en: Oṃ, salutations to Śiva;
salutations to the supreme deity, whose self has conquered the three qualities (guṇas), who is eternal, whose form is yoga, and who is the cause for the cessation of saṃsāra. || 1 ||
Salutation to the wise Mahādeva, the twenty-sixth principle who is the primary cause of persistence, destruction, and creation, and who expands [the universe];
[I bow] at the great field of Prajāpati, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Kālindī.
At Prayāga, the supremely meritorious gateway to the world of Brahmā,
sages of purified souls whose sins had been destroyed by austerity performed their daily rites on the full moon day for the purpose of bathing at the sacred ford. || 3-4 ||
Not seeing the Sūta, who was devoted to truth and well-versed in the Purāṇas, those sages,
having bathed in that great holy place (tīrtha),
saw the Sūta approaching for the purpose of offering salutations with a joyful heart.
They prepared a place for him to rest and arranged a seat for his stay. Then the Sūta, endowed with all virtues, bowed down to all those eminent sages and took the seat offered to him.

O virtuous one, in ancient times, while the inhabitants of the Naimiṣa forest were engaged in a sacrificial session dedicated to Brahman, the sages who had attained perfection through austerity questioned him as he sat there:
"The narrative known as the Bhārata and the supreme Purāṇa have been recounted by you. (8)
Therefore, you appear to us as the son of Satyavatī in person.
He knew the ultimate meaning of all scriptures and was devoted to truth and righteousness.
He is constantly devoted to the worship of the twice-born; therefore, you ought to question him.
That which excels the Purāṇas and is like the Bhārata narrative.
O Tattvas, we indeed wish to ask about the birth of the wise Kārttikeya.
For all these sages are solely devoted to your worship.
Their minds were filled with eager longing to hear about the birth of Skanda.
Thus addressed at that time by those perfected, foremost of sages, the charioteer—
He spoke these words, which expressed the true state of affairs, to all the sages.
Listen, all you sages, to the account of the birth of Kārttikeya.
Devotion to Brahmanas, great magnanimity, and valor exceeding that of the thirty gods. ||14||
When the great-souled Śuka had departed for the supreme abode out of a desire for liberation,
Vyāsa, tormented by grief for his son, gazed upon Tryambaka.
Upon merely seeing Maheśāna, Vyāsa became free from all suffering.
Then the sage, the son of Satyavatī, wandered through the worlds. ||16||
Then, on the peak of Mount Meru, he beheld the first-born son of Brahmā.
To Sanatkumāra, the giver of boons, who is endowed with the sovereign power of yoga.
He stood in a celestial chariot resembling the sun, possessing a brilliance like fire.
By sages who have attained perfection through yoga, high-souled ones endowed with austerity. ||18||
By those who know the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and who are endowed with the knowledge of all the scriptures of dharma.
It was surrounded by those who had acquired all branches of knowledge, appearing as if it were the four-faced Brahmā himself. ||19||
Then Vyāsa saw that great-souled sage standing there.
He paid homage with supreme devotion, as if to the Grandfather himself.
Then the son of Brahmā beheld Vyāsa, who had arrived there, endowed with great splendor.
Embracing him with supreme affection, he spoke these auspicious words. ||21||
By good fortune, O knower of dharma, you have attained this through the grace of the Supreme Lord.
Free from sorrow, you have arrived; ask, and I shall speak.
Then, having heard the words of his son, the bull among sages [Brahmā]—
The wise ones spoke these words that had long resided within their hearts.
How was the birth of the wise Kumāra Kārttikeya?
"What is its cause, or from where does it arise? Indeed, I wish to know this."
How was he the son of Rudra, and how was he the son of Agni and Gaṅgā?
And how indeed did he become the son of Umā and Svāhā?
And how did he [behave] toward Suparṇī, the Mothers, and the Kṛttikās? ||25||
Who was that one who first arose, what were his austerities, and what was his prowess?
For this deludes all living beings; speak it exactly as it is.
Sūta said:
Thus questioned, that radiant one, the most excellent son of Brahmā, [replied].
The omniscient one spoke everything to Vyāsa, the performer of effortless deeds.
Listen to that, O sinless ones, as it is being recounted by me according to its true nature.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
I take refuge in the Lord Īśāna, the omniscient and unconquered.
To Mahādeva, the Great-Souled One, the Lord of the entire universe. ||1||
That whose power is unimpeded and whose sovereignty is universal, as well as his lordship and pervasive mastery, are declared to be the results of his own actions. (2)
Having bowed down to that divine Soma, being self-restrained and pure,
I shall describe for one desiring to know the ancient narratives the auspicious origin of Skanda—
the descent of the body of the god Rudra, the Supreme Self. (3)
The consecration for the sake of Prajāpati, as well as the seizing of the head;
the vision of the members of the six families and the dismissal of the Cakra; the origin of Naimiṣa and the conclusion of the sacrificial session.
In that [account] there is the arrival of Brahmā, as well as the practice of austerity;
the manifestation of Śarva and the birth of the Goddess.
The truth regarding the dispute, as well as the curse of Dakṣa, the origin of the army, and the self-choice marriage (svayaṃvara) of the Goddess; ||7||
The granting of boons by the gods and by the wise Vasiṣṭha;
and the birth of Parāśara and of the high-souled Vyāsa. ||8||
The occurrence of the conflict between Vasiṣṭha and Kauśika,
the desolation of Vārāṇasī, and the description of the greatness of the sacred field (kṣetra);
the presence of Rudra here and the grace bestowed upon Nandin.
The vision of the Gaṇas and their narration in its entirety;
the invocation of Kālī and the performance of ascetic penance;
the birth of Somanandin and likewise the granting of boons. || 8.2.10–11 ||
The state of being Gaurī, the obtaining of a son, and the very birth of the Goddess;
the motherhood of all spirits by Kauśikī, and likewise the lion becoming her chariot. ||12||
The abode of Gaurī on the Vindhya mountains, the meeting of the Vindhya range with the Sun, the majesty of Agastya, and the slaying of Sunda and Nisunda. (13)
The destruction of Niśumbha and Śumbha, the slaying of Mahiṣa by her, and the consecration of Kauśikī... ||14||
...and also the granting of the boon;
likewise the birth of Andhaka, and the binding of the earth. ||15||
The slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa and likewise that of Hiraṇyakaśipu;
the subduing of Bala, and also the agreement of the Goddess. 16.
The departure of the gods, as well as Agni’s role as their messenger, the granting of boons by the gods, and the dismissal of Śukra. ||17||
The birth of the messenger, the sight of Andhaka by the Goddess, the distress and agitation caused by Śailādi and others, and the hundredfold form of the Goddess. 18.
The bestowing of boons upon the noble ones, the hymn of praise by Śiva and others, the arrival of the god, and likewise the narration of what had occurred. ||19||
The narrative of the devoted wife and of service to the teacher;
the narrative of Pañcacūḍā and the invincibility of Taijasa.
The arrival of the messenger, the conversation, and his dismissal;
likewise, the dialogue with the Asura Andhaka and the journey to Mount Mandara. ||21||
The arrival of the Gaṇas, as well as the hearing of their enumeration,
and then the conflict with Andhaka in a great battle.
The gift of half his body, the taking in of Aśoka’s son, the birth from ashes and Soma, and likewise his dwelling in the cremation ground. ||23||
The birth of Kubera, the wise king of the Yakṣas;
the subduing of the lords of serpents; and the felling of Śikhara.
And even the subjugation of the three worlds, including Śakra himself.
The presentation of the divine army and the consecration as commander-in-chief. || 25 ||
And there was indeed the arrival of the one known as Nārada, who had been sent by Tāraka.
The fierce slaying of Tāraka and the expedition to Bhadravaṭa. ||26||
The slaying of Mahiṣa and the destruction of Krauñca as well.
The extraction of Śakti and the auspicious slaying of Tāraka. ||27||
The arising of fear among the gods and asuras, and the battle concerning the three cities.
The account of Prahlāda’s form and the narrative of the ungrateful man.
The great good fortune of the Brahmins is proclaimed in detail. ||28||
Having understood this correctly, one should indeed become an attendant to the Youth.
Strong and endowed with intelligence, he obtains a son who is highly esteemed. ||29||
Thus ends the second chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Listen to this divine narrative, which destroys all sins.
Being narrated by me, it is wonderful, full of many meanings, and consistent with the Vedas.
Having heard which, even one who has committed evil deeds shall go to the supreme destination. ||1||
It should never be given to an atheist, one who lacks faith, or to a deceitful person.
One should relate this discourse likewise to a man who is envious.
This [should be given] to a son, to a disciple who is righteous and free from malice.
O Great Brahmā, it should be told to one who is devoted to the gods.
O Brahmin, this should always be told to one who is devoted to the gods,
as well as to one devoted to Kumāra, and indeed to one who possesses faith.
This secret should always be spoken to ascetics of purified soul;
then he spoke with a heart surrendered [to him]:
"In ancient times, Brahmā was produced within this egg by Prajāpati Tvaṣṭṛ."
Enveloped by darkness due to that lack of knowledge, Brahmā did not recognize his father.
Thinking "I am alone," he surveyed all the worlds;
yet, though endowed with the power of austerity and yoga, he saw no other there.
And when addressed as "son, son" by the wise Śarva, Brahmā bowed down with palms joined in reverence and sought refuge in him alone.
Having bestowed upon Brahmā the power of creation together with knowledge, Śambhu—
And the Supreme Lord possesses the power of making himself invisible to the worlds.
Thus, O Vyāsa, this eternal Upaniṣad has been declared by me,
having heard which yogins attain Maheśvara through meditation.
Desiring a son for the sake of progeny, he indeed performed intense austerity.
As that great-souled one was engaged in fierce yoga and penance,
his father became well-pleased with him in a very short time.
He obtained a vision of him, and [the Lord] said, "I am the giver of boons. Bowing down and placing his joined palms upon his head, he praised him:
"Salutations to the Supreme God, the creator even of the gods! ||14||
Salutations indeed to the Creator, the sustainer of the world, the Lord of Brahmā;
to the one who is endowed with power yet remains unattached,
who is infinite, immeasurable, and beyond the reach of the senses.
To the all-pervasive one, who was previously pervaded, the sustainer, and the impeller;
to him who has performed the act of impelling and who effects the arrangement of the principles (tattvas);
to the original impeller of primordial matter (pradhāna) and the bestower of power upon the qualities (guṇas).
To the one who bestows vision upon all and who is himself the very act of seeing;
to the grasper of objects and the performer of restraint;
to the creator of the mind, the senses, and indeed the Veda.
To the creator of the qualities of all beings, likewise the giver of power,
the maker of the cosmic egg, to me, the inconceivable, the first-born,
the immeasurable Father— being eternally pleased with us, grant us the *śakvarī* [hymn].
To him whose power of immeasurable qualities and sovereignty is indeed unimpeded—
while he was thus praising him, O Vyāsa, Maheśvara, the God of gods,
being pleased, then spoke himself to his son Brahmā as he stood bowed before him.
"Since this subtle [nature] has been known by you, O child of great splendor,
therefore you shall attain renown in the worlds by the name 'Brahman.
And since I have been called 'Father' (Pitṛ) by you, O best among the wise,"
Therefore, your status as Grandfather shall attain renown in the world.
And because you have performed such fierce and most difficult penance for the sake of progeny, I grant you the office of Prajāpati, O self-restrained one.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Gods created embodied women;
those eight primary elements (prakṛtis), along with the modifications and the senses,
and all states of being, approached the God in their own forms.
Then the God, endowed with his own splendor, said to them:
"Accomplish this consecration today; do not delay.
Taking each their own respective divine and inconceivable essence, they [prepared it]. || 27-28 ||
The exceedingly radiant Prajāpati was consecrated here;
there, yogins who know the truth of yoga behold this subtle one with their divine eye and sing of him as the ancient one endowed with the three qualities.
"O Lord, Rudra is indeed the creator of all beings and of you as well;
together with us, you are the one who sets the world in motion.
That god, who possesses the application of supreme sovereignty, has been properly propitiated."
He consecrated Brahmā, his first-born son, over the Prajāpatis.

To that Supreme Lord, who out of reverence fashioned this world called "the Body" (tanu) joined with various paths of yoga, who is endowed with infinite yoga, who through his powers of illusion (māyā) is the kinsman of the three worlds, and who is ever-vigilant—to him [I bow]. 3.1–3.2

Having bowed with devotion to that God, the Lord of Beings, who dwells eternally within the minds of all, who perceives both the auspicious and the inauspicious, whose very movement is salutation, I perpetually seek refuge in him who is subtler than the subtlest.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Coronation of Brahmā as Lord of Creatures," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having then obtained the status of Lord of Creatures (Prājāpatya), he proceeded to create progeny.
Those creatures being created did not multiply for him.
Thus, as the Grandfather was performing that creation but remained devoid of power,
he then began once more to practice austerities for the sake of further creation.
Having learned of his asceticism for the sake of creation, the Lord of the Three Worlds,
pervading the universe with his splendor, approached his presence;
the Creator, the Lord of the World, revealed the entire universe within his own body.

Possessing the power and sovereignty of great yoga, surrounded by hosts of those who have attained perfection through knowledge, Hara—the Lord of Gods and Master of the Great Elements—himself arrived. Pervading the entire universe with his supreme own splendor, he stood there. || 4–5 ||
Śambhu said to the Grandfather, "O child, ask for a boon.
Brahmā mentally chose him as his son for the purpose of creating the worlds.
Knowing that intention of Brahmā, the Supreme Lord [spoke].
Thinking, "This one is deluded," the Bestower of Boons himself spoke:
"Since you have come here as a father while desiring a son,
by my command a son shall be born who is an embodiment of myself."
And he, my Gaṇanāyaka, shall become your son;
having become Rudra incarnate, O fool, he will humble you.
Furthermore, he shall bestow upon you the sovereignty over all vidyās and over all yogas in every respect.
The lordship over the *bala* [ganas] and the mastery in the employment of missiles—these have been granted by me to him;
they shall all immediately attend upon him.
The bow Pināka, the trident, the sword, and likewise the battle-axe.
A water-pot, a staff, the Pāśupata weapon,
the thunderbolt of universal destruction, and the discus of reabsorption—
endowed with all such powers, your son shall thus come to be.
When that great-souled one had spoken thus and vanished,
Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, desiring a son, then performed a sacrifice; offering oblations with great exertion and accompanied by intense concentration, he performed the rite.
With his hand holding the fuel-stick, he wiped his forehead;
a drop of sweat born from the contact with the fuel-stick fell from his forehead onto that blazing fire, doubled by its own intensity.
For that splendor of Maheśvara was deposited in Brahmā and transmitted by him. 16.
Impelled by the God of gods, he fell into the consumer of oblations;
at that very moment, having remembered that supreme boon, Rudra was dispatched as a leader of the Gaṇas and immediately became [one]. 17.
And that fire born of moisture, having first been joined with the flame,
quickly became red and then turned blue once more;
thus, by virtue of being both blue and red, that Lord came to be known as Nīlalohita.
The glorious three-eyed one with ten arms, as if covering Brahmā,
[is addressed] by names beginning with Śarva and by forms beginning with Water.
Having praised that all-pervading god, Nīlalohita, the imperishable,
and having recognized him as the creator of all who is established in the great elements,
that Lord then created various other beings in the world.
He too, having established himself in yoga and endowed with sovereign power,
entered all the worlds and sustained them at all times.
Then, from Brahmā, there were born the auspicious sons Dakṣa, Dharma, and others.
All creatures, teeming with gods and humans, were created;
then, after a long time had passed and kalpas had come and gone again and again,
when this present kalpa arrived, he sustained the creatures through his yogic power.
When the livelihoods were established, when the creation of the world had proceeded,
and when the progeny had increased, while Brahmā was performing a sacrifice at Prayāga, those six ṛṣis of noble lineage, whose vows were highly praised, [arrived].
The Marīcis, the Trayas, the Vasiṣṭhas, as well as the Kratus, the Bhṛgus, and the Aṅgirases—all whose sins were consumed by ascetic penance (tapas). ||27||
Approaching Brahmā together during the interval between rites, they said:
"O Blessed One, we are completely enveloped by a great darkness. (28)
Exhausted and disputing, we do not see what is beyond this;
O Lord, this doubt has long resided within our hearts. (29)
For you indeed know, according to reality, our supreme cause;
what is higher than all beings, and who is more powerful in every respect? (8.4.3)
By whom is the universe presided over? Who is eternal, and who is everlasting?
Who is the creator of all beings and the impeller of primordial nature (prakṛti)? ||3 1||
The high-minded one employs all beings in all tasks throughout the universe;
whose elements are under his control, and who is the director of all? (3.2)
"How may we see him? Tell us this in its entirety.
Thus addressed, Brahmā then spoke in the presence of all—the gods, the ṛṣis, the gandharvas, the uragas, and the rākṣasas.
Those among the yakṣas and asuras who were the instigators of beings,
along with the piśācas and others who were in their vicinity,
rose up with palms joined in reverence and uttered the words "Rudra" three times. || 34-35 ||
He can be seen through austerity alone and by no other means;
he is remembered as the creator of all beings and as one who possesses great power.
All beings are subject to his will; by him this world is sustained. ... [all] paid homage to that Great Soul.
The sages said:
O God, what is that great austerity by which that Lord may be seen?
Tell us that, O Lord of Gods; and grant us a boon. (38)
The Grandfather said:
"Perform a great sacrificial session (sattra), free from the defects of speech and mind;
and I shall tell you the region in which you shall carry it out."
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having created that mind-made discus, he spoke to them:
"This discus has been hurled by me; follow it without delay!"
"Wherever its rim should break, that place shall be auspicious for asceticism.
Then he released that discus, and they followed after it;
as it moved swiftly, the place where its rim finally broke—
That place is known by the name Naimiṣa; it is meritorious and honored everywhere. ||42||
It was worshipped by gods, humans, and siddhas; by fierce rākṣasas and divine serpents;
by yakṣas along with hosts of gandharvas and piśācas; by all the apsarases and the sons of Diti.

He was praised by self-controlled Brahmins endowed with tranquility and yoga, by all the lords of the earth who visit sacred fords, and by Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Cāraṇas, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, and the Pitṛs. ||44||
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Origin of the Six Families," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Having reached that Naimiṣa forest, the sages of blazing splendor performed a great divine sacrificial session lasting for a thousand years.
All were one-pointed in mind, free from possessiveness and egoism,
constantly meditating upon the Lord of Lords, together with their wives, sons, and sacred fires.
They were all established in Him, devoted to Him, united with Him, and taking refuge in Him.
Performing all their activities, they were mentally absorbed in him alone.
Perceiving their state of mind, the glorious Mātariśvan, of great ascetic power, who moves through all living beings and is the impeller of all creatures, [approached]. ||4||
The auspicious Lord, assuming a physical form, granted his vision to those performing the sacrifice;
having seen him and having worshipped him as the imperishable Mātariśvan, [they were filled with joy].
The sages, firm in their vows, questioned him as he sat upon his holy seat concerning the entire origin of the world, as well as its dissolution,
its complete maintenance, the genealogies, and the ages and manvantaras.
The entire history of the dynasties, as well as the divine measures [of time], likewise.
The origin and dissolution of the eight classes of divine beings, the creation of the ancestors, the remainder [of the creation], and the measurement of Brahmā;
the entire course of the moon and the sun, as well as the movement of the stars and planets.
And the state of all the lords of the islands, and the dharma of the continents in its entirety. ||9||
The Lord explained all of this in its entirety: the establishment of the system of castes and stages of life, and the performance of sacrifices. 8.5.10.
And for a thousand divine years, they remained thus absorbed in that [meditation].
Then, in a divine form, there appeared the auspicious Sāvitrī, whose speech was the Sāman, whose eyes were the quarters of space,
whose nose was the Yajus, whose head was the Atharvaśiras, and whose tongue was the Śabda (Veda).
Logic is her ear, etymology her skin, and she moves through the verses, feet, and words of the Ṛgveda.
Time is her arm, the rains her hand, and she bears the days as her fingers.
She possesses the digits as her joints, and likewise the months as her fingernails.
With her breasts exalted by the knowledge of the divine sciences (*śikṣā-vidyā*), her waist conquered by *chandas* (prosody), and her navel indeed the *mīmāṃsā* (investigation);
with her hips broadened by the *purāṇa* (ancient lore) and her heart’s desire fixed upon the *dharmaśāstra* (treatises on law). || 14 ||
Her thighs were the stages of life (*āśrama*), her knees the social classes (*varṇa*), her ankles the sacrifices (*yajña*), and her toes the fruits [of action].
Her body was the worlds and the Vedas, adorned with the auspicious hairs of the Vedic meters (*chandas*).
Faith was her garment, and she spoke of the dharma of yoga. || 1.5–1.6 ||
Emerging from the center of the altar and flowing with supreme waters, they reached its end and, having bathed at the final sacrificial lustration (avabhṛtha), joined with Vāyu.
They questioned that god Vāyu of great intellect: "Whose daughter is she? || 17 ||
That one of great splendor spoke to the sages who were permeated by righteousness.
"You are all purified by your asceticism, and great merit has been performed by you, since this holy river has come here from the world of Brahmā.
This is the one named Sarasvatī, the ornament of the world of Brahmā. (19)
First, she has come to this world of mortals for the sake of your success;
there exists no one more meritorious than her in the three worlds.
The sages said:
How did this highly meritorious [river], which goes to the world of Brahmā, come into existence?
What was the cause therein? We wish to know this.
Vāyu said:
In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history,
the dialogue between Brahmā and Sacrifice (Yajña) in former times.
In ancient times, having performed sacrifices with blazing splendor, the divine Brahmā created all beings, both the immobile and the mobile.
Having seen this, the radiant god, endowed with supreme splendor,
gazed upon those worlds with his four lotus-like faces;
the high-minded one looked again and again at the gods and others, as well as humans and the rest.
He thought: "There is no one equal to me in the world, nor anyone superior. ||25||
I, who swallow and emit all these creatures established in the seven worlds—among gods, humans, and animals. ||26||
For I am indeed the creator of all beings; no other whatsoever exists.
There is no one equal to me anywhere as a ruler or as a maker of the worlds. (27)
While he was thinking thus, the high-minded Sacrifice arrived;
and that radiant being said to him, "O great-minded one, do not think in this way."
For this delusion of yours will lead to your destruction; such a thing is not fitting for you today, who abide in goodness and are self-born.
"You alone are the creator and there is no other; nevertheless, this does not bring you glory.
For I am indeed the sustainer of living beings and likewise of the entire world."
"I shall not fall into delusion, O Lord, as you proclaim.
To him Brahmā then said: "O All-pervading One, you are not the sustainer;
for I alone am the sustainer and likewise the destroyer of all beings."
The beings were created by me; you alone are deluded in this matter.
Then Veda, who was extremely radiant, arrived there deeply agitated;
and the lord Veda said to those two, "This is not a god."
"I am the best because I have never spoken a falsehood;
listen to who is the creator of all beings, including you two. (34)
The Supreme Lord Mahādeva, Rudra, the omnipresent Master, is he by whom I was given to you, and by whom you were made the Prajāpati. (35)
This sacrifice and its origin, as well as I who am established therein—everything has indeed been produced from that; there is no other creator for us anywhere.
To him who spoke thus, the divine Brahmā addressed this knowledge:
"I am the leader and likewise the creator of all the Vedas. (37)
"By my grace, you are indeed the Veda and this is the sacrifice; of this there is no doubt.
You two are deluded, or else unrighteousness has been committed by you both otherwise. (38)
"Perform penance; then you shall be liberated from your sin.
When he had spoken thus, a great sound indeed arose.
And a circle appeared, shaped like the solar disc,
situated high in the sky with a great sound;
and it, falling from there, descended to the surface of the earth.
Having reached a grove in the Himalayas, resounding with the cries of various birds.
Having remained in the sky for a long time, he indeed descended to the earth.
Then Brahmā, the Grandfather, having gazed upon all the quarters with his four lotus-like faces,
did not see him stationed in the firmament.
He created a fifth blazing face situated upon his head.
With that [weapon], he beheld him stationed in the sky, possessing a splendor equal to ten thousand suns,
having the form of the solar disc, sounding, and terrible to behold.
Having created that fifth head of his, which was indeed born of great wrath—

Resembling the fire of universal destruction, it grew as it was about to swallow [the world]. As it increased, resembling the submarine fire (vaḍavāmukha) and possessing both brilliance and sound, that god appeared with a blazing orb.
With the nail of the thumb of his left hand, as if in mere disdain,
he swiftly severed that great and terrible fifth head of Brahmā.
Then, his head severed by the blazing [weapon], afflicted by intense suffering and deprived of consciousness,
he fell down, abandoned by the practice of yoga;
he was like a great tusked elephant with its tusks broken, or a bull of Śiva with its horns shattered.
Like the sun with its rays fallen to the surface of the earth, he shone;
then, like one who has risen from sleep, having regained consciousness, that great ascetic praised Mahādeva, who was stationed within the solar orb, with a piteous voice. || 49-50 ||
Brahmā said: Salutations to the thousand-eyed one, and indeed salutations to the hundred-eyed one;
salutations to the one with the wide-open mouth, and indeed salutations to the hundred-faced one.
Homage to the one with a thousand faces, indeed homage to the one who is all faces; homage to the one with a thousand feet, indeed homage to the one who is all feet. ||52||
Salutations to the thousand-armed one and to the one whose hands are everywhere;
salutations to the creator of all and to you, the witness of all.
Salutations to the one with the color of the sun and to the one who severed his own head.
Salutations to the creator of emanation and dissolution, and likewise to the creator of maintenance.
Salutations to the one with a thousand lingas and a thousand feet;
salutations indeed to the one whose linga is the act of withdrawal and whose linga is water.
To Him who moves within, who is all-pervasive, and who fulfills primordial nature;
to Him who pervades all beings and impels the Puruṣa;
to Him who is distinguished by the objects of the senses and likewise acts as the regulator. ||56||
To all that has been and is to be, and to that which is eternally in the midst [of existence], [salutation]. 57.
O All-pervading Lord, you alone are the creator of the worlds and likewise the bestower of mantras;
it behoves you to show favor to me, who have come for refuge and am self-controlled. 58.
As he was thus praising with a state of perfect and supreme devotion,
the Lord of the Gods then granted him divine vision.
With that vision, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, then [beheld].
In a celestial chariot radiant as the sun, he beheld a mass of splendor;
from its center, he then heard a great voice—
profound, sweet, well-composed, and characterized by perfect meaning.
"O clear-sighted one, you were previously urged by the Lord, crying 'Son!
Son! And that Nīlalohita who was born from the sky for you—this is he of whom I spoke earlier when I was searching for a son."
That leader of my gaṇas, who shall become an embodiment of me,
will attain supreme knowledge and, O fool, will humble you. This severing of your head is the fulfillment of his fruit.
Therefore, be at peace now, for this has been brought about by me alone.
O high-minded one, the divine head, consisting of upward-moving knowledge,
has arisen from this sacrifice which has strayed onto a wrong path.
"He alone shall cut off his head for some other reason;
however, I am pleased with this hymn. What shall I give him, O sinless one? Vāyu said.
Then that Blessed One, delighted, bowed with auspicious words and,
joining his palms in reverence, spoke to that Lord who was both visible and invisible:
"O Blessed One, the mere sight of you does not afflict me with sorrow."
For I desire that you always carry his head upon your own.
O Lord, I do not recall this severing of my head;
furthermore, I desire that you alone should restrain me from further acts of unrighteousness.
"And so, having observed your purpose, I shall see you as you wish. Having heard this petition of Brahmā, the Lord of the World replied: || 8.5.70 ||
"He himself, known as Sutasoma, who is my own form as Nīlalohita,
shall cut off the head of the sacrifice and he shall also sever your head.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the gods vanished right there.
When that Great God had departed, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
together with the sacrifice and the Vedas, returned to his own world.
Vāyu said:
The mortal who hears this secret, which is equal in meaning to the Vedas, shall,
upon the dissolution of the body, attain union with Brahman.
And he who recites this daily in the presence of Brāhmaṇas—
Freed from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
This divine narrative is not to be told to those who are without sons, nor to disciples, nor to yogis;
it should not be told to one who lacks knowledge, nor to the deceitful, nor to the arrogant.
One should always recite this great, divine instruction on dharma in an assembly of Brahmins and physicians.
Such a man finds an opening here in this world, and upon the dissolution of the body, he shall enter the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Then that blessed god, Kapardin Nīlalohita,
by the command of the Supreme Lord, took hold of the head of Brahmā.
Having seized that blazing head and assumed a deformed appearance,
he set out for alms, employing the play of yoga.
O brahmins, he likewise went to the abode of the gods for the sake of alms;
yet no one gave that lord a fitting alms-offering.
Then the god proceeded to the residence of the high-souled Viṣṇu;
standing at its door, he uttered the auspicious word for alms.
Then Viṣṇu, having perceived that [demon] with his hand raised toward him through his yogic vision and having understood Śiva’s divine play, caused a stream of blood to flow.
And then that vast [stream] fell for a hundred and fifty yojanas;
O best of Brahmins, as it fell, it flowed for many years.
Not even half of the skull of the Grandfather was filled.
Then the God, smiling, spoke these auspicious words to him: ||7||
A maiden is given in marriage but once; fire is kindled but once;
kings speak [their word] but once; and alms are bestowed but once. (8)
"I am pleased with this fitting gift of yours, O giver of honor!
Choose a boon, O Lord of Gods; indeed, I am the granter of boons to you today. (9)
Viṣṇu said:
"This alone is a praiseworthy boon, that I behold Śaṅkara, the radiant lord of the gods, with his matted hair."
Then the god, beholding the shadow upon the nectar situated in the skull-cup,
created a divine person, powerful and resembling Viṣṇu.
He said to him: "You are indeed imperishable, free from old age and death;
you are without rival in battles, and you are the immediate companion of Viṣṇu."
The illustrious one, who performs the work of the gods, spoke these supreme words to Mahāsena:
"Since your birth was from the *nārā* (waters) during the battle, you shall therefore be known by the name Nara; moreover, you shall be dear to him. || 13 ||
Vāyu said:
Having then consoled that man and cast him aside, he went to the abode of Brahmā immediately after Viṣṇu; and those two also entered the house.
Whoever, having obtained this human birth here, should hear or recite this,
shall be endowed with supreme fame and honored in the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Birth of Man," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vāyu said:
Having reached the world of Brahmā, the Blessed One, the protector of all worlds, stood at the gate, saying, "Give me alms, give me alms. (1)
Seeing him thus transformed, with his skull-hand ornament, Brahmā recognized him through great yogic power and praised the Lord of the World.
Then the God, pleased with him, said, "I am the giver of boons;
choose a boon without anxiety, whatever dwells in your mind. (3)
Brahmā said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, I desire that this mark be made by you, O Lord of the world, by which this world may be marked with a sign. (4)
Having heard those words of his, the Blessed One, the best among speakers,
replied "Om," O Brahmin, signifying that everything was as he had said.
By his mere meditation, this divine-sounding speech issued forth from the mouth of the goddess; bowing low, she stood there present. (6)
Then the Goddess spoke to her, as if reviving her with her voice:
"Since you, having become imperishable, have issued forth from my speech. (7)
Therefore, O Goddess, you shall become the presiding deity of all vidyās,
because you have taken refuge in my mouth, the Veda which is the essence of Brahman.
Therefore, O radiant one, you shall attain fame in the world as Sarasvatī,
after you have nourished this world with your waters of essence.
Furthermore, you shall be the savior of all the worlds; of this there is no doubt.
And the gods, together with the Grandfather, will grant you a share of the sacrificial offerings.
Thus, this skull of Brahmā of immeasurable power,
having reached this world, remains in this most beloved place.
There, the Lord of the Devas, the Master, placed that great, divine skull— blazing with radiant flames— at the front of the *kuśa* grass.
Then, seeing it thus established, all the attendants of the Great-Souled One [were amazed].
They let out a tremendous roar, making the ten directions resound.
...in that famous place... it was rent asunder. By that terrible sound, the Asura known as Hālāhala, the thorn in the side of the gods, went toward that region. || 14 ||
Unable to endure [this], the evil-souled Yajñaśāsaka, blinded by anger, was invulnerable to all living beings due to the boon granted by Brahmā;
he was surrounded by hundreds of Asuras who had assumed the forms of buffaloes. || 15-16 ||
Beholding that buffalo, the thorn in the side of the gods, rushing forward in a rage, the Lord of the Gaṇas spoke to all the attendants of the wielder of the Pināka bow:
"O leaders of the Gaṇas, this wicked one is indeed a thorn to the gods throughout the three worlds."
"He comes toward you in a rage; therefore, slay him!
Then all those leaders of the Gaṇas, filled with fury, pierced the approaching enemy of the gods with their spears and deprived him of his life.
When he was slain, the god then gazed upon all the quarters;
from them there emerged powerful female piśācas with faces like those of piśācas,
who approached that god while reporting his death to them.
And being consumed by them in every way...
|| 2.1 || they then reached that very abode ordained for the gods and others; from there and everywhere, the Siddhas and Asiddhas constantly devoured him. || 2.2 ||
Therefore, they were proclaimed by the wise Lord as the Kapālamātaraḥ (Mothers of the Skull),
because the skull was established in that place by the wielder of the Pināka bow;
for that reason, it is celebrated throughout the three worlds as Mahākapāla.

Just as it had happened when that skull was established, that place became renowned as Śivataḍāga, which liberates one from all sins. Then Brahmā, surrounded by hosts of deities, arrived there. ||24-25||
Having addressed Kapardin, he accepted that region;
a field extending half a yojana all around shall undoubtedly become the Siddhakṣetra of the Great-souled One. 26.
For the wise know that *śma* means sin and *śāna* means destruction; because it is purified through meditation and observances, it is designated as *śmaśāna*.
It is the secret [place] of the God of gods, supremely dear and unsurpassed.
In this way, a person there shall abandon every single evil deed. ||28||
Having fasted for three nights and worshipped the bull-bannered god, one shall obtain the entire fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices. || 29 ||
And that person who shall there renounce his dear life-breaths will attain equality with the gods of the Guhyaka hosts.
Vāyu said:
Then, having established two auspicious images of the God there,
Sureśvara quickly constructed a beautiful temple for Rudra.
By merely approaching that place, one brings about the destruction of sin and attains the world of Rudra; thus spoke the Grandfather.
And where the Lord of the World cut off his head, that place became a most meritorious and auspicious region by name. ||3 3||
Then the Lord, together with his attendants, having assumed a transformed appearance,
vanished from the sight of all the gods.
And this imperishable site of Kapāla, which was joined by the Lord of the Gods with the fruit of bathing at all sacred fords (tīrtha),
is even today seen there as a great divine lake.
O best of Brahmins, that place is known as Mahākapāla; there, heaven is said to be imperishable.
This auspicious, divine teaching of the Dharma is a great lake honored by Indra, the gods, and the asuras;
it is a detailed description of the nature of the Great Skull, beneficial for plunging into the worlds of the Lord of Gods and beyond. (37)

The man who always recites or hears this circle of lunar mansions, praised by those whose wealth is austerity and by hosts of Siddhas, which is equal to the celestial realm, goes to heaven, highly honored. (38)
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Installation of the Skull," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vāyu said:
"In this manner, indeed, this Blessed Lady follows after the world of Brahmā."
For the sake of the accomplishment of your dharma, he emerged from the center of the altar. ||1||
Sanatkumāra said: When their thousand-year sacrificial session had thus concluded and the Sarasvatī had begun to flow, the Grandfather (Brahmā) went there.
Brahmā said:
"Perform once more this sacrifice here for the sake of the Lord God;
when obstacles arise for you, then your austerity shall become free from blemish. (3)
Having overcome that very obstacle and having performed radiant austerity, you will attain the great yoga; being thus disciplined, you shall then behold Śaṅkara.
Having said "So be it," when he had departed, those of great vows, being diligent, then performed many various kinds of sacrificial sessions (satras). ||5||
O twice-born ones, having made this entire earth free of Soma,
they then desired to press King Soma after having summoned him.
Then that Soma too was eclipsed by the evil-minded Svarbhānu, who remained invisible while moving transversely; consequently, they became distressed.
Having gone there, all those sages brought Purūravas, the inhabitant of Kalāpagrāma, and consecrated him as king over them.
And those illustrious ones said to him: "O Lord, our Soma has indeed been stolen by someone;
therefore, may you bring it back here quickly, without delay. (9)
When the lord, having been addressed thus, could not find [him] despite searching,
he then spoke to the brahmins, bowing down and oppressed by fear.
"O Lord, having exerted the utmost effort, I have searched for Soma;
yet I do not know by whom he was taken, nor where he has been led. (11)
To him who spoke thus, all the sages of celebrated vows, being enraged and highly agitated, said to the high-minded son of Ilā: 12.
O father, you have been made king by us who were afflicted by fear;
yet that fear has not been removed for us, nor are you even capable of understanding it.
With your mind excessively attached to sense objects, you do not perceive this through yoga;
therefore, by persisting in hostility toward the twice-born, you shall meet with death.
We ourselves shall indeed bring back the king, who is so difficult to find;
by our own ascetic power, O Indra among kings, behold our supreme strength! 15.
Then all those sages, whose sins had been consumed by austerity, praised Gāyatrī, the source of the Vedas, with pleasing words. (16)
Then, as they were offering praise, Gāyatrī, the source of the Vedas, appeared in embodied form and spoke these words to those twice-born ones: ||17||
"I am pleased, my children; what shall I do for you today? I am a granter of boons to you.
Speak, and that shall be accomplished this very day; of this there is no doubt. (18)
The sages said:
"O Goddess, Soma has not been brought by anyone; he has been taken away by some very wicked soul.
Bring him back! Salutations to you! This is our supreme boon. (19)
Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus, she reflected and, seeing with her divine eye,
transformed herself into a female hawk and quickly went toward the Asura Śvarbhānu.
While the Asuras were distracted, she took the Soma and returned;
having arrived, she said to those sages, "This Soma is here; let it be pressed."
Having approached him and obtained the great fruit of their sacrifice, those twice-born sages thought, "Our austerity has become stainless. (22)
Then Brahmā himself, having arrived there along with the gods, serpents, and others, spoke to those sages: "Perform penance; do not delay."
Having gone together with Brahmā to Maināka, the best of mountains, they performed austerities with all the hosts of gods, their minds fully concentrated. 24.
After a long time, for those whose selves had been refined through austerity, there arose an engagement with yoga that was characterized by subtlety; thereafter, they [proceeded].
Those sages, together with the gods, joined in meditation with Brahmā;
fixing their minds upon Maheśvara, they remained as motionless as stones.
Then Mahādeva, the wielder of the Pināka bow, blue-and-red in hue,
approached that place in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun;
for he, perceiving them to be permeated by that state of being, was moved by his supreme nature.
He spoke with a roar like a thundercloud and a sound like a hundred drums.
O gods, including Brahmā, along with Viṣṇu, the sages, and the cāraṇas!
I bestow upon you divine vision; behold me as you desire. (29)
Sanatkumāra said: Then they all beheld a celestial chariot, possessing the splendor of ten thousand suns, resembling Mount Meru, and adorned with various jewels.
In its center stood a very great, blazing fire, radiant, encircled by garlands of flames, and adorned with rays of light. ||31||
With a face made terrible by fangs and eyes like blazing fire,
his matted hair was tawny like the three sacrificial fires, and he wore a girdle bound with serpents.
He has polished earrings, holds a trident and a spear in his great hands,
carries the Pināka bow, a staff in his hand, and wields a mallet and a thunderbolt.
Holding swords and spears in his hands and bearing a discus, with his phallus erect and a rosary in his hand, he was difficult to behold for those who had not disciplined themselves.
Adorned with garlands and ornaments by the moon, the sun,
and the planets, all those gods beheld him with their divine vision—
him, upon seeing whom death could never occur even for a mortal. (35)

Through their ascetic power, the sages—whose vision was granted by the Lord of the Sky (Viśvabhūti)—bowed with joy to Bhava, who is as stainless as the moon, while he was engaged in his yogic discipline; they were accompanied by the gods.
Having observed that the Time of the Great Lord of Asuras was unbearable even when reflected upon by the mind,
they— having abandoned all concern for their own existence— bowed down and, together with the gods, offered praise to the Source of the World.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Vision of Rudra," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having beheld the Lord of the Gods of gods, those deities, headed by Brahmā and Indra, [were filled with wonder].
Having prostrated before the one whose vehicle is the bull, they praised him with desired words. ||1||
The Grandfather said:
Salutations to Śiva, who is accompanied by Umā, the remover of the fear of his devotees;
salutations to him who holds a trident-tip in his hand and carries a water-pot. (2)
Salutations to you, O Blue-throated one, whose teeth are formidable;
to the three-eyed Hara, whose eyes blaze like the fires of the three sacrificial altars. ||3||
Salutations indeed to the wielder of the Pināka bow, and salutations to the bearer of the thunderbolt;
salutations to him who has a serpent as his sacred thread and who is adorned with earrings.
Salutations to the one who bears the discus, to the one who wears a tiger skin,
to the one who has a black antelope skin as an upper garment, and likewise to the one who wears a girdle of serpents.
To the giver of boons, to the son, likewise to him born of Sarasvatī,
to him whose eyes are the moon and sun, and to him who holds a rosary in his hand.
Salutations indeed to the one with thousands of garlands of flames, to the upward-pointing Liṅga;
salutations to the dweller of the mountain, who formerly took away my head.
To the destroyer of Hālāhala, the bearer of the excellent skull-bowl, the one who rides the finest celestial chariot, and my very own progenitor. (8)
Salutation to the bestower of boons, to the most excellent one, to the one who delights in the cremation ground;
salutation always to the creator of man and to the sustainer of the world. 9.
To the creator of all origins and dissolutions, the helper of all,
the lord of sages and deities, and the sovereign of all beings— O Lord of gods, who are auspicious and gentle, be gracious to us, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees.
Sanatkumāra said: While Brahmā was thus offering praise, that god of gods, the lord of the worlds,
being pleased, spoke to those gods and sages who had been strengthened by their austerities.
O gods, I am pleased with this true austerity of yours, O sages and deities. Choose a boon; I shall grant it—let it be spoken after due deliberation. (12)
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O best of Brahmins, having gazed upon all those who were satisfied and strengthened by their asceticism, Brahmā spoke these words merely by the sight of them.
Brahmā said:
"O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to us, then become auspicious, gentle, and visible to us. (14)
He is pleasant to deal with, always contented in mind, and ever intent on what is beneficial and wholesome in all his undertakings, O Śaṅkara. (15)
"O God, bestower of thousands of boons, let him be granted to us, together with the Goddess, his son, and the hosts of gods. (16)
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by Brahmā, that Blessed One,
the best of gods and a knower of all yoga, emitted his own great and divine splendor.
From half of his splendor, he emitted a meteor from his mouth;
the Blessed One, assuming a universal form, said to it, "Become a woman. (18)
Having pervaded the sky along with the atmosphere, as well as the earth, by her majesty,
she stood established there, shining like a flash of lightning, and approached the Lord of Gods.
The Lord, smiling, said to that lotus-eyed goddess:
"O Goddess of pure smiles, worship Brahmā, the giver of boons."
Having promised "So be it," she began to perform austerities;
and Rudra said to those sages, "Listen to [the means] for my gratification."
O you whose wealth is austerity, listen to what I say regarding the fruit of those who possess such fruit:
they are immortal, free from old age, free from disease, and exempt from rebirth. (22)
"Devoted to me and endowed with austerity, you shall dwell right here;
and this hermitage is most excellent, situated upon the supreme mountain Svarṇaśṛṅga. (23)
This place on Mount Maināka shall indeed become meritorious and pure; of this there is no doubt, since I, Svarṇākṣa, am stationed here.
I created the goddess Svarṇākṣī, and because of her, that place is known as Svarṇākṣa. O Ṛṣis, you six families are ascetics rich in penance. ||25||
"Commanded by me, you shall dwell there indeed at Svarṇākṣa;
that sacred field extends for a yojana in every direction—of this there is no doubt. || 26 ||
It was frequented by gods and gandharvas and served by throngs of apsarases;
it was filled with lions, elephants, and śarabhas, and crowded with tigers, bears, and deer;
it was teeming with many kinds of birds and thick with creepers, trees, and shrubs.
A celibate student, observant of restraints, having conquered anger and mastered the self,
having fasted for three nights and offered a sacrificial oblation (caru),
shall dwell in the world of Brahmā even if he dies anywhere.

Whoever should likewise behold me here, the bull-bannered one, even against their will, shall obtain the fruit of a thousand cows through my grace. And having died here according to the prescribed rule, he shall wander with me.
"As long as the worlds endure, and as long as this mountain Maināka remains,
so long shall you move about with me by my grace, O gods.
Having spoken thus to those sages, he looked upon them with a gentle eye.
Even as all were looking on, he vanished right there.
Sanatkumāra said:
"The mortal who hears this, or causes the twice-born to hear it,"
Having attained that fruit, he too shall move about free from death.
Victorious is the bearer of the clouds, the time of the end for all beings,
who removes the afflictions of ascetics devoted to tranquility and self-restraint.
The remover of birth and death, he moves among those who act righteously;
endowed with various instruments, he travels through the air and walks upon the earth.
He is the shatterer of the city of Madana and the taker of eyes and teeth.
Free from fear and dejection, he is the leader of all beings.
Constantly proclaiming [the truth], the God of gods is the observer of his own consciousness, the ornament of hands and feet, and the all-seeing.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Bestowal of Boons," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
That goddess, having been addressed by Tryambaka, performed penance for a very long time.
At times she was without food, and again she subsisted on a single leaf.
Furthermore, she subsisted on air and even more so on water;
and Brahmā, perceiving her to be intensely radiant as she was thus engaged in the practice of austerity, [approached her].
He said, "Speak, O Goddess, for I am pleased; what may I do for you?
She replied, "O God, having obtained as my husband the three-eyed Lord who possesses the luster of the moon, may I wander happily through all the worlds; salutations to you. (3)
Brahmā said: "Indeed, it is not by that very body with which supreme austerity is performed that the Supreme Lord, the Master Śambhu, is attained. (4)
Therefore, through that very yoga, you shall become the daughter of Dakṣa Prajāpati in this world; having been born as such, you will obtain Rudra as your husband.
Then, having heard those words, that wise goddess,
the daughter of Dakṣa and the most eminent of yogis, was born through her yogic power as Satī.
Dakṣa gave that blameless woman as a wife to Tryambaka at the word of Brahmā; upon her he begot his mind-born sons.
There were many thousands of Rudras of immeasurable splendor, equal in strength to himself, radiant, and free from old age and death.
Seeing them being cleansed, Brahmā forbade him:
"O Lord of the gods, do not create offspring who are exempt from death."
"Create other offspring, may it be well with you—beings endowed with death.
Because he replied, "I am standing firm," he was therefore known as Sthāṇu.
The God of gods said:
"O Brahmā, I shall by no means create subjects joined with death;
I stand firm today because of your word, and I am not to be addressed by you again."
But these high-souled and mighty beings who have been created from my mind—
all of them shall indeed wander with me as performers of sacrifice.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O Vyāsa, after some time had passed, Dakṣa, on account of the curse,
summoned his other sons-in-law along with their wives and honored them in his home.
Filled with rage, he did not invite Satī along with Tryambaka;
but Satī, having understood all of that, went and spoke to her father.
O you of excellent vows, I am both the eldest and the most distinguished;
it does not behove you to honor these women along with their husbands while excluding me. (15)
Then, overcome by anger and his senses impaired by wrath,
Dakṣa looked at him and spoke as if burning him with his gaze.
"O virtuous one, these women, together with their husbands, worship me with affection;
but you do not worship me in that way, O lady of great vows, along with your husband. (17)
Ascetics rich in austerity enter my house accompanied by their wives;
therefore, I consider them always to be the most excellent, and for that reason I honor them. (18)
Therefore, O daughter, accept whatever worship I perform for you today, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious; or else, go wherever you please. (19)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, her face blazing with anger and exceedingly provoked, that auspicious woman did not accept the unwelcome and inferior worship, and she spoke this to him: [8.10.20]
"O father, since you perform this unwarranted worship toward me—which is praiseworthy, faultless, and supreme—you are, in fact, censuring me. (21)
Therefore, I shall abandon this body of mine for the sake of your son; for what is the use of this inauspicious life to me, now that I have been treated with such disrespect?
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having mentally offered salutations to Tryambaka, she who was the source of speech, being highly agitated, spoke these words: ||| 23 ||
"O Lord, wherever I may be reborn in a body again by my own will, may I there also be born as a virtuous woman, free from delusion. ||24||
"May I become the lawful wife of the wise Tryambaka.
Then, having performed the concentration upon the fiery goddess through meditative absorption, she— 25 ||
She indeed consumed her own body with the fire arising from within herself;
and the highly illustrious Tryambaka, perceiving the Goddess to have become thus, [acted].
Approaching Dakṣa, he who was skilled in speech spoke these words:
"Since I have been censured by you, while the others have been praised separately. (27)
Therefore, during the Vaivasvata Manvantara, these sons-in-law of yours shall again be born as your sons-in-law at a sacrifice, accompanied by their wives.
"And you too, O King, shall become a Kṣatriya by my curse;
you shall be born as the son of the Pracetasas from the daughter of the Śākhis.
And there, I shall create obstacles to the dharma for you, who are of cruel deeds. (29)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Dakṣa, with a heart truly burning with grief, spoke to him:
"If my own daughter was indeed spoken of by me, or even if she was abandoned by me again..."
"O Lord, what have I done here? I am always her master;
since you have cursed me, therefore, O Śaṅkara, you too shall dwell eternally upon the earth alone, and never in the intermediate space."
And having given you a share in their sacrifices, O Mahādeva of great splendor, all the twice-born shall everywhere perform the purificatory ablutions.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that three-eyed god, smiling, spoke to him:
"Of all the worlds, Bhūrloka is said to be the foundation."
I alone sustain it out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds;
for when this is sustained, all the worlds remain eternal.
Therefore, I shall remain here forever, not by your will;
for the twice-born, desiring to give, have already allotted shares to others as well. (35)
They touch water for the sake of purification and offer a portion to me;
furthermore, they perform what is auspicious for the increase of dharma itself. ||36||
Having given, they touch [the recipient] again for the very sake of the increase of Dharma. ||36||
For just as pure people carry away the floral offerings of the gods, yet, desiring to touch what is impure, they cast them aside and then touch water. (37)
Just as these bulls among Brahmins, wishing to give to me and to others, touch the portions of water, what cause for lamentation is there in that? (38)
But you, scorched by my curse, a perverted and lowest of men, being deluded in soul, shall procreate a son upon your own daughter. (39)
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus cursed Dakṣa, the blessed Lord, the master of the universe,
endowed with great splendor, ceased speaking and departed as he had come.

We bow down to the eternal one, whose eyes are like the moon, the sun, and fire; whose face is like the moon and whose eyes are like lotus petals; who is borne by a bull, who possesses an immeasurable flood of virtues, and who wears the crescent moon. 41.
He who, being firm in his vows, hears this account of Dakṣa’s curse and the bodiless state of the Goddess, or causes it to be heard by Brahmins,
shall be liberated from all sins and attain the world of Rudra. ||42||
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Curse of Dakṣa," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Once, Kaśyapa, the foremost among bipeds, arrived at his own home.
Himavat asked this question: "What indeed brings renown in the world?
O Sage, by what means may the worlds become inexhaustible and one attain supreme fame? Likewise, tell me how one may be worthy of honor among the virtuous."
Kaśyapa said:
"O highly fortunate one, all this is obtained through offspring;
my fame, along with that of Brahmā and the sages, was established through offspring. (3)
"O Lord of Mountains, do you not see why you ask me this?
O Mountain, I shall relate that which was seen by me in the past.
While I was traveling to Vārāṇasī, I saw [something] stationed in the sky."
A divine, incomparable, and irreproachable celestial chariot resounded;
beneath it, in the place of the womb, I heard cries of distress.
Having discerned them through my ascetic power, I remained there, invisible.
Then, O Lord of Mountains, a brahmin who was observant of vows, pure,
whose soul was purified by ablutions at sacred fords, and established in supreme austerity, arrived there.
Then, as that twice-born one was walking along, he was threatened by a tiger.
O mountain, that well then entered that region where it was;
there, afflicted and tormented by grief, the twice-born one saw the sages hanging from a clump of *vīraṇa* grass within the well, and he questioned them. || 8-9 ||
"Who are you, hanging head-downwards from this clump of vīraṇa grass, suffering? O sinless ones, by what means will your liberation come about?
The ancestors said:
O you who have performed meritorious deeds, we— your father, grandfather,
and great-grandfather— are suffering because of your wicked actions.
"O illustrious one, this is hell, situated here in the form of a pit;
you are a clump of vīraṇa grass, and we are hanging from you. (12)
O Brahmin, for as long as you live, we shall remain;
once you have died, we, being evil-minded, will go to hell. (13)
If you enter into marriage and procreate a son of superior qualities, by that means we shall each be liberated one by one.
"Not by any other austerity, my son, nor by the fruit of sacred fords;
therefore, O one of great intelligence, perform that [deed] and deliver your ancestors from fear. (15)
Having promised "So be it," and having propitiated the bull-bannered god,
he raised his ancestors from the pit and made them leaders of his attendants.
And he himself, beloved of Rudra and known by the name Sukeśa,
became a highly esteemed and powerful leader of Rudra’s hosts.
Therefore, O Lord of Mountains, having performed severe austerities, procreate a most virtuous offspring; through that, you shall attain fame.
Sanatkumāra said: Having been thus addressed by the sage, the lord of mountains remained steadfast in his observance and performed extensive penance, by which Brahmā was indeed gratified.
Then Brahmā, having approached him, said, "I am the giver of boons;
speak, O mountain of good vows, for I am pleased with this austerity of yours."
Himavat said:
"O Blessed One, I desire a son adorned with all virtues;
grant me this boon, O Lord, if you are pleased with us. (21)
Brahmā said:
"O Lord of Mountains, a daughter of excellent complexion shall be born to you;
by her power, you will attain abundant fame everywhere. (22)
Worshipped by all the gods and surrounded by ten million sacred fords,
you shall be purifying and meritorious in every respect even for the gods.
O auspicious one, she shall be your elder sister, and the others shall follow after her.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus, Brahmā then vanished on that very spot;
and in due time, that lord of mountains begot [a son] upon Menā.
Aparṇā, Ekaparṇā, and likewise Ekapāṭalā;
Ekaparṇā [is associated with] the banyan tree, and Ekapāṭalā with the *pāṭala* tree. (25)
Āśritā and Aparṇā, however, were without a leaf and without a dwelling;
they practiced austerities for a hundred thousand years, difficult to perform even for gods and dānavas.
Sai-kaparnā provided her food with a single leaf,
and Eka-patala likewise prepared it with a single *pāṭala* flower.
When each full thousand had passed, those two would take their food;
but Aparṇā remained without food, and her mother addressed her thus: ||28||

Distressed by maternal affection, she cried out, "Umā! Thus addressed by her mother, that goddess, who had performed difficult austerities, became renowned in the worlds by that very name, Umā, and was honored by the gods. ||29||
This entire world, both moving and unmoving, consists of these three young maidens;
by their ascetic power, they shall sustain the worlds as long as the earth endures.
All three of them had asceticism for their bodies, were endowed with the power of yoga,
were all great yoginīs, and were all possessed of perpetual youth.
The mothers of the worlds and those who practice celibacy always favor the worlds through their own ascetic power.
Umā was the most excellent and the best among them, a woman of supreme complexion;
endowed with great yogic power, she attended upon Mahādeva.
And her son was Dattaka Uśanas, that delighter of the Bhṛgu lineage.
Asitā, who was of a single color, gave birth to Devala as her son.
Among those maidens, the third, Ekapāṭalā,
attended upon Jaigīṣavya, the son of Śataśalāka.
Śaṅkha and Likhita were also his two sons, born not from a womb;
and as for Umā, that woman of excellent complexion whom I have described to you—
Then, observing that the entire three worlds had been completely scorched by the power of her asceticism, Brahmā spoke these words.
Brahmā said:
"O Goddess, O beautiful one, why will you torment the worlds with penance?
This universe was created by you; do not destroy it. (38)
"For you indeed uphold all these worlds by your own splendor;
speak, O Mother of the World, what is it that you desire? Be gracious unto us.
The Goddess said:
O Grandfather, you know in truth the purpose for which this penance is being performed by me; why then do you ask me again? (8.11.40)
Brahmā said:
"O Goddess, O sustainer of the worlds, he for whose sake you exert yourself with ascetic penance will himself come here and choose you as his bride."
He is the supreme lord of all the gods, the sovereign of the lords of all the worlds;
we, together with the gods, are subject to his will and speak as his servants.
The God of gods, the Lord of supreme lords, will himself come to the shore of the world;
he will appear in a noble form, yet deformed and misshapen, resembling the appearance of some ordinary man. (43)
Maheśvara, who dwells in the world of the mountains, the lord of the moving and the unmoving, is the first object of knowledge;
though his face is equal to the moon even without the moon itself, he stands here in a fierce and terrifying form. 44.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Granting of Boons by the Goddess," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Then the Blessed Lord Brahmā spoke to her in a melodious voice:
"O Goddess, O auspicious one, he by whom you were created cannot exist without you."
"That Lord of Gods shall be your husband; do not perform penance.
Then, O Vyāsa, Brahmā circumambulated the daughter of the mountain.
She vanished from her sight, and she too ceased [speaking].
Having said, "It is well," that goddess departed for her own hermitage.
Having taken refuge by the aśoka tree that had grown at the gate, she stood there;
then Hara, who bears the moon as his tilaka and removes the suffering of the thirty gods, arrived.
Assuming a deformed appearance, he became short and thin-armed;
his nose was bent, he was hunchbacked, and the ends of his hair were tawny.
And with a distorted face, he said, "O Goddess, I choose you as my bride.
Then Umā, perfected in yoga, recognized that Śaṅkara had arrived.
With her inner being purified,

she who was fond of brahmins, her eyes like beautiful flowers, spoke to him with the desire to perform the ritual acts, having honored that brahmin with water for the guest-offering (argha), water for the feet (pādya), and the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, I am not independent; my father is my lord, as is the Lord of the Immortals (Śiva).
Those two are indeed the masters over my giving, for I am a maiden, O bull among the twice-born. (8)
"Go and entreat my father, the imperishable Lord of Mountains;
if he gives me to you, O Brahmin, that shall be pleasing to me.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that Blessed Lord, the powerful deity, remaining in that very same deformed state, said to that king of mountains: "O lord of mountains, give Umā to me."
Recognizing him as the imperishable Rudra in his transformed form, he became afraid of the curse and, with a troubled mind, spoke these words: ||| 11 ||
O Blessed One, I do not hold the Brahmins—who are the deities of the earth—in contempt;
however, O one of great asceticism, hear that which was previously desired by me. (12)
"O Brahmin, a svayaṃvara for my daughter shall take place, honored by all;
whoever she herself chooses there, he shall become her husband. (13)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of the mountain, the high-minded Lord whose banner bears the bull approached the Goddess and spoke this. (14)
"O Goddess, it has been heard that you have been commanded by your father to hold a svayaṃvara;
O sinless one, whomever you choose there shall indeed be your husband."
Therefore, I take my leave; I shall depart, O fair-faced one, for you are difficult to find.
Having rejected one so handsome, how could you choose someone like me? (16)
Sanatkumāra said: Then she was addressed there by him with the very intent that had been expressed; he spoke of the disposition placed within Rudra and likewise the grace of his mind.
Having approached the Lord of Gods, he said: "Let your mind not be otherwise;
I shall choose you alone, and never any other being whatsoever. (18)
Or perhaps you have some doubt regarding me in any way, O Brahmin;
here and now, O illustrious one, I choose you for my heart's desire. (19)
Sanatkumāra said:
Taking a cluster of blossoms that was situated there,
the Goddess placed it upon the shoulder of Śambhu and said, "You have been chosen by me."
Then that Blessed Lord, thus entreated by the goddess,
spoke to Aśoka as if reviving him with his speech.
"Since I have been honored by you with this cluster of beautiful flowers, therefore, though abandoned by old age, you shall become immortal. (22)

He can assume any form at will, he is the flower of desire, he goes wherever he wishes, and he is my beloved; he is enriched with all ornaments as his flowers and possesses the fruits of all trees. ||23||
"You shall be the consumer of all foods and the one from whom nectar flows;
you shall be the possessor of all fragrances and will become a steadfast favorite of the Goddess. (24)
Fearless and perfectly at peace, you shall wander through all the worlds;
and this hermitage is exceedingly renowned as Citrakūṭa.
Whoever undertakes this journey seeking merit shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
and wherever he may die, he shall go to the world of Brahmā. ||26||

And whoever here, endowed with self-restraints, should completely renounce their life-breaths, shall become a Great Lord of the Gaṇas (Mahāgaṇapati), joined with the ascetic power of the Goddess. ||27||
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus and then taken leave of the daughter of Himavat, the Lord,
the creator of the world and protector of all beings, vanished from sight.
When that Blessed One of immeasurable soul had departed, the goddess too remained standing there with her face turned upward,
and then sat down upon the rock.
When that great archer, the Lord of Creatures, had departed, she,
looking up at him, became despondent like a night devoid of the moon.
Then Śailajā heard the sound of a distressed child in a lake filled with water near her own hermitage.

Then Śiva himself, the God of gods, having assumed the form of a child for the sake of sport, became seized by a crocodile in the middle of the lake. Thereupon, he who is the cause of the manifestation of the phenomenal world resorted to his power of yoga-illusion (yogamāyā).
Having created that form in the middle of the lake, he spoke this: ||3 3 ||
"May someone come here and save me, whose mind has been snatched away by this crocodile!
Alas, what a tragedy! Still but a child, I have not yet attained my heart's desire;
I shall meet my death in the mouth of this wicked-souled crocodile."
Though seized by a crocodile and suffering, I do not grieve for my own body. (35)
Just as I grieve for my father and my ascetic mother,
who will surely give up their lives upon hearing that I have met my end in the jaws of a crocodile—
those two, so fond of their son and having but one child, will certainly abandon their very breaths. (3.6)
"Alas! What great misery it is that I, having undertaken a vow while still a child, shall go to my death struck down without having performed any austerity.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard that cry of the distressed Brahmin, the beautiful queen rose and ran to where that twice-born man was staying. There,
she of moon-like countenance beheld a boy of lovely form.
Being swallowed by that grasping [grāha], he remained there trembling.
That illustrious and noble crocodile, seeing that the goddess had approached,
seized her and quickly went into the very middle of the lake.
Being dragged away, that radiant youth then uttered a cry of distress.
Then the goddess, afflicted with grief upon seeing the boy, spoke, she who is devoted to great vows. (41)
"O King of Grāhas, O Great Being, release this boy who is indeed my only son!
O you with great tusks and fearsome prowess, let him go quickly!
(42) The Grāha said:
"O Goddess, whoever approaches me on the first sixth day—that has been ordained as my food by the creators of the world from of old. (43)
"O illustrious daughter of the king of mountains, this man has surely been sent by Brahmā on the sixth day; I shall not release him by any means.
The Goddess said:
"O King of Grāhas, by virtue of the supreme austerity I have practiced on the peak of the Himavat, release this child; homage be to you! (45)
The crocodile said:
"O Goddess, daughter of the lord of mountains, do not let your ascetic merit go to waste;
even the King of the Gods himself is not able to release him. (46)
From Śarva, the fierce wielder of the trident, who was pleased with me as my lord,
[I obtained] immortality, invincibility, and indeed inexhaustible strength.
Furthermore, you yourself have granted him the power to seize and release, as well as imperishable knowledge;
therefore, I tell you that he shall not attain liberation.
Or else, O Goddess of auspicious countenance, you have great compassion for this child;
tell me what I should do so that he may thereby attain liberation.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of the Grāhas, speak quickly that which is not censured by the virtuous;
that has been done, of this there is no doubt, for the Brāhmaṇas are firmly honored by me. (8.12.50)
The crocodile said:
"Whatever penance you have performed, even if it be very slight in the end, give all of that to me; then you shall obtain liberation. (51)
The Goddess said:
"O great crocodile, whatever merit has been earned by me since my birth—all that I give to you; release the child before me. (52)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the crocodile, empowered by that asceticism, blazed forth;
like the sun at midday, he became difficult to look upon. (53)
And with a joyful heart, he said this to the Goddess, the sustainer of the world:
"O Goddess of great vows, what was this that you did without deliberation? (54)
For the acquisition of ascetic merit is indeed painful, yet its abandonment is not praised;
therefore, O lady of pure smiles, accept both this asceticism and this child. (55)
"I am pleased with your devotion, O Brahmin; therefore, I grant you a boon.
Having been addressed thus by the crocodile, she, who was firm in her great vows, spoke these words.
"O great crocodile, having reflected well, you have brought about the liberation of the fool;
there is no austerity superior to that of the Brahmins—indeed, the Brahmins are considered by me to be the most excellent. (57)
"O Lord of Grāhas, you know that once I have given something, I do not take it back;
for no man, O Grāha, would ever reclaim what has been given. (58)
"This has been given by me to you; indeed, I do not take it back.
Let this remain with you alone, and let this child be released. (59)
Having been addressed thus, he then praised her, released the child, and paid homage to the goddess who shone with the splendor of the sun; then and there he vanished.
Then, even as a child, he was released from the grasp of a crocodile on the shore of the lake;
like a treasure found in a dream, he vanished right there.
Thereupon, considering the expenditure of her ascetic merit, the Goddess, daughter of the Lord of the Snowy Mountains, [reflected].
Resolving to exert herself, she began once more to perform ascetic penance. ||62||
O Vyāsa, knowing that she desired to perform further asceticism, Śaṅkara himself spoke these words: "Do not perform penance."
"O Goddess of great vows, this ascetic power was granted to me by you;
therefore, it shall become inexhaustible for you in a thousandfold way. (64)
Having thus obtained this supreme and inexhaustible boon through her ascetic penance, the virtuous goddess remained there filled with joy, awaiting her svayaṃvara.
Indeed, that man who always recites this account of Śambhu’s conduct during his childhood shall, upon the dissolution of the body, become purified and a Gaṇa equal to Kumāra. (66)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
On the vast expanse of the Himalayas, crowded with hundreds of celestial chariots...
In the course of time, however, the svayaṃvara of Śailaputrī took place. ||1||
Then that king of mountains, Himavat, skilled in meditation,
understood that his daughter had been consecrated by the God of Gods.
Although he already knew [the answer], the Great Mountain, desiring to perform the proper rites of hospitality,
then proclaimed the self-choice marriage of the Goddess throughout all the worlds.
"May my daughter choose the Supreme Lord in the presence of all the inhabitants of the world, including the gods, dānavas, and siddhas. (4)
"Only that is well-done, praiseworthy, and conducive to my prosperity,"—having reflected thus, the Lord of Mountains placed Maheśvara in his heart. (5)
In the worlds up to the realm of Brahmā, the best of mountain lords,
having made that region filled with jewels for the Goddess, caused a svayaṃvara to be held.
Then, O Vyāsa, as soon as this proclamation had been made for the *svayaṃvara* of the daughter of Mahīdhra,
the gods and all other inhabitants of the world arrived, having assumed celestial attire.
Seated upon a throne of full-blown lotuses, he was surrounded by immeasurable *siddhas* and yogins.
Having been informed by him, the king of mountains, his grandfather, arrived there. ||8||
Bearing a thousand eyes, that king of the gods, possessing a noble form adorned with divine ornaments, garlands, and sandalwood paste,
mounted Airāvata, the foremost of all lordly elephants, from whose temples flowed streams of trickling ichor.
Having ascended, the king of all the immortals, bearing his thunderbolt, came before the gods;
like the sun, he illuminated all directions with his divine form, which surpassed [all others] in splendor and majesty. (8.13.10)
Mounting a golden celestial chariot with fluttering banners, he arrived swiftly with great speed;
