adorned with earrings blazing with the brilliance of jewels, he stood in that chariot which resembled the splendor of fire and the sun.

The son of the brahmin Kaśyapa, Āditya—who bears the name Bhagavat—approached from nearby; he possessed a stout, well-formed body and was adorned with necklaces, his majesty being equal to that of splendor, strength, and sovereign command. (12)
Taking up his staff, Kṛtānta arrived with speed, mounted upon a terrifying buffalo;
his body was as massive as a great mountain, and his beautiful attire was adorned with gold and various jewels. (13)
Samīraṇa, the sustainer of the entire world, ascended his celestial chariot and approached,
scorching all the lords of the gods and asuras by entering into their splendor with his own superior brilliance.
Vahni, approaching into the midst of the lords of the gods, set forth blazing and wearing a magnificent raiment;
his slender body was illuminated by various jewels as he traveled through the world in a foremost, celestial chariot.
Having ascended, that lord of all sovereigns, the king of kings, proceeded with haste;
beautiful in form, he gladdened all the lords of gods and asuras by his radiance and his attire. (16)
Having ascended a celestial chariot of blazing form, variegated with great jewels, the Moon arrived;
his slender body was dark-hued, his attire was most exquisite, and he was adorned with all manner of fragrant garlands bound upon him. (17)
Mounting Tārkṣya, who resembled a mountain, that wielder of the mace arrived swiftly;
likewise, those two best of divine physicians, the Aśvins, quickly ascended a single celestial chariot.
The two heroic ones, Manohara and Ujjvalacāruveṣa, arrived at the assembly of the gods;
Śeṣa followed, possessing the brilliance of a blazing sun and fire, bearing a thousand hoods that flickered with the color of flames. || 19 ||
Accompanied by other great-souled nāgas, he ascended a celestial chariot and approached the sons of Diti, the great asuras, who possessed a splendor equal to fire, the sun, Indra, and the wind.
Having assumed an attire suited to his excellence,
that king of the Gandharvas, possessing a beautiful form, traveling in a celestial chariot with divine women, approached the assembly of the gods.
Accompanied by hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases, he arrived there at the command of Śakra;
and other gods, the lords of the inhabitants of the triple heaven, also came, each having individually assumed a beautiful attire. (22)
The Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Kinnaras arrived, having mounted the backs of celestial chariots;
and there, within that assembly of the lords of the gods, was the Lord of Śacī, his form distinguished by a majesty exceeding the authority of kings.
Deluded by the power and sovereignty of kings, he exerted himself excessively and in vain;
for she was the cause of the three worlds, the mother of the universe, and the mother of both gods and asuras. (24)
And the consort of Śambhu, the Puruṣa, the supreme Prakṛti described by the Purāṇas, that wife of the Supreme Lord came to the home of Himavat for the sake of her purpose, due to Dakṣa’s anger. (25)
Thus, because they did not know them, delusion entered those lords of the gods;
for they had come for the sake of boons and were utterly bewildered, since they had been rendered so by the Lord. (26)

Then, with celestial nymphs dancing, with throngs of Gandharvas singing beautiful songs, and with hosts of gods, asuras, and other denizens of heaven standing there in various forms and attire; ||27||
Seated upon the back of a celestial chariot variegated with jewels and gold, her body fanned by waving yak-tail whisks,
the goddess set forth forcefully, holding a fragrant garland of flowers from every season.
Sanatkumāra said:
While the Goddess stood holding the garland in the assembly of the gods,
Śakra and the other deities arrived, having come to the svayaṃvara.
Out of a desire to test the Goddess, the omnipresent Lord Śambhu suddenly became a five-crested infant and lay down upon the surface of her lap.
Then, suddenly, the goddess, perceiving through her yogic concentration that the five-crested child was standing there, rejoiced, filled with affection.
Then she, whose resolve was pure and who had obtained the excellent fruit of her desire,
remained as if liberated, having fixed him alone within her heart.
Then, seeing the infant lying in the lap of the goddess, the gods consulted among themselves, "Who is this? and, being greatly distressed, they became exceedingly enraged.
Raising his arm, the slayer of Vṛtra hurled the thunderbolt at him;
that raised arm of his remained fixed in that very position.
Paralyzed by Śambhu, the God of gods, who had assumed the form of a child, he was unable to hurl his thunderbolt nor even to move his arms. (35)
Then the powerful god Āditya, the son of Kaśyapa, known as Bhaga,
being deluded, raised up a flaming club and desired to hurl it.
Then the Blessed One likewise paralyzed his arm;
shaking his head, Viṣṇu looked at him with anger.
The Lord indeed caused baldness to come upon his head as well;
Pūṣan, gnashing his teeth with his teeth, looked at Śarva, deluded.
As soon as he was seen by Śambhu, even his teeth fell out;
Yama’s staff was paralyzed, and the fire’s brilliance and the moon’s luster were eclipsed. (39)
The Lord likewise paralyzed the strength of Vāyu and that of all the other inhabitants of heaven, as well as their power, splendor, and yogic mastery.
Then, while those gods remained thus filled with indignation,
Brahmā, deeply agitated, respectfully applied himself to meditation.
He perceived the Lord of the gods of gods seated upon Umā’s lap;
having recognized the Supreme Lord, he quickly rose up with reverence. 42.
The Grandfather (Brahmā) prostrated at the feet of Śambhu and praised him with ancient Sāman chants and meritorious, secret names.
You are the unborn, the immortal, the divine, the creator, the destroyer, the all-pervading, the supreme;
you are primordial matter, the individual soul, the ultimate principle, Brahman, the object of meditation, and the imperishable. 44.
He is the nectar, the Supreme Self, the Lord, the Great Cause;
He is the creator of Brahmā, the fashioner of primordial nature (prakṛti), the creator of all, the Supreme Lord. ||45||
O Lord of the gods of gods, you truly cannot be known even by the inhabitants of heaven;
nor, O God, can you be known even by sages who are masters of yoga.
O Great God, you exist immeasurably through your own divine play;
O Lord, you alone remain throughout the great creation and the great aeon. 47.
"O Maheśvara, even I do not know your activity;
how then can the gods know that which is profound and of an inscrutable nature?
And this, O Lord, is your eternal Prakṛti, the cause of creation."
Having assumed the form of a wife, she has come as the cause of the world. ||49||
Salutations to you, O Lord of the World, and always salutations to the Goddess as well.
By your grace, O Lord of Gods, and by your command, [I have created] the subjects.
"These gods and others who were created are now deluded, bewildered by your yoga;
show them favor so that they may become as they were before. (51)
Then, having thus petitioned the Supreme Lord, the immensely radiant Brahmā spoke these words to all those gods who had been paralyzed: ||52||
"You gods are all deluded; you do not recognize this Śaṅkara, the god of gods, who has arrived here as the very cause of my own birth. (52)
This Rudra is Mahādeva, Śarva, Bhīma, and Kapardin;
he is Ugra, Īśāna, the Self, the Unborn (Aja), and Śaṅkara as well. ||53||
The God of gods, the supreme abode, the Lord, Paśupati, the Master;
the creator of the world, the sustainer of the world, and the cause of the world's maintenance. ||54||
O lords of the immortals, go quickly for refuge together with me to this very Lord of Gods, the Supreme Self, the imperishable one. (55)
Having heard the words of Brahmā, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the sovereign,
laughed and enlightened all the gods, O guardians of the world.
In this very way there is no doubt, just as Padmasambhava has said:
"In a previous creation, O gods, Maheśvara was indeed with me. (57)
Pervading the world with his manifold forms, he remains established therein;
therefore, becoming his very self, go for refuge to Hara.
Then all those inhabitants of heaven were likewise paralyzed;
with minds purified by their inner disposition, they bowed mentally to Śarva.
Then Maheśvara, the God of gods, became pleased with them;
he then swiftly restored the bodies of the deities as they were before.
Then, while all the gods were thus engaged in their efforts to ward him off,
the Lord of Gods assumed a most wonderful three-eyed form.
Because of his splendor, the gods requested eyes from that omnipresent Lord;
to them, he gave his supreme eye, which possesses the power of vision through his own body.
The Supreme Lord of Gods granted [this]; then they beheld the Lord.
Having seen the Supreme Ruler, who bears a third eye, they [were filled with wonder]. (63)
Brahmā and all the other lords of the gods quickly became his wheel-rims;
then the goddess, delighted, stood before the dwellers of the three heavens.
They placed a garland of flowers at the feet of the one of immeasurable splendor;
and having cried out, "Excellent! Excellent!", those deities again paid homage to the Lord along with the Goddess, bowing their heads until they touched the surface of the earth.
Then, O Vyāsa, in the meantime, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [arrived].
The one of great splendor spoke thus to Himavat, the great mountain: "Indeed,
you alone are praiseworthy, worthy of worship, and venerable to us all,
for you possess this great connection with Śarva."
"Let the marriage be performed quickly; why do you remain in suspense?
Then Himavat, having bowed to that god, replied to him:
"O God, you alone are the cause by which my prosperity has arisen through Śarva."
"Your grace has arisen spontaneously, and you alone are indeed the cause;
therefore, O Grandfather, ordain their marriage as is appropriate.
Having heard these words, the Grandfather, the king of mountains, [acted accordingly].
"O Lord, let the marriage be performed," he said to the god.
Śaṅkara replied to that world-guardian, "As you wish.
And at that very moment, O Vyāsa, a city was fashioned by Brahmā.
For the purpose of Maheśa’s marriage, there were various jewels for adornment:
diverse gems and precious stones, gold, and pearls. ||73||
Approaching in embodied form, they adorned that supreme city.
The ground was variegated with emeralds and beautified by golden pillars;
its walls were made of crystal and beryl, from which hung strings of pearl necklaces.
In that delightful city of Śiva, which had been constructed for the purpose of the wedding.
The moon and the sun shone equally there upon the great earth, illuminating the abode of Maheśvara, the high-souled God of gods. ||76||
Taking up a delightful fragrance from the bull, the wind blew with a pleasant touch, manifesting its devotion toward the Lord.
There were the four oceans, the supreme gods headed by Śakra,
the celestial rivers and great rivers, as well as the Siddhas and Munis;
all the Gandharvas and Apsarases, along with the Nāgas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas.
The Guhyakas, other Khecaras, Kinnaras, and Devacāraṇas. ||79||
Tumburu, Nārada, Hāhā, and Hūhū were the singers of the Sāman hymns.
Taking jewels and musical instruments, they arrived there filled with joy.
There, the sages whose wealth was their asceticism, with joyful minds, recited in their entirety the sacred wedding mantras sung in the Vedas. ||8.1||
All the mothers of the world and all the daughters of the gods, entirely,
sing with joy at the wedding of the Supreme Lord.
There, the six seasons stood present in embodied form, bringing equal joy through their various fragrances;
they had arrived for the wedding of Śaṅkara, delighted by the deep thundering of masses of dark clouds. || 83 ||
It was illuminated on all sides by peacocks crying out "kekā" and dancing,
and it was beautified by cranes— white, yellow, and pale— as well as by the shimmering streaks of flickering, tawny lightning. || 84-85 ||
With fresh *śilīndhra* mushrooms and *kandala* sprouts just appearing, with creepers and trees putting forth beautiful young shoots,
and resounded by swarms of frogs languid with passion— awakened by the onset of auspicious rain-showers—
even the most resolute of passionate women, whose minds were previously uplifted by pride toward their lovers, [now succumb]. (86)
In an instant, she was made captivating by the charming cries of peacocks which caused the hearts of men to falter;
likewise, she shone intensely with the rainbow of Indra, which was curved like the crescent of the moon, possessed a beautiful form radiant with three colors,
and hovered near the mass of clouds.
With breezes that were cool due to being mixed with thick water, fragrant from contact with various flowers,
and enchanting, the wind caused the beautiful tresses of the celestial women to tremble.
The orb of the moon was obscured by thundering clouds, while lovely *dūrvā* grass sprouted from the sprinkling of fresh water.
She was gazed upon with longing by the wives of travelers, who watched her with reverence as she was shrouded in the smoke of their sighs.
Rich with the sound of swans' anklets, with uplifted breasts, her girdle like a flickering streak of lightning, and her eyes clearly like lotuses;
she is like a flock of swans terrified by the roar of a mass of dark clouds. ||91||
With the tips of its blue lotuses reddened by the falling streams of pure water,
and with the beauty of all its limbs fashioned from the pollen of fragrant flowers, the rainy season arrived for the prosperity of the Mountain’s Daughter at her wedding.
Freed from the mantle of clouds, with breasts emerging from the sheaths of lotuses, resounding with the anklets of swans, and making all the quarters of space most delightful;
with broad sandy banks for hips and warbling cranes for a girdle. (93)
She is enchanting with eyes as expansive as full-blown blue lotuses;
her lips are like ripe bimba fruit, and she smiles with teeth like kunda flowers; she is adorned with a line of body hair as dark as a fresh, young śyāmā creeper. || 94–95 ||
With her excellent necklace of moonbeams gliding across her lofty chest,
she delighted the hearts of all the inhabitants of heaven;
she spoke with a sweet voice that was like the humming song of a swarm of female bees.
Adorned with beautiful earrings resembling clusters of swaying white water-lilies, she held fingers made of sprouts from the tips of red *aśoka* branches;
she was further embellished with garments composed of heaps of those very flowers. ||97-98||
Her feet were like the tips of red lotuses, her rows of nails like jasmine flowers;
her beautiful thighs were like plantain trunks, and her auspicious face was like the moon. ||99||
Like a beloved woman, the enchanting autumn arrived, affectionately touching the gods with gusts of wind mingled with lotus filaments;
she was like one who has cast off the bodice of white clouds, her face being the orb of the full moon.
With eyes like blue lotus buds and beautiful breasts just beginning to emerge,
with winds fragrant from the pollen of various flowers, and bringing delight to the hearts of all— autumn arrived there for the goddess’s wedding, sounding like the tinkling anklets of a swan. 101.
Flooding the mountain rocks with exceedingly cool waters,
the two seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira arrived, possessing incomparable splendor.
With those two seasons having arrived, that Himavat, the best of mountains,
quickly shone like silver as they rained down a powder of frost.
Then, with that thick and beautiful shower of frost, the Himālaya shone like the ocean Kṣīroda; meanwhile,
the winter season destroyed the trees in the snowy regions.
Like a wicked man who has suddenly achieved his purpose,
that mountain shone with its peaks covered by layers of frost,
like a lord of the earth with large, white parasols.
The pale, vast, glorious,
and auspicious mountain peaks shone like lofty palaces. In the caves of that lord of mountains, which were exceedingly filled with various kinds of deer, [the sounds echoed].
Streams of frost, white as the rays of the moon, fell like streams of cow’s milk;

breezes, cool from contact with droplets of ice and their bodies laden with heaps of many flower-pollen, blew gently, causing the extremely fine garments of the lords of the hosts of immortals to flutter slightly. (108–109)
The spring season, its harshness shaken off and its faults removed, with the sprouts of the mango tree as its ear-ornaments,
quickly came to the Himalayas for the sake of serving the Daughter of the Mountain.
When he had reached that mountain for the purpose of attending the wedding of the Daughter of the Mountain,
clusters of trees and thickets appeared on all sides, adorned with flowers as their crest-ornaments.
Fragrant, auspicious, and very cool breezes blew repeatedly, their bodies laden with the pollen from the tips of various flowers; they intensified the passion of the gods and the celestial nymphs.
Likewise, there were lotus ponds filled with clear water, adorned with the blossoms of red and blue lotuses.
Just as women become most beautiful when the tips of their breasts have only slightly begun to emerge. || 1.13 ||
Due to the nature of the season and the arising of passion, the male cuckoos, with wings tucked against the blossoming branches,
warbled their full song, which was pleasing to the ears of the celestial nymphs.

The foremost of the celestial elephants drank with great joy the waters of the lakes, which were neither too hot nor too cold, turned tawny by the pollen of lotus filaments, and made resonant by pairs of ruddy geese; they drank from those pools surrounded by excellent *priyaṅgu* trees, which were even more beloved than their own mates.
They shone as if threatening one another with their flower-clusters.
Upon the peaks white as snow, clusters of blossoms appeared like elders who had gathered for some solemn purpose. There,
flowering Aśoka creepers clinging to the Śāla trees shone resplendent.
Like amorous women whose forms are embraced by their lovers' necks,
the *mālatī* creepers shone as if conversing with one another, their clusters of blossoms being sung over by swarms of intoxicated bees. (118–119)
The waters were made blue by blue lotuses and white by the pale stalks of lotus fibers;
likewise, they were rendered intensely variegated by petals half-bitten by intoxicated bees.
In some places, upon the vast waters, there were golden [lotuses], while in others, there were emerald ones growing without interval.
In some lakes, lotus groves with stalks of beryl sprang up on all sides. || 121 ||
There were beautiful ponds adorned with lotuses and water-lilies,
resounding with the cries of various birds and featuring rows of golden steps.
O Sage, the peaks of that mountain, densely covered with well-flowered *karṇikāra* trees, shone as if they were made of gold.
All the quarters became pale-red with *pāṭala* trees, their forms trembling in the wind, bearing flowers that had just begun to open;
and the dark-blue *aśoka* trees shone like the peaks of mountains of black collyrium.
In full bloom upon the mountain, the trees grew as if in mutual rivalry;
and the groves of *kiṃśuka* trees, resounding with the humming of bees,
appeared on every slope of the mountain.
Then the splendor of that Himalaya was like that of Tamāla thickets,
as if masses of dark clouds were nestled within its recesses;
and it was graced by towering Campaka trees with exceedingly broad branches and flowers in full bloom.
At that time, the Himālaya shone exceedingly with the cries of intoxicated male cuckoos;
hearing those sweet, impassioned sounds of the cuckoos from all sides, the peacocks with their fluttering wings let out a cry as melodious as their own.
By their sounds, the Bodiless One— his strength augmented, his flower-bow and arrows in hand, and fully prepared— set himself to pierce the limbs of the celestial women.
With its sharp sunlight and generally warm reservoirs of water,
the summer season arrived at the Himalayas for the purpose of serving the wedding of the Goddess.
And there, it was further graced by many trees with their abundance of blossoms.
He adorned the peaks of the snowy mountain on all sides. ||13 1||
And during that season, delightful winds blew there,
bearing the fragrance of *pāṭala*, *kadamba*, and *arjuna* flowers.
The ponds, filled with clusters of blossoming lotuses whose forms were reddened by filaments,
resounded upon their banks with flocks of kalahamsa geese.
Likewise, the kurabaka trees as well, their forms pale with blossoms,
appeared upon all the peaks, frequented by swarms of bees.
And on the broad slopes of the mountains, bakula trees released beautiful flowers on all sides.

Thus, O hero among sages, the six seasons— adorned with all manner of flowers and diverse attire, and delightful with the songs of various birds— approached for the sake of the prosperity of the marriage of the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain.
Then, when the assembly of all beings had thus gathered and was filled with various musical instruments, my father Brahmā himself [arrived].
Having adorned the Daughter of the Mountain with a wealth of yogic ornaments, the Knower of the World took her and caused her to enter the city. (138)
Then Brahmā once again addressed the omnipresent Lord:
"Standing in the position of preceptor, I shall offer oblations into the fire. (139)
"If you grant me permission, this ritual procedure must be performed.
To that god, Śaṅkara—the god of gods and lord of the universe—spoke. (8.13.140)
O Lord of the Gods, do whatever you desire;
O Brahmā, O All-pervading One, I shall carry out every word of yours, the Master of the World. (141)
Then, with a joyful heart, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, bowed down and joined the hands of the God and the Goddess in the yogic union (yogabandha).
Agni himself stood there with palms joined in reverence, accompanied by the great mantras sung in the Vedas, which had appeared before him in embodied form.
Having offered oblations according to the prescribed rule with clarified butter and that very nectar,
one should cause that god Agni to be circumambulated three times.
Having released his hand-clasp, accompanied by all the deities and all his mind-born sons, he was filled with joy in his innermost soul.
When the marriage ceremony was completed, O Vyāsa, she bowed to the bull-bannered Lord;
for by means of yoga alone, she had become one with Umā and Parameśvara.
"That supreme marriage has been performed, which the gods do not know anywhere.
Thus I have related to you all this auspicious Svayaṃvara and the most wonderful marriage of the god, as you listen. 147.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Marriage of Umā," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Now, when the marriage of Bhava, of immeasurable splendor, had taken place...
Having attained incomparable joy, the gods together with the Grandfather (Brahmā) praised Maheśvara with pleasing words while bowing down:
"Salutation to the one whose linga is the mountain; salutation indeed to the Lord of the Mountain."
Homage to him who has the speed of the wind, to the multiformed, and to the unconquered;
homage to the destroyer of afflictions and the bestower of auspicious prosperity.
Homage to Nīlaśikhaṇḍin, and homage to the Lord of Ambikā.
Salutations to the one whose form is the wind, and salutations indeed to the one of a hundred forms.
Salutations to the one whose form is Bhairava and to the one with deformed eyes.
Salutations to the one with a thousand eyes and to the one with a thousand feet.
Salutations to the secret essence of the Vedas, salutations again and again to the limb of the Veda;
salutations to the one who paralyzed the arm of Śakra, and to the sprout of the Veda.
Salutations again and again to the lord of the moving and the unmoving, and to the one who brings peace.
To the one whose linga rests upon the waters, whose linga is as vast as the end of an eon; ||| 7 ||
Homage to the one adorned with a garland of skulls, homage to the one wearing a wreath of skulls; homage to the one with a skull in hand, to the fanged one, and to the wielder of the mace. ||8||
Homage to the Lord of the three worlds and to him who is bowed to by the seven worlds;
homage to him who holds the khaṭvāṅga staff in his hand and who removes the suffering of the Pramathas. ||9||
Homage to the one who struck off the head of the sacrifice, who removed Kṛṣṇa’s hair,
who cast down the eyes of Bhaga, and who took away the teeth of Pūṣan.
Homage to the bearer of the Pināka bow, the trident, the sword, the scimitar, and the mallet.
Homage be to the Death of Death and to the one with the third eye.

Salutations to the one who brings an end to the end-maker, and salutations to the dweller of the mountains; salutations to the one with golden seed (Suvarṇaretas) and to the wearer of conch-shaped earrings;
salutations to Vāḍvali, the destroyer of yoga, and the teacher of yogins.
To the one whose eyes are the moon and the sun, and who has an eye upon his forehead; || 13 ||
Homage to the one who delights in the cremation ground and to the bestower of boons in the cremation ground;
homage to the Lord of the gods, to Tryambaka, salutations again and again. ||14||
Salutations to the one whose laughter is like a hundred thunderbolts, who is devoted to the Veda, who is unconquered,
who is ever virtuous as a householder, who wears matted hair, and who is a perpetual celibate;
salutations to the one with a shaven head and a half-moon on his cheek, salutations to the Lord of all creatures.
To him who was performing austerities in the water and who bestows the sovereign power of yoga.
Salutations to the peaceful one, to the self-controlled one, to the cause of dissolution and creation;
salutations again and again to the performer of grace and to the performer of maintenance.
Salutations to Rudra, to Vasu, to Āditya, and to the Aśvins.
Salutations to the Father, to the Sādhya, and indeed salutations to the Viśvedevas.
Salutations to Śiva, to Śarva, to Ugra, and to the Giver of Boons.
Salutations to Bhīma, to the Commander of the Army, and salutations to the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati).
Salutation indeed to the pure one who licks [the world], to him who is newly born;
salutation to Mahādeva, the wondrous, and to Citraratha. || 8.14.20 ||
Salutations to you, the Pradhāna, the immeasurable, the effect, and the instrument;
salutations to the Puruṣa, who brings about the desires of the Puruṣa.
Salutations to the one who possesses the qualities of Pradhāna through its union with the Puruṣa.
To the one who sets in motion both primordial nature and the person in every respect. || 22 ||

Salutations to the one who knows the performed and the unperformed, who bestows the connection with the fruits [of action], who knows the time in all circumstances, and who moves according to the rules of discipline. ||23||
Salutations to the creator of diversity and the bestower of the functions of the qualities;
salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; salutations to you, O Creator of all beings.
O Lord, may you be auspicious, gentle, and pleasant to behold; indeed, be like the moon to us.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus praised by all the gods, that Blessed Lord, the Master of the Universe and Lord of Umā, spoke these words to the immortals.
O gods, O deities, I am pleasant to behold and gentle; tell me, O sinless ones, what you desire most, for I shall grant it to you. Speak! (26)
Then all those gods, including Brahmā, bowed down and said:
"O Blessed One, let it be so; let this boon remain as requested. (27)
"When there is a task to be done, you shall grant us our desired boon.
Having said "So be it" to them and dismissed the gods, Hara then entered his abode along with the Pramathas and the worlds.
But he who sings of this wonderful festival of Hara in the presence of deities and brahmins, upon the dissolution of his body, shall become equal to the peerless Gaṇeśa and attain happiness. (29)
Sanatkumāra said: O son of Parāśara, whoever should hear or recite this hymn of praise,
having become a dweller in the heavenly world, he is honored like the king of the gods.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Hymn on the Marriage of Umā," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: When the Lord had entered the palace and was well-seated upon an excellent throne,
Accompanied by his wife Rati, the cruel Manmatha became intent on piercing the God.
[He was] that evil-souled one, the lowest of his lineage, joined with improper conduct,
who tormented all the worlds and was devoid of compassion toward everyone.
He was the creator of obstacles for the sages together with their observances and vows,
and he had come together with Rati in the form of a peacock.
Then, O Vyāsa, he looked with his third eye at the Lord of the Gods who desired to pierce him as an assailant, regarding him with contempt.
Thereupon, the fire born from his eye, possessing thousands of garlands of flames, [burst forth].
Having concealed his true intent, he burned the Lord of Pleasure along with his retinue.
As he was being consumed, crying out piteously and discordantly in distress,
and seeking to propitiate that god, he fell to the surface of the earth.
Then Manmatha, the tormentor of the world, his limbs enveloped by fire,
fell down and in an instant was reduced to ashes.
But his wife, deeply distressed, lamented piteously for him.
Weeping and filled with compassion, she entreated both the god and the goddess.
Hearing her lamentation, those two gods, whose very nature is compassion, looked upon the sorrowful woman, comforted her, and spoke to her. (8–9)
"He is certainly burnt, O blessed lady; his rebirth here is not expected.
Even though he is bodiless, he will perform all your tasks for you in due time."
But when Viṣṇu becomes the son of Vasudeva, O auspicious lady,
then he shall indeed become your husband, the son of that [Viṣṇu], for the sake of pleasure.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having obtained that boon, she— the beautiful-faced wife of Kāma—
went to her desired place, filled with joy and free from fatigue.
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus burned away Kāma, whose mind was deluded, Śaṅkara spoke to the daughter of Himavat with devotion toward that best of sages.
"The eminent brahmin named Vasiṣṭha, holding me in his heart, is performing austerities;
O lady of great vows, I shall go there to grant him a boon.
Having spoken thus to the goddess out of affection for his devotee, the Lord then—
The powerful lord went to the hermitage of the sage Vasiṣṭha, who was performing austerities.

Then that scorcher of enemies [Parāśara] approached Vasiṣṭha, the best among the excellent sages, the most eminent, the foremost of those who practice austerities, and a tiger among ṛṣis, as he was performing penance.
When a full thousand years had passed, the Blessed One approached him—who was like a blazing fire—and said: "Tell me, what shall I give you?
O twice-born one, I grant you divine vision; behold me along with my retinue."
Having seen that Lord Īśāna, he bowed his head to the Master,
placed his joined palms upon his head, and praised him with a joyful countenance.
Vasiṣṭha said: Salutations to the golden liṅga; salutations indeed to the Vedic liṅga.
Salutations to the thousand-fold liṅga; salutations indeed to the fiery liṅga.
Salutations to the ancient Liṅga; salutations indeed to the Liṅga of the Vedas.
Salutations to the supreme Liṅga; salutations indeed to the Liṅga of Brahman.
Salutations to the Liṅga of the three worlds; salutations indeed to the Liṅga of the conflagration.
Salutation to the mountain-liṅga; salutation indeed to the liṅga of stability.
Homage to the secret liṅga, whose path is the liṅga of the seven continents;
homage to the liṅga of all objects, whose limbs are the liṅga of all worlds.
Homage be to the unmanifest liṅga; indeed, homage to the liṅga of the intellect.
Salutations to the one whose mark is the ego-sense; salutations indeed to the one whose mark is the elements.
Salutations to the one whose mark is the senses; salutations to the one whose mark is the subtle elements.
Salutations to the one whose mark is the Puruṣa; salutations indeed to the one whose mark is existence.
Salutation to the one whose upper sign is *sattva*, and salutation indeed to the one whose sign is *tamas*;
salutation to the one whose upper sign is *rajas*, and salutation indeed to the one whose sign is *sattva*. ||25||
Homage to the Liṅga of the Sky, and indeed homage to the Liṅga of Radiance;
homage to the Liṅga of the Left, Above, and Below, and indeed homage to the Liṅga of Sound. ||26||

Salutations to the one whose mark is the Ṛgveda; salutations indeed to the one whose mark is the Yajurveda. Salutations to the one whose mark is the Atharvaveda; salutations indeed to the one whose mark is the Sāmaveda. 27.
Salutations to the one whose mark is the constituent parts of sacrifice; salutations indeed to the one whose mark is sacrifice itself.
Salutations to the one whose mark is the end; salutations to the one whose mark is followed by the Vedas.
Grant us supreme yoga and offspring equal to yourself;
O God, grant us imperishable Brahman and supreme tranquility, O All-pervading Lord; grant our lineage immortality and an inexhaustible mind devoted to dharma. (29)
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, when the Blessed One was thus being praised by Vasiṣṭha of immeasurable soul, he was gratified; and being pleased, he spoke this to him.
The Blessed One said:
"I am pleased with you; I grant all this that is in your heart, as well as the supreme, subtle, imperishable yoga that fulfills all desires. (31)
"And you shall have a divine son equal to yourself, endowed with the power of austerity and yoga; moreover, O best of sages, various forms of knowledge shall manifest within you.
Self-restraint, tranquility, fame, contentment, and freedom from anger [shall likewise be yours]."
They shall be yours eternally, and you shall possess immortality in every respect. ||33||

O Brahmin, may there be for you always the state of being independent, the state of being invincible, and the state of being imperishable; may there be no destruction of your lineage, and may your intellect regarding dharma be undecaying.
Speak of other boons as well; I grant them to you, O best of sages.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Blessed One, O All-pervading Lord, everything that has occurred and all that is currently happening is known to you.
O God, let that by which I may know the future be ordained for me. (35)
The god said:
"It is not possible to know how one might act according to one's own will in the future;
nevertheless, you shall know it through my grace—be at peace."
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Blessed One, O best of gods, all that is to happen in the future is known to you; O Lord, it shall be exactly as you intend, O Master."
The God of gods said:
"It is my firm conviction that the future cannot be made otherwise;
how then could one make it otherwise? (38)
"Thus it is; there is no doubt in this matter regarding that which has been performed by me. Therefore, O imperishable one, you shall again show favor to your son.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus, O brahmin-sage, the blue-and-red god Kapardin vanished in an instant while that seer was looking on.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Bestowing of Boons upon Vasiṣṭha," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Having obtained those boons, our grandfather, the venerable Vasiṣṭha, begot a son who was equal to himself in splendor. (1)
Sanatkumāra said: By that boon from the trident-bearing God of gods,
he begot [a son] upon Arundhatī, who was endowed with the power of asceticism and yoga.
The eldest of his hundred sons, a son named Śakti who was most devoted to Brahman,
[was born] to that high-souled descendant of Vasiṣṭha from his very childhood.
Devotion toward the one who has the bull as his banner arose with great intensity;
once, for the sake of offspring, he propitiated the Lord of Umā.
Mahādeva, pleased with him, said, "I am the giver of boons. Then, having seen that Lord, he spoke these words with a bowed face: ||5||
O Lord, with what shall I praise you, who are the master of the entire world?
O All-pervading One, you sustain all the worlds by yourself through your own law.
You alone are the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment, the agent, the action, and likewise the instrument;
you are the producer, that which is produced, and the very act of production in every respect.
"O Lord, O Ruler of the Gods, I desire a son named Ātman, equal to me in virtues; let this boon be granted to me. Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, to him who was speaking thus, the Lord, the best among speakers, smilingly spoke,
making all the quarters resound with his voice.
"I have been requested by you, O Śakti, and he shall be born to you—a bull among sages who will be equal to you and a knower of all the Vedas. (8.16.10)
And having thus arisen from the seed-nature by its own inner self, it no longer exists as that seed-nature, because it has entered into another state of transformation. (11)
Thus, this self of ours, which was designated as having come into being, will not exist by its own nature once it has undergone a change of state through transformation. (12)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus to him, the god, laughing and looking on, that yogi of exceeding splendor suddenly vanished from sight. 13.
When that Great God had departed, your grandfather Śakti, having reflected upon those words, thought, "It is even so. (14)
Then, after a very long time had passed in that auspicious place,
he became radiant like fire through his great ascetic penance.
O one of great wisdom, the king Kalmāṣapāda, his mind having been stolen by a Rākṣasa, became enraged and devoured the sage Ṛṣyaśṛṅga while Adṛśyantī was carrying her excellent embryo. (16)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
Why did that king devour that sage who was endowed with ascetic power?
And for what reason was the king’s mind carried away by the Rākṣasa? ||1||
There was a powerful king named Mitrasaha, for whom Vasiṣṭha acted as priest.
His son was Saudāsa, who possessed a splendor equal to that of Indra and the moon.
Śakti approached him and said, "Having been initiated, I shall observe my vow."

Therefore, O King of kings, grant to me, who have always been a flesh-eater, that which I have come here for: pure food, endowed with all excellent qualities, possessed of great luster, and intended for me alone in solitude. (3–4)
When he had said, "So be it," that high-minded one departed;
then, at that moment, the Rākṣasa vanished from the sight of the king.
O best of sages, he had the cook inform him of that for his sake;
then, O dear one, when the day had passed, that self-controlled lord of men, remembering it,
summoned the cook and spoke to him like one in distress.
Saudāsa said:
"O Mṛtavaśas, I have promised the wise son of my preceptor that his flesh, prepared as food, shall be provided by me this morning at night. (7)
"Therefore, act so that it may be done quickly, lest time should not cease.
Thus addressed, the cook Mṛtavasu then spoke.
O King, O bull among men, you did not tell me before;
at present, there is not even a small amount of flesh that you desire. (9)
By the gift of even a small amount of flesh to many kings, and by the bestowing of nectar, nothing at all remains [of that merit]. || 8.17.10 ||
The king said:
"I know your every purpose, and I know your wicked deed;
I know that the meat was but a small amount, and that this task was of such a nature."
"Quickly seek out some flesh wherever you think the hunter is."
Sanatkumāra said:
While searching for meat with great effort, he did not find any at all;
when he had not obtained any flesh, he then spoke to the lord of men.
"I am one who has been pierced by the arrow of desire; tell me, what may I do for you? (1.2)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus by the cook at that time, O lord of men, the king said nothing to that cook; he became despondent.
Having found this opportunity, a Rākṣasa named Rudhira, incited by Viśvāmitra, entered the king.
Then, he was possessed by that evil-minded Rākṣasa, Rudhira.
The one of great splendor spoke softly into the ear of the cook.
"Go, and having brought some human flesh—
whether from a donkey or even a camel— you should quickly prepare it.
Furthermore, will he recognize that it has been prepared by you during the night?"
"Bring it quickly, for it possesses both flavor and fragrance. || 17 ||
Sanatkumāra said: Having been thus addressed by him, O Vyāsa, the cook then took human flesh from a certain remaining person who had offended the king.
Then, at the hour of midnight, he beheld that best of sages, whose splendor was like the form of the sun and whose brilliance equaled a blazing fire;
he honored him with water for the hands, water for the feet, and the most excellent seat.
Having honored him according to the prescribed rite, he should then present food to him.
Having touched that food which had been brought to him, the great ascetic became enraged; and as if laughing, he agitated the king.
Śakti said:
"O lowest of kings, the feeding of Brahmins is not fit for Rākṣasas;
it is not given by one who knows the ritual rules, yet you treat me with contempt. (22)
"Since you wish to give this Rākṣasa as food to me, therefore, by this very act, you shall become a man-eater. (23)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed in this manner, that radiant king then reflected upon it;
with his eyes red with anger and his mind possessed by a Rākṣasa, he spoke.
"Since you have addressed me thus, 'Become a man-eater,' therefore, O twice-born one, I shall devour you along with your brothers. (25)
Having consumed [the flesh] for the sake of purification, I shall thereafter be freed from the curse;
then, having restrained my senses, I will practice pure austerity. Permitted by your father, I shall dwell in heaven as long as I desire. (26)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, "The Curse of Kalmāṣapāda," in the Ambikākhaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa, within the collection of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that king, having abandoned his own kingdom along with his wife...
He entered the forest; there dwelt a man-eater of great strength. ||1||
Then, right there in front of him, Śakti, the great sage, destroyed the splendor [of Viśvāmitra].
Then, even as Vasiṣṭha looked on, he destroyed his hundred brothers.
Thereafter, having witnessed that terrible slaughter of his sons, the powerful son of Brahmā [Viśvāmitra]—
Vasiṣṭha did not, therefore, release his anger toward Kauśika.
He was tormented exceedingly by the great grief for his son;
that powerful son of Brahmā tied a large stone around his neck.
She cast herself into the river to dwell there for a hundred nights;
thus do the sages of celebrated vows call her.
Then, having bound her firmly with nooses once more, the self-controlled one released her into another [river].
In her, Vipāśa was conceived; from that, she became known as Vipāśā.
Then, having approached the pond, fasting and with senses conquered,
he remained there subsisting on air alone, causing his own body to wither.
Then he heard the melodious sound of someone departing while reciting; thereupon, he applied himself once more to meditation. ||8||
Then his wife, whose every limb was beautiful, with full and elevated breasts, and with a dejected face and downcast eyes, approached him standing before Śakti.
He said to her, "From where do you come, and to whom does this sound belong?
She then spoke with a piteous voice, saying, "I heard it from those who were speaking. (8.18.10)
Adṛśyantī said: "O Guru, from the very moment you departed from this hermitage due to grief for your son,
I have been devoted to you, O Blessed One."
O Lord, this sound of your grandson studying has been heard by me even while he was still within your womb; therefore, do not give way to unbearable sorrow.
Sanatkumāra said:
"O child, I now have hope for my life," he said.
And he said to him: "O evil-souled one, I would burn you along with your kinsmen!
But what use is it to me that you are burned? Go, you are released, O wicked-minded one!
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that released rakshasa, a doer of cruel deeds, being dejected in spirit and terrified, suddenly bowed down and went into the presence of Kaushika.
When the night-stalker had departed, the king, bowing his head to the sage, [remained there].
He then propitiated him, and he spoke these meaningful words.
O Indra among kings, there is indeed no fault on your part for being possessed by a Rākṣasa;
rather, it was by him that your sons were brought about, and the Rākṣasa was merely the instrumental cause therein.
"Rule over this beloved kingdom of your father and grandfather, O Indra among kings!
Tell me, O bull among men, what dear service may I perform for you today?
The king said:
"I desire, O Blessed One, a son begotten by you, O Acyuta, upon this queen—a great being. Therefore, do what is pleasing to me.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having said, "So be it," O observer of great vows, he begot upon his wife a son of great renown named Loṣṭaka. Then,
having consecrated that son Loṣṭaka upon the throne, he—
Then, together with his wife, he went to the forest and remained there devoted to asceticism. ||24||
In time, Vasiṣṭha’s son Śakti had a powerful son by Adṛśyantī; he was indeed your son named Parāśara. (25)
Then the wise one regarded Vasiṣṭha as his very father; and he repeatedly addressed his father and preceptor, saying, "Father! Father! (26)
Then, at one time, having learned that his father had been devoured by a Rākṣasa, he then performed a rite for protection against Rākṣasas through asceticism and mantras.
Thereupon, fifty-five crores of Rākṣasas of cruel deeds [were summoned].
The one of great splendor offered [the oblation] into the fire; then Brahmā arrived swiftly. ||28||
Having approached and honored him along with Vasiṣṭha, the Lord,
together with the sages and the deities, spoke this to Parāśara.
Brahmā said:
They gratified the deities with sacrifices preceded by mantras;
for this is indeed the eighth station of the gods—do not you be such [as to lose it].
Parāśara said:
Together with the gods, I shall consume all the worlds with fires;
having burnt them, I shall spread forth other worlds there—of this there is no doubt.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those haughty words of his, the divine Grandfather spoke these words to him,
consoling him with gentle speech.
The Grandfather said:
"O great sage, what you have done is exactly as you say; there is no doubt about it.
All of this must be forgiven by me out of a desire to do what is pleasing to you."
"O highly fortunate one, those by whom my father and his brother were suddenly devoured—
let them alone be offered as oblations into the fire while Viśvāmitra looks on.
May there be well-being for all others everywhere, including the gods together with the Rākṣasas."
Satisfied by his resolve, he uttered this meaningful and exalted speech: ||3.5||
"O illustrious one, restrain the grandson of Vasiṣṭha.
Then all the gods, with palms joined in reverence, bowed down to that great sage. (36)
And that sage, filled with wrath and endowed with the power of asceticism and yoga,
having split open the blazing fire through the application of his penance,
[spoke]. Sanatkumāra said:
Then the gods, together with the gandharvas and preceded by the Grandfather (Brahmā),
having recognized his power, worshipped Parāśara. And when those most wicked-minded rākṣasas had been slain, [the gods continued their worship].
Then, with the constant approval of Brahmā, he brought the sacrificial session to a close.
Sanatkumāra said:
"Whoever, having become pure, causes this to be heard by the twice-born at the time of a śrāddha or during a rite for the gods, the rākṣasas do not harm him."
Having heard this account of Parāśara— which originates from one of undaunted birth, arises from the performance of pure speech and action,
and brings about the spiritual success of the lineage— they departed.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Sacrifice to the Rākṣasas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
"O Vyāsa, in this manner your father performed the Rākṣasa-sacrifice;
and having completed it, he again quickly engaged himself in ascetic penance."
Vasiṣṭha, the imperishable one, having approached him who was radiant as the sun through his ascetic power, spoke these meaningful words with great affection.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Desiring sons, the Pitṛs indeed performed extremely difficult austerities and produced a son endowed with ascetic power and knowledge.
Those who know the Vedas understand that he who possesses a disciplined lineage, who is endowed with knowledge and asceticism, shall by effort attain the divine state. 4.
O Lord, though endowed with immediate ascetic power, possessed of knowledge, and graced with fame,
he was the best among those who have sons, yet he was deprived of offspring.
Therefore, O best of those who observe vows, go to discharge your debt to the ancestors;
procreate a son quickly, and do so equally with Bhāvanā.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha,
that radiant one reached Mount Maināka and performed a most difficult penance.
After a long time, when he had been purified by his ascetic penance, the Lord of Umā granted him a boon; and he chose as his boon a son.
Having obtained the boon, he returned and searched for a perfectly pure field where his son might be born. (9)
Wandering about, he then beheld Kālī, the daughter of the king of the fishermen, who had attained the status of his own daughter and possessed a divine form.
In ancient times, he begot upon Adrikā— the most excellent of Apsarases, born from the womb of a fish, arisen from the seed of a fish, auspicious, and composed of Brahmanic splendor—
that great ascetic, having first granted her a boon.
[He was born] from you, the source of austerities and the promoter of the Śrauta and Smārta rites.
Your son was Śuka, the best among the knowers of the Vedas;
he had four sons and one daughter of slender waist.
Vyāsa said: O Brahmin, such was the supreme enmity between Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha;
I wish to know further how it came to an end. (14)
Sanatkumāra said:
While Parāśara was still in the womb and the son of Gādhi had become his enemy,
the two of them were dwelling in their own hermitage at Kurukṣetra on the banks of the Sarasvatī.
There, recollecting his enmity, the wise Viśvāmitra,
out of wrath, slew the hundred sons of Vasiṣṭha while he was engaged in ascetic observances.
The sage Viśvāmitra, full of prowess, also spoke there. ||17||
"Bring Vasiṣṭha here alone to a secluded spot, quickly, as he is bathing here in the Sarasvatī with its great current. (18)
Having been addressed thus, she went to Vasiṣṭha and spoke to him in her distress;
and Gādheya, for his part, spoke to the great river as he had been told.
"Do so, O illustrious lady; take me wherever you desire.
Let not that cruel son of Gādhi cast upon you a curse that is difficult to overcome."
Sanatkumāra said: Then, as Gādheya was offering oblations to the sun when it had reached the meridian,
that auspicious river flowed toward Vasiṣṭha with its current.
Seeing that best of sages carried away by the current, O Vyāsa, he said: "He has been forcibly snatched away by you through deceit."
Therefore, by this act, you shall become full of blood;
thus cursed by Viśvāmitra, that river which bestows happiness upon the world flowed with terrible blood,
as well as flesh and fat.
Then Triśvāmitra, having gone to the lord of the gods, said:
"O Kauśika, give me your thunderbolt;
for I shall slay Vasiṣṭha, that lowest of Brahmins, who has acted wickedly."
"O Śakra, his sons of evil mind have been slain by me;
yet even after killing them, O Lord of the Gods, there will be no peace for me."
Śakra said:
O best of beings, Vasiṣṭha and you yourself possess the knowledge of Brahman within your own selves; let these [others] partake of the Soma, and may you be released to know [the truth]. (27)
Then, O descendant of Kālī, that son of Gādhi, becoming violently enraged, forcibly cast Śakra out of his body by means of yoga.
Having entered that body of the enemy of Vṛtra, the powerful one stood there seeking a vulnerability, with his hand raised to strike with the thunderbolt.
While the sages themselves were looking on, he split that blazing fire into seven pieces with his hundred-jointed thunderbolt.
Then, having quickly gathered the fragments himself, the sage reassembled his own body and, filled with anger, spoke these words:
"Stay, O Kauśika! Now that you have been seen by me, you shall not depart."
Indeed, from Divākara, headless trunks fell by the hundreds of thousands. ||3 3||
Indeed, blood fell from the sky in profusion,
and most inauspicious winds blew, scattering the celestial chariots from the heavens.
Then there were various portents such as these, foreboding the destruction of the world: the Vedas of the Brahmins vanished, and likewise the Nagas ascended into the sky. || 35 ||
Having seen him, the gods and sages said to the son of Gādhi:
"O Vasiṣṭha of great splendor, and you, O righteous son of Gādhi,
we two are immortal, free from old age, and endowed with the power of asceticism and yoga."
For there is no destruction for you two, nor will you bring about destruction.
The two gods fought with one another for the sake of all the worlds, like two elephants in rut fighting each other in the forest. || 38 ||
Just as there is great destruction from the crushing of creepers and trees,
so too [is there destruction] from the enmity that has arisen between you two high-souled ones.
The ruin of the worlds will clearly come to pass, there is no doubt; therefore, [I shall bring about] the destruction of the worlds along with the ṛṣis. (8.19.40)
"Let there be friendship between you two, and let there be an end to enmity.
Having been addressed thus by the sages together with the deities, the son of Gādhi [Viśvāmitra]—
"Let it be so," he said to them, amazed by their splendor at that time;
then all the dwellers of heaven spoke likewise to Vasiṣṭha as well.
Thinking, "He too is just like that," he formed a friendship with him.
From that time forth, indeed, the entire world— both mobile and immobile—
rejoiced, filled with happiness and affection, free from all distress.
Sanatkumāra said: Now, in connection with the holy fords (tīrtha), the sages who had assembled there showed her favor,
by which she became possessed of clear water.
Then, after a long time,
having recognized that patience of Vasiṣṭha,
Viśvāmitra, that bull among sages and possessor of great splendor, abandoned his enmity toward Vasiṣṭha. ||46||
In this way, those two best of sages abandoned their mutual enmity.
Sanatkumāra said:
"The Brahmin who hears this, or causes the Brahmins to hear it,"
One whose human effort is unwearied crosses over difficult terrains that are otherwise most hard to traverse. || 48 ||
With beings who dwell in the magnanimity of three generations, he shall be highly exalted and possess radiant, beautiful attire;
he shall become equal to all the kings of the immortals and sport at will in Triviṣṭapa.
Thus it came to pass, O Vyāsa, between Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha.
And for the sake of the welfare of the worlds once again, this enmity has come to an end.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Averting of Hostility," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said: Now, that which the two lords of gods, Umā and Hara, performed when united together—
Tell me all of that in its entirety, O great sage.
Sanatkumāra said: Then Umā and Hara, the two blameless ones, having come together with one another,
[beheld] the son of Śilāda, the brahmin who was a restrainer of Śakti.
And that son, who was not born from a womb, having propitiated Maheśvara and attained equality with Rudra, shone as a great lord of the Gaṇas. ||4||
Vyāsa said: How was Nandin born, and how, having propitiated Śaṅkara,
did he attain equality with Śambhu as well as the office of his doorkeeper?
Sanatkumāra said:
There was a rishi named Śilāda, virtuous in soul and full of vigor. Because of his conduct and character (śīla-vṛtti), he became known as Śilāda.
The twice-born man beheld those ancestors hanging down,
having entered that terrible hell where the lineage has been severed.

Addressed by them, you, O best of the twice-born, should indeed propitiate that imperishable god, Mahādeva, who is the desire of the subjects and the lord of the world, for the sake of obtaining a son.
"He who is capable of delivering you will grant you a son.
Having heard their words, he then went for refuge to Śiva.
As he was performing austerities for a thousand years, the wielder of the trident [appeared].
Śarva, surrounded by his hosts, declared, "I am the granter of boons."
Having beheld Soma, the Lord of Gods, he prostrated at the feet of the All-pervading One and praised the Sovereign of the Devas with a voice faltering with joy. Śilāda said:
Salutation to the supreme deity, the Great Lord (Maheśa), the Great Soul;
salutation to the creator of all the lords of the gods, the husband of Brahmā. Salutation to the destroyer of the body of Kāma, the cause of the origin of Yoga.
Salutations to you who dwell upon the mountains; salutations to you who are attainable through meditation. ||13||
Salutations eternally to the Lord of the sages, salutations to the Lord of the gods;
salutations indeed to the Lord of the worlds and to the Lord of the yogins. Salutations eternally to Pradhāna, the source of creation... [to Him who brings forth].
Salutations to the giver of boons to devotees, and salutations to the omnipresent one.
Salutations to You, the Lord of the transformations of the subtle elements, the senses, and the gross elements, together with the *guṇas*; salutations to You, the sovereign and all-powerful Master.
Salutations always to the Lord of the universe and to the Creator of the universe; eternal salutations to the Lord of Prakṛti, who transcends the Puruṣa. || 17 ||
Salutations eternally to the Lord, who is attainable through yoga, who is the cause of the origin and destruction of saṃsāra, and who bestows all desires. 18.
Homage ever to the one worthy of refuge; homage to the one whose form is smeared with ashes.
Homage to you who hold the *yoga* in hand; homage to the Lord of Splendors. (19)
Salutations always and eternally to the Creator of the three worlds, who abides as the sun, wind, fire, water, moon, ether,
and earth. O Lord, your rest shall be proclaimed from another limb of this hymn.
Since you alone are the cause of the maintenance and destruction of this world,
O Lord of Gods, grant your supreme favor to me who am without refuge and seek refuge in you; be a bestower of boons, O Sustainer of the Universe.
Sanatkumāra said:

The twice-born who, being pure and observant of vows, recites this stainless hymn in the morning before the twice-born—him neither Brahma-rākṣasas, Piśācas, Sādhyas, Yakṣas, nor men, serpents, or Pūtanas shall harm. (23)
Then that Blessed Lord, being praised along with Umā, said:
"I am the giver of boons; speak what is in your heart."
Then Śilāda worshipped the god who spoke thus, and he addressed the Lord of Gods with faltering words: [25]
"O Blessed One, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me,
I desire a son equal to myself— one free from death and not born from a womb.
Having spoken thus, the three-eyed Lord was then delighted.
Having said to him, "So be it," he vanished right there.
When that great archer had departed, the highly honored sage returned to his own hermitage and then related [the events] to the sages:
"The prince, who resembles a fire that fulfills all desires, replied [as follows]."
Having seen that prince thus arisen, blazing with radiant splendor, he—
Realizing, "This is a Rākṣasa," he did not approach him out of fear;
yet the prince, though born in such a manner, approached his father of blazing splendor with a distressed soul and cried out, "Father! Father!"
When, even though addressed as "O dear one," he did not welcome that [proposal],
then Vāyu uttered a melodious sound in the sky.
Vāyu said:
O Sālāṅkāyanī, this son of yours, who was given by the god Śambhu in the past as one not born from a womb—he is here; rejoice in him!
"O best of the twice-born, because this theft was committed by Nandikara,
your son shall therefore be known by the name Nandin.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, at the word of Vāyu, he embraced Nandin;
taking him by the hand, he led him to his own hermitage, which increased his joy.
He performed for him the rites beginning with the tonsure and the vow;
and having done so, he taught him the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches in their entirety.
He also mastered Ayurveda, Gāndharvaveda, the Dharmaśāstra with its defining characteristics,
the behavior of elephants, and the discovery of the nine treasures.
All the arts, as well as the knowledge of omens, the medical treatment of the host of spirits, and whatever constitutes the conduct of the Mothers; ||38||
And whatever movement there is of all the serpents, and whatever exists among the collections of scriptures and the eight grammars; ||3.9||
Likewise, one should study the Purāṇas and the Itihāsas in their entirety,
as well as the five points that pertain to the investigation of the hosts of luminaries.
The Mātṛbhūtagraha-tantra is considered the supreme teaching for yogins;
Vyāsa then studied it all in fifteen years.
He was skillful, pure, undepressed in spirit, pleasant of speech, free from envy,
always beloved by all the world, and a delight to the eyes of many.
Then, in his seventh year, two sages, gods whose wealth was their asceticism—
Having reached the hermitage, the two of them, whose vigor remained unimpaired, [approached] Śilāda.
Having honored them according to the prescribed rule, Śilāda, a man of great asceticism,
bowed down to those two who were seated comfortably and highly revered upon their seats.
Those two named Mitra and Varuṇa, endowed with the power of austerity and yoga,
were cognizant of all beings in the three worlds, including the mobile and the immobile.
Supported by them, he too sat down upon an excellent seat.
The virtuous and steadfast one, who increases his family lineage, spoke properly;
and being well-pleased, he called his son Nandin.
He prostrated with his head at the feet of those two blameless ones;
then those two divine beings bestowed upon him their blessing for eternal devotion to the service of his elders and for imperishable worlds.
Sanatkumāra said: Then Śilāda, having received the blessing of the two gods and having dismissed Nandin, being afraid, questioned those two best of sages.
Śilāda said:
"O best of sages, for what reason did you both fail to bestow a blessing of long life upon my son, who is so blessed?"
Mitra and Varuṇa said:
"O dear one, this son of yours is universally esteemed, yet he has a very short lifespan;
he shall indeed sustain his life for only one more year beyond this. (51)
Sanatkumāra said: Then, tormented by grief and distressed by the calamity concerning his offspring,
he dismissed those two tigers among sages and lamented alone.
Hearing the sound of him lamenting out of grief,
his son Nandi came there and saw his father thus exceedingly distressed.
Nandi said:
"O father, by what sorrow are you so tormented that you weep?
From where has this grief arisen? O father, I wish to know. (54)
Śilāda said:
"My son, why would you abandon your life for the sake of a boon?
The two sages spoke thus, and then they entered me. (55)
Nandi said:
"It is true, O dear one, that the divine sages did not speak a falsehood;
nevertheless, death shall have no power over me, so do not grieve. (56)
Śilāda said:
"What is your austerity, what is your knowledge, what is your yoga, and what is your exertion, by which you will evade such terrible death, my dear son? (57)
Nandi said:
"O father, I shall not evade death through asceticism nor through knowledge;
by the grace of Mahādeva alone shall I conquer death, and not otherwise. (58)
I shall behold the god Śaṅkara; thereafter, death shall not be mine.
Death being destroyed, I shall dwell for a long time with you in peace and contentment. ||59||
Śilāda said:
"In the past, after performing extremely difficult austerities for a thousand years,
Mahādeva was seen by me, since you were obtained as my son."
How does one behold Mahādeva? This is what I wish to know.
Nandin said:
"The Lord is not seen through austerity, nor is he seen through knowledge;
the Supreme Lord is seen only by means of the mind. (61)
"I know this by which I shall see Śaṅkara;
sent by you, I shall go and behold the Three-eyed One before long, O father—of this there is no doubt. Therefore, release me quickly."
"In a very short time, you shall see me freed from the suffering of death and having accomplished my purpose; therefore, release me—whether I am standing, lying down, running, or even fallen. (63–64)
"Do not wait, thinking 'Death shall come for me later'; realizing this, attain tranquility.
Even if thousands of Deaths and hundreds of millions of Yamas were to rush at you, tormented and with clubs, nooses, and raised weapons," (65)
Nevertheless, they are never capable of causing you any distress.
"Indeed, these will not cause me even a hair's breadth of distress.
Having descended into the divine water and assumed a state of pure being,
and having practiced the Raudra chapter, I shall then behold Śaṅkara."
For me, who am engaged in recitation, devoted to Rudra, and absorbed in his nature, the many [omens] of death and time shall cause no affliction. ||68||
Sanatkumāra said:
Perceiving him speaking thus with a pure intellect,
the great ascetic, whose soul was undepressed, dismissed his son with fortitude.
Having saluted his father’s feet with his head, that highly illustrious one,
having performed a circumambulation, set forth with firm resolve.
Having paid homage to all the sages, that noble-minded one, desiring to behold Śiva— the remover of the distress of those who bow before him— became a sage with a mind fixed on the Divine.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "Nandin’s Entry into Austerity," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Nandin departed from there and went to the best of rivers,
renowned as Bhuvanā, which brings welfare to all the worlds.
Having entered it, the wise and radiant one remained there with one-pointed concentration; then, fearing death, he recited the Rudra-mantra with a composed mind.
While he was reciting there with single-minded devotion, by virtue of that blessing,
when one crore had been recited, the God was indeed pleased.
Sanatkumāra said: Having descended from there once more, with his self likewise restrained,
he recited another ten million [mantras], meditating solely upon Rudra.
Then, when the second crore [of years] had elapsed, the bull-bannered Lord approached him and said, "I am the giver of boons. ||5||
He said: "O Blessed One, O Lord of Gods, O All-pervading One, by your grace I desire to recite ten million plus one more [times]. (6)
"So be it," the Blessed One replied once more;
then the high-minded one went to his own abode together with the Goddess.
Then he recited another ten million Rudra-mantras;
thereupon, O twice-born one, he became like the sun at the end of an eon.
O Vyāsa, when his three peaks were completed, the god Soma, possessing a blazing luster, approached that place together with his attendants.
Taking him by the hand, he drew him from that water of his conduct and,
touching Nandin with his own hand, Kālahasta said:
The God of gods said:
"O Śailāda, I am the granter of boons to you, gratified by this penance.
Well recited by you, O wise one; tell me what is in your heart. (11)
Śailādi said:
"By your power, O Lord, I shall indeed chant another ten million [times] once more. O All-pervading One, if you are pleased with me, O God, I choose this boon. (12)
The Blessed One said to Śailāda: "O son of Ambikā, I am pleased with you.
Whatever desire you choose today, I shall grant it all to you. (13)
"Shall I become Brahmā, or Viṣṇu, or Indra, or yet another? Shall I become an Āditya or a Rudra? Tell me, what shall I do for you? (14)
Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus by the God, he bowed his head at His feet and praised the destroyer of the cities, desires, limbs, sacrifices, and mountains.
Salutations to the God of gods, to Mahādeva;
salutations indeed to the destroyer of the body of Kāma, to Nīlakaṇṭha.
Salutations to the destroyer of the Tuṣita heaven, and to the subduer of the three worlds.
Salutations to the one with the staff at the end of time; salutations indeed to the one with the fierce staff.
Salutations to the one whose hands and feet are everywhere, and whose eyes and faces are everywhere;
and to the one who exists pervading everything, being the source of all.
Salutations to you who are gold-hued and likewise beyond the senses;
salutations to the golden-liṅga, and indeed salutations to the universal liṅga.
Salutations to him whose color is like the moon and the sun, the Lord of Yoga, the unconquered.
And to the one who holds the Pināka bow in his hand, and to the one who holds the trident and mallet in his hand.
Salutations indeed to the one who carries a quiver, to the one who wields a sword, and to the bearer of the battle-axe;
salutations to the chariot-warrior, to the one clad in armor, and to the Great Lord. Salutations to the one with the trident in hand, and to the wielder of the fierce staff.
Homage to the Lord of the Gaṇas; homage to the Lord of the Rudras. Homage to the thousand-eyed one; indeed, homage to the hundred-eyed one.
Homage to the Lord of the Ādityas; homage to the Lord of the Vasus.
Salutations to the Lord of the Earth, salutations to the Lord of the Sky;
salutations to the Lord of the heavenly world, salutations to the Lord of Umā.
Salutations to him who is attainable through yoga and the bestower of all yoga.
To the one meditated upon by those in meditation, and who is praised by those in meditation. || 25 ||
To Death, to the Wielder of the Staff of Time, to the Great-Souled Yama, to the Lord of the Gods, and to Him of Divine Constitution; ||26||
To the one who bestows wealth for the sake of sacrifice, who grants heaven and victory;
to Savitṛ, the source of all the gods, to Dharma, who possesses manifold forms;
to the immortal, the most excellent, who is praised by all the gods.
To the one who severed the head of Brahmā and of the great-souled Sacrifice;
to the fierce destroyer of Tripura and the remover of all inauspiciousness;
to the one whose form consists of half the body of Umā and who has an eye in his forehead.
To the husband of Mahiṣa and Andhaka, to the Supreme Seer,
to Brahmā, to the Teacher, to the Brahman, and to the progenitor;
to the teacher of Kumāra and to the bestower of boons upon Kumāra.
Salutation indeed to Halin, to Muśalaghna, and to Mahāhāsa. || 31 ||
To him who holds the noose of death in his hand, who wears Takṣaka as his sacred thread;
who is accompanied by lightning, clouds, and wind, and likewise rides upon a bull;
who dwells in the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, and resides on the summit of Mount Meru.
To the dweller of Kailāsa, the friend of the Lord of Wealth;
to him to whom half of Viṣṇu’s body was given, and who is the granter of boons to him;
to the one who is the sacrifice for all beings and who has compassion for all beings.
Salutations to you who have the primary elements as your internal constituent, who bestows life upon living beings, who are the object of thought, and who are indeed the conceit itself;
salutations to the one being awakened, to that which is to be awakened, to the seer, and to the eye.
Salutations to the toucher and likewise to the sense of taste;

salutations to the sense of smell and to the smeller, and indeed to the sense of hearing and to the hearer; salutations to the holder of the hand and to the hand, and likewise to the foot and to the one who possesses feet.
Homage to you, the creator of bliss, and homage to you, bliss itself; homage to the speaker and to the one who possesses speech, to the Great Soul who consists of those subtle elements;
homage to the subtle, to the gross, and to the qualities of sattva and rajas.
Salutations always to Tapa, and to the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña), the unconquered;
salutations to Viṣṇu, the creator of the worlds, and to the Lord of creatures;
salutations to the Seven Seers (Saptarṣi) who are performing austerities and who are themselves ascetics.
And salutations to the one devoted to Brahman, likewise to Durvāsas;
to the artisan, the lord of artisans, the wise Viśvakarman. ||41||
Salutations to you, O Atri, Bhṛgu, and Vasiṣṭha;
salutations to the Being, the Lord of Beings, and to the Master. ||42||
He stands and he moves, he sings and he even dances; to the one who is beyond necessity, beyond destruction, ageless, and immortal. (43)
To the one who is imperishable and yet the very dissolution [of all], likewise unobstructed;
to the one who cannot be entered by anyone, whose nature consists of both the visible and the invisible. ||44||
Salutations to you, O Blessed One, the subtlest among the subtle; salutations to you, O Blessed One, the Great Self, the Lord of all, the three-eyed Śiva. 45.
Salutations to you, Lord of all worlds; salutations to you, Creator of the world.
Neither through lordship over the gods nor even through the state of Brahmā do I [desire this]. (46)
"O Lord of Gods, not as Viṣṇu, nor as Indra, O Protector of Beings;
O Īśāna, I desire from you an eternal and imperishable state as a Gaṇa.
May I always behold you, gracious, together with your Gaṇas, Ambā, and your retinue."
"I wish to see him, O Lord of Gods; let this boon be granted to me. ||48||
O Lord, having previously granted me a state of existence, you have now again caused it to revolve;
O Protector, you alone are my refuge, for I never behold any other. (49)
And for one abandoned by you, swift destruction is certain; there is no doubt in this matter.
I see no other auspicious refuge for him than you, O Antaka.
"O Lord, accept me who am devoted, faithful, intent upon you, and reliant upon you; let this be the boon granted to me forever. (51)
Sanatkumāra said: That man who, rising early in the morning, recites this with an undistracted mind, shall,
upon the dissolution of the body, become equal to Nandīśvara.
Whoever should constantly hear this or cause it to be heard among the twice-born, having obtained the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice, is glorified in the world of Rudra. ||53||
O Vyāsa, having heard this sin-destroying hymn even once, wherever one may die, one shall not fall into an evil rebirth. He who,
with a self-controlled mind, constantly studies this supreme hymn and always worships the God...
What need has he for various sacrifices, gifts, pilgrimages, or likewise for well-performed austerities? || 55 ||
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the Lord of the Gods of gods [spoke] to him who was endowed with supreme devotion.
With eyes filled with tears, dejected, he bowed his head at [his] feet. || 1 ||
Taking him up with her two most pleasant hands,
that woman of supreme majesty raised him and wiped the eyes of Soma, which were filled with tears.
Then the Lord, his soul gratified, spoke to him as if nourishing him with his speech,
while looking upon all the leaders of the Gaṇas together with the Goddess.
The God of gods said:
"O sinless one, I know your devotion to me, and I know your distress.
O Śailāda, listen now to the future outcome of all this."
Immortal, abandoned by old age, eternally free from suffering, inexhaustible and indeed imperishable—such shall he be, together with his father and his circle of friends. (5)
Gaṇapa is indeed dear to me; he possesses my own vigor and my own prowess.
He is always dear to me and is ever by my side.
"You shall possess my very form and be endowed with the power of great yoga;
your island shall be possessed of supernatural powers and the Ocean of Milk, the source of nectar.
I grant you a dwelling there, and you shall always take delight therein."
Then, having removed from himself a garland made of lotuses, ||| 8 ||
The one of great splendor fastened that divine garland upon Nandin;
with that garland suspended around his neck, Nandin shone resplendent. || 9 ||
Three-eyed, ten-armed, and glorious, like a second Śaṅkara, the Blessed Lord Hara then took [him] by the hand with his own hand and said:
"Speak; what supreme boon shall I grant you today?"
And this hermitage has been thoroughly sanctified by your asceticism.
Known as Japyeśvara, he shall become my secret [shrine];
the sacred field extending for a yojana in every direction shall be divine and surrounded by hosts of gods.
Crowded with Siddhas and Cāraṇas and frequented by hosts of Apsarases,
this supreme secret field of spiritual attainment will undoubtedly become such.
Whatever a person performs by deed, thought, or word—
Whatever is auspicious or inauspicious here, all that shall become auspicious for one who possesses it. || 14 ||
When it is recited as a mantra, it will indeed be equal to the Rudras;
mortals who die anywhere shall go to your same world.
Then, taking water drenched with matted locks, pure as a pearl necklace—
Having said, "Become a river," the one of great asceticism released her.
Then that auspicious river, possessing divine waters and water like jewels, was holy and beautiful;
it was crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks and graced by *cakravāka* birds.
A great river, filled with groves of lotuses and water-lilies, flowed from the mountain;
assuming a female form, she stood before the god with her hands joined in reverence and her head bowed low,
her eyes possessing the luster of blooming lotus petals.
Then the God spoke to that river who had herself approached him.
"O Goddess of auspicious countenance, since you have issued forth from the matted locks and the water,
you shall therefore be known by the name Jaṭodā, the best of rivers. And whoever, being pure and with a restrained mind, performs a bath in you— "
Having obtained the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha), he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Sanatkumāra said: Then [the Lord showed] Nandīśvara, who possessed exceeding luster, to the Goddess...
Saying, "This is the theft of a son," he caused him to bow down at his feet.
Having smelled him on the head and stroking him with both hands, she drenched him out of maternal love with the three streams flowing from her breasts. 23.
As the goddess gazed upon the god with her milk, white as a conch shell,
those three streams of hers flowed forth as the river Oghavatī.
Then Hara spoke to that auspicious river Trisrotasī;
seeing the river Trisrotasī, O bull among sages, he was exceedingly delighted.
He let out a roar, and from that sound another river came into being.
Because that great river originated from the bellowing of the Bull (Vṛṣabha). || 26 ||
Therefore, the bull-bannered god spoke to Ḍhitkirikā; the deity then bound upon him a wonderful crown made of gold, most marvelous,
and earrings born of nectar.

Seeing him thus honored in the sky, the cloud Prabhākara— the vehicle of the gods— rained down, accompanied by thunder and flashes of lightning. As he was being consecrated, two streams then flowed forth in abundance.
