the Sandhyās and the Saptaricas, as well as all rivers and lakes;
and the seven oceans—all the divine tīrthas are present here in their entirety. ||88||
They shall go to the Bhāgīrathī at Kāśī on all festival days. ||89||
O daughter of the Mountain, know me as Avimukteśvara residing in Kāśī,
as well as all the meritorious shrines upon the earth that belong to me.
They always enter, arriving on every auspicious festival day,
at the Liṅga in Kedāra, the Liṅga in Mahālaya,
the one situated at Madhyameśvara, and likewise Paśupatīśvara. ||91||
Śaṅkukarṇeśvara, and likewise both Gokarṇeśas;
Drimi-caṇḍeśvara, Bhadreśvara, and Īśvara;
Sthāneśvara, Ekāmra, Kāleśvara, and Ajeśvara. ||92–93||
Bhairaveśvara, Īśāna, and likewise him who resides at Kārohaṇa—
whatever other meritorious places there are on my earth,
all of them without exception enter me in the city of Kāśī.
This secret has been proclaimed for all meritorious festivals;
by it, even for a dying creature, the immortal state is attained here, O auspicious lady, through my being seen after one has bathed in the Gaṅgā. ||95-96||
One immediately attains what is equal to the fruits of all sacrifices performed hundreds of thousands of times; indeed, what could be more excellent than this? (97)
"O Goddess, among all the foremost sanctuaries in heaven, on earth, and even in the mountains, know for certain that there is nothing superior to this in its entirety. (9.8)
This supreme place is eternally frequented by Brahmā, Arka, Vaiśvānara, Śakra, Candra, Varuṇa, Kubera, and Vāyu, together with the hosts of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Siddhas. ||99||
O Daughter of the Snowy Mountain, this place of mine is always secret; this field is exceedingly meritorious.
Indeed, ascetics who have awakened to reality resort to it, for it bestows the fruit of accomplishment free from sorrow. (8.29.100)
Those virtuous men who dwell in this field,

who always behold me with reverence day after day, being pure, bathed, and ever devoted to me— they, being mortal, are freed from fear, sin, and suffering, their ritual actions being perfectly purified.
Having pierced through the dense thicket of the web of bonds of worldly existence, they attain supreme liberation.
Thus it is: this sacred field, most secret to me, is filled with gods, crowded with various trees and creepers, and adorned by the Ganges;
having reached the Bhāgīrathī here in Vārāṇasī, my own abode.
Having attained the merit of a hundred horse-sacrifices, he goes to the world of Brahmā.
O Goddess, there is nothing more meritorious than this, nothing more secret anywhere,
nothing more auspicious than this, and nothing dearer to me than this.
Having reached this field of mine, frequented by gods and Siddhas, a mortal [attains success] through the power of his good deeds.
He shall become renowned among all gods and asuras, and upon death, he shall go to that supreme state.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the Lord [established] gardens as well as places for himself.
Having thus spoken to the daughter of Himavat, he then moved on once more.
Then he beheld the Brahmin Jaigīṣavya, whose wealth was his asceticism,
the son of Śataśalāka, performing supreme penance;
he had established the *liṅga* of the God of gods and was constantly worshipping it.
Lying upon ashes and smeared with ashes, he delighted [him] with dances and songs.
Purified by recitation, by the sounds of the *vṛṣaṇa* drum, and by austerity, he was pure;
and as he lived in this manner, endowed with supreme devotion— ||4||
The Blessed One, having approached suddenly, spoke these words:
"O Jaigīṣavya of great intelligence, behold me with your divine eye. (5)
"I am pleased and I am the giver of boons; speak what is in your heart.
Thus addressed by the God, he beheld the three-eyed Soma, and bowing his head at His feet, spoke with supreme joy.

Jaigīṣavya said: Salutations to the one who has accomplished all aims; salutations indeed to the one perfected in yoga. Salutations to the one who holds the Pināka bow in hand, and to the one whose abode is the Himavat mountain.
Homage to him who possesses the speed of the wind, who is always to be meditated upon by those engaged in meditation;
homage to Soma, to Hema, and to the wearer of the golden garland.
Homage to the Lord of the Gaṇas, and homage to him whose senses are tranquil;
to the one who provides assistance in yoga, and to the one who brings about immediate peace. ||9||
Homage to the remover of death, and homage to the remover of grief;
homage to the bestower of success, and to the perfected one who grants success.
Homage to the sustainer of all worlds and the lord of all worlds;
homage to the one of fivefold color and the dispeller of saṃsāra.
Homage to the one who has reached the further shore of saṃsāra and the supreme beyond the shoreless.
Salutations indeed to you yourself, who are both the mantra and the mind, difficult to comprehend.
Homage to the knower of the divisions of time, and to the one who possesses all parts;
homage to the one who dwells within the principles, and homage to the Lord of the Pretas. 13.
Homage to the one free from anger, homage to the Lord of Anger;
homage to weariness, to the weary one, and to the remover of weariness. Homage to the knower of the essence of knowledge, to the wise one, and to the one who bestows knowledge.
To one who is attached to asceticism and to one who is devoted to sovereign power.
Homage to him who is followed by wisdom, who turns back ignorance;
homage to him who possesses all-pervasive power, whose mind conforms to all states of being. || 1.6 ||
Salutations to the one whose path is self-restraint and tranquility, who removes the messengers of death;
salutations to the Lord of Śailādi and to the protector of the hosts of Śailādi. ||17||
Homage to the secret of yoga, homage again and again to the giver of yoga!
O Blessed Lord, Master, grant me all my desires with your whole being.
Sanatkumāra said:
Being thus praised with supreme devotion,
he was pleased and, being further gratified, spoke these words to him.
The God of Gods said:
He is indeed ageless and immortal, entirely free from all sorrow;
he is a great yogi of great heroism, endowed with the sovereign power of yoga.
And by the power of this secret field of mine, which is eternal, you shall attain the supreme and great sovereignty consisting of the eight qualities of yoga. ||21||
"O best of the twice-born, you shall become a renowned teacher of Yoga (yogācārya).
And whoever shall worship this *liṅga* fashioned by you according to the rule,
having passed through seven births, shall attain the state of a Lord of Yoga."
O Jaigīṣavya, that twice-born man who, having reached this cave,
applies himself with a disciplined mind for seven nights, is liberated from all sins;
within a month, he shall know his former birth and what he previously studied.

By staying for one night, one purifies one's own destiny and delivers one's ancestors; by staying for three nights, one delivers even those who have passed away seven generations back. Beyond this, what more shall I give you today, Jaigīṣavya?
Jaigīṣavya said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, this desire residing in my mind is what I wish for;
therefore, I desire nothing other than that which is superior to the imperishable yoga. (26)
May you possess constant devotion toward Soma, the lord of the Gaṇas;
likewise, may you have freedom from pride, as well as patience, tranquility, and self-control.
Furthermore, do not commit any act of humiliation, nor show contempt for his splendor.
"O God of great splendor, I always desire these boons.
The God of gods said:
"These shall be yours, as well as invincibility against yogins."
And if you so desire, you shall indeed have a vision of me. ||29||
Sanatkumāra said: Then that blessed Lord, the son of Parāśara, together with Umā,
Sananda, and his attendants, [arrived] out of a desire to bestow grace upon his devotees.
While the Yakṣa king was performing his austerities with Maheśvara held in his heart,
the Lord of Gods then went before him to grant a boon.
Then he beheld the son of Visravas, who had three feet and short arms, thighs, and feet, performing severe austerities.
Having seen him, O Vyāsa, the god then spoke to Kubera, who was radiant with splendor,
purified by asceticism, and reduced to mere skin and bone.
The God of gods said:
"O son of Viśravas, I grant you divine vision.
O great being, behold Soma and me with your divine eye."
Then, having seen the Lord of Gods accompanied by Ambā and preceded by Nandin, he prostrated himself; being utterly exhausted, he was unable to rise up.
Observing him to be weak and incapable of rising, the Lord—
He said, "Arise! May it be well with you; may your ancient strength return to you. (36)
Then, rising up, Kubera stood on his knees, remaining there while gazing at the goddess with a sidelong glance from his eye. ||37||
This is that daughter of the mountain, honored by all the worlds;
she is the mother of these three worlds, endowed with the power of great yoga.
Oh, the vigor of her asceticism! Oh, her radiance! Oh, her strength!
She who indeed attained the status of wife to the Lord of all the worlds.
Sanatkumāra said:
Beholding him whose mind was thus disposed and [beholding] Pārvatī, [he spoke].
The goddess perceived this, and having perceived it, the Supreme Sovereign became enraged.
Enraged, she burned the brilliantly shining left eye of Kubera,
as a blazing flame of fire consumes a withered thicket.
Furthermore, she of auspicious countenance, whose source was asceticism, set her mind upon his destruction; then Hara spoke to her.
"Do not be angry, O Goddess, with this ascetic Yakṣa who is your devotee;
for he is illustrious and righteous, and especially so because he is devoted to you. (43)
"O auspicious one, it was out of curiosity that he gazed upon you;
O Great Goddess, show favor to this child of the Giver of Wealth.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, O Master, he gazes upon me with humility all at once;
why, O God, does he not measure my virtues while standing before me? (45)
He who, out of delusion, would attempt to leap over those whose splendor is immeasurable would perish with his strength diminished, like a moth that has flown into a fire. (46)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having thus beheld the enraged Śaṅkarī, whose eyes were copper-red with anger,
he spoke these sweet and gentle words to the daughter of the Mountain King.
I speak to you, O highly fortunate one, O gateway for the two worlds: do not be angry.
By you the entire world was created; you are primordial nature, O Sovereign of the Gods. 48.
Since this is the theft of a son, O Goddess, you ought not to be angry;
especially as you are looking upon the mother of your son, O beautiful one. (49)
There is no fault in him, nor is his mind deluded regarding you.
Therefore, O Goddess, Mistress of the Gods, show favor to this Kubera, who has sought refuge in you and bows before you, according to his desire.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by the God of gods, that daughter of the mountain king showed him favor;
being pleased, she spoke these words.
The Goddess said: "O sinless Kubera, whatever transgression you committed has been forgiven by me;
I am pleased with you. Do not again commit such an offense against one who possesses such splendor. ||52||
"But as for this eye of mine which has been burnt while you were looking on, let it remain just so—tawny and glowing. (5.3)
Marked by this [sign] in the world, you will undoubtedly become renowned by the name Ekākṣipiṅgala, honored everywhere. ||54||
"This conduct of yours, as well as this austerity, shall be imperishable and undecaying;
and through my grace, supreme good fortune shall also be yours.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus, the goddess of auspicious countenance then became silent;
thereupon the Blessed One said to Kuvera, "I am the giver of boons. Then, released by the god, Kuvera was delighted in his heart.
Bowing with his head and palms joined in reverence, he praised the God and the Goddess. ||57||
Kuvera said: Salutations to the one who holds a spear in his hand and wears an excellent crown;
salutations to the bearer of bracelets and to the bearer of the mirror.
Salutations to the one with hair on all limbs; salutations again and again to the one with long hair.
Salutations to the wearer of a girdle; and salutations to the wearer of a sacred grass belt. ||59||
Salutations to her who possesses variegated crests; salutations to the wearer of tawny matted locks.
Salutations to the embodiment of knowledge; salutations to the sovereign of all beings.
Salutations to her who bears the name Tārā; salutations indeed to the one with the chest of a lion.
Homage to her who bears the foremost jewel; homage to him whose crown is the crescent moon.
Homage indeed to Prakṛti, and homage be to Puruṣa;
homage indeed to Buddhi, and homage truly to Ahaṃkāra.
Salutations to Delight and to Bliss, salutations again and again;
salutations to the ritual act, to the action, to the undertaking, and to the completion.
Salutations to the sacrifice, to the mantra, to the sacrificial fee, and salutations to the *ṛc* verse.
Homage to the Sāman, to the Yajus, to the Chandas, and to the Stuti; homage!
Homage to Gṛhī and Vedī, to Svāhā and Havis;
homage to Lakṣmī and Śrī, and homage to Dharma and Vedhas.

Salutations to desire and to delight, salutations to him who is dispassionate toward worldly prosperity; salutations to accomplishment, as well as to nourishment, contentment, and patience—salutations again and again.
Salutations to the Svadhā offering, to the Kavya, and salutations again and again to the Havya.
Homage to the one to be known, homage to knowledge; homage to Śarva, homage to devotion. ||67||
Salutations to Kāla, to Mṛtyu, who exists for dissolution and for origination, for stability and for wandering in saṃsāra, and for liberation and for final release.
Salutations to you, O Blessed Lord, O God, Lord of the World, together with the Goddess.
"Grant us [our desires], O Lord of the past and the future, that which resides within my mind.
Sanatkumāra said:
"He who, having risen at dawn, recites this hymn daily,"
Whether he be a Brahmin, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or even a Kṣatriya, if he performs this recitation,
the Lord of Wealth (Dhaneśa), being pleased with him, bestows great wealth;
and the blessed Soma, being pleased, grants him his desired goal.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus praised by Kubera, the Lord of the World said, "I am the giver of boons; speak, O son of Viśravas. (72)
Kubera said:
"O Blessed One, may I always receive your grace and possess eternal devotion toward you;
O Lord, may this be my boon. (73)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having granted all of that with the words "So be it," the Blessed Lord Śiva then bestowed upon him eternal friendship along with his own self.
The God of gods said:
"Take this palanquin, drawn by men and free from attachment;
O Lord of the worlds, having mounted it, you shall travel to whatever worlds you desire. (75)
And take this very divine thunderbolt, characterized by its irresistible nature; let this weapon be yours, which shall be unbearable for your enemies.
And I grant you this weapon; it shall be known by your name, celebrated as the Kaubera, which deludes all embodied beings. (77)
Sanatkumāra said: Then that god, with a satisfied soul, bound upon his head his own irreproachable garland, which possessed a brilliance like the form of the sun.
The Lord of Umā, being well-pleased, indeed fastened a beautiful garland of blossoming lotuses around his neck;
having granted him a full vision of himself and the status of the Lord of Wealth.
The Blessed Lord Soma departed from there to another desired region.
Sanatkumāra said: "He who [listens] to this entire account of the granting of boons to Kubera..."
Whether he listens to it or causes others to hear it, being always composed,
that man— when he dies— is born wealthy, endowed with beauty, accompanied by sons and grandsons, and possessed of noble lineage, wisdom, and strength. || 81-82 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the highly fortunate goddess, accompanied by Śambhu, reflected upon the five-crested Apsarases who were performing penance. ||83||
With slender limbs, full of devotion, and their sins burnt away by asceticism,
their hearts drawn by compassion, they addressed these words to the God:
"Grant a supreme boon to these women who are performing penance."
"I grant your desire, O Īśāna; you should deign to permit this.
Having heard her petition, the Blessed One spoke thus:
The God of Gods said:
"Act thus, O highly fortunate one, to grant the desired favor to your devotees;
for these Vaidikī Apsarases are known as the Pañcacūḍās. (86)
"Having placed you in their hearts, they suffer; O Best One, let a boon be granted to them.
Then, thus urged by the God of Gods, Pañcacūḍā approached and spoke these words.
"I am pleased, O Apsarases; behold me directly, you of pure smiles! I grant you your desired boons, whatever resides in your hearts. (88)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus by Pārvatī, those auspicious Vaidika Apsarases, beholding the Goddess, bowed their heads at her feet and prostrated before her. (89)
With eyes full of tears and dejected, restraining themselves by their own effort,
they placed their joined palms to their heads and praised him together in unison.
The Apsarases said:
"Salutations to Siddhi, salutations to Tuṣṭi; salutations to Kriyā and to Buddhi. Salutations to Kīrti, salutations to Satya, to Ulkā, and likewise to Iṣṭi. (91)
Salutations to the auspicious Earth, to Śrī, to Lakṣmī; salutations again and again.
Salutations to Sudhā, to Svāhā, to Svadhā, and to Diti.
Salutations indeed to Taḍit, and salutations again and again to Saudāmanī.
And salutations again and again to Sāvitrī, to Gāyatrī, and to the Mother of the Vedas. || 9.3 ||
Salutation to the Daughter of the Mountain, to Intelligence, and salutation to Memory;
salutation to the Dweller on the Mountain, and repeated salutations to Rudrāṇī.
Salutation to Primordial Nature, and salutation to Moonlight and Prosperity.
Salutation to Śobhā, to Dīpti, and to the radiance of the sun and the planets; salutation to Gatyā, to Gati, to Indrāṇī, and to Muktā. Salutation to Niyati, to the river, to Gaṅgā, and to Sūti.
Salutations to the cause and to joy, salutations to the activity of the instruments;
salutations to continuity and to Irā, salutations to the activity.
Salutations again and again to Vāruṇī, to the refuge, to peace, and to beauty.
Salutations to Kauśikī; salutations again and again to Kātyāyanī.
Salutations to Sannati and salutations again and again to Mahimā. Salutations to Aṇimā; salutations again and again to Laghimā. || 98-99 ||
Salutations to you for worship, and salutations to Śitibāhu and Sṛpti;
salutations to you, O Saṃjñā, and salutations to Gīr and Smṛti.
Salutations to you, O Sarasvatī; salutations to the tongue and to vision.
Salutations to the slayer of Mahiṣa, and likewise to Śumbha and Niśumbha;
salutations to her who has a lion for a chariot, and salutations again and again to the wielder of the trident.
Salutations to the bearer of the mallet, and salutations again and again to the one clad in armor.
Salutations to the wearer of earrings, salutations to the sustainer of the world;
salutations to the bearer of the bow and salutations again and again to the wielder of the sword.
Salutations to the one who possesses a peacock-feather banner, and to Dhāriṇī, and to the wielder of the *paṭṭiśa* spear.
Homage be to Bhūtamātṛ, and salutations again and again to Skandamātṛ. And indeed, homage to the mother of Viśākha and Śākha, and to Naigameśa as well.

Salutations always to the noble one, the source of all the gods, and the deity of the forest; salutations again and again to Śikhaṇḍinī. Salutations to Nīlaśikhaṇḍinī; salutations again and again to Dīrghaveṇī.
Homage be to the slender-waisted goddess and to Wealth;
homage to Fortitude, homage to Purity, and repeated homage to Fame. 1.07.
Salutations again and again to her who bestows good fortune upon women and to Dhāriṇī; salutations again and again to Rākā, Anumati, and Sinīvālī. || 108 ||
Salutations to Action, to Faith, and salutations again and again to Intelligence; salutations be to Retention and salutations again and again to Reasoning;
salutations be to Discernment and salutations to the source of the *vaṣaṭ* call.
Homage to Samādhi and to Spṛhā; homage to Cittī.
Homage be to Vedanā; homage again and again to Bṛhadukthī. Homage to Prabhā and to Śuddhā; homage to Śuci and to Śuddhi. || 111 ||
Salutations again and again to the consort of Tryambaka and to Vidyā;
salutations again and again to Dīkṣā, to Dakṣiṇā, and to Jvālā. ||1 12||
Salutations again and again to Bhavānī, for the engagement of the senses and the cessation of karmas, for the hearing of all the Vedas, and for the sustenance of all embodied beings;
salutations to Durgā, the savior from difficulties, the upholder of all who possess bodies.
Salutations to you, O goddess of all deities; salutations to you, O source of the world's existence.
Salutation to Peace, salutation to Beauty, and salutation to the consort of Hara;
salutation to Aditi, to Dānavī, and repeated salutations to Vitānā.
Salutations to Śivā and Kartrī; salutations to Prabhāvā. Salutations to Mṛkaṇḍvī, to Mārddavāhū, and likewise to Surabhī.
Salutations again and again to Vinatā, to Lakṣmī, and to Surasā.
"Salutations to you, O blue-throated one; salutations to you always from every side. Being well-disposed toward us, grant us everything that resides within our hearts.
Sanatkumāra said:
Any man or woman who, being composed, recites this constantly, shall abandon all sin committed during the nights without exception.
And he who, O Vyāsa, being self-restrained, constantly recites it while lying down, [attains the same]. || 118 ||
He shall abandon what was done by day, and upon death, he shall go to a happy rebirth.
And whoever should constantly listen to this or always cause the twice-born to hear it, he, upon the dissolution of the body, shall become beloved of Pañcacūḍā. || 8.30.120 ||
And whatever mortal, reciting this, should give up his life-breaths so difficult to abandon, he—
completely freed from all sins— shall rejoice for ten million years in a celestial chariot brilliant as the sun and frequented by hosts of Apsarases.
And that man who, observant of the religious rules on the lunar day, worships the Goddess with supreme devotion and recites [the mantra], is liberated from all sins;
by the mere recitation and through his austerity, when the body is cast off, he who possesses devotion [attains liberation].
Having become an attendant of the Goddess, he is glorified in the holy world.
Sanatkumāra said:
Praised by those very [goddesses], the Goddess remained in the presence of the God.
With a joyful countenance, Pañcacūḍā spoke these words:
"Listen, all you Apsarases, to the great fruit of this asceticism, and also to the fact that you, O beautiful ones, have sought refuge in me with supreme devotion. (124–125)
By my command, you shall be free from old age and sorrow, forever joyful in mind, and beloved by all the world. Furthermore,
speak without hesitation whatever else resides in your hearts.
"I shall give you everything; know that, do not delay, and do not suffer distress.
Pañcacūḍās said:
"O Goddess, it is known to you that all women exist for the sake of men's purposes."
They remain our supplicants only so long as their business is not completed;
once their task is finished, they become to us like strangers. (1.28)
"Therefore, O Goddess, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to us, then,
O Great Goddess, let all men be under the control of all women.
The Goddess said:
"From this day forward, in all the worlds, may men always be under the control of all women, and may they carry out every task for them everywhere.
Both before and after [all other wealth], gold, cattle, and women [shall be theirs]."
They shall grant all enjoyments and remain entirely submissive in every way;
even while committing many various offenses,
they will always remain dear and no evil shall ever arise.
Having fallen under the sway of women, they will commit acts of violence even against their mothers, fathers, brothers, friends, and even their sons;
though they perceive their transgressions, faults, and very deformities.
"By my boon, their senses are so deluded that they do not run away from men at all.
Sanatkumāra said: Then she, the wife of the God of gods and daughter of Himavat, [spoke].
Taking up a garland of flowers, the lady of auspicious countenance,
smiling, said to her beloved, "Become a woman," O imperishable one;
and as that garland was being whirled, those parts of it which were shattered upon the ground— *13.5–6*.
Those lotus-eyed women became flowers.
He said to them: "In former times you were all free from old age and decay;
you were the enchanters of the world and the binders of the hearts of men. (137)
Having entered the three worlds through the playful manifestations of sight and touch. ||138||
...you shall make men subject to women;
and all men shall always be devoted to you. ||1 39||
By my splendor, the conduct of all women shall become auspicious—
for the sake of men’s attainment of sexual enjoyment with women, and for the sake of women’s own pleasure—
as well as their auspicious rites and purifications of the limbs, whether divine or human. (8.30.140)
Having assumed many forms, those women entered [them] at all times.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, having thus created them at that time and having dismissed them, the Goddess spoke to the Apsarases: "Tell me, what more shall I do for you?"
With delighted minds, they said, "O Vyāsa, may we indeed become the inevitable [prey] of gods, humans, and even Rākṣasas.
Then the god said to them, "In this world, you shall be so. (143)
Then the Supreme Lord, accompanied by the Goddess, Nandin,
and all his attendants, the powerful master who casts down the eyes of Bhaga and strips away the pride of the Daityas, entered his own abode. (144)
He who is a flood of lotuses, snow, and camphor; the destroyer of the fire of the sacrifice of desire;
one who travels upon clouds and bulls; the ender of all suffering; whose banner is the bull of battle; the moon-crested Lord—departed. (145)
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Bestowing of Boons upon Jaigīṣavya, Dhanada, and Pañcacūḍā," in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, within the section on the Vision of Vārāṇasī.
Vyāsa said:
"O Blessed One, by what means did Piṅgala attain the status of a Gaṇa?"
And that one of great splendor attained the status of a consumer of food in Vārāṇasī. || 1 ||
"How did Kṣetrapāla come into being, and how did he attain the state of being beloved?
O son of Brahmā, I wish to hear this explained by you.
Sanatkumāra said:
Listen, O Vyāsa, how that Piṅgala obtained the status of Gaṇeśa, the role of the provider of food for the worlds, and the city of Vārāṇasī as his abode. ||3||
The illustrious and powerful Yakṣa, the son of Pūrṇabhadra, was known as Harikeśa; he was devoted to Brahman and righteous. ||4||
From his very birth, he possessed unsurpassed devotion toward Bhava; he was intent upon His blessings, intent upon His salutation, steadfast in Him, and devoted to Him alone. ||5||
Whether sitting or lying down, walking, standing,
eating, or even drinking, he meditated only upon Rudra.
To him, whose mind was thus disciplined, his father Pūrṇabhadra spoke.
"I do not consider you my son, you who were born in such a contrary manner.
Indeed, this conduct does not belong to those of the Yakṣa lineage;
alas, you Guhyakas are by nature cruel-hearted."
"O son, why do you eat raw flesh and why are you so inclined toward violence?
Do not act thus; this is not the way of life seen among the high-souled ones.
That very mode of livelihood which was ordained by the Self-born Creator is the one praised. (9)
Harikeśa said: "Even if it were created by the Self-born One himself, a livelihood that is censured and always condemned by the virtuous must be abandoned, unless it be otherwise. (8.30.1)
Therefore, householders should not perform the duties belonging to other stages of life (āśramas).
By abandoning their human nature through various such actions,
they would lose both their divinity and their very status as humans.
"If their karma was ordained as leading to that attainment, then behold, my karma too was ordained for that same end; there is no doubt in this.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by his son, the powerful Pūrṇabhadra said:
"Go forth quickly; go wherever you please.
Then, having abandoned his home, relatives, and kin, he departed.
Having reached Vārāṇasī, he performed a very difficult penance.
Becoming like a pillar, with unblinking eyes, resembling dry wood or a stone, he remained motionless, having completely restrained the collection of his senses. 15.
Then, as he remained thus incessantly devoted to that [practice] and intent upon its blessing,
a thousand divine years passed by.
O Vyāsa, he was overrun by an anthill,
being devoured by ants with mouths like diamond needles, and pierced in the very same way.
Devoid of flesh, blood, and skin, and possessing the luster of a *kunda* flower, a conch shell, or the moon, every one of them became nothing but bone; and the god thought thus. || 18 ||
In the meantime, the Goddess requested Śaṅkara:
"I wish to see this very garden once again at all times;
indeed, I have a great curiosity to hear about the majesty of this sacred field."
Because this is dear to you, and because its fruit is supreme.
Thus addressed by Pārvatī, the Lord of the World, the God,
began to relate everything that had been asked according to the proper order.
And Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, went forth together with Pārvatī;
the divine wielder of the Pināka bow showed the garden to the Goddess.
It was beautified by various kinds of flowering shrubs in full bloom, lovely and bent down by the spreading of creepers;
it was surrounded on all sides by *priyaṅgu* trees with burgeoning flowers, and by well-flowered *ketaka* trees covered in bristling blossoms.
It was densely covered everywhere with fragrant tamāla thickets and bakula trees in full bloom,
as well as forests of aśoka and puṃnāga trees in splendid flower, their clusters of blossoms swarming with swarms of bees.
In some places, birds, dusted with the pollen of blooming lotuses, uttered their beautiful and melodious songs.
It resounded with cranes, swans, and water-fowls, and with the charming cries of intoxicated gallinules;
in some places it was made resonant by the calls of ruddy geese, in others it was joined by flocks of *kādamba* ducks;
in some places it echoed with the noise of *kāraṇḍava* birds, and in others it was filled with swarms of intoxicated bees. ||25-26||
It was frequented by female bees intoxicated with honey and adorned with lovely, fragrant flowers;
in some places it was hidden by mango trees laden with blossoms and by tilaka trees entwined with creepers.

It was inhabited by Vidyādharas and Siddhas who sang songs, accompanied by throngs of Apsarases who danced eternally; it was served by various kinds of joyful birds and resounded with the cries of intoxicated Hārīta birds. ||28||
In some places it was frequented by deer who had formed herds, their minds agitated and cowed by the roar of the king of beasts;
and in other places it was adorned with lakes and ponds filled with various kinds of beautiful, blossoming lotuses. (29)
Delightful with blue-throated peacocks hidden in the dense *nicula* reeds;
delightful with the warbling of birds intoxicated with joy;
and with intoxicated bees clinging to the branches of flowering trees.
Its branches, at their extremities, were adorned with the beauty of fresh young shoots.

In some places, the lovely creepers were bitten by elephants; in others, beautiful trees were embraced by climbing vines; and in other spots, it was frequented by the wives of the *kiṃpuruṣas*, who moved with the languid grace of amorous play.

It was resplendent with numerous celestial temples of the gods, which were as white and charming in form as beautiful peacocks, whose crests were scraped by the clouds like the warbling of pigeons; and it was illuminated by many shrines that seemed to smile with the profusion of scattered flowers. (32)
The celestial path was graced by reservoirs of water adorned with canopies of thousands of blooming blue and red lotuses;
it was filled with birds and clusters of shrubs and branches, variegated by the patterns of flowers fallen from the intervening paths. || 33 ||

It was illuminated by lovely *aśoka* trees with lofty tops, whose branch-tips were bent down by the weight of clusters of blue blossoms, producing pleasure for the ear through the songs of swarms of intoxicated bees;

at night, it attained a unity with the moonlight through its blooming *tilaka* flowers, while the tips of the *darbha* grass shoots were nibbled by herds of deer who slept, woke, stood, and moved within its shade.
Its vast waters are pure, with lotuses stirred by the wind from the wings of swans; on its banks, peacocks dance amidst groves of blossoming plantains;
in some places, the ground is colored where their moon-like tail-feathers have fallen; and in every region, flocks of intoxicated hārīta birds sport joyfully, hidden among the foliage. (35)
In some places its regions were frequented by *sāraṅga* deer; in others, it was covered with various heaps of flowers;
and in yet other places, there were groves of trees where joyful, intoxicated *kinnara* maidens sang most sweetly.
In some areas, the trees were surrounded by the dwellings of sages, where flowers were strewn about and scattered overhead.

In some places it was filled with tall, massive jackfruit trees, thick with fruit from root to crown; in others, it was delightful with the sound of golden anklets from the wives of the *siddhas*, who were hidden within bowers of flowering *atimuktaka* creepers. There, bees clung to the clusters of blossoms on lovely *priyaṅgu* trees, while copper-colored *kadamba* flowers were dappled by swarms of bees.
At its edge, the tips of the trees were shaken by breezes laden with heaps of flowers, while in front, thickets of bamboo were being torn apart by the lord of the gods' elephant.
Bestowing liberation upon embodied beings who perceive with apprehension the herds of frightened does scattered within the thickets. || 39 ||

It was filled with lovely *tilaka* trees, white as a mass of moonbeams; with *aśoka* trees resembling vermilion, saffron, and safflower; and with *karṇikāra* trees equal to refined gold, all laden with clusters of flowers upon their vast branches. In some places they resembled powdered collyrium, and in others they were like coral.
In some places, the ground was strewn with flowers resembling gold.

With hundreds of birds warbling among the *punnāga* trees, bent low under the weight of clusters of red *aśoka* blossoms, its borders delightful, its breezes dispelling fatigue, and with bees sporting over the blooming lotuses—[such was the garden]. (42)
Then the Lord of the World, the sustainer of the entire universe, together with the daughter of the Snow-Capped Mountain and his beloved lords of the Gaṇas,
showed the Goddess a most enchanting grove, vast with various trees and filled with intoxicated cuckoos.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, the garden has been shown, endowed with supreme beauty;
you ought to speak here once more of all the virtues of this sacred field. (44)
Having heard the greatness of this sacred field, Avimukta, at that time, I am indeed not satiated; therefore, speak further to me.
The God of gods said:
"This most secret field, Vārāṇasī, is always mine;
it is at all times the cause of liberation for all living beings. (46)
In this place, O Goddess, the Siddhas, always established in my vow,
constantly bear various outward marks and long for my world.
With disciplined minds and conquered senses, they practice the supreme Yoga.

It was crowded with various trees and creepers, frequented by diverse birds, adorned with lakes rich in lotuses and water-lilies, and always graced by throngs of Apsarases and Gandharvas; it was auspicious. || 48-49 ||
I am pleased with my dwelling here; hear now the reason why:
he whose mind is fixed on me, who is devoted to me, and who has offered all his actions to me. (8.30)
Just as one attains liberation here [in Vārāṇasī], it is not so anywhere else;
for those intent on recitation and meditation, whose minds are unattached to worldly knowledge,
and even for those struck by darkness and delusion, such is the destiny of men in Vārāṇasī.
At the time of departure from this world, Maheśvara himself bestows the Tāraka Brahman, by which one becomes absorbed in That.
Thus is my divine city, the great one, more secret than the secret.
Brahmā and the others, as well as the perfected ones (siddhas) who seek liberation, know this;
therefore, this field is dear to me, because here my delight resides.
Since it has not been abandoned by me, nor shall it ever be abandoned.
Therefore, this field of mine is known as Avimukta (the Unreleased). For liberation is not attained even by bathing or by devoted service at Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, Gaṅgādvāra, or Puṣkara. ||55-56||
Because it is attained here, this place is superior;
whether liberation occurs at Prayāga or here, it is through my acceptance [of the devotee].
This very place is remembered as even greater than Prayāga, the foremost of all sacred sites (tīrtha).
Jaigīṣavya, that great ascetic who has attained supreme perfection,
[did so] through the majesty of this sacred field and through his heartfelt devotion to me.
The cave of Jaigīṣavya is most beloved and is desired as a dwelling place for yogins.
For one who meditates upon me there constantly, the fire of yoga blazes intensely;
he attains the supreme state of absolute liberation (kaivalya), which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
It was here that Mārkaṇḍeya, of great austerity, attained the highest perfection.
Likewise, the Bālakhilyas and the Siddhas [reside] in this most difficult-to-attain field;
the Ātreyas and the Bhārgavas have attained perfection in this most difficult-to-attain field,
along with sages whose emblems are unmanifest and who are knowers of all philosophical systems.
Liberation is attained here, which is never found elsewhere;
and to them I grant unsurpassed mastery in yoga,
as well as union with my own self and the desired station.
That great-souled Kuvera, having dedicated all his actions in that manner,
indeed attained the status of Lord of Wealth through the very service of this sacred field.
O Goddess, by worshipping me right here, he shall attain unsurpassed perfection.
The son of Parāśara, the yogi, the seer Vyāsa of great austerity,
shall be my devotee and the one who establishes the system of the Vedas;
O lotus-eyed one, that bull among sages also delights in this sacred field.
Brahmā also, together with the sages, as well as Viṣṇu, Vāyu, the Sun, Śakra the king of the gods, and other celestial dwellers [were present]. || 68 ||
O lady of excellent vows, the high-souled ones here worship Me, the Lord of all; having become single-minded, they always worship Me alone.
And by my grace, Ālarka shall regain this city;
having restored it as before, he shall fill it with the four social orders.
Having enjoyed that prosperous land, crowded with people, for a very long time,
he will eventually attain me alone, having surrendered all his life-breaths to me.
From that time forward, O lady of beautiful limbs, even those who dwell in this sacred field— whether householders or ascetics— who are my devotees and devoted to me, shall,
by my grace, attain liberation which is otherwise most difficult to reach.
Even a man whose mind is attached to sense objects and who has abandoned delight in the Dharma,
if he dies in this sacred field (kṣetra), shall not enter saṃsāra again.
As for those wise ones who are free from the sense of "mine," who have attained perfection, and who have conquered their senses— ||73-74||
Established in their vows, remaining steadfast in their states, they have been meditated upon by me on all sides;
having attained the dissolution of the body, these wise ones are freed from rebirth. ||75||
O lady of virtuous vows, when I am pleased, they shall attain supreme liberation;
whereas one who practices yoga for thousands of future births might only eventually reach it,
here in this very life, through death, he attains supreme liberation.
The person who has abandoned the conduct of those who slay Brahmins, those who slay cows, those who violate the teacher’s bed, and thieves; who is restrained in his own proper livelihood;
and whose grief is liberated from the firm bonds of worldly existence—such a person comes to my city, Vārāṇasī. ||77||
O Goddess, this great fruit of this sacred field, Avimukta, has been told by me to you in brief; it is the supreme secret. (78)
O Sovereign Goddess, there is no secret accomplishment higher than this.
Those on earth who know yoga and are devoted to yoga understand this;
this alone is the supreme knowledge, and this alone is the supreme auspiciousness.
This alone is the supreme Brahman; this alone is the supreme state.
O daughter of the King of Mountains, Vārāṇasī is the delightful city that constitutes the very essence of the three worlds, and it belongs to me forever.
Where even those who have committed various misdeeds, upon the destruction of their sins, attain freedom from passion and reach liberation through sacred hearing;
if any man should somehow come to the city of Vārāṇasī—

One should employ that means so that one may not depart again, if one desires a fruitful birth; for what else is there that yields such fruit? If one desires the supreme state, one should cast off the body in the city of Kāśī.
O Goddess, this entire field, filled with various trees and shrubs and blossoming with flowers at will, is known to me as most beloved.
Embodied beings who die here attain the supreme state.
This very state is indeed called liberation and Śiva-hood; there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Vārāṇasī," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
In the meantime, the Lord spoke to the Goddess, the daughter of the Mountain King.
"O noble lady, let us go to grant a boon to the Yakṣa, who is our devotee."
"O lady of excellent hips, my devotee has had his sins burnt away by penance;
O Mistress of the World, he is worthy to receive a boon from me.
Having spoken thus, the God, the Lord of the Universe, then [departed] together with the Goddess.
The Yakṣa went to where he was staying, emaciated and covered with veins;
and he granted him divine vision, by which he beheld Śaṅkara.
Sanatkumāra said: Then,
O Vyāsa, the Yakṣa slowly opened his eyes and beheld the God with His attendants, seated upon the bull-bannered vehicle.
The God of gods said:
"I grant you a boon: first, visibility throughout the three worlds, as well as the essential strength of your body; behold me, free from all affliction."
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having obtained the boon with his body unhurt,
he stood bowing at [his] feet, placing his joined palms upon his head.
And, being urged by that region with the words "I am the giver of boons," he said:
"O Blessed One, grant me unwavering and exclusive devotion toward you. (7)

"May I be the provider of food for the worlds and likewise possess imperishable lordship over the Gaṇas; and may I dwell forever in your abode, Avimukta. O Lord of Gods, I desire this unsurpassed boon to be granted. (8)
The God of gods said: "Freed from old age and death, devoid of all sorrow,
you shall become a leader of the Gaṇas, a granter of boons, and honored by all."
Invincible against all, endowed with the sovereign power of yoga,
you shall be a giver of food to the worlds and a protector of the field;
possessed of great strength and great being, devoted to Brahman, you shall be dear to me.
Tryakṣa, Daṇḍapāṇi, and likewise Mahāyogin—
Udbhrama and Saṃbhrama are your two attendants;
by your command, they shall cause agitation and confusion among the world.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, having thus made the Yakṣa the lord of the Gaṇas, the Blessed One,
the Lord of Gods and Sovereign of the Suras, departed for his own abode together with him.
Then, having seen the goddess there, the God of gods, whose banner is the bull,
spoke quickly to Mandara as he was performing austerities for the sake of obtaining a boon.
The God of gods said:
O Goddess with eyes like full-blown lotuses, O slender-waisted one, I shall go to Mandara,
the best of mountains, desiring the boon of your favor.
Accompanied by his wife, his sons, and his circle of friends,
that best of ascetics indeed sought refuge with me on Mandara, the foremost of mountains;
O Pārvatī, five thousand divine years have passed today.
"The best among those who perform austerities performs penance through his total absorption in me.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, take me also to Mandara, with its beautiful caves."
O Lord, Sovereign of the entire world, I shall find no delight here without you.
Then the Supreme Lord, the God, smiling, said to her:
"Avimukta must not be abandoned; how can you wish to depart?"
The Goddess said:
"I shall dwell right here and I shall go to Mandara;
therefore, O God, this place shall become Avimukta."
The God of Gods said:
"It is even so, O Pārvatī, O lady of beautiful hips, as you say;
for by virtue of my sovereignty, O Goddess, you are all-pervading in every respect, just as I am."
Sanatkumāra said: Then that blessed Lord Hara, the omnipresent Soma, mounted his bull and, accompanied by Sananda and his attendants, proceeded toward Mount Mandara.
Having gone there, he saw Mandara performing supreme austerities in that world; and having seen him, he spoke to him.
"O Lord of the Mountains, I am the giver of boons; I am greatly pleased with your asceticism.
Choose a boon as you desire, and I shall grant it all to you.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by Śarva, he beheld the Lord of the Three Worlds,
and having bowed to Soma, Sanandin, and the one whose vehicle is the bull,
he gazed again and again upon Hara and again and again upon the Goddess.
And counting them again and again, he bowed down to Nandin.
Seeing him thus agitated, Hara, his eyes clouded with tears of joy,
again invited the Mountain to choose a boon.
The God of gods said:
"Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—for I am the giver of boons to you, O Mountain.
I wish to grant you whatever you desire; choose a boon, O Supporter of the Earth. (28)
Mandara said:
"O Blessed One, O God of gods, O Lord of the world, if you are pleased with me, I desire this from you: [the favor] for Soma and his retinue."
O Lord of the gods of gods, I desire that my self be eternally purified by the touch of your feet, together with Soma and his retinue.
"O God, O Teacher of the World, I desire no other boon from you;
let this very boon be granted to me, O Lord of the Universe.
Sanatkumāra said:
"So be it," the Giver of Boons then said to Mandara;
"I shall dwell within you forever along with Nandin and the Goddess.
And you too, O best of mountains, shall be free from old age and death."
And by my grace, you shall become impenetrable even by the thunderbolt.
Delightful to all beings, adorned with gold and jewels, crowded with throngs of apsaras, and frequented by gods and siddhas. ||34||
Sanatkumāra said:
Then he created there a great house made of gold, O Vyāsa, which was of supreme quality; there is nothing anywhere equal to it.
Even for Brahmā there is nothing like it, let alone for anyone else;
it is renowned by the name Vṛṣa for its splendor, stature, and radiance.
Vyāsa said:
O Blessed One, son of Brahmā, Lord of all masters of yoga!
I am not satiated by your narration of the deeds of the God of gods.
He is the bull, the beloved, and the vehicle of great power;
by whom was this great sound of the high-souled Maheśa brought forth? (38)
Whose son was he, whose grandson, and how exactly was he born?
What was his austerity, and what was its fruit? This I wish to know. (39)
Formerly, he was the cloud that brought forth existence and the vehicle beloved by Rudra;
how could he have abandoned that and set his mind upon a bull?
Sanatkumāra said:
In ancient times, Veda was born as the first-born son of Brahmā;
Yajña became the second, and they appointed him to his office in the world.
Employed by the slayer of Brahmā himself, who desired to increase his progeny, that [sacrifice], which causes the nourishment of the world, did not increase [them] in their entirety. ||42||
Yajña said:
"O Blessed One, I have been employed by the Self-born Creator for the sake of the world's success; yet I do not possess such power. Seek another, for salutations be unto you."
The God of gods said:
"Become a cloud; success shall be yours among the worlds.
Then, with waters as nectar, you shall cause the worlds to flourish. (45)
Yajña said:
"O Cloud, if your state brings about the accomplishment of my worldly goals and is auspicious, I shall carry you on my back, O abode of lightning."
Then, O Vyāsa, having realized that he was not possessed of sufficient power, Acyuta performed a very great and most difficult penance as his sacrifice.
Then, O observer of noble vows, the god Śarva became pleased with that sacrifice.
He said, "I am the giver of boons," and he chose a boon from the giver of boons:
"O you of great splendor, just as I carry you in the form of a sacrificial oblation, even so shall I carry you, the imperishable one, in the state of a rain-cloud. (8.31.50)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having replied, "So be it," the Blessed One, O Vyāsa, fashioned the cloud Jīmūta— which possessed the form of a sacrifice and was exceedingly radiant— into the state of a vehicle.
But when, O Vyāsa, the head of the great-souled Dakṣa was swiftly severed by an arrow while he was sacrificing— that sacrifice of immeasurable splendor— then [Śiva],
having taken that headless sacrifice as his vehicle, cast it away.
Vyāsa said:
How did the Blessed One destroy Dakṣa’s auspicious sacrifice? And what was the cause here, O Brahmin, by which the Lord struck it down? ||53||
Sanatkumāra said:
O best of sages, the curse has already been fully described along with its cause;
now hear from me once more this ancient account in detail. ||54||
For in ancient times, he emerged from the mouth of Brahmā as he was sneezing,
equipped with a bow, a quiver, and arrows, and with his fingers bound by leathern arm-guards.
He was armed with a sword, wore a crown and garlands, had earrings and armor;
he was broad-chested, possessed great energy, and was a man with the luster of gold.
Brahmā himself addressed him by the name Kṣupa. Indra chose him as king, the guardian of the world on earth.
He said: "If you grant me your own weapon, the thunderbolt."
"Then I shall become a king on earth; otherwise, it does not please me.
Indra said:
"This thought shall become your hand; the thunderbolt will come to you, and not otherwise."
"So be it; may it be well with you; become a king for the welfare of your subjects.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus, that radiant one indeed became a king upon the earth.
And at that time, Cyāvani became the friend of this Dadhīci.
Having met with him and seated comfortably on an excellent throne, he, being delighted, engaged in conversation of manifold meaning again and again. (61)
Then, O Vyāsa, there arose between them once again a passion born of their birth,
as to whether the Kṣatriya was superior or not, and whether the Brāhmaṇa was superior or not.
Kṣupa said, "The Kṣatriya power and the Brahmanical power," while Dadhīca said, "The Brahmanical power.
Then, for the sake of that cause, neither of them would desist.
Moreover, because of his sharpness and likewise his superior asceticism—
O Vyāsa, because of the preeminence of his status as a Brāhmaṇa and because it was ordained by fate,
the highly effulgent Dadhīca became enraged; he struck him on the head with his left hand,
and that [other] one struck him with a thunderbolt.
Cut in two by the vajra, that imperishable one summoned Śakra and said:
"You are a great yogin; you are capable of joining yourself back together."
Dadhīca, by means of his power of yoga-illusion, restored his body to its former state and sought refuge with Śarva.
Having propitiated the Lord of the Gods, he obtained supreme invincibility.
From Śaṅkara, he obtained the state of possessing adamantine bones, indestructibility, and freedom from decay;
as well as compassion for all beings and the status of a great yogin.
He returned again to see Kṣupa, and once more a friendship was formed between them.
And Rāga, who had been born as before,
was struck by Kṣupa with his left foot; then,
taking up a thunderbolt, he struck him again.
And that thunderbolt caused neither pain nor distress to him, O Sage.
Then, realizing that the high-souled one was invulnerable,
Kṣupa approached Nārāyaṇa and propitiated him for the sake of a boon.
Urged by the gratified Viṣṇu with the words "I am the giver of boons," that high-minded Kṣupa bowed down and spoke thus to Viṣṇu, O Vyāsa.
Kṣupa said:
O Hṛṣīkeśa, there was a brahmin-sage named Dadhīca who was truly incapable of being slain; he was my friend, and he always said to me:
"I am not afraid of a god, nor of a Rākṣasa, nor of an Asura."
"You ought to act in such a way that [he] might say, 'I am afraid of a Piśāca, or a Yakṣa, or of age, or of a human.
Having been addressed thus by the lord of men, that Viṣṇu, the creator of the world, [acted accordingly].
Having said to him, "So be it," he went to the hermitage of Dadhīca;
O Vyāsa, having entered the hermitage, he was honored by Dadhīca.
Having saluted him and joined his palms in reverence, he spoke this to Dadhīca:
"O Blessed One, best of Brahmins, whose splendor is equal to that of the Grandfather Brahmā,
I choose a single boon which you ought to grant me."
O best of Brahmins, I have been propitiated by Kṣupa through his auspicious deeds.
And when he was told, "I am the giver of boons," O great sage, he chose a boon, saying: "You have said 'I am afraid'; by my grace, tell me what it is. (80)
There is no doubt that for the Brāhmaṇa there is fearlessness toward all beings;
endowed with the power of great yoga, he is also invulnerable to all.
"Nevertheless, O Lord, speak that for my sake today without fear.
And then Dadhīca, though released by Viṣṇu, spoke sweetly.
He said repeatedly to Janārdana, "I do not fear.
"I shall not say 'I fear'; it has not been said by me, nor is it being said by me now.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed, Cakrapāṇi, overcome with rage,
raised his discus and spoke to Cyāvani, displaying his fearlessness:
"Those who become even more powerful must indeed act in this very manner."
Out of affection, they speak to a weak person as if he were their own master. || 85 ||
O Discus, if you do not see him, thinking "I am afraid," then it will take your well-nosed head and cast it down upon the earth.
Dadhīci said:
"O Viṣṇu, why do you wish to cause me distress by raising your discus in vain?
By the grace of Tryambaka, I am not within the reach of your discus."
However, out of a desire to investigate, I shall go for refuge to the Guardians of the World;
having learned of their lack of agency, I will then go to Śaṅkara.
Having spoken thus, Cyavana ran toward Varuṇa;
having sought refuge with him, the Lord granted him freedom from fear.
There, a terrible and terrifying battle took place between the god Viṣṇu and the wise Varuṇa for many years.
When Varuṇa had been subdued, the son of Cyavana approached Yama;
he too, who grants fearlessness, was defeated in battle by Viṣṇu.
Then Vyāsa approached the fire, and he too was defeated by him;
thereupon Cyāvana, taking a handful of *kuśa* grass, [struck him]. 92.
Having returned to his own hermitage, he said, "Stay! Stay!
[He thought: "For the sake of testing the world-protectors, I sought refuge with them."
All those [demons] were indeed powerless; their supreme strength resided in me alone.
Today, I shall destroy all your pride, arrogance, and that wonderful power of yours. Wait now, O Janārdana! (94)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, a tumultuous battle occurred, causing the hair to stand on end, between Nārāyaṇa and the high-souled Cyavana. ||95||
By means of yoga, Dadhīca caused those weapons and arrows released from Nārāyaṇa’s hand to settle within a handful of kuśa grass.
Then, through the power of Viṣṇu’s yoga, they emerged from his limbs.
All the gods, clad in armor, fought together with Viṣṇu.
Enraged, he cast all of them— without exception, along with their weapons and their mounts— into his fist, with the sole exception of Viṣṇu.
Then, O Vyāsa, all the immortals were placed within a handful of kuśa grass by the high-souled Dadhīca through his yoga and spiritual power.
Then Brahmā himself, having approached Viṣṇu, who was agitated in appearance and bewildered by the onset of anger, spoke these words:
"O Govinda, what is the use of this constant effort toward the twice-born?"
Furthermore, do you not know how, after Dadhīca had performed his penance and received boons from Śarva,
he attained through the grace of the Supreme Lord invincibility, supreme yogic power, and even mastery over all qualities? || 101–102 ||
He himself obtained the essence of adamantine bones from the Lord;
yet, O God, those such as you do not act with hostility toward Brahmins.
Therefore, turn back at once and ask forgiveness from this best of the twice-born.
Then, having heard the words of Brahmā, that Viṣṇu, the creator of the worlds, [acted].
Having understood that power of the high-souled Dadhīca through his yoga,
[Indra] asked forgiveness from the lord of sages and then returned to his own abode.
Brahmā too, the protector of the three worlds, having consoled and honored that ṛṣi, [departed].
Then, O Vyāsa, he vanished from sight along with all the immortals.

The immensely radiant Dadhīca also performed severe penance in his own hermitage for the sake of propitiating Mahādeva, subsisting only on air and water. Then, as he was thus engaged in austerity, he became resplendent like the sun.
The three-eyed Lord was gratified, and being pleased, he spoke these words:
The God of gods said:
"O Cyavana of noble vows, I am well-pleased with this austerity of yours."
"Tell me what you desire; indeed, it shall be accomplished by me.
Dadhīci said:
"O Blessed One, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me,"
"I desire all the gods, conquered by you, together with Viṣṇu.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, laughing, the giver of boons [spoke] to Dadhīca, the best of sages.
"So be it," said Hara, the remover of the distress of those who bow before him,
to him. When that auspicious boon had been granted by Tryambaka at that time,
the sage considered his enmity with Kṣupa to be truly settled.
Seeing him meditating in that manner, the Lord whose banner bears the bull said: "O Brahmin, choose another boon; I shall grant it to you."
Dadhīci said:
"O Lord, since this enmity has arisen because of the granting of a boon by you,
let there be a place here for you named after this [enmity], O Unborn One."
The God of gods said:
"This supreme place shall be renowned by the name Sthāneśvara;
it will extend for one *krośa* and be filled with various flowers and creepers."
In this place, a man who, having undertaken the highest observance,
fasts for three nights, bathes properly in a river,
feeds a Brāhmaṇa, and is endowed with righteousness, shall worship me. (116)
Completely liberated from all evil, he shall attain my world. ||1 17||
And this Sthāṇu-tīrtha shall come into being; likewise, it is the destroyer of sins.
For one who bathes here obtains the full fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
And this glorious banyan tree stands where I am now situated.
The great Sthāṇuvaṭa tree, known by my name, is capable of granting a boon. || 11.9 ||
There will be no doubt; hear from me also the fruit of this:
whoever stays here for a day and night, self-controlled and restricted in diet, has himself performed the unsurpassed Sthāṇu-vow.
Completely liberated from all evil, he shall become a leader of my host (gaṇapa).
He shall be known as Akampana, the great one, endowed with the power of great yoga;
and he who is self-controlled over his vital breaths, or likewise, self-restrained according to the Yamas. || 121–122 ||
A person who renounces [this] shall obtain great merit as its fruit;
liberated from all sins and freed from all bonds, he becomes like Nandi, a lord of the Gaṇas, omnipresent, and belongs to me. 123.
"Whoever stays here at Sthāneśvara for even a single night shall indeed exhaust all [their sins] without exception.
With a mind completely liberated from all evil, he shall become a most formidable lord of my Gaṇas.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Dispute between Kṣupa and Dadhīca," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
At that very time, O Vyāsa, Dakṣa Prajāpati,
the king born of the son of Pracetas, performed the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha).
There, the fire-god, incited by mantras, then carried the sacrificial portions for all the classes of gods;
and the goddess, the daughter of the mountain king, beheld him as he was carrying them.
Recalling that enmity and the very cause of the curse,
Girijā spoke to him, awakening him to his former state with words that were both artful and sweet, and endowed with reason.
O God, you are the refuge and the resort of all the gods;
O Lord of all the gods, how can the sacrifice proceed without you? (5)
"O Bhava, this Agni carries the sacrificial portions for the gods; he is not yours, O Maheśāna. What is the reason for this, O you of exceeding luster?
O Lord, this task cannot be accomplished through conciliation without valor."
This foolish and arrogant king, the son of Pracetas,
remembering his former enmity, will certainly not grant it unless he is commanded;
furthermore, O Lord, the boon was granted to Dadhīca by you at that time.
"The time for this has arrived; let it be performed for that purpose.
Sanatkumāra said:
"O Vyāsa, having been addressed thus at that time, the Blessed Lord whose banner is the bull [Śiva]..."
Laughing, your father said to the goddess, "O lady of pure smiles, O fair-hipped one, O auspicious one, in a former birth you were the daughter of Prajāpati;
knowing my inner thoughts, O goddess, you speak thus. (8.32.10)
"O beautiful lady, no one in this world desires suffering for their father.
Thus was she addressed then by the god Vyāsa, whose soul is pure.
Then the large-eyed goddess, with a frown upon her forehead,
pressed the tip of her nose with her hand out of anger, she who possesses a pure smile.
As that nose was being pressed, an intense radiance [emerged].
She was born as a woman with a frowning face, four tusks, and three eyes;
she wore leather arm-guards and finger-protectors, was clad in armor, and girt with a waist-belt.
Equipped with sword, bow, quiver, and banner;
twelve-faced, ten-armed, slender-waisted, and dark as the night; with full breasts, broad hips, thighs like an elephant’s trunk, and imperishable. (14)
The goddess of auspicious countenance addressed that goddess, saying, "Bhadrakālī."
Then she said to the God: "O Lord, this [creation] has been fashioned by me;
you too, create another host worthy of it. Salutations to you! (1.6)
Then the god beheld his own radiant shoulder;
from it was born a divine being who seemed to burn the three worlds,
his face adorned with a frown and his hands bound with leather arm-guards and finger-protectors.
Wearing armor, with quiver fastened, armed with arrows, sword,
and bow; three-eyed, four-armed, with a body as firm as a diamond, and youthful—
he was created as the lord of the Gaṇas named Hari, and having bowed down, he stood before him.
Having joined his palms in reverence, he spoke to the God of gods who was with Umā:
"Command me, O Lord of the Suras; O All-pervading One, tell me what must be done by me."
Then the Blessed One said to Hari, that leader of the Gaṇas: "Go and destroy the sacrifice of this son of Pracetas."
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, perform this task quickly together with Bhadrakālī.
Then that wise and blessed Lord created from his own limbs various Gaṇas, the lords of the Gaṇas, who could assume any form at will and bore diverse appearances.
He properly touched his arm, and from that, the mighty ones were born. ||23||
"O Lord, there were then ninety-one crores [of them].
The Blessed One said to them: 'O sinless ones, destroy the sacrifice!
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, surrounded by that vast army resounding with the roar of the ocean and the thunder of clouds and lightning, those two proceeded;
and the God, together with Pārvatī, [arrived] near the hermitage of Raibhya.
Standing there, he beheld that deed of the lords of the Gaṇas which brought about the destruction of the sacrifice.
Sanatkumāra said:
"The trees belonging to Kanakhala are situated near Gaṅgādvāra."
And there was a mountain with golden peaks, resembling Mount Meru.
In that region, the sacrifice of Dakṣa took place at that time;
and the formidable army of the lords of the Gaṇas arrived, led by Kālī.
Having arrived there, all those highly fortunate ones, possessing the radiance of blazing fire,
spoke to the sacrificer, the officiating priests, the sages, and the gods:
"We are indeed all attendants of Śarva, the Supreme Self."
"Those who have arrived here desiring [their shares], grant them their desired portions!
By means of austerity, sacrifice, strength, or discipline;
by sovereignty, or yoga, or whatever else—since you were formerly [the recipients] of these."
For all that [belongs] even to us, and we too are sharers in its portions; moreover, since the gods are our masters, they have thereby attained the right to a share. || 3.2 ||
In matters of sovereignty, power or ascetic merit is the cause; of this there is no doubt.
Both of these belong to us alone, and therefore sovereignty is our rightful prize.
Now, O best of divine sages, if this is the command of someone, let it be said:
"The portion must be given to you, but not to us. ||34||
"Tell us who makes it known, for we shall understand from that.
Thus addressed by Hari, all those led by the gods [replied]. (35)
"O lords of the hosts, the mantras have declared that you are entitled to a share.
The mantras replied to the gods, "You are those whose minds are afflicted by darkness."
Because you did not worship Maheśvara, who deserves the first portion, even though you were urged by them with mantras, they did not give you any shares at all. (37)
Then those mantras departed from there to the eternal world of Brahmā;
thereafter, Śakra and all the other gods spoke to the lords of the Gaṇas.
Having abandoned...
we shall attack and slay all of you who have come here to fight. ||39||

Having heard those words of theirs spoken with pride, Hari, the conqueror of enemies, laughed and spoke these powerful words to them all: 40. Having heard those words of theirs spoken with pride, Hari, the conqueror of enemies, laughed and spoke these powerful words to them all.
The mantras were not made authoritative by you who are arrogant in your strength;
therefore, because you have acted with violence, I shall today destroy you along with your boasts.
Together with the officiating priests, their sacrificial portions, and the sacrifice itself, I shall destroy all those who cause them to perish. 42.
Having spoken thus, the radiant and powerful Haribhadra and the enraged Bhadrakālī both rushed toward the gods.
And the leaders of the Gaṇas, filled with rage, uprooted the sacrificial posts and hurled them;
the leaders of the Gaṇas likewise [attacked] the Hotṛ priest together with the Prasthātṛ and the horse.
Having seized them, they all became enraged and threw them into the current of the Gaṅgā;
and having bound the sacrificer with a noose, they led him away at their pleasure. ||45||
Some destroyed the sacrificial altars, others the *kuśa* grass, others the *sruva* ladles, and still others the *camasa* cups; some threw them about, while others set the sacrificial halls on fire.
Even Haribhadra, blazing with energy, [restrained] the hand of Indra as it was being raised.
The undaunted-souled one likewise paralyzed the other inhabitants of heaven.
With an angry countenance, he struck out with the tip of his bow and, while they looked on, felled the eyes of Bhaga and the teeth of Pūṣan.
And that terrible discus of Viṣṇu, possessing the splendor of the sun at the end of an eon, was paralyzed by him of undaunted soul; held in his hand, it did not waver.
Having struck down the Tuṣita gods, who were intent on battle and eager for combat,
with the Vāyavya weapon, he cast them to the earth;
and that god [further] struck all the other gods who stood ready for war.
The blameless one, using that excellent weapon of delusion, completely bewildered him.
And whatever kings had come there desiring to see [the spectacle],
he forcibly sent them all back to their own homes by the power of his weapons.
Thus, the sacrificial ground was utterly devastated, with its jars shattered and its sacrificial posts and archways broken.
Seeing the great hall set ablaze, Yajña fled away.
Then, as he was fleeing toward the sky in the form of a deer,
Hari fixed an arrow and severed his head.
Taking up another arrow, the powerful Vīrabhadra—
He pursued that sacrifice which was fleeing in the form of a deer;
it approached Vīta, who was bound by two [nooses], as it sought to attain the state of a star.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus, O Vyāsa, having been humiliated by the Gaṇas as well as by Kālī and by the divine Hari himself, they all came for refuge.
Then Hari, together with Kālī, said to all those gods, including the sages and the world-protectors, who had sought refuge: "Go to Soma, the Unborn;
propitiate the Lord of Gods, and then there will be peace for you. (57)
Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus by Hari, those gods, though filled with indignation, went forth composedly to propitiate him, even as they were overcome with pain and grief.
Then, not very far from there, those high-souled ones, with their minds fixed upon him, beheld the Lord together with Sāmba and his attendants.
Having seen him, they bowed down and loudly praised that one of blazing splendor.
Having placed the Brahman priest at their head with words worthy of the Āhavanīya fire,
the gods said:
"Salutations to you, O slayer of the enemies of the gods, O crusher of the sacrifices of the asuras!"
O Great Sacrifice, O Great Being, praised by hundreds of great sacrifices! || 61 ||
Salutations to the destroyer of the sacrifice and the giver of the entire essence of the Vedas;
to Viṣṇu, who assumed the form of Śipiviṣṭa and struck down Narasiṃha;
and to the dweller on Mount Mandara, the giver of all that is auspicious.
To the one who possesses a great celestial chariot, who creates obstacles for the seasons;
to the one who brings an end to mantras and who performs the mantra-vow;
to the destroyer of Pūṣan’s teeth and the remover of Bhaga’s eyes.
Salutations indeed to the one who paralyzed Śakra, Viṣṇu, and the discus; salutations to the leader of sacrifice and to the one who brings about the origin of sacrifice;
salutations to the one who is attained through the granting of boons and to the progenitor of Brahmā.
To you who wear a tiger skin and whose garment is a black antelope hide.
Salutations likewise to the father of Nara, who wears an excellent garland;
to the progenitor of Viṣṇu, and to Jaya and Vijaya.
Salutations to the destroyer of wrath, and to the one whose offspring is Vīrabhadra.
Salutations to Harṣa, salutations to Kopa, and salutations to the creator of Gaṇeśvara.
Salutations to the one who causes remorse for the gods, and to the one who fixed the arrow upon the deer.
Homage to you, O Blessed Lord; homage to you, O Blessed Śiva.
Salutations to you, O Lord of all worlds; salutations to you, O Creator of the world.
By you this entire universe was created—both the sacrifice and the gods who destroy the sacrifice.
Be gracious; do not be angry with us, and do not bring about our destruction.
Sanatkumāra said:
For one who, having risen in the morning, recites this daily with self-restraint,
no forms of obstacles shall ever arise.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed, the Lord of Gods— the soul of all and the creator of all— then spoke these words with a smile to those who stood praising him.
The God of gods said:
"I am not angry; you are always exceedingly dear to me.
For if I were angry, your life would cease in an instant."
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, the Lord, desiring the welfare of the gods,
then caused all those deities to enter by means of his yogic power (yogamāyā).
In order to cause amazement by his power within his own body,
those [gods] then entered the body of the high-souled Lord;
they beheld that wondrous world, joined with the seven worlds.
Having wandered through all those worlds, they were all filled with fear.
There they saw the five-eyed Gaṇapa, the Hero; by him all those tigers among the gods were instantly cast upward and, remaining unwearied,
they departed for another world.
Those highly fortunate ones beheld a city resembling the sun,
enclosed by a vast wall made of crystal,
and adorned with various beautiful peaks that shone with gems and gold. || 78–79 ||
Beyond that, O best of gods, I beheld in their midst a beautiful city extending for seventy million yojanas on all sides,
divine and encircled by a silver wall with the luster of the moon.
In its center, at the very top, is a supreme city extending sixty million [yojanas] in width.
It was well-enclosed by a rampart made entirely of Jāmbūnada gold;
and in its center, there was another [city] measuring five koṭis.
O best of sages, those gods beheld it in its center, surrounded by a rampart made of sapphire stones.
It is four million yojanas in equal extent and circumference,
and it is completely enclosed by a wall made of lapis lazuli stones.
In the center of that city was a beautiful realm extending for three million yojanas,
completely surrounded by a wall variegated with all kinds of jewels.
Within those [walls] were the provinces, entirely free from all suffering.
They were all endowed with pure lineage and possessed perpetual youth. ||86||
Free from hunger and thirst, devoid of disease and sorrow,
they are immortal, liberated from old age, and always joyful in mind.
They are adorned with various long ponds and reservoirs.
With various and wonderful trees that always bear flowers and fruits,
other auspicious trees there produce all kinds of food;
others produce ornaments, and still others produce all types of garments.
Others [brought] all kinds of flowers and all kinds of fruits;
others likewise [brought] all manner of objects, as well as auspicious honey not produced by bees.
O Vyāsa, there are other trees of great splendor that yield milk;
they all constantly flow with cow's milk. The entire ground is made of jewels, auspicious, and covered with golden sand.
Here the waters burst forth from the earth, as do the mountain springs.
In them there is neither anger nor greed, nor war, nor hatred, nor envy;
there is no delusion, nor pride, nor any other defects.
In its center is another auspicious city, two koṭis in extent.
It was adorned with a rampart made entirely of rubies.
Having passed through such cities as these, the gods then [reached the city] which extended for ten million yojanas and was surrounded on all sides by fire.
Those best of gods beheld a great, divine, and endless city that was without gates, resembling the fire of universal destruction and difficult to look upon;
having seen it, they were filled with supreme wonder and fear.
To those lords of the gods, who were trembling with terrified faces, O Vyāsa, the five-eyed leader of the Gaṇas said: "O gods, let there be no fear for you;
this is that very great and terrible city, enveloped by a fearsome fire."
O great-souled ones, you must behold that for whose sake you have come here. || 9.8 ||
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, that mighty five-faced one, with his spear blazing like fire,
created a gateway while the hosts of gods looked on.
Having entered, those high-souled gods, accompanied by the five senses,
beheld that great city, which was divine and filled with lions.
Among those beings who were like Mount Meru and Mandara, possessing claws and fangs,
terrible, fire-colored, enraged, and of exceeding splendor,
one powerful lion then tore through their bonds.
Enraged, with his great mane hanging down, he pursued him.
At the terrifying roar of that lion, all the denizens of heaven,
their faces dejected, went to Pañcākṣa for refuge.
Pañcākṣa said: "Do not fear; O gods, I shall now show the Lord to you.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed, they suddenly beheld Śarva together with Umā;
yet, O Vyāsa, neither that city, nor the lion, nor anything else was seen.
Trembling with fear, they approached the Lord for refuge;
then the Blessed One, who is worthy of being sought for refuge, spoke to them while smiling.
Addressing all the gods who were trembling with fear, the Lord of the Gods said:
"Indeed, you have seen my wrath in its terrifying form as a lion."
By one of them alone, who was fierce, you have all been threatened;
for if I were ever to release them all out of anger, [it would be disastrous].
There is no doubt that all of you will cease to exist in a mere moment;
this goddess, the daughter of the mountain, is angry with you.
Appease her, O gods, for I am not angry with you.
Sanatkumāra said: When the Lord had spoken thus, the fierce, copper-eyed goddess rose up and created from her mouth another goddess who was terrible and increased fear.
With a face made terrible by fangs, possessing many feet, hands, and fingers,
she bore a bow, axe, fierce sword, discus, trident, and arrows;
she possessed the splendor of a thousand blazing suns and was the universal form itself.
Her body was ten thousand yojanas in measurement.
Overwhelmed by her and being struck from all sides, those gods were unable to stand before her, like herds of deer before a tiger.
Then, their hearts distressed by the fear of Kālakarṇī,
those gods entered the heap of ashes standing beside the Lord out of fear.
Seeing them who had entered the mound of ashes seeking refuge, [the Lord spoke].
The Goddess restrained the gods, whose limbs were smeared with ashes, from approaching the Goddess.
The Goddess said:
"O Kālakarṇī, turn back! Do not slay these best of gods;
they are devotees of Paśupati, their forms smeared with ashes. (11.5)
This is the Pāśupata vow proclaimed by Paśupati in ancient times;
that bathing with pure ashes is the highest of all baths.
O best of gods, these [beings] must certainly be favored by the Blessed One.
"Since they have entered into the ashes, do not destroy them.
For these fierce animals, by virtue of that entry into the ashes, have now all become leaders of the Gaṇas; O Īśvarī, they must not be slain by you."
"Death has no power over those whose minds are dedicated to Śaṅkara;
for I have performed this entire vow, which fulfills all desires.
Having been addressed thus by the Goddess, Kālakarṇī assumed a terrifying form.
She turned back from the gods and abandoned the anger that had arisen. Seeing that Kālakarṇī had desisted, the gods then praised the daughter of Himavat, as their most terrible fear was pacified.
The gods said:
