[Praise] the excellent consort of Hara, the wife of Mahādeva, the beloved Ambikā of Tryambaka; the single-syllabled Vāc, Umā, the destroyer of worlds, the auspicious wife of the God of gods; white as a conch, a kunda flower, the moon, a pearl necklace, or water, with fierce tusks, victorious in battle, difficult to behold, possessing inconceivable and fierce vision, large-eyed, clad in yellow silk garments, bearing a great trident, bells, banners, and flags; fond of divine perfumes, clarified butter, and incense; holding in her hands the staff of Time, a sword, and a shield; carrying vessels filled with fat, blood, entrails, and marrow; [the goddess] of the quarters...

We take refuge in the Dakṣiṇā, whose silken bands are bound with beautiful gold, whose eyes are like the fire at the end of an eon, who emits loud bursts of laughter; she who acts according to her will, who is uninjured by the weapons of the Bodiless One (Kāmadeva), the renowned army of heroes, the river dwelling eternally on Mount Mandara, the celestial one, the destroyer of Kānasī, Asura, and Mahiṣa, the shatterer of Dundubhi, the slayer of Sunda, the death of Niśumbha; she who creates the splendor of the light of the moon, sun, and fire, the bestower of desired objects, the remover of the pain of grief and suffering, the fierce one who grants all desires.

She who brings an end to the Destroyer of Ghanā; likewise, she who destroyed the power of the sage Jāmadagnya; the Queen of Kings; the charming Karālā; Kṣapā; Daṇḍanīti; Sthiti; Siddhi; the beloved and auspicious Kālarātri; Aparṇā; Samādhi; the refuge for all; she who delights in dwelling upon the Lord of Mountains; the eternal one of the Milk Ocean; the auspicious Mahākiṃkiṇī; she whose hair is disheveled and standing erect; she possessing the luster of a blazing fire and the hue of twilight clouds; she who wears leather arm-guards and finger-protectors; the three-eyed one; she who wears a garland of matted locks and red lotuses.

I take refuge always in that unique goddess who is Viśalyā, born from the fire-eye of the bodiless god of love; she whose garland is bound with a golden chain, who possesses a long braid and beautiful tresses, who is endowed with glory and fame; she whose variegated banner is fixed with peacock feathers, who is royal and the bestower of peace; she who has a hundred serpents for her armlets, who is intoxicated by the life-force of great Dānavas; she whose body and hair are rough with funeral ashes, who has great knees and a protruding belly; she who wears a serpent as a sacred thread, whose half-face is raised, whose eyes are half-closed, whose hands bear fresh ornaments, and who wears a great girdle and various hanging garlands.

I praise Pārvatī, the primordial and supreme Goddess, who delights in great clouds, musical instruments, and fierce drums, and who loves dance, song, laughter, chatter, and joy; she who is beyond recitation, fire-offerings, fasting, dwelling, wandering, and perfuming; whose essence is known through great yoga and follows a fierce path; whose firm resolve is bound by the fierce sound of the bowstring and bells; whose intense and fierce roar resembles the falling of great thunderclouds, the vajra, or the ocean; she who is the ritual for the initiated, the wife of Virūpākṣa, who dwells within half the body of Hara, and who emerged from the flame of her own mouth.

She is the presiding goddess of all sciences, whose nature consists of restraint, observance, and self-control; she is the auspicious daughter of the lords of mountains, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, and the one who occupies half the body of Bhava. She is the one who felled the teeth of the Sun with her hand, paralyzed the foremost hand of the lord of the gods, and removed the hair from Viṣṇu. Drawn by a great lion as her vehicle, she is the Great Terrible One who strikes fear into even the fearsome, the mother who consumes Skanda and the Moon, and the foremost of those who devour the elephant-faced god. She is the one who brought about the birth of Viśākha, and the progenitor of Nandin and Naigameṣa.

We take refuge in her who is the primordial fire-drill for the entire world, the worshipful Mother of yogins, the Yoginī being meditated upon; she who is steadfastness, unattainable by gods and brahmins through great yogic reasoning; she who is the abode of the distinguished, the beloved, and the virtuous; she who is Lakṣmī, the source of the worlds Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Janaḥ, Tapaḥ, and Satya, and the source of majesty; she who is the cause of the senses, the creator of ego and the subtle elements (tanmātras); she whose activity consists of darkness, goodness, and passion; she who is the supreme activity, the power of Maheśa, as well as consciousness, and that which is conceivable through all-encompassing knowledge.

Direct us toward the goddess Umā, our mother; O Mother, being pleased, grant us happiness. She is the auspicious wife of Mahādeva, whom we contemplate with single-minded consciousness and constant meditation. Whatever cruel deed has been done by us, may you, being pleased, destroy it for us today—just as she who was born from the body of the great Sun destroys frost. Whatever we have done in the past across thousands of millions of births, whatever we shall do, and whatever we are doing now—all that, grant to us entirely, and grant us every object of our desire.

"Likewise, O Goddess, may you today bestow upon us health, vigor, prosperity, knowledge, discernment, and intelligence; as well as retention, reasoning, deliberation, refutation, fortitude, the state of nobility, and divine progress, along with constancy in Dharma and whatever other virtues there may be. To you, O Goddess, be homage! (123–144) Sanatkumāra said:
Thus was the Goddess praised by the gods with joyful hearts.
And by the grace of Tryambaka, the Goddess, being pleased, spoke this to the gods: "Go all of you, free from anxiety; I am pleased with you, there is no doubt. (145) The Goddess said:
"Go all of you, free from anxiety; I am pleased with you, there is no doubt."
Do not do this again, O gods, lest destruction befall you.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that god, the matted-haired Nīlalohita, the slayer of the enemies of the gods, smilingly restored all the deities to their natural state.
And the Lord of Gods said to them, "Go, free from anxiety;
when the sacrifice is to be performed, then indeed this shall be yours."
With his head restored, he was joined together with this mantra by the son of Diti.
Then the god gave him the Atharvaṇa hymn of praise and the imperishable mantra that effects the joining; and he spoke these words in a melodious voice.
The God of gods said:
"O best of gods, let this sacrifice attain equality with the constellations;
and let this Lord Hari also become its pursuer of the deer."
Bhadrakālī, Hari, and these hosts of great strength—
all of you shall forever be auspicious to you, O immortals.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, all those gods together with the Brahmās bowed their heads in prostration and spoke these words to Śarva: || 152 ||
O Lord, O God, Master of the Suras, let this most excellent sacrifice belong to you alone; O Imperishable One, it shall be honored for a hundred years.
"In all sacrifices, we give you every portion.
Thus addressed by all the gods, the Lord of Gods, the Sovereign of the Suras, [spoke]. (154)
Then the gods beheld Maheśvara assuming his own infinite and supreme form, auspicious and composed of all the deities. 155.
Upon their heads, arms, thighs, and feet, as well as on their bellies, hands, and stomachs,
they beheld high-souled sages whose wealth was their asceticism.
Having assumed that form at that time, Śaṅkara spoke to the gods:
"All of you are great-souled beings, born from my own body. (157)
And behold your own bodies as being composed of me;
then, O Vyāsa, those deities saw the entire world as consisting of Rudra. 158.
And not seeing themselves, their minds were filled with wonder;
thus did that Lord of Gods display his own power to them.
He said to the tigers among the gods: "Indeed, these manifestations have been seen;
whoever worships whichever form with supreme devotion, being endowed with it," (8.32.160).
"O gods, assuming that form, I myself accept the worship; I have no need for sacrificial portions. O gods, I give back all those portions today. Go now, all of you, freed from your distress."
The gods said:
"O God, this supreme secret has been revealed to us by you.
Any mortal who shall know it thus will attain the imperishable worlds. (162)
And this place, O Blessed One, known as Bhadreśvara, shall become the best in the world, the most meritorious of all meritorious sites. (163)
Thus, this eternal Rudrakṣetra extends for a yojana in every direction;
one who dies here shall become a leader of the Gaṇas, beloved by you, O Lord.
O destroyer of sacrifices, he who constantly recites this upon rising at dawn,
or causes it to be heard by the Brahmins, is liberated from all sins;
and he who, having bathed in this Bhadrakarṇahrada, worships Hara [is likewise freed].
Having prepared the sacrificial porridge (caru), the pure one should feed the Brahmins.
That man, liberated from all sins, wherever he may die,
rejoices in the midst of Apsarases like another god in heaven. O Lord, O Blessed One, O Master, regarding that which was spoken by you while standing there:
"O Hara-Bhadrā, by your grace, let this merit become eternal. || 1.68 ||
"O Slayer of Sacrifices, O God, let that merit which belongs to one who has properly performed the Aśvamedha sacrifice accrue here to the man who always worships you.
And whatever best of men shall give up his life here,"
"That host of Haribhadra shall possess great power.
Sanatkumāra said:
"So be it," and having spoken thus, he [went] to Mandara, which has beautiful caves.
The blessed Śarva, accompanied by hundreds of his attendants, departed like Soma.
The gods, together with the king, remained at that place as they pleased;
Brahmā and Viṣṇu followed behind the gods.
Having traveled a short distance accompanied by both of them, the Lord [proceeded].
Not far from there, he said: "Stay, O Viṣṇu of great strength! (173)

Then that best of men, having bowed at the feet of Hara, stood leaning upon a mango tree; thus he became a hunchback. Because Hari stood in that place leaning upon the mango tree, [it was called Āmrakūṭaka].

While gazing at the Lord of Gods, that region became known as Kuvjāmraka, a prosperous sacred field of Viṣṇu; it is meritorious and bestows the fruit of a thousand cows for every nivartana measured there. || 175-176 ||
Having gone not very far from there, O Vyāsa, the Lord again spoke to the Grandfather, "Return," and he entered the sky. ||177||
When that god had ascended into the sky, Brahmā, with palms joined and face upturned,
circumambulated him clockwise, bowed down, and then departed from there.
Because Hara was thus circumambulated by him at that place, [the site became known as Pradakṣiṇā].
The whirlpool of his own body was formed by his meritorious deeds;
therefore, that beautiful region became renowned as Brahmāvarta. A person who bathes there obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice. || 179-180 ||
Having prepared the sacrificial oblation (caru) there and likewise fed the twice-born, he shall then cast off his life-breaths and attain the world of Brahmā. ||181||
Then, having arrived together with the gods led by Viṣṇu,
Brahmā performed a glorification of Paśupati at Bhadreśvara.
Having installed that *liṅga* there and performed an exceedingly brilliant worship,
he bathed in the Bhadrakarṇahrada lake and went to heaven together with the gods. As he was departing, Dakṣa then spoke this to Brahmā:
"O Lord, tell me, who am asking you, what must be done by me? (184)
The Grandfather said:
"Propitiate the great archer Śarva, the fierce one with matted hair;
then you shall attain the completion of the sacrifice and the eternal worlds."
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, having been thus addressed in truth by the god Brahmā,
he then fashioned a linga at Kanakhala and worshipped Rudra.
When a hundred divine years of Prajāpati had passed,
Mahādeva, smiling on the summit of the mountain, said to the daughter of the mountain:
"O Goddess, the son of Pracetas stands engaged in ascetic penance, self-restrained."
Behold him, established with a mind fixed entirely upon me.
Then, seeing Mahādevī standing there subsisting on air alone,
worshipping Maheśvara at the Liṅga with supreme devotion,
the Goddess, thrilled with joy, spoke to the God who is worshipped by all the deities.
With palms joined in reverence, O Vyāsa, the Goddess spoke to her husband, the lord of all the gods:
"This one is mean-spirited, evil-minded, arrogant, conceited, and wicked."
Having been humiliated by you through this misfortune, I have come to you alone for refuge. || 191 ||
Therefore, O Maheśvara, you ought to forgive this wicked-natured one who has sought refuge in you; for his sake, I propitiate you as his devotee.
The God of gods said:
"O Goddess, you yourself grant him his desired boons as you please;
permitted by me, O fair-browed one, you alone bestow the boon upon him."
Sanatkumāra said: Then those two lords of the gods, having come together and surrounded by their own attendants, said: "Behold, O Dakṣa; we are both pleased [to see you] with our divine eye."
O highly fortunate son of Pracetas, you who possess great ascetic power and are the bestowers of boons!
For the sake of pacifying the curse, I grant you this desired boon:
may you obtain the fruit of that sacrifice which was destroyed by my attendants.
O illustrious one, become my Gaṇeśa, capable of assuming any form at will;
you shall be imperishable and immortal, free from suffering and grief, O highly fortunate one, and shall remain ever by my side. 197.
The Goddess said:
Listen further; what else might Maheśvara grant?
For he, when entreated by you, would surely bestow even a most difficult boon.
Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus by that daughter of Himavat, the high-minded Dakṣa, with palms joined in reverence and bowing down, spoke these words: 199.
Dakṣa said:

We, together with our wives, have sought refuge in that god who is the cause of the creation and destruction of the three worlds, whom the foolish do not know as the one and only unspoken being, the wielder of the Pināka bow who removes the misfortunes of his devotees. (8.32.20)
Because of our ignorance, our lack of divine nature, and our excessive pride and delusion, we did not indeed worship him along with the daughter of the mountain;
that Lord of the Gods, being enraged, gave us a curse—we have now come for refuge to that deity together with his wife. ||20.1||

We have gone for refuge, together with our wives, to that God who is the creator of the hosts of gods, yakṣas, and rākṣasas; of the siddhas, the sons of Diti, the lords of the dānavas, and of men; and of all beings—beasts, deer, birds, and reptiles.
He who, out of anger, created from his forehead the great lord of the Gaṇas, the lion-king Hari, whose form possesses immeasurable power.
And we, together with our wife—who is endowed with immeasurable virtues and power—have come for refuge to that god and his consort.

We, together with our wife, have come for refuge to that god who conquered the gods—those protected by Varuṇa, those guarded by Savitṛ, those accompanied by Brahmā, those with the hundred-sacrificed Indra, those with Viṣṇu and Vāyu, those led by Indra, and those possessing great weapons in the ocean of battle. (204)

Whatever impurity or evil has been done toward you, whether through ignorance or through the defects of passion, hatred, and delusion—may Śarva, the soul of the universe, forgive all of that today for me and my wife, by virtue of his nature as one of great majesty. (205)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having thus praised the Lord of Gods with eyes clouded by tears,
he stretched out his arms and fell to the ground with his entire body.
Then, O illustrious one, the powerful god himself, together with the goddess, raised up Dakṣa, who had sought refuge and whose eyes were blurred with tears.
Her tears fell there upon the ground in the form of drops;
having coalesced, O best of Brahmins, they became a river.
Then the God spoke to that river, which was endowed with auspicious qualities.
O Goddess, since you have emerged from a drop of Arjuna’s tears, [you are called Arundhatī].
Therefore, O auspicious one of great renown, you shall be known by the name Arjunī; reaching every sacred mountain peak, you shall carry forth [the waters],
and indeed, one who bathes in you shall obtain the fruit of the horse-sacrifice.

And one who dies on this bank of yours, whether by natural means or otherwise, shall not undergo rebirth in the human state nor fall into an evil destiny. Furthermore, he who has fasted for three nights, having prepared and offered the *caru* oblation, [shall attain the same]. || 212 ||
"Having bathed, you should feed a Brāhmaṇa; he too will go to the world of the cows (Gavāṃloka), O one of great splendor, and from there he shall not fall.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having thus created the river and bestowed his favor,
the Lord of the Gods then comforted Dakṣa and spoke to that king.
The God of Gods said: "Therefore, let that fear of yours be gone; O dear one, become my Gaṇeśa.
Speak again, O virtuous one, what desired boon shall I grant you?"
Sanatkumāra said: Then Dakṣa, having bowed down, spoke with auspicious words;
repeatedly taking heart and looking again and again, he said: [Verse 2.1.6]
Dakṣa said:
"If you are pleased with me, O God, let this place be yours, O Imperishable One—pure and meritorious. Let this be my boon, O Śiva. (217)
The God of gods said:
"These two daughters of a sage, having undertaken difficult penance, have been eating only grain for a full year by that wicked man. (218)
"O highly fortunate ones, since you two and Dakṣa have performed [this act] here, this place shall therefore become my station named Kanakhala. (219)
And there is a great and most meritorious sacred ford, comparable to the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean;
herein there are no sinners, nor the deceitful, nor atheists, nor those possessed by pride.
They shall indeed always be able to depart, but never to remain;
by my splendor, one who dies here shall not undergo rebirth.
Having approached this place, bathed, and likewise prepared the sacrificial oblation (caru), [one shall attain liberation].
His soul liberated from all evil, he was honored in the world of Śakra.
Then, there in that place, he appointed Gaṇapati as Haribhadra’s minister;
out of affection, he gave him Kālī as a wife, who was preeminent in every virtue.
And he bestowed excellent, vast, and divine islands, as well as those surrounded by seas of clarified butter, upon many groups of Bāhuja kings. ||224||
Sanatkumāra said:
"Thus, O Vyāsa, that sacrifice of Dakṣa was indeed destroyed by Śambhu;
and how the head of the sacrifice was severed has been related to you."
Vyāsa said:
O Lord, that divine and terrible goddess born from the mouth of the Goddess—who causes fear even to the gods—where has she gone, and how did this happen? I desire to know this.
Sanatkumāra said:
When the Blessed Lady was praised by the best of the gods who were prostrate before her, then that Mother of the World (Sāmbikā) spoke to him, saying, "Tell me, what shall I do for you? (227)
Then Brahmā, having bowed with great reverence to Mahādevī, said: "O Sovereign of the Gods, let her become my daughter."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having said "So be it," Umā gave her daughter to that goddess;
and he too, having said "You are Death," appointed her to a terrible task.
The goddess who is auspicious in taking away the life-breath of all living beings was herself appointed by Brahmā to perform that task;
with her arms raised, O Lord of Gods, she remains ever-diligent in this work through you and me.
He who [listens to] this unsurpassed account of the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the installation of Bhadreśvara, and the very grace bestowed upon Dakṣa; || 23.1 ||
Whether one recites it, hears it, or causes even the twice-born to hear it,
one is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the heavenly world.
[The wrathful glance] of Bhaga’s eye at Dakṣa’s sacrifice became a forest fire.

For the sake of attaining happiness, I have sought refuge in Śaṅkara— the sacrificial fire for the god of love, whose body is radiant with the crescent moon, the preceptor of the gods at the time of sacrifice, and the sovereign protector of the seven worlds. (23.3)
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, "The Destruction of Dakṣa’s Sacrifice," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: O bull among sages, listen to how the Bull bore the Lord [Śiva].
Having paid homage to the bull-bannered Lord (Śiva), I shall now fully declare that to you:
in former times, the Great Being Dharma, accompanied by Yajña,
performed an immense and most difficult penance of renunciation.
Having reached the Himavat mountain,
they subsisted on air for twelve thousand human years; thereafter, they further subsisted on leaves for ten thousand [human] years.

Then, after a short while, the god Hara of great splendor, together with his hosts whose forms were identical to his own, granted them his vision. Having seen those many Maheśvaras of similar radiance, the two of them [were amazed].
They both thought to themselves, "Who indeed among us could be the lord?
Then, having looked at each other, they consulted together and reflected again and again.
In their midst, they beheld Maheśvara, the treasury of splendors;
having bowed with great reverence to Bhava, the god in their midst, those two of measured luster placed their joined palms to their heads and offered praise.
The two sacrifices said:
"Obeisance to the Lord of the three worlds, who is clothed in the directions, whose nature is immortal;
who dwells at the crossroads and delights in the crossroads. (8)
To the god who has four manifestations, who has three eyes, and who is Bhava;
to the one with four faces, the pure one, who moves within the lattice-work [of the heart]. ||9||
To the one who bestows grace upon Indra, to the one who effects grace upon Brahmā,
to the god whose liṅga is erect, to the one who intoxicates and yet is free from intoxication.
Homage to the one of golden hue and likewise to the sun-eyed;
homage indeed to the one with pure hair and to the long-tongued.
Homage to you, the many-footed; homage, homage to the one-eyed.
Salutations to the Thousand-Bell, and salutations indeed to the Thousand-Eyed. 12.
Salutations indeed to the wielder of the Pināka bow and to the one with the banner; salutations again and again.
Salutations to the thousand-headed one and to Saṃvarta; salutations again and again. || 13 ||
Salutations ever to the one worthy of praise; salutations again and again to the slayer of enemies.
Salutations to Bhava, to the auspicious one, and to the creator; salutations again and again. Salutations ever to the excellent one, and likewise to the bestower of boons.
Salutations eternally to Gokarṇa; salutations to the Lord of Sovereignty. ||1 5||
Salutations to Viṣvaksena; salutations again and again to Prabhāsa.
Salutations to you who are Tennada; salutations to you, the giver of life.
Salutations to the initiator; salutations indeed to Padmamāla.
Homage to Mahāratha himself; homage again and again to Bhairava! || 17 ||
Salutations indeed to the four-faced one, salutations to Mahādeva;
obeisance to Brahmā, to both the immovable and the moving.
Obeisance to him who takes the form of a woman, to the fortunate one; salutations again and again.
Salutations to you, the Middle One; likewise, salutations to you from every side.
Salutations to you, the one who permits and the thinker, the impeller of all beings.
O Lord of the World, grant the desires sought by us both.
Sanatkumāra said:
He who constantly praises with this [hymn], endowed with self-restraint, shall be fulfilled in all desires and attain his desired goal. (21)
Sanatkumāra said: Then the Lord restored all those hosts to their natural state— Nandin, the Goddess, and even himself.
And he said to them both, "I am pleased; let the desired boon be accepted."
The two gods said:
"O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to us, then even when we have entered into other births, may we always carry you, O Lord of Suras."
And this secret place has been intensely cultivated by us through austerity;
by your grace alone, O Lord of the Gods, may it become meritorious. ||24||
The God of gods said:

This supreme secret of mine is an excellent abode destined to come into being; indeed, by merely casting a five-arrow’s distance [toward it], one who has died shall become a leader of my attendants (gaṇapa).
Since you have remained here, honored by us, with the thought "I am in the middle," therefore let this be renowned by the name Madhyama (the Middle). 26.
Having attained another birth, you two, being highly honored and exceedingly powerful, shall sustain the worlds after becoming my vehicles. ||27||
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having thus addressed those two best of gods, the Lord departed for Mount Mandara, which has golden caves, together with his hosts of attendants.
After the gods had departed with their hosts for a long time,
the auspicious Surabhi then propitiated Rudra during this Manvantara.
Pleased by her asceticism for a thousand years,
Bhava appeared before her, O Vyāsa, and said, "I am the giver of boons.
She chose as her boon an incomparable son, the best among all living beings.
And other sons of great being, worthy of sacrifice, the most excellent of gods. ||3 1 ||
Likewise, he gave his daughters and other beautiful world-sustainers;
then the god gave everything and indeed departed from sight.
When that Great God had departed,
Surabhi gave birth to a son, a bull of radiant splendor, who was the first-born among all beings;
likewise, she bore the eleven auspicious Rudras as the younger brothers of the bull.
And those seven maidens gave birth to those cows who are the sustainers of the world. ||34||
Having performed his daily rites every morning, that bright bull would always approach and pay homage to his father, mother, and likewise his grandfather,
who was served by elephants from the four quarters.
The forest is the abode of hosts of Siddhas, where indeed that [river] born of the nectar of immortality flows. || 36 ||
It was divine, with the nectar-like taste of dūrvā grass, capable of healing wounds and burning sensations.
Once, while wandering in that forest, he became weary and afflicted by thirst despite being full. ||37||
The king of bulls, the son of Surabhi, went to drink from the ocean;
having plunged into the great ocean, he then opened his mouth wide in anger, making it a massive gape that reached the very middle of the sea and swallowed the timi and timingila fish.
He drank the water of the ocean, yet he did not attain satisfaction. ||39||
While he was drinking, fourteen thousand lords of the Daityas, all equipped with swords and arrows and with bows in hand, stood ready for battle.
Resembling Śakra, and like Yama, Kāla, and the fire of destruction,
the great-souled sons of Maya rushed with speed toward Vṛṣabha.
[Seeing] those Daityas thus enraged, bearing swords, mallets, and lances—
That one of great strength drank them up along with the waters of the ocean.
Seeing those [waters] already drunk and those being drunk, all the inhabitants of the sea were suddenly terrified and cried out in distress.
Then the blessed ocean, being drunk up and deeply distressed,
approached the Mare’s Mouth (Vaḍavāmukha) and sought refuge with Saṃvarta.
And that exceedingly powerful fire, highly incensed, gave him [protection].
Having approached Vṛṣa, Abhaya spoke these words with palms joined in reverence.
Saṃvarta said:
"This auspicious abode of the Daityas is a refuge for all beings;
you, O valiant one, ought not to deprive it of its waters."
The Bull said:
"O Agni, it did not occur to my mind to dry up the ocean entirely.
Since you are its protector, I shall therefore not do so today."
Whatever pride and arrogance you have, whatever strength and whatever manliness, show that to me, O Lord of Sacrifice; I shall drink it right before you. (48)
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, the lord of bulls began, out of impetuosity, to drink up the ocean— dwelling as he was in the submarine fire— to leave nothing remaining.
Anala said:
"You are no match for me in power, nor do I have any enmity toward you;
however, since I am bound by this task, I shall indeed perform it accordingly."
"You shall not drink; I will protect the ocean in my presence.
I shall restrain you, O boastful son of Surabhi! (5.1)
Sanatkumāra said: Then the illustrious Fire-god, possessed of great luster, leaped up and seized him by the throat; though he was powerful, he could not move from that spot.
He then vomited out that water which had been drunk, except for the portion belonging to the Dānavas.
Indeed, all of them were completely consumed by his internal fire.
Sanatkumāra said: Then the fire Saṃvartaka, having released Kakudmin who had been restrained, said, "Go, O lord of bulls; I do not kill you."
I am indeed capable of burning you, but you are incapable of killing me;
nevertheless, I do not roar, for what is the use of roaring for those who are truly powerful? ||55||
Sanatkumāra said:
Having dismissed the bull, Agni quickly went to his own abode;
the bull also departed, overwhelmed by grief and sorrow.
The radiant bull, the son of Surabhi,
being oppressed by sleep and overwhelmed by sorrow, departed while reflecting thus:
"I am weak, yet Vahni is powerful, by whom I have been so humiliated."
Having become the lord of my life, I have not been deprived of my vital breaths;
yet all my strength and likewise my roaring were in vain,
like that of a rain-cloud in the sky devoid of water.
Today, firm in my resolve and established in my vow, I shall renounce my life,
so that such a humiliation of my pride may never happen to me again while I am weak, seized by an enemy, and evil-minded.
"I consider death to be superior to life; what is the use of living?
Sanatkumāra said:
While the bull was reflecting thus, he heard an auspicious voice from the sky.
"O bull, you must not fear; do exactly what I tell you."
Seek refuge in Rudra, the lord of all gods, who is more powerful than all;
through him, O lord of the gods, you shall conquer the Fire-god.
He is undoubtedly the creator of all beings, beginning with Brahmā;
O Bull, he will dispel all this suffering of yours.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard this from the great-souled Sādhya,
the one of great splendor reached the Himavat mountain and performed extensive penance.
When he had been devoted to that for a thousand years and was intent upon those blessings,
the Blessed One, the Lord of all beings, together with Ambā and his attendants, spoke to him.
The God of gods said:
"O son of Surabhi, O highly fortunate one, I am pleased with you, my dear son. Name the boons you desire, my child; I shall grant them to you, however many there may be."
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having beheld the Lord Īśvara together with Ambā and his attendants, he, being well-composed, bowed his head at the Lord’s feet with palms joined in reverence. ||68||
Gazing at him again and again and bowing down repeatedly, he said: "O Lord of the World, I desire indeed imperishable ascetic power;
O God, as well as unsurpassed strength and inexhaustible mastery over yoga."
I am your vehicle, and yet I have been thus insulted by Agni.
"O Lord of Gods, O Imperishable One, I wish to see the fire of universal destruction (saṃvartakānala) dwelling within the mouth of the submarine mare (vaḍavāmukha), subdued by you. Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus, the son of Satyavatī, after granting those boons,
rubbed his left side and created a single Rudra—
wearing a crown and garlands, three-eyed, and adorned with earrings and armlets.
To him— broad-chested, clad in armor, bow in hand, possessed of great strength,
with leather arm-guards and finger-protectors bound on, and bearing a sword and divine weapons—
he said, "Go to Rudra, who dwells in the Mare’s Mouth."
Having bound the blazing fire of universal destruction, bring it here!
Sanatkumāra said: Having bowed at the feet of that Soma,
the leader of the Gaṇas went swiftly to the ocean and beheld the consumer of oblations (Agni).
Having waged a powerful, most terrible, and hair-raising battle,
he bound Saṃvarttaka and brought him before the side of the gods.
Vyāsa said:
"What was that battle between the Lord of the Viśas and Pāvaka like?
I wish to know this; tell me, O best among speakers.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having gone there, the leader of the hosts, enraged, with eyes red with anger, then spoke these meaningful words to the fire Saṃvartaka: ||78||
Gaṇapa said:
"The Lord of the entire universe, the God adorned with the crescent moon, commands you, O Vahni: 'Propitiate this Bull.'"
"Accompanied by your friends, say to that bull among men, 'I am prostrate before you';
remain under his command and do whatever must be done. (8.33.80)
Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus and having heard those words of the God of gods, Nala,
not being overly elated, spoke these meaningful words.
Anala said:
"I am forever the servant and follower of that very God of gods;
he will never appoint me here and then employ me elsewhere."
"Go and speak to the three-eyed Lord in my name:
'If he speaks to me again, then I shall do accordingly. (83)
Gaṇeśvara said:
"Alas, those who are considered wise but are excluded from both strength and knowledge,
when addressed in this manner, behave exactly as you describe me."
The command of those who are powerful and those who possess authority is decisive even once;
moreover, he indeed is the best of messengers who accomplishes the objective. ||85||
Thus, I, a powerful messenger, have been dispatched here by that mighty creator of the world, the wielder of the Pināka bow, for the sake of accomplishing all purposes. ||86||
"If you do not carry out my word, then today indeed,
having bound you with great nooses while you are quivering, I shall lead you into the presence of the Sustainer of Heaven."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus, that radiant one, his eyes blazing like fire with anger, rushed toward the leader of the Gaṇas and cried out, "Stay! Stay! (88).
As he was rushing forward with speed, that powerful expert in weapons struck him with the Parjanya weapon;
he [the opponent] blazed up with great force.
Then, as he approached nearby blazing and overwhelmed with rage—
With a great thunderbolt weapon, he struck him in the middle of the chest.
Then, struck by that weapon, even though he was possessed of great speed,
the lord of fire stood for a moment bewildered and agitated, like a smokeless flame.
Then, seeing that great fire quivering as it was bound by the excellent noose of Rudra, the Lord of the Gaṇas, overcome with anger, bound him with his two hands. Indeed,
having seen him fallen, bound by that supreme noose—
His sons and circles of friends, with various weapons in their hands,
rushed at the leader of the Gaṇas in anger by the hundreds and thousands;
but that leader of the Gaṇas, having utterly defeated them, [confronted] that Fire-god.
He quickly presented him to Hara, like a sacrificial animal at a ritual; Mahādeva, beholding him who had been brought—the consumer of the ocean—[635]
He said to the bull, "Tell me, what should be done for him?
Observing that wretched man of dejected mind, the great bull [spoke]. 96.
Bowing his head to the feet [of the Lord] with palms joined in reverence, he spoke thus:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Great Sovereign of all the worlds! (97)
"O Lord, Master of this assembly, this greatness of yours has been witnessed.
O One of Great Strength, this wretched and powerless one has also been seen.
Let him be released, O Best of Gods; he is as good as slain, there is no doubt."
For all his sons have been slain, as indeed have all his friends in every way. ||99||
"O Lord, the slaughter of this wretched one is not desired by me; let him be released.
Having heard these words spoken by the bull, Maheśa was pleased and, smiling, then released that burner (Agni).
And that Rudra is liberated from old age, grief, birth, and death. || 101 ||
Having made him the lord of the Gaṇeśvaras, the Sovereign granted him a continent renowned by the name Manoramaṇa, which possessed great prosperity.
O Vyāsa, it was divine, moving at will, adorned with palaces made of bright Jāmbūnada gold and endowed with everything that fulfills every desire.
At that time, all the gods, led by Brahmā, were present there.
Having approached the God of gods, they spoke these words according to the facts:
"O Blessed One, O Slayer of the enemies of the gods, O Best of Deities, this bull was formerly occupied by you; that powerful one has now filled it with his roar."
O Lord, out of pride he has rendered the entire three worlds unsettled;
O protector of beings, he courses through the sky at great speed with his celestial chariots,
causing the gods to tremble and making a roar as he moves.
Now he has obtained his boon from us once again;
O Lord, let that means be devised so that he does not act [against us] in that same way.
O Lord of Gods, O Protector of Beings, you alone are our refuge and our resort.
O Lord, you are the protector in every way for those who are constantly overcome by fear. 108.
The God of gods said:
"I shall ordain for you all such that no fear shall arise and all the worlds may forever remain in well-being."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the blessed Vyāsa, the god of gods of great splendor,
by virtue of his boon, created Gaṇeśa, who wore beautiful earrings.
With a face split open as far as his ears, he was of massive body and great strength;
his arms were like great iron clubs, and he was firm with a body as solid as a diamond.
He had large tusks and a broad chest, and he wielded a great sword and a great bow.
He had blazing embers for eyes, was three-eyed, and radiant with armor;
he bore two inexhaustible quivers and wore garments of skin,
holding an arrow in one hand and a bow in the other.
Adorned with planets and stars, illuminated by lightning and the sun,
and with the sky as its upper garment, he shone like the peak of Mount Meru.
Addressing him clearly by the name "Prabhākara," the Blessed One said this:
He spoke to that Prabhākara in the presence of all the gods:
"O Prabhākara, mine of virtues, you have been commanded by me;
endowed with supreme sovereignty, restrain the force of Vṛṣa."

"And for the sake of your residence, I give you the celestial Indradvīpa. Jyotsnā shall be your wife, and likewise, being commanded by me, you shall become my Great Gaṇapati, free from old age and death."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then all the deities, together with Brahmā, bowed to him and departed for their own abodes; and the god, whose vehicle is the bull, shone forth.
From the mouth, Dharma is the bull; the sacrificial rite is said to be the hindquarters.
The moon and sun are his two eyes, and Brahmā is seated upon his head.
Varuṇa is on his tongue, and Vāyu himself moves within him.
Viṣṇu, Bhaga, Pūṣan, and Śakra were stationed in his feet;
the remaining Ādityas likewise resorted to his shanks, while the Rudras took refuge in his thighs, ears, nose, neck, lips, and jaw. (8.33.120–121)
His weapons were his hooves, and the discus and thunderbolt were on his two horns;
Mitra himself was in his anus, and his tail was all kinds of gifts.
All the mountains were his bones, and his dung became auspicious prosperity.
And his urine, O Vyāsa, became divine, immortal, and purifying.
O Vyāsa, all the sages became his body hairs, and the constellations in their entirety became his limbs; the planets became his auspicious-looking joints,
while the sacrificial offerings, Vedic sacrifices, mantras, hymns, and fruits [became his other parts].
His flesh became the earth, and his blood the rivers and oceans.
The seven worlds were indeed the mouth of that being of incomparable splendor;
his hands were the rays of light, and his marrow was the medicinal herbs.
Animals are like mantras, as are sinews and creepers;
likewise, climbing plants, trees, shrubs, and other auspicious forest-dwellers.
The *nāḍīs* (channels) were his *nāgas*, and the *vasus* were the accumulation of his semen;
the two gods, the Aśvins, are remembered as his stomachs for undigested and digested food;
the clouds were his skin, and the garlands of lightning... [were his hair].
...the yakṣas, gandharvas, and apsarases likewise. || 1.29 ||
From them were born the veins, the arteries, intoxication, and pride;
as well as human mothers and various kinds of living beings.
The pores of that great-souled bull were likewise [the gods].
Thus the blessed Lord, the Great God, endowed with supreme sovereignty,
became Saurabheya Mahādeva, who embodies all the gods.
Whoever hears or recites this account of Saurabheya’s birth and deeds according to their true nature, as well as his entire majesty—
being ever pure and undepressed in spirit— is liberated from all sins.
And when he dies at the proper time, he shall attain the world of Rudra. || 133 ||
This should never be given or even heard by a deceitful person,
nor by an atheist, a wicked person, or one of evil deeds.
It is [meant] for a son, a disciple, or a righteous, high-souled person.
This eternal secret should be given and heard by one who is pure.
May that Maheśa— who possesses the power of the worlds and the Vedas, by whom all goals are accomplished,
and who has great strength whose roar is like the thundering of clouds and the ocean— be forever well-disposed toward you.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Origin of the Bull," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
"In this manner, O Vyāsa, the Blessed One, the Lord of the Gods, having released the cloud..."
He became borne by a bull, just as I have described to you.
Vyāsa said:
How did the blessed goddess Kṛṣṇā attain a fair complexion? What was the cause of that as well? Indeed, I wish to know this.
Sanatkumāra said: Seated on the plateau of Mount Mandara, Umā and the Destroyer of Kama then took delight together with the Pramathas, who assumed various forms.
Then, while the Lord was sporting there, he addressed that noble lady as "Kṛṣṇā" in the course of conversation; she, being high-minded, became enraged.
Mahādeva, of great luster, embraced her as she was angry and,
remaining unperturbed, spoke these sweet words of consolation once more.
The God of gods said:
"O Goddess, O sinless one, do not give way to anger; O imperishable Creator of the universe, this was merely a jest on my part when I uttered the word 'Kṛṣṇa'."
"From this day forward, O fair-faced one, I shall not speak to you with such words; abandon your anger...
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard the God speaking thus, the daughter of the mountain king attained supreme satisfaction and spoke these words in a melodious voice.
The Goddess said:
"You are the teacher of all the world, worthy of worship, and indeed my husband.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus, the wielder of the Pināka bow was pleased by those words offered by the Goddess.
He invited her to choose a boon, and she was requested for this boon.
The Goddess said:
"Whenever you address me as 'Kṛṣṇa,' O best among speakers—"
At that time, O Lord, my heart seems as if it were being torn asunder. || 1.2 ||
I inform you, O Lord of All, [of him who possesses] unsurpassed golden complexion;
he is the sustainer of the world, the sovereign of the gods, whose prowess is equal to his own self;
he is the leader of all the deities and the destroyer of all the Daityas. || 13–15 ||
If you are pleased with me, O God, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then you should deign to permit me to perform penance. || 17 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Bhava, laughing, said to her, "Of what use is asceticism?
Whatever is desired through asceticism, that I shall grant to you this very day."
Thus addressed, Girijā said: "O Blessed One, while this intense penance is being performed, you alone shall be the giver of boons to me according to my desires."
Then, having been thus requested by him who perceives the purpose of all actions, [the king spoke].
Having bowed at the feet of Śiva, who possesses immeasurable splendor,
that goddess arrived in an instant at Himavat, the best of mountains,
which was adorned with the hermitages of the foremost sages. ||21-22||
Having reached Lake Mānasa and likewise that Bindusaras, as well as the divine Pāṇḍuśilā and the very source of the Gaṅgā;
then, having reached Mahālaya and likewise the Devadāru forest. ||23-24||
Having reached other excellent forests beyond that, the virtuous lady went further north of the mountain and beheld a single,
divine, and exceedingly beautiful peak situated in a secluded place.
Divine, consisting of gold, and covered with all medicinal herbs. ||26||
It was completely surrounded on all sides by auspicious surfaces of sapphire, great sapphire, and blue stones, and by wonderful trees made of jewels.
In some places it has the luster of a heap of collyrium and even of crystal;
in some places a divine golden stone, and again in some places a variegated gemstone; in some places a peak of red arsenic, and in some places resembling yellow orpiment.
With *śāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees, as well as *priyāla* and *āmra-ātaka*;
with *aśoka*, *campaka*, *lodhra*, *kadamba*, *āmra*, and *atimuktaka*; and with *nāga*, *punnāga*, *tilaka*, and fragrant *candana* trees. || 30 ||
It was adorned with *dhātakī* and *ketakī* trees, as well as *uddālaka*,
variegated plantains, date palms, and jackfruit trees;
it was further beautified by *bakula* and coconut trees, and by clusters of lotuses.
With kapittha, khadira, bhavya, and pārāvata trees as well.
It was covered with vine-arbors and likewise with mango groves,
which were always endowed with flowers and fruits and possessed the luster of beautiful gold;
it was further adorned with waterfalls and rivers.
It was resounded on all sides by the sweet warbling of birds.
It was filled with peacocks and cātaka birds, crowded with swans and ruddy geese, and made resonant by cranes, wagtails, and green pigeons;
it teemed with jīvañjīva birds and was thronged with buffaloes and bears.
It was frequented by lions and tigers and crowded with *śarabhas* and elephants;
resembling Mount Meru and Mandara, it bestowed the fruit of all merit.
It was as delightful as heaven, yet inaccessible to those of evil deeds and cruel actions.
Adorned with splendor, it was like a magnificent garden in personified form.
There, some trees bore honey-like fruit and granted every desire throughout all seasons;
others there were beautiful trees known as "milk-yielders" (kṣīrin).
Other trees bore all kinds of flowers and fruits;
other golden trees likewise blossomed and fruited,
while yet others produced all manner of edible fruits and foods everywhere.
Furthermore, great trees produce human and divine fruits of six flavors;
others produce garments, and even ornaments within their fruits.
Likewise, other trees provided various kinds of beds and ornaments;
and other trees produced honey free from bees, resembling nectar. (42)
Others produce various enjoyments as well as ornaments;
others bring forth women, and still others, human beings. (43)
The entire ground of that divine mountain peak is made of jewels;
a fragrant breeze blows there, being neither too hot nor too cold.
As long as the Great Goddess had not yet reached that mountain,
Rudra created it for the sake of pleasing her;
and by his very grace, that mountain peak remains inaccessible.
[This was] for all the hosts of gods and for all living beings in every way.
Sanatkumāra said:
On that excellent mountain, the Goddess performed a most difficult penance.
Wearing two beautiful garments made of bark that served as instruments for dharma,
she at times subsisted on fruits, at times on leaves,
at times she lived on water, and at times she fed only on air.
On one occasion, that lady of beautiful countenance stood on a single foot facing the sun, having restrained the entire collection of her senses. 49.
The goddess, who offers salutations to Mahādeva, is devoted to Mahādeva and is dear to Mahādeva; she seeks a boon for the sake of a son. (8.34.5)
Ajaikapāda, Rudra, as well as Dindimundeshvara, Kapalin, Bharabhuti, and Mashadhi, together with their followers. ||51||
And Nikumbha, whose anger has subsided, and Bhūtamohana, as well as Kāladaṇḍadhara and likewise Mṛtyudaṇḍadhara. ||52||
And likewise [he saw] the wielder of the Brahma-staff and the wielder of the terrible discus,
as well as the terrible ones who move through the intermediate space in the cardinal and intermediate directions—
these secret leaders of the hosts, invisible and facing in all directions.
Long ago, Mahādeva appointed them for her protection;
yet those lords of the Gaṇas, though possessed of immeasurable power, guarded that mountain neither from above nor from below, nor indeed from any side, remaining invisible everywhere. ||54-55||
Even though that mountain peak was being guarded by them in such a manner, the gods, dānavas, and gandharvas were unable to approach its vicinity;
this was all the more so because she had previously placed those [ornaments] upon the surface of the beautiful rock.

From them was born the river Bhūṣaṇā, whose waters are a source of merit. People even today behold that auspicious river, renowned as Alaṅkāradhārā, which destroys sins and possesses waters at all times. ||57-58||
O Vyāsa, on the very same day that the goddess, the daughter of the mountain, remained there in that manner, a tiger also approached her.
With a massive mouth, he was terrifying, with tawny and stainless eyes;
armed with claws and fangs, he was formidable and a source of terror to all embodied beings.
Emerging from the mouth of the cave, the one of great strength yawned;
then, beholding the goddess, he prepared to devour her,
for he was paralyzed by her ascetic power and thought only this.
"I have never before seen such a beautiful woman by the side of Śarva; considering the power of her asceticism, I believe she is not human.
Or rather, she has been constantly devoted to Maheśvara."
"The daughter of the Himalayas sports on Mount Mandara together with the God;
what need then has she for penance, since her husband is the wielder of the Pināka?
This other woman, possessing such beauty, must have undertaken penance and self-restraint for some other purpose."
"Endowed with such great splendor, this auspicious lady cannot be slain by me here today for the sake of food, since I have been rendered motionless by her. Therefore,
I shall wait upon her until the change of time occurs."
"Later, when she is dead, I myself shall devour this weak woman as I please,
like a sage afflicted by hunger eating fruit in a hermitage.
Having thought thus, that tiger remained at a distance from the goddess.
With his gaze fixed, his ears and tail erect, he sat and gazed at her;
and she too, the Goddess, seeing him standing there with his eyes turned upward,
remained unattached and always directed her mind toward him as one who bestows grace.
Vyāsa said:
While the goddess was intent upon the practice of austerity, what did the three-eyed god, the lord of the deities, do? This I wish to know.
Sanatkumāra said:
Listen to this which the god spoke when she was thus disposed toward him, her heart’s desire being fixed upon obtaining a son. (71)
While the Goddess was absorbed in penance, the Lord whose banner bears the bull came to bestow his grace upon the high-souled Upamanyu.
Once, that sage [received] excellent milk at his maternal uncle’s house. (72–73)
Having drunk the remnants of the *homa* offering, which were exceedingly sweet, from the *agnihotrin*,
he remembered them and said to his mother, "Mother, give me milk.
Distressed, his mother gave him flour, having stirred it with water.
Seeing that flour which had been brought forward as "milk," the sage then [spoke]. (75)
She said to her mother, "This is not milk. Then she spoke:
"Child, where can there be milk for us, or food for ascetics?
Propitiate Mahādeva; he will grant you everything."
Thus addressed by his mother at that time, he was overwhelmed with pain and grief.
Facing the Sun, standing restrained on one foot, he sought refuge with his whole being in the god Śaṅkara;
with his mind, he constantly meditated upon Hara, the remover of the distress of those who bow before him.
He remained for one thousand divine years subsisting on fruit alone. ||79||
The second year he subsisted on withered leaves, and the third he lived on water;
devoted to Mahādeva and having conquered his senses,
he remained for a thousand years subsisting on air alone.
When the fourth thousand autumns of the sage were fully completed, Śarva,
being pleased, then granted him a vision in the form of Śakra.
Śakra said:
"O Upamanyu, O highly fortunate one, you have accumulated great ascetic merit.
I am pleased with you; choose a boon, my son, whatever you desire."
Upamanyu said:
"Welcome to the King of the Gods, the sovereign of the three worlds!
Today I consider my own great penance performed to be free from all blemish."
I, who behold Indra, the lord of the three worlds and guardian of the quarters—here is water for the feet, here is the respectful offering, and here is the seat of grass. (84)
"And let this madhuparka be accepted by you, O Lord of the Assembly.
Tell me what I shall do; ask for it, O one of great strength.
Know that it is already accomplished, provided it is something that can be easily done by me. (85)
Śakra said: O Brahmin, in former times my father was your supreme friend and devotee;
out of that affection, seeing you established in asceticism, I [have come].
"Come here while you are still suffering; tell me, what shall I give to you?
Upamanyu said:
"O best of gods, I do not desire even the sovereignty of the gods from you."
I am a devotee of Mahādeva; therefore, I desire a boon from him. ||87||
Śakra said:
"Even the gods do not behold Mahādeva, the lord of the assembly;
you shall not see him either, O best of Brahmins. Tell me what is in your mind."
"O observer of great vows, I have come here out of affection for your father; for according to dharma you are my son. Therefore, speak, and I shall grant it to you.
Upamanyu said:
"You have performed your duty as my own kin; I have been honored by you, O Lord.
Depart, for I shall not ask for a boon from anyone other than Rudra. || 8.34.90 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed, the radiant Maheśvara, appearing in the form of Śakra, spoke:
"You will repent later; what can Rudra do for you?"
I am departing; may it be well with you, and may this undertaking of yours be free from obstacles.
O Lord, you should indeed remember me when you set out toward Rudra. (92)
Sanatkumāra said: When Indra had departed, Rudra then assumed his own form and,
remaining unperturbed, showed himself to him and spoke these words in a melodious voice.
Rudra said:
"O highly fortunate Upamanyu, behold me, freed from your distress.
Speak, having deliberated with your mind, whatever boon I shall grant you. (94)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having beheld the Lord of Gods and having bowed his head in prostration,
he spoke these words while remaining humble and reflecting deeply within his mind.
O Blessed One, who are always worshipped by the hosts of gods, if you are pleased, O Īśāna, grant me that which I ask; salutations to you!
Without depending on any substance whatsoever, whether human or divine— ||96||
One should eat milk-rice that has been offered unasked.
The God of gods said:
O best of the twice-born, here in this world there is nothing whatsoever that exists without depending [on something else].
"Therefore, O Great Sage, tell me [how one may attain this], even by taking refuge in a blade of grass.
Upamanyu said:
"O Blessed One, by your grace, I do not take refuge in anything at all."
"And this undertaking is for that purpose; therefore, grant it as requested.
The God of Gods said: "O Sage, there is no milk-rice for you without something to support it.
Having spoken thus to him, Mahādeva vanished right then and there.
Then, having vanished from that place, the wielder of the Pināka bow assumed the form of Brahmā for the sake of testing him and spoke to him once more.
Brahmā said: O Upamanyu, O one of great wisdom, your auspicious penance has been well-performed. I am pleased with you; choose a boon, and I shall grant it as you desire.
Upamanyu said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of all worlds, salutations to you, O Lord who creates all!
O God, O Protector of the world, my ascetic penance has been well-performed, since I behold you."
I am a devotee of Maheśvara, devoted to him and intent upon his grace;
therefore, O God, I choose no boon from you other than this, without a doubt.
Brahmā said: O Brahmin, Rudra did not give you even that milk-rice, which is difficult to obtain;
how then could he grant you any other supreme boon here?
"Shall I grant you the state of Prajāpati, or even the state of a god, or even immortality;
or shall I grant you the status of Indra, or the status of Soma, or the status of Viṣṇu? (106)
"May you become a world-protector, honored by all the worlds. Speak, what shall I give you today? Release Maheśvara;
that Īśāna will not give you even a single blade of grass, however small."
Upamanyu said:
"O Lord, nothing at all was taken by that high-souled one;
he is the lord of all beings, and there is no master over him."
The Lord performs all the tasks of petitioners according to His will;
He may grant me a gain, or He may not grant it. || 109 ||
What is the use of much prattling? I choose that which he has given;
whether it be hell or the state of a beast—what else could it possibly be? (8.34.1) 10.
"O Grandfather, I do not desire from you the status of Viṣṇu nor the status of Śakra. Depart, O Lord of all gods; do not undergo this fruitless distress.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by that brahmin seer, the Lord, the Master of the Gods,
then spoke these words again to him there for the sake of a boon;
and Upamanyu, too, fixed his mind immovably upon Īśāna.
The god also became silent and vanished right there.
Knowing his meditative absorption, the three-eyed Lord of the Pināka bow assumed his own form and revealed himself to him at that very moment.
Three-eyed, with matted hair, large-eyed, wearing earrings, and with blazing eyes;
bearing garlands of flames, glorious, and having a girdle bound with serpents. || 11.5 ||
He wore a serpent as his sacred thread and was clothed in a tiger skin;
he had a black antelope skin as an upper garment and likewise carried a water-pot.
He held a staff and a trident, possessed a great laugh, and was surrounded by many hosts of attendants.
He said, "O son, O son! I am pleased with your asceticism."
"By my grace, you shall become immortal, free from old age, devoid of all suffering, glorious, and able to assume any form at will. (119)
"Take this island, created by me, which moves at will;
it is surrounded on all sides by the ocean of milk and rice."
Having become one possessed of the power of great yoga, omniscient and pleasing to behold,
eat rice with milk, my child, always together with your kinsmen.
"O ascetic of noble vows, I bestow grace upon all seven of your ancestral lineages and upon this entire family as well.
O brahmin-sage, let all these who are your kinsmen become [prosperous]."
By my grace, O great beings, you shall always subsist on milk-rice.
Sanatkumāra said: Having received that boon and bowing his head to Bhava, he,
with a disciplined mind, placed his joined palms upon his head and offered praise.
Upamanyu said:
Salutations to the Lord of all the immortals; salutations again and again to the Lord of the universe.
Salutations to the remover of all afflictions, and salutations to the dispeller of sorrow.
Homage to the one with the speed of the wind; homage to the one whose form is the wind.
Homage to Kāñcanamāla; indeed, homage to Padmamāla.
Homage to the slayer of the enemies of the gods, and indeed homage to the one of fierce speed;
homage to the lord of the ancestors and gods, and indeed homage to the destroyer of the sacrifice.
Salutations to you who take the form of a woman and who assume all forms;
salutations to the destroyer of Kandarpa, and repeated salutations to the creator of the universe.
Salutations to the all-pervading noose, and salutations indeed to the inconceivable one;
you alone are our refuge and our highest good, and you are always our very heart.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having smelled him on the head, comforted him, and bid him farewell,
the venerable Lord Vyāsa, that powerful master, departed toward Sukeśa.

He made Upamanyu—who was blazing with the luster of fire and who sought to surpass Indra (Śatamanyu) through his ascetic penance—bow down before Hara; and by granting him a boon, he then removed his fierce anger. Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter of the Skanda Purāṇa, titled "The Granting of the Boon to Upamanyu."
Sanatkumāra said: Thereupon, O Vyāsa, that blessed Lord again made Sukeśa, the leader of the Gaṇas, a Brāhmaṇa devoted to austerity and truth.
Vyāsa said: How did that Brahmin formerly attain the state of Gaṇeśa?
By what austerity was the Lord pleased to grant him the status of Gaṇeśa? (2)
Sanatkumāra said:
There was a Brāhmaṇa born in the lineage of Vasiṣṭha, truthful in speech and pure,
who was devoted to pilgrimages and dedicated to fasting.
Once, while staying in a foreign land, he saw on the path in the forest a terrible tiger standing there, its mouth wide open, with claws and fangs as its weapons.
Having seen him, that Brahmin then quickly abandoned the path and entered a vast,
terrible forest devoid of living beings.
There he saw, leaning against a clump of vīraṇa grass in front of him, men hanging down, wailing, and deeply afflicted with suffering.
Seeing those twice-born ones hanging there with their heads downward, he asked, "Who are you? and they spoke this to him: ||| 7 ||
The ancestors said: "O evil-minded one, we are all your ancestors, hanging head-downwards in this hell; we hang from you, O Vīraṇa, because of your own fault. (8)
"Men desire sons with the thought, 'These will deliver us from hell'; but you, instead, will cast us, who are already suffering, into it.
The Brahmin said:
"O grandfathers, by whatever austerity I have acquired through visiting sacred fords, and by whatever merit I have performed since birth, by that means may you lift me up from this pit."
The ancestors said:
"We cannot be raised up from this pit by asceticism, nor by sacrifices, nor by any other means; do for us that which we tell you."
"Procreate a son endowed with virtues and devoted to austerity;
then, if you so deem fit, we may be released from this pit. (1.2)
The Brahmin said:
"I have undertaken this vow, thinking 'I am one whose vital energy is drawn upward. I shall not take a wife, and I shall indeed deliver my ancestors."
Then, having abandoned them in that manner and being overwhelmed by great sorrow, he went to Rudra for refuge; thereafter, his ancestors vanished.
When his ancestors had thus disappeared, the twice-born one then subsisted on air alone;
becoming like wood, clods of earth, or stone, he remained there without breathing.
Fixing his mind on Rudra, steady and well-composed,
he stood in the open air reciting the Rudras with his heart.
When that month was completed for him, there arose a great wind and rain.

It was the crusher of all beings, unbearable and accompanied by terrifying sounds. Yet, despite that great rain, he felt neither pain nor defeat at that time; rather, he remained perfectly steadfast. (17–18)
Then, when the seventh month had elapsed, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, assuming his own form, spoke to that best of the twice-born.
"I am pleased with you; may it be well with you, O observer of noble vows, because of this asceticism.
Choose a boon, O brahmin-sage, whatever dwells in your mind.
Then Sukeśa, seeing Nārāyaṇa standing before him, [spoke].
He said, "O Śaṅkara, I do not desire a boon from you."
Viṣṇu said:
"Enough of this persistence regarding Hara, O brahmin-sage;
he cannot even be seen by the gods, much less by humans."
Sukeśa said:
"Whether I am capable of being seen by you or not—what is the use of these deliberations of yours?
Whether I am a bad grasp or a good grasp, my mind is nevertheless fixed upon the Lord."
O Lord of the Wheel, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious,
I desire no boon from you, nor from anyone else whatsoever. For even you, O God, are entirely absorbed in that very deity.
Because you worship him and praise him, he is therefore called the most excellent.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having understood his resolve, the blessed Lord Hara was satisfied;
casting off the form of Viṣṇu, he resumed his own form. (26)
And he said to him, "O best of Brahmins, become my imperishable attendant (gaṇapa), free from death, abandoned by old age, and devoid of all suffering. (27)
Endowed with sovereignty, you shall be dear to me and my foremost attendant.
And this divine mountain named Trikūṭa, created by me,
which moves at will and is filled with golden palaces— I offer it to you.
And for whose sake, my son, you have exerted yourself to please me. || 29 ||

O sinless one, all these ancestors have been delivered from the terrible hell by you, their excellent son; they have come before you as Gaṇeśa. Free from suffering forever, they shall become your servants.
These lords of the Gaṇas shall become subject to your will.
"You shall become renowned by the name Sukeśa,
and you shall always move about endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers."
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having seen his ancestors along with their kinsmen delivered from hell and endowed once more with the status of a lord of the Gaṇas, worthy of worship; ||| 3 3 ||
With a joyful mind, he approached Maheśvara with his head bowed and palms joined;
then, his face beaming with delight, that master of speech spoke.
Sukeśa said:
"O Blessed One, the status of Gaṇapati and sovereignty have been obtained by me;
likewise, immortality, inexhaustibility, and the boon of agelessness."
These ancestors have been delivered, and these leaders of my hosts have been appointed;
moreover, this mountain that moves at will has been obtained by me through your grace. ||36||
O Great God, O Soma, Sovereign of the foremost lords, O one of ever-gracious countenance, O granter of desires, I desire you exceedingly as one who is most beautiful to behold. (37)
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by the high-souled Sukeśa, the Blessed One spoke as follows:
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, all this shall come to pass."
"Taking refuge on this mountain together with these excellent and noble ones,
go, my child, to your desired destination and protect the gods and the brahmins.
Then the God dismissed Sukeśa, the leader of the Gaṇas.
Soma vanished from the sight of all who were looking on.
Sukeśa, too, remained on that mountain in the city which resembled heaven,
and he earnestly questioned his ancestors regarding the true nature of the hells.
Vyāsa said: O Brahmin, for what purpose did the leader of the Gaṇas question those ancestors,
and how did the ancestors there explain it to that wise one?
"O dear one, I wish to hear from you this matter exactly as it is, whether in detail or in brief— beneficial and bringing all happiness.
Sūta said:
Thus addressed, that lord, the son of Surasṛk and architect of celestial chariots,
having completed his task and being the enhancer of the world of the gods, spoke these words which destroy all previously committed evil deeds.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Bestowing of Boons upon Sukeśa," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: On that peak of Trikūṭa, in the city fashioned by the gods,
he was seated in a divine golden celestial chariot crowded with women.
Having then summoned all the ancestors and worshipped them according to the prescribed rites,
he beheld them seated comfortably and spoke these words.
Sukeśa said:
"O gods, it is by your splendor that all this sovereignty of such a kind exists; it was brought about by you, whereby I have been made a partaker of happiness. (3)
The ancestors said:
"Do not speak such a falsehood, my son; let there be no unrighteousness for you here.
By our grace, O son, you shall never possess sovereign power."
But we, being driven into a terrible and most dreadful hell, have attained through your asceticism and prowess a happiness that is very difficult to obtain. ||5||
Just as we have been delivered from hell by you, our excellent son, so do we see no other way; for you are blessed, truly our son.
Today, for many thousands of years, we [have dwelt] in hell.
We would have been cooked in a terrible place for our evil conduct, had you not been our kinsman.
O son, many living beings who are self-restrained there, yet are extremely wicked and devoid of asceticism, are tormented in that most terrible place. (8)
Sukeśa said:
"O ancestors, never before have I spoken falsely, nor do I speak it now;
for such was my sovereignty at that time through the power of you all."
Listen well to me as I speak; do not disregard my words. O ancestors, I do not hold the gods in contempt—who indeed would hold them in contempt?
The ancestors perform those deeds on earth that are esteemed by the virtuous.
And they always pray: "May our subjects be abundant. || 11 ||
Those who are righteous, grateful, and devoted to virtuous deeds will constantly rescue us from remaining in the pit of hell.
Because they perform that duty and do not fall away from their own dharma,
that dharma, when properly practiced, produces auspicious progeny.
They are righteous, generous, grateful, and established on the path of the virtuous;
they are devoted to their fathers and everywhere intent upon the liberation of their ancestors. 114.
Thus, by you all, through righteousness and supreme meditative concentration, I have been produced, endowed with ascetic power, and entirely devoted to you alone.
Having propitiated the god, I have further delivered my ancestors from hell.
"This is the power of you all, as well as your well-performed asceticism.
O ones of great wisdom, what falsehood could there be here in my words? And this is the auspicious Vedic revelation, O best among the knowers of the Vedas. (1.6–17)
If you consider yourself an authority because you were made by yourself, [then know that] you arise from limb after limb; you are born from the heart. 18.
"You are indeed my very self, named 'son'; live for a hundred autumns! I have arisen from your limbs and from your heart;
thus, by means of my own self, I shall deliver myself and you."
Therefore, you all should consider that everyone [is saved] by means of meditative concentration (samādhi).
For it is by one's own karma that people are rescued from the terrible intermediate state;
no other person of dull intellect can cross over by means of another's karma.
"For the ripening of the fruits of the actions of living beings is ordained by their own karma.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then those very ancestors were addressed in this manner by that high-souled one.
With eyes full of tears, they then spoke these words out of joy.
The fathers said:
"Who else but you would speak thus, unless one were approved by the Lord?"
These words of yours are fitting for you, a righteous and high-souled being. ||23||
O son, how could the Lord of all gods not properly unite with sacrifices one who is not such as you, just as the bull-bannered god has united with you? 24.
"You are the Sustainer, for you are our kinsman; you are the progenitor, O Great-minded One!
You alone are our father, and we are indeed your sons—of this there is no doubt.
In this regard, O Great-minded One, we shall relate to you an ancient account."
You ought to consider that which has been sung in the Śruti and the Smṛti for our sake. ||26||
The Pitṛs said: "O sons, you were created by Brahmā with the command, 'Sacrifice to me.
Yet they sacrificed to their own selves; at that, Brahmā became enraged with them. (27)
Enraged, he said to them, "You shall lose your consciousness.
Thus all those inhabitants of heaven were cursed by Brahmā as they gathered together.
Overcome by suffering and grief, they were dejected; yet, beholding him so gracious, they then praised him, bowing their heads and speaking thus. (29)
"O Lord, our consciousness has been lost; restore it to us, O Master! And forgive us, O Lord of Gods, for that which we have done out of ignorance. (8.36.30)
Then, having been addressed thus by those gods, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, spoke these words of compassion to the prostrate deities: |||31||
Brahmā said:
"O beings of great courage, perform penance according to the prescribed rules;
thereby you shall cast off all the sin born of transgression."
The gods said: "O Lord, O Sovereign Creator of All, that very designation by which we might know those expiations is not known to us, O Protector of the World. (33)
Brahmā said:
"Ask your own sons; from them you shall obtain what is beneficial. Furthermore, O knowers of dharma, do not lose your composure again, nor act otherwise than this."
The Pitṛs said:
Then those tigers among the gods questioned their sons regarding expiations,
duties, and the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs and in full detail.
Then those auspicious sons, being self-restrained, reported all that exactly as it had happened through their supreme meditative concentration. Thereupon,
they regained their senses and likewise attained their desires.
Filled with joy and delight, they addressed their own sons.
The gods said:
"O sons, you are not our sons; rather, we are indeed the sons born of you, by whom eternal knowledge has been bestowed upon us whose consciousness was lost. (38)
When they had spoken thus, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, arrived there;
and the highly illustrious one spoke these words to all those gods.
Brahmā said:
The gods do not speak falsehood; truth abides among the gods.
For all of you have been called "sons," and "fathers"—that is indeed no falsehood. (8.36.40)
Therefore, your fatherhood toward your sons shall be eternal and imperishable;
of this there is no doubt, for you are sons in every respect.
Indeed, secret doctrines are never told to one who is not a disciple.
Son and disciple have the same purpose; therefore, you are all sons in every respect.
Through sons, fathers cross over, and they cause those sons to cross over as well.
Having caused them to cross over, they attain the status of "fathers" through that very deed.
And you have likewise been delivered from hell by your sons out of ignorance;
therefore, these indeed are fathers and you are all sons. Because he protects, he is called "father" (pitā), or because he procreates, he is also "father. (44)
And because both of these [qualities] reside in their sons, fathers are considered as such by you;
therefore, they are [endowed with] Brahman...
[and possessed of] power.
The ancestors invited them with desired boons as they pleased.
Then the ancestors chose for themselves the first right of sacrifice:
"He who, without having sacrificed to us, should sacrifice to the gods, shall not obtain the fruit thereof. || 47-48 ||
And being joined with sin,
they all departed from there just as they had come, together with Brahmā. (8.36.50) The Pitṛs said:
Just as we, O son, were rescued from the hells by you with our minds restored and our consciousness renewed, and were once again exalted;
therefore, you are our venerable father, whom we follow. ||51||
...the seventh.
Bowing down with palms joined in reverence, he spoke these words to his ancestors:
"It is exactly as you have said; your auspicious words are not false."
"For it has been declared that all are fathers to one another.
O lords of the Gaṇas, grant me this further boon;
for by means of this, my desired question has indeed been stated, O best of the twice-born. (54–55)
The Pitṛs said:
"O Supreme Lord, there is nothing unknown to you.
You wish to explain the truth here for our sake as a standard of authority. (56)
"Tell us what is not already known to us; we shall indeed relate that to you—whether heard or experienced—as it truly is and according to our ability.
Sukeśa said:
"Sirs, you have been tormented in the most dreadful and terrible hell;
therefore, you who possess the knowledge of the scriptures undoubtedly know the true nature, the conjunction, the temporal distinctions, and the sequence of all hells. (58)
I wish to hear all of that, for my curiosity is indeed great:
how many are those hells, what is their extent, and what is their basis? What is their form, who is cast into them, and how indeed do they suffer so intensely? (8.36.59–60)
And how does a living being suffer, and likewise, how is he rebuked?
After what length of time is he liberated from hell? Once liberated, by what means does he arise, and how does he transmigrate again? || 6.2 ||
"O ones of great wisdom, relate all of this in its entirety, in detail, and exactly as it is; for my curiosity is indeed supreme."
To him—the foremost among Upendra, Pitāmaha, Īśvara, and Īśa; who has realized the treasury of the true nature of reality;
whose yoga is marked by the destruction of evil and leads to liberation—they declare this to be the supreme yoga for every yoga.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Great Fortune of Sukeśa," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then those ancestors [considered] his establishment regarding his own son.
The immutable ones declared it to be known as Sumarmāṇa. ||1||
The ancestors said: "O son, your father Suśarman, world-renowned,
will explain to you in accordance with the truth that which has been mentioned by you."
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O brahmin-sage, the high-minded Suśarman, having taken leave of him, spoke these words to Sukeśa, that being of great courage and foremost among the Gaṇas.
Suśarman said: "O Sukeśa, we have not ourselves fallen directly into the ocean of hell;
yet, with our hearts resting upon you, we shall fall without you."
But, terrified by those torments, we reflect day and night:
"Of what nature are those most dreadful hells, so terrible to hear about? (5)
Therefore, O Lord of the Lords of the Gaṇas, listen as I describe to you the hells that have been proclaimed, according to my wisdom and according to what I have heard. (6)
Difficult to approach, extremely impassable, and terrifying to all living beings—
therein is the first hell, renowned as Yamalācala;
the second is named Śālmalī, and the third is Kālasūtraka.
The fourth is Kumbhīpāka, and the next is Asipatravana. ||8||
Likewise, Vaitaraṇī is the sixth, and Ayoghana is the seventh;
the eighth is Padma, and Mahāpadma is the next.
Raurava is the tenth, and Mahāraurava as well;
the twelfth is named Tamas, and likewise Tamastamataras.
These are the great hells, and there are others as well;
for each one, eight secondary hells (ucchrayas) have also been proclaimed. O Lord, within these secondary hells, there is torment interspersed with intervals of rest.
But in the others there is no rest; for this is proclaimed as the distinction. || 1.2 ||
The constant suffering of those men arises from their sinful deeds;
however, as their sin is exhausted through its gradual depletion, their sequence [of rebirths] will now be described.
O Gaṇeśa, it is impossible to state the full measure of this individually.
Due to the mastery over that karma, through its exhaustion, he perceives the end. ||14||
