Everyone who has fallen into hell does not see its end;
hear from me, O Vyasa, how those whose sins are exhausted perceive it.
Having fallen into the terrible hell by his own evil deed, the doer of wickedness [remains there].
Being driven along most piteously, he takes refuge in a single direction.
Having traveled quickly on that road extending for many yojanas, and having failed to reach many others, he turns back from its end. || 16-17 ||
Turning back from there once more, driven along, he goes senseless;
having gone toward another direction, he likewise turns back again. (18)
Having thus gone in all directions, yet not finding an end, he becomes distressed;
he wanders there piteously, for no one exists here [to help him].
At the end of the torment, yet before the end of his sin,
he then perceives once more that which is limited and entirely circumscribed.
One is liberated from that by means of the great gate;
for in this way, all hells are indeed infinite, inexhaustible, and imperishable.
No calculation in yojanas can be made for them;
rather, it is by the time that a living being falls down again, suffering in misery. ||22||
Listen, O Lord, O sinless one, as I describe this:
having committed sinful deeds, at the end of their exhaustion, the evil-minded person,
afflicted by disease and mental anguish, then casts off his own body.
Bound with great nooses by the messengers of Yama and impelled by suffering,
O Lord, he is led along a rugged path, his form distorted,
being pierced here and there by iron thorns. ||24-25||
Being smeared on all sides with the mud of hair, marrow, and bones,
he falls again and again into uneven pits and is further shattered;
in some places, he is overwhelmed by a great rain of stones.
There, his head-hair, knees, feet, arms, and the joints of his thighs were severed. ||27||
He is dragged by the messengers of Yama and further pierced by thorny trees;
he is stretched out, split apart, and bound fast with creepers.
Thus, O Lord, by means of paths that cause suffering in many such forms—
Led helplessly by the afflictions, one goes to the abode of Yama. 29.
Then, having not reached Yama but from afar by Yama’s command,
he approaches Citragupta and is made to hear of the karma that was performed.
Then Soma, Agni, Varuṇa, Vāyu, and Sūrya—these serve as witnesses there, declaring for all living beings what has been done and what has not been done. (31)
Having been thus addressed, examined, and interrogated by Citragupta,
the afflicted one is cast into hell with his feet upward and his head downward.
And he struck them with exceedingly sharp-pointed arrows, as well as with battle-axes, slings,
mallets, javelins, and long spears.
With iron bars, saws, thunderbolts, chisels, ploughs, stones, wedges, pestles, and indeed with alkaline flour; 34.
Being struck day and night by blazing, terrible weapons and even by a rain of fire, he cried out piteously and profusely.
For a thousand years he attains the auspicious hell;
having fallen there, he remains exceedingly miserable as he is tormented once again. ||36||
For ten million years without rest, he falls into the depths of hell;
and once released from that great hell, he takes refuge in another place of torment.
Touched by the cool wind, he finds happiness there;
having attained that respite, he then forgets his torment. (38)
In a dream lasting but a moment, he was dragged away by a Rākṣasa;
and as he was being dragged by him, he was once again afflicted by pain and grief.
Having lamented piteously and excessively in many ways, he remained there; then that Rākṣasa dragged him back once more toward the place of torment.
It indeed torments that living being, though he possesses consciousness and occasional respite;
there, for a thousand years, he is truly tormented once again.
Indeed, he remains for exactly as long as it takes for another terrible birth to come about;
thus, through his sinful karma, he undergoes eight such births.
In this cycle of existence, those lowest of men who go to those terrible hells are reborn as creatures such as worms and insects. || 43 ||
I shall describe them to you in brief, O son:
the first hell that was mentioned by me is Yamalācala.
Men who are destined for the great hells go there at the end.
There were two mountains teeming with bears, elephants, lions, and tigers; crowded with *śarabha*s and elephants, and filled with many serpents;
[and they were also filled] with birds of various forms and with men with uplifted weapons. ||45-46||
They are joined by leafless trees with thorns like needles and diamonds;
between those two is indeed a single level space covered with needles. ||47||
They were likewise surrounded by upward-pointing, adamantine-beaked, and impenetrable [thorns],
and on all sides encircled by a wall of iron, while on the other side they were hemmed in by terrible men with weapons in their hands.
And even in the sky, those two were completely covered by an iron net.

Those men who violate a woman who does not desire it, those who assault another's wife, and indeed those who defile a maiden; those who misappropriate a deposit, as well as those who steal meat—go there. (8.37.50)
Those who steal flavors, those who defile others,
those who destroy the collection of the senses, those who assume false marks of asceticism,
those who kill deer and wild beasts, and those who eat the flesh from the backs [of animals]— [these are the ones excluded]. || 51-52 ||

O son, those who eat meat in vain and those who commit acts of violence—these lowest of men go to the mountain of Yama. And that lowest of men who does not perform [funeral rites] when twins have been born [to him], [goes there as well]. || 5.3 ||
And that man of impure soul undergoes the penance;
being pursued by those men as described and being cut by their weapons, he reaches that mountain. ||54-55||
There he is devoured by enraged tigers, śarabhas, hyenas, serpents, cats, birds, and iron-beaked creatures.
And if, while being devoured by them, he climbs a tree, [he is still not released].
There he is pierced by those sharp thorns and indeed by birds;
then, if he wishes to go to its ravine or cave, even there he is burned by fire and, afflicted by suffering, turns back. ||57-58||
If, however, a terrible interval between those two is encountered, there the man's feet are pierced with fierce needles. ||59||
Seeing that he was divided and unable to escape,
those two immovable ones quickly joined together and tormented him exceedingly, like sugarcane in a press.
Being thus oppressed by the two immovables, he became as distressed as if crushed in a machine.
Wailing piteously, he indeed undergoes that torment.
Furthermore, whether it has been eaten, torn apart, devoured by birds,
or burnt, a new body is born once again.
Thus, being driven along for many years in great suffering, he reaches the gate and emerges; yet, upon reaching the heights, he is cast down.
He falls toward this mountain of Yama, which possesses fierce velocity and is joined with the fruits of manifold sinful deeds.
He who listens to this constantly with intense devotion shall never again enter into that state of fierce evil.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Yamalācala," in the description of the hells within the Skanda Purāṇa. Suśarman said:
Hereafter, I shall again describe the Śālmalī hell.
There, men who have committed very grievous sins go;
O Lord of the Pre-eminent, there are many thousands of *śālmalī* trees,
all of which are lofty, terrible, and extend for many *yojanas*.
They possessed great branches, great leaves, and were covered with large thorns;
they were completely enclosed by a massive iron wall and were all topped over with a great net.
Many men with angry faces stand there. 44.
Holding vajras, staffs, and stones, and bearing swords and mallets—
with various other forms of weapons in their hands—
those most terrible beings violently torment helpless creatures.
And there they were also being cut to pieces by Rākṣasas of cruel deeds.
Afflicted by sensation and deeply distressed, he flees in all directions;
wherever he goes, there he is struck down.
And when they have fallen into pits, the exceedingly cruel Rākṣasas, having seized them from all sides, cut them to pieces with weapons of various forms. || 8 ||
Proclaiming the sins committed in the past by that evil-minded one, and rebuking that man of wicked conduct who had indeed fallen somewhere; ||| 9 ||
Then, rising up with his limbs mangled and pursued by the rākṣasas,
he reaches another region filled with needle-like thorns.
There, being pierced again by fierce needles and iron thorns, he cries out in agony and falls down, overwhelmed by extreme suffering.
There too, having encountered him, those with various weapons in their hands [assail him].
Rākṣasas indeed rush toward one just as enemies attack an enemy. || 1.2 ||
If, rising up from there with speed, he climbs a tree,
he is pierced and even cut by the sharp thorns found upon it.
With his ears, eyes, nose, and lips torn away by birds of various forms with iron beaks, he fell upon the surface of the earth.
There, they are pierced in all their limbs with fierce needles;
thus do those suffering there undergo various kinds of torments.
Listen as I declare those of evil conduct who fall [into hell]: he who sets fire to a house, he who administers poison, and he who approaches a woman of low birth. (1.6)
He who emits semen in a male, a poisoner, a seller of meat, one who travels by sea, a wicked-souled person, and he who eats delicacies all alone; || 17 ||
He who does not honor a guest, he who observes false vows, the one who has spilled the Veda-water (*brahmocchiṣṭa*), the naked ascetic, and the twice-born man who enters [the womb] as a woman;
the village watchman, the priest of a village, and likewise the teacher of Śūdras—[these are those from whom one should not accept food]. (18)
Likewise, a greedy usurer and one who sells the Veda. (19)
These evildoers go to the place known as Kūṭaśālmalī;
having emerged after two crores of years, they indeed return once again.

Having been cast down upon the height, they rest there for a short time and are then cast again into that hell until their sin is exhausted. O Sage, this same rule is recorded for the other hells as well.

He who, though his nature be curious, listens with self-restraint to this account of the intense suffering of those who perceive [objects]— an account as difficult to traverse as a mountain for the virtuous— shall certainly not go to the Śālmalī hell.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Kūṭaśālmalī [Hell]," in the description of the hells within the Skanda Purāṇa. Suśarman said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the hell named Kālasūtraka.
It is well-enclosed on all sides by a great and high wall;
likewise, it is covered even in the sky with a net of iron.
Just as this one is enclosed, so too are all the hells enclosed.
Those who are highly elevated [in status] should also be known; I shall not describe them further.
There, those lowest of men who are haters of the world go.
Those who abduct a woman, or likewise one who sells cows—
One who reviles Dharma, the Self, and the Brahmins;
one who deceitfully conceals the scriptures from his teachers;
and one who likewise reviles his teacher, his father, or his mother—[these are those who must be avoided]. ||4-5||
He who reviles his father-in-law, his elder brother, or other elders, as well as he who treats them with contempt; likewise,
he who violates the rules of the stages of life (āśramas) and all secret doctrines.
O twice-born one, he who takes what has not been given shall indeed go there;
those evil-minded, lowest of men, having fallen into that terrible hell,
shall remain for a full three crores of years.
At the word "Death," they go forth wailing and deprived of their senses. ||8||
Having repeatedly measured out their evil deeds with a great black cord,
they violently sever the limbs of those beings with weapons that have blunt tips.
By those servants, who are tireless and unwearied day and night,
when the time is fulfilled, the creature then attains its height;
having rested there, that creature is then cast back again into hell.
Until all the evil he has committed is exhausted without remainder. || 1.1 ||

Whoever should hear this Sūtra on the Doer of Many Evils, this Sūtra on Worldly Deeds that are Difficult to Perform, shall not go to that hell of the Yama-world, the Kālasūtra, where there is that fierce suffering. || 1.2 ||
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "Kālasūtra," in the Description of Hells within the Skanda Purāṇa.
Suśarman said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the most terrifying Kumbhīpāka hell.
At that time, it was indeed terrifying for the listeners whose minds were undisciplined.
There, the cauldrons of Brahmā were as large as mountains of collyrium,
filled with oil, glowing like fire, and exceedingly difficult to endure.
When those [rivers] are heated, the mighty and terrible Rākṣasas bind the evildoers one after another and cast them in while they cry out most fearfully. (3)
O Lord, living beings are cooked there for four million years;
understand from me, as I speak them, who those are.
One who bakes bricks, as well as one who bakes jars,
he who destroys those two, he who sets fire to houses,
and he who destroys food and drink in the forest, in the threshing floor, or in the cow-pen— [these are all to be avoided].
One who creates obstacles to feeding, a destroyer of sacrifices, and a burner of sacrifices;
one who performs fraudulent deeds and likewise one who is a false witness;
one who piles up sacrificial fires falsely and likewise one who brings forth sacrificial fires falsely. || 6–7 ||
The one who gives false results and the one who reviles the Vedas,
as well as that lowest of men who steals the tools of artisans—
such people are made to pass through there, finding rest only upon being raised up again.
Having reached [the end], they fall again into hell until its exhaustion.
Indeed, that person who hears of this ripening of karma— the culmination of many evil deeds—
does not go to that hell of wicked self, the ripening of the *kumbhīpāka* torture which inflicts such agonizing suffering.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of Hell: Kumbhīpāka," in the Skanda Purāṇa. Suśarman said:
Hereafter, I shall further describe the Asipatravana hell.
The hell of the evildoer is a place of suffering that strikes fear into all beings.
There, trees known as "Sword-leaved" (Asipatra) are difficult to approach;
they have many great branches and are exceedingly dense and tall.
Their leaves are terrible, sharp, and resemble swords;
they are superior to those made of iron, for they are not indeed made of iron.
O Mahāmati, those [leaves] are distinguished by their sharpness for cutting;
they are covered with such leaves and likewise possess thorns.
There, living beings bound by their evil karma are guarded by rākṣasas.
Being struck by swords and clubs, as well as by other great weapons,
and being consumed by fire, they flee toward those trees; yet,
upon seeing them approach, even the leaves fall from them.
Great and sharp [weapons] indeed cut them down;
with their heads and necks severed, they depart from that region.
Having gone there, they are repeatedly assailed by Rākṣasas and by trees difficult to approach;
for five crores of years, they remain there in great misery.
Then, once released from those, they indeed enter into high elevations.
Having found rest there, they all [were cast] again into the Ucchraya hell. || 9 ||
Those sinful men who go to that terrible hell are cast down helpless and deluded until their evil karma has reached its end.
I shall fully declare those [sins] to you; listen attentively, O twice-born one!
That evil-minded person who destroys a tree that has been treated as a son— ||1||
The evil-minded man sells [the wood] either in a grove or in a village;
likewise, he fells a tree that has grown in a hermitage, on a path,
in a pond, in a garden, or in temples dedicated to the gods.
Whether in a house, at a water-station, on the bank of a river, or at a crossroads—
wherever they may have grown— the evil-minded person who destroys trees, shrubs, creepers, bushes, or even grasses, [is reborn as a tree]. || 13–14 ||
For that fool who destroys [a tree] for the sake of its shade, flowers, or fruit, or for the sake of performing his own work, meets with that very same fate. || 1.5 ||
And he who plucks the roots, flowers, and fruits for his own sake and for the gratification of his desires, and not for the sake of the gods or the ancestors; || 1.6 ||
He who obstructs a river, he who fills up wells,
and that lowest of men who cuts down a tree for the sake of its leaves or bark,
or destroys that tree— he incurs the same [retribution]. || 17 ||
And whoever harasses creatures that have approached his shade,
or frightens those who are near his own dwelling, or even drives them away—
all of them fall into that great, elevated hell.
Having crossed over from there, those of inauspicious deeds go once more into saṃsāra.
But he who, with an unwearied mind, should hear this account of hell— the place of misery for evildoers—
he, a man of meritorious deeds and one who knows the self, does not encounter that place named Asipatravana.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Forest of Sword-Leaves," in the description of the hells within the Skanda Purāṇa. Suśarman said:
Hereafter [I shall describe] the river Vaitaraṇī, which destroys all sins.
Listen attentively, my son, to [the description of] the river Vaitaraṇī, which brings fear through its evil deeds. My son, that formidable river has banks carved away by axes;
it is filled with hair, bones, and blood, and possesses a highly caustic liquid.
It was crowded with *ullumpakas*, *gardabhas*, crocodiles, and even tortoises;
with porpoises, *nakras*, *tantukas*, and even *rākṣasas*;
and with large-toothed, massive-bodied flesh-eaters.
And it was completely covered by those trees growing on the banks, which possessed sword-like leaves.
And it was covered by long moss as if by a canopy;
on its bank was a formidable forest teeming with śarabhas and bears,
crowded with tigers and leopards, and filled with lions, elephants, and donkeys.
There, those who have performed evil deeds are tormented by those tigers and other beasts.
Then those suffering beings are cast into that most terrible river;
having fallen there, my child, they are entangled by weeds and moss.
Bound together by a canopy, they are devoured by those [beings] with their beaks;
being burned by alkaline water, they cry out in their suffering. (8)
They remain there for sixty million years until the exhaustion of their evil karma;
once liberated from that, they are indeed cast down again and again into the heights.
All those who were cast down helplessly and deludedly into the high precipices of hell find rest there until their sin has reached its end;
having emerged from these precipices, they return once more to the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
Furthermore, among those who have crossed over from the various hells,
one *koṭi* of time increases further and further for each individual height.
For all of them, it increases separately for each one.
In brief, O son, it increases by a thousand years.
But those of wicked mind who go to that terrible hell—listen to them as they are correctly described by me, O sinless one. (13)
He who curses a river, he who treats her with contempt, he who enters her while naked, or he who has sexual intercourse with her;
or he who spits, or voids urine, or even discharges excrement into her—[he incurs the same fate]. (14)
He who steals water from fields, gardens, or those belonging to people; he who destroys the embankments of rivers, and likewise he who breaches a tank or a man who defiles lotus ponds; || 16 ||
Whether she be wicked or virtuous, whoever defiles a woman, or that evil-minded man who steals or destroys a lotus-lake (padminī); || 17 ||
Those lowest of men who bring fear to a caravan or to any living being shall all fall into a terrible hell. ||1.8||

He who, being self-restrained, constantly hears this [teaching] which destroys impurity and subdues uncleanness, shall not go to the impassable river Vaitaraṇī, which must be crossed through meditation. ||19||
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, named Vaitaraṇī, in the Description of Hells within the Skanda Purāṇa.
Hereafter, I shall describe the hell known as Ayoghana, which destroys sins and strikes terror into all living beings. (1)
There, those terrible men, resembling Yama, the servants of Yama—possessing great strength and great courage, and likewise all masters of yoga—[stand]. || 2 ||
Just as blacksmiths take a lump of iron heated by fire,
seize it with tongs, and place it upon a solid anvil,
so too do they strike it with other heavy hammers; even so are living beings there treated.
They are struck by terrible Rākṣasas who threaten them most cruelly;
thus, for seven times ten million years, they pass their time through their own karma, undergoing horrific torments in those elevations. ||4-5||
I shall now fully describe those men who go to that great, towering hell— those irreproachable lowest of men:
he who would strike his father, his mother, or even one worthy of honor with his foot.
Or likewise, one who strikes any other woman with his hand or with a whip and the like; or one who steps over a renunciant, or even fire;
or one who, for the sake of wealth, brings death upon a child.
Whether it be a woman, a man, or a eunuch, that lowest of men who seeks to deceive his brothers over some matter of property indeed [is such]. (9)

Whether it be a father, or a mother, or even a sister, or a husband who deceives his own wife, or sons who deceive their parents— the destination of those [deceivers] is said to be hers [of the deceived]. (8.43.10)
And for that evil-minded person who would desecrate the images of the gods, sacred pilgrimage sites,
or divine sciences and scriptures— that is said to be their destination.
He who constantly hears this [account], which is the cause of the conjunction of many sins and the perpetual destroyer of happiness—
For one who strives, that terrifying hell—difficult to traverse, like a descent into battle—does not come to pass. || 1.2 ||
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, named "The Iron Hammer," in the description of the hells within the Skanda Purāṇa.
Suśarman said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the exceedingly difficult-to-traverse Padma hell.
It is unattainable for those of virtuous deeds, yet it brings terror to those of evil deeds. ||1||
There, a fire named Tāpana blazes as if being blown upon; living beings are scorched there and become the color of fire. ||2||
All of them, resembling lotus petals, were being heated here and there;
in the midst of that stood a great iron pillar.
Having gone there, they hide themselves from him; yet that fire is exceedingly fierce.
Thus, even upon those lofty peaks, they endure a constant and terrible suffering.
Listen to me regarding those men who go to that state free from attachment:
he who would approach the wife of his guru, or he who would steal the property of his guru. ||5||
He who consumes or repeatedly destroys the property of the gods,
he who seizes the wealth of a Brāhmaṇa or even forcibly retains it;
he who steals the property of children or the wealth of women— [these are all equal].
He who abandons eunuchs, and he who would kill one who has come for refuge. ||7||
He who covets another's wealth, he who misappropriates the property of the gods, he who eats all things indiscriminately, and he who sells water—[these are equal to the killer of a cow]. || 8 ||
One who sells Soma, one who extinguishes fires,
one who hurls fire [at others], one who hurls poison,
and a man who kills unarmed people in battle with a weapon; ||9||
Whether they are begging, or likewise sitting down,
or even turning their backs, or engaged in conversation with another— all such men there go [to hell], being of unrefined intellect. (8.44.10–11)
He who, being self-restrained, constantly hears this account of the abode of Death— the dwelling place of manifold miseries—
shall not go to that hell of fierce sorrow, which is like death itself and the very seat of Time.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, named Padma, in the Description of Hells within the Skanda Purāṇa. Suśarman said:
Beyond that is another hell, Mahāpadma, which causes the hair to stand on end.
There, those terrible henchmen of Yama, who resemble Yama himself,
mercilessly cut away the flesh from the bodies of sinful beings with blunt weapons and give it back to them again and again.
Having devoured their own flesh, those doers of evil deeds become like lotus petals and are burned in the fire day and night.
Furthermore, when iron has been liquefied by a terrible fire,
the cruel servants of Yama pour it back into their mouths.
Likewise, there are women made of iron and men with a radiance like fire.
Having come together from here and there, they run about and embrace one another. ||5||
And there are many trees there, beautifully flowering and laden with fruit;
afflicted by suffering, they take refuge in them, and they too rain down fire.
And there are many other rocks there, which they cling to when they reach them.
Then those women, glowing with the color of fire, burn those men intensely.
Thus has this great hell, Mahāpadma, been fully described;
it is for the man who steals gold and for the man who violates his mother. (8)
He who approaches his mother or his son, he who corrupts the Vedas or violates his vows of celibacy, he who is envious, he who is ill-behaved, and he who honors the śramaṇas. ||9||
That outcaste who might speak the Veda, or even listen to it, or likewise take it up with a wicked mind, or shows contempt for Brahmins. (8.45.10)

One should not listen to or recite the secret doctrines belonging to the Brahmins, nor those pertaining to other stages of life (āśramas), in the presence of one who is not authorized [to hear them]. || 11 ||
Likewise, that twice-born man who provides food to wicked śramaṇas, nirgranthas, and ajīvakas, falls into hell. ||12||
He who, being of evil conduct, speaks ill of Yoga, or of the ancestors, or of the grandfathers, or of the lords of Yoga, or even of the dharma of Yoga— (13)

The Vedas, the social classes, the stages of life, and the sacrifices—all these belong to him; that rogue who delights in reviling them becomes an atheist and a rationalist, and everyone follows his lead.
Everything I have spoken is the truth; it is exactly so, without a doubt. (14)
Thus they are driven there, bound by the fruits of their own karma;
then, connected by what remains, they are born among the wombs of insects.
The wise and intelligent person who, being forever free from greed, delusion, and sorrow, listens to this after reflecting upon it—
that one, whose self is impelled by the divine law, goes indeed to heaven and never returns to that [world of suffering].
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, named Mahāpadma, in the Description of Hells within the Skanda Purāṇa.
Hereafter, I shall further describe the Raurava hell,
where those living beings, bound by their own karma, remain helpless.
Those who go there, afflicted by suffering and grief, are destined for the Great Hell;
since that sound "ru" is heard there, it is called Raurava.
Or rather, because it is terrifying (bhīma) again and again, it is therefore called Raurava.
But when full, it burns from the cow-dung fuel with extreme ferocity. ||3||
In its center is indeed a pillar of iron, possessing the luster of molten gold;
there, the creature, sinking deeply, is helplessly scorched as it enters.
Uttering cries of distress, he fell down unconscious;
then, with great effort, he raised himself up by his own power.
Having reached yet another place, he should enter it in the same manner; then,
having leaped up from there, if he takes refuge in a pillar,
he is burned by that as well, and having abandoned it, he should enter again.
Thus he is tormented there for many years, experiencing extreme suffering.
Released from there, he again undergoes various elevations;
for men who drink liquor yet teach the Dharma go to that place.
A killer of a father, a killer of a mother, a killer of a brother, and likewise a killer of a guru;
those who delight in verbal disputes and are revilers of such [virtuous people];
a cow-killer, and one who is extremely cruel toward living beings as a tamer—[these are the ones].
The one who cuts the throat and the one who uses false measures—whoever performs such actions [is reborn as a bird]. 8.46.10

The elder brother whose younger brother marries before him, the younger brother who marries before his elder brother, one who delights in cremation grounds, one who has united with the son of a remarried woman, and he in whose house a paramour resides—
all these men go to the Raurava hell.

Whoever should hear this account of Raurava, the most terrible hell for evildoers, shall certainly attain the highest state; he would not go to Raurava even in thought. Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, named Raurava, in the Description of Hells within the Skanda Purāṇa.
Suśarman said:
"O son, hear from me about another great hell, Mahāraurava, which is a place of torment for the wicked; there, my child, are streams, water, and ponds."
There were pits filled with cow-dung and others glowing like gold, as well as trenches filled with fire;
there were many pillars made of iron and trees covered in numerous thorns;
and there were Rākṣasas of various forms, bearing sharp weapons and missiles.
There, a living being is completely bound by abundant evil.
Falling down with a distorted form and crying out again and again, he was quickly struck on the head by the rākṣasas as he lay there. ||4||
He is cooked intensely and most cruelly in a fire-colored pit of cow-dung;
then, distressed by that burning and suffering supreme agony,
he plunges into a pond for the sake of allaying the heat.
There, afflicted by double the pain from heated caustic lye, he suffers. || 6 ||
Rising up in haste, he climbs either a tree or a pillar;
there he is pierced by those sharp thorns as if they were made of iron. ||7||
Indeed, in the Agnikulyā hell, wailing piteously in many ways,
he thus goes along being tormented, crying out much while afflicted by thirst;
yet when he seeks to resort to a stream to drink, even that [stream] for him then becomes of iron.
If water flows with the color of fire, one afflicted by fainting will die from it. 9.
And when his torments are complete, he is released from that great fear;
yet at that time, the creature is subjected to extreme cruelty amidst the elevations.
There goes the king-killer, the one who insults the wife of a king, he who gives hope but does not fulfill it, and he who defiles sacred fords. 11.
A thief, a slanderer, one who subsists on women, and a doer of evil;
one who prevents the giving of gifts to the sacred fire, to a cow, or even to a Brāhmaṇa. || 1.2 ||
That lowest of men who sells his own wife or his offspring, or who steals the sacrificial vessels of the fire and even the slightest possession of the yogins; 13.
Or those men who support thieves, as well as Brahmins appointed to office and those appointed to matters of dharma; ||14||
The cow of a Brahmin who maintains no sacred fire that is tawny-colored;
one who performs the Agnihotra sacrifice improperly; one who serves food at the daily rites;
the killing of a prince; and whatever one might contemplate during a famine—[these are causes for loss].
That man who causes the ruin of a kingdom, the loss of a wife, or the loss of wealth;
or whoever brings about the devastation of a country or commits acts of terror—
all of them go to the hell known as Mahāraurava.
Whoever should hear this constantly will certainly abide in a righteous mind;
he shall not go to that terrifying hell, Raurava, nor to Ugraraurava.
(18) Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "Mahāraurava," in the Description of Hells within the Skanda Purāṇa.
Suśarman said:
There is another terrible hell named Tamas, which is most fearsome;
falling into it, one is struck down by Rākṣasas even before reaching the ground. (1)
With swords, mallets, and spear-tips; with clubs, pestles, and battle-axes; with terrifying iron bars, chisels, thunderbolts, spears, and hatchets.
Struck by others in various ways who are enraged and utterly merciless,
he faints, is seized by darkness, and falls into that hell.
With his body destroyed and his form stupefied by darkness,
bound by a continuous succession of suffering, he undergoes intense torment;
for, seized by darkness, he remains without refuge in that most dreadful state.
The creature experiences torment; therefore, it is called *tamas*.
Whatever torments of many kinds have been described, the evil-minded one undergoes them all there as a result of his own sin. (5–6)
Even when his destination is reached and he has crossed over by means of his own karma, a living being, bound by the fetters of karma, is made to rise up once again. ||7||
The killer of a Brahmin, the killer of an embryo, the drinker of liquor, and that Brahmin who,
blinded by delusion, creates an obstacle at a watering place for thirsty cows, or who, having summoned them, reviles them— he is the lowest of men. (8)

He who constantly hates Brahmins, he who reviles a petitioner, he who steals the scriptures, and the man known as a cow-killer; the follower of Kapila, one of false views, and the one who reviles the purpose of the Vedic dharma—[these are all equal]. || 8.48.10 ||
The reviler of Brahmins, the defiler of the Veda, dharma, and artha,
as well as atheists and evil-minded men— these indeed go there.
O you whose senses are ever vigilant, he who hears this [account] consisting of darkness is likewise overcome by darkness.
He never goes to that hell consisting of darkness, which brings terrible suffering to living beings.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "Tamas," in the Description of Hells within the Skanda Purāṇa. Suśarman said:
Listen further to the description of the most terrible hell, Tama-tamara.
Where there is no light at all and no vision functions, a man falling there is rendered unconscious;
because of that darkness, it is called *tamas* by the Rākṣasas of hideous form. ||1-2||
Having fallen there, that fool is severely burned by the fire;
then, rising up again with great force, he is sightless and unconscious.
He is cut and even torn apart by Rākṣasas of cruel deeds;
afflicted by that as well, he likewise flees to another region.
There too, seized by them, he is slaughtered like a sacrificial animal.
Then once more, unconscious, he was cast into wells and difficult places. ||5||
And having plunged into the fire-ash pit, he is born there crying out;
thus, experiencing many such torments, he becomes exceedingly miserable. (6)
Having reached the end of hell, one is cast down from heights;
this applies to one who causes an abortion and to one who desires sovereignty. (7)
Even here, this unworthy servant is intent on the murder of his king;
he who, being no teacher himself, undertakes the work of teachers. ||8||
He who destroys the sciences of the treatises along with their medicinal herbs, as well as diseases along with their remedies; he who praises the Dānavas;
and that teacher who, out of malice, does not impart instruction—[these are the ones to be avoided]. 9.

He goes to that terrible, impenetrable hell consisting of darkness. Then all those denizens of hell, having seized the ungrateful man and bowed down to Yama, speak together with the servants of Yama: ||| 11 ||
"O Blessed One, we are not capable of destroying this evil;
therefore, look for another means here and show us your favor, O Lord. (12)
Thus addressed, the Blessed Yama, lord of the pretas,
then questioned those most excellent sages who were skilled in the meaning of all dharmas.
"O Blessed Ones, how might there be atonement for this ungrateful and evil-minded man for his most terrible sinful deed?
Then all those sages, having looked with their far-reaching vision, [spoke].
They indeed spoke these words to Yama, the best among the upholders of dharma: ||1 5||

For the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and likewise for one who has broken his vow, an atonement has been prescribed by the virtuous; but for the ungrateful person, there is no atonement.
Then that blessed Lord, the excellent son of Mārtaṇḍa, gave his command to the denizens of hell: "All of you, [bring] this man! || 17 ||
"You shall purify him; go, for his destination is said to be no other.
Then, at his word, all those most terrible hell-beings sequentially tormented the evildoer.
He who takes away the food provided by his master and he who takes away the funeral offerings for his ancestors; likewise,
he who receives instruction and does not give the teacher’s fee,
he who, having been nourished, does not follow his benefactor, and the man who causes such a person to be killed— [these all go to hell].
He speaks of the faults of what has been done, yet performs it only half-heartedly;

he does not remember what has been done for him, and he reviles the stages of life (āśramas). Likewise, he fails to support his mounts, those who have sought refuge with him, and those who have rendered him assistance.
He who speaks jesting words even to servants devoted to their duties and likewise to those who act for his welfare, as well as to his wife and laborers; ||23||
Manu declared that all those who say, "Nothing was given by him, nor was any oblation offered," are ungrateful, along with the sages.
The ungrateful, the deceitful, the nihilist, and one whose doubts have been severed—
all these go to those very places that I have described.
Furthermore, the progenitor, the one who performs the initiation, and he who imparts knowledge— [these too are worthy of honor].

The protector from fear, the provider of food, and these five others are remembered as fathers. One should abandon those lowest of men who speak of their faults, who are envious, and who are intent on doing them harm.
He who betrays a friend and is evil-minded, who proclaims the faults of others, and he who does not return a favor nor act kindly toward one who has previously done him a service; ||28||
All these men are wicked; all are devoted to what is unwholesome.
Bound by their sinful deeds, they fall into the hells.
All of these have been declared by me to be destined for the great hells.
Only those people who have committed evil deeds go toward the heights.
Whoever should hear or recite this terrible account of darkness,
unrighteousness shall turn away, and he shall go to the abode of Brahmā.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Darkness," in the section on the description of hells within the Skanda Purāṇa.
Hereafter, I shall explain the cycle of worldly existence;
how those who have emerged from hell transmigrate in brief.
Those evildoers whom I have described as being in the first hell are born in the wombs of worms due to their remaining karma.
Having transmigrated into the womb of worms for hundreds of thousands of years,
they are thereafter born again as monkeys and then as hyenas.
When they are subsequently born among cattle,
then, after a remainder of exactly one hundred births,
they are born among humans; of this there is no doubt.
If they do not commit any further sin there,
then they indeed obtain a pure birth once again;
nor shall they ever again encounter the terrible cycle of worldly existence.
Those whom I have mentioned in the second [chapter] are liberated from their remaining karma;
they are born among worms and insects for six hundred thousand times.
Likewise, they go again for a hundred times ten thousand;
they are born from the womb of a fish for that same duration, without a doubt. (8)
Then they become tigers and bears, and from there they attain the state of cattle;
they are reborn among humans as despised beings due to their own karma.
Now, those who were described by me as the third group of evildoers—
They were liberated from that karma, yet remained enveloped by its remainder.
They are born among worms and insects for six hundred thousand times, and likewise for another ten thousand times as birds. (1.1)
Then there are lions, snakes, cattle, and later humans;
furthermore, those who were described by me as doers of evil deeds belong to the fourth [class]. ||12||
All of them, however, are born with their karma remaining in the wombs of worms—
eight hundred thousand and sixteen thousand more.
For from those wombs they are born again as deer;
and when released from the state of a deer, they are born again as donkeys. (14)
Then they become wild oxen, and then oxen, and then human beings;
those whom I have mentioned as being in the fifth stage also [attain this] through their remaining karma.
Indeed, they are born among worms and insects for ten million lifetimes,
and likewise among elephants, camels, and horses.
Then, having attained the state of a cow, they obtain human birth;
being liberated from the sixth [state] by means of their remaining karma,
they are born among worms and insects for twice the duration of those previous births.
From that, one koṭi [of breaths] makes a louse; from that, a fish, and then a pig. ||18||
Having attained the state of a buffalo thereafter, one is born as a human from the state of a cow;
yet in that human state, one is born both contemptible and diseased.
Released from the seventh [state], he is born among worms and insects;
for three hundred million [lives] he likewise attains the state of a tree.
Thereafter he becomes a creeper, then a shrub, and then he is born as an elephant.
Having attained the state of a cow, he is thereafter born as a human;
then, released from the eighth [birth], yet bound by the remainder of his karma, he is born among worms and insects for two times ten million births. ||22||
Then, by way of becoming medicinal herbs, he is born among shrubs and kusha grass;
thereafter, released from the state of being a cow, he is born as a contemptible man.
Having emerged even from the ninth [birth], yet bound by the remainder of his karma,
he is born among worms and insects for fifty million births, and thereafter as a bird.
Then he indeed becomes a fish for that long, and likewise a reptile; then for that same duration he becomes a dog, and thereafter a kinnara.
Released from the state of a kinnara, he is then born among cattle.
Then, released from the womb of a cow, he is born among human beings.
Having emerged even from that tenth state, the worm undergoes six crores of births; by the remainder of his karma, he is then born as a monkey. (26–27)
For that long he was a monkey here, for that long a cock, for that long a crow, and likewise a jīvañjīvaka bird.
He is born as a tree, a child, a cat, and an ant;
thereafter, having been born among cattle, he is born among human beings.
Released from the Mahāraurava hell, he remains in great suffering for seventy million [aeons].
Born among worms and insects through successive births, one attains the state of a fish;
thereafter, one becomes a dog, a donkey, a cat, and a parrot;
then one becomes a cow, and subsequently a eunuch among humans.
Released from that hell, that being, still deeply afflicted, undergoes eighty million births as worms in excrement;
thereafter, he is born again as a dog, and repeatedly as a cakravāka bird.
Then, having attained the state of a frog, one is born among deer and birds;
one is also born as a *kiṃnara*, a leopard, or even a *śarabha*. After that, having reached the state of a cow, one attains human status.
Released from that darkness of hell, he is indeed born among worms and insects due to his remaining karma alone; he undergoes ninety million births.
From that he becomes a crow, and after that a vulture;
then a bird that eats vomit, and then again an owl.
Then he becomes a tree and a shrub, and thereafter indeed a wild animal.
Then that cow and the human being as well perish while still in the womb. ||37||
Being born again and again for a hundred thousand years,
he is born repeatedly as one afflicted by disease and loathsome.
But he who, having experienced all these hells, is born here once more—
He experiences all the various states of existence within the entire cycle of saṃsāra.
If, by the turning of time, he should ever attain human birth, even there he repeatedly enters lowly wombs. (8.50.40)
Unwelcome to all beings, suffering and likewise afflicted by disease,
he assumes a deformed appearance, corrupted by his own past action.
A hater of gods and Brahmins, excluded from all vows,
liberated from all dharma, devoid of virtuous conduct,
disrespectful, ill-behaved, eating anything whatsoever, and a reviler of Brahmins— [42]—
"Deprived of sacred fords and temples of the gods, and abandoned by the rites of *svadhā* and *svasti*,
he is born through his own karma as one who is not to be praised by the world. Suśarman said:
"All this has been told to you in its entirety, my son, in brief—
the true nature of the hells and the distinctions of their sequence according to my understanding.
Sanatkumāra said:
Whoever listens to this with devotion always on the sacred festival days, or properly causes the twice-born to hear it, is liberated from all sins. (45)
It brings merit, fame, long life, and leads to heaven; it accomplishes all goals.
It should be heard and recited constantly by one who desires prosperity. (46)
But this [work], which brings about all goals and happiness, is certain, of great power, bestowing a happy rebirth, and auspicious;
it should always be studied and retained by a Brahmin of concentrated mind, for it is eternally equal to the Vedas. 47.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Course of Saṃsāra," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, Sukeśa, having then heard this from his father with a very dejected expression, [spoke].
Afflicted with grief, he then contemplated that state of living beings.
With his mind overwhelmed by anxiety and struck down by sorrow,
his intellect being clouded, he did not perceive the means for the liberation of those beings.
When he, having fallen into deep thought, did not address those ancestors, then all those ancestors spoke thus to Sukeśa: || 3 ||
The ancestors said:
"Why do you worry so excessively? From what source does this anxiety come to you, O sinless one?
Since you are the son of the Lord, this [suffering] is not ordained for you. (4)
Sukeśa said:
Having heard what you have related concerning the suffering of living beings born of their own karma, I reflect upon how there might be a means for their liberation. (5)
The ancestors said:
"O son, disregarding decay, there is no liberation for them;
for in this world, the destruction of one's own performed karma is held to result from its experience."
And enjoyment in hell is inevitably ordained for a living being;
yet those denizens of hell cannot be removed without the exhaustion of their karma.
Indeed, a wise person should not undertake those matters which are impossible to achieve.
Just as one crossing the ocean reaches the death of the sea itself, so does [the world] reach you, O Death. ||8||
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by his ancestors, that radiant one, overcome by desire,
bowed down and said to them, "Do not despise me, for I am your son."
What power do I have to forcibly deliver those beings to auspiciousness?
It is the grace of Mahādeva that will deliver them from their miserable states.
"Just as you have crossed over, so too shall all those creatures dwelling in hell, though they are bewildered, cross over; of this there is no doubt.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having taken leave of them, that high-souled leader of the hosts entered the waters of the ocean; remaining within the water, he—
pure in soul, motionless, and well-composed— then recited the Rudra hymns.
As that great-souled one was engaged in yoga while performing his recitation (*japa*),
O Vyāsa, the entire triple world was scorched by his ascetic power (*tapas*).
Thereupon, all the gods then spoke to the Grandfather (Brahmā).
"What is this, Blessed One? We are all tormented and rendered helpless. Whose power is this asceticism? To whom does such yoga belong? (15)
"O tiger among gods, who is this that performs such severe austerity?
[I shall go] while he does not yet burn [me], and while he does not yet become enraged. (1.6)
"O Lord, fulfill all his desires.
Thus addressed by those gods, the Blessed One, the best of deities, said:
"Let there be no fear for you; he is not one who acts contrary to our will."
He is this very one, the high-souled leader of the hosts of the God of gods. || 18 ||
Seated within the waters at the edge of the ocean, the practitioner of yoga recites the Rudra-mantras;
O mighty ones, he harbors no evil intent toward the worlds.
He considers himself capable of rescuing even the denizens of hell from that very hell;
therefore, if you so desire, go and bow down to Rudra.
"Let the desired boon of this god be granted.
"So be it," they all replied, having come together with Brahmā. (21)
Having gone to Mount Mandara without agitation and being ushered in by Nandin,
they beheld the Lord Īśāna and, having praised the All-pervading One, spoke as follows.
O Blessed One, Sukeśa, your beloved leader of the Gaṇas, having cultivated compassion for living beings, performs difficult penance. (23)
O Lord of the World, fulfill their desire with its fulfillment;
having heard their petition, Bhava, the God of gods, [acted accordingly].
Then Brahmā, accompanied by the others, arrived in the presence of Sukeśa;
so too did the ocean and other sages who were firm in their vows.
Taking up the water of honor (arghya), they bowed hundreds of times to Śaṅkara who had arrived.
Then the God of gods spoke these words to him, the best of the leaders of the Gaṇas: ||| 26 ||
Vyāsa spoke sweetly, bringing pleasure to the mind and ears:
"O child Sukeśa, arise; ask for whatever you desire. (27)
"I shall grant all of that to you, for you are indeed like Nandi to me.
Then Sukeśa, having risen and praised the Bull-bannered Lord, [departed].
Having prostrated, he again requested his previously desired wish:
"O Lord, men who have committed evil deeds go to the hells. (29)
O Lord, my heart is tormented with grief for them;
O Master of the World, may they all be completely liberated.
"Act accordingly for me this very day; this is the boon requested by me.
O Lord, as for those men who are currently being cast into the hells,"
"O Lord of the Gods, I entreat you for their sake that they may obtain liberation.
Then the God, granting what was requested, spoke as follows: ||32||
"Let it be so for you, my child; the men in the hells are liberated.
By this devotion as well as by your compassion, you are dear to me."
"Be especially free from anxiety, endowed with supreme sovereignty.
Then all those hell-beings ascended celestial chariots.
Then, having approached the God of gods, they bowed down to Sukeśa as well. The Lord spoke again to Sukeśa, the leader of the Gaṇas:
"He who indeed delivers certain living beings from calamities..."

Having become their father in the Dharma, he does not behold cyclic existence. For even that being who, with his mind, always desires to liberate living creatures from the afflictions, being a soul of Dharma, is himself liberated from all sufferings.
And he who, having acquired merit for himself, bestows it upon living beings for their happiness,
he too is completely liberated from all sufferings.
You, moreover, are endowed with supreme yoga and sovereign power.
"Who else on earth is equal to you in being intent upon the deliverance of living beings?
Sukeśa said:
"O Blessed One, by your grace, all this shall come to pass for me."
"O Lord, from where did I derive this power? O All-pervading One, this was brought about by you alone."
Furthermore, there is no other task or duty remaining for me that is in my mind;
I am your servant and slave. That I am such as this is not surprising. ||41||
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O Vyāsa, that Blessed Lord, having dismissed the leader of the Gaṇas,
proceeded to Mount Mandara, surrounded at that time by all the immortals.
Even the gods, having seen from all sides the hell-beings situated in their celestial chariots and observing that the suffering of the world had been stilled, departed as they had come. (43)
Whoever should hear or recite this "Deliverance from Hell" shall never despair even when encountering suffering.
Having heard this entire ritual procedure for yoga and its samayas, a person [attains this] constantly.
Even a person of sinful nature does not encounter such terrifying and utterly merciless misfortune by taking refuge in sin;

however, he who approaches this [text] here, remaining constantly endowed with purity, and recites it in the assembly of gods, Brahmins, and physicians, being firmly devoted to Śaṅkara at all times—[for him there is no fear]. (45)
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Liberation from Hell," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
Furthermore, which doers of auspicious deeds do not go to that hell?
O Brahmin, even those who take delight in evil deeds—this is what I wish to know.
Likewise, what is the most excellent and auspicious destiny for women? By what ripening of karma does this come to pass? This I wish to know.
Sanatkumāra said:
O giver of honor, hear from me about those men who, though devoted to evil deeds, do not go to that most miserable hell. ||3||
One who maintains the sacred fires does not go to hell, nor does one who wears the three-stranded cord, nor one who observes the cow-vow;
nor he who has performed the horse-sacrifice, nor he who has gifted a thousand cows;
nor he who is constant in private Vedic study, nor that twice-born man who recites the Rudra hymns.
And he who delivers Brāhmaṇas from calamities ending in death;
and he who serves a Brāhmaṇa who is diseased, distressed, helpless, and afflicted by suffering—by such means as these, a man is joined with merit. || 5-6 ||
He who provides a Brahmin, who is destitute but endowed with Vedic study, with the necessities for living at home, does not behold hell.
Likewise, he who, with a disciplined mind, protects a cow that is submerged, fallen, and deprived of strength,
does not go to that [hell];
and he who [protects] Maheśa with supreme devotion and meditative absorption.
If one worships him constantly with devotion, he never departs from that person.
But for others, there is indeed rebirth in saṃsāra; of this there is no doubt.
O Vyāsa, those Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, who are devoted to the six duties, and who are established in the dharma of the self, do not go there.
Endowed with austerity and purity, they were compassionate and firm in their vows.
Those twice-born who have desisted from accepting gifts and are devoted to the Lord,
and those Kṣatriyas who are always prepared for the protection of their subjects—
if they give up their lives in battle, they do not go to hell.
The Vaiśyas were engaged in the occupations of livelihood, established in justice and righteousness. || 13 ||
Those whose livelihood is uninterrupted and who worship the gods and Brahmins do not see hell; they are proclaimed to be destined for heaven. || 14 ||
Those devotees of the three castes who are free from pride, and especially those Śūdras who constantly serve the Brāhmaṇas—
they do not see hell; having died, they have gone to a happy state.
And among all four castes, men [should seek] Śiva with devotion.
Those devotees who have dedicated all their actions and states to Śarva, remaining ever-vowed to him, do not go to hell; they attain the supreme goal. || 17 ||
Furthermore, those who, having constructed a temple, worship the God of gods, indeed rescue their other ancestors from hell as well. (18)
Even those by whom lotus ponds, reservoirs, and lakes were dug, and who planted groves of trees, do not indeed go there. || 19 ||
Those who constantly provide protection for the twice-born and for others who are suffering do not go there;
nor indeed do those who are ever free from anger and who worship the gods and the brahmins.
And those who are constantly devoted to giving do not go to a lower state. ||21||
Those who are devoted to speaking the truth, who avoid wicked undertakings,
and who are engaged in the practice of their own duty, do not see hell.
Therefore, one who is devoted to the worship of the *liṅga* is liberated from everything;
likewise, the pure meditator who always recites the *gaṇas* is freed. But the yogi, even while committing all manner of sins, is not defiled.
For women, however, the husband is always the supreme deity.
Therefore, those who reflect upon dharma do not look to anyone else, whether in action, thought, or speech; whatever they give or offer in sacrifice, [it is to him]. (24–25)
A woman who abandons her husband does not enjoy the fruit thereof;
however, she who is devoted to the service of her husband through thought, word, and deed, and who, even when her husband has died, desires no other man in her mind— [she enjoys that fruit]. (26)
Whatever merit she performs, she offers all of it to her husband;
such a woman does not go to any of the hells, even in thought. ||27||
She does not at all undergo the entire terrible cycle of existence;
but for others, O observer of noble vows, there is no doubt that they go to hell. (28)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having thus shown favor to Sukeśa, the Lord who has the bull as his vehicle also went to the hermitage of Kāṣṭhakūṭa.
He favored that brahmin Kāṣṭhakūṭa, whose wealth was his asceticism.
Vyāsa said:
O Blessed One, what was the austerity of that high-souled Brāhmaṇa, and in how much time did he obtain a boon from Maheśvara? 8.52.30.
Whose son was he, whose grandson, and what was the name of that most excellent being?
O Blessed One, I desire this auspicious account to be told by you in detail. (3.1)
Sanatkumāra said:
In the lineage of Gautama, there was a lordly brahmin named Kṛṣṇa;
his son was the famous Bhūmanyu by name.
He had a wife named Yaśas, a daughter of Rātri, who possessed beautiful eyebrows. Once, after he had performed his marriage, that Gautama named Bhūmanyu—
Enveloped by old age, he found no son through her;
afflicted by grief, that man skilled in speech said these words to his wife:
"Through a son, people desire the worlds, and they also become free from debt. (34)
I am overcome by old age, yet no son of mine is seen.
"Therefore, O auspicious lady, being permitted by me, do you take some kinsman of my own lineage for the sake of a son; I entreat you with palms joined and bowed.
Suyaśā said:
"I have not heard this from you, nor has it been spoken by you, O sinless one;
for how could one like me even conceive such a thing in her mind? (37)
Born in the lineage of the Atris, I have entered the family of Gautama;
how could one such as I commit this act, which is censured by the virtuous? (38)
One should seek wealth, lives, and pleasures through austerity;
sons, family, and worlds—perform austerity, O great sage! (3.9)
For by means of asceticism Śakti obtained that son Parāśara,
and the great sage Cyavana obtained Aurva through his own asceticism.
Vasiṣṭha begot Indrapramati through Kapiñjalī,
and Śilāda likewise begot a son, Nandin, through the power of austerity.
Therefore, you too should perform austerity with perfect concentration.
You shall obtain an excellent son, endowed with the power of great yoga.
Indeed, having seen me in the past, Atri himself, the son of Brahmā, said:
"This woman shall become the mother of a virtuous son; that shall not prove false. (43)
"O Lord, whatever merit has been acquired by me through austerity, by virtue of your grace, may you, endowed with that as well as your own [merit], propitiate Rudra. ||44||
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus, that radiant one, filled with supreme shame and permitted by her in this manner, went for refuge to Rudra.
And he, having arrived at the Narmadā quickly and filled with joy,
sat down upon its bank and remained there for years subsisting only on air.
But that brahmin did not at all achieve his purpose by that deed;
therefore, being even more distressed, he remained engaged in breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Then, after one year, the omnipresent Lord said to him:
"O Brahmin, why do you afflict yourself thus? You have no son anywhere."
"O sinless one, there is no fruitless theft [of asceticism] for you, as you have no son.
Thus addressed, he became despondent and lost all hope regarding the birth of a son. (49)
He thought of death rather than returning to his own home;
deeply distressed, he gathered wood and took up fire.
Lamenting and afflicted by great sorrow, he desired to burn himself;
Rudra, observing that extremely difficult resolve of his, [acted]. (51)
"Son! Son!"—thus an invisible voice spoke deeply:
"A son shall be born to you; go, and do not commit such a rash act. (52)
"And that son of yours shall be known by the name Kāṣṭhakūṭa.
Then, with a joyful mind, the brahmin of great asceticism went and [conceived] in his wife.
He begot a son, the great sage Kāṣṭhakūṭa;
then, with the passage of time, the thought occurred to him regarding the conditioned world.
"This father of mine is unable to teach me due to his old age;
therefore, I shall depart without taking leave of my father for the sake of [learning] the Vedas. (55)
Having gone there, that illustrious brahmin, having properly bowed his head to his mother and father, spoke these words:
"I was born as a son to you two for the sake of dharma, not out of desire. (56)
"He will be our savior, and likewise that of our ancestors;
there is no doubt that our lineage shall remain unbroken.
And by means of this excellent son, we shall in every way attain the worlds we desire. (57–58)
"I am your son, desired by you both, so that I might be free from debt to my ancestors;
yet I am unskilled in the duties of dharma and excluded from the Vedas and the Smṛtis. (59)
"Because of the ignorance of the performer, the ancestors were made miserable by that act;
you too shall sink into hell and dwell there for a long time like a wicked man.
Furthermore, you are incapable of teaching day after day due to your old age. (8.52.60)
And because of affection for your son and because of [your] duty, you will not maintain it properly.
Moreover, this mother of mine will never approve of me being properly disciplined by you, thinking, "This is my only son. || 62 ||
Therefore, it is my thought that I shall always resort to another preceptor who is constant in austerity, utterly pitiless, and endowed with wisdom;
for I do not perceive anyone in you two who possesses such qualities. || 63 ||
One should constantly perform service at their feet, thinking thus: ||64||
And this must not be hidden from you; I have considered whatever is auspicious or even inauspicious for you both, for you are my supreme refuge. (65)
When they had been addressed thus by their high-souled son,
the parents stood for a moment with eyes filled with tears;
then, having smelled, embraced, and wiped their beloved sons out of affection, they spoke as follows.
Bhūmanyu said:
"O son, service to the ancestors, which is commensurate with dharma, is of two kinds;
it must be performed with diligent effort by a high-souled son. (67)

Service to the body in this world and the gift of Dharma in the next—by these the ancestors cross over and attain imperishable desires. Among these, we do not desire the worldly as much as that which is beneficial for the life hereafter. (68)
Therefore, perform that action which pertains to the world beyond;
go and study both the Śruti and the Smṛti of those who perform virtuous deeds.
Suyaśas said:
"O son, act exactly as your father, who has realized the self, tells you;
act in such a way that Lord Bhava may become the granter of boons to you.
O high-minded one, you were carried in my womb with great hardship."
And thus, it has been obtained through many hardships for the sake of accomplishing all goals. ||71||
Your father, having abandoned his life-breaths— which are exceedingly difficult to give up— through fierce asceticism,
obtained you, Bhava, from Mahādeva; therefore, act in a manner worthy of him,
O son, so that he may be pleased by you and the two of you, living together with Jīva, may be reunited.
"Let us both be so; therefore, practice correctly.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, permitted by them and having his head smelled [as a blessing], he—
Having performed a circumambulation, that self-possessed man departed.
Dismissed by those two, he then went toward Cyavana,
like an oblation offered with the Ṛg and Yajur Vedas being cast toward Varuṇa.
Having approached him, he was made successful by that [sage] who was pleased,
just as a mantra preceded by ritual formulas becomes effective when the gods obtain their sacrificial portion.
Then, once that son had departed, the father met his end.
Then Kāṣṭhakūṭa, having returned from his studies and being highly virtuous,
beheld his mother looking wretched— like a lotus pond devoid of water, like a night without the moon, or like royal fortune stripped of its command.
Weeping, her eyes filled with tears, lamenting and deeply distressed. ||78||
But Kāṣṭhakūṭa, seeing her overwhelmed with grief,
spoke these words to her, as Jayanta spoke to Paulomī when Śakra had been defeated:
Kāṣṭhakūṭa said:
"I have already heard this, and the funeral rites for the deceased have been performed.
Do not set your mind on grief; this is the eternal law."
O Mother, for the gods, the ṛṣis, and the great-souled yogins—how much more so for mortals! Do not grieve for that one whose wealth is asceticism.
Indeed, I myself was created by him as his very self through his own splendor.
Behold me, O Gāyatrī, your son, who has accomplished his purpose.
All the Vedas have been studied by me, along with their limbs (Aṅgas) and sub-limbs (Upāṅgas), in full detail; likewise, all the Upavedas and the entire Adhyātma have been mastered by me.
Whatever is to be known by men, all that is indeed knowledge;
likewise, everything that is to be heard has been heard, and the yogis have also been worshipped. ||84||
Rejoicing with even greater intensity and filled with joy, she said:
"O Great Being, protect me always, as Gāyatrī protects the sacrifice.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of that high-souled one, which were indeed true, his mother,
weeping with even greater sorrow, spoke to him.
Suyaśas said:
"O son, this is not my sorrow that he is considered dead;
for this is the destiny ordained for all living beings subject to mortality. (87)
And he too, that great-souled one endowed with ascetic power, has accomplished his purpose;
indeed, there is nothing here for us to grieve for him.
But I grieve for myself, O son, who have been left bereft of him.
I have not died following him; rather, I am longing for your arrival. ||89||
Neither wealth, nor enjoyments, nor kinsmen, nor sons, nor even relatives remain for women where the husband stands; if the husband is there,
then everything is theirs, but without the husband, nothing exists at all.
For everything is a source of sorrow for those women who have neither husband nor son.
Moreover, this is my further grief that today,
though I am joyful, I do not welcome you, my son, being united with the illustrious Ravi by Viṣṇu.
For many times he said to me, "Kāṣṭhakūṭa will come here;
once he has completed his studies, I shall choose his auspicious daughter as my daughter-in-law.
This daughter of Uda, the son of Kaśyapa, is exceedingly virtuous.
I shall choose that woman of virtuous vows as my bride from Kāṣṭhakūṭa.
Then I shall see that son of firm vows together with his wife;
indeed, having seen him accompanied by his wife, I shall fetch the sacred fires.
When, satisfied by the hand-taking ceremony of my son's wife, shall I [be so fulfilled]?
I shall perform many virtuous deeds through both mind and speech. ||96||
Thus, for him who possessed his heart's desire, who was like a father to his son, and whose son was so dear, this thought did not occur: "O son, you are burning me!
For previously, as you were departing in his presence, I had indeed spoken to you.
"May we both live so that we may see you, yet even that did not come to pass.
Today my heart, though made of the essence of diamond, does not shatter; for it is only because I still behold you here, O son, that I am not once again a non-existent being."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, like a female osprey bereft of her mate, that highly illustrious woman,
afflicted by great sorrow, lamented and fell upon the surface of the earth.
Kāṣṭhakūṭa, having burned her—who was afflicted by grief, fallen, lifeless, and unconscious—with fire, lamented in great distress:
"Alas, O father! For me, who am evil-minded and ignorant of dharma! || 101 ||
"Where have you been? You do not speak to me today, even though you were with your wife.
Did I not direct you, as if delighted, saying, 'Go and study'? Having returned today after completing my studies, why do you not address me?"

"Surely I, your son, was obtained by you through supreme austerity and meditative absorption from Rudra, the God of gods; why then do you not speak to me? O sinless one, what wrong have I done to you, along with your wife?"
"Since you have come with my mother and do not greet me warmly at all—alas, I am undone by this one wicked son of mine, so evil-minded!
I consider this world to be without a king, since he does not slay me, a killer of my father. (10.6)
Thus he lamented, O Vyāsa, along with many other sages.
Once he had been established and consoled, that man of great asceticism performed no water-libation rites; instead,
having touched water with palms joined in reverence, he made this vow in the midst of the sages— a vow difficult for all beings to perform.
From this day forward, I shall not take a breath in any way whatsoever;
the vital airs residing within my body shall never move again.
Devoid of both closing and opening my eyes, I shall remain with one foot planted and my arms raised upward.
"I shall become like wood, clods of earth, or stones; of this there is no doubt.
As long as I behold Rudra and likewise my father, together with his wife, so long shall this vow remain mine. (8.52.110–111)
Sanatkumāra said: Then, being watched by those sages, that man of great asceticism remained right there, constantly meditating upon Maheśvara.
O Vyāsa, while he remained thus devoted to his father,
Lord Śaṅkara himself became pleased on the eighth day and spoke to him.
The God of Gods said:
"O Kāṣṭhakūṭa, O sinless one, I grant you divine vision.
Behold me with full confidence, for I am invisible even to yogis.
Speak, my son, whatever boon is fixed in your heart."
I shall give it; there is no doubt. Having reflected well, tell me.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having beheld the Lord of Gods who was like the rising sun, he fell at his feet in joy and spoke these words in a melodious voice: ||| 11 || 6 ||
Kāṣṭhakūṭa said:
"O Blessed One, my mother and father have been joined with death by Time;
O Lord, I desire this as a boon: that both of them may live."
The God of gods said:
"Both of them, afflicted by death, have fallen into a terrible hell;
it is not possible to restore them to life. Choose something else from me."
Kāṣṭhakūṭa said:
"O Lord, I do not desire any other boon whatsoever.
This undertaking is for the sake of my father; therefore, grant it. Salutations to you! || 119 ||
The God of Gods said: "If the body of the deceased still exists, it is indeed possible to reunite it with life this very day; however, this is not possible for one who has been cremated."
For those two, there is indeed no body, nor likewise any other instrument;
and as that father of yours was in terms of his physical form, so shall you be.
Give up this body, and then they will both become living beings.
Kāṣṭhakūṭa said:
"Indeed, there is nothing that those two cannot accomplish if it is deemed necessary to be done;
for the rising of Dhruva was seen even without a physical body."
"Moreover, O Lord, I have no pleasure in being without my body for those two;
therefore, O God, accept my body if you so deem fit."
This has arisen from his very limbs, limb by limb;
therefore, O Lord of Gods, withhold it, for I have no need for this.
Sanatkumāra said: Then that blessed Lord, smiling, O best of sages, being pleased in heart and desiring to unite him with auspiciousness, replied as follows.
The God of Gods said:
"O son, best among those who follow the path of dharma, this test has been conducted by me.
I am well-pleased with this devotion to your father; listen to my words. (1.26)
Inexhaustible and imperishable, free from old age and death,
and endowed with sovereign power— you, my beloved, shall become a leader of my hosts (gaṇapa).
Known as Kāṣṭhakūṭa, you shall be possessed of the strength of all yogic powers.
"You shall travel in a celestial chariot made by me that moves at will.
And all these sages, ascetics in this hermitage,
shall become your attendants and lords of the Gaṇas."
They shall be inexhaustible and immutable, endowed with the power of great yoga, and equal in sovereignty; of this there is no doubt.
And this father of yours, O son, Bhūmanyu, together with his wife—

Having become your very own follower, you have arrived as my equal. I grant you this divine Śveta mountain, adorned with celestial chariots, moving at will, and resembling heaven itself, as your dwelling place.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that blessed Lord, having shown favor to that powerful one,
went back to Mandara, and he too returned to his desired place.
While the queen, engaged in ascetic penance, remained upon her father’s peak,
the god performed all this that has indeed been described.
The man who hears this account of the deeds of the God of gods, or causes it to be heard by the twice-born, shall not fall into an evil state of existence. ||1.35||
One who studies this constantly, being pure and of restrained mind,
attains liberation from the body and goes to the world of Rudra.
Thus [ends] this supreme [work], which destroys many sins and brings about union with Rudra.
And he who recites this "Establishment of Virtues" does not, upon death, go to a state of wretchedness.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Great Glory of Kāṣṭhakūṭa," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
Indeed, that divine and imperishable Goddess is the daughter of Himavat.
For how long did she practice penance that is so extremely difficult to perform?
And how did she, who is the fire-drill for kindling hundreds of boons, obtain her boon?
O best of the twice-born, I wish for all of this to be told.

Sanatkumāra said: Listen; after some time had passed, the Goddess performed a most difficult penance, becoming self-restrained, with palms joined in reverence, and likewise concentrating her mind. (3)
Aiming her eyes and her mind at the sun,
she stood with unblinking gaze, as if bound to a tree like a wooden image.
Gazing at the sun with her eyes fixed on Suvarcala, she remained standing; with one foot planted and her arms raised, she became breathless.
For a thousand divine years, she stood as motionless as a stone.
Accompanied by a tiger, Rudrāṇī was engaged in asceticism and observed auspicious vows. || 6 ||
Neither did she suffer any exhaustion, nor was there any loss of strength;
for that queen remained steadfast in her asceticism just as before.
By the power of her asceticism, the entire world, including all things stationary and moving, remained afflicted by distress as if struck by universal destruction. ||8||
The sun did not shine too brightly, nor did the moon illuminate; the luminaries became obscured by darkness, and the Siddhas did not travel through the sky. (9)
Their celestial garlands withered and their celestial chariots fell;
even in heaven they found no happiness, and a sense of longing arose within them.
All the directions and the entire triple world are smoking;
the movement of the Vidyādharas is broken, and their weapons are blazing.
Deer, tigers, lions, cats, owls, mice,
serpents, and mongooses also moved about together in one place.
Then all the gods, having assembled together, said to one another:
"This reversal seen in these three worlds cannot occur without a cause."
There must be a great cause for this; it cannot be without a cause.
Therefore, being ignorant of this, we have fallen into every kind of error. (14)
"How shall we remain so deeply distressed? Let us go into the presence of Brahmā.
Having said this, all those gods, led by Bṛhaspati, [departed]. (15)
Having gone to the palace of Vairāja, they bowed down before Brahmā;
duly honored by Brahmā, they sat down according to their rank.
Questioned by him regarding the cause of their arrival, they, afflicted by grief in their hearts, said:
"O Blessed One, O All-pervading Lord, you perceive the entire reality of the world as if it were before your very eyes. (17)
"O Lord, tell us why this world has become so perverse today.
Having heard those words of the frightened ones, he who knows all yogas [replied]: 18.
He spoke these words, sweet, gentle, and profound:
"This is the goddess Haimavatī, Rudrāṇī, the sustainer of the worlds; with her mind disciplined, she performs penance, established in unwavering yoga. (19)
Indeed, by means of her meditative absorption, a thousand divine years have passed for her,
as well as two hundred years and another hundred autumns.
"O gods, this is the power of the asceticism performed by her through yoga,
by which the worlds have fallen into a state of reversal.
The gods said:
If, by her power, this great fear of calamities arises, she will further burn the worlds; therefore, restrain her.
For that goddess, endowed with ascetic power, is even more radiant than the night;
she would undoubtedly burn up these worlds along with us. ||23||
Therefore, for the sake of the welfare of the world, and even at our word, act in such a way that the virtuous and beautiful lady may be turned back. ||24||
The Grandfather said:
"So be it; go, O sinless ones, and be at peace.
By granting this desired boon, I shall establish Rudrāṇī."
Then, after the gods had departed, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
[ascended] a bright golden celestial chariot, crowded with hundreds of altars,
bound with networks of tinkling bells, and illuminated by strings of pearls.
With pillars made of sapphire and likewise with lattices of gold from the Jāmbūnada river.
It is surrounded on all sides by bells of universal form, and illuminated by diamonds, sapphires, lapis lazuli, great blue gems, and other jewels. || 28 ||
It was covered with suitable spires marked with crystal,
and it was indeed made entirely of metal, fashioned by the God himself;
for it consisted of the five elements and remained in its primordial state.
Connected with a network of exquisite sounds like the beautiful resonance of a bell,
it was adorned with eight strings of pearls and encircled by sixteen rows of tinkling bells;
that celestial chariot, possessing great radiance, had twenty altars therein.
Adorned with fifty thousand divine characteristics and likewise with jewels and gems,
and provided with many seats situated throughout the world,
Brahmā ascended that celestial chariot together with his sages.
Likewise, together with the Vedas, the mantras, and all the Śāstras as well.
In its center was a divine, firm seat consisting of a golden lotus;
there sat comfortably Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds.
