By his side were Sāvitrī and Gāyatrī, both of radiant splendor.
The Ṛgveda is on his right side, and the Yajurveda is on the west;
the Sāmaveda is on the north, and likewise the Atharvaveda is in front. Therein are the expiations, the duties, the observances, and the austerities.
Various kinds of gifts, sacrifices, and likewise well-performed rites; the seven sacred utterances (vyāhṛtis), as well as all the worlds;
the mountains and the rivers, as well as the mothers of the world.
The world-protectors, the overseers of creatures, Dakṣa, and likewise Dharma;
Bhṛgu, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Marīci, Aṅgiras, and the highly illustrious Ruci. ||38–39||
R̥bhu, Sanātana, Virāja, and Mahātapas, as well as the Pitṛs and the Devas—these are the progeny of Brahmā. || 8.53.40 ||
Earth, wind, space, water, and likewise light—
these very elements as they were enumerated, as well as the oceans and the directions,
and the sciences and the performers of dharma, stood before him.
The Brahmadaṇḍa, the Daṇḍa, and likewise the Kalaśa made of gold. || 42 ||
A water-pot was at both his sides, a splendid sacred thread was [on his body], and likewise the syllable Om was before him. ||43||
The rosary, yoga, and the mantra to be recited stood before him;
Svāhā, Svadhā, Vaṣaṭ, Vauṣaṭ, and Agni were at his sides;
and Yama, the restraints (niyamas), and many means of accomplishment (sādhanas) were likewise present.
Then all these became the attendants of Dharma:
compassion, pity, generosity, and faith, together with modesty;
likewise, all the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) that accompany the side of the sacrifice became the attendants of the sages.
Then all the gods whatsoever who dwell in the world of Brahmā quickly ascended and stationed themselves on every side. ||47||
When they had thus all ascended that celestial chariot and were seated comfortably, Brahmā exhorted them.
That [chariot] was urged on by him, the foremost of those skilled in yoga, who travels everywhere in the most excellent of great celestial chariots.
He proceeded by means of a power that followed the mind, just as the mind moves by its own impulse, as if driven by the Creator of all.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Departure of Brahmā," in the *Devīvarapradāna* section of the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, by means of that celestial chariot, the wise four-faced creator of all went to Mount Mandara, which possesses caves of variegated stones.
Having reached that vast, incomparable, and exceedingly radiant place, which was pleasing to the sight even from afar, he saw those seated in the assembly and spoke as follows: ||| 2 ||
Behold this auspicious abode of Rudra, invisible even to those of meritorious deeds, and possessing a splendor like the form of the sun, even for the gods. ||3||
Having entered this, the sacrificial glory of the gods does not depart;
there is constant victory in battles, and even the greatest righteousness as well.
This was created by him himself through his own mind, he of incomparable splendor.
For indeed, there exists no house in this world equal to his. || 5 ||
Having entered this, the righteous soul does not experience suffering again;
nor does he undergo rebirth, for he has attained eternal sovereignty.
This state is indefinable, even for yogis, due to its constant union with yoga.
But how could even a great person describe this otherwise?
This [cloud] of our chariot, struck by the wind in anger,
increases in size like the peak of Mount Vindhya along with the mountain itself.
This [being] stands obstructing the path of our celestial chariot,
above, across, and below, by the splendor of the God of gods.
Having created this blinding darkness, that Medhas himself,
wearing a garland and with thunderbolt raised in hand, advanced against him, roaring aloud.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that Blessed Lord Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
having steadied himself upon the pinnacle of that celestial chariot, stood there with palms joined in reverence.
And then they praised the god Śarva, the fierce one with matted hair;
and all those sages, well-restrained and seated upon their celestial chariots,
illuminated the entire world, both the stationary and the moving.
Then that cloud, having released its rain, went to its own place.
All the directions became stainless and a great light shone intensely;
and perceiving him reciting that mantra, the Lord whose banner bears the bull,
the Sovereign of the Gods, spoke these words to Nandin who was standing at the gateway:
"This Brahmā has come here in his celestial chariot to see me.
Tell me the purpose for which you have come; I already know it. Accomplish that task and depart quickly, for the time for it has arrived."
Sanatkumāra said: Having been thus addressed by Rudra, Nandin, the leader of the Pramathas,
while still standing at the gate, spoke these words to Brahmā, who was seated in his celestial chariot.
Nandi said:
"The Blessed One knows for what purpose you have come;
indeed, perform that task quickly, for the time for it has now arrived."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having offered salutations mentally to Śambhu and having performed a circumambulation, he departed for Mount Mandara.
Having bypassed the entire Mandara mountain, that high-minded one traveled through the middle of Śākadvīpa and arrived at Jambūdvīpa.
He was gazed upon by the gods and by sages firm in their vows.
Having approached Himavat, the best of mountains, he spoke this: || 31 ||
This lofty and radiant peak of Himavat stands here;
from afar it is perceived as resembling the sun at the end of an eon.
Here dwells that mother of the world, like a nurse tending her own biological son. ||22||
Protecting the entire world, the daughter of the mountain performs ascetic penance.
Oh, how meritorious and fortunate indeed is this peak in every respect,
since the Destroyer of Desire will unite it with a bridegroom for the sake of the Mountain’s Daughter!
Behold the power of the asceticism of this goddess of virtuous conduct, for having seen this peak, we shall not see rebirth again. ||25||
Even as he was speaking thus, the four-faced one arrived at the gateway of Śikhara by means of his celestial chariot, accompanied by all the sages.
There, the ministers of Rudra stood with weapons raised in their hands.
Threatening them and crying out, "Stay! Stay!", they advanced.
To them, Brahmā spoke with gentle words, preceded by consolation;
praising them all with joined palms and a liberated mind, he said: || 27-28 ||
Brahmā said: "O you all, great-souled ones, you are endowed with sovereignty;
for you are indeed imperishable, immortal, and likewise unimpeded."
Endowed with the power of great yoga, you are invincible in battle by anyone;
O supreme lords, who could surpass you, even Śakra himself?
"O God of gods, by your command I have come here from Mandara;
please grant me permission to bestow a boon upon the Goddess.
The lords of the Gaṇas said:
The high-minded God himself shall be the giver of the desired boons to the Goddess;
indeed, the Goddess should not even mentally think of a boon from anyone else.
The Lord Maheśvara is capable of bestowing grace upon the entire world;
he bestows grace upon you as well—how much more so, then, upon the Goddess, O Lord of the World?
The Grandfather said:
The high-minded Mahādeva is unable to grant a boon;
he who thinks of the God in such a manner shall never come to be [liberated]. (34)
It is said that the goddess Pārvatī does not wish to leave the side of the Blessed One;
therefore, the god Śiva has sent me here from him to request the desired boons.
Sanatkumāra said: Then those lords, with disciplined minds, beheld the Great Lord, who was worthy of being seen, and the World-Protector, who had granted them permission.
Then, O great sage, all those appointed ones, having understood the matter, spoke there to Brahmā, the cause of the world, and to the lords of the Gaṇas:
"O Grandfather, we have learned that you have been sent by the God of gods."
"O Lord, enter now with Pārvatī, desiring to grant her a boon.
Then the Grandfather (Brahmā), having descended from his celestial chariot, quickly alighted upon that mountain peak variegated with various minerals.
Then that king of mountains, a vast mass of great rocks from which streams of precious minerals flowed,
shone like the divine mountain of sunrise, radiant with the released sun.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Arrival of Brahmā," in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, within the section on the granting of boons to the Goddess.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the Daughter of the Mountain suddenly beheld him as he approached.
Surrounded on all sides by those highly fortunate sages,
he was like the sun, the source of splendor, at midday with its rays;
she [then] honored him with the guest-offering (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
Rudrāṇī worshipped the four-faced one who had approached her. ||2||
Brahmā said:
Having become the mother of the world and having likewise sustained the universe,
why do you now wish to consume the world further with this ascetic heat?
O Goddess, do not destroy this world after having created it while engaged in ascetic penance;
having understood this, sustain this world—salutations to you.
O sinless one, O goddess, bestower of boons, this world and I myself were created by Rudra from you in the past; do not bring about our destruction.
O Rudrāṇī, by your ascetic power, the entire world—both stationary and moving—is sustained.
He suffers like a lotus uprooted from the water at midday in the summer heat. || 6 ||
"Or what is it in your heart, O Goddess, even if it be very difficult to accomplish?
Choose a boon; I shall grant you all of them, O daughter of Himavat.
The Goddess said:
O Lord Īśāna, O four-faced God, you are the granter of boons;
this devotee is devoted to me and is always dear to me, O Master. ||8||
"O Lord of the World, first subdue this tiger; then you shall grant me a boon.
Today, for a thousand years, he has remained before me, meditating with unblinking eyes and motionless ears."
"Bestow a boon upon him, O God; for I am not yet a seeker of a boon. || 8.55.10 ||
The Grandfather said:
"This wicked-souled beast has come here to devour you.
O Goddess, his mind is not pure; he is cruel and evil-minded."
Behold this evil-minded one; his mind has no regard for your welfare.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having heard those words, Rudrāṇī, the creator of the worlds,
beheld with her divine eye that act of rashness committed out of ignorance.
Previously devoted to no other, yet defiled by the fault of his birth, he then became one who understood the truth; thereupon, the daughter of Himavat spoke.
O Blessed One, who indeed in the worlds, while existing in the state of an animal, remains motionless, with ears and eyes fixed, and fasts for even a single divine day? (14)
Why would he who possesses such great majesty remain for a thousand years? He has not been reborn among the animals. (1.5)
"Whether this one be evil-minded or not, let him be of great strength;
'he is to be favored by me'—let this indeed be the boon granted to him. (16)
Sanatkumāra said: Then that blessed Lord, the four-faced Grandfather,
spoke these words to the Goddess while the sages were listening.
Even outcasts may attain perfection here through association with the noble;
just as this man, though a doer of cruel deeds, shall attain unsurpassed perfection. (18)
Therefore, noble ones should always be served even by one who constantly commits evil;
for a person who stays near those free from sin quickly attains accomplishment. || 19 ||
"O blameless one, this wicked-minded sinner is worthy of your favor;
therefore, O Goddess of gods, grant him whatever boon pleases you."
The Goddess said:
"He is immortal, free from old age, inexhaustible, and likewise immutable;
he is endowed with the power of great yoga and possessed of supreme sovereignty."
And may this Lord of the Gaṇas be my beloved, if you so desire.
The Grandfather said:
"So be it; may prosperity be yours. All this shall come to pass.
You know the minister of Brahmadatta, that wretched Brahmin."
Although he had long possessed devotion to you, he fell into the state of a tiger due to a curse;
furthermore, this Yakṣa was formerly the gatekeeper of Pāñcāla.
"Because this joy has been produced for him today by you and me,
he shall therefore become famous by the name Somanandin.
And whoever should praise him in times of distress, in wildernesses, or in moments of fear— "
They know no fear of tigers, lions, or leopards.
O Īśānī, tell me also what your heart's desire is,
so that by the command of the Supreme Lord, I may grant you everything.
The Goddess said: "O Blessed One, I desire a divine complexion with the luster of gold;
and may I become renowned in the world as Gaurī, O Lotus-born One. (27)
The Grandfather said:
"So be it, O Mother of the World, O you whose wealth is asceticism!
Choose another boon; may prosperity be yours, O Goddess, for I grant you a boon."
"This great austerity practiced by you for the welfare of the world is not matched by a suitable bridegroom;
therefore, let another be sought.
The Goddess said:
"I desire, O Blessed One, a son who shall be the foremost among all upholders of dharma,
possessed of great strength and great energy, and honored by all the worlds.
The Grandfather said:
"O Goddess, you shall have a son endowed with the power of great yoga;
he shall be invincible to all beings and possessed of the eight qualities of sovereign power. (3.1)
The conqueror, the slayer, and likewise the instructor, he is indeed ageless and unslayable;
he is forever beyond reproach and the most excellent among all living beings.
He is eternally a child, yet handsome, a knower of dharma, and a lover of dharma.
He is the protector of gods and brahmins, the learned one, and indeed the omniscient one.
He has six faces and twelve arms, and likewise holds a spear in his hand;

he is devoted to Brahman, a refuge for all, and the destroyer of the hosts of those who hate the gods. He is not born from a womb, possesses great splendor, and is indeed the creator of happiness for the worlds.
He spoke this slowly and then became silent.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having granted those boons and having performed a circumambulation, the Lord of Gods [departed].
Having ascended that celestial chariot, he then departed for his own world.
When he had departed, Rudrāṇī too, preceded by Somanandin, took her place in the sky like Rohiṇī followed by Budha;
she was like Gāyatrī following the Mantras, or as Śacī follows Jayanta. || 37 ||
Thus does that Rudrāṇī shine, preceded by Somanandin.
Whatever wise man, being free from sloth, recites this always in the morning, for him Somanandin and Hara, the bestower of boons, shall not bring fear. (38-39)
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Granting of Boons to Somanandi and Devī," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said: O Blessed One, regarding that which was previously described by you in the description of the hells—
Having committed an evil deed, men indeed go to hell.
All those who have performed good deeds become endowed with the happiness of heaven;
whereas Brāhmaṇas, having committed evil deeds, fall into miserable states and calamities.
How then do they again attain the great fruit of heavenly happiness?
Or how, having entered many wombs among the mixed castes,
do those who have performed good deeds once again attain an auspicious destiny?
Sanatkumāra said:
Listen, O Vyāsa, to an ancient account as it was heard among the Daśārṇas,
concerning the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of seven disciples of a twice-born man.
There was a renowned and pure Brāhmaṇa of the Kauśika lineage named Suparvan.
He was righteous, generous, and learned, honored by the brahmins.
He had seven disciples who were indeed dull-witted, yet devoted to serving their teacher; learn their names from me. ||5-6||
Ātreya named Kaṇḍara, Upamanyu and Dāmana, Śāṇḍilya, Hāla, Gārgya, and likewise Vidala. ||7||
Śaiśira, Gautama, Daṇḍakīla, Kāśyapa, Vidarbha, and Hārīta—these seven are renowned. ||8||
Then the preceptor, possessed of great ascetic power, said this to those brahmins:
"Having gone from here in a short time, go to the beautiful Surūpī, who was given by her patron."
"Go quickly to the city of Māhiṣmatī and bring [the fire] for the sake of the oblation.
Thus addressed by him, those men from Māhiṣmatī set out without delay.
Returning from Gāmā with only a small amount of earth,
they then encountered a drought as a famine unfolded.
Overcome by hunger, they all became uncertain of what to eat.
When the seventh day had arrived, they were without food and deeply distressed.
They addressed that village, saying, "Let us eat; why do you sit idle?
Among them was one named Kaṇḍara, born of the lineage of Atri. || 13 ||
He said to them, "Do not eat this cow belonging to our guru;
for even death on account of the guru is praiseworthy for us, though we may be unwise. (14)
"Let us not go to our destruction, consumed by the anger of our preceptor.
When they, being tormented by hunger, did not at all accept those words,
he then spoke these meaningful words to them once more:
Or perhaps, O wise ones rich in asceticism, you have resolved to eat them.
"Let us not consume this in vain; let us consecrate it for the sake of the ancestors.
O auspicious ones, let there be no loss for us here through these two faults. (17)
"In this way, we shall certainly be joined with only a small fault.
Having been addressed thus and having properly understood his words, they, remaining unperturbed,
sprinkled that milch-cow for the sake of the ancestors.
Then, O great sage, having consecrated it according to the rules and having offered it, || 1.9 ||
Then, having offered oblations into the fire and each having partaken [of the meal],
they tied a single calf around their necks and brought it to the preceptor.
Then, seeing that calf, the twice-born one asked them about the cow.
Those cruel men said, "A tiger killed her on the road. ||21||
Then, having heard their words and suspecting those evil-minded ones,
the great ascetic beheld with his divine eye that she had been devoured by them;
thereupon, his eyes red with rage, he seemed to burn them up as it were.
Seeing his calf, he spoke, deeply afflicted by compassion:
"Indeed, she was eaten by you, yet the truth was not told to me.
Because of that deed, a miserable fate shall befall you."
Pleased by those disciples, that Brahmin of great splendor spoke these words once more to them all out of compassion: ||25||
What has been spoken by me is true; it shall not be false.
But for those whom we have assisted, they themselves shall determine what is auspicious.
"You must not remain near me now by any means;
having seen this young child, my son, lest I consume you—go!"
Then they all, together, having lost their senses and being distraught,
were joined with time as they reflected upon the words of their preceptor.
O Vyāsa, that auspicious river named Daśārṇā has holy waters.
On its bank was a divine, renowned, and most radiant forest.
There lived a heroic and powerful hunter named Kṣupaka;
he had sons of great strength born to him by Citakā.
Caitaka gave birth to those seven esteemed sons;
they all became hunters and were indeed renowned as the Caitakas.
Carrying their bows, they roamed about, slaying deer and birds.
Lions, tigers, elephants, and boars of every kind; || 3.2 ||
Listen to me as I recount those names they bore in their state as hunters: Kāṇḍāru was named Arjunaka, and Damana became Siṃhaka.
Hālabhū, Vyāghraka, Vidala, Śarabha, as well as Śaiśira, Himavat, Hastika, and Daṇḍakīlaka; ||34||
Vidarbha and Vajraka—these indeed are their names;
as flesh-eaters, they roam individually through that terrible forest. ||35||
All these predatory creatures, destroyers of living beings, had entered into a wicked womb;
wandering about at times, they likewise slaughtered deer.
Having reached the hermitage of their preceptor by virtue of their well-performed deeds,
all those deer there became agitated with fear.
Observing the deer thus terrified, that brahmin of great asceticism—
He gazed in all directions and saw the hunters who had arrived.
Having recognized through meditation that his own disciples had fallen into the state of hunters, he, overcome with compassion and desiring their welfare, spoke to them. (3.9)
Formerly, I was served with devotion by you brahmins;
yet because of that very action, due to the curse incurred from the killing of a cow,
you have now attained this wretched state of hunters, a life of violence.
And that cow was eaten for the sake of a rite for the ancestors; it was not out of malice. ||41||
Therefore, having fallen from this state, you shall be endowed with the memory of your former births;
having become deer at Kālañjara, you shall then become cakravāka birds on a lake. Thereafter, having become swans on an island in Lake Mānasa, you shall indeed [attain liberation]. ||42||
Furthermore, having become human again, conscious in birth after birth,
you shall— through my grace, being high-souled and unwearied, and joined in yoga—
be liberated from all sins and attain the world of Brahmā. ||43-44||
Having heard this, their former memory then arose, and the thought occurred to them: "This is our preceptor. (45)
Then, loathing the actions they had performed in their previous births,
they circumambulated [the place] and departed toward Daśārṇa.
Having reached the bank of the Daśārṇa and consulted with one another, [they proceeded].
Remembering their former births, they chose death itself. ||47||
Then, among those who had reached a decision, there was a certain Brahmin named Kāṇḍarīya;
he was a hunter named Arjunaka, and he spoke these words: ||48||
"Sirs, that which was previously spoken by me has not been done by you; now that [the consequence] has arrived, do not disregard my words. (49)
I shall proclaim what is most beneficial; listen and act accordingly, so that we may be liberated from this birth and not lose our mindfulness.
Fathers desire sons for their own nourishment and for their deliverance;
and we have been begotten by that great-souled hunter and likewise raised with hardship by our mother and father. (51)
"How can we desire death without having taken leave of those two?
If you think that they should be dismissed after being consulted, we shall unite ourselves with the highest good; this is for your ultimate benefit. (52-53)
If they do not dismiss us,
we shall remain intent on serving them until they both have died;
then, having perfected our souls, we shall be entirely free from debt.
"We shall go to that meritorious state; this is our supreme good.
Saying "So be it," they all accepted his words and, reflecting upon their former births, returned to their very homes. (55–56)
Then, seeing them returned, their father and mother Citrakā were filled with supreme joy and spoke these words to them:
"O dear sons, today you have come home after a very long time."
"Today we have become truly and firmly deluded; why was this delay made? (58)
Cītaka said:
"O sons, my father is overcome with hunger today; out of affection for his children, O dear sons, he does not eat this cooked meat, nor does he drink this liquor. (59)
Sanatkumāra said: Despising even their own births, all those born of sinful wombs spoke these auspicious words to Kṣupa and Citaka: || 8.56.60 ||
"Sirs, eat without obstacle for the sake of nourishment and peace;
we ourselves do not eat here today, for we shall eat tomorrow—of this there is no doubt.
Then, on account of their old age, the two were unable to endure hunger at that time.
They took their food and became thoroughly satisfied.
Beholding them both satisfied, they all bowed their heads in every way and then spoke these words with effort and in unison: || 62-63 ||
"O parents, we are utterly weary of this birth;
we wish to renounce it, so you ought to grant us your permission. (64)
Having heard those words of theirs, their father,
his eyes clouded with tears, embraced all his sons and said this to them:
"O sons, in former times I was a brahmin of celebrated vows."

He was the highly esteemed friend of the royal sage Divodāsa. Once, while practicing archery intensely with his bow in a delightful forest, he said this to me: "O King, you do not know how to handle this bow."
"Unknowing what this affliction is, you act in vain. Thus the king spoke. "The knowledge of mantras is prescribed for Brahmins;
in matters of invitation and feeding, the twice-born are indeed skilled in speech. (68–69)
Laughing, I said to him, "Bring me my bow,
so that I may discharge an arrow at the target you have named for me.
Thus addressed, he then presented me with the bow and the arrow.
He said, "Then, aiming at the target, I discharged an arrow.
There stood a brahmin, a wanderer among deer, firm in his vows.
Pierced by that [arrow], the radiant one died instantly."
Thus, having observed that he was dead, I was dismissed by that king.
Out of fear of the terrible sin of killing a Brahmin, he questioned his father; the father replied, "You have no fear; how could the sin of killing a Brahmin be yours? (74)
Having passed through hundreds of different births, this was seen by the Self-Existent One;
therefore, with supreme devotion, I remained for many years intent on the service of my father,
together with this wife of mine.
In time, my father also was joined with death. 76.
And she remained right there with this very woman, O sinless ones; then, after a long time, I was struck down by a cow. And as I fell into the fire, this fair-eyed woman descended after me, weeping.
"Thus I was struck by a cow, and by the killing of a deer while wandering as a hunter."
O sons, due to my sin, I fell from the status of a Brahmin at birth and was born as a hunter;
thus, through a thousand births, I have been born into this most dreadful state.
Yet, by means of that devotion to my father and through his perfect propitiation—
"Through fasting, my mindfulness is restored and knowledge also arises. || 8.56.80 ||
"I know that all of you Brahmins have indeed fallen due to your actions regarding the cow,
and likewise that your consciousness has been lost through the curse of your preceptor.
Later, by his command, all of you sons shall indeed have your minds liberated."
And likewise, all those of great strength have today regained their senses.
For this mother of yours knows you well; she is virtuous and ever devoted to her husband.
Do that which I tell you today, for it is dear to me. ||83||
Then, all of you, being unwearied, shall attain what is most excellent; you shall be free from disease and sorrow, and you shall not lose your consciousness.
O sons, this is undoubtedly my final birth among human beings.
"Having died from here, I must go to the auspicious abode of Brahmā.
You all should wait for me for some time without weariness.
When I have gone to heaven, you shall perform whatever is beneficial; do not grieve."
"Furthermore, sons must necessarily serve their mother and father when they are in great distress;
there is no duty more powerful than this.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, filled with wonder, their grief vanished and free from envy,
they waited upon him for that duration of time until those two departed their lives.
Having properly performed the funeral rites for those two who had passed away,
all seven of those hunters then purified themselves by means of fasting according to the prescribed rule at the great river Daśārṇā.
Furthermore, on Mount Kālañjara, seven deer were born.

Remembering their former birth there due to the fall from the wind-god's chariot, they then purified themselves and were reborn among the ruddy geese. Learn from me now those names they bore in their state as deer.
For he was long-lived, invincible, and unshakable as the force of the wind. ||92||
Śrīpārśva, Śaṅkhapāda, and Somalakṣya as the seventh—
remembering their former births and feeling mutual affection—
they suddenly gave up their lives together by leaping from the mountain peak.
Those seven [types] are likewise found among diseases and among wild animals. || 94 ||
Having taken birth there, they were then born again as birds on Śaradvīpa;
thus it became known as Śaradvīpa, a beautiful lake among the Kāmpilyas. ||95||
There too, those seven brothers were born as *cakravāka* birds;
they are remembered as Maruddeva, Śikhaṇḍin, Rathanemisvara, Śikhin, Jīva, Vṛkṣa, and Dhvaja. (96)
Once, while they had been reborn there,
the immensely radiant King Aṇuha of Kāmpilyaka came to that region in person.
Having reached that lake, he was filled with joy along with his women.
Having reached the Mandākinī, he sported there with the Apsarases like an immortal god.
Seeing him thus sporting there with the divine Maruts,
that Cakravāka bird felt a longing for those very sensual pleasures.
"If I were indeed his son, I would surely obtain the kingdom; then I would enjoy these sensory pleasures—of this there is no doubt. (8.56.100)
Knowing his thought, the second one, known by the name Cakra and called Śikhaṇḍin, then spoke to him while laughing:
"You have contemplated both the status of a prince and a kingdom."
"In that matter, may I be your priest; this is also my own desire.
Then, having understood what was thought by those two, Rathanemisvara reflected: "In that case, O Lord, may I be your minister."
Sanatkumāra said: While those three were thus reflecting,
the other Cakravākas then became enraged and spoke these words to them.
"What you have thought is inconceivable, for you are seekers of sense-objects.
Therefore, once you are released from this, you shall obtain your heart's desire.
Having cursed them, he observed that they were dejected in mind, and then [he spoke] to them again.
By whom that state of being a prince and even the kingdom itself was contemplated. || 1.06 ||
Out of compassion, they spoke these words to him whose mind was lost,
employing many qualities of consolation, as if they themselves were suffering.
"O Lord, by your power we have crossed over this hardship;
you are our provider of wisdom and are indeed considered by us to be a bridge.
For had you not spoken, the cow would have been offered to the ancestors."
And we would not serve our fathers; consequently, there would be no recognition [of them]. || 1.09 ||
"By your power, this manifestation of our yogic sovereignty has occurred;
therefore, we shall speak further of what is for your own welfare—listen to us."
O lord of men, you will remain with a heart attached [to worldly things] for as long as you,
along with your companions, do not hear these true words of mine;
but once you have attained the knowledge of yoga, you shall reach an auspicious state.
Sanatkumāra said: Then all those great birds, united and with disciplined minds,
completely relinquished their state as birds and entered another womb.
Then all those hunters, as well as the deer called Cakras, having been consumed by the sage’s anger, were born again in human bodies; those three alone became lords of yoga in the kingdom.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Curse of Kauśika," within the Narrative of the Seven Hunters in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Those four teachers, moreover, were birds who acted according to their own will.
They were born as sons of the high-souled Yāyāvara brāhmaṇa.
When they were born, the Brahmin, a man of great austerity, brought about their livelihood without any distress,
guided by their good fortune.
Having performed the Vedic vows and studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches, they [proceeded].
They practiced yoga alone, being devoted to it and having it as their ultimate goal.
The other three as well, O Vyāsa, impelled by their own past actions,
attained that birth which they had previously contemplated.
For the first son born of Aṇuha was known as Brahmadatta; one son of Aṇuha was born, and the second was the son of his family priest. ||5||
Then, having attained that birth, those three became like the three ministers;
they were like the three fires, or like the three worlds.
Those three great-souled ones grew like the three oceans.
When they had acquired their learning and were proficient in their respective duties,
their fathers, with joyful hearts, entrusted them with their own tasks.
Aṇuha bestowed the abundant kingdom upon Brahmadatta;
then, accompanied by Kīrtimatī, he departed for the forest.
But the priest Dhṛtarāta, being the master of his own duty, [installed] his son [in the office].
Having left him there, he whose vows were highly praised then departed for Pañcāla.
The minister Sudhanvan, however, having established his son Brahmadhanvan— the steadfast one— in his own office, departed together with his wife.
When they had gone to their respective worlds, the powerful Brahmadatta [reigned].
He indeed ruled the kingdom together with Pañcāla and Brahmadhanvan.
While thus governing the kingdom, performing sacrifices, and enjoying [its fruits],
those virtuous ones passed many years in happiness.
Then, after a long time, he dwelt happily in his home with his wife and his circle of friends, like Kubera in the Puṣpaka chariot.
Then, the Knower of All Sounds observed an ant acting out of its own will, offering flatteries to another ant.
Having discerned through his knowledge that such a state existed even within the womb of a worm, he reflected upon it.
O sinless one, as he laughed aloud with an open mouth and made a sound like that of a bird,
his blue-lotus-eyed wife, seeing that laughter of his, became enraged and said: "What is this strange thing that you have displayed today?"
Greatly agitated, the king sought to appease his beloved, who was dearer to him than life itself; yet that fair-faced woman did not become placated with him.
When she was not satisfied even though much that was true was being said to her,
he then propitiated Viṣṇu for the sake of winning her favor.
Having gone to the Sālavana forest together with Pañcāla,
that great man, preceded by Brahmadhanvan, traveled in a magnificent chariot.
There, on the seventh day, he was sent forth by Viṣṇu.
That tiger among men went to his own excellent city, Kāmpilya.
At that very time, four auspicious brahmins, endowed with great yoga, said this to one another:
"We have accomplished our purpose; what work remains for us here, staying among mortals?"
Let us go to our own Brahma-source; let us be liberated from this great fear.
Those three companions of ours are indeed sinking;
let us awaken them here so that they do not meet with defeat.
Then all those twice-born ones, having bowed to their father, said:
"O father, we are masters of yoga, perfected indeed by our own actions."
We take our leave and shall depart for our own womb created by Brahmā;
having cast off these human bodies, do not release us—salutations to you! (25)
The father said:
"Fathers desire sons, thinking, 'They will deliver us from fear.
O sons, that fear is both of this world and difficult to overcome in the next. (26)
Being bound by debt and not having released your own pledge, how do you go away—may it be well with you? Do you not perceive the unrighteousness [of this]? ||20||
The sons said:
"O father, we are masters of yoga; we shall grant you worlds free from affliction, of which there is no doubt, reaching which you shall no longer grieve. (28)
"O father, how could we, as your sons, allow you not to attain the status of a Brahmin? Listen, for we shall likewise provide for your wealth even in this world. (29)
"Take this letter and show it to Brahmadatta;
as soon as the king reads it, he will provide for your livelihood.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that bull among sages, their father, knowing their power, considered all that to be exactly so and further approved it.
Then, having bound themselves in postures, those ascetics departed with disciplined minds;
and your father, of exceeding splendor, beheld them as they had become like luminous bodies.
Taking that letter and reflecting upon his sons,
he went swiftly to Kāmpilya, desiring to see the best of kings.
And that king, having come from the Sāl forest, entered the city;
and from afar, a brahmin presented that letter to him.
Having observed auspicious omens, that lord of men,
saying "Bring the letter," took his place upon that great chariot.
He then stood at the city gate in that magnificent vehicle.
Brahmadhanvan held the parasol, while the Pāñcālas fanned his face. ||3.6||
Then, having taken the letter, he read it calmly;
and in that letter there were two verses which brought auspiciousness.
Those who, though afflicted by the slaughter of a cow due to a curse imposed by their guru,
became grateful through devotion to their father, were all born with auspicious destinies.
These were the seven hunters among the Daśārṇas, and the deer on Mount Kālañjara.
The ruddy geese on Śaradvīpa and the swans on Lake Mānasa—
even they were born in Kurukṣetra as Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas. Having set out upon a long journey, why do you despair?
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those two verses, the three of them were as if they had drunk poison;
having then fallen into a swoon, they regained consciousness and entered the city.
Having entered the city and the palace, they remained unwearied,
deliberating thus and so, and set their minds upon the forest.
And that illustrious wife approached the lord of men.
Filled with joy, she spoke thus to the king together with his circle of friends.
Having become a lord of yoga, you were nevertheless attached to all kinds of enjoyments;
therefore, for the sake of awakening me, you then summoned your anger.
I know you to be an expert in the cries of birds, and I know you to be a fowler;
therefore, O King, knowing this, I am intent on awakening you. (45)
Therefore, O King, endow this Brahmin, their imperishable father,
with wealth today, and having consecrated his son in the kingdom,
let us both go to the forest tomorrow; do not delay any longer.
Having performed all those duties together with his wife, the king, observing his vows,
departed for the forest and ascended to heaven through yoga. When he had gone, Pañcāla also performed extremely difficult austerities.
He performed the breaking of his fast and indeed attained the state of a Yakṣa;
and in time, the high-souled Brahmadhanvan, firm in his vows,
beheld the goddess, the daughter of Himavat, through his ascetic penance.
Then, seeing her who grants boons, Brahmadhanvan spoke to that auspicious lady.
I desire the power to assume forms at will and your devotion forever; furthermore, when I have fallen into great distress, I desire to be uplifted by you alone from that state. (51)
Having said, "So be it," she then departed for her desired destination;
meanwhile, the evil-minded Brahmadhanvan became intoxicated with passion.
Having previously been righteous, he was now tormented by unrighteousness.

Deluded by passion, he approached maidens and the wives of sages everywhere, assuming the form of their husbands; yet no one recognized him as he behaved in such a manner, even among those closest to him.
Now, there was one known as Āla, a great ascetic who lived among the deer;
his wife was named Sudharmā, who was truly beautiful.
For the gods, the Siddhas, and the Cāraṇas declare:
"This beautiful woman is peerless in beauty among all others in the three worlds. And he did not perceive any difference between her and his wife.
"At what time will her separation from her husband occur?
Having heard that she was so beautiful and virtuous, Brahmadhanvan,
desiring her separation from her husband, assumed the form of a tiger.
Then, O Vyāsa, having assumed a very large, deformed, and terrifying form,
that fool struck fear into the deer with his mere sight.
At that time, O Lord, the herd of deer was terrified by the fear of the tiger.
He became invisible, his speed as swift as the mind;
and Hāla too, seeking to live, fled at that time along with the deer.
Sudharmā, that beautiful Brāhmaṇī, also fled out of fear of the tiger.
Due to her female nature, she did not follow the herd of deer that had fallen [into the trap];
and seeing her all alone, the evil-minded Brahmadhanvan [seized her].
Casting off his tiger-form,
he addressed her with gentle words full of consolation, as she was tormented by fear.
"Do not fear; let there be no dread for you, O blessed one. I am your husband here, O slender-waisted lady. That king of beasts has gone; take heart, my beloved. (64)
Having regained her composure, she of great renown beheld that form resembling her husband, and thought in her heart: "He was seen by me together with those deer."
Seeking to save his life, he fled; how has he come back again?
O wicked one, the Lord of the Gods always assails me without weariness.
"Since he has arrived here desiring to lust after her, why should he not be one who harbors inner malice?
Therefore, I shall clearly behold this wicked man with my divine eye. (67)
Sanatkumāra said: In the meantime, Brahmadhanvan took her by the hand and, being delighted, spoke this to her: "What are you reflecting upon in your heart?"
"Do not embrace me now, for I have emerged from the very jaws of death.
Surely I am your beloved husband; do not be angry, O woman of excellent complexion. (69)
Then, out of wickedness, he kissed her on the cheek;
and the evil-minded one, having embraced her, pressed his limbs against her limbs.
He loosened her waist-knot and forcibly drank from her lower lip;
and that beautiful woman recognized him as wicked by that deed.
Sudharmā said:
"O fool, you are not my husband; you are Śakra, there is no doubt about this.
O evil-minded one, I am no longer an object for Madana. (72)
Thus addressed by her, he who was completely cast off fell upon the surface of the earth and assumed his own form.
Then, with eyes copper-red with anger, she seemed as if she would consume him with her gaze.
Having gazed upon his face, she of the beautiful brows spoke these words:
"Many wives of sages have been seduced by you with your wicked mind;
yet no other woman like me has ever been encountered by you before. (74-75)
Now behold this difficult-to-attain fruit of that action previously performed by you, received from my presence. (76)
"Having assumed whatever form you used to frighten the deer here by force, you shall wander in that very same form for many years;
moreover, you will be unable to kill any human being anywhere. ||77||
"And when the sixth mealtime arrives, you shall obtain a deer for food.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having addressed him thus cruelly, the high-minded woman of auspicious conduct—
He went after those very deer; then, not seeing his wife, he too was tormented by grief, thinking she had been killed. While lamenting, he saw her and, embracing her, spoke thus: || 8.57.80 ||
"By good fortune you have arrived, having escaped from the jaws of death.
I hope, O beautiful one, that you were not seen by that king of beasts.
Sudharmā said:
That lion was not a beast of ill-will, nor was he anyone capable of assuming forms at will;
he had come for my sake and was consumed by me like a moth.
That evil-minded one, due to my curse, has returned to his natural state as a tiger.
Like King Saudāsa, who by the curse of Śakti assumed the body of a Rākṣasa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of hers, Hāla, who knew the true principles of dharma and artha, [spoke].
With his divine eye, he beheld the imperishable Brahmadhanvan.
That compassionate one said this to his virtuous wife:
"O daughter of Atri, you have committed a wicked deed—a deed censured by the righteous. (85)
O virtuous lady, this great destruction of the vast power of his asceticism has been wrought today; yet women are not defiled, just as rivers are not by those who bathe in them.
And it is not possible to crush you, who are well-guarded by Dharma,
just as it is impossible for men to eat food concealed with poison.

Clad in armor and prepared for battle, they gathered together with the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas.
The *rakṣasas* remaining from the oblations in the fire were taken up by the son of Śakti;
the gods, being weak and terrified, sought refuge [with him].
The *yakṣas*, the best of the immortals, are always dependent upon Kubera.
And he, being diligent, performs the work of the foremost gods.
"O best of asuras, since there is no one more powerful in the worlds than the enemies of the Daityas, a state of dual policy (dvaidhībhāva) is not appropriate.
When the Dānava Mahiṣa had spoken thus with confidence in the assembly, [the ministers replied: 123.
The great asura Druma spoke these words, which were very clear and meaningful:
"How can the victorious gods, endowed with power, form an alliance with us, who were previously defeated in battle while being weak?"
Having quickly prepared our fortresses, both mountainous and watery,
let us remain in a state of waiting after declaring war, constantly intent upon victory.

Constantly destroying sacrifices, vows, and observances, as well as the system of social classes and stages of life in this world, they sought to strike down everything on all sides. Then, through the destruction of the world, the path of righteous action was severed.
"Having recognized that the gods have been humbled, we shall advance against them clad in armor.
Then they all approved his words,
just as living beings accept food when death is near.
The enemies of the gods rose up, intent on the destruction of the world,
like oceans overflowing their bounds at the time of universal dissolution, agitated by the winds.
He was as dark blue as a rain-cloud, with limbs that were thick, rounded, and elevated.
Then, wearing a pearl necklace as white as the rays of the moon,
Sunda leapt up from his seat,
churning like the ocean at the end of an eon, garlanded with foam.

Thereafter, his younger brother Nisunda—whose vehicle was water, whose arms were like iron clubs, whose large eyes were red and long, who caused terror to his enemies, and whose mind remained undaunted—did not leave his seat at that time. || 13.2 ||
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Exertion of the Daityas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, for the destruction of the worlds, the leader of the Dānavas set forth.
The army was crowded with rutting elephants and swarming with chariots and horses.
Then that army of Dānavas scattered in every direction,
like the waters of the ocean tossed by the wind at the time of universal dissolution.
Some slaughtered the Brāhmaṇas, while others crushed the Vaiśyas.
Some devoured the Kṣatriyas, while others devoured the Śūdras; they swallowed,
licked, ate, and broke everything on all sides—
the food and sacrificial offerings at the sacrifices, as well as the banners and the sacrificial posts, O enemy of Mura.
Resounding with the sound of the study of the Vedas well-recited, where the groves and trees were honored by the foremost of sages,
where there were abundant stores of bark garments, deerskins, and darbha grass, and where there were mountain torrents of cool water flowing in endless abundance.

Others, having spread out, destroyed the hermitages where wild rice and *gavedhuka* grass were gathered near the edges, where deer, bears, and monkeys slept in confidence, and which were filled with the canopy of smoke from sacrificial fires.
Some asuras, whose luster was like that of aged serpents,
seized the matted locks of the sages and tore them out, washing them with the water of sacred fords.
Other asuras, having cast them down, ground them into the earth with their feet.
The sages [beheld them] like blazing fires, as if for their own destruction. ||8||
Some subduers of the Dānavas touched the heads of the sages’ wives with their hands, palms, and likewise with waters purified by merit.
Then, perceiving their own impending triumph, they set out on their journey.
Having summoned forces from all sides for the destruction of the world, they,
on an auspicious day, under a favorable constellation and at a victorious moment,
struck the war-drums and performed rites that bring victory.
Having summoned powerful beings equipped with armor and excellent elephants,
the asuras properly honored them and bound on their mail according to the prescribed ritual.
The two sides of the machines were filled with polished iron arrows,
and they fastened bamboo poles full of spears across them.
And those appointed to the middle and the two flanks bound on tomaras, kaṇapas, spikes, spears, discs, and axes. || 14 ||
He prepared his supreme weapons and well-tempered arrows,
which were fully equipped with fragrant feathers and cloth, and possessed sharpened tips.
They placed iron breastplates, shaped like the crescent moon and possessing a luster like that of the young moon,
upon their neck-chains, positioned between the two masses of their heads.
And the elephant-riders fastened beautiful, golden garlands of razor-sharp blades upon the frontal globes of the elephants.
And the Dānavas raised up long, variegated Vaijayantī banners, clearly marked with their own insignia, for the elephant division. 18.
Great-sounding bells were fastened to the heads of the principal elephants;
there were also very long yak-tail whisks, as radiant as the rays of a swan.
And for each one, there were four beautiful female elephants.
The warders of the enemy's elephants were stationed in front by the Daityas.
They made young horses, mounted by youths who were trained and skilled in weaponry, armored with iron mail and equipped with metal mesh, the vanguard.
Then other Daitya warriors followed— armored, clad in mail, bearing polished swords, with foot-soldiers in front of them pursued by archers,
and others wearing iron mesh armor.
Mounted upon horses that had been bathed and dressed in yellow cloths, they were girt with bound swords.
Then some disciplined young men, having bathed and performed auspicious rites,
yoked the chariots with horses of the swiftest speed.
Then some mounted chariots adorned with gold, equipped with weapons and banners, and resounding with networks of tinkling bells;
having heard that the army had been thus prepared, he who is honored by armies [set forth].
Sunda, the tiger among Dānavas, having performed the auspicious rites,
went forth on an excellent chariot made of gold, with beautiful poles and fine wheels,
adorned with various wonderful jewels and decorated with floral patterns and figures of animals and birds.
Then, having mounted a divine chariot adorned with banners and flags, drawn by horses swift as thought and yoked with those most exultant, he departed. (28)
Clad in armor, with his sword girded and white chowries being waved,
he was being praised on all sides by charioteers, panegyrists, and bards.
Even Niśuṇḍa, having mounted a war-elephant whose dark temples were covered with bees intoxicated by rut,
quickly went forth.
And other Dānavas there [departed] on chariots, horses, and elephants.
Extremely joyful, skilled in battle, and well-armored, they marched forth,
placing the great asura Tārakākṣa at the head of the army,
accompanied by many brave warriors on chariots, elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers.
Having quickly stationed the great asura Balonmatta at the rear with his fourfold army, and having placed Mahiṣa as the protector of the flanks,
he assigned Meghasvana and Mahāsvana to both sides.
With a vast army, those two proud Dānavas, the destroyers of their enemies—
Sunda and Nisunda in the midst, along with Maya, Śambhu, Khara, and Mura—
were armored, powerful, heroic, and capable of tearing asunder the enemy forces.
Those best of Dānavas set forth with great resolve toward heaven,
like the clouds of the *saṃvartaka* wind driven at the time of universal dissolution.
Having learned of their approach, [Indra] together with the inhabitants of the celestial realm...
Having departed, Śatakratu quickly went to Janasthāna.
Then, having ascended the peak of Meru, those enemies of the gods, together with all their forces, established their camp in the Nandana grove.
Then, having provided protection for the army on all sides, the lords of the Daityas took up their respective well-ordered and spacious quarters.
Then, having been granted permission by the foremost of the Dānavas,
all the Dānavas removed their armor and all their equipment at that time.
Having mounted the female elephants, the soldiers slowly removed their armor and quickly laid aside their weapons from the intoxicated tuskers.
Then the Dānava soldiers removed their armor, cast off their breastplates, and laid aside their variegated body-protectors.
Some Dānava soldiers bound to the wish-fulfilling trees those elephants whose bristling hair had subsided, who had bathed and drunk, and whose fatigue had vanished.
Some powerful nāgas, with bees clinging to them from their rutting ichor, shattered the wish-fulfilling trees, causing the terrified, intoxicated, and bewildered birds to flee.
Some powerful elephants, dark with rut,
rubbed their temples against the rows of bees that clung to the blossoms on the Kalpa trees.
Some elephants, intoxicated, plunged into the river Mandākinī,
whose banks were made tawny at their edges by the filaments of golden lotuses.
The horse-grooms bound the horses, which were freed from their sets of battle armor, whose minds were serene, whose bodies were rubbed down, who had drunk water, and whose fatigue was removed. (47)
Then they brought from the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) fine garments, most excellent variegated garlands, and sweet fruits.
Some Dānavas, their forms reddened by its pollen, joyfully went to the river Mandākinī and broke the golden lotuses there. ||49||
Some soldiers brought heaps of mandāra flowers;
others fetched many sweet fruits. (8.61.50)
Having stayed there for one night and having beaten their drums, the Dānavas,
prepared according to that same method, set out for Amarāvatī.
Then, by the sound of trumpets, the trumpeting of elephants,
and the lion-roars of the Daityas, Amarāvatī itself seemed to tremble.
Then, beholding the city empty, those best of Dānavas,
greatly delighted, spoke thus while roaring with a terrifying sound:
"Victorious is the enemy of the gods, the lion-like lord of the Daityas, Sunda!"
With arms firm and beautiful, a broad and expansive chest,
eyes lovely, wide, and long, a voice like the rumbling of water-laden clouds, and the gait of a rutting lordly elephant— he was the conqueror of Indra’s city. (54)

Following that, there arose Nisunda, the lord of the Dānavas, who was victorious over the foremost of the gods; he possessed beautiful, reddish, and wide eyes, moved with the playful gait of a lion, was invincible in battles, and was a conqueror of the best of the thirty deities.
He had the sound of a beaten drum and possessed thick, long thighs and arms. ||55||
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Entry into Amarāvatī," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having conquered the two lords of the Daityas, those two who were endowed with prowess ascended to heaven.
Together with the Daityas, they went to the Vindhya mountain, a mass of lofty rocks.
Having duly honored the Daityas and then dispatched the two brothers,
they both took delight at the foot of the Vindhya mountains, where the slopes were covered with blossoming trees.
Then Brahmā, having learned of the defeat of the gods by the two Daityas,
reflected with a one-pointed mind upon the proper means for their destruction.
Taking up every single sesame seed from the jewels,
he created a woman of beautiful appearance, with lovely limbs and a sweet voice.
The Grandfather (Brahmā) gave her the name Tilottamā;
at that time, she appeared as the very model for even the most divine women.
Her face was exceedingly full, her eyes like those of a blue lotus, her speech possessed the sound of a swan’s cry, and her gait was like that of a rutting elephant.
Seeing Lakṣmī, she became bashful and covered her face with a lotus; and the deities of the garden trembled at the sight of the beautiful-limbed woman’s body. (7)
Having brought her forth, the Creator then spoke to Indra, the subduer of Pāka:
"Previously, Madana was consumed by Śambhu with the fire of his eye."
Let us all go to the side of the wielder of the Pināka bow for his manifestation;
having propitiated him, we shall then act so that Madana may exist once more. ||9||
Then those enemies of the Asuras, together with Brahmā and her,
went to the peak of Mount Vindhya where the blessed Lord Hara resides.
Not seeing Śarva there, those best of gods meditated,
all of them reciting the *praṇava* with their minds fully surrendered to Śiva.
Then, in the midst of those dwellers of heaven, a Liṅga rose up,
well-compacted and firmly joined, like a mass of radiant energies.
Then, from it, a voice with clear syllables issued forth loudly:
"This wicked one, a thorn to the ascetics, has been consumed by me.
For your sake, I shall release him; he will perform your task.
Let this woman circumambulate me from all sides."
Thus addressed by Maheśa, she performed a circumambulation,
placing her hands— soft as red lotuses— in añjali upon her head.
Then, from that previous form, there issued forth from the mouth a three-eyed being of immeasurable splendor and beauty, with a serene countenance and lovely lips. Then,
a radiant light issued forth from the moon-like face of the wielder of the Pināka bow.
He quickly entered that woman, who was as radiant as the autumnal sun.
Then that beautiful one bowed to the southern form;
thereupon, a radiant face emerged from the Teacher of the Gods.
Resembling a cloud heavy with water, possessing a terrifying roar, shining with formidable fangs, and having eyes with glowing red corners. || 19 ||
Then, a brilliance exceeding that of the sun issued from his right mouth;
being beheld by all the gods, it entered the most excellent of women.
She then immediately bowed down before his western form.
Then, from her mouth, there emerged a supreme three-eyed being.
Then, a blazing radiance issued forth from the moon-like face of the enemy of Madana and swiftly entered that very same most excellent woman.
Having assumed a physical form, she approached Uttara and bowed with palms joined in reverence.
Her face emerged perfectly full and very serene.
From it, a radiance issued forth, possessing the brilliance of the sun and blazing fire,
and quickly entered that very woman of excellent complexion.
For the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods, four faces of the God of Gods issued forth toward the cardinal directions; it was not out of wonder at her beauty. ||25||
Because the Lord of Gods had previously consumed the fire residing within himself and thereby rendered Madana ashes, he showed favor to that most excellent woman.
And there Śiva spoke these words to all the gods:
"O best of gods, because she has circumambulated me and you all in a clockwise circle, therefore this place shall be mine."
On the Vindhya mountain, there will be one known by the name Maṇḍaleśvara. || 28 ||
Whoever performs this circumambulation of Maṇḍaleśvara, by him the earth with its seven continents has been circumambulated;
for I, the bestower of boons, shall always maintain my presence here. (29)
Having beheld Īśāna, the Lord of the Maṇḍala, a man who is self-restrained shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice and attain my world—
a realm crowded with many perfected beings (siddhas) and frequented by kinnaras and serpents (uragas).
It will always be appropriate for you and dear to me. || 31 ||
"This Tilottamā, for whose sake you, O best of gods,
have created her with undistracted focus— she shall accomplish that task of yours.
Upon seeing her, those two Daityas were infatuated and tormented by passion.
As they go toward each other's destruction, this very [conflict] shall come to pass.
"Undecaying and immortal, the most excellent of all Apsarases and auspicious,
she shall always be worthy of worship and salutation here in this place.
Sanatkumāra said:
When Maheśa had spoken thus, the gods, their minds well-pleased,
then dispatched that woman for the purpose of slaying the two Daityas.
And Brahmā, whose vehicle is the lotus, gave her as companions Wrath,
Pride, Death, all the Seasons, Envy, and Intoxication.
Then, having dispatched Kāla, Mṛtyu, Moha, Viṣāda,
and that goddess Tilottamā,
those gods of immeasurable splendor all indeed resolved themselves into a single body.
"Who, who, and which one among you has arrived here today, O bulls among the gods? (38)
Then, having bowed again to that Supreme Lord standing in the center while the gods were being compressed into a mass,
he became known there as Piṇḍāreśvara, because he remained stationed in the midst [piṇḍya-madhye] of them.
Having beheld the Lord Piṇḍāreśvara with devotion, a human being— ||| 8.62.40 ||

Freed from all that is impure, one becomes a member of the Gaṇa upon the dissolution of the body. Indeed, all those lingas on earth and the abodes of the Four-faced One (Brahmā) become visible once this [truth] has been seen. ||41||
Then all those deities, having performed their duty with diligence, [departed].
Having prostrated before the Supreme Lord, they returned to their own abodes;
she too, with her lovely face and side-glances, and full, uplifted breasts, [departed]. (43)
Then, as if captivating the minds of the gods with her graceful movements,
she set out toward the southern quarter, where the two Dānavas resided.
Then, as the two lords of the Daityas were wandering through the delightful foothills of the Vindhya mountains, whose ridges resounded with the songs of birds, they beheld her standing there.
Clinging to a branch of an *aśoka* tree in full bloom, frequented by intoxicated bees, she was wearing a variegated silken garment and a bound jeweled girdle;
she sang sweetly, passionately, evenly, melodiously, and without distraction. (46)
It is perfectly adorned with notes that are high, low, and exceedingly high. || 47 ||

Like the personification of the perfection of asceticism, like Fortune incarnate, like Rati herself attained in bodily form, and like the splendor of the moon—those two foremost of Dānavas [vied for her], each thinking, "She is mine alone! She is mine alone! (48)
Having approached the goddess, the two of them simultaneously grasped her hands.
Then, their minds possessed by pride, intoxication, anger, and envy,
those two foremost of asuras became exceedingly enraged with one another.
Gadā, Antaka, Kāla, and Mṛtyu quickly entered into them both.
Then, seizing their clubs, the two enraged warriors struck one another.
Then, struck there by each of them with a single blow,
they became despondent, their entire bodies shattered, deluded by the curse of Śiva.
Falling unconscious upon the ground like two trees severed at their roots,
they then emerged from there, their minds overcome by passion.
The two souls of those two chief Dānavas, together with Śukra, then departed from there; they were the life-breaths of those two evil-minded ones.
The two youths, possessing all beautiful limbs, quickly became powerful;
there, one boy said, "I am Śumbha, the enemy of my foes. (55)
Then Niśumbha said, "I am one, and the other there is a child.
Thereupon, Vindhya approached those two boys of immeasurable luster.
He commanded his wife, "Protect these two children," and then both those sons of the lord of the Dānavas grew up there.
Just as at the end of the dark fortnight the moon and the ocean [rise] simultaneously,
so too did those two subduers of enemies perceive their birth from the two Dānavas.
They performed most rigorous penance, subsisting on leaves, water, and air;
propitiated by them through their asceticism, the Lord came there and spoke.
"I am pleased with you both, my sons; what boon shall I grant you? Those two heroes chose this boon: "May we always be invincible and never subject to death."
Having heard that prayer of the two of them, the Grandfather replied:
"The death of these two sons must inevitably come about by some means or other. (61)
"O Lord of Daityas, immortality does not exist for anyone other than the gods.
To Brahmā, who had spoken thus, the two Dānavas requested a boon.
Having both reached a firm conclusion, their hair standing on end with joy, they said:
"O Grandfather, O God, may we never suffer defeat by Death, except for that maiden who is the Mother of the World. (63)
Having said, "So be it," both of those sons of the lord of the Daityas [departed].
The creator of the entire world vanished right there;
then, having ceased their intense asceticism and performed auspicious rites, the two of them—
wearing crowns, clad in armor, and adorned with necklaces and armlets— [remained].
Their limbs were smeared with yellow sandalwood paste, and they were dressed in yellow silk garments.
Having heard of the attainment of boons by Śumbha and Niśumbha from the Grandfather (Brahmā), those two best of Dānavas roamed through the delightful plateaus of the Vindhya mountains.
The Dānavas dwelling in the depths of Pātāla arrived, filled with joy:
Śambhu, Maya, Ghana, Keśin, Naraka, Namuci, and Druma.
And other millions of arrogant enemies of the gods who had survived the slaughter, all those Dānavas together, settled upon the plateau of the Vindhya mountains. || 69 ||
In that place strewn with heaps of flowers from various trees, creepers, and shrubs,
there were archers equipped with swords and adorned with variegated ornaments.
Like clouds in the sky accompanied by Indra’s bow and lightning,
the Dānava Maya then spoke there to those two best of Dānavas:
"O Daityas, the entire three worlds were enjoyed by your two fathers in the past; why then are they not taken back by you two now? (72)
Having utterly defeated all the assembled gods at the forefront of battle, those who were indeed the allies of your parents, the enemies of the gods, [have been slain]. (73)
"These very companions of yours in battle are intoxicated with strength," said Maya, the lord of the Daityas; then the great Asura Śumbha,
looking at the face of Niśumbha, spoke these words.
"O Daityas, having now divided the entire Bhūrloka among all of you and ourselves, we shall conquer all the gods at the front of the battle. Then that best of Asuras himself seized Jambūdvīpa.
The Lord gave Śākadvīpa to his younger brother Niśumbha;
he gave Śālmalidvīpa and Gomeda to the Dānavas.
He gave Krauñcadvīpa and Kuśadvīpa to the Daityas,
and the lord of the Daityas offered Puṣkaradvīpa to Bhārgava.
Having thus quickly divided the entire earthly realm at that time, [he departed].
Sacrificial offerings, reverential salutations with joined palms, obeisances, all sacrifices, and every virtuous deed—||79||
Having snatched them away from the gods, the Daityas and Dānavas seized them;
thereafter, the sacrifice of the high-souled Kaśyapa proceeded.
Then, having arrived at that sacrifice, the enemies of the gods began to destroy it.
"For now, O Kaśyapa, we hold sovereignty over the entire world of mortals.
In every circumstance, you ought to perform this sacrifice for us.
Thus addressed by the Daityas, Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci, then spoke.
Smiling as it were, he spoke these words, profound and meaningful:
"Having made the three worlds your own and having conquered all the immortals in battle,
you Daityas ought now to take for yourselves all the sacrificial portions."
Thus addressed by him at that time, the best of the Daityas and Dānavas—
Having mustered their entire strength and performed the rites of battle,
those Daityas and Dānavas— whose conduct was established in auspicious moments, lunar mansions, and days—
set forth on chariots, elephants, and horses.
Having properly stationed their protective forces behind, in front, and on both flanks, they set out intent on victory, desiring to conquer the gods.
Having learned of the arrival of those enemies, the subduer of Pāka (Indra) [prepared for battle]. || 86–87 ||
Having arranged all the defensive works for his own city, he, being well-prepared, fought against those who were united and seeking to conquer heaven. ||88||
On auspicious lunar days, asterisms, moments, and astrological divisions,
he duly honored the sages and paid homage to the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Accompanied by all the hosts of gods, having performed the auspicious rites, he set forth upon the elephant Airāvata,
who possessed four tusks and resembled a peak of the Himavat mountains.
Having mounted Airāvata, who constantly showers streams of rut-fluid, [he was held] by a great golden staff encircled by the rays of jewels. || 91 ||
With a radiant parasol held aloft,
he was fanned by whisks as pure as the mass of rays from the autumn moon.
He was honored by sages with blessings and shouts of victory, and by yak-tail whisks whose interiors were inlaid with clusters of rays from jeweled handles. 93.
Being praised on all sides by sūtas, māgadhas, and bards,
he then [proceeded] to a wide, level expanse devoid of trees.
Bṛhaspati arranged the Padmavyūha formation for the gods,
placing Śatakratu at the pericarp (kaṇikā) together with the Maruts.
And he placed the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas upon the petals;
and upon the filaments, he placed Yama, Kāla, Kubera, and Varuṇa as well. ||96||
The preceptor fashioned an infinite base joined with serpents upon the stalk,
and [he arranged] the other gods together with the hosts of Rākṣasas and Gandharvas.
Furthermore, he arranged a lake surrounded by lotuses;
then, having heard the sound of the Dānavas' musical instruments, the denizens of heaven [prepared themselves]. ||98||
Delighted, they beat their drums and blew their trumpets in great throngs;
hearing those sounds of the denizens of heaven mingled with the noise of musical instruments, [the people rejoiced]. 99.
The lords of the Dānavas, being fully prepared, exerted even greater effort;
then those Dānavas beheld the lotus-array (*padmavyūha*) of the celestial dwellers.
There, those of immeasurable prowess questioned Bhārgava regarding the breaking of that formation.
Thus questioned by the foremost of the Dānavas, the wise Bhārgava, remaining unperturbed, reflected upon the breaking of the array and then spoke thus to the Asuras: || 101 ||
"Scattered on all sides like heaps of frost, O enemies of the gods, the array of the lords of the deities has been completely destroyed.
Thus addressed by the high-souled Bhārgava, the Daityas [responded]. || 102–103 ||
Having quickly let out a lion’s roar and charging from all sides,
a battle then ensued between the armies of the gods and the dānavas,
as they struck one another with various sharp weapons.
Horsemen fought with horsemen, elephants with elephants, and chariots with chariots;
proud foot-soldiers fought with proud foot-soldiers in the battle.
Some were pierced by iron arrows, and others were cut down by battle-axes.
The warriors of both armies fell lifeless;
"Cut! Pierce! Strike now! Stay, you fool! Where are you going? [they cried]. (107)
Thus these words, uttered by warriors in battle, rose up;
that field of battle became drenched with fat and blood, strewn with armor and coverings, and mired with the mire of slain elephants and horses.
Then, being oppressed there by those Dānavas, the denizens of heaven—
wounded and for the most part slain— took refuge with Śakra alone;
the chief Nāgas sought refuge with Ananta, and the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas with Kubera.
When the array of the gods had been broken, the Daityas and Dānavas were overjoyed;
uttering loud lion-roars and repeatedly striking their musical instruments,
they rushed forward in battle, fully prepared, against the subduer of Pāka.
Then, having raised his elephant, Śakra, enraged, crushed the army of the Dānavas with his hundred-jointed thunderbolt; Pākaśāsana set fire to the dwellings of the Dānavas on all sides.

Then, like a blazing fire in the heat of summer consuming dry undergrowth, Śumbha approached in battle and spoke to Śakra: 1.14. "Then, like a blazing fire in the heat of summer consuming dry undergrowth, Śumbha approached in battle and spoke to Śakra."
"O Śakra, you have been seen by me today; you shall not return alive.
Then Brahmā, having arrived, spoke thus to the best of the gods:
"O gods, you must not fight with the Daityas; those enemies of the gods are invincible to you."
"You must not fight, you must not fight, O gods, with the Daityas of great strength!"
For these enemies of the gods had previously obtained boons and were thus unslayable; therefore,
having heard his words, all the denizens of heaven vanished from that battle and quickly departed with their armies and vehicles.
Then the Daityas, greatly rejoiced, struck their musical instruments once more and, roaring loudly,
spoke these words, exulting in battle.
In that battle, amidst the darkness of dust trampled by the hooves of horses and amidst throngs of infantry terrified by the roar of elephants and chariots,
Śumbhasiṃha remained free from fear and despondency.
Victorious is he who conquered the gods, whose roar is like that of a great rain-cloud.

Following him, victorious is Niśumbhasiṃha, the lion of battle, who triumphs in the foremost of conflicts; he possesses long, thick, and muscular arms, a broad, beautiful, and high-arched chest, a gait like that of the king of beasts, and a voice like the thundering of a water-bearing cloud.
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Victory over Śumbha and Niśumbha," in the Devāsura-saṃgrāma of the Skanda Purāṇa.
Now, having defeated the gods in battle, the enemies of the gods then went together to the Vindhya mountain, where clouds were resting upon its peaks.
Having duly dispatched all those Daityas and Dānavas,
the two of them then took their pleasure together on the Vindhya mountains, in a cave where Kinnaras sang;
there, a great Asura named Mūka served as their protector.
On the mountain peak, he beheld the goddess, blazing as if with splendor;
she was endowed with auspicious marks and adorned with holy ornaments,
appearing there like the very personification of the success of meritorious deeds.
Then Mūka, his eyes wide with wonder upon seeing the goddess,
went in his mind to Śumbha, the best of the Dānavas, thinking:
"Since she is beautiful in all her limbs, she is the foremost among all women."
Likewise, among men, this Śumbha, the moon among the lords of the Daityas, is preeminent;
for him, who has a broad chest and long eyes, a dark-eyed woman with expansive hips would be a fitting wife. (6–7)
Having reflected thus in her mind, she spoke to that slender-waisted woman:
"Who are you, O lady with eyes like those of a frightened and bewildered young doe?
Who is your father, O faultless-limbed one, and who is your mother, O sinless one?"
"For what purpose do you dwell here on this mountain frequented by dānavas?
Thus addressed by Mūka, the Great Yoginī, the Sovereign of the Gods,
perceived in her mind that the time for Śumbha and Niśumbha had arrived.
Preceded by a smile, she who was skilled in speech spoke these words:
"Know me to be a human woman who has made her dwelling on this mountain."
"My learned father, the son of Atri, who wandered the earth, has gone to heaven;
leaving me behind while I was still a child, my mother too has followed her husband.
O Dānava, I was then commanded by my mother after she had bestowed these weapons upon me."

"Dwell on the delightful Vindhya mountain and always practice yoga. "O lion among men, O tiger, I am that very person; observing the word of my noble lady, I dwell here on this best of mountains, which is frequented by elephants and deer."
Having heard these words of the goddess, Mūka, his mind filled with joy,
went in haste to see Śumbha, the foremost of the Dānavas.
Then, having approached Śumbha, his eyes blossomed wide with delight.
He seemed to announce the sight of that unprecedented jewel through his very gestures.
Seeing him with eyes wide with wonder, Śumbha, whose own eyes were red and long, then said to Mūka: "O Dānava, why are you so pleased? (17)
Thus addressed by Śumbha, Mūka spoke these words:
"Today I have beheld an unprecedented jewel among women upon the peak of the mountain."
There is no woman so beautiful among humans, nor even among the gods;
neither among the rākṣasas, nor the yakṣas, nor in the cities of the gandharvas.

"O King, never before have I seen such a beautiful woman among the Nāgas, the Siddhas, or in the palaces of the lords of the Daityas. Who are you, to whom do you belong, and for what purpose do you dwell here on this mountain?"
Questioned, she spoke these words: "I am indeed the daughter of Atri;
by my mother's command, I dwell here upon the peak of the Vindhya mountains.
Having thus informed her husband, that Dānava fell silent.
Then, in the heart of Śumbha, along with the speech of Mūka,
Desire found an opening for the destruction of the enemies of the gods.
Thereupon, the lord of the Daityas, his mind agitated by desire, spoke:
"Go, Mūka, and for my sake entice that slender-waisted woman. || 24 ||
Thus addressed by Śumbha, that Dānava rose up quickly and went to where the Goddess had previously been sighted.
Seeing that Dānava standing before her with palms joined in reverence, the goddess then asked Mūka, "For what purpose have you come?"
Thus questioned by Kauśikī, the Dānava Mūka replied as follows:
"Noble lady, I am the messenger of Śumbha, come into your presence. (27)
Then the Goddess, having smiled and looked upon him with a gracious gaze, spoke thus to the messenger who had arrived: "What did that Lord of the Asuras say? (28)
Thus questioned by the goddess, the mute one then spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"Noble lady, Śumbha, the lord of the Daityas, chooses you as his wife."
O deer-eyed one, among all his wives, you are the foremost, belonging to that lion among Dānavas, Śakra, the conqueror in battle.
Thus addressed by him, the Goddess of the Immortals laughed and said:
"Behold these arms of mine; know me to be one for whom battle is the bride-price.
Only after conquering me will that Daitya be worthy to make me his wife."
Or let him, slain by me, become food for crows and jackals. ||32||
To the goddess who had spoken thus, Mūka said as if laughing:
"O beautiful lady, what need have you for war with the Dānavas and Daityas, your husband?"
Even the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra, though mounted upon the shoulders of Airāvata, was unable to look upon the face of him who was enraged in battle. (34)
Having heard those words of his, the Goddess spoke as if smiling:
"O lowest of Dānavas, go and inform Śumbha that even all you lords of the Daityas are but blades of grass to me on the front line of battle. (35)
Since you have come to me as an envoy, therefore you are not harmed.
Then, having bowed to her, the mute man went to the side of the enemy of the gods;
and being permitted by him, he began to relate [the matter]. (37)
O best of Dānavas, that maiden was requested by me for your sake;
she said, "I am one whose bride-price is battle; you should take me away only after defeating me. (38)
Furthermore, O King, that woman, filled with pride and wonder, spoke thus: "The Daityas are but grass to me in battle. (39)
Having heard those words spoken by Mūka at that time,
that best of Asuras could not endure them, due to his anger, pride, and passion.
Then, having risen, the lord of the Dānavas went to the beautiful assembly hall,
which had pillars and balconies made of crystal and was adorned with gateways of variegated jewels.
Upon that great, firm, and well-spread golden lion-throne,
the mighty-armed one sat down comfortably, like Varuṇa.
Then Niśumbha also sat down upon an excellent throne,
his chest at that time dappled by the mass of rays from his jeweled armlets.
Following those two, the great beings— the Daityas and Dānavas—
