entered a delightful cave of the Himavat mountains, like clouds darkened by rainwater.
Then, when those kings of the Daityas and Dānavas had sat down, Śumbha, with a voice like the rumbling of thick clouds, spoke these words: ||45||
My protector, the Dānava Mūka, was on Mount Vindhya;
on a peak of the Vindhya, he beheld a maiden of beautiful form. (46)
"I am the bride-price for battle," she said; "I was not sought by you for my sake. O Lord of Daityas, she indeed spoke further words to me regarding the blades of grass. (47)
Having forcibly conquered that proud maiden in battle,
I am eager to bring her here this very day, even as she struggles and remains powerless.
Then, having heard his words, the mighty-armed great asura named Śambhu laughed loudly and said this to the lord of the asuras: |||49||
"O King, all women by their very nature are of a fickle disposition; they should be appeased but once. You ought to take her back. (8.63.50)
Then, having heard the words of Śambhu, Maya, the best of the Dānavas,
whose eyes were like freshly blossomed blue lotuses, spoke.
O Lord of the Gods, what is her form, or what is her activity? What are the attendants by her side, or what are her constant implements? (52)
When Maya, whose prowess was like that of a rutting elephant, had spoken thus to the lord of the Daityas,
the lord of the Daityas then urged Mūka, who was standing by his side:
"O best among the wise, [explain] that question which Maya has asked."
But the mute man then began to relate all of that.
Always well-established, free from distraction, with a terrifying face and fangs, she has eight arms, is dark as a rain cloud, possesses a beautiful nose, and has a lovely voice. ||55||
All her weapons were always kept ready, along with her principal armor and various beautiful ornaments. (56)
"Her form surpasses the sun, and her radiance exceeds the moon"—
having spoken thus in the assembly of the Daityas, Mūka then ceased speaking.
Then, sighing deeply, the great Asura Maya,
skilled in speech, spoke these words of auspicious conclusion in the assembly.
Surely, a *kṛtyā* has been conjured by the gods defeated in battle;
she has come to the Vindhya mountain for the destruction of the enemies of the gods. (59)
Therefore, enough of that for you, O King; there are slender-waisted maidens with long eyes and beautiful limbs in the dwellings of the Daityas and Dānavas.
Having properly acquired those suitable, sweet-sounding instruments, O King,
sport as you please, constantly remaining within the interior of the palace.

When these words had been spoken by Maya in the assembly of the asuras, the great asura Śumbha then spoke these words, laughing in this manner: evam ukte tadā vākye mayenāsurasaṃsadi | prāha vākyaṃ tadā śumbho vihasyetthaṃ mahāsuraḥ ||62||
If she was created by the gods as a *kṛtyā* under the command of the Dānavas, then she will not cease until she has swiftly slain the Dānavas. (63)
"As long as she has not yet launched her active assault against us, you ought to seize her by force and quickly bring her under your control. (64)
Then all those foremost among the Daityas and Dānavas,
impelled by Time, reflected upon the words of the king of the Daityas.
Then, having addressed these words to all the lions among the Daityas present in the assembly, the conqueror of the Lord of the Gods flew up,
trailing his pure and bright lotus-like necklace.
Like a rain-cloud in the monsoon season, bent low by the weight of fresh water.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter in the dialogue between [Mahat and Ara] in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having struck their kettledrums and donned their armor, those Dānavas and sons of Diti [set forth].
Then they equipped their chariots, elephants, and horses for battle. ||1||
Then the Daityas brought elephants that had been taken to fetch water,
their trunks swollen with rut, and offered them incense and morsels of food.
Likewise, he gave girths and well-fashioned breastplates,
neck-chains, and goads made entirely of iron and adorned with gold and jewels.
Then, the elephant-riders mounted upon their female elephants from all sides duly donned various kinds of armor.
They properly fastened quivers and arrows with their openings facing sideways and upwards;
they also fastened all weapons on both sides. Furthermore, they arranged seats for all three, each in its respective place.
Then, banners of victory were raised aloft.
The Dānavas, clad in armor and wearing iron mail, mounted horses that had been bathed and watered;
they held their tails in hand and carried girded swords.
Some chariot-warriors mounted their chariots, which were yoked with horses,
equipped with weapons and banners, well-prepared, and possessed of excellent axles and poles.
Then Śumbha and Niśumbha, the two brothers and lords of the Dānavas, [prepared for battle].

Having mounted their chariots, which were equipped with weapons and banners, made of refined gold, and yoked to prancing horses, the two great asuras— clad in armor, intoxicated by their own strength, fully prepared for battle, and standing apart— advanced.
Those two broad-chested youths, having performed the auspicious rites for victory,
went forth while being praised by Magadha bards, panegyrists, and heralds who marched before them. Then, having struck the musical instruments in great numbers, they began their journey.
The Asuras were all around that mountain where the goddess Kauśikī resides.
Then the banners of the lions among the Dānavas fell as they were about to depart; and jackals, stationed in the blazing quarter, howled inauspiciously.
Dust, grey like the interior of a pigeon's belly, fell from the sky.
And above the army, vultures and crows wandered about.
An adverse wind, laden with dust, blew against them;
the sky roared harshly and the earth trembled.
Perceiving the signs of defeat, the enemies of the gods approached,
as if helplessly dragged away by the God of Death.
Then the lord of the Daityas commanded the guard Mūka:
"Go and say to that slender-waisted woman, 'Pay the toll.'"

Having gone there at his word, he bowed to Kauśikī and said: "O Noble Lady, please accept the bride-price being offered by the enemy of the gods. Having replied, "So be it," she dismissed that Dānava.
Resorting to yoga, Kauśikī increased in power through great yoga.
Then, from her limbs, there emerged excellent women,
terrible to behold, equipped with weapons and wearing leather arm-guards and finger-protectors;
Vāyasī was surrounded by ten million women who had the faces of crows.
With that many Upakās and Kokilās, she becomes Mahābalā. || 21 ||
Pracaṇḍā is surrounded on all sides by goddesses with lion faces,
and Ugrā is protected on every side by those with tiger faces.
The sinless Jayā was surrounded by goddesses with elephant faces, and Jayantī, of great strength, by those with peacock faces; she was encompassed by immeasurable hosts,
while she herself was honored by those with horse faces and those with swan faces, who were filled with majesty.
And Prabhāvatī was surrounded by those with faces like wheels, who possessed great strength;
Śivā was surrounded by those with the faces of jackals, who were inauspicious to enemies in battle;
and Saramā was surrounded by those with the faces of dogs, being exceedingly difficult to conquer.
Vijayā was protected on all sides by those with the faces of hawks, and surrounded by those with the faces of herons who slay enemies in battle. (26)
In battle, Niyati was surrounded by others who were difficult to conquer, with faces like cormorants;
Aśani was resounded by many with faces like cocks;
and there were Revatī, Vṛṣadaṃśā, Pūtanā, and Kaṭapūtanā.
Ālambā, the Kinnarī Śaṣṭhī, and Śakuni Mukhamāṇḍikā;
Alakṣmī, Adhṛti, Lakṣmī, Potakī, Vānarī, and Spṛhā—these and others were born from Kauśikī, all possessed of great power. || 28–29 ||
Surrounded on all sides by many women wearing various costumes and bearing diverse armor and weapons,
Kauśikī quickly created golden chariots equipped for battle.
Yoked with horses swift as thought, they were equipped with weapons and raised high banners.
[She saw] horses with their equipment, elephants intoxicated with rut,
weapons, armor, and various musical instruments.
And that great Yoginī spoke to those goddesses standing before her.
"O goddesses, Śumbha and Niśumbha, those two brothers who are thorns to the gods,
have indeed come to lead me away after defeating me in battle at the front of the fray;
they have arrived together with the Daityas and Dānavas, intoxicated by their own strength."
"I shall slay those two; as for the remaining enemies of the gods, they are already slain.
You shall become free from old age, immortal, and possessed of great strength.
Having thus granted them this boon and instructed them at that time, [he departed].
The goddesses, highly fortunate, have resolved to engage in battle. || 3.6 ||
Then that steadfast lady mentally conceived a great chariot for herself;

and the daughter of the King of Mountains immediately bestowed upon her that very chariot she had thought of—one possessing a splendor equal to a blazing fire and encircled by garlands of rays from jewels. (37)
Before him, Kauśikī beheld a well-crafted golden aerial chariot,
equipped with various weapons and armor, and yoked to mighty, victorious lions with swaying tawny manes who had conquered the enemy forces in battle. ||38-39||
He was resplendent with a preeminent golden banner, raised very high and firm, its radiance scattered by dancing peacocks and shining with the luster of jewels;
at that time, Vijayā took up the parasol, and Siṃhī became the charioteer.
Then Jayantī and Jayā fanned her with chowries.
Thereupon, having donned her armor and taken up various weapons, she—
having received blessings for victory and auspiciousness— ascended the divine chariot.
With a sunshade raised high above his head, possessing the luster of the full moon,
he was fanned by beautiful whisks with variegated handles, white as the rays of the moon.
Then, having struck their musical instruments, they sounded various kinds of notes.
The goddesses, well-united with the Goddess, became her vanguard.
At that roar, the hearts of the Daityas trembled;
the elephant and horse forces of the Asuras discharged excrement and urine.
The world of mortals seemed to tremble, the oceans were as if agitated, the lords of mountains shook, and the vault of the sky was filled. ||46||
Then that army of deities, adorned with banners and standards, shone brightly as it resounded with the blare of musical instruments and was crowded with gleaming white swords. ||47||
Variegated with rows of cranes, accompanied by Indra’s bow, and possessing a great roar, it was like a mass of water-bearing clouds in the month of Nabhasya, together with lightning. ||48||
Then, restraining himself, he advanced toward the lord of the Daityas;
the host of gods moved with such speed that it seemed to contract the ten directions.
Then the enemies of the gods beheld the approaching army, with its various lofty banners raised high.
Producing terror with a great roar, it rose up like a mass of clouds at the time of universal dissolution.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Army," in the Battle of Śumbha and Niśumbha within the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then those deities, enraged, struck the foremost of the Daityas with various weapons, and they [the Daityas] pierced them in turn in the battle.
Then the Daityas, equipped with diverse weapons, struck the goddesses in the fray.
The weak were made strong, and the heroes conquered their enemies in battle.

Horsemen mounted on horses [attacked] foot-soldiers, and foot-soldiers [attacked] foot-soldiers; chariot-warriors stationed in their chariots [attacked] those in chariots, and elephant-riders [attacked] those mounted on elephants.
Chariots, elephants, and horses [assailed] chariots, elephants, and horses respectively.
Brave foot-soldiers struck down horsemen, and brave horsemen struck down foot-soldiers;
even the goddesses, enraged in battle, destroyed the infantry, cavalry, chariots,
and elephants of the lords of the Dānavas with spears, javelins, and axes.
Having thrown the heroic Dānavas to the ground, they crushed them with their feet;
some of the enemies of the gods they split apart with their fists.
In that battle, some goddesses tore open the chests of those filled with pride and drank the blood of the enemies of the gods along with their very lives.
Others, rising up with great speed, [seized] the weapons that had been shattered into pieces.
The enraged gods struck them with fists as hard as thunderbolts.
Some elephants, their temples darkened by the flow of rut-fluid,
being exceedingly furious, crushed the chariots of the gods in battle.
Some elephants, with rows of intoxicated bees clinging to their temple-walls and their riders slain, slaughtered both Daityas and gods.
Some, clad in armor and with bright swords whirling in their hands, cut down the host of the gods, while the gods likewise struck down the Dānavas.
Some elephant lords, having recognized their intoxicated elephants by scent even though their faces were concealed,
suddenly struck them after smelling that odor, despite being held fast by their drivers.
Great bows were being drawn by the mighty leaders of the army of monkeys.
They faltered on the field of battle like cranes in the autumn nights in the sky.
With the sounds of musical instruments, the slapping of bowstrings, the cries of elephants and horses, and the rattling of chariot wheels,
that entire Vindhya mountain— with its hollows and caves filled to the brim— seemed to tremble then.
The goddesses, having driven back the enemies in battle, roared loudly at the forces with great force.
With hearts full of joy, the Daitya warriors, having repelled the goddesses in battle,
let out shouts; their forces, slightly drenched with blood, moved back and forth there like great forests shaken by the wind, with their sprouts raised aloft.
The severed heads of those leading warriors, radiant with various golden ornaments,
lay fallen on the battlefield with the goddesses, shining like lotuses whose stalks have been cut.
Repulsed by the deities, with its elephants fleeing in terror and its horses and warriors struck down,
that army became like a swinging pendulum as the lion-like lords of the Daityas turned back to attack.
Striking out in battle, the roaring enemies of the gods fell, resembling mountains of black collyrium.
The lordly elephants, their various bells bound on by the gods, were struck by excellent arrows that pierced their vital organs.
Having rushed forward with speed against their forces, those [arrows] struck them and fell swiftly in battle,
like the waters of rivers driven back when they encounter the great ocean at the time of its swelling tide.
The goddesses and the Daityas shone in that great assembly, their arrows locked with one another,
like clusters of stars appearing when the dense clouds have vanished and their light is released.
Then, having proclaimed their names, the lords of the Dānavas quickly emerged from their own army, mounted upon their chariots.
Enraged and well-prepared, those foremost of chariot-warriors drew their variegated bows.
The goddesses also, standing upon their chariots, became even more resolute and rushed forward with speed in their wrath;
then Mṛtyu, her anger inflamed, advanced against Meghasvana with a chariot of refined gold, while Ṣaṣṭhī followed behind.
Then Lakṣmī was joined by Druma, Kānti by Maya in the midst of battle, Saramā by Mura,
Caṇḍā by Ghana, Niyati by Khara, and the wrathful Prabhāvatī by Dhundhumāra.
Those Daityas, their minds eager for combat, approached the goddesses with their arms and weapons.
Unable to endure [the enemy], those renowned for their pride, well-prepared on their own chariots, advanced swiftly.
With undaunted spirits, they discharged in battle the finest arrows of the gods—whose shafts were made of refined gold and radiant as light—released from bows drawn back to the ear. || 25-26 ||

Then the goddesses likewise discharged infinite arrows— sharpened, well-feathered, capable of traveling great distances, and piercing the vital organs— at those approaching leaders of the Dānava hosts.
Those various excellent arrows, released by one another and interlacing,
shone like the combined splendors of the sun and moon gathered together on a cloudless full-moon day at the close of day.
Severed by the divine weapons in battle, the arms of the lords of the Daityas fell from their hands still grasping their weapons.
Deprived of their splendor, massive and thick like lordly serpents whose tongues have been swallowed,
the enraged Ṣaṣṭhī then loosed showers of arrows at Meghasvana in that battle.
As they came toward her from all sides, the Daitya cut them down by the hundreds in the sky with his own shafts.
Then, seeing those arrows cut down, he quickly discharged other, swifter ones;
the Daitya, for his part, repeatedly severed those incoming shafts with volleys of many arrows. (31)
Having cut down those arrows, the son of Diti again discharged ten gold-feathered shafts with his sixth finger;
having swiftly warded them off with her own sixth finger, Ṣaṣṭhī pierced the Daitya with arrows of golden feathers.
Pierced by them, his body smeared with blood and greatly distressed, he became somewhat speechless;
his own charioteer then bore him away from that battle on a chariot adorned with gold.
Kārtasvana loosed arrows with variegated golden shafts at the goddess in the encounter.
Mṛtyu cut those arrows down with floods of his own shafts, broad-feathered and yet not even approaching their mark.
Having cut his arrows with his own variegated shafts, he pierced him in the chest with sixty-five;
thus quickly pierced by them, he shone like a cloud in the sky split by the rays of the sun. (35)
Then Death quickly struck his horses with separate arrows having golden shafts.
Thereupon, the Daitya, leaping from the chariot whose horses were slain, seized a shield and a polished, excellent sword;
with eyes extremely red with rage, he rushed impetuously toward the Goddess.
As he was falling, Death cut that shield into hundreds of pieces with his sharp-pointed volleys of arrows.

With his shield-covering severed, the lord of the gods raised a sword with a sharpened edge and rushed toward Death; at that moment, he appeared in the sky like a cloud flashing with lightning toward the star Rohiṇī.
As he was charging in battle like Death itself, Mṛtyu struck him with arrows resembling fierce serpents at his vital points;
having targeted them precisely, he swiftly deprived him of his life-breaths.
On the field of battle, Lakṣmī, invincible through her showers of excellent arrows, overwhelmed that tree-like warrior— who possessed the grace of a lordly elephant—
with sharp, straight shafts released from his ear-tips, adorned with beautiful golden feathers.
Those various straight-flying arrows with beautiful feathers fell upon the limbs of the tree in the battle;
with those diverse shafts clinging to it, that great tree shone as if inhabited by flocks of birds.
Then that lord of the Kimpuruṣas pierced Lakṣmī with ten well-feathered arrows.
On the face, that wise one [placed] one equal to the full moon; and on the two arms, separately, with eight hundred [petals]. || 42 ||
While they were not thinking [of him], he fixed sharp arrows into the mouths of those with beautiful faces;
and into the bodies of many other women, he separately lodged well-feathered shafts with gold-polished nocks.
Then, with a sharp crescent-headed arrow, the lord of the Daityas severed the tip of Lakṣmī’s banner on her chariot;
he quickly pierced her four horses with four arrows and struck her charioteer with a shaft.
Thereupon, taking up an iron bolt (nārāca), Lakṣmī struck the charioteer of that enemy of the gods in battle.
He pierced the horses individually with arrows and swiftly cut down the banner of the chariot. ||45||
Then, tormented by his incomparable arrows,
the horses of that [opponent], as if seeking to protect their own lives, bore him away from the field of battle without his chariot.
Kāntimaya covered Bāṇa with hundreds of arrows, and Bāṇa likewise covered Kāntimaya with volleys of sharpened shafts.
Then, as if by falling mists, a thick darkness enveloped the space between the two of them there.

In seizing, aiming, and drawing back; in their positions, the sequence of movements, the grip, and the exertion—by means of the qualities of their training, they both excelled one another in the midst of the combat.
Maya cut down those arrows consisting of splendor, and Maya’s splendor [cut down] the arrows polished by Kānti;
though both were invincible, they found no opening whatsoever against one another.
Maya’s splendor discharged straight-flying arrows with shafts polished with gold into his horses, his driver, his charioteer, his banner, and into all his limbs. (8.65.50)

And Maya, with sharp arrows, completely covered Kānti— along with his chariot, charioteer, beautiful and variegated banner, and excellent horses— as a cloud covers a forest glade with showers of rain.
Then, enraged in battle, Kānti [struck] Maya with a preeminent iron shaft (nārāca) furnished with fine feathers.
Then he quickly slew the enemy's charioteer with eight arrows, and his eight horses as well.
Then Maya, his horses and charioteer slain and deprived of his chariot, took up a sharp-edged sword;
perceiving through its brilliance the prowess [of Saramā] in battle, he abandoned the fight and leapt into the sky.
On the field of battle, Saramā pierced Mura, the leader of the hosts of Dānavas and Daityas, with her sharp arrows.
The Daitya also struck Saramā with straight-flying arrows, fletched with the feathers of vultures and peacocks.
Then the enraged Goddess cut his variegated bow with a sharp crescent-headed arrow (bhalla).
Thereupon, taking up another bow, he pierced the four horses of the Goddess.
Struck by the arrows of the lord of the Daityas, those horses became distressed and vomited blood.
They fell upon the ground in battle, gasping for breath, and all together they quickly gave up their lives at once.
Then the goddess Saramā, enraged, raised her sword with its bright edge and,
leaping into the sky, struck the driver and the horses of great size belonging to the asura.
Then Mura, having leapt into the sky with speed and having slain the horses and charioteer out of anger,
pierced the Goddess in the chest with ten extremely sharp arrows resembling fierce serpents.
Disregarding those arrows, Saramā then severed Mura’s bow.
His bow severed, that enemy of Indra quickly abandoned the battle and vanished from sight.
And he pierced the fierce cloud-like Daitya as he was rushing forward in combat with sharp-pointed, gold-feathered arrows.
Pierced by them, the lord of the Daityas shone like a dark rain-cloud struck by the rays of the moon.
Disregarding those arrows, the fierce Rāvaṇa, raining down a mass of shafts like a cloud, rushed forward;
and as he approached, he pierced the principal horses of the chariot with his fierce, well-feathered arrows.
The Daitya also cut down the goddess’s banner with its lofty top and struck her horses;
abandoning their chariots, the two of them descended to the ground and, grasping excellent shields and swords, exerted themselves.
In the midst of the arena, they strode about the circle, touching the ground with the tips of their toes;
moving with such lightness of foot along various paths, the two of them never left an opening for one another.
[She performed] the *abhipluta*, *uccapluta*, *siṃhapāta*, *nivṛttaka*, *ākrīḍitaka*, *ūrdhvabāhu*,
*khagāpayāta*, *abhihatāpayāta*, *niṣaṇṇaka*, and *āviddhaśirobhighāta* [movements].
Then, leaping up with speed, Caṇḍā swiftly severed his neck.
With his head severed, that Daitya quickly fell upon his chest onto that battlefield. || 65 ||
With his body smeared with blood, the bull-like warrior then fell lifeless upon the earth;
he shone like a dark cloud in the sky, its vast form streaked by the twilight.
Niryāti pierced Khara in the chest with sharp, well-feathered arrows tipped with gold.
And with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla), he cut down the standard of him who was charging directly toward him in the battle.
Pierced by them, he, the slayer of enemies, rushed forward in fury, desiring to kill the Goddess;
then, seizing a heavy mace, his body smeared with blood, he swiftly hurled it at the Goddess.
That mace, released by the foremost of the Dānavas, was beautiful with its various golden bells that shone brightly.
He quickly crushed the chariot of Niyati, along with its charioteer and its banner whose tip was raised high.
Leaping swiftly from her own vehicle, Niyati, her eyes rolling and bloodshot with rage,
approached that chief of the Danava warriors and split his head asunder with her sword.
With his head split open and streams of blood flowing,
that Dānava shone upon the earth like a mountain with its peak shattered by a thunderbolt, streaming with veins of mineral ore.
Prabhāvatī struck him with straight-flying, well-feathered arrows.
With ten sharp-pointed arrows, broad-chested and possessing a color like a mass of rain-clouds, she struck the sixteen horses of the enemy of the gods;
having slain the charioteer with one arrow, she cut down his banner with another. ||72-73||
Dhundhu hurled a mace heavy with a thousand *bhāras*, adorned with beautiful golden bells;
as it came flying toward her, Prabhāvatī shattered that weapon released by the lord of the Daityas into a hundred pieces.
Seizing a massive iron club (*parigha*), the Daitya leaped from his mount and rushed forward on all sides.

On the field of battle, the goddess—who was as dark as a mountain of collyrium and like Death himself with staff in hand—struck the approaching lord of the Dānavas with well-feathered arrows. Disregarding all the arrows of the goddess, he rushed toward her at the head of the fray out of rage. (75–76)

Whirling that iron club, which was like the staff of Yama and forged of steel, he who possessed arms as thick as a bar lowered it upon the chariot; just as Indra hurls his thunderbolt upon the flank of a mountain,
he shattered that chariot of the goddess— along with its horses, driver, banner, and golden wheels— in an instant.
Struck by that iron club, the goddess retreated from there with great speed.
Seeing her then departing from that place, that chief of the Dānava warriors seized that very iron club and rushed toward her,
like a dark cloud in the sky pursuing the star Citrā.
Leaping up, she shattered the club with sharp-edged arrows (kṣurapra) and other excellent celestial weapons.
Then, raising his fist tightly, the Daitya leaped once more into the sky.
The Goddess swiftly struck that Dānava in his vital organs with excellent arrows that pierce the vitals;
pierced by those well-feathered, life-penetrating shafts, that chief of the Dānava warriors vanished from sight.

Then, the enemies of the Lord of the Gods, having abandoned the battle as the chief warriors departed with their prowess and manliness destroyed, raised a great roar and stood upon their excellent elephants, grasping their weapons. Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Battle of the Goddess," in the Śumbha-Niśumbha conflict of the Skanda Purāṇa.

Sanatkumāra said: The goddesses also, having learned of their efforts, mounted with diligence those excellent elephants—pure, exuding streams of ichor, possessing fine tusks, and endowed with praiseworthy bodies, trunks, and flanks. (1)
With well-formed, prominent, and rounded frontal globes; with beautiful, curved ears and fine manes;
with excellent dental ridges and eyes like those of the kalaviṅka bird; with broad chests and straight spinal columns. ||2||

[He saw] war-horses of the prime of their age, well-trained, with broad forequarters, equipped with armor and weapons and adorned with variegated bells, with their great standards and banners raised high. (3)
Then those herds of elephants, adorned with banners and flags and decorated with various wonderful weapons, appeared like forest groves come together in the woods.
Those Daityas also shone as they stretched their six-fold bows upon the heads of their elephants.
Accompanied by Indra’s weapon and containing the sound of thunderbolts within, they were like clouds resting upon the mountains. ||5||
In that slaughter, those armies, urged on by their elephant-riders,
rushed fearlessly at one another like masses of clouds driven by the wind.
Charging with speed against the elephants, other elephants— with tusks as white as lotus stalks bound with iron bands—
struck them on the frontal globes in battle, their faces darkened by rutting ichor.
And some, stretching out their trunks, rushed toward the scent of the temporal juice (*dāna*) from all sides.
Though goaded by mahouts with goads, nooses, and words, they remained arrogant with rut.
Sharp, razor-headed arrows severed the raised sunshades,
while various colorful banners and diverse standards fell from the elephants as they struck one another.
The warriors fell down, groaning loudly as they were pierced by the gods' arrows in their vital organs;
vomiting blood with foam from their mouths, they still held their strung bows in their hands.
The elephants fell down on all sides, struck through by excellent arrows that had penetrated their vital parts.
In the battle against the lords of the Daityas, they were struck down by the goddesses like boulders from mountain slopes driven by the wind. ||1 1 ||
Seeing the leaders of the Mātaṅgas fallen lifeless upon the field of battle— resembling the great blue mountains—
some rutting elephants, having circled them and lowered their heads, trumpeted with their trunks.
Severed heads adorned with earrings, arms still clutching weapons and smeared with fine sandalwood paste,
fell from the elephants of the demon leaders in battle, struck down by the sharp razor-headed arrows of the goddesses.
The bows of the chief enemies of the gods resounded loudly on all sides as they were struck, and they let out great roars.
The bowstrings vibrated violently as they were drawn and released, and the elephants, pierced by the arrows, sank down to their knees. || 14 ||
The earth is strewn with falling elephants, pierced by arrows, their broad backs adorned with lofty banners;
driven by the wind, they resemble the foothills of mountains covered with palm trees.
The Nāgas struck the elephants, and the Daityas struck the goddesses and the daughters of Diti;
the lordly elephants and the Daityas, enraged and full of wrath, rushed there against the other elephants.
Due to the masses of elephants, resembling mountain peaks, that had fallen on all sides scorched by weapons, the ground became impassable during that clash between the gods and the dānavas. (17)
Seeing their own forces overwhelmed in battle and their elephants slain by the goddesses,
Śumbha and Niśumbha, the two lords of the Daityas, mounted on their chariots, arrived at the field of combat accompanied by vanguard infantry,
cavalry, and elephants, and by throngs of the enemies of the gods.
With their massive arms like iron clubs, they drew their variegated bows and prepared themselves for battle.
Having learned of their arrival at that time, the goddess,
stretching her bows in battle, urged on the lions of her chariot, which were adorned with swaying, tawny manes.
By the very sound of her bowstring, the goddess brought about the loss of speed in the horses, the deprivation of rut in the great elephants, and the confusion of mind in the enemies of the gods.
Having exerted the utmost effort in battle, all the arrows of the enemies of the gods fell upon the earth without reaching the Goddess, as if proclaiming the defeat of the Asuras;
just as the sun pervades all things mobile and immobile with its rays throughout the days.
In that same manner, the Goddess pervaded the forces of the lords of the Daityas on the field of battle with floods of arrows.
Swiftly, lifeless horses fell; rutting elephants, their ichor flowing, stumbled;

and all the foremost warriors of the enemies of the gods trembled together in the fray, struck by her shafts. Just as a fire, ignited by blazing flames, burns through dry thickets without restraint, so did she consume them.
In that same manner, Kauśikī consumed the armies of the enemies of the gods with blazing volleys of arrows in battle.
Just as at midday the sun makes the shadow of all things, both stationary and moving, very short,
so did the goddess make that army of enemies remaining few in number small indeed in the battle.
Then, having summoned the goddess, the two lords of the Dānavas drew their great bows and discharged arrows;
with sharp, well-feathered shafts, they covered Kauśikī in the arena of battle.
With bows, monkeys, and banners as their targets, those two mighty-armed ones, their hearts overwhelmed by rage, remained intent on the fight.
In the battle, the two lords of the Daityas struck excellent, well-feathered arrows at the goddess.
Then, disregarding those volleys of arrows, the Lord of the Daityas— she who destroys the pride of enemies—
pierced the two Daityas in battle with excellent, well-jointed arrows, gold-feathered and adorned with beautiful wings.
Disregarding the arrows, the two heroic Daityas seized their maces, which were adorned with brilliant and beautiful bells;
whirling them with extreme effort, they hurled those massive weapons upon the Goddess in the field of battle.
Having sliced them into hundreds of pieces in the sky with well-feathered arrows that had golden and lovely shafts, [the gods struck them down].
The Goddess severed their various armor with other sharp-pointed razor-headed arrows. ||3 1 ||
He struck down the horses and the charioteers, and cut away the two variegated banners from the two chariots;
furthermore, he pierced the vital organs of the enemies of the gods with other excellent gold-feathered arrows.
Then Śumbha and Niśumbha, the lords of the Daityas, casting aside their chariots while tormented by excellent arrows,
seized two superb swords and flew into the sky, which appeared dark blue from their sharp blades.
Then, in a cloudless sky as blue as a polished sword,
the Goddess, having rushed forward with great speed and seized them by their necks,
quickly crushed those two lords of the sons of Diti.

Then, their strength suddenly shattered and all the joints of their limbs crushed, they vomited frothy blood from their mouths while being praised by the lords of sages, who were free from fear and despondency. ||34||
With their impurities gone and their eyes red at the corners,
those two lions among the Daityas fell upon the surface of the earth.
(35) Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Śumbha and Niśumbha," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Then the denizens of heaven— the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Marutvān, the Maruts, and the Aśvins— came to see Kauśikī and the Vindhya mountain.
Dharma, Aṅgiras, Uśanas, Dakṣa, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, Kaśyapa, Pulastya, Pulaha, Agastya, Sanaka, Ātri, and Sanandana; ||2||
The Apsarases, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, Nāgas, and Mahoragas;
the Upavedas, the sacrifices, the Vedas, the sciences, and Sarasvatī. ||3||
The oceans, rivers, mountains, and various sacred fords;
the Mothers, the world-protectors, the constellations, Dhruva, and the planets—
then those radiant deities spoke to the goddess of great splendor.
The enemies of the Asuras sat there, their minds filled with great joy.
"O Goddess, by slaying those two lords of the Dānavas, those two of great strength who were thorns to the three worlds, you have removed the painful dart of suffering for all people."
O Goddess, the sages are now offering purifying oblations;
they recite the Vedas aloud and observe their sacred vows.
O Goddess, this sacrifice with abundant sacrificial fees is now being performed by the Brahmins;
and in their leaf-huts, the sages lie down in comfort, full of trust.
The virtuous ones, O Goddess, who have taken refuge in the path of the righteous, dwell there free from fear.
Furthermore, the path of virtuous practice, having been interrupted, has now appeared once more in the world. ||9||
By your grace, the world-protectors bear their heads held high,
and the breeze blows pleasantly, mingled with the pollen of flowers.
O Goddess, O Great Yoginī, daughter of the Mountain, by your grace the rivers flow with waters that are clear and cool, free from all fatigue;
and now, O Daughter of the Mountain, the mountains have been restored to life once more.
Free from fever, they carry forth the water of cool and sweet cascades.
The serpents now bear their hoods high, marked with the auspicious svastika and the wheel;
and the oceans, filled with confidence, rest in peace.
O Goddess, by your grace, the celestial nymphs (apsarases) now wander about freely.
In the sky, pure with truth, their eyes were languid with playful charm. || 14 ||
And now, O Goddess, the Siddha women serve you with full confidence upon the mountain peaks where sandalwood trees are in full bloom.
By their very nature and from drinking honey, the yakṣas, whose eyes are like red lotuses,
now roam upon the ridges of Mount Gandhamādana.
Free from fatigue, the earth now bears [them] with ease.
The remainder [of the world] was surrounded by the hoods of Śeṣa, which were encircled by canopies of rays from his own jewels. || 17 ||
"You are the mother of the worlds, bestowing fearlessness upon those who are afraid. O Goddess, choose your desired boons and be consecrated as Acyutā. ||18||
Thus addressed by the gods, the Goddess spoke as if smiling slightly:
"I wish to see my father, who bears the incomparable crescent moon upon his crest;
and I wish to see my mother, the daughter of the mountain, who is exceedingly gracious."
And when you have been permitted by my parents, you shall then consecrate me.
Thus addressed, the gods then reflected with undistracted minds upon Mahādeva,
who was accompanied by his consort and possessed immeasurable splendor and prowess.
Then those gods beheld the God of gods, the Lord of Umā,
standing before them like the concentrated mass of all splendors.
He bore upon his head the weight of matted locks, tawny at their tips, which seemed to carry a blazing fire as if they were radiant flames. ||23||
He was bathed in holy ashes as white as crushed camphor,
appearing like a towering silver mountain crowned with clusters of golden creepers at its edge.
He eclipsed the splendors of the gods with his own brilliance,
like the sun at midday obscuring the flames of lamps.
He bore upon his head a slender crescent of the moon, slightly curved, emitting nectar-like water, encircling one side;
He wore a lion’s skin with its fur slightly disheveled;
his body was streaked along its edges by the rays from the jewels on the hoods of a great lord of serpents that slithered across his chest.
And he saw Bhavānī standing at his side, radiant with her own splendor,
wearing a red silken garment produced from the wish-fulfilling tree.
She bore upon her head a full-blown mandāra garland, frequented by swarms of intoxicated bees and tawny with a profusion of pollen.
Adorned with excellent ornaments made of gold, fashioned by celestial artisans, variegated, and encircled by the rays of jewels. || 3.1 ||
She bore upon her neck an unblemished, unsurpassed single-string necklace that was radiant, pure, and as stainless as the rays of the autumn moon.
Then all the gods, with faces bowed in reverence, rose up and fell at the lotus-feet of the two of them with hearts full of joy.
Then Mahādeva, looking up at Kauśikī, spoke these words:
Invincible to all beings, a great yogin of great splendor. ||34||
"You shall wander through the worlds, unimpeded everywhere.
And all these deities, O blameless one, shall worship you with devotion, offerings, and oblations by the grace of you. (35)
O sinless one, you shall always be the granter of boons to your devotees.
And be quickly consecrated by the gods, O destroyer of asuras;
being ever worshipped, O imperishable one, protect the entire world of mortals.
And having embraced Kauśikī and smelled her head, the illustrious Śarvāṇī, being pleased, said: "By my power, you shall become [great]."
Just as the gods, yakṣas, great serpents,
gandharvas, sages, and siddhas worship me, so too, O blameless one, shall they worship you everywhere; devoted, they will praise you, O imperishable one.
Thus, having granted her that boon, the Mountain-Daughter and the Bull-bannered Lord [departed].
Then, having been saluted by the gods, the two imperishable ones vanished.
Thereupon, the Lord Indra commanded Viśvakarman:
"Let a divine assembly hall, like Sudharmā, be constructed here at once."
And Śatakratu likewise commanded all the seasons in this manner. ||42||
"Let the ground be quickly and properly adorned with heaps of various flowers;
let the breezes, fragrant with the pollen of shrubs, bushes, creepers, and trees, blow pleasantly here, captivating the minds. (43)
May the clouds drench the slopes of the Vindhya mountains with their holy waters.
Let the peacocks, overjoyed, cry out loudly in every direction;
let them dance all around, displaying various and wonderful movements. (45)
All the hosts of Apsarases should set aside their flavors, emotions, and graceful charms;
and the Gandharvas, with sweet voices, should set aside their fine lutes.
Let songs be sung everywhere in harmony with the *layatāla* rhythm,
and let celestial drums be struck vigorously on all sides.
Quickly struck by rough hands, the great-sounding [lutes], possessing variegated forms,
were set in motion by a gentle breeze, with rows of bees clinging to them.
And let divine showers of flowers fall upon this spot;
let banners of variegated forms be raised on all sides,
and flags of diverse shapes with well-fashioned golden staffs.
Then, the immensely radiant Viśvakarman quickly constructed there a beautiful palace with pillars blazing with various jewels,
featuring wonderful gem-encrusted altars and gate-towers made of diamond and crystal, and fashioned from Jāmbūnada gold.
With stairs whose broad steps were made of sapphire, draped with hanging strings of pearls,
adorned with banners and flags, and resounding with the ringing of bells,
it was like the personified success of asceticism, self-restraint, and sacrifice risen up in visible form.
Then the deities saw flowers from different seasons. ||53||
There, the winds blew, carrying many various flowers that were equally endowed with excellent fragrance;
they were filled with floral filaments, pleasant to the touch, and sweetly scented.
Bells rang out repeatedly as they stirred.
The gods and gandharvas sang, and the hosts of apsaras danced.
Then the sages praised Kauśikī with auspicious hymns;
she was filled with all kinds of jewels, medicinal herbs, fragrances, and holy waters.
There, auspicious jars made of gold and jewels were brought;
they were supported by four lions made of rubies with manes of diamonds. ||57||
It was as if golden and being carried away by its own splendor, as though it were breathing;
its surrounding circle was inlaid with a network of light from all kinds of jewels. ||58||
And Viśvakarman fashioned a magnificent seat for the Goddess, while she was being praised from all sides with hymns and shouts of "Victory! (59).
Then Kauśikī, the daughter of the God of Gods, sat upon that divine throne together with the sages and the deities.
Having had the rites for auspiciousness performed by the Brahmins while the sacrificial fire was well-kindled,
they were dressed in two white garments produced from the wish-fulfilling tree.
Her limbs were adorned with strings of pearls, and she was decorated with white garlands and unguents;
then the Seven Sages, Viṣṇu, Dharma, Yajña, and Prajāpati [arrived].
The Ādityas, Kaśyapa, the Rudras, the world-protectors, the sacrificial fires, the lords of mountains, the earth, the Gaṅgā, the moon, the Maruts, and the Aśvins;
the oceans, the Vasus, Lakṣmī, Sandhyā, Kīrti, and Sarasvatī. ||63||
The lords of the nāgas, the lords of the birds, and various excellent rivers.
Taking all the jars, they consecrated Kauśikī with [water] that possessed great splendor and jeweled handles, resembling the orb of the full moon.
Śatakratu himself took up the extended umbrella,
while [attendants] held long chowries with golden handles, as pure as the rays of the moon.
Then the world-protectors consecrated her with those riches;
and thereafter, the glorious Indra, the subduer of Pāka, spoke to Kauśikī.
O Goddess, protect the entire earth; you are my sister, O Imperishable One.
Show favor to your devotees, O Sovereign, and destroy the thorns of the immortals.
Wander through all the worlds, honored by the hosts of Siddhas. 68.
Having spoken these words to Kauśikī, the King of the Gods, accompanied by the hosts of the thirty [deities] and wearing shimmering, white necklaces of lotus fibers,
then flew up from the Vindhya mountains, scattering dark clouds— bowed down by their burden of water— throughout the sky in every direction.
Whoever should constantly hear this, or recite it in the assembly of the virtuous,
having attained happiness in this world, shall go to the supreme goal.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Consecration of Kauśikī," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Then those deities, born from the body of the goddess Kauśikī—
The highly fortunate ones settled them in various regions and cities. ||1||
And Pralamba settled Bahuputrā in Laṅkā;
he settled Lambauṣṭhī, Vṛṣadaṃśā, and Kinnarī in Siṃhala. ||2||
One should worship the goddess Revatī at Gokarṇa, Mukhamaṇḍikā among the Pāṇḍyas, Aśivā among the Ābhīras, and Śānti on the banks of the Varaṇā;
likewise, one should worship the goddess Prabhā at Vatsagulma and Lakṣmī on Mount Kola.
The *upaka* among the Persians, and the *vāyasī* among the Yavanas. ||4||
He settled Pracaṇḍā in Tuṣāra, Lambikā in Kośala,
and both Jayā and Vijayā in his own city;
he settled Prabhāvatī among the Kaliṅgas and Jayantī in the city named after the Nāga.
And she [is known] as Ṣaṣṭhī among the Kaśmīras, and as Saramā among the Malayas.
And Pūtanā in Supīra, Mṛtyu in Pṛṣṭapura,
Bāhumāṃsā in Koṭivarṣa, and Kaṭapūtanā in the Pauṇḍras.
In the Middle Country, one should worship Aspṛṣṭā; among the Barbaras, Kinnarī;
in Vārāṇasī, Nirāyāsī; and Citraghaṇṭā in Kauśikī.
Mahākālī is in Mahākāla, and Vānarī is among the Śabaras;
all the remaining deities are in the villages and the cities.
In the mountain fastnesses, Kauśikī established her residence.
Then, after some time had passed, at Svarṇākṣa, the one of great asceticism— where Viṣṇu had obtained a boon by propitiating the god Śaṅkara— [established his own].
The discus named Sudarśana, which is like the end-maker of enemies.
There dwells a highly fortunate rishi named Gautama Śaradvān;
the goddess, having been invited by him, then went to his sacrifice.
Having learned of her arrival there, the valiant son of Śumbha,
the Dānava named Mahiṣa, quickly came to that place.
Well-knit, broad-chested, with a long neck and a fine tail, possessing curved horns, broad hooves, and a wide, elevated head. || 14 ||
With a mind fixed on enmity, cruel, a great being exceedingly difficult to conquer,
roaring with a mighty sound harsh as the crash of a thunderbolt,
resembling a mountain of collyrium in appearance, he was arrogant in his strength and eager for battle.
The son of the lord of the Dānavas stood blocking the path of the goddess. || 16 ||
Having perceived his arrival, Vindhyavāsinī, the mistress of yoga,
went swiftly to that place where the lowest of demons was located.
Then, seeing the goddess, his eyes became even redder with rage.
The Dānava approached with speed, exerting great effort. || 18 ||
With his tail raised, the tip of his sharp horns, a broad chest, and hard, upright ears,
he— resembling a dark mountain with eyes as copper-red as *guggulu* resin— rushed with speed toward the Goddess.
Seeing that son of the lord of Daityas, Mahiṣa, rushing toward her with fury, Kauśikī—

the slayer of the lords of Asuras— stood upon the earth with her beautiful, wide, copper-hued eyes blazing with wrath. Approaching the goddess with supreme arrogance born of his strength, the son of the king of Dānavas assailed her.
He struck her on the chest, where her necklace dangled, with his horn as hard as Indra’s weapon.
Having endured that blow of his at that time, she seized the buffalo by the horn with her trunk;
then, whirling it high in the air on all sides in her rage, she cast it down onto the surface of the earth as it gasped for breath. ||22||

Seizing the hair of the enemy of Indra and forcibly placing her foot upon his head, she took up a trident and pierced him in the back; she swiftly deprived the Daitya of his life-breaths. His horn was as hard as a thunderbolt, resembling a dark blue cloud.
Having then slain Mahiṣa of arrogant pride,
she, being showered from all sides with a rain of various flowers,
went to her dwelling on Mount Kauśika.
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Asura Mahiṣa," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
O Blessed One, knower of all worlds, whose splendor is equal to that of the Grandfather (Brahmā)!

O Brahmin, O great sage, after performing extensive penance and receiving her desired boon from Brahmā— the state of having a fair complexion— what else did the goddess, the daughter of Himavat, do at the conclusion of her austerities?
And what auspicious boon did Somanandin and Śārdūla obtain?
Tell this to me who asks you, for I am your devotee and bow before you.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having paid homage to Mahādeva, the supreme, eternal Brahman,
whom the Sāṃkhyas always recite as the twenty-fifth principle (puruṣa).
And the yogins, as well as the twenty-sixth principle (the Puruṣa), Brahmā and the other celestial dwellers,
bowed their heads with supreme devotion to that Three-eyed One.
O Vyāsa, [I shall tell] how the meeting of Śaṅkara with Gaurī took place.
I shall declare all of that to you; listen, O best among those who know yoga.
Having performed extremely difficult austerities on that peak of the Himalayas,
she then became fair-limbed, with a luster like pure gold;
thereafter, Śarvāṇī set her mind upon beholding Śaṅkara.
Having reached Mount Mandara together with Somanandin,
the goddess saw at the entrance of her husband's palace, stationed at the threshold, Nandin, the leader of the Gaṇas, bearing a blazing spear. ||8-9||
Then, seeing her devotee Nandīśvara, the daughter of the Mountain King spoke with affection: "Come, my child; it has been a long time since you were last seen. (8.69.10)
Nandi, beholding that fair-limbed woman who shone with the luster of gold,
was filled with great joy and fell prostrate at her feet.
Then, having prostrated, that wise one praised the daughter of the mountain:
"Homage to Siddhi, to the Great Goddess; homage to Rati, to Gati. (12)
You are action, you are the cause, and you are primordial nature as well as liberation itself;
you are splendor, radiance, contentment, peace, and the supreme source of well-being.
She is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), destiny (niyati), death (mṛtyu), the twilight (sandhyā), lightning (vidyut), day (ahar), and night (kṣapā);
she is the earth (pṛthivī), Kauśikī, Śrī, Śarvāṇī, and the beloved of Śarva. 14.
Gaṇamātā, Diti, Pavitrā, Vindhyavāsinī, Kṛṣṇā, Kātyāyanī, Gaurī, Bhūtamātā, and likewise Īśvarī. ||15||
"O Goddess, be gracious toward me, your devotee who bows down before you.
Then the Goddess, seeing Nandin prostrate at her feet, [spoke].
She said, "I am the giver of boons," and he chose an auspicious boon:
"I desire you to be forever pleased with me; this is my supreme boon. (17)
Saying "So be it," that large-eyed woman entered;
Nandin went before her, and Somanandin followed behind.
She shone between the two like the crescent moon between two planets;
having beheld her from afar, the God of gods was filled with joy.
The one of great splendor arrived with eyes wide open in agitation;
the goddess fell at the feet of the wise God of gods.
Then the God, the best among the gods, having gazed again and again at the Goddess, the daughter of the mountain king who had arrived there, spoke to her.
"By good fortune you have a joyful countenance; by good fortune your asceticism has borne fruit.
By good fortune you possess this excellent complexion, fair and with the luster of gold.
O Goddess, it is most pleasing to us in every way that you have come here."
Having fulfilled his vow here, from where has this tiger come to you?
Thus addressed by her husband with words tender with affection, the goddess then related her entire history to the god.
The goddess said:
"O Lord, because you previously addressed me as 'black-complexioned,' my limbs were then overcome with resentment and I desired a fair complexion.
Having gone to a peak of the Himalayas, I engaged in great austerity. (25)
Constantly thinking only of you, she remains standing on one foot.
On the very same day that I undertook my ascetic penance there, this tiger Somanandin appeared before me. ||27||
Mahādeva remained there, endowed with supreme devotion;
for a thousand divine years, I remained engaged in that ascetic practice.
For that same length of time, he too remained near me, gazing with his tail, eyes, and mouth motionless, abstaining from food. (29)
At the conclusion of my ascetic penance, Brahmā, the granter of boons, arrived;
O Lord, I previously requested a boon from him for his sake.
Therefore, O God Śaṅkara, this immortal one, free from old age and sorrow, has been made my attendant by your side; and at your command, O Grandfather, he has assumed this form. || 3.1 ||
The God of gods said: "O Goddess, I am well-pleased with you; choose a boon as you desire.
This king of beasts, Somanandin, the foremost of my attendants and possessed of great strength—"
"O beloved, as my Nandīśa is, so shall yours be;
whatever else you say, I shall do all of that for you.
The Goddess said:
"O Mahādeva, O Śaṅkara, I desire to see once again that place where supreme penance was performed by you together with me.
Sanatkumāra said:
When Pārvatī had spoken thus, the Supreme Lord said:
"O lady of beautiful limbs, it pleases me also to go there, O imperishable one."
Having summoned Nandin and thousands of his attendants, he went together with the Goddess to that beautiful peak of the Himalayas where you had performed your austerities,
to the great mountain Himavat.
Being repeatedly saluted by gods, Vidyādharas, Siddhas, Gandharvas, and the best of sages,
and being praised from all sides, the Lord,
the playful Master of the Gaṇas, mounted the back of Nandin. || 37-38 ||
Having reached the Himavat mountain, he arrived at that region;
having reached that peak, which was beautiful and adorned with minerals.
The Lord of the hosts was highly pleased and rejoiced; then,
seeing him arrived, the Mountain appeared in embodied form and,
bowing with palms joined in reverence, waited upon Mahādeva.
Having fashioned that sacrificial pit on that most excellent peak,
the wielder of the Pināka bow favored the lord of mountains with a boon.
By my grace, you shall become immortal, free from old age, devoid of all suffering, and indeed unbreakable even by the thunderbolt. (42)
"O best of immovable things, you shall become a purifier from sin;
you will attain fame in the world as 'Gaurīśikhara'. ||43||
O best of mountains, merely by seeing you raised high from afar, people shall be liberated from all their sins and shall go to the supreme goal. (44)
He who, having stayed for three nights with pure vows, ascends you, beholds Gaurī, worships her, and gratifies a Brāhmaṇa; ||45||
Whether it be a woman or even a man, he shall go to the world of Gaurī;
and whoever here gives up his life with self-restraint and a concentrated mind,
having attained the status of a leader of the Gaṇas, he shall wander together with me.
And here itself, O Gaurī, your presence shall be constant at all times. ||47||
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus to that best of mountains, the three-eyed God of gods,
accompanied by Pārvatī, wandered about there in every direction.
Then, O Vyāsa, that lord saw a golden stone adorned with jewels;
he said to the goddess, "Behold this stone. (49)
The Goddess said to the Lord of Gods: "I have performed austerities here;
this place is dear to me, as well as to Somanandin."
Then Bhava, out of affection, bestowed his grace upon that stone at that time:
"Whoever shall remain pure and fast for three nights upon this [stone],
by him penance will have been performed, and he shall go to your world."
That mortal who, being pure, should stand on one foot for a single day; ||52||
Having become intent upon the Tapanīya [Upaniṣad], devoted to you, and having you as his supreme refuge, he too shall go to your world and shall become a leader of the Gaṇas. ||53||
And whoever shall here renounce their lives on this stone, though they are difficult to give up—
even he, having performed arduous penance, shall go to the world of Brahmā.
And this region of the mountain is the abode of Somanandin.
Whoever should do so for a day and night, he too would become equal to Nandin. ||55||
Then the Lord, wandering about, questioned Pārvatī once more:
"O Daughter of the Mountain, how did these pools come to be here?
Being thus questioned, the Goddess spoke these words in reply.
"O Lord, O Master, when I arrived here to perform ascetic penance,
two great streams repeatedly flowed from my breasts;
these [streams] formed two ponds of white water with vast expanses."
O Lord, when I renounced my ornaments in order to perform penance, streams of water flowed from them and fell down instantly. (59)
And thus, O Lord, this second auspicious pool of water was created for me;
and when that supreme golden complexion was obtained by me from Brahmā,
then a black sheath emerged from my body.
From that sheath, this third vessel was produced. ||61||
O Lord of Gods, having worshipped you in this place according to the prescribed rites,
I have performed the fire-ritual with oblations accompanied by mantras.
These bark garments from the trees are ready for you to wear;
this bright black antelope skin was previously set aside by me.
Then, having heard the words of Pārvatī, the Lord Mahādeva,
filled with supreme affection, replied to the Goddess at that time.
Since your pond, radiant as the moon, was filled with the water from her breasts,
these two shall attain supreme renown as the "Breast-Pond" (Stanakuṇḍa).
The man who, observing a fast, bathes here, worships the deities, gratifies all the ancestors with libations, and feeds the Brāhmaṇas [shall attain great merit]. ||66||
That [merit] of yours shall be inexhaustible, and you shall indeed have a retinue;
O lady of beautiful countenance, this stream that flows from your ornament— ||| 67 ||
This shall become renowned by the name Alaṃkāradhārā;
whoever bathes in it and offers libations to the ancestors, [shall attain great merit].
That act of faith shall become inexhaustible, and one obtains the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice;
for this great pool of yours, Nīlatoya, possesses auspicious waters. (69)
"This shall become famous everywhere as Nīlakuṇḍa;
whoever, being self-restrained, bathes here and offers libations to the ancestors and the gods," [shall attain great merit].
All that shall become inexhaustible for him, and he is liberated from all sins;
and when that man dies, O Goddess, wherever it may be and in whatever manner, [he attains the supreme state]. (71)
By bathing here and performing the fire-ritual, a pure Brāhmaṇa shall become Mahāgaṇapati [through the grace] of Kauśikī Vindhyavāsinī. (72)
"By him, the Agnihotra sacrifice shall have been offered for twelve years.
Having spoken thus, O best of sages, Mahādeva rose up.
Then the Lord, taking the bark garments that were upon the trees,
said, "Become a river," and cast them down as if laughing.
O Vyāsa, they then became a beautiful river of clear water.
Adorned with various trees growing on its banks, it was beautified by swans and ruddy geese.
The best of the gods spoke to that great river of holy waters:
"Since you have emerged here from the bark garments, you are the foremost among rivers. (76)
"Therefore, you shall become the most meritorious place in the world;
having bathed in you, a person is quickly liberated from all sins. (77)
For one who gratifies the ancestors with a śrāddha, that offering shall become inexhaustible.
And he who, being composed, gives a tawny cow here to a Brāhmaṇa,
O lady of beautiful countenance, shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Because you ascended to the summit and performed penance here. ||79||
This place shall become renowned everywhere as Agrāraṇya;
it is auspicious, yielding great fruit and great merit, and bestowing all perfections.
It is the supreme peak of Gaurī, extending over five yojanas.
Having fasted here, bathed, and being endowed with supreme devotion, [one should worship]. ||81||
Upon the dissolution of the body, he shall abide resplendent in a celestial chariot.
This black antelope skin of yours is of great merit and removes all sins;
whatever Brahmin beholds it, for him heaven is not difficult to attain.
Whatever fruit is obtained in the Naimiṣa forest and whatever fruit is obtained at Puṣkara;
O Goddess, having seen the black antelope skin, the twice-born man obtains that very same [merit];
and I shall dwell here perpetually with you, O beloved. 84.
"O Goddess, whatever human being worships us while we are stationed here shall become a leader of our attendants and traverse the entire world.
Having thus favored the Lord of Mountains together with the daughter of the King of Mountains, the Lord of Sages—
Followed by the gods and the perfected ones (siddhas), Śarva returned once more to Mount Mandara. ||86||
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Bestowal of the Boon upon Kośīśilā, Stanakuṇḍa, Ajinagaurī, and Śikharagaurī," in the *Devīsamāgama* section of the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
Vyāsa said:
Having gone once more to Mount Mandara together with the Daughter of the Mountain, the Lord...
"O great sage, tell me what Mahādeva did.
Sanatkumāra said: "Having come to Mount Mandara together with Pārvatī, Hara..."
He sports in a divine golden chariot, adorned with all kinds of jewels.
In that most excellent city, which had been fashioned by his mind, there were beautiful staircases crowded together upon surfaces of variegated silk-like stone slabs. ||3||
The Lord of the Universe was being served by the lords of the Gaṇas, great yogins led by Nandīśvara, as well as by perfected beings and the best of sages.
Thus he dwelt together with the Goddess, being likewise honored;
while that wise God of gods was thus playing, O Vyāsa. (5)
Then the thousand-eyed Indra, the moon, and Vāyu arrived;
having reached the city gate, they saw Nandin standing there.
With palms joined in reverence, they spoke, desiring to see Śaṅkara:
"O Nandin, you ought to act in such a way that we may behold the Lord of Gods.
Then Nandin, having approached, stationed himself at the entrance.
Śambhu informed [her] that the three gods had arrived.
O daughter of Nanda, when the God of Gods commanded,
"Let them enter," those three gods then entered into the presence of Śaṅkara.
Having prostrated, they stood together gazing at the omnipresent Lord, the bestower of boons.
Then the Lord of the World spoke to them as they stood with their heads bowed in reverence.
"O gods, what is your business? For what purpose have you come? Speak, O immortals; I shall grant you all whatever you seek. (11)
Then the thousand-eyed god spoke these words to Śaṅkara regarding the slaying of the exceedingly powerful lord of the asuras, Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Although Viṣṇu, the crusher of enemy forces, had slain that lord of the Daityas, he did not abandon that terrifying Nārasiṃha form; instead,
O Lord, he assumed his own original appearance.
O Lord of Gods, by that form, though it was cruel, he desired [our] welfare.
"O Śaṅkara, we do not remain here out of fear having attained liberation; rather,
O Supreme among Gods, you ought to show us favor so that Mādhava may likewise cast off that lion-form."
Then the god of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow, spoke to Śakra.
O Śakra, just as Viṣṇu will cast off his terrifying lion-form, so shall I do; O Śakra, let the fever of your mind depart. (17)
Then Vāyu addressed the god Śaṅkara:
"You ought to act in such a way that I may no longer be bodiless. || 18 ||
Having heard the request of Pavana, the three-eyed Lord granted him a most massive body, by which he became embodied; then,
O Vyāsa, that high-souled Śaśāṅka made his petition.
"In former times, I was cursed by Dakṣa, saying, 'You shall become one whose body is afflicted by consumption.
Grant me your favor so that I may be freed from this consumption.
Having heard the moon's petition, the powerful Lord spoke these words to him:
The one of great splendor spoke this to Śaśin as he bowed down:
"After performing penance at Prabhāsa, you shall become free from consumption.
Having thus obtained the boon, all three of those best of gods departed.
Vāyu, Soma, and Sahasrākṣa each entered their own abodes. || 23 ||
Vyāsa said:
O Blessed One, how was that Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu slain by that Narasiṃha? And what was his power?
Tell me, who am asking this, what was his vigor and what was his austerity? 24.
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, there was a wife of Kaśyapa Prajāpati named Diti;
she was the daughter of Dakṣa, and she gave birth to two sons.
Having consecrated Hiraṇyakaśipu as the elder and Hiraṇyākṣa as the younger,
he formerly became the king of the Daityas by the decree of Brahmā.
Then, among the Dānavas, the exceedingly powerful Vipracitti was the Indra, and among the gods, the thousand-eyed one; thus this triad of Indras shone forth.
Then, O Vyāsa, while they were ruling the three worlds at that time—

The Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, desiring to seize the kingdom of Śakra and intending to bring the three worlds under his own control, fixed his mind upon ascetic penance. Having gone to the southern quarter, he established himself on the Śrīparvata mountain.
The immensely powerful king of the Daityas performed intense and great austerity;
he offered oblations of fuel-sticks and sacrificial porridge mixed with his own blood into the fire.
With arms raised and without support, his gaze fixed upon the sun during the day, and standing on one foot with eyes half-closed, he remained there, firm in his resolve.
The powerful one remained thus for two thousand divine years;
by his great asceticism, the three worlds were thoroughly agitated.
Then Brahmā, the best of gods and whose vehicle is the lotus, approached him.
"Choose a desired boon, O King," he said respectfully.
Having seen that Lord Brahmā, the granter of boons, the king of the Daityas requested a boon, O Vyāsa; hear what he desired:
"O Blessed One, if you are pleased, O All-pervading Lord, let this be my boon."
May I be immortal, indestructible, free from old age, and possessed of great strength. ||35||
Neither by a hand-held weapon nor by a missile, neither by night nor by day;
neither by something wet nor by something dry, neither by a man nor by a woman. ||36||
Brahmā spoke to him from within, and he addressed him in return:
"Therefore, O Lord, death shall come to me in a different manner. (37)
Having said to him, "So be it," Brahmā, the best among the foremost of gods,
the Grandfather, departed quickly for his own city, peaceful and pleased.
Then that Hiraṇyakaśipu, the best of all asuras and the son of Diti,
having conquered Śakra himself, ruled the kingdom.
Having brought the three worlds under his own control and having conquered all the inhabitants of heaven,
Śakra himself became Vāyu, Yama himself,
Dhaneśa, Varuṇa, and Agni— he himself became everything. (8.70.40)
"Bow down to me and worship me; I am Brahmā together with Purandara," so that Asura spoke to all the sages, the Siddhas, and the Brahmins.
Vyāsa said:
O best of sages, regarding that which you have called Śrīparvata—how indeed did it come to be known as Śrīparvata? What is its merit, and what is the fruit thereof?
Sanatkumāra said:
"Ah, O you of noble vows, I shall indeed tell you that which you ask me:
concerning where the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu performed his great penance."
On that mountain of great merit, the god of gods, whose banner is the bull and who possesses great luster,
took perpetual delight together with the goddess Umā.
While the God was staying there, the Goddess, daughter of the mountain king,
[beheld] great yogis who had attained perfection through austerity and possessed a radiance like that of fire or the sun.
O great sage, after they had performed circumambulation and prostration before Śambhu,
the Lord of the World, seeing them as they repeatedly departed, questioned them.
"Who are these perfected gods, the lords of yoga, who have bowed down to you?
Then the Supreme Lord, the God, smiling, spoke to her: 47.
Those great-souled ones, perfected in yoga and established in the Pāśupata yoga,
who here, O Goddess, having propitiated me, gave up their lives—
these are they, whose bodies have attained perfection and who move about according to their own will.
They shall go to the supreme state, the ultimate goal for the attainment of liberation. ||49||
Then, having reflected for a very long time with eyes wide with wonder,
Śarvāṇī addressed these most venerable words to the God.
"O Lord of Gods, O All-pervading One, I shall likewise exert such effort so that I too may attain this same perfection; for I have come here for that purpose."
Then, assuming the form of Śrī, that most beautiful goddess performed great penance there for a thousand years.
And the god of great splendor granted her a boon equal to theirs:
"O beautiful lady, regarding the entire system of spiritual science (adhyātmatantra) proclaimed by me," ||53||
"You shall become a perfected Mahāyogeśvarī, possessing knowledge for the sake of others; and this glorious mountain shall be known by your name. ||54||
Known as Śrīparvata, adorned with various forms,
it shall become a place of great merit for a hundred yojanas all around.
And whoever comes here, O Goddess, daughter of the mountain, to you and to me—
A mortal who, having bathed and become pure, performs worship, shall go to my world.
But he who shall here give up his life on Śrīgiri, the best of mountains,
will become three-eyed and able to go at will, and attain the status of a Gaṇapati.
And those who, having come here, shall perform a circumambulation of the mountain—
And your hosts shall be joined with the abodes of Śarva. ||58||

On the Śrīparvata mountain, which is exceedingly beautiful, frequented by hosts of perfected beings (siddhas), and variegated with fragrant flowers— those pure men who, having cast off the defects of impurity, behold me;
They travel through the sky in celestial chariots yoked with birds.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Bestowal of the Auspicious Best of Mountains," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
While that Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was thus ruling at that time...
A great length of time passed, O Vyāsa, throughout the three worlds with all their moving and non-moving beings.
Possessed by great pride, his mind agitated by the intoxication of prosperity, he held all the gods in contempt and did not regard dharma.
Overwhelmed by anger, he [disregarded] all the gods together, headed by Śakra.
Even though they had been displaced from their own kingdom, he caused them great distress.
Being tormented, they all went for refuge to Brahmā, saying:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, Grandfather of great splendor!"
O sinless one, the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, having obtained a boon from you, has seized the entire three worlds and robbed us of our kingdom in heaven. ||5||
"He constantly inflicts insults upon us as a means of avenging his enmity;
driven away by him, we have all come to you for refuge.
O Lord of Gods, show us favor so that he may no longer remain our enemy."
The powerful Hiraṇyakaśipu was an enemy of the world who had abandoned all righteousness.
Thus addressed by the gods at that time, the lotus-vehicled Lord,
possessed of great wisdom and acting for the welfare of the gods, spoke these words:
"The ascetic power of that evil-minded king of the Daityas has been exhausted."

"That enemy who has brought you to such hardship and seized your kingdom—by him I was previously entreated for the supreme boon of being unslayable by all; and he, having been confounded by my magic power, spoke of a loophole. (8.71.10)
O mighty ones, as soon as the king of the Daityas became senseless upon seeing that opening, at that very moment I attained satisfaction in my mind.
Go today, all of you together, to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu; speak to that Acyuta for the sake of his destruction.
"Having assumed the body of Narasiṃha, he will slay the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu by striking him but once; thereafter you shall attain peace.
"So be it," they all replied, having prostrated before the Grandfather.
The gods, acting with reverence, came together to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Then, seeing the gods standing before him, the immensely radiant Viṣṇu spoke with gentle words, uttering speech that was captivating to the ear:
"Welcome to you; for what purpose have you come?"
All of you are worthy of my worship; you are my most venerable friends.
O dwellers of heaven, whatever task is in your minds that must be performed by me, speak it briefly, and I shall carry it out immediately without hesitation.
Thus addressed by Viṣṇu, the gods, led by Śakra,
spoke with joyful faces while offering praises to Janārdana.
O Lord, from Hiraṇyakaśipu, the exceedingly powerful king of the Daityas,
a very great fear has arisen for us; our kingdom in heaven has been seized,
and we have been subjected to humiliation by him, O best of gods.
That son of Kaśyapa, a hater of Brahman, devours the entire world.
O Hṛṣīkeśa, slayer of all enemies, act in such a way that this Daitya may be slain by you; let this boon be granted to us. (21)
Then Viṣṇu, having meditated for a long time and reflected upon a means for their destruction, spoke to the gods—the best of deities—as if refreshing them with his words:
"So be it, O best of gods; I shall do everything according to your word."
"Since I am telling you this, O lords of the Daityas, you who possess great strength:
let you also, O observers of noble vows, enter my body.
Having become composed of all the gods, I shall slay your arrogant enemy."
Then all the gods entered the body of Viṣṇu;
and he too, having become powerful and having assumed a terrifying form,
the man-lion (Nārasiṃha) of great splendor, adorned with claws and fangs.
Viṣṇu went, shining brightly, to the city of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Having seen that garden outside his [the Daitya's] palace, filled with flowers of every season, Nṛsiṃha stood there greatly amazed at the lion-like Daitya.
It was adorned on all sides by campaka, aśoka, and jātī flowers, as well as by kadamba and bakula trees, and by fragrant blossoms of every kind. ||28||
With lakes covered by lotuses and adorned with swans and ruddy geese,
and with trees that grant every desire, the forest was like the Vaibhrāja grove.
But Nṛsiṃha, moving with playful gait and fierce with intoxication, shattered that [tree]; like an elephant in full rut, he agitated the lakes.
Moving here and there in the midst of the forest,
he shone like the lofty peak of Meru, the king of mountains, standing firm.
Then, having approached that Man-lion, the powerful forest guards, filled with rage, sought to restrain him; but the mighty one struck them down as well.
Then those gods who remained after the slaughter melted away there;
having gone, they reported that matter to Hiraṇyakaśipu at that time.
Having heard those words of theirs, the exceedingly powerful king of the Daityas—
Having summoned Prahlāda, Anuhrāda, Namuci, Bāṣkali, Bali,
and all the Dānavas headed by Vipracitti,
he said: "Go quickly, bind the lion, and bring him to me."
"Bring him here, O lords of the Daityas; he must not be killed by any means whatsoever.
This lion cub shall become a plaything for my goddess," she said.
Having heard this, all the Asuras, led by Vipracitti, [acted accordingly].
Having gone to the garden together, they saw the Man-lion standing there.
Standing at a distance, they hurled nooses, which Mādhava cut asunder;
then he, like a lion, utterly put the Dānavas to flight.

Then, their companions having been slain, those Daityas went dejected to the side of the king of the Dānavas and reported everything to him at that time. Thereupon, the powerful King Hiraṇyakaśipu himself became enraged.
Mounted upon his chariot and fully armored, he rushed furiously toward Narasiṃha.
That mountain-like chariot, equipped with weapons, was swiftly whirled around by the king of lions and cast down, being ground to powder upon the surface of the earth.
Then the Daitya, his chariot shattered, with eyes bloodshot with rage,
uprooted a tree and hurled it with force at Nṛsiṃha.
Thereupon, that tree fell upon the body of the lion-king.
Like a clod of earth thrown against a stone, it was reduced to powder. ||43||
Then, having seized Hiraṇyakaśipu, the lion struck him once with his palm and swiftly deprived him of his life.
Having let out a great lion’s roar, the omnipresent Lord Hari, with his nails made of diamond,
tore open the chest of the Daitya, which resembled a massive mountain.
O son of Śakti, when that great Daitya had been slain by Viṣṇu,
those Dānavas who were not killed entered the netherworld (rasātala).
Śakra regained his great sovereignty over heaven, free from all thorns;
and all those dwellers of heaven likewise took possession of their respective kingdoms.
Then the god who bears the trident and has the bull as his emblem arrived there.
O Vyāsa, that which I have told you was requested by the gods.
In order to cause Viṣṇu of wondrous deeds to abandon his leonine form,
he then became a Śarabha, resembling a peak of the Himalayas.
With four hind legs, sharp fangs, and great strength,
he approached Narasiṃha and roared with focused intent.
Then the lion, seeing the śarabha standing before him, [prepared for battle].
Overcome by great anger, he struck him with his palm. ||51||
Though struck by that lion, the śarabha was not at all disturbed;
then, having struck the śarabha—who possessed a body like adamant and great strength—[the lion fell]. ||52||
He himself fell into distress through the touch of that great-souled one;
then Viṣṇu, having meditated for a long time, realized that Śaṅkara had arrived.
Having bowed his head to him, he proceeded to offer this praise:
"Homage to Śarva, to Rudra, to the commander of the army, and to the bestower of protection. (54)
Salutation to the supreme deity, to the highest Brahman;
salutation indeed to Time, who has the form of Yama, and to the staff of Death.
Salutations to the creator of the end and to the destroyer of Death itself;
salutations to the one who holds the Pināka bow in hand and who wields the fierce arrow.
Salutation to Caṇḍa, to Vāmadeva, and to the Lord of all Yogas;
salutation to the Sovereign of Knowledge, salutation to the Lord of Brahmā. ||57||

Homage to you, Kālacakra, the slayer of the foremost of asuras; homage to the wheel of the fire of universal destruction, the bringer of the end of the dissolution. Homage to the Lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa, whose very self is Nara-Nārāyaṇa.
And to me alone, the giver of boons and the bestower of all desires. ||59||
