Salutations to Śarabha, who is beautiful in form, who is well-clothed in a tiger skin,
the lord of the Nandīśvara Gaṇas, and the master of the hosts.
Salutation to the Lord of the senses, the Master of the mind;
salutation to the Lord of primordial matter (pradhāna), salutation to the Lord of the gods. ||61||
Homage be to the Lord of Existence; homage to the Lord of the Principles.
Homage to the Lord of the moving and the unmoving; homage to the Lord of all beings. ||62||
Salutations to the Lord of the three worlds and to the Lord of the worlds;
salutations to me who bestows yoga, and likewise to him who bestows sovereignty; salutations to the giver of invincibility and likewise to the giver of that which is beyond recitation.
O Blessed One, I am established in you, I find my ultimate goal in you, and you are my supreme refuge;
I have come to you for shelter—be gracious to me always.
Whoever should hear this constantly, being pure and with a disciplined mind, [shall attain the highest state].
Having reached the world of Rudra, he shall become an attendant of the God.
It brings merit, fame, long life, and leads to heaven; it destroys sin.
To hear it, to listen to it, and likewise to remember it constantly [yields these same fruits]. || 66 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus being praised by Viṣṇu,
the Lord of the World spoke these most venerable words to Hṛṣīkeśa.
"O Viṣṇu, this meritorious and auspicious boon has indeed been granted to you by me:
the restoration to your own womb of one who was attached to a non-womb.
Thus, you, Viṣṇu of great splendor, shall always possess the boon obtained from me."
At that time, the ocean gave birth to you as one born of an animal womb.
You have accomplished every task; Hiraṇyakaśipu has been slain. Come, go now to your own most wonderful and auspicious birth.
Then the most excellent Śarabha stepped upon that lion with his feet and joined Keśava once again with a divine body.
Then, having granted a boon to Viṣṇu, the slayer of Daityas, he whose banner bears the bull, [departed].
Having said, "Be established in your true nature," he vanished right there.

Having granted that incomparable boon to Viṣṇu, the Sustainer of the World—being gazed upon by the eyes of the wives of the gods’ cities as he slew the Daityas—departed for his own supreme abode, which is praised by the great sages, while bearing a chest resembling the luster of a dark rain cloud and holding his trident in hand. || 73 ||
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Rescue of Narasiṃha by Śarabha," within the account of Hiraṇyakaśipu in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all yoga, I have heard this most excellent narrative."
O best of sages, I wish to hear from you what has transpired.
Having then removed that lion-form of Viṣṇu, what else did the wise one whose banner is the bull do? I wish to know this.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Bhava, the god of gods, having brought Viṣṇu— who is his own source—
to Mandara, wandered there together with the Goddess, he of great splendor,
through the delightful forest regions and the mountain cascades.
The Lord of the Gods adorned [the place] by crawling all around.
Knowing that the immutable Lord Śaṅkara was delighted by the sight of the forest,
the two seasons of autumn and spring arrived there together.
Then, all the trees and the lakes on every side [began to bloom].
They suddenly and simultaneously released various kinds of flowers.
There were enchanting ponds covered with lotuses and water-lilies, frequented by swarms of bees and inhabited by swans and cranes. (7)
Species rich in fragrance quickly came into being along with the *campaka* trees;
likewise, there were *aśoka* trees with fragrant flowers and *atimuktaka* vines.
Fragrant breezes, pleasant with every kind of scent, attended upon the God;
and they beheld that most excellent forest, strewn with flowers of every season. ||9||
Taking the flowers himself, the Lord of Gods, the Master of the Universe,
with a joyful heart, adorned the Goddess, the daughter of the Himavat mountain.
Then the Lord of the Gods [beheld] Nandīśvara standing at his side and himself;
thereafter, Pārvatī, having bowed to the Lord of the Gods, spoke this out of affection.
The imperishable Mother of the entire world spoke these words:
"O you whose banner is the bull, how shall I have a son born of my own body?"
Your heroism and your power are honored by all the gods;
O Mahādeva, act accordingly if you hold me dear.
Thus addressed by the Goddess, the three-eyed God of gods,
possessed of great splendor, spoke these words out of a desire to do what was pleasing to the Goddess.
"Let it be so, O Queen of Gods! I shall make this petition of yours fruitful, O Ishani, so that he may become your son. ||15||
The most excellent among all the lords of the gods, endowed with the power of great yoga—
he under whose control this entire world shall remain, O beautiful lady.
"Even before you departed to perform that penance, this boon was indeed requested by you for the sake of a son; therefore, I shall certainly grant it to you."
Having spoken thus, those two gods— the daughter of the mountain and the Lord of the Universe—
wandered together with Nandīśa as the teachers of the world.
Beholding all the gardens, they arrived at the Vindhya mountain.
Then, having reached the supreme golden peak of the Vindhya—
which was filled with caves and caverns and joined by various waterfalls— [they stayed there].
A mass of clouds accompanied by lightning, like a solidified mountain peak.
It was endowed with various trees and rocks, joined with various flowers,
filled with the fragrance of various perfumes, and auspiciously radiant with gold and jewels.
Having created in its center a city of great supernatural power,
divine, composed of jewels and gold, and enchanting to both gods and asuras,
the two of them, endowed with supreme sovereignty, entered that city together.
Then the imperishable Goddess commanded Nandin:
"O child Nandin, lord of the Gaṇas, you must stand thus at the gate so that no one may enter here,
not even the subtlest atom of air."
Having placed that command upon his head, Nandīśa, the lord of the Gaṇas,
stood at the entrance, manifesting an exceedingly unbearable splendor.
Then, engaged in yoga, the two gods—
Pārvatī and Bhuvaneśvara, the source of the entire world—
assumed their supreme forms and remained for a very long time, those two of great splendor, for the sake of obtaining a son.
O great sage, that supreme yoga which occurred between the goddess and the trident-bearing God of gods cannot be described by me, nor even by Brahmā;
for this Supreme Lord is superior to Brahmā and to those such as myself. (27–28)
One must necessarily relate in the scripture exactly as it occurred and exactly as it was heard;
therefore, O Vyāsa, since you are dear to me and my disciple, I shall speak to you.
O great sage, while they remained thus established in the application of yoga,
a thousand divine autumns passed by.
Then there appeared terrible and terrifying omens:
the entire earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembled;
the rivers went dry, and the lord of rivers was agitated.
The sun became lusterless, and the wind blew hot.
Meteors fell most dreadfully, and the quarters of the sky became exceedingly terrible;
thus the Earth, terrified by these portents, sought the cause of auspiciousness.
He went for refuge to Viṣṇu and, having approached him, reported his distress:
"O Lord, many terrible portents have occurred most intensely. (34)
Therefore, being exceedingly distressed, we have today come to you for refuge.
Then the Lord Viṣṇu addressed all the gods with these words: ||| 35 ||
Then all the inhabitants of heaven, led by Bṛhaspati,
having gathered together in one place, engaged in various kinds of discourse.
Then the one of great intelligence, the son of Aṅgiras, spoke these words:
"This is the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, the God of gods, the three-eyed one. (37)
The immensely radiant one was united with the daughter of Himavat for the sake of obtaining a son, through the yoga of the Supreme Lord, for a thousand divine years. ||38||
Then, for Pārvatī who had spoken thus, terrible portents occurred that struck terror into the world; what more need be reflected upon here? (39)
"Let us all go together with devotion to praise the bull-bannered Lord, so that a son born of his own body may be granted to the Goddess, O lords of the gods. (8.72.40)
"O immortals, inform the Lord of Gods accordingly and very quickly.
Thereupon, Vaivasvata spoke words that issued forth from his wrath.
For what reason are you all so deeply distressed?
If this son of the God of Gods is indeed devoted to us, [why does he not protect us]? || 42 ||
"He shall not be a malevolent one; therefore, O gods, we shall forgive him.
But if he should become harsh toward us or a malevolent one, then I shall bind that boy with the noose of Time."
"O immortals, I shall bring that cruel one under my control, together with Death. ||44||
"If Purandara does not hurl his thunderbolt at his head,
by which that fool will be split in two and shall give up his life so difficult to abandon," he said much in this manner, his eyes bloodshot with rage.
The righteous Viṣṇu, who knows the supreme truth, spoke these words.
"O son of the Sun, you speak with great confidence,
being under the sway of anger and ignorant of the ultimate truth!
For he who shall become the son of Śambhu through Girijā— " [47]
Whoever shall become subject to you will be like a fool. ||48||
"Will this man, or another born subject to birth and death, arise as the son of the Sun, by whom you shall be brought under your control? (49)

O son of the Sun, even if the time is not yet complete, you will not be able to destroy the youth; how much less so the son of the Trident-bearer? For the splendor of the Blessed Lord Śambhu shall be unsurpassed.
O Lord Śakra, how could he possibly come under the power of death at your hands? || 51 ||
"O gods, I speak for your benefit if my word is to be carried out:
let us all go together to propitiate that Hara."
"The boon that was granted to us at our self-choice marriage remains with Śaṅkara;
we shall choose that very boon, the foremost Pinākin. ||53||

"Since a son born of the body will not be produced for the Goddess, Śambhu will not procreate a son who is unfriendly to us. We ourselves are all the sons of the omnipresent Śaṅkara, born before him. || 54 ||
O lords of the gods, he cannot be seen through austerity, nor can he be known through knowledge.
"He who bears the bull upon his banner can be seen through supreme devotion.
Come, let us go to where Śaṅkara resides,
so that by establishing the highest devotion we may behold Śaṅkara."
And the god Agni himself shall enter into his presence.
"O best of gods, [this shall be done] for all the gods through their very manifestation.
Having heard these words of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor, [the gods spoke]. (58)
Led by Bṛhaspati, those celestial dwellers, the best of gods, with joyful hearts and full of satisfaction, uttered these words: "Excellent! Excellent! (59)
Then, accompanied by Viṣṇu, they went to that supreme peak and addressed these words of praise to the god Agni:
"O Agni, you are the benefactor of all the gods and are entirely imperishable."
Having entered, protect us all and report this to Śaṅkara.
"O best of gods, act in such a way that Lord Śaṅkara, having emerged,
may look upon us as we stand bowed down in devotion.
When all the gods had spoken thus, the Fire-god replied:
"O gods, there is indeed nothing that must not be done by me toward you.
Yet, I lack the power to behold Hara, the supreme Lord of the Gods, united with Pārvatī; and you yourselves are greatly distressed. (63–64)
"Your word is not to be transgressed, yet this hardship is exceedingly great for me.
O gods, like a messenger, I shall enter and perform a great act of daring.
Having said this, he went quickly to that abode of the one with matted hair (Śiva).
There he saw Nandin, possessed of supreme luster, standing at the gate;
he stood there having blocked the entrance, wielding a blazing spear.
Seeing him, the Fire-god then looked all around.

"There is no means whatsoever here for even a minute creature to remain once it has entered," he reflected, and went to that very Nandin for refuge; then the god Agni, with palms joined in reverence, offered praise to him.
Homage to the Lord of the Gaṇas, and homage to Caṇḍa, the wielder of the trident;
homage to the Lord of the Army, and always homage to the one whose self is Śarva. 69.
Salutations indeed to Hālāhala Rudra and to Nīlarudra;
salutations to Itirudra and likewise to Ārdrapaṭa.
Salutations to you, Svapnarudra; salutations to you, Bhasmarudra.
Homage to Rudra of the cremation ground; homage to you, the ten million Rudras! || 71 ||
Homage to Piṅgalarudra, the lord of the Rudras;
homage to Pramatharudra, and homage to you, Bhūtarudra. ||72||
Salutation to you, Virūpākṣa, to Rudra, to Śvetarudra;
salutation to you constantly, O God, salutation to you constantly, O Śiva. ||73||
Salutations to you, O ever-compassionate one; salutations to you, O lover of your devotees.
O Lord, you are [the refuge] for me, your devotee, who desires the welfare of the gods. ||74||
"Be a granter of boons, O Lord of Nandin; do not direct your anger toward us, O Master.
Then Nandīśvara spoke to the Fire-god who stood there offering praise.
"O Vahni, O best of gods, I am pleased with this devotion of yours. Speak, O divine one, what is dear to you? What may I do for you, O Hutāśana? (76)
Then the Fire-god spoke to that boon-granting Nandin who stood before him:
"O Lord, if you are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me... (77)
"O Lord of Gods, let me be granted entrance for the sake of the gods' business into the abode of the God of Gods; O All-pervading One, let this be my boon. (78)
Nandin replied to him: "This boon is indeed difficult to grant;
you will not be able to see that Lord of Gods when he has entered into yoga. (79)
"O Maheśāna, the imperishable creator of the world, together with the Goddess—
nevertheless, O Anala, this boon must indeed be granted by me to you.
Go, O Fire-god, becoming exceedingly subtle and difficult to perceive."
"Having entered, depart quickly, so that the act of your arrival remains unknown. 81. Permitted by Nandin, Jātavedas, filled with joy, became subtler than light and merged with a ray of the sun. 82.
Having entered the palace of Śambhu, he then approached a jeweled pillar;
illuminating that pillar situated amidst fire-gemstones, he shone upon it repeatedly. (83)
There he beheld the Lord of Gods and the Goddess Bhuvaneśvarī;
then that bearer of oblations (Agni) praised the two deities in his mind.
Being thus extolled, he displayed his affection for the Goddess.
Seeing the pillar, Hara spoke these words to the Goddess:
"O Goddess, O beloved, this jewel-pillar appears as if it were radiant;
it praises me along with you. I shall grant it an auspicious boon. (85-86)
The Goddess said:
"O Mahādeva, O Lord of the Gods, act thus for this devotee who praises you along with me; grant him an excellent boon."
The God of gods said:
"I am pleased with your devotion and humility, O you who dwell within the center of the jewel.
Speak whatever task you desire; all that shall be yours."
Agni said:
"O Lord of the World, the gods, staying outside, desire to see you.
O Blessed One, act in such a way that they may all behold you. (89)
The God of Gods said: "So be it, O best of gods! Having emerged from among the inhabitants of heaven, I shall grant you a vision, O Vahni, out of a desire to do what is pleasing to you."
"So be it," he replied; thus authorized, the Fire-god emerged from him and, having informed the gods of his mission, stood there, established in yogic concentration.
Then the Blessed One, the God of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow, came forth.
He went quickly to that place where the gods were assembled. || 92 ||
Then, having beheld Mahādeva, the bull-bannered god, all the deities bowed their heads in reverence; filled with joy and full of delight, they offered hymns of praise.
Salutation to the thousand-eyed one and to the thousand-footed;
constant salutation to the Lord of the great, the Lord of the gods. ||94||
Homage to the one who delights in the cremation ground, who is beautifully clothed in a tiger skin;
to the one who severed the head of Brahmā, and who indeed granted boons to Viṣṇu.
Homage to the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice; homage to you, O Tryambaka.
Homage to the Lord of Beings and to the Destroyer of Pradhāna! || 96 ||
Salutations always to the wielder of the Pināka bow, to the one whose self is united with all yoga; salutations indeed to Nīlaśikhaṇḍin together with his consort. ||97||
Salutations to the one who is unattached to desires, and salutations indeed to the one who is attached to desires.
Salutations to Śarva, the All-pervading; salutations to the one with the staff and the one with matted hair.
Salutations to the one who has become the self of all; grant us that which is in our hearts. 98.
Thus being praised by all the foremost of the gods, Mahādeva replied to those deities who stood before him with bowed heads:
"O gods, I am well-pleased; tell me, what shall I grant to you?"
Bowing down once more, those gods spoke these excellent words: || 8.72.100 ||
"O Lord, O All-pervading One, that bridegroom who was chosen by you at our own self-choice marriage—let us all together entreat him; it behooves you to grant him to us."
O Lord of the World, this yoga which you have practiced for many years for the sake of a son for the Goddess—withdraw it; salutations to you!
O you of great splendor, inauspicious omens are seen;
O Lord, the earth is ill-supported and we are greatly distressed. (10.3)
"Therefore, you ought to act in such a way that this son may not be born from the body of the Goddess as he was before, but rather as a god.
Having heard those words of theirs, the God of Gods spoke these words:
This is a great boon sought by all the foremost of the gods;
nevertheless, out of a desire to do what is pleasing to you, I grant it.
However, for a long time, this great splendor has been restrained by me.
"For he beholds this supreme and unfailing station.
Then, O best of sages, having been addressed thus by the God, those gods—
The gods, led by Brahmā, remained together in silence.
Then, from among them, Vahni spoke to the Lord of the World:
"O God, O Protector of the Three Worlds, offer this supreme splendor into me."
Then Bhava offered his own supreme splendor into the fire.
Having offered it all therein, the Supreme Lord became pleased; Śaṅkara said to the consumer of oblations, "Choose a boon. || 8.72.110 ||
Then Vahni, having prostrated before the Lord, the All-pervading One, requested boons:
"I desire that this son of yours be celebrated by my name;
may I be immune to curses, and may I behold you eternally."
"O Śaṅkara, may I bear this [knowledge] with ease and may I release it;
though I consume all things, may I remain untainted, and may no sin accrue to me.
O Wielder of the Trident, may the gods and the sacrifices find their foundation in me."
May I be Bhūteśvara and may I indeed be Paśupati;
may I become your very body, your embodiment, and your refuge. (114)
"O Lord of Gods, I desire this boon to be granted by you.
"So be it," said the All-pervading Lord, and he bestowed all of that upon Vahni.
Then, having dismissed the gods, the God of gods, whose banner bears the bull, departed.
He entered his residence once more, and the Goddess addressed him:
"O Lord of the Three Worlds, where did you go, and why have you returned here so quickly?
What was that most weighty matter for which you went forth?"
Then the Lord of the Gods spoke to Pārvatī, whose face was clouded with anger:
"O Goddess, O beloved, I have departed in haste at the request of the gods."
Then, O lotus-petal-eyed one, the Goddess spoke to the God, the Lord of the entire world, by those devoted and deeply distressed ones standing outside.
"How did you know, O Lord, that the gods of the triple heaven had arrived outside in a state of terror? And by whom was this told to you, O All-pervading One?
The God of Gods said:
Having entered, O Goddess, the Fire-god took his place by a jeweled pillar and,
offering praise, announced to me all the gods who were standing outside.
"O Goddess, it was by your very permission that I granted him the boon.
Thereupon, the blessed Pārvatī became enraged and spoke to Nandin.
"O evil-minded one, how did that fire enter you while you were standing here at the door?
Then, she became violently angry and placed a blue lotus upon his ear.
Having seized that lotus, which was like a thunderbolt and blazed like twelve suns, he hurled it at Nandīśa.
For the purpose of slaying Nandin, he rushed forward fiercely as if bursting apart;
and crying out, "Nandīśvara has been killed!", Śaṅkara rose up. ||125||
Having said, "O Bhava, may it be well; quickly take the lotus," Umā, the goddess, then regained her composure.
"Alas! What a great calamity has been committed by me under the sway of anger!
Somehow Nandin, the leader of the great hosts of attendants, has not been killed. (127)
Then, taking that ear-lotus from the hand of the god,
the goddess quickly threw it into the lake, saying, "May it be well with you."
Having spoken thus, the goddess then threw that lotus from her ear;
it became a lake upon the ridge of the Vindhya mountains, shining with many lotuses and water-lilies.
Crowded with swans and cranes and graced by ruddy geese,
it is known by the name Bhadrotpala, situated near Hemaśṛṅga.
Having bathed there, a person is quickly liberated from all sins;
there, gifts and the libations offered to the ancestors always become inexhaustible. (13.1)
And a man who dies here attains the same world as Nandīśvara.
Then the Goddess, the daughter of the Mountain, spoke these words again to the God: ||132||
"O God, what did the gods say to you, and with what kind of boon did they worship you?
Then the Lord of Gods, whose banner is the bull, spoke thus to the Goddess.
"O Goddess, O fair-faced one, I have come forth at the request of the gods;
this yoga which you possess, O Mistress of the World, is for the sake of a son for the Goddess. (1.34)
"Here, thousands of terrible and inauspicious omens are seen;
the entire earth is terrified, and we ourselves are deeply distressed."
"Therefore, so that this son is not born from the womb of the Goddess,
let this boon be granted, and he shall be a praiseworthy offspring.
Then, O Sovereign Lady, that wondrous splendor was cast into the fire by me for the sake of a son.
You shall become glorious, possessing six heads and twelve eyes.
Having heard those words of his, he cursed the sons of the Mountain-Dweller and the immortals:
"Since my son was not desired in their bodies by those evil-minded ones within their own wives, therefore those gods shall not obtain a son."
The Earth, too, her senses impaired by my curse, shall remain bewildered;
though she obtains many husbands, she shall never obtain a son.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the goddess ceased, having cursed the gods along with Indra;
she was known by the name Kaiṭabhā, a holy one who bestows many boons.
On a golden peak of the Vindhya mountains, there was a beautiful, auspicious Gaurī;
for that is indeed a holy sanctuary and the stone known as Ramaṇā.
O Vyāsa, the man who goes there shall, upon death, become a leader of the Gaṇas.
Then all the gods arrived there together with Agni;
they were pale, overcome by dejection, burdened with shame, and filled with anxiety.
When they had reached the gatekeepers, Nandin announced their arrival to Śaṅkara.
Having entered and received permission, the gods said to the Lord:
"O Lord of the Three Worlds, we are unable to endure this splendor."
Save us, O Lord of the world of the gods, so that we may be free from our feverish distress!
The asura Andhaka performs exceedingly difficult austerities;
therefore, O God, O All-pervading Lord, a very great fear of him is seen by us. (145)
The God of gods said:
"O gods, let there be no fear; I myself shall slay Andhaka, that excellent son of Hiraṇyākṣa who has exerted his prowess for your sake."
And you all must go to the vast forest situated in the midst of Meru, known by the name Śaravaṇa, which is twelve yojanas in extent and holy. || 147 ||
O preeminent deities, having split open your bellies there,
that supreme and radiant splendor of mine shall emerge.
"O best of gods, your bellies shall also attain the state of gold.
Having heard those words, they bowed their heads to Bhava and went to the glorious Mount Meru and that auspicious Śaradhāna.
There, having then split their wombs, that splendor emerged.
Resembling the fire at the end of an eon and difficult for even the gods and asuras to behold, the glorious and exceedingly beautiful Mount Meru quickly became [transformed]. (1.51)
Everything became golden, the supreme splendor of Maheśvara;
a divine wind blew, carrying the fragrance of flowers from all seasons. And by the piercing of their bellies, they attained a state of supreme gold.
In heaven, divine drums resounded spontaneously without being struck;
showers of fragrant flowers fell repeatedly,
and there arose the sound of invisible beings offering salutations.
Seeing and hearing such things as these, O observer of noble vows, the best of gods went joyfully to the wielder of the Pināka bow and reported everything to him.
Then, dispatched by Sthāṇu, they returned to their own worlds with delighted faces. ||155||
Having heard these harsh words spoken by the gods who were filled with joy,
the goddess— honored in her heart, the mother of yoga, the bestower of boons upon the wise, and the ordainer— was delighted; and knowing the news of the birth of her son, she remained there.
And she, whose lotus-feet were touched by the heads of the gods, attained satisfaction in her heart.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Origin of Skanda’s Birth," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
Whose son was this Andhaka? What was his heroism and what was his prowess?
And how was he slain in battle? Tell me all of this.
Sanatkumāra said:
Listen, O Vyāsa of great intelligence;
I shall relate to you, O twice-born one, all this as it happened—the ancient account of Andhaka in its entirety.
Two sons were born to Kaśyapa by Diti; those two became Daityas:
Hiraṇyakaśipu was the elder, and Hiraṇyākṣa was the younger brother after him.
At that time, Hiraṇyakaśipu was the eldest king there;
when that hero had been slain by the wise Narasiṃha,
Hiraṇyākṣa became king, saluted by all the Daityas.
"He was childless; it is heard that he performed austerities for the sake of obtaining a son. (5)
Having reached Śaṅkukarṇa at the confluence of the Indus and the ocean,
the son of Diti performed austerities in order to behold the god who wields the Pināka bow.
Vyāsa said:
How did that divine, purifying, and world-renowned sacred field of Maheśvara, known as Śaṅkukarṇa, which accomplishes all goals, come to be?
You should explain to me what the fruit is and what the attainment of merit is.
Sanatkumāra said: Formerly, indeed, the Blessed Lord Kapardin Nīlalohita,
having come to the ocean of the Indus for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worlds, [spoke].
He began to perform a penance inconceivable even to the gods and asuras;
thereafter, for the sake of protection in all ten directions,
the Lord of the World stationed thousands of leaders of his hosts (gaṇas), such as Nikumbha and others.
With ears like those of a boar, large tusks, thick eyes, and a thick nose;
with short feet and hands, a gaping mouth, and terrifying to behold;
covered with a tiger skin and draped over with a leopard skin.
Having summoned the very powerful Gaṇeśa, who is known as Śaṅkukarṇa, to his side, the Blessed One spoke this.
"O child, protect this forest together with your own hosts of Gaṇeśvaras, so that the gods may not enter it, for as long as this vow of mine lasts."
Having thus performed that protection, Mahādeva, whose banner is the bull,
practiced there a great, terrible penance that is exceedingly difficult to perform.
Then all the gods, led by Śakra, arrived at that place.
Hindered by Śakukarṇa, they did not move even a step forward.
The gods said:
"O Gaṇeśas, we [wish to see] the god Śarva, the fierce one with matted hair."
"O sinless ones, we have arrived here on business to see him; let him be shown to us. Being distressed at not seeing him, we shall perish, O lords of the Pramathas.
Śaṅkukarṇa said:
"O gods, you are not able to see the Lord in any way whatsoever.
Practice austerities, may it be well with you; then you shall behold Śaṅkara."
The gods said:
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, O you of great splendor, let there not be the destruction of the worlds!
Therefore, grant us an entrance; show us favor, O Lord. (18)
Śaṅkukarṇa said: "Let the worlds perish, or let you perish; entrance shall not be granted.
The Lord of the World, the Master, will create them again once they have perished."
He alone is the creator of all beings, and likewise their destroyer;
O gods, who else besides that omnipresent Lord is capable of destroying the worlds?
"We shall not open the door; our command is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Having been addressed thus, the gods reflected and went to the abode of Brahmā.
Then those best of gods reported this to Brahmā.
Then Brahmā said to the gods: "O gods, go with me once more to the leaders of the Gaṇas, so that I may bring about your restoration.
Thereupon, those dwellers of heaven went together with Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
They returned once more to that very place where Śaṅkara was staying;
then that lord of the Gaṇas,
Śaṅkukarṇa, blazing as if with splendor, blocked them once again.
Then Brahmā spoke these words to him, which were consoling and full of meaning: ||| 25 ||
O Lord of the Gaṇas, there is indeed no wickedness whatsoever among the gods.
By your grace, let the gods behold the bull-bannered God.
Bowing their heads to you, the gods, led by Indra, [pay homage].
And I, together with Viṣṇu, would entreat you, O Lord of the Gaṇas.
Having heard those words of Brahmā, that lord of the Gaṇas, enraged, raised his sharp-edged spear and spoke these harsh words: ||| 28 ||
"O gods, this prostration of mine to you is not at all heavy;
rather, the command of Śambhu is weightier. No one has the right to enter here.
O Brahman, how is it that those who were forbidden have been appointed for the purpose of guarding?"
"Having transgressed the command of the Lord, we grant him entrance.
Having heard those words of the high-souled Gaṇeśa,
Brahmā, filled with supreme shame, went into a secluded place.
Then all the gods, seeing the Grandfather filled with shame,
spoke these words to the Lord of the Gaṇas, their bodies overcome with anger and wrath.
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, you have no shame; how can you revile your guru?
For the Bull-bannered One will certainly not approve of you speaking thus.
Furthermore, O Gaṇa, do not treat us with such contempt."
"Today we are prepared; we shall destroy your life!
Having heard those words of theirs, Śaṅkukarṇa, filled with rage, looked askance at the denizens of heaven and spoke these words in his fury.
"O gurus, why should I fear you, lords of the rākṣasas?
Having propitiated Śaṅkara, you have attained this supreme divinity."
"You too, O best of immortals, are members of the host of the Lord of the Gods;
we too are masters of supreme yoga, leaders of the hosts of that wielder of the trident.
Are you equal to us, O dwellers of heaven, or are you inferior?"
"Since we behold and follow the Lord of the Gods, therefore we are always more worthy of honor than all the other gods.
We look upon you without fear; enter, O immortals! (38-39)
"Behold today the terrible power of the lords of the hosts;
whatever strength you possess, whatever yoga, whatever austerity, and whatever exertion you have—"
"Show all of that to us, and then you shall see my power.
Having heard those words of his, all the gods became exceedingly arrogant.
With weapons firmly grasped, they quickly rushed toward Śaṅkukarṇa;
O Vyāsa, as those gods who considered themselves heroes were attacking, [Śaṅkukarṇa]— 42.
The immensely powerful Śaṅkukarṇa seized their strength through yoga;
thus, all those foremost of gods had their power restrained.
Unable to take a step, they stood motionless like pillars.
When the gods were thus restrained, Viṣṇu, the best among strikers,
rushed with speed toward Śaṅkukarṇa, the lord of the Gaṇas.
Then that powerful one, by means of yoga, paralyzed the body of Viṣṇu.
Resorting once more to his yoga, Viṣṇu, endowed with sovereign power,
fought with Śaṅkukarṇa, and he in turn fought against him.
O best of sages, as those two lords of yoga were thus engaged, ||| 46 ||
A very great battle took place between them by means of yoga itself.
Having restrained Viṣṇu, that most wonderful Gaṇeśa, the beloved of Śarva, engaged my father in combat through his yogic power.
Then, employing subtle yoga, Brahmā entered into all beings.
Whatever being Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, entered,
there he beheld Śakukarṇa standing before him.
Having abandoned the gross elements, the Lord entered the subtle elements (tanmātras).
Then the Grandfather, whose soul was absorbed in yoga and who had attained the supreme state of yoga, beheld there the senses, the principles, and the constituent elements;
he saw Sthūlaśiras, Śakukarṇa, and Mahābala.
Now, in the meantime, O Vyāsa, twelve thousand divine years passed for the trident-bearing God of gods;
and, O Vyāsa, the vow of that high-souled one was completed. ||52-53||
When that vow was completed, Śaṅkara, possessing a splendor like the fire at the end of an eon, gazed upon all the directions as if bringing them back to life.
Seeing all those inhabitants of heaven thus subdued,
the god then restrained Śakukarṇa by means of gentle persuasion alone.
O child, O lord of the Gaṇas, you have carried out my command correctly;
release all these gods and do not disregard them, O lord of the Gaṇas.
Thus addressed by the God, Śaṅkukarṇa, the lord of the Gaṇas,
dismissed all the deities and stood near the God.
Then all the Suras as well, filled with supreme shame,
bowed with the highest devotion to the Lord of the gods, the All-pervading One.
Then the God, who knows the Self, laughed at them as they stood there ashamed.
Addressing Viṣṇu in a melodious voice, he spoke together with Brahmā:
"O lords of gods, this lord of the Gaṇas is always devoted to my command;
O best of deities, may whatever has been done by him be forgiven for you."
"Tell me what must be done, and for what purpose you have come."
Brahmā said:
"O Lord of Gods, this illustrious Gaṇeśa Śaṅkukarṇa has indeed destroyed our strength through his yoga; let a boon be granted to him."
May he always grant us his own vision from beyond.
The God of Gods said:
"This very place shall be known by this name, pure and renowned throughout the world;
it shall be celebrated as Śaṅkukarṇa, as well as the auspicious Sthūleśvara. (62)
Extending for a yojana in every direction and endowed with all sacred fords (tīrthas),
it is graced by the fruits of all sacrifices and possessed of the fruits of all gifts. Whoever comes here, prepares the sacrificial oblation (caru), and worships me with diligence— || 63 ||
By fasting for a day and night, he shall go to my world.
Whoever dwells here for a year, having observed some form of restraint,
shall attain supreme yoga and become equal to Śaṅkukarṇa.
And whoever, established in self-restraint, should give up their life-breaths here in this field,
shall become a great Gaṇapati upon the dissolution of the body;
the Śrāddha offered here will become inexhaustible for the ancestors.
And these women are endowed with sovereign power and possessed of the strength of asceticism and yoga.
"O gods, depart free from anxiety; you shall behold me constantly.
Then the Lord, the Sovereign, having granted this boon to the gods, vanished on the spot while granting them constant vision at will.
When that Great God had departed, Brahmā, surrounded by the foremost of the gods,
installed a linga there and established numerous sacred fords (tīrthas),
such as the meritorious Daśāśvamedhika and Pañcāśvamedhika.
Having established sacred fords for the gods, he departed for his own abode.
This, O Vyāsa, has been recounted to you regarding the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean. ||71||
The supreme abode of the Blessed One is pure and renowned throughout the world;
it is crowded with perfected beings and celestial musicians, and frequented by hosts of apsarases.
O Vyāsa, having gone to that forest which was endowed with many flowers and fruits and was always resounded by the songs of birds, the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa [remained].

For the sake of a son, he performed austerities while meditating upon the Three-eyed Lord. Then the God, whose banner is the bull, went there with his attendants to the beautiful peak of the Himavat mountain known as Maināka. (74)
The supreme lord of yogis remained as the eternal, transcendent Brahman. ||75||
Then the goddess, having approached, stood slowly behind him and closed the eyes of Śambhu with her two lotus-like hands.
Thinking, "He does not know," the daughter of Himavat then played;
at that moment, O Vyāsa, the world became blind.
For it had become invisible due to darkness, just as it was before; then the God, having understood that, created a third, imperishable eye upon his forehead,
situated above and possessing a brilliance equal to the fire at the end of an eon.
By the splendor of that eye, the mountain was reduced to ashes. || 79 ||
Seeing her father thus consumed by the wielder of the Pināka bow,
Pārvatī withdrew her hands and stood dejected at her husband's side.
Then the God, seeing Umā with a dejected countenance,
looked again at that mountain with a gentle eye.
As soon as he was seen in that state, he became as he was before;
seeing her father restored to his natural form, the daughter of the Mountain King, her face beaming with joy, bowed down and spoke to her husband. ||82||
"O Lord, for what reason was this mountain reduced to ashes by you? And for what reason, O Master, was it restored once again to its natural state? (83)
Having heard those words of hers, the Supreme Lord said:
"O Goddess, at whatever time my two eyes were closed by you..."
"Then all the worlds became blind, enveloped in darkness. Therefore, O Goddess, for the sake of light, this eye was created by me upon my forehead, with which this best of mountains was burnt. (85)
And having observed you so distressed because of the slaughter of your father, O auspicious lady, [I shall act]. 86.
"For your sake, O fair-hipped one, I have been restored to my natural state;
yet, while this world was seized on all sides by intense darkness, I was born blind through my own power, O Goddess. (87)
"I shall give that son to Hiraṇyākṣa, who is performing austerities."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, surrounded by his hosts, took hold of Andhaka and,
having arrived at the ocean Sindhu, spoke to Hiraṇyākṣa.
"Behold me, O son of Diti; I grant you divine vision.
I am Śarva who has come here, O Daitya; choose a boon as you desire.
Rising up, Hiraṇyākṣa bowed his head to Bhava.
He quickly requested a boon from the God, saying, "Grant me a son. ||91||
The best of the gods spoke to him as he bowed his head at his feet:
"O tiger among gods, this son of yours, the eldest of a hundred sons,
must not be treated with contempt by you, O lord of the asuras, on the grounds that he is blind."
"This son of yours shall become great, endowed with the power of asceticism and heroism.
No one other than me shall be able to slay him.
Then that blessed Lord, having granted him that auspicious son, [departed].
Taking his son Andha with him, that great asura Hiraṇyākṣa went once again to the beautiful peak of Maināka.
Having gone to his own city of Aśmaka, he said to his high-minded wife:
"O Goddess, this son has been granted to you by the Blessed One himself. (96)
"Nurture him through yoga; do not be negligent at any time.
Out of affection for him, she looked upon him and milk flowed from her breasts. (97)
Being nourished over time, Andhaka grew up;
and when he reached youth, he reflected thus:
"Fie upon my life as a blind man! Death itself would be better for me."
I, who am blind and do not see my home, kinsmen, or relatives. || 99 ||
Blessed are those men in the world who, remaining undaunted, go forth by themselves after having looked upon the faces of their kinsmen and spoken with them as they pleased;
for they may achieve their purpose even with a clod of earth, a blade of grass, or even a corpse.
"Shame on me, a doer of evil, who has not been favored by him!
This Daitya, my father, always protects me out of affection for his son; he does not slay one who ought to be slain, for he causes the depletion of his treasury. (1.01–1.02)
Deluded by affection, he does not understand this agony of mine;
I myself shall perform that task which is prescribed by the wisest.
For, by undertaking great asceticism, I shall indeed become possessed of sight.
Having thus reflected in many ways, that very wise man, though blinded, [acted].
Having taken leave of his mother and having bowed down to his father,
the wise one, having made his resolve and being firm in his determination, departed for the sake of asceticism.

For a long time he was gazed upon by his father, whose face was flooded with tears of grief and whose soul was exhausted by fatigue, and by his mother, whose face repeatedly shed tears; blinded by the piercing cries of their intense sorrow, exhaustion, and the pain of separation, he sighed deeply.
Meditating upon the god who is the lord of Umā, Andhaka departed from his home to perform austerities.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Departure for Austerity," in the Legend of Andhaka within the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O best of Brahmins, having gone there at that time, the son of Hiraṇyākṣa—
Gaṅgādvāra is an auspicious gateway, an unsurpassed forest of asceticism. ||1||
There is a divine place named Kanakhala, where the river Hairaṇvatī flows;
there all the trees are indeed golden, known as the Kanakhalas.
There, where in ancient times Dakṣa performed a sacrifice together with the gods,
and where his sacrifice was formerly destroyed by Mahādeva—
there he worshipped the God, having bathed and being of restrained mind.
Having paid homage to the deities, he spoke these words:
Andhaka said:
"In that penance grove where the gods and various living beings [dwell]..."
I go for refuge to them all; may they grant me the perfection of asceticism. ||5||
From this day forward, I shall perform a most difficult and severe penance,
so that I may obtain my desired boons or meet death which destroys life.
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, O son of Parāśara, that one of great strength then subsisted on air for a year, free from fatigue.
Likewise, bathing at the three sessions of the day, offering oblations into the sacred fires,
devoted to the worship of the gods, and intent upon recitation and burnt offerings;
every year, when it was fully completed, he would cut a piece from his own body, the size of a grain of rice.
Then the great asura offered a portion of his flesh into the fire.
O best of sages, in this manner, as he daily offered his own flesh, a thousand divine years passed for him.
His father-in-law, white as a conch shell, water, nectar, the kunda flower, or the moon,
remained solely devoted to austerity until nothing but his bones and veins remained.
Endowed with that ascetic power, he then rendered the sun lusterless.
The self-controlled one made Soma together with the planets and stars;
just as that very sun illuminates with its splendor,
he dried up the ponds, the riverbanks, and the lakes.
Then Andhaka, through his ascetic power, paralyzed the wind;
the Siddhas did not move in the sky, and their celestial chariots fell.
Having seen the form of that austerity, Śakra suddenly created hundreds of obstacles, yet he did not waver.
Then Brahmā, approaching him, spoke to the Dānava Andhaka:
"O great Asura of mighty strength, you have performed a terrible penance;
I am pleased with you, O mighty-armed one of noble vows—become possessed of sight! (16)
"Let your body return to its natural state as it was before, O Lord of the gods;
speak further of another boon that resides in your mind. (17)
Sanatkumāra said: Having then become possessed of sight and with an uninjured body,
he bowed down and spoke directly to Brahmā, the creator of the worlds.
Andhaka said:
"O Blessed One, if you are pleased with me, and if my ascetic practice has been successful, O Grandfather, grant me invincibility against the gods in battle."
Great strength, as well as illusions and even immortality—
this I desire, O Lord of Gods, if you are a granter of boons to me.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, the all-pervading Lord laughed and spoke these auspicious words once again to the son of Hiraṇyākṣa.
"O son of Diti, I do not grant immortality to the Daitya;
however, there shall be a condition for you—state it yourself.
Andhaka said:
"If there were a woman who is indeed the mother of the world and I did not bow to her, then my death would occur; otherwise, I am indeed free from death. (23)
Brahmā said:
"Let it be so for you; indeed, as you have spoken today, you shall become Andhaka by name and shall attain renown in the world. (24)
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus to Andhaka, the thorn in the side of the gods, the Blessed One departed for his own abode, and Andhaka ceased [his assault].
Having bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā and worshipped the god according to the prescribed rites,
and having offered oblations into the fire, the wise one then took leave of the penance grove and,
accompanied by his companions and the lord of the Daityas, went into the presence of his father.

With a joyful heart, having become mighty through asceticism and his desire increased, he who gratifies the enemies of the gods, radiant and resembling a cloud driven by the wind, went once again into the presence of his father. (27)
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Obtaining of Boons by Andhaka," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Having gone with those eight Dānavas to that city nearby, he—
Having accomplished his purpose, Andhaka returned and reported [the matter] to his father. || 1 ||
Then, O Vyāsa, Hiraṇyākṣa, the lord of the asuras, who had brought this pleasant news,
gave many jewels as well as desired objects;
at that time, the king himself, together with all his friends and their vehicles.
Accompanied by his wives, he went swiftly like the moon with its clusters of stars.
Having traveled not very far into the forest, which was filled with *aśoka* and *campaka* trees,
the illustrious one reached his son, who resembled another Budha.
Seeing his son’s purpose accomplished, the lord of the Dānavas was filled with joy;
out of affection, he embraced him and repeatedly smelled the crown of his head, asking:
"How, by what means, and in what time were these boons obtained by you?"
Being questioned, he related everything exactly as it had occurred:
that granting of the boon and his own greatness.
Having heard this, those tigers among gods roared like the oceans.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having placed his son Andhaka upon that chariot, Hiraṇyākṣa quickly entered his own city together with those friends.
Accompanied by his son, that Daitya shone with a fulfilled heart,
like the sun moving through its zodiacal sign together with Saturn.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having entered, that lord of the Daityas spoke to his circle of friends,
just as an Adhvaryu priest addresses the other officiating priests standing at the Sānnāyya sacrifice.
Hiraṇyākṣa said:
Listen now to that which has long resided in my heart as a task to be performed;
it must be carried out by all of you, who possess terrible prowess.
"Previously I desired that, having accomplished my purpose, once I have arrived here in this city of Andhaka, I would indeed celebrate the Kaumudī festival. (12)
"I shall perform the Great Splendorous Night (Mahāprabhā) for the god who destroys sacrifices; let all that be done without hesitation."

"By my command, let it be proclaimed throughout this city— in its squares and assembly halls— that for fifteen days, beginning with the day of the Kaumudī festival, [the streets shall be illuminated]."
And let there be three nights for the god;
and let those who are his friends— the lords of the Daityas and the mighty Dānavas—
come here from all directions and take their delight.
And in our school, those auspicious brahmins beginning with Śukra— ||| 1.6 ||
“May the Nāgas, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and likewise human beings—
all of them come together and enjoy themselves with me.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by the wise Hiraṇyākṣa,
the lords of the Daityas then did everything exactly as they had been told by that enemy of the immortals.
O son of Śakti, he swiftly dispatched messengers to the Daityas along with the Dānavas,
as well as to the other factions of his own side,
saying: "The mighty King Hiraṇyākṣa invites you."
Accompanied by your circles of friends, go forth, desiring to see him.
Victorious is the king, the powerful lord of the Daityas, Hiraṇyākṣa!
All those who hate the Daityas and the enemies of the Dānavas have been slain.
For the victory of the sons of Diti and for the fear of the Ādityas, the King orders the Kaumudī festival for you, beginning from dawn. (23)
And let the city be made ready with streets well-swept and smeared with cow-dung for the night of the god Rudra, which destroys the gods.
"May all the city-dwellers be clothed in new, unwashed garments; may they wear garlands, have bathed their heads, and have been provided with gifts and food in due order.
Let the singers sing and let the actors and dancers dance."
Let banners be raised upon the houses, the streets, and the marketplaces;
and let the houses always be plastered and adorned with heaps of flowers as well as various kinds of incense.
Let all [the images] be adorned with garlands and clusters of forest wreaths;
let the Brahmins be fed, and let the auspicious proclamations be made. ||28||
And everywhere there were the sounds of Vedic chanting and proclamations of auspicious days,
as well as the lighting of lamps throughout the night on the royal highways and within the houses.
Let indeed uninterrupted wicks soaked in abundant oil be prepared;
let the youths wander everywhere together with women, taking delight, laughing, singing, and devoted to dancing. (8.75.30)
Let the musical instruments be played; let the wives of the Daityas dance! || 3.1 ||
He performed the auspicious worship of Mahādeva with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
he presented various kinds of oblations, grand ablutions,
and abundant garlands adorned with all manner of foods to be chewed and eaten.
And lamps of various forms, as well as drinks and flavors. ||33||
"Offer various fruits, meat, cooked rice, and non-arid delicacies, adorned with gold and jewels, to the Lord.
Let animals be bound here, and let the best of the twice-born be fed. (34)
If any inhabitant of the city should ever fail to do all this, the king of great renown shall inflict corporal punishment upon him. || 3.5 ||
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus made his proclamation from atop the elephant's back, the bell-ringer returned once more to his own home, and the Kaumudī festival arrived.
At that time, all the people in the city did everything exactly as instructed;
the king too was self-restrained, bathed, pure, and possessed of a disciplined mind. (37)
Day after day, Vyāsa, exerting himself with diligence, bathed him with pure *pañcagavya* and fragrant oil. (38)
With milk, clarified butter, curd, and many auspicious juices;
with flowers, fruits, seeds, and gems, all accompanied by water. ||39||
With fragrant ashes and scented water,
the king himself [offered] ten hundred jars for each [of the two].
Day after day, O Vyāsa, the king worshipped Tryambaka with perfumes, flowers, incense, recitations, and offerings;
having thus performed the worship, he then fed other brahmins.
Having performed [the rites] with sacrificial animals, gems, and even jewels, ||42||
Being praised with offerings of food, beds, seats, and other gifts, he went to his home;
likewise did the other lords of the Daityas and the exceedingly powerful Andhaka.
O best of sages, they all acted exactly as the king had commanded;
then the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa seized Andhaka.
O Vyāsa, reciting this [hymn] of Rudra, he caused him to fall from his feet:
"O son, may this gracious Lord always be well-disposed toward you. (45)
You should cultivate devotion toward this Supreme Lord;
he is to be saluted and worshipped, for there is no teacher higher than him.
You should always worship this Supreme Lord with devotion. (46)
Sanatkumāra said:

Having spoken thus and prostrated before Śaṅkara, that great Asura, the lord of the Asuras and Dānavas, departed—wise and fully satisfied—to his own abode, just as the Lord of the Gods [Indra] would go to his own. ||47||
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Great Kaumudī Festival," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, on that Kaumudī night, the Daityas and Dānavas, together with their women, [celebrated].
The gods, their minds filled with passion, gazed [upon her] as if they had returned to heaven.
There, a certain woman with beautiful outer corners of her eyes placed a divine lotus over her face,
as if out of fear of the Moon, for the sake of protecting her lotus-like countenance.
Another, having approached her beloved, struck him with her foot in intoxication,
as the moon strikes a full-blown autumn lotus with its ray.
Other noblewomen, unaccustomed to royal highways,
took off their sandals upon seeing the ground paved with crystal.
And others, O best of Brahmins, lifted up their garments out of fear that it was water.
As they walked along the royal highways, they beheld the ground strewn with jewels.
A certain woman, abandoned by her lover because he was infatuated with another, had departed from her home; touched by the rays of the moon, she fell down, languid with passion. 5–6.
Having fallen, that noble woman spoke thus to Soma:
"Once again you burn me with your sharp rays, as if I were a lotus pond. (7)
"Indeed, you revive medicinal herbs that have been scorched by the sun;
why then do you not firmly revive me, who am utterly consumed by passion?
Some beautiful women are swinging other women upon swings."
With forms as flickering as ripples, they appear like the moon reflected in water.
Some mighty Daityas sing together with women,
just as Gandharvas do with Apsarases in the Nandana grove.
In some places the royal highway shines, crowded with many women, like that auspicious and divine celestial path in the sky, variegated with stars. ||1.1||
In some places, the sound of anklets and girdles, like that of cuckoos,
shone forth— pleasing to the ear of the listener and kindling the subtle fire of passion;
in other places, O Vyāsa, there was the sound of women devoted to their lovers as they dallied with their beloveds.
A sweet voice, which agitates the heart, is heard.
Thus, O Vyāsa, that festival occurred, full of many wonders, increasing the joy, happiness, and confidence of the Dānavas at that time. || 13-14 ||
When that assembly hall was once again established as it was before,
O Vyāsa, those Dānavas returned to their former nature and gathered together;
terrifying and roaring, they entered the divine and enchanting hall.
With pillars made of Jāmbūnada gold and altars of diamond and lapis lazuli; richly adorned with hanging strings of pearls and decorated with the finest garlands of flowers;
[furnished] with diamonds, lapis lazuli, sapphire, great sapphire, and mango sprouts. || 16–17 ||
It was adorned with rubies, crystals, and emeralds as well,
encased in a divine lattice, and beautified by variegated tinkling bells.
It was endowed with trees bearing abundant flowers and fruits that grant all desires,
as well as beautiful oblong ponds and many beds and seats;
it was free from fatigue, overflowing with abundance, and devoid of all suffering.
Filled with all desired objects and crowded with many women and men,
the Daityas, overwhelmed with pride, entered that divine assembly hall—
Prahlāda, Anuhrāda, Sini, and Vāskala as well. || 8.76.20–21 ||
Virocana and Bali, as well as the renowned sons of Bali—twelve thousand in number, of whom the exceedingly powerful one was the eldest. (22)
There was a king named Bāṇa, a master of great illusion who possessed a thousand arms;
he had ten thousand other sons,
as well as the Dānavas Mura, Dhamuṣu, Maṇḍa, and Vipracitti.
Kāla, Hayaśiras, Sambara, and Kālasambara; ||24||
Also Viśruta and Indradamana, the Dānava Kālanemi, as well as Sunda and Niṣunda, Vipāka, and Pāka. (25)
Rāhu and Śataketu, Dhvaja, Tāra, and Satāraka;
Mahiṣa and Dundubhi, as well as the exceedingly powerful Kālaka. ||26||
And Andhaka, as well as Aṭi, Baka, and Śarabha;
Svarbhānu, Vṛṣaparvan, Madhu, and Kaiṭabha;
Mahākāya, Śatānanda, and Śatadundubhi.
And Kārttasvana, and Hastin, and Bala, and Naraka as well. ||28||
Dhvāṅkṣa, Mūka, and Ivala; Vātāpi along with Asṛpuñjika; Kaṇḍala, Mīḍha, and the famous Durloma;
Dhundhu, Śatamāya, Śatāvarta, and Dussaha.
Candra and Sūrya, as well as Nara, Devāntaka, and Narāntaka. ||8.76.30||
Brahmahā, Yajñahā, Ilvala, Pilvaka,
and Maya, the best of the Dānavas, as well as the renowned sons of Maya—
these eight thousand, all of whom were firm in their resolve. ||3.1||
And Vṛtra, the best of the Dānavas, as well as Namuci and Bāṣkala; ||3 2 ||
Śatodara, Vyaṃsa, Tāthāya, Hradodara,
Keśin, Pralamba, Kabandha, and Dhenuka.
Hāla, Gārgyaśiras, Kuśa, and likewise Śambhu; as well as Gaganamūrdhan, Sāluka, and Śālva;
Meghanāda, who is renowned, and likewise Mahānāda. ||34||
Kharotha, Khararoman, and the Dānava Sūcīroman;
Parigha, Uparigha, Daṇḍa, and Kāśyapa; Dundubhi of massive body, and the group known as the Saiṃhikeyas. || 35–36 ||
Likewise, there were Hālāhala and Andhakāraka;
the Paulomas numbered sixty thousand, as did the renowned Kālakeyas;
and the Kālakañjas numbered eight thousand—these were the thorns in the side of the gods.
And there were three crores of the mighty Nivātakavacas;
all these enemies of the gods have been counted as sixty crores in total,
excluding those on their side who are humans and even serpents.
O Vyāsa, there were also twenty crores of Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Yakṣas, and birds;
all those enemies of the gods, having entered that assembly hall, were filled with pride.
They shone like rain-clouds in the monsoon accompanied by lightning and meteors;
they were like thundering clouds, like smoky mountains, like bellowing buffaloes, and like approaching banners. || 8.76.40-41 ||
Like portents that have broken loose, like venomous serpents,
like elephants in rut, and like winds driven with speed,
they stood filling that assembly hall for the purpose of harassing the gods.
Then the chamberlain, having approached, spoke thus to the king:
[43] "O Vyāsa, having first bowed his head and touched the ground with his knees, the youth, seated comfortably upon the lion-throne, addressed the king. [44]
With palms joined in reverence, he spoke properly with smooth words and syllables:
"May the Lord, the bringer of victory to all the asuras, be victorious! (45)
"Let it be known that Prahrāda and all the others, led by Vipracitti, have arrived at the assembly; whatever else you deem fit to do, please perform. (46)
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having heard that all the enemies of the gods had arrived at the assembly hall,
the king suddenly rose up like the banner of Indra during a festival.
He wore a crown, possessed large tusks, hair like *muñja* grass, and a broad jaw;
his mouth was gaped open as far as his ears, and he had a great protuberance on his head.
With arms reaching to his knees, round eyes, tawny eyes, and hair standing erect; possessing a body as firm as a diamond, he was a great yogi of immense strength.
Resplendent with his crown like the rising sun,
his chest adorned with a magnificent necklace like a cloud accompanied by cranes,
Vyāsa set forth with his son like the personified Himavat mountain.
Then that best of the lords of the Dānavas, his earrings encircled by the rays of various jewels,
entered the assembly hall— which was surrounded by the foremost of the Asuras and Daityas— just as the sky is filled with rising planets.
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Entrance of Hiraṇyākṣa into the Assembly," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, having gone to that assembly, he beheld the Daityas and Dānavas.
Just as Indra [subdues] the intoxicated clouds that have appeared during the rainy season. ||1||
As he entered, all the enemies of the gods then rose up and cried out "Victory!", just as the Vedas do when the Grandfather [Brahmā] appears.
"Arise! the lord of the asuras said to them all, like a serpent encountering the fivefold illusion and seizing the winds.
That great asura Hiraṇyākṣa shone at their head, like a rutting great elephant in the midst of a herd of young calves. ||4||
Then, seated upon a divine and excellent throne made of Jāmbūnada gold,
that king of the enemies of the gods shone like a great cloud accompanied by lightning resting upon a peak of Mount Meru. ||6||
Then the Asuras sat down in silence,
desiring to create water at the proper time, like towering dark clouds.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having perceived their gestures and knowing the right time to inspire them with joy,
King Hiraṇyākṣa himself spoke to those enemies of the gods.
All of you, O Mahāmāyās, listen with self-restraint and equanimity, like disciples hearing the words of a teacher—timely and beneficial. (9)
My brother was indeed dear to me; as the eldest, he was as venerable as a father.
King Hiraṇyakaśipu was high-souled and true to his promise;
he was righteous, generous, a performer of sacrifices, a giver of gifts, and endowed with ascetic power.
He maintained the sacred fires, was learned in the four Vedas, and brought happiness to all living beings. || 11 ||
For the sake of the kingdom, he was slain by the gods through their deceit, their minds being deluded;
because of his suffering, O great Asuras,
I am tormented and withered like a blossoming lotus uprooted from the water in the summer heat.
"I am capable of inflicting punishment upon those enemies of the Asuras;
however, I am not inclined to do so for the sake of protecting you children there.
Therefore, I shall myself inflict that punishment upon the enemies of the Asuras alone."
I shall go, there is no doubt; O gods, let there be no fear for you.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, those Dānavas were filled with joy;
yet, overcome with great shame, they looked at one another.
Then his younger brother Vipracitti, who was possessed of great strength,
bowed down to that brother and spoke these words, which were meaningful and sweet.

There is no doubt, O Great Being, that you alone [could defeat] the enemies of the Asuras, provided they do not stand in battle having resorted to some kind of illusion. They are weak; there is no doubt, for it is through deceit that they are strong. 18.
Having propitiated me with your head bowed, listen to what I say;
O Hiraṇyākṣa, this has been well-established through sound reasoning even by children.
"That it is to be grasped" has been proclaimed by those learned in the scriptures.
King Hiraṇyakaśipu, our eldest and most excellent brother, though he too thought "I am capable," was slain alone by the gods. (8.77.20)
O King, even Hari, though possessed of great strength, was forcibly slain by those who were powerless;
therefore, O Lord of Asuras, I address you while weeping, for we are but children to you, not they.
"Endowed with the power of asceticism and yoga, and possessed of various illusions, we are capable of slaying those defilers of their lineage through fair combat;
remembering our enmity, we shall destroy the gods. (23)
Just as you have no sleep because of the slaying of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Likewise, O Great King, do not treat us like fools; for wherever you shall engage us, O King, whether on even ground or uneven, [we shall follow]. (25)
We shall surely cross over that [host] like young fish crossing the ocean;
this Prahlāda, together with his brothers, sons, and friends,
alone shall summon them all, just as a lion summons great elephants.
This Bali, the lord of the Daityas, alone is capable of harassing all the gods, including Indra,
as well as Yama and the Lord of Wealth;
and this Bāṇa, his son, is a king who possesses a thousand arms.
These two brothers, Sundas and Nisundas, both possessed of mighty arms, are alone intent upon destroying all the gods. ||29||
Both of them, alone in battle, were intent on slaying the gods;
so too were the valiant Maya, Sāraka, and Tāra. (8.77.30)
And there are other heroic Dānavas capable of harassing the gods;
they too are all exceedingly powerful, and we are always strong.
We shall slay all the gods, just as hunters kill deer in the forest.
"This glorious Andhaka is a hero who has received a boon from Brahmā;
he will surely carry them all away by force in battle to the abode of Yama.
Indeed, it was by relying upon him that [the city] was protected by him."
"We shall wage a great war that will strike terror into the gods;
formerly we were all gods, and later they became the gods. (34)
"How indeed can we fear them, like śarabhas before lions?
Having heard those words of his, Andhaka, the lord of the asuras, [spoke].
There he spoke these words, gladdening the lords of the Dānavas:
"O King, we are possessed of great strength, while those gods are devoid of power.
Behold all the deities, led by Yama, already slain."
Today [I shall slay] that evil-souled, lowest of his lineage, the murderer of the king.
Today their mother Diti shall experience sorrow...
Behold, I alone have slain the youngest of the Ādityas!
Stay, all you Dānavas; I am sufficient for these evil-minded ones.
Death has come upon us, the slayers of the king. ||3 9||
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, O Vyāsa, the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa, desiring victory over the enemies of the gods, spoke to the Dānavas.
"Today the Puṣya asterism is present, which is the cause of our strength;
this very day, O Dānavas, all of you must quickly set out, clad in armor. (41)
Then those Dānavas, filled with joy, quickly equipped their mounts suitable for battle against the oppression of enemies:
"Quickly make yourselves ready; let us go toward the gods! || 42 ||
A tumultuous noise indeed arose from their mounts.
Like the sound of the Ocean of Milk stirred by a gentle breeze, he cried out:
"This lion is mine! This leader of the elephant herd is mine! (44)
"To whom does this chariot belong, so fully equipped with the implements of war?
Come, go forth with speed; wait but a moment! (45)
"Let all the lords of the Daityas depart; we shall follow behind.
Ascend your chariot, O hero! What need have I for a chariot today? On foot alone, I shall slay the enemies of the gods in battle this very day. ||46||
Thus, that most charming sound of those enemies of the gods,
mingled with the resonance of flutes and lutes, was like the lamentation of women.
Then Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu, a man of great asceticism, approached them at that time.
Gladdening the lord of the Dānavas, he said this to Hiraṇyākṣa:
"I have today established peace for you and provided protection along with the Dānavas.
Slay all the gods in battle; there shall be no defeat for you. ||48-49||
"I shall support you, along with your servants and kinsmen,
as you fight, just as another sacrifice sustains the worlds.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having performed a circumambulation and bowing his head to Śukra,
he went out from the palace with Bhārgava at his head.
Then there were kettledrums, conchs, cymbals, drums, and horns;
as well as *sāḍastama*, *diṇḍima* drums, *bhāṇḍa* drums, together with *paṭaha* drums.
Jhaṃrjharī drums, dardura drums, sunava drums, and likewise mardala drums; kaṭaṃkaṭas, pepukas, and also ekapuṣkalas—[all these were sounded]. || 53 ||
Pañcākṣas, saridhīkas, mukundas, and likewise murajas,
as well as labhakas and jalamattas, were sounded by the thousands;
and there were singers singing and praising, along with sūtas and māgadhas.
Having had auspicious rites performed by divine women and the elders of the lineage,
she beheld at the gate the chariot prepared for her— the divine, firm, golden vehicle, a hundred *nalvas* in measure, which Hara had used as his own celestial mount.
With three thousand divine, unattached white horses, swift as thought, capable of going anywhere at will, and free from the suffering of fatigue;
the renowned charioteer of that chariot was named Sārthavāha.
O Vyāsa, the son of Garuḍa was an auspicious bird capable of traveling at will.
Honored by the king with the title of "Rāja" and with blessings, he ascended the single-wheeled chariot just as the sun ascends its chariot. || 58-59 ||
Wearing armor, with his quiver fastened, armed with arrows, sword,
and bow, he likewise had his finger-guards made of iguana skin bound on and a neck-guard secured.
Adorned with a great banner and a parasol,
and with many victory-pennants, he resembled a cloud accompanied by cranes.
Then his parasol, resting upon his diadem,
shone like the moon on a full-moon night, manifesting the luster of a cloud;
and his khaṭvāṅga banner gleamed as if it were scaling the heavens.
Like a blazing comet risen for the purpose of destroying the three worlds. ||63||
O Vyāsa, the chariot of the high-souled Andhaka was likewise at that time, possessing a roar like that of a great rain-cloud.
Then, when told by him, "Now go," the charioteer urged on three thousand excellent horses belonging to the enemies of the gods toward the chariot.
Urged on by him, those swift horses, possessing the speed of the wind and capable of going wherever they desired,
bore that great chariot like the seven horses of the Sun.
Then, in front of him, Śukra appeared in a chariot rumbling like a cloud, just as Budha appears in the sky when it is rising;
and on his right side was the Dānava Andhaka.
Having reached the southern course, just as the sun stands for the world,
Vipracitti took his stand on the second side,
like the Himavat, the best of mountains, to the land of Bhārata. ||68-69||
Then some went behind and others in front, according to their pleasure; other heroic Dānavas followed like planets around the moon.
O best of sages, that army of those who were marching shone as it moved,
like clouds accompanied by lightning and thunder at the end of the rainy season.
He proceeded amidst the sound of neighing horses, the trumpeting of rutting elephants, the flapping of limbs, the clapping of hands, and shouts raised with lion-like roars.
Indeed, he went forth accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments, the roaring of lions, the neighing of horses, and the fierce trumpeting of elephants.
The terrifying army of the Dānavas advanced, making the earth resound with the noise produced by their arms and shouts. ||73||
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Departure of Hiraṇyākṣa," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana said:
"O Blessed One, when the sons of Diti had departed for Amarāvatī..."
What did those immortals do? I wish to know this.
How was it hidden from them, what was the mantra, and what was their conduct? And what answer did those gods finally arrive at through their efforts? (1–2)
"Being righteous, generous, learned, and with their doubts severed, they were beloved by the entire world; what did those deities do?
Sanatkumāra said:
Listen, Vyāsa, to how the gods obtained the upper hand and how the armored Asuras countered whatever was directed against them. ||4||
While the Daityas were thus exerting themselves, terrible portents indicative of fear for the gods arose intensely in Amarāvatī;
there, flesh-eating birds wandered everywhere above.
The garlands of the gods withered, and an inauspicious odor blew.
The horses and other animals did not neigh, and the elephant became dejected.
Without clouds, everything became terrifying, and much blood fell from the sky.
O son of Śakti, weapons are blazing with smoke, headless trunks appear in the sun, and a battle is seen right here. (8)
O Vyāsa, between those two men there was a cry of "Alas! on all sides;
it caused the gods distress and even affected their minds. (9)
The left eyes throb, yawning occurs,
and birds utter cries that portend fear;
furthermore, the fire there blazes with a harsh and rattling sound.
Having seen these and various other portents indicating danger, Śakra spoke these words to his preceptor Bṛhaspati: ||11||
"O Blessed One, what is this terrible fear that has arisen for us, since these fierce and most dreadful portents are foretelling it? (1-2)
I do not believe these portents are without cause, nor indeed is their significance small for us; for these fierce omens, as terrible as the end of an eon, are signaling something dire.
Having heard those words of his, Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods,
looked upon him, reflected with his intellect, and then spoke these words.
What you have said is true, yet it is not without cause;
there will undoubtedly be a very great reason for this. || 15 ||
In former times, Hiraṇyakaśipu, the lord of the Daityas, was the cause [of our downfall];
he was slain by Narasiṃha, and our kingdom has been regained once more.
Today, for twelve thousand years, all the worlds have been enjoyed by you, great-souled ones who are perfectly at ease. (17)
The lords of the Daityas, together with the Dānavas, lie down devoid of energy;
and in Pātāla, the sons of Danu remain struck by misery and grief. ||18||
Hiraṇyākṣa, the lord of the Daityas and the foremost of Hiraṇyakaśipu’s sons,
is surely approaching now,
surrounded by all the lords of the Daityas and Dānavas, seeking revenge for his slain brother.
The lord of the Daityas, possessed of great strength and prowess, was accompanied by his sons and grandsons.
Moreover, his son Andhaka was made immortal by Brahmā;
since that youth cannot be slain, fear has arisen among you.
Therefore, O great beings, all of you, well-armored and clad for battle, wait until this portentous event has passed. (22)
Having heard those words of his, Śakra then said to all the gods: "Prepare yourselves for battle, having made a firm resolve. (23)
A great danger has arrived; do not remain inactive!
Lest the lords of the Daityas, having encountered us, slay us as the intoxicated gods [slay their enemies]. (24)
Then Vāyu, having approached Śakra, the destroyer of all asuras,
spoke with palms joined in reverence in the very assembly of the gods.
"O Goddess, this Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa, surrounded by all the Asuras,
approaches intent on slaying you, remembering the slaughter of his brother.
Therefore, O mighty one, you should be fully armored and [proceed] together with us."
Arise for victory, O Lord of Gods, for the destruction of the enemies of the gods! 27.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, that high-souled Lord, the King of the Gods himself,
[bestowed] an impenetrable, divine armor adorned with gold.
Having himself duly bestowed it with mantras upon his son,
Śakra, whose voice resounded like a thundercloud or a drum, fastened it upon himself.
Clad in that armor, the majestic Śakra shone brilliantly.
Like Mount Meru, immovable and surrounded by clouds accompanied by lightning and meteors,
the Lord Bṛhaspati himself then bound upon him arm-guards, finger-protectors, and radiant hand-shields with sacred mantras.
He bound to him two inexhaustible quivers and a sword born of nectar, which could not be worn out by arrows and other weapons, using a mantra;
then he gave him a most formidable bow with five thunderbolts and an arrow.
He properly bestowed upon him the victory-increasing [weapon] consecrated with mantras.
Then the valiant one showed him auspicious objects:
a full jar, a weapon, and also Airāvata.
Adorned with many divine ornaments by the preceptors dwelling in Kalpa,
and worshipped and perfumed, as well as incensed by the Krodha and Darpaṇa deities;
then the god mounted that elephant at that time.
Then the Lord, mounted upon the elephant Airāvata— endowed with auspicious marks, possessing four tusks, and dripping with rut—
shone like the rising sun atop the crest of the Eastern Mountain.
Then, with a white parasol,
the king of the gods shone like the great mountain Śveta, O great sage, when accompanied by the moon;
his face, exceedingly radiant, gleamed as it was fanned with chowries.
Like a great lotus in full bloom in autumn, fanned by swans, he sits there;
and at his side is Jayanta, the righteous son of Śakra, who shines like Kārttikeya, the beloved son of Rudra. || 39-40 ||
Then the mighty Yama, mounted upon his buffalo Puṇḍra and preceded by the Staff of Death (Kāladaṇḍa), arrived surrounded by ten crores [of followers]. ||41||
And Kubera went forth, surrounded by many Rākṣasas,
as well as Yakṣas, Puṇyajanas, and other deities;
they numbered twelve crores and twenty thousand.
And likewise eight hundred, and again eight more. ||43||
The god Varuṇa went forth with ten hundred sons; they were all surrounded by aquatic creatures numbering twenty-one crores. ||44||
Then the god Anala, surrounded by ten crores [of followers],
went forth together with his son, along with his circle of friends and kinsmen.
Then Vāyu, of great splendor, all-pervading, and of great speed,
possessing immense strength, marched forth with ten akṣauhiṇīs.
O Vyāsa, all the Ādityas went forth, surrounded by twelve akṣauhiṇīs; each one of them was a warrior skilled in divine weapons.
Likewise, the Rudras, possessed of great illusion and great strength,
emerged one by one, each surrounded by sixteen akṣauhiṇīs;
the Vasus with ten, and both the Aśvins with eight.
In the same way, all those divine Aṅgirasas were surrounded by seven akṣauhiṇīs.
The Yāmas, the Dāmas, the Sādhyas, and those Lekhas who possess great strength—
all of them also assembled together with ten hundred crores.
There were twenty crores of great-souled Gandharvas, sixty-four of Pannagas, and twenty of birds. ||51||
Fifty million Piśācas were assembled there,
as well as [thousands] of high-souled kings.
This entire divine army was gathered together there.
Having seen that vast and boundless, supreme power of the gods.
The king of the Jīvajīvas, who was a knower of the supreme dharma, said:
"O Blessed One, let an array be formed so that [we may overcome] those evil-minded ones. || 54 ||
Having heard those words of his— words concerning that which is unassailable, immeasurable, and which even Bhārgava does not know— Bṛhaspati, possessed of vast intelligence, [reflected].
In the presence of the gods, he said to Śakra, the lord of the deities:
"O great archer, there is nothing that the great Bhārgava does not possess within me. (56)
O Pākaśāsana, he whose distinction you do not perceive should not be treated as an equal;
for that highly renowned great yogi, Uśanas, knows what you do not.
And I do not know that at all, for he is indeed superior to me;
yet, O Lord of Śacī, it was because of his sharpness and pride [that he acted thus]. 58.
One may act with negligence toward them, and they are not found everywhere; yet I [approach them] with a sense of wisdom, with extreme gentleness, and with [other virtues]. (59)
Vigilant in all respects and protected by your troops,
