I shall always surpass him in intellect, O Lord of the Gods;
therefore, I will form for you an array of great brilliance in the shape of a hawk.
By which you shall defeat those Dānavas in battle for some time. || 61 ||
Then that Blessed One Jīva, the great yogi, assuming the form of a hawk named Śyena for the sake of the gods' welfare, created an array of exceeding splendor;
at its neck he placed the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) as well as Varuṇa.
And indeed Anala, Vāyu, and Jayanta, the son of Śakra. ||63||
Jīva made Yama his crest-lock, and both Mṛtyu and Kāla his head;
he made his mouth Jīva, and the moon and sun his two eyes.
That twice-born one indeed made all the Rudras his one wing,
the Ādityas his second wing, and Purandara the middle of him.
The Vasus were his feet, and the Aśvins were his great soles;
the Gandharvas and the Pannagas likewise took refuge in his nails.
Great beings among the birds and mighty piśācas he made his tail; serpents and other gods he then made his belly;
and kings stood upon his feet, while he placed the bhūtas beneath his soles.
All the gods who were members of the assembly, who possessed great strength and great energy. || 68 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Having formed that array of birds and having consecrated it with a mantra, Bṛhaspati spoke these words to the king of the gods: ||| 69 ||
"This array has been devised by me, having made the King of the Rākṣasas its center.
Beyond this, no further task of formation remains for us.
O Śakra, protected by the gods, conquer the enemies in battle!"
And by me, through meaningful words, mantras, and the power of ascetic penances. ||71||
Perform your duty to the best of your ability, for you are indeed immortal, O King.
Let all the gods, too, fight as immortals, O King of the Suras;
through our good fortune, victory shall be attained, O bull among gods, and not otherwise.
Slay the enemies, O mighty-armed one; let there be no fear in you in battle. ||73||
Then conchs, kettledrums, tabors, and ḍiṇḍimas,
as well as āḍambaras, nambhas, kṛkavākas, and horns,
along with mardalas and various peṣukas, sounded on all sides.
At that sound, a great joy of battle arose among the warriors;
they let out lion-roars and made sounds of clapping their hands and striking their arms. ||75||

Then the gods, led by Indra and other principal deities, went forth with conchs and mṛdaṅga drums, their hands radiant with all their infallible weapons, desiring victory and seeking the slaughter of the enemy. Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Formation of the Battle Array," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
When the army of the gods had thus been arrayed and stood ready for battle, clad in armor,
the terrible and fearsome force of the Dānavas came into view.
Seeing that army of the Dānavas, all the gods, together with Indra,
let out lion-like roars mingled with the sound of musical instruments.
That immense roar, O Vyāsa, like that of the ocean being churned,
filled the entire world with a sound like the thundering of clouds at the end of an eon.
Then all those tigers among the Dānavas, having seen the supreme gods...
Having properly arrayed their army, they stood and gazed intently at one another.
Seeing those leaders of the Dānava hosts standing there looking on,
O Vyāsa, Hiraṇyākṣa himself spoke to Bhārgava:
"These gods stand here fearlessly, having formed this military array."
"We shall completely defeat the Dānavas in battle," they thought.
Therefore, O Bhavānī, quickly create for us as well a counter-array of illusion that will shatter this very array of the gods. (7)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having said, "So be it," he drew his crescent-shaped sword and strove to sever the head of that bird from its body.
Upon its peaks, however, he placed the Dānavas Prahlāda and Andhaka,
as well as the Dhārās, the Nivātakavacas, the Paulomas, and the sons of Kālakā.
Virocana, Bali, and Vipracitti along with his younger brothers, as well as the brother of Prahlāda together with his circle of friends and kinsmen.
The great yogi made Hiraṇyākṣa his backrest and the king his cushion;
then Bhārgava, the scorcher of enemies, spoke to him with confidence:
"This is appropriate for you at this time, and it is beneficial in every respect."

"This great array has indeed been formed for you by me, capable of breaking the arrays of the gods. Act with propriety—may prosperity be yours! Protected by me, let all of you, skilled in various weapons, guard one another."
All the gods were as if unaware of Mahāmāyā.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then conchs, kettledrums, cymbals, drums, and cow-horns, as well as āḍambaras, ḍiṇḍimas, and paṭahas of great sound [resounded]. 14.
And thousands of other various kinds of musical instruments were played,
which indeed bestow intoxication and strength upon both gods and dānavas.
Then, commanded by the lords of the Dānavas with the words "Crush them!", the Dānavas,
being struck from all sides, began to trample the army of the gods.
The gods, too, prepared for battle, endowed as they were with the power of asceticism and yoga.
They struck the Dānavas, who had committed offenses, with various weapons.
From the falling heads of those who were being struck down, and from the elephants as well,
there arose a most terrible sound, like that of splitting bamboo canes.
As the bows were drawn and the arrows were released,
there arose a great sound there, like that of mountains being split asunder.
With bhindipālas, śaktis, and tomara weapons being hurled,
the entire sky became covered as if filled with fireflies.
With heads, feet, and arms cast down, that battlefield became uneven in an instant. ||21||
With elephants resembling mountains, with excellent horses and the finest chariots,
and with headless trunks dancing about, the battlefield became difficult to behold;
it was further covered with parasols, necklaces, armor, and hand-guards.
With golden neck-ornaments, threads [of gold], beautiful crowns, armlets, and even earrings; || 23 ||
With various neck-protectors, fine silk garments, and jewels; with variegated saddle-cloths and even arms adorned with ornaments.
With maces, trident-staffs, bells, and even goads,
the surface of the earth there shone like the sky covered with celestial lights.
Enraged, that great chariot-warrior seized him by the hair, even though he himself was deprived of his chariot.
The powerful one, having leaped upon the chariot of the charioteer, slew him by force.
And there, another mighty-armed one, having swiftly struck the elephant, hurled the chariot away like a handful of *kuśa* grass at a sacrifice. (27)
Leaping up from his elephant when struck, he [the opponent] sent him to the abode of Yama with arrows resembling venomous serpents. 28.
Even when his rider was slain and fallen upon the earth,
this horse stood by his feet, just as a self-controlled disciple attends to his sleeping teacher.
When the warrior Sāsūti was slain, these excellent horses carried the chariot like men who, though intoxicated, carry the sacred scriptures through their knowledge.
Furthermore, although this bull among the gods was firmly bound by the Daitya,
he wound his arms around him and proceeded toward the presence of the deities.
"Behold, he severed the trunk of this charging elephant;
slain by that very same elephant, he fell to the earth. (32)
This one was joined with another, and having come, he was slain by yet another; that one too was killed by a god, and he in turn was struck down by another. (3.3)
These and many other foot soldiers, having gathered together in great force and confounded the chariot-warrior, struck him down fearlessly. ||34||
Thus do the sky-faring Siddhas, as well as the Rishis and Charanas, govern,
take delight, smile, and perform recitation;
and the Apsarases even carry away the warriors slain there in battle.
Even the Piśācas rejoiced and the Nikumbhilas danced;
that music of the Gandharvas, consisting of shattered, broken, and torn instruments,
became a "war-music" (yuddha-gāndharva) that increased the fear of cowards.

Then the gods and asuras, whose entire bodies were wounded by mutual blows, remembering their enmity and desiring victory for the sake of sovereignty, struck one another, having assumed forms equal to those of Rākṣasas.
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Battle between the Gods and the Asuras," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
While that great and terrifying battle was thus proceeding...
Then the gods indeed surrounded the Dānavas on all sides.
Death, Time, Yama, Kṛtānta, as well as Strife; Deceit, the Diseases, Enmity, and the powerful Wrath;
all those hells and all the messengers of Yama from every side.
The pretas and the ancestors—these are the four classes. || 3 ||
O gods, Vāmana and the immensely powerful Kiṃkaras all entered that [Vāmana] and struck down the Dānava host;
their limbs were mangled by the messengers of Yama, and their chests and flanks were shattered.
The Daityas groan upon the earth like sinners in the hells;
crushed by swords and shields, bound by the noose of Death, and all fallen under the power of Kṛtānta, the sons of Diti are being torn apart. ||5-6||
Being struck down by both Death and Yama, those lords of the Daityas,
finding no protector anywhere, wandered here and there.
Thus, being tormented, they struck those very beings as they wandered here and there;
then a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the army of the Dānavas.
"Excellent! Excellent! was the cry that arose from the gods as they worshipped Yama.
Then there came the son of Prahrāda, known as Virocana;
he approached on an elephant and crushed the army of the gods.
Together with that great illusory elephant, he rushed forward.
Having circumambulated Yama like another Droṇamegha,
he [assailed him] with many sharp, iron arrows whose points were unblunted.
He rained down upon Varuṇa, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), and Vāyu as well;
having then shrouded the splendor of the sun with his sharp arrows, he then overwhelmed the gods like a cloud at the time of universal dissolution. 12.
With all their limbs pierced by those arrows and being struck again and again,
all the gods in an instant became unconscious;
they could no longer perceive him whether he was departing or approaching, whether he had not yet reached them or had already arrived, or whether he stood far away.

Whomever the Daitya beheld from whichever direction, him he struck from that very spot. With his bow perpetually drawn, the Daitya became as difficult to look upon as the sun surrounded by a halo, like the fire risen at the end of an eon.
Then, O Vyāsa, as he was shooting in this manner, the wise Varuṇa cut down that very great bow while threatening the lord of the Dānavas;
Vāyu, meanwhile, stripped away his armor on all sides with sharp arrows.
With a blow from his thunderbolt, Dhaneśa slew his elephant.
Seeing him thus struck down, both Bali and Bāṇa,
along with Prahlāda and their brothers, rushed toward the world-protectors.
As they were thus rushing forward, the mighty world-protectors (Lokapālas) crushed their wheel-protectors with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Vāyu [struck] Bāṇa’s bows as he drew them back with his shafts.
Vyāsa cut them off simultaneously; that was like a marvel. ||8.80.20||
With his bow severed, he became enraged and then discharged javelins;
Vāyu hurled them with force toward another direction.
Furthermore, he struck his horses again with straight-knotted arrows.
Greatly distressed, he indeed sent them along with their charioteers to the abode of Yama. || 22 ||
Leaping down from his chariot in anger, that mighty one of great strength seized a mace and rushed impetuously toward Śvasana. As he was thus swiftly attacking with his mace, the Wind-god likewise—
With arrows shaped like venomous serpents, he cut that mace to pieces.
And Bāṇa, the best among strikers, though his mace had been cut away,
seized another mace, hurled it, and laughed.
As Bāṇa’s mace, moving through the sky, came rushing with speed,
Vāyu seized it and, like one undaunted, hurled it toward another direction.
Then, O Vyāsa, seeing that his son was deprived of his chariot and severely afflicted by Vāyu, Bali quickly placed him upon his own chariot.
Those two lords of the Dānavas, prepared upon a single chariot,
shone like the sun and the moon joined together on the full-moon day.
Then, a battle took place between them and those others.
Then, perceiving that they had been restrained by the mighty world-protectors,
all the Nivātakavacas, the armored Kālakeyas,
the Paulomas, the Saiṃhikeyas, Śambara, and Kālaśambara [advanced].
And the great Daitya Andhaka, as well as the renowned Hiraṇyākṣa—
all these Dānavas, eager for battle and not abandoning their formation,
exerted a great force with their immense speed, like mountains accompanied by clouds.
Then, as they were still rushing forward, the powerful Yama restrained them with his staff;
they stood still, fixed like figures upon a painted cloth.
Seeing all those Daityas brought to a halt out of fear of Yama, [he spoke].
Andhaka approached Yama and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
Having arrived in his great chariot, he repeatedly drew his bow.
The valiant one pierced Yama in the forehead with ten arrows,
Mahiṣa with five, and likewise Kāla in front of him with six.
Whirling his bow, which possessed a radiance equal to Indra’s rainbow, he struck Death with ten arrows and Kṛtānta with seven; then,
roaring like a thundercloud, he pierced the deity once more.
"I am Andhaka, the eldest son of Hiraṇyākṣa and possessed of great strength," he proclaimed, "and a boon was granted to me by Brahmā.
While he was speaking thus, the powerful son of the Sun quickly [appeared]. (37-38)
Enraged, he shattered the chariot, striking it down with his staff;
for when that chariot along with its bow had been crushed there,
Andhaka then raised his mace and rushed with speed toward the Lord of the Dead.
With a blow of his staff, he too crushed that mace to pieces.

Enraged, he struck him again on the head with his staff, just as a sage who has conquered his senses is struck by the objects of the senses. Then, the unimpeded staff was struck back by Andhaka. ||42||
Seeing it struck down before them, the lords of the Dānavas laughed;
they let out lion-roars accompanied by musical instruments and made resonant sounds with their arms.
They cried out again and again, "Excellent! O Andhaka!"
Then Andhaka also, approaching and roaring like the ocean, struck Mahiṣa with his palm and felled him to the ground along with Yama.
Thereupon, a cry of "Alas! Alas! was raised by the gods, while the Dānavas shouted, "Seize him! Seize him!"
O son of Śakti, the array of the gods was broken.
Then those three— Mṛtyu, Kāla, and Kṛtānta—
overwhelmed with rage, bound Andhaka with many nooses.
Then that exceedingly powerful lord of the Daityas, having severed the nooses,
bound Kṛtānta with the noose of his own arm.
Bound by the noose of his arm, Kṛtānta was overcome with rage.
Having lifted Andhaka up, the powerful one carried him away by force.
Seeing his own son being carried off, Hiraṇyākṣa struck Kṛtānta very violently and firmly with sharp arrows.
That one of great strength pierced all his limbs and even his joints with sharpened arrows; thus transfixed, he stood firm.
Seeing that [city] laid open by his arrows, all the gods, together with Indra, stood ready to protect it, their weapons raised in their formidable hands. || 51 ||

Then, amidst the hosts of asuras and suras, there arose that great and most fierce sound of musical instruments—of *kikhara*, *mṛdaṅga*, flutes, lutes, *paṇava* drums, *sughoṣa* drums, and *kaḍiṇḍimānaka* drums. ||52||
Thus ends the eightieth chapter in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the section on the war.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Hiraṇyākṣa, seeing the Lord of the Gods approaching before him, [acted].
He said to the charioteer, "Take me to Indra. ||1||
Urged by him, and himself urging the horses at that time,
he brought him to the Lord of the Gods, just as Agni carries the offered portion.
Then, standing within the range of an arrow's flight, that bull among asuras addressed the thousand-eyed lord of the gods, who was mounted upon the shoulder of an elephant.
O Śakra, whatever strength you possess, display it without delay;
for we are the former gods, and indeed the entire triple world belongs to us.
O best of gods, having rightfully established [the kingdom] according to the order of seniority, you have now abandoned justice and killed my brother once again. ||5||
Having become deceitful through their confidence, they later attained divinity;
we are the former gods, and you are not gods at all.
"Either I shall take away the lives of all you who fight today, or, having slain you here along with your followers, I shall make an offering of you. (7)

"I shall become free from debt to my brother, who was slain by you through your illusory power. Having spoken thus, O Vyāsa, the valiant one drew his powerful bow and pierced [Kumbhakarṇa] in the forehead with five sharpened arrows.
Pierced in the forehead by him with five arrows,
that king shone like Mount Meru enveloped by the rays of the sun.
Then, as he was walking about once more, Śakra took up his thunderbolt, cut his bow, and struck him again.
By that excellent blow, he saw the quarters of the sky ablaze;
not seeing [his opponent], he took up another bow and drew it once again.
The king cut that down for him, as well as another and yet more;
then, seizing a spear, he hurled it in his wrath.
It came flying toward him, blazing-mouthed and fierce, like the very sister of Death.
The king cut it with his thunderbolt; it was like a marvel. ||1 3 ||
Then, raising another splendid mace, the enraged Hiraṇyākṣa rushed forward with speed like a lion toward an elephant.
As he was thus swiftly attacking, [he saw] that mace adorned with gold.
The king cut him into many pieces, just as an atheist rejects both dharma and artha.
Then Vipracitti, Śini, Bāṣkali, Maya, Śambara, and the Dānava Asiloma [attacked him]. || 15–16 ||
Tāra and Kāraka, as well as Indradamana; Kālanemi, Ṣaṇḍa, Vipāka, and Pāka;
Ilvala, Namuci, Vātāpi, and Kālamuñjika.
All these great illusions rushed toward the Lord of the Gods. || 18 ||
Then, as they were still charging forward, the wrathful Rudras and Ādityas hemmed them in, just as powerful lions restrain elephants in a secluded place.
A most terrible battle ensued between them and those [demons].
Like intoxicated elephants in the forest, they collided with one another.
There, O Vyāsa, the one named Aṃśa, the son of Āditya, drawing his bow with a chariot that roared like a cloud, rushed toward the Dānavas. He struck Vipracitti with ten arrows and Śini with five.
And with three arrows he struck Vāṣkali in battle, with five Maya,
Saṃvara with twenty, and likewise Asiloman, Tāra, Tāraka, Ilvala, and Namuci.
Vātāpi, Indradamana, Vipāka, Pāka,
Kālanemi, Ṣaṇḍa, and likewise Āmī-sṛmuñjika—
all these he pierced with ten arrows each.
And as they were drawing them back in battle, the god Āditya, possessed of light-handedness,
simultaneously cut their bows and let out a roar.
Then he [further] destroyed their horses, charioteers, and divine victory-banners.
As if laughing, O best of Brahmins, he cut them into many pieces with his arrows.
Those great archers, their horses and charioteers slain on all sides,
all rushed toward Aṃśa with speed, brandishing their swords.
Like the peaks of great mountains or like roaring clouds, those Dānavas were,
without any agitation,
covered up to their knees by that Āditya with arrows filling their ankles and reaching even to their knees.
Then, casting off their share, they departed with speed toward another direction. ||29||
Then the gods raised a great sound of musical instruments,
as well as vast lion-roars and abundant shouts of "Bravo!
And the blessed Aṃśu, having drawn his bow which resembled Indra’s rainbow—
He wrought a great slaughter among the Dānavas and the Daityas. ||3 1 ||
That best of strikers, with his arrows, struck down the heads of the lords of the Dānavas like ripe fruits, just as the wind blows them away. ||32||
Some, rendered headless by arrows, run on with their bodies;
having fled swiftly from the battle, they fall lifeless upon the earth. ||33||
Others, though possessed of great strength, fell with their arms and thighs severed,
groaning fiercely like men situated in hell.
With all their limbs covered by arrows and bound together by those very shafts, they wander here and there, just like embodied beings in saṃsāra. ||35||
There was no Daitya or Dānava of great strength there who could not be pierced by the fierce arrows of the high-souled Aṃśa;
the forest appeared as if it were a blossoming grove of Bandhujīva flowers.
Or like aśoka and kiṃśuka trees, so did the army of the Daityas appear. ||37||
"This is a portion, this is a portion," "No, this is it, and that is it"—
thus, O Daityas, did they perceive everything as being composed of portions, afflicted as they were by fear.
He too, with his bow perpetually drawn, was like the sun surrounded by a halo.
Whichever Daitya he beheld from wherever he stood, him he pierced with feathered arrows; indeed,
at that time, neither taking up his shafts,
nor fixing them, nor even drawing his bow was perceived by the Daityas and Dānavas.
His great bow appeared drawn into a complete circle;
at that time in battle, he was seen like the sun at midday.
Possessing a divine bow, light-handed and powerful, with his bow always drawn into a great circle, he consumed his enemies in battle like a wind-fanned fire consuming a great heap of dry fuel. ||42||
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter in the Yuddha-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
While those lords of the Daityas were being driven hither and thither by her through her partial incarnations (aṃśa),...
Seeing this, Bala, the master of great illusions, said to his charioteer:
"Take me to where that evil-souled one, who is consuming our army, is;
I shall send him to the abode of Yama with my sharp arrows."
As he was thus rushing forward, that best of strikers then cut down his standard with an arrow and struck each of his horses one by one.
And with a crescent-headed arrow (bhallena), he swiftly struck off the head from the body of the demon;
he then pierced that very demon in the forehead with five arrows.
Those five arrows shone upon the forehead of that Daitya.
Like rays of the sun emerging from a dense cloud,
the powerful Daitya, also an archer, then rose into the sky in a rage and,
O Vyāsa, covered Aṃśa with many arrows.
Just as a cloud pours forth rain, as Indra hurls his thunderbolt, as the sun sheds its rays, and as the moon emits frost—
so did that Dānava Bala, the best among strikers, strike out with pride.
He showered Aṃśu alone with sharp arrows that pierce the vital organs;
the lord of the Dānavas also cut his banner into many pieces,
rendered the horses devoid of speed, and left the charioteer without a chariot.
He shattered the bow with many arrows; he,
the fierce one of great illusion, rendered the other deities also powerless according to their respective portions and let out a roar.
In some places he resembles the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati), and in others he is like the Sun.
In one place he was like the moon and fire; in another, equal to the stars and planets;
in one place resembling a mountain; and in another, assuming the form of a vulture.
In some instances, having entered the sky, he became invisible and discharged arrows.
With their bodies covered in arrows—cut, pierced, and torn asunder—the entire host of the gods appeared motionless like mute men;
the sound of musical instruments had vanished, and the neighing of horses was silenced. || 13–14 ||
Shaken by the trumpeting of elephants, filled with the cries of exhausted warriors, and rendered motionless, that army appeared like a scene depicted in a painting. 15.
O Bala, whichever god there looked upward at him, the exceedingly powerful Bala made his face [unrecognizable] with arrows;
they became devoid of movement, as if established on the path to liberation. || 16–17 ||
Seeing all of them thus despondent in that great ocean of an army, Vāyu, Jayanta, Pūṣan, and Bhaga—those of immense strength—[approached]. || 18 ||
Roaring, they warded off those arrows of that army;
O highly fortunate one, Vāyu [warded them off] like rain from a cloud.
The powerful one seized those being released, those already released, and even those yet to be released;
laughing as it were, he cut down Bhaga’s divine bow,
and likewise Pūṣan’s body-armor and Jayanta’s two quivers.
The gods, possessing a splendor equal to the sun, struck him with sharp arrows;
then that powerful bull among the Danavas was assailed by the gods.
O Vyāsa, he of terrible prowess fought with trees born of the forest;
at that time, those auspicious trees were hurled by him in many ways through his strength.
Then Kratu, with his arrows, struck the lords of the gods; thereafter he went toward the mountain, seizing its great peak along with its deer, wild beasts, and kinnaras.
Uttering an exceedingly terrible and great roar,
he fell with such force, like a powerful wind driven by its might.
He seized that very horn and struck it down upon the head of the Asura;
at that time, he [slew] ten million powerful Dānavas in battle.
He struck down that mountain peak, which had been released by Bala and was making a great roar.
Seeing those sons of Diti, the Dānavas, slain by that peak,
and seeing those fierce gods, the demons were shattered by the thousands.
With chariots, horses, and elephants, as well as on foot;
others, seeking to save their lives, then abandoned their mounts and fled by the thousands, uttering great cries of distress. ||28-29||
Then, as they were fleeing, the Dānava Hiraṇyākṣa approached them,
along with the Danuja Vipracitti and the mighty Prahlāda.
Then Maya, the Daitya Andhaka, and Tāraka, the scorcher of Śakra,
spoke to all the Dānavas and Daityas who were overwhelmed with fear.
"O tigers among the Dānavas, O Daityas, enemies of the gods!
Why do you flee? Stay! Let there be no fear for you, O Dānavas!
Where have you gone, O Dānavas, and will you find happiness or not?"
Not knowing his strength, these gods who were formerly possessed of great power do not crush him while he remains in Pātāla, nor do the best of the Asuras;
yet these lowest of their kind will utterly destroy him, even in Pātāla. || 33-34 ||
"Do not go; turn back and protect yourselves by all means!
O Daityas, do not fear for your lives here, but rather [protect them] through fair combat."
Where has your state as Danujas gone? Where has your nature as Daityas gone? Where has your enmity with the gods gone, and where has the seizure of your kingdom gone? (3.6)
That fortitude which you possess, that pride of yours, your lineage and your birth, and that roar you previously uttered—the time for all of it has now arrived. (37)
Then the Daityas spoke: "We are not children;
indeed, each one of us individually is capable even of destroying the gods. (38)
Today, this very moment has arrived for him here; why do you flee?
From now on, I shall know all that roaring of yours. ||39||
"O Daityas, do not fall into vain fear here like autumn clouds;
turn back, you who are ignorant of dharma, and fight with firm resolve!
O lowest of your lineage, behold the great deed of me and my sons!"
"O Dānavas, I am the illustrious Hiraṇyākṣa, the son of Kaśyapa.
And this is my son Andhaka, who received auspicious boons from Brahmā;
he possesses the prowess that belonged to Hiraṇyakaśipu, O best of Asuras. (41–42)
I possess twice that amount; behold it without hesitation.
And today, O Dānavas, witness all of them slain by me.
Even if all the gods were to stand before me in battle today, once the enemies of the asuras have been slain, the three worlds shall be free from anxiety.
O best of asuras, with me and Indra, you shall enjoy happiness without feverish distress.
"Let there be no fear for you here today; remain as the virtuous ones stand, watching me together with my son in battle.
Sanatkumāra said:
O best of Brahmins, having been addressed thus, they all turned back again, overcome with great shame like elephants tormented by a goad.
Their lotus-like faces were shrouded by their parasols, and their countenances were devoid of color, possessed as they were by shame.
Distressed by fear, they did not stand before that king, like small fish in the water before a whale.
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Asuras' Shouting in Battle," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O Vyāsa, those Dānavas retreated from the front of the battle.
Then they performed that difficult task with a force like rivers surging into the ocean:
Prahlāda, Anuhrāda, Śini, Bāṣkala, Virocana, Bali, Bāṇa, and another Bali who was a thorn to the gods. || 1-2 ||
Vipracitti, Ṣaṇḍa, Hrada, Śatodara, the Asura Yama, Vyaṃsa, Śatāvarta, and Hutodara. ||3||
Keśin and Namuci, as well as the Asura Indradamana; Maya, Mura, Tārakākṣa, Vidyunmālin, and Prabhākara. ||4||
Tāra, Tāraka, the renowned Baka and Aṭi, as well as Mūka, Kubha, and the two of great roar, Kārtasvana and Mahārava. (5)
Vātāpi and Celvala, as well as Ilvala and Kabalvala; Ketu and Śataketu, Rāhu and Svarbhānu.
Śambara, Namuci, and Kālaśambara;
Dundubhi, Mahiṣa, and Śatadundubhi as well. ||7||
Kālanemi, Vipāka, Pāka, and likewise Duryodhana;
Hastī, Sundan, and Sunda, as well as Śarabha and Kāla. ||8||
Vṛṣaparvan, Śatākranda, Śatāvarta, Dhenuka, Pralamba, Baka, Gaja, and likewise Hālāhala. (9)
The Sainhikeyas are renowned, as are the Paulomas, the sons of Kālaka,
the Nivātakavacas, and likewise the Bāleya hosts.
And all the sons of Bāṇa were renowned as the Kālakhañjas;
Vṛtra, Vṛtta, and his hosts, as well as others of great strength.
O best of Brahmins, as that army was roaring, a great momentum then arose from it,
like the mighty surge of the ocean king toward the shore.
Mixed with the abundant lion-roars accompanied by the sound of musical instruments, along with the clatter of chariot-rims, the neighing of horses, and the trumpeting of elephants—
that tumultuous noise, O Vyāsa, filled the three worlds.
For even the gods, though well-prepared and established with every effort, [are unable to prevail].
With eyes long and copper-red with rage, they received those Daityas;
and as they were being struck down on all sides with swords and *śataghnī* weapons,
the sky then became variegated like it were filled with meteors.
O best of sages, heads pierced and severed by arrows indeed fall upon the earth like ripe fruits from palm trees,
adorned with crowns, necklaces, armlets, and radiant waist-bands.
With gold coins, fine silk garments, bracelets, rings, and earrings; || 18 ||
With elephant-ornaments, hair-combs, and ivory-handled fans;
with yak-tail whisks, umbrellas, and jewels as well.
With divine golden turbans and highly radiant armor,
and with heads, feet, hands, and faces of great splendor.
With goads, blankets, and yokes shining with gold,
the night of battle there shone like another sky filled with stars.
"Stay! Stay! Where are you going? There is truly no escape for you today!
I am standing here; strike me! I have no fear; stay before me!
"Why do you roar vainly in the sky like clouds in autumn?"
"Quickly show your prowess through action; today your roaring has been rendered fruitless.
You fool, you do not strike in this manner; do not look about, but stand firm!
Stay, stay! Where will you go after killing my beloved son? || 23-24 ||
"I stand here; today I shall lead you to the abode of Yama.
Today, O lowest of gods, I shall inflict upon you that entire, most unbearable agony. (25)
"My arrows shall destroy you; stay, stay before me!
O lowest of Dānavas, I am a god; I am not afraid in battle.
Speaking thus, they fought like rutting great elephants.
Thousands of warriors there were intent on slaying one another. ||27||
Having thus addressed one another, they sent word to the place of sacrifice;
and all the Siddhas and Cāraṇas remained stationed in the sky. ||28||
They accomplish their goals, they sport, and they roar like clouds;
"This Dānava here, my husband, has been slain in battle by me. (29)
"This god is your husband; do not set your heart on another.
Why are you thus possessed by greed? Why do you examine one superior man after another? (8.83.30)
"There is no taking by force here; read the document, do not be hasty!
Why is your mind dissatisfied? Be content, O beautiful one! (3.1)
"This portion has been granted to you by the gods; take it and go to your home.
Thus do the apsarases speak here, and they laugh as well.
When the warriors were slain in battle, they likewise engaged in quarrels;
their sweet, bird-like chatter was mingled with the sound of their girdles and bracelets.
Hearing that [noise] again and again, those warriors fought on, free from fear.
Leaping and bursting forth, they made all the directions resound. ||34||

That battle shone forth, resounding with the trumpeting of elephants and the leaping of those incensed by it, echoing with the roars of lions, instilling fear in gods and dānavas, and bringing an end to life.
Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Battle," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: At that time, that foremost sacrifice of battle took place there for the sake of the kingdom.
There, the powerful god Sahasrākṣa himself was the sacrificer. ||1||
The lord of the gods, together with the deities, is considered his *kuśa* grass;
his arrows are regarded as various weapons, and the *sruva* ladles are those by which the oblation is offered.
The vital breaths are declared to be the oblation, and the fire is Death of great splendor.
The mantras were his divine weapons, and the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) were his heads.
Soma was the victory there, and the Rudras became the Adhvaryu priests;
the Ādityas were the Bahvṛcas, and the Vasus performed the office of the Hotṛ.
Brahmā himself was present there as the god Bṛhaspati, while the two Aśvins performed the duties of the Śāmitra; thus did the sacrifice proceed.
The Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa, along with his followers, became the sacrificial animal there;
thus did that sacrifice of the Daityas shine forth, O Lord of the Cool Season.
The performer of sacrifices, Hiraṇyākṣa, became the leader of the Daityas and Dānavas;
Vipracitti was the Hotṛ priest, and the Dānavas were the Prasthātṛs.
Udgātṛ was Prahlāda, Śukra was Brahmā of noble vows,
and the thousand-eyed Indra was the sacrificial animal;
thus did that imperishable one perform the sacrifice while that great and terrifying sacrifice was proceeding.
Indra approached the exceedingly powerful Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa.
The mighty Vāyu quickly approached Vipracitti;
Aṃśa became entangled with Saṃvara, as did Bhaga with Bala;
Pūṣan was joined with Virocana, and Mitra with Bali.
Varuṇa was with Bāṇa, Yama with Andhaka;
Ilvala was with Jayanta, and the Moon with Maya;
Rāhu was with Ahirbudhnya, and the Kāpālin with Śataketu. || 1.1–1.2 ||
Ajaikapād fought Kālanemi, Jvara fought with Kārtasvana,
Aryaman with Prahlāda, and Dhara with Anuhlāda.
Dhruva was joined with Hrada, and other mighty warriors were likewise joined with others; then the exceedingly powerful Hiraṇyākṣa, having firmly drawn Indra’s bow,
pierced the elephant in the region of its frontal globe with a single arrow.
He struck the Lord of the Gods in the region of the collarbone with five arrows,
pierced him in the forehead with six, and again struck the elephant with seven.
Pierced by those arrows, that elephant shone as it flowed with blood.
Streaming with red chalk water, he was like a white king of mountains.
Then Śakra, enraged, struck him on the cheek with his hundred-jointed thunderbolt,
O Vyāsa, and let out a roar.
That lord of the Daityas regarded the blow of the thunderbolt as a powerful strike of flowers.
Remaining unperturbed, the powerful one struck Śakra himself along with his elephant.
The elephant, pierced by him, appeared with blood flowing from its wounds;
it blazed up in anger like a fire fed with oblations, and it roared.
Exerting great speed and urged on by the goad,
he quickly seized Hiraṇyākṣa’s chariot by its pole.
Seizing him, that best of elephants tossed him up and hurled him away,
just as the white-eared Indra, having lifted a cloud-covered peak of Mount Meru, hurls it down.
Having traveled for a moment with great speed, that excellent chariot shone as it fell.
O best of sages, just as the sun was formerly struck by Svarbhānu along with his chariot,
so too did a swift elephant approach the chariot of Hiraṇyākṣa, which stood firmly upon the ground there, desiring to seize it.
With his trunk extended and his eyes, ears, and tail held rigid,
the elephant charged with speed like Garuḍa toward a serpent.
Beholding him rushing forward with such velocity, the best of the Asuras—
Then he bore him through the sky, like Garuḍa bearing a serpent.
The elephant likewise followed that revolving circle, wandering with its gaze, ears, and tail motionless, while its trunk was extended. ||26||
A cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from both armies, and cries of "Excellent! Excellent! were likewise heard; yet then, the hosts of gods and daityas became as silent once more.
"Excellent, O Daitya! and "O Hiraṇyākṣa!"—thus did others cry out as that lord of the hosts of gods shone while wandering upon the shoulder of his elephant.
Like a fierce buffalo mounted upon the lord of mountains, the great asura Hiraṇyākṣa, the king of the Daityas, whirled around three times. ||29||
Having driven away the elephant like a swift wind, the immensely powerful lord of the Daityas stood upon his chariot;
and fighting with his bow firmly drawn,
he surrounded the king of the gods on all sides with sharp arrows.
O Vyāsa, he was then struck by those arrows in his vital organs and joints;
with a thunderbolt-like weapon, he shattered his armor into a hundred pieces and cut through all the harnesses of the horses as well. ||3.1–3.2||
The powerful Śakra, as if laughing, cut the reins held in the charioteer's hand and the golden whip into many pieces. || 33 ||
Then his horses, their traces severed, bolted away at their own will;
Hiraṇyākṣa, however, leaped down and struck them with his mace.
With his sword, that great asura [struck] both the elephant and the lord of the gods;
by that blow, the elephant abandoned that best of chariots.
O Vyāsa, discharging excrement and urine, that powerful one then fled away,
crushing the mountain and causing the best of gods to whirl about.
Even when struck by the sword, the mighty King of the Gods felt no pain in the battle, nor did he suffer...
[37] That one of great strength, though struck by the lord of the Dānavas’ elephant, which was exuding the scent of flowing ichor, remained unharmed.
Unable to endure it, he set forth, having been struck down in battle by the crushing Hiraṇyanetra.
Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the section on the battle.
Sanatkumāra said:
Vipracitti, the master of great illusion, [assailed] Vāyu with many swift arrows.
The son of Danu covered him with arrows, just as a cloud-giver covers the earth with rain. ||1||
Then, O Vyāsa, with his bow drawn into a circle and covering [the sky], he discharged sharp-pointed arrows like a swarm of locusts or like the ocean [sending forth its spray]. ||2||
Just as rainfalls come from clouds and the like, just as moonlight comes from the moon, just as rays come from the sun, and just as snow comes from the Snowy Mountain (Himavat). //3//
Thus, those masses of arrows issued forth from the bow drawn into a circle by Vipracitti;
as those arrows were falling, seeking to shroud the sun, the powerful one [Vālin]—
The Blessed One, Anila, struck down the asuras with great speed.
By those arrows, many of that Daitya's Dānavas were slain;
mangled, they groaned upon the earth like men dwelling in hell.
Seeing them thus slain, the great asura Vipracitti leaped down from Vāyu’s chariot and fought a hand-to-hand struggle.
As he remained intent on battle, the strength of Vāyu increased;
and the gods thought that the son of Danu had been subdued.
Then, springing up with great speed, the mighty Hiraṇyākṣa struck Pavana firmly on the cheek with his mace. By that powerful blow from Hiraṇyākṣa...
...and something else entirely; from that very [source], he [obtained] the gift. 8.85.10.
Having abandoned them, the one of great strength quickly went to another land;
O best of sages, this was also the case for Aṃśa and Saṃvara. 11.
A terrible battle ensued, increasing the delight of the spectators,
as the mighty Saṃvara swiftly fell upon Aṃśu.
Displaying his great agility, he properly severed the golden banner;
having split the bow into five pieces, he sent it indeed to the abode of Yama.
Then he struck off the head of that charioteer from his body so that it fell to the ground;
furthermore, he pierced him with sixty-four arrows.
That Dānava, having quickly entered into a terrible and dark illusion,
[assailed him] with rocks, thunderbolts, maces, and even iron clubs.
O Vyāsa, on the field of battle, he struck down the god Aṃśa along with his chariot using shields, swords, slings, and iron clubs.
Beholding that great terror being unleashed on all sides,
the bewildered Aṃśa abandoned the battle and fled elsewhere out of fear.
Having summoned his strength, Bhaga, standing in a chariot that thundered like a cloud, cried out "Stay! Stay! to that Daitya and pierced him with a feathered shaft.
Taking up an arrow, that powerful great chariot-warrior of the asuras swiftly pierced Bhaga in the palm of his hand and let out a roar.
Then, having approached him, as if laughing by means of his illusory power,
he struck him on the chest with his foot and returned once more to his own chariot.
Seeing his agility, heroism, lack of confusion, and valor, all the gods and asuras honored him, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent! (21)
Then Bhaga, overcome with shame, was struck by that foot;
indeed, he destroyed his chariot along with its charioteer with the mace.
Having then reduced him to nothing but a name, he roared like a thundercloud;
Bala, meanwhile, abandoned his chariot, which had been crushed along with its horses.
Standing on the ground, the powerful one severed Bhaga’s divine bow;
then he struck him in the forehead with a stone-tipped arrow.
Furthermore, O Vyāsa, he pierced his two hands with seven arrows;
and as he was grasping his bow, he cut through his back with force.
Furthermore, Bhaga then took yet another and yet another from him.
The pestle was the root of Time (Kālamūla), possessing the brilliance of a fire that destroys all things. ||26||
Having said, "You are slain," he hurled that club which destroys strength.
As that mace came flying toward him, Bala, the preeminent among the Dānavas, [seized it]. (27)
Nandin paralyzed him with arrows, just as one might paralyze death itself for oneself; then, perceiving that his club was thwarted, that Asura once again—
With the tip of his bow, the powerful one struck him on the head;
then, seizing the chariot along with its driver by the pole, he [dragged it] again.
Like the wind casting a mountain into the ocean,
the god Pūṣan hurled Virocana away with many swift arrows.
Enraged in the battle, he pierced him,
and he in turn pierced him back with seven sharpened arrows that pierce the vital organs.
Then the powerful Pūṣan, enraged, drew back his great bow and released a terrible, life-ending shaft that possessed the brilliance of the sun at the end of an eon;
aiming it at the enemy, he cried out, "You are slain! (33).
As he rushed forward, roaring in many ways and illuminating all directions, vomiting forth meteors and sparks, and leaping with great speed toward his enemies; ||| 34 ||
And that great lord of the asuras, having leaped down and seen him shining with a luster equal to the sun,
and deeming him irresistible, abandoned his own chariot and, entering the sky, stood there.

Having reduced that charioteer, his great chariot, and his excellent all-pervading weapons to ashes in an instant—just as fire consumes its fuel—he departed for the divine sky in an invisible form. 36.
Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, "The Battle," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that Dānava Virocana, whose chariot had been burnt, remained stationed in the sky.
Quickly drawing his sword, he [discharged] sharp arrows at Pūṣan.
The valiant one cut down all those who were rushing toward him and even his own bow;
then he struck him again on the head with a sword.
By that well-dealt blow, his head streaming with blood, he quickly fell upon the seat of the chariot like a banner whose festival has ended. ||3||
Seizing him as he fell, that mighty lord of the Daityas quickly hurled the king of the gods while roaring like a cloud.
Mitra pierced Bali in the region of the collarbone with three arrows;
Bali, with a single broad-headed shaft (bhalla), severed his bow. ||5||
Then he struck him again in the heart with another [arrow];
stunned and nearly dead, he sank down upon the seat of his chariot.
O Vyāsa, the charioteer then drove away that dejected man who had approached out of fear of death; thereupon, the Daityas cried out in lamentation.
Varuṇa pierced Bāṇa with a hundred arrows;
then the powerful Bāṇa [pierced him] with five hundred bows.
Drawing them back simultaneously, the enraged one discharged as many arrows;
then Varuṇa, with great agility, struck them down even as they were falling upon him. ||9||
Having divided each arrow into five parts,
Varuṇa, the powerful one, smiling, pierced all of his bows with five shafts.
He cut it with sharp arrows, and that was like a marvel;
then the demon, his bow being severed, hurled a mace at him.
Seeing that mace shattered, the powerful one then created more maces;
yet, being then occupied with one, he did not perceive those other maces.
And all those [arrows], without being pierced, fell upon him;
one, having crushed his crown, fell to the surface of the earth.
And some let fall their terrible bows from the grasp of their hands.
A certain woman hurled a firm, divine banner onto the surface of the earth.
Then one [goddess] struck the chariot and swallowed the dust; others struck those maces upon his chest, thighs, belly, and hips.
Falling down, most terrible and causing great fear, they brought him intense suffering;
thus was he deprived of his chariot by that wise one with great difficulty.
Varuṇa, having released him, went to another part of the battlefield;
Yama, having encountered Andhaka, urged him on, saying, "Stay! Stay! || 17 ||
Then he hurled a staff at his chariot from there.
Having crushed his chariot into hundreds of thousands of pieces, he [proceeded]. ||18||
Yama returned once more and stationed himself there just as before;
the mighty Andhaka also, casting off his chariot, stood with mace in hand.
He rushed toward Yama, emitting fire as if out of rage;
as he was charging with speed, Yama himself, the King of the Ancestors, [confronted him].
With his very staff, Yama reduced the fierce mace to ashes;
then, laughing, he spoke forcefully to him.
That abode which belonged to you has been destroyed by me;
now, having purified you as well, I shall lead you today back to my own abode. 22.
For I am the Lord, the cause of death for the entire world;
having encountered enmity with me, where will you find release from life at the end?
Today I shall slay you; let the world be made very firm.
"Or rather, O Andhaka, today he has gone to bondage, and previously [you] went to my city;
you shall see all these enemies of the gods right there before you. (24)
Sanatkumāra said: Then, as Yama was speaking thus, the fearless Dānava Andhaka, his eyes blazing with fire from rage, spoke angrily to him.
I am the proud Andhaka, son of Hiraṇyākṣa, the destroyer of the gods;
endowed with the power of great yoga, I am no ordinary Dānava.
Having cut portions of flesh from his limbs and other parts, each weighing one karṣa,
he offered them into the fire for eight hundred and five years.
Satisfied, Brahmā granted me eternal and auspicious immortality;
I am that very one known by the name Mahāsattva, the subduer of death—of this there is no doubt. (28)
You have not brought about my death, like a hare for a lion in the forest;
rather, I shall be the cause of your death—of this there is no doubt. (29)
"Today, by slaying you, a wicked soul who causes terror to all the worlds, I shall bring about the welfare of the three realms; such is my resolve. (8.86.30)
"You have always been an enemy to the gods, intent on their displeasure;
yet, once you are slain, you will become dear to them today. (31)
For by taking the lives of living beings, you have never before encountered any great being; therefore, you are always free from fear. (32)
Terrified by fear of you, the gods are unable to slay you;
therefore, they desire the nectar and other such things, and they worship you constantly.
If you, the cruel one, are slain today, they too will undoubtedly feel no such joy at the death of the gods as they would if you were immortal. (34)
Today, at the end of my body, I shall utterly destroy my pride, my arrogance, and even the greatness of my yoga, along with my very life-breaths.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus threatened by the lord of the asuras, the son of the Sun struck that tiger among asuras on the head with his staff.
And Kāla struck him in the heart with his very hand,
while Mṛtyu swiftly struck him on the head with a thunderbolt.
And Yama cast a terrible noose around his neck;
with a mace, he struck him on the cheek as if with a heavy iron bar.
Struck by those unerring weapons and missiles, the demon Andhaka was not afflicted with pain, just as one might be when showered with flowers.
Neither nooses, nor the staff, nor even the iron bar bind him;
furthermore, other intense sufferings do not lead to his pain.
Then a great shout was raised by all the Dānavas in every direction; musical instruments were sounded, and Andhaka rejoiced exceedingly. 41.
Impelled by their shouts of joy and his own intoxicating prowess, he [advanced].
O Vyāsa, having roared like a cloud, he rushed toward Yama himself.
Having gone there with great speed, although he was being struck by the servants,
he of immense velocity struck Yama on the chest with his fist.
And again, he struck the buffalo on its head with his foot;
both of them, being overwhelmed, wandered there for a short distance. 44.
O best of sages, having abandoned Andhaka, they both departed quickly;
then Jayanta, reaching Celvala, pierced him with ten arrows.
Elvala quickly cut down his banner adorned with jewels,
as well as the harnesses of the horses and his golden whip.
Without their traces, his horses, becoming agitated, abandoned the chariot;
neighing and leaping away, they departed, and he became deprived of his chariot.
Abandoning his chariot, the powerful son of Śakra stood upon the ground and struck down Ilvala’s horses, charioteer, and banner. ||48||
Then both of them, having been deprived of their chariots, were indeed intent on conquering one another.
At that time, they would have pierced him with sharp arrows from their bows. ||49||
Having warded off each other's arrows and having countered weapon with weapon, the two roared like two oceans.
Then the glorious son of Śakra, having found that opportunity,
cut his bow with a crescent-headed arrow and roared again and again.
That Daitya, his bow shattered, whirled a sword with the brilliance of blazing fire and hurled it; [Viṣṇu] then cut that down as well.
Having seized another's fallen mace, adorned with gold,
he whirled it and hurled it, then fled away with great speed.
Just as the son of Diti cut that terrible mace with straight-jointed arrows,
he [Indra] likewise cut his bow.
Then, just as that son of Aditi seized his sword,
the Daitya struck him on the chest with his left foot.
That mighty Jayanta seized his very foot and whirled him around,
roaring like a thundercloud.
Then a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the host of asuras, as they cried out, "Go! Save the lord of the Daityas, Ilvala, quickly! (57)
The gods uttered lion-roars and the sounds of conchs were abundant; musical instruments were played, and cries of "Excellent! Excellent! arose.
Then Jayanta, the powerful son of Vidhātṛ, whirled the lord of the Daityas around like a wheel, roaring like the clouds at the end of an eon.

Then Hiraṇyākṣa himself, as well as Śumbha, Bala, Bāṇa, Vipracitti, Śambara, and Virocana; those Daityas known as the Kālakeyas, the Paulomas, and the sons of Siṃhikā— 8.86.60. Then Hiraṇyākṣa himself, as well as Śumbha, Bala, Bāṇa, Vipracitti, Śambara, and Virocana; those Daityas known as the Kālakeyas, the Paulomas, and the sons of Siṃhikā—
And the Nivātakavacas surrounded him on all sides.
He [was struck] by them with those arrows, maces, iron clubs, and long javelins.
And he was struck violently with many other various weapons.
Being struck by him, that god Jayanta, the son of Śakra,
cast him onto the path of Hiraṇyākṣa and fled toward where the deities were.
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Battle," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Maya, overwhelmed by rage, tormented the divine Moon.
Roaring like a thundercloud, he [assailed him] with arrows resembling venomous serpents. ||1||
As he was shooting arrows here and there, Candra, as if laughing,
split each one into seven pieces and pierced Maya with five arrows.
Then he pierced him in the forehead with a spotted arrow;
and the god laughed again, putting him to shame.
While he was laughing, that highly provoked man quickly pierced him deeply in the forehead with a heron-feathered arrow, just as an obstacle strikes one who is firm in his vows.
Then the god, letting out a roar, cut down his banner and sent his wheel-protectors to the abode of Yama with his swords.
Seeing that fickleness of his, Maya, the best of the Dānavas,
then resorted to divine illusion and became Rāhu.
Having become Rāhu, that lord of the Daityas rushed toward the Lord of the Gods, who bears the mark of the hare,
just as Rāhu [once] did with a chariot thundering like a cloud.
Then that god, born of the nectar of immortality, recognized that illusion.
He indeed struck him, who stood in the sky as if at a non-junction, with three arrows.
That great asura, a master of great illusion, warded off those arrows by means of his own magic power and rushed toward the cool-rayed moon.
Then the Daitya, seizing his divine chariot of great splendor which was drawn by Nāgas, struck it against the pole and let out a roar.
Having approached Rāhu, the planet of the moon,
Ahirbudhnya pierced him with five arrows and struck down his banner.
Leaping from his chariot, the imperishable one struck him with his fearsome mace, completely pulverizing his bow, banner, and horses.
Greatly agitated, he seized the blazing thunderbolt with its hundred bells, like the bride of Death; he grasped it as Antaka seizes the noose of Death.
Whirling that fierce weapon, which resembled the staff of Yama,
he forcefully hurled it toward Rāhu, just as the king of clouds hurls lightning.
Blazing like a great meteor and as radiant as a thunderbolt from a cloud,
it fell upon Rāhu's head like a thunderbolt upon a mountain peak.
Then, by that blow, he did not feel any pain;
laughing heartily, the exceedingly powerful Rāhu exerted great speed.
Enraged at Ahirbudhnya like the king of birds toward the serpents,
the Blessed One, the best of gods, beheld him as he was rushing forward.
He departed along a path other than his own, just like a serpent;
and the heroic Śataketu followed him in a chariot that thundered like a cloud.
Enraged, he rushed forward in battle and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
As he charged, the wearer of skulls pierced his heart with heron-feathered arrows.
Like a thunderbolt hurled against a lofty mountain peak,
that best of grahas had his heart shattered by Rudra.
Confused, he fell upon his own chariot like the lofty banner of Indra;
then a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the Daityas, and they cried out, "Seize him! Seize him! (21).
"Excellent! Excellent! the gods cried out like thunderclouds;
then Andhaka, Hiraṇyākṣa, Vipracitti, and Virocana [spoke].
Śambara, Celvala, Bāṇa, and Bali,
as well as the Kālakeyas along with the Paulomas and the Nivātakavacas—
many other Daityas likewise surrounded that Rudra.
With those arrows, maces, clubs, *prāsa* spears, and *tomara* javelins, [they struck]. 24.
They obstructed that god, threatening him again and again.
Being struck by those many [demons], O best of sages, the god moved away with speed from the vicinity of the enemies of the gods. 25.
Ajaikapād challenged the lord of the Daityas, Kālanemi, who was armed with a mace and irresistible with his club, just as Viṣṇu once challenged the powerful Madhu. 26.
Those two of great strength, skilled in combat and with maces in hand, moved in circles,
intent on each other's defeat like two planets.
But Kālanemi, filled with rage, took up a mace adorned with gold,
which had a hundred bells and a loud laugh-like sound, and was as wondrous as the tongue of Death.
Having whirled him around repeatedly while bellowing like a bull, the Daitya hurled him toward Rudra, as Skanda hurls his spear at a mountain. 29.
Like a thunderbolt released by Śakra descending upon a mountain,
or like a mighty flash of lightning, that Rudra of terrifying prowess [encountered it].
Śveta outstripped him with speed, as if deceiving Death himself who had arrived;
and Rudra, the best among strikers, cried out, "Stay! Stay! [31]
Having whirled his terrible mace, he brought it down upon the Daitya;
by that blazing mace of fearsome form, the Daitya [was struck]. (32)
Struck on the head, he saw all the directions as yellow;
then the Daitya, once again whirling his mace with great force, [attacked]. (33)
Having displayed various *maṇḍalas*, the one of great strength struck Ajaikapāda on the shoulder with his mace.
And he too, struck by him like a mountain by a thunderbolt, entered the earth afflicted with pain; that was truly like a marvel. (35)
Rising up with speed, the mighty and enraged Rudra moved counter-clockwise, circling the Daitya from his left side within the mandala.
Having whirled his mace once more, he brought it down upon the Daitya;
that mighty Daitya, by that blow, spun around three times. ||37||
Having steadied himself once more with his mace, he struck Rudra in the belly.
Struck by that mace, he was like a mountain shaken by the wind. ||38||
He fell to the ground with great force, like the mountain Śataśṛṅga in ancient times;
then, approaching him as he lay fallen, [the Lord] seized the one of noble vows by the foot.
Having whirled it around, he hurled it; yet that [weapon], though fierce like the fever of gold (Kārtasvana), remained ineffective against Rudra, the best among strikers, for he was immortal.
He struck him simultaneously on both breasts with ten sharp, broad-headed arrows.
And Kārtasvana, with an arrow, cut his radiant bow into many pieces,
and then pierced him again with feathered shafts.
Rudra, too, having swiftly whirled his staff which accomplishes all purposes, hurled it toward Kārtasvana’s chariot.
Like a cloud striking a mountain with rain, he struck him— who resembled the fire at the end of an eon and possessed the brilliance of a hundred suns and fire— with a multitude of arrows.
Being struck by them, Daṇḍa blazed up even more intensely like a fire kindled by oblations,
and he rushed forward with great speed.
But Kārtasvana, knowing that his rod was unimpeded, [acted].
Abandoning the chariot with speed, the powerful one stood in the sky. 45.
And the staff, having approached the chariot along with the horse, the driver,
the banner, and the pennon, reduced them all to ashes and departed once more.
As long as the staff had not yet fallen upon him, the powerful Kārttikeya pursued Rudra on his chariot and assailed him with arrows. 47.
Having cut down his banner and bow, as well as the harnesses of his horses,
he deprived Jvara of his chariot and struck him on the head with a sword.
His soul overwhelmed by the fear of being struck by the sword, that Rudra abandoned the assembly of his enemies and quickly fled elsewhere on foot, O best of sages. 49.
His mind was perverted by the destruction of his own kindred, yet he possessed the luster of red sandalwood ointment.
Leaving behind that enemy of preeminent prowess, they fled in all directions with their divine forces.
Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Battle," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Aryaman [struck] Prahlāda, the bull among the Daityas, with many arrows.
He struck the terrible chariot and shattered its banner.
The heroic Prahlāda, too, having abandoned his excellent chariot, fled like Rāhu at the appointed time flees from the sun that dispels the darkness. ||2||
And as his enemy rushed forward with speed, bewildered, Aryaman struck him with many arrows, just as a cloud strikes a mountain with rain. ||3||
Without even counting the arrows, the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu rushed forward with speed,
impelled by anger, pride, and arrogance.
Seizing the pole of his gold-adorned chariot along with the charioteer,
he then struck it out of joy and let out a roar.
Anuhrāda, having reached Dhara, was pierced by him in the middle of the chest;
drawing his sword with speed, he approached Dhara's chariot.
Having severed his banner, his horses, his charioteer, and even his bow, and having placed him upon his shoulder, he returned once more to his own chariot.
By that deed, Dharā became severely oppressed by the Daitya;
and in this same way, other mighty gods were [afflicted] by other lords of the Daityas.
Some were conquered, some were threatened, and yet others stood ready for battle once more;
then a tumultuous conflict ensued between the gods and the dānavas.
The battle between those desiring to conquer one another brought fear to the timid;
then there arose kettledrums, conchs, and paṭahas, as well as sekyas and puṣkalas.
O Vyāsa, thousands of jharjharī drums, pepukas, ḍiṇḍimas, and cow-horn trumpets were sounded by both sides in the army. 11.
Then [there was a river] with a flowing torrent of blood, where banners and flags were the trees,
and it abounded with elephants and horses as its crocodiles, while chariots were its prominent tortoises.
Abounding with hair-foam, with bowstrings for its cords, with hissing weapons for its frogs, and with silken garments and parasols for its froth; 13.
And the Uṣṇīṣavarahaṃsā, as well as Karapādaśiropalā.
Her necklace and armlets are like grains of sand, and her crown is a full-blown lotus.
A terrible river, consisting of the mud of fat, blood, and phlegm, and destroying life and vitality, began to flow, carrying away elephants, horses, and chariots. (15)
In that [river], the rākṣasas bathe, drink, and take their pleasure;
they also dance in various ways, inspiring fear in those who are timid. (16)
Vultures, jackals, dogs, cats, and crows;
They sported while devouring eyes, hands, feet, and entrails.
"This is my elephant's foot; this is my bandage of fat;
this is my bright trunk; and this is my arm, which bestows blood. (18)
"This is mine, this is not yours; take it, look!"—thus did those cruel flesh-eaters engage in quarreling there. (19)
Having abandoned their slain bodies there, other great chariot-warriors departed for the assembly hall of Brahmā in celestial chariots crowded with women.
Others, performers of evil deeds, being struck by those blinded by rage, fall into a terrible hell, crying out again and again. (21)
Some, making a piteous sound, were afflicted by [the god of] love.
Men die in battle by the hundreds and by the thousands. ||22||
Some were biting at grass, while others cried out, "O brother! O son! Thus the people, weeping and terrified, gave up their lives with great difficulty. (23)
Some great chariot-warriors among the gods and asuras,
their lips bitten together and their vital organs pierced by arrows, fell to the earth like trees.
Inauspicious jackals howled, and the Rākṣasas let out loud bursts of laughter;
likewise, men, elephants, and horses uttered cries of distress.
There were lion-roars from the brave, the loud sounds of arms being brandished,
the twanging of drawn bows, and the clamor of musical instruments.
Then Indra, Dhaneśa, Yama, and the powerful Kāla, as well as Varuṇa, the Maruts, and all the Viśvedevas, [arrived]. ||27||
Mitra, Jayanta, Bhaga, Pūṣan, and Aryaman, as well as Rudra in the form of Kāpālin and the Vasus of great strength. ||28||
Nāsatya, Dasra, and the Pṛśnis, the best of gods—these and other eminent deities, mighty of arm. (29)
The powerful [gods] exerted their force against the strength of the Dānavas,
roaring like oceans or like fires at the end of a Yuga.
Like tempests out of season, like great mountains immovable, like bulls bellowing, and like massive elephants; ||31||
They were like seizing crocodiles, like sharks tearing [apart],
like raining clouds, and like roaring lions.
They all, with great speed, checked the entire force of the Dānavas.

That army of the Danus and Danavas, its momentum shattered by Devavega, though still exerting itself, became supportless and utterly overwhelmed, like a blade of grass caught in the mouth of a fire. 33.
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Battle," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
As they were being driven by that force, broken and once again suffering...
For the sake of protection, Hiraṇyākṣa, whose eyes were exceedingly blazing, seized his position.
And Andhaka, the great illusionist, and his brothers who were equal to him,
[led] a hundred thousand chariots, all of whom were non-retreating.
And Prahlāda, the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, together with his brother;
and Vipracitti, together with his brother and those sons of Siṃhika.
Crying out, "Seize him! Seize him!", they then advanced against the gods;
a most terrible battle then ensued between them.
Just as Indra, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Pūṣan [restrain] crocodiles in a riverbed or elephants in the forest, they held back Hiraṇyākṣa.
Having come together, they struck all their vital points with sharp arrows;
indeed, they shattered the variegated bows of those gods who were discharging them.
The radiant lord of the Daityas, by the power of his illusion, brought them to a standstill;
those [weapons] were then rendered motionless by the Daitya through his magic.
They did not bow as they had before, and so they became truly agitated;
that Daitya, a master of great illusion, then roared with a sound like the thundering of clouds.
He bound their limbs on all sides with the illusory power of his weapons;
and seeing those mighty ones thus bound and rendered incapable of action, [he spoke].
The charioteers quickly bore them away from that field of battle with their vehicles.
Then Kāla, Yama, Dhaneśa, and Mitra likewise [departed].
Varuṇa, all the Vasus, and the two mighty Aśvins, with weapons raised and filled with wrath, stood there crying out, "Stay! Stay! (11).
They rushed with speed toward the great asura Hiraṇyākṣa;
as they were attacking him in battle, that Daitya was overwhelmed with rage.
In the battle, he pierced the armor of all of them with his sharp arrows;
their armor shattered, they all had faces blazing with rage. ||13||
Then they indeed discharged their foremost weapons, which were likewise irresistible.
Yama cast his staff at him, and likewise did Kāla... ||14||
Dhaneśa [Kubera] took a terrible thunderbolt, Varuṇa a noose, Bhaga a fearsome mace, and the other gods likewise took their various weapons. ||15||
That Daitya, his soul undaunted, even as he laughed, paralyzed them with arrows that pierce the vital organs,
just as Bhava paralyzed the hand of Śakra.
Then, the great chariot-warriors among the Dānavas, being delighted, offered shouts of "Well done!
and honored the great Asura Hiraṇyākṣa.
Others said: "This is no wonder for the son of Diti in battle—for he was begotten by Kaśyapa, as were we and our lord. (18)
Others let out lion-roars and loud shouts with their arms; being delighted, they likewise sounded all kinds of musical instruments.
Thus, in that great battle, many words of praise were heard from the Dānavas as they were greatly delighted, O son of Parāśara.
Perceiving their great joy and that defeat of the gods at that time,
Vāyu, who moves through all living beings, rushed toward the asuras.
That wind-god [Prabhajana] was on a chariot measuring a thousand nalvas,
equipped with banners on all sides and garlanded with hundreds of flags.
Suddenly, it came into view, making a great noise as it was restrained with effort by the charioteers through its speed, filling all the directions.
Then, remaining unperturbed, he struck the king of the Daityas with five sharp arrows.
Having brought it from that place a yojana away, he quickly released it.
Then Andhaka struck with sixty arrows, and Vipracitti with seven.
Having pierced [them] with fifty, and again with seven by seven. ||25||
At that very moment, he pierced all the Daityas and Dānavas,
as well as the sons of Puloman and the Nivātakavacas.
Pierced by him with many arrows, those foremost of asuras were scattered in all directions and remained at a distance of a yojana apart.
And whatever maces, clubs, and spears they released,
the blessed Vāyu caused them all to fall upon the Dānavas.
Struck and being struck violently by the weapons discharged by themselves,
they fled in all directions, uttering cries of distress.
That wind of great velocity shattered the best of chariots,
and furthermore, it filled their eyes with a shower of dust.
Then, terrified by fear, they did not discharge their arrows; likewise, they did not employ other weapons, but remained standing there, joining their palms in supplication. ||31||
Having observed that deed of his, the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa, the son of Diti, spoke to all the Dānavas in reproach: ||32||
"Fie on all your strength, O Daityas! Fie on your pride! Fie on your prowess!
Abandoning the battle without agitation, go and attend to the duties of women!"
"You fools, who stood in the midst of battle while life still remained, have been shattered by a single gust of wind; fie upon that counsel you previously gave! (34)
Or rather, as I have said: "You are children, exhausted by the fatigue of passion. (7)
That is not so; there is no doubt, for you have acted like children. || 35 ||
"All of you remain like children, guarding your own lives;
behold, I alone shall conquer this wind. (36)
Then that powerful and imperishable son of Diti, having become a mountain,
completely warded off that wind-force from all sides.
Having perceived that Anila had been warded off by Parvata, Andhaka leaped forward and bound him with the noose of his arms. (38)
Then that powerful Vāyu, bound by the noose of his arms,
swiftly seized Andhaka and leapt up into the sky.
As soon as he had risen up, seizing the Dānava Andhaka,
Rāhu swiftly brought down a most terrible mace upon his head;
and the exceedingly powerful Vipracitti likewise rushed at his feet.
Like a great crocodile seizing fish in the vast ocean, he seized him; by that powerful blow, he became overwhelmed and fell within the range of living beings.
With his hair entangled in the shoulder [of the demon], he was whirled around by Vipracitti;
as he was being spun about, he appeared with his necklaces, garlands, and garments slipping off. 42.
O best of sages, seeing it whirling like a blazing brand at night, the gods together with Indra were once again struck with wonder. 43.
The exceedingly swift Veghas rushed forward, crying out, "Seize him! Seize him!
But the Daitya Vipracitti [beheld] those enraged ones with their weapons raised. 44.
Beholding many [enemies] in the battle, the leader of the Dānava hosts roared like a cloud, repeatedly producing a terrifying sound like the wind. 45.
He hurled the thunderbolt at Śakra as if against a mountain;
and he too, having been struck by it, regained consciousness, O one of great strength. 46.
Having manifested his power, he stood before the Lord of the Gods with palms joined in reverence;
then Vāyu and all the gods, together with their followers, did likewise. ||47||
Grasping their excellent weapons, they rushed toward the lords of the Daityas;
a most terrible battle then ensued between them. 48.
Like proud lions with śarabhas in a solitary place, some there were struck down by a powerful blow and rendered unconscious. 49.
Crying out "Excellent! Excellent!", they cast off their lives after stretching their vital breaths upward;
others, endowed with great strength, rushed forward joyfully toward Indra.
Some of the best among the gods and dānavas protected the hero who was struck down by the enemy like a good son, even after they themselves had slain very many. ||51||
Some of the immensely powerful gods and daityas, having approached unarmed, reproached themselves for not being wounded by sharp weapons. (52)
Desiring a righteous battle, they laid down their weapons and fought;
many lords of the Daityas there, possessing terrible prowess, engaged in combat.
And those gods who are indeed not struck never strike [others] at any time; all the foot-soldiers there fight with foot-soldiers.
The battle proceeded thus: horsemen with horsemen, chariot-warriors with chariot-warriors, and likewise elephant-riders with elephant-riders.
Thus, indeed, the battle between those gods and the Dānavas continued for eight hundred years, being most terrifying.
Then the Daitya Mahāmāya, mounted upon an elephant with the splendor of a rain cloud,
bore a massive iron spear that possessed the brilliance of the fire at the end of an eon.
Virocana, who resembled a cloud dark as a cuckoo or collyrium, fled then toward the gods, as if they were arrows discharged from his left side. 58.
With his rutting elephant, whose mouth resounded with a tumultuous roar, he rushed toward the Lord of the Gods and cried out, "Stay! Stay! (59)
Then, as he was still falling, the Blessed Lord Pākaśāsana (Indra) struck him in the region of the collarbone with a terrible arrow, and [the demon] let out a roar.
Having endured that blow, that Daitya of terrifying prowess then pierced his [the opponent's] uplifted hand with a lance.
Then, from his hand which had been pierced by the lance, [he took] that which was adorned with gold.
That divine bow, possessing a radiance equal to a great thunderbolt, fell down.
Then, while he was thus distracted, the exceedingly powerful lord of the Daityas swiftly pierced his elephant in the region of the frontal globes with a lance.
He was shattered by that Daitya in the forest like an elephant in rut, who,
unrestrained and unchecked, gradually loses its strength.
Being thus slaughtered by the Daityas and Dānavas, those Ādityas, afflicted by fear, fled in all directions in every way. ||65||
Then conchs, kettledrums, and various other musical instruments were sounded,
and those esteemed by the Daityas and Dānavas let out lion-like roars.
That great army, protected by the gods, though its ranks were cut, pierced, and torn asunder by the elephant and further churned by the Daityas,
shone like the ocean lashed by Mount Mandara during the churning.
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Battle," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having beheld that divine army [surrounded] by the leaders of the Daitya and Dānava hosts...
O Vyāsa, they were being slaughtered violently, like deer by tigers in the forest. ||1||
The enemy of darkness, possessed of great splendor, Soma, the best among strikers;
he of sharp form and most cooling rays, with the Wind himself as his charioteer. ||2||
Both of them were properly clad in armor, both were holding their bows, and they had fastened their leather arm-guards and finger-protectors, as well as their quivers.
Equipped with swords and bells, and adorned with banners like two elephants,
both heroes of great prowess stood ready to fight the Daityas.
Soma, however, pierced the heart of the Daitya, the great Asura Hiraṇyākṣa, with ten sharp arrows that penetrate the vital organs. ||5||
With his heart pierced by Soma, that Daitya, though firmly exalted,
fell into a state of delusion, O Vyāsa, like Mount Krauñca struck by a spear.
Having observed him thus, the charioteer drove away the chariot together with the Asura from the Great Illusionist (Mahāmāya), just as treasures depart from the Lord of Wealth (Dhaneśa).
Then there arose a cry of "Alas! from the Daityas, and "Excellent! Excellent! from the deities;
"Seize him! Seize him! was shouted by the Daityas, and "Do not seize him! by the deities.
Then kettledrums, conchs, small drums, and cow-horns were sounded by the gods, indeed, to arouse joy and passion.
Then Andhaka and Tāra, Tāraka and Namuci, Vipracitti and Śambara, and the Dānava Mahāmāya— ||8.90.10||
Dhundhu, Kārtasvana, and the exceedingly powerful Rāhu;
Śataketu, Śatāvarta, Puloman, and likewise Vilva. (11)
Vātāpi, Kālanemi, Śatāvarta, Śatodara, Mahāpārśva, Andhaka, Musuṇḍa, and Suṇḍha. ||12||
Durloma, Vakrabandha, Viroma, Rodha, Mārīca, Subāhu, and Śvetakuṇḍali. ||13||
Vṛṣaparvan, Atikāya, Śarabha, and Siṃha; Narāntaka, Devahana, and he who is Yajñahana. (14)
The two Daityas Sunda and Nisunda, as well as Śakratāpana, Prahlāda, Anuhrāda, Śini, and Bāṣkala. (15)
Virocana, Bali, Bāṇa, and the exceedingly powerful Vātāśva;
then Maya, Tārakākṣa, Vidyunmālī, and Prabhākara. ||16||
Dundubhi and Mahiṣa, Ariṣṭa and Riṣṭa, Keśin and Dhenuka, as well as Ajaka and Vyaṃsa. ||17||
Likewise, there were Gaganamūrdhan and the Dānava Asiloman; also Sūcīloman, Tuhuṇḍa, Huṇḍa, and Paratāpana. ||18||
Hastin, Duryodhana, Vipāka, Pāka, Bala, Mura, Naraka, as well as Mūka and Indradamana. 19.
Aśvagrīva, Śambara, and likewise another, Kālasaṃvara;
Śālva, Śatabhuja, Drumas, and the Dānava Vyaṅghra. ||8.90.20||
Madhu and Kaiṭabha, as well as Mahāsaṃgara, the renowned Chāyāgraha, and the famous Seṃhikeyas; ||21||
All those celebrated sons of Bali known as the Hālāhalas, as well as all the sons of Maya and the Nivātakavacas; ||22||
The Paulomas, the Kālakeyas, and those who are the sons of Vipracitti—these and many others esteemed among the Daityas and Dānavas. (23)
All of them directed their speed toward the god Candra, like buffaloes [attacking] elephants, or as [beasts attack] a śarabha. ||24||

Just as obstacles [hinder] one who is striving, just as sensual desires [hinder] one intent on liberation, just as the objects of the senses [hinder] yoga, and just as harmful things [hinder] one who is suffering; ||25||
Just as serpents [assail] Garuḍa, or as bees [swarm upon] a tree, so did all those Dānavas, grasping their excellent weapons, [attack him]. ||26||
They rushed toward the cool-rayed god with the roar of great clouds;
as they were attacking, O Vyāsa, the enemy of darkness (the sun) seemed to laugh.
He cut down all the raised weapons with his arrows from every side;
then that god, filled with wrath, [struck] them all once again. ||28||
With sharp arrows he pierced their hearts and let out a roar;
and with cold frost, the imperishable Lord of the Stars [shone].
With eyes bloodshot with rage, he struck all the asuras;
pierced by his arrows and severely tormented by the cold, they were utterly overwhelmed.
The lords of the Daityas remained right there, as if fixed upon a painted canvas;
even the god Candra stood in the battle with his bow drawn into a circle.
Roaring like a rain-cloud, he shattered all the lords of the Daityas;
O best of sages, whether they were Dānavas or Daityas, whoever they might be—32.
At that time, all of them indeed took up arrows against him, who was like the moon.
Whenever he moves any limb whatsoever, O dear one, the Daitya [is aware] there at some time.
