In that battle, wherever the Daitya warrior spoke, the Lord pierced him with various sharp arrows and let out a roar.
The Moon also buried eight arrows in his mouth;
all those foremost of Asuras stood motionless like the mute, their entire bodies pierced by arrows as if they were figures fixed upon a painted canvas. (35)
Just as that divine Lord Candra, the destroyer of the Dānavas,
so too did the divine Vahni afflict the Dānavas in battle.
That formidable army—crowded with chariots, horses, elephants, and warriors, and overwhelmed by scattering drops of blood—is sinking like a herd of elephants mired in the mud. (37)
Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Battle," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
In that army, by means of that Soma of incomparable splendor, [the enemy was overcome].
While being struck, that great illusory Asura then regained his composure.
Hiraṇyākṣa, the son of Diti, filled with rage, spoke thus to the heroic son of Garuḍa, the charioteer in battle: ||2||
O Lord of Birds, you feel no shame here in this ocean of battle,
since today you carry me away from the fray by means of your chariot.
"What will all the asuras and the mighty daityas say:
'Our king, the scorcher of enemies, has been defeated in battle by his foes'? (4)
Seeking his own life, that evil-souled one has abandoned us, these fools, and fled from the battle to some unknown place; shame on me, a doer of inauspicious deeds! (5)
Having become the son of Kaśyapa, he was a respected brother to the Daitya.
The Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was endowed with the power of great yoga.
In the presence of all the Daityas and likewise the Dānavas, how was the king, the lord, and the hero himself defeated by his enemies? (7)
Or rather, you are indeed the son of Garuḍa, who belongs to the side of the gods;
you favor that very side and do not protect me.
Today, I am no longer able to sever your head, adorned with its earrings, from your body.
O lowest of the bird clan, cut [it] with this sharp sword! 9.
"You were my friend in the past, like a childhood companion;
therefore, having protected you, I let you go—you are released, though you are at fault."
Having heard those words of his, the charioteer, the lord of birds,
spoke with gentle speech to the great asura Hiraṇyākṣa.
"Do not be angry, O best of Dānavas; O Daitya, I am not your enemy. I have been brought here from the battlefield quickly indeed for the sake of protection. (12)
O Lord of the Dānavas, the charioteers who are learned in the scriptures say that the husband and wife, as the driver and the rider of the chariot, are devoted to one another. (13)
Just as a charioteer must protect his beloved passenger from the blows of weapons,
so too must he protect the chariot, for it is the chariot that brings victory to its master.
You, however, were pierced and bound by the enemy in battle.
Thinking, "He might become incapable," I have thus quickly removed him. ||15||
Having regained your breath and summoned your strength, you shall again arm yourself for battle and conquer your enemies in combat; thus have you been sent away.
O Daitya, for those high-souled ones who set out at the proper time and return at the proper time, clad in armor, victory in battle is not difficult to attain.
And I am not unbeneficial; I have always acted for your benefit. Do not harbor suspicion, O Lord of Daityas; I swear this by my entire truth. (18)
Moreover, it is not unknown to you that an oath was previously made by me:
"In the same way as Amṛtapas, death does not exist for me. (19)
"I am the son of Garuḍa; having left the gods, I have sought refuge with the Asuras.
Out of affection for you alone, O Daitya, do not harbor any suspicion toward me. (8.91.20)
This army is being tormented by both the Moon and Fire;
protect us quickly, O mighty-armed one, for you ought not to grieve.
"O Great King, resorting either to illusion, to your bow, or to your strength, slay your enemies; let not the sons of Diti become enraged. (22)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that great asura, having embraced the king of birds,
rushed forward with speed in a chariot that thundered like a cloud.
Then, as he was still charging forward, both Sūrya and Candramas likewise severed his banner in battle with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Then, O Vyāsa, having pierced him in the forehead, those two gods, Śaśin and Pāvaka,
let out a loud roar like the clouds at the end of a Yuga.
Seeing that agility of theirs, the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa destroyed that coolness with the foremost of weapons, the Āgneya.
Having burned [him] with a shower of snow, he then, having once again deluded him by means of his magic power,
quickly became Rāhu and rushed at him.
Then, being seized by that Rāhu, the Lord of Birds abandoned the battle and fled elsewhere; thereupon the Daitya let out a roar.
Indeed, when that storehouse of snow had vanished, all those Dānavas recovered their spirits and once again waged war against the hosts of gods;
they roared like clouds struck by thunderbolts, making the ocean resound with their clamor.
The great chariot-warriors among the Daityas and Dānavas, those preeminent riders, were taking breath;
desiring battle once more, they were like great tusked elephants dwelling in the forest.
Thus ends the ninety-first chapter in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the section on the battle.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having beheld the Lord of the Constellations, the Blessed One, the Bearer of Oblations (Agni), [spoke].
Having fled out of fear of the Dānavas, he now stood on foot, ready for battle. ||1||
With his arrows, he reduced the Dānava’s chariot— along with its driver, horses,
banner, and pennants— to a state of union with ashes.
Then, filled with rage, he rendered that divine bow stringless with a straight-knotted arrow and cried out, "Stay! Stay! (3)
Then Andhaka, Rāhu, Prahlāda, Maya,
and other foremost Dānavas surrounded Kṛśānu.
Then, leaping down upon them, he burned their bows, their chariots,
and their variegated banners, and let out a roar.
Assuming a hideous form and making the quarters resound on all sides, that best of Vasus burned the variegated armor and the heads.
O Vyāsa, while they were crying out "Alas! Alas! there, the Blessed One, who is indeed unassailable, shone as he scorched their tongues, remaining within the cave like a lamp.
Scorching the faces of certain Dānavas,
he— possessing great radiance— was like the enemy of darkness (the sun) scorching full-blown lotuses.
But for some of the lordly elephants, the Blessed One’s fire consumed their gold-adorned trunks, just as a forest fire consumes serpents.
The blessed Fire consumed the arrows and the bows, as well as the sword-fittings, and even all the elephants and horses without exception.
Being struck down, those lords of the Daityas, deprived of their weapons and armor, wandered here and there in great misery. ||11||
As those enemies of the gods were being consumed, blazing with fire, King Hiraṇyākṣa himself became the rain-cloud. ||12||
Then that lord of the Daityas, having become like a cloud, swiftly extinguished that fire with showers of rain, like the Saṃvartaka cloud.
Observing that the fire-god was thus pacified and distressed,
Vipracitti struck him in the forehead with sharp arrows.
Then, as he was shouting, Maya, the best of the Dānavas and a great Asura, drove even more most terrible arrows into his mouth.
O Vyāsa, as his mouth was thus split open, a terrible smoke, resembling collyrium, rose from his body like a wind. (16)
By that smoke, O Vyāsa, the sky, the heavens, and the earth were entirely filled with that great [smoke], so that nothing could be discerned.
By that sound, by their cries, by the proclamation of their names,
and even by the touch of hands, they then led one another to the abode of Yama.
Neither a god was recognized there, nor a Daitya, nor even a Dānava.
Not knowing this situation there, they established these [names]:
the Daityas called him Āṭi, while the deities called him Baka.
At that time, he struck down those Daityas who were calling out "Baka! there.
Calling out "Sura!
and "Āḍi!", that battle continued in this manner for a thousand years.
Indeed, there was great fear for the Daityas in the darkness, along with the gods.

In that darkness, there occurred a most terrifying and exceedingly fierce battle, flowing with streams of blood from the gods and asuras—who, though desiring the welfare of the world, were intent on its destruction. (22)
Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Battle," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, at that time, the banner of Agni rose up.
And being struck by the wind, it indeed underwent extreme dissolution. ||1||
Then the entire sky indeed became completely clear;
all the gods and the Daityas could see one another.
Then conchs, kettledrums, tabors, and drums, as well as Sughoṣakas, Ḍiṇḍimas, and broken kettledrums, [resounded] on all sides. (3)
In both armies, they were struck down by the hundreds and by the thousands;
then Śakra, the lord of the gods, Yama, and likewise Vaiśravaṇa [also fought].
Both Pūṣan and Bhaga, Aryaman and Mitra as well, Jayanta, the Maruts, and all the Rudras and Ādityas [were there]. ||5||
With great speed, those of immense velocity crushed the Dānava army;
there, seizing a powerful bow that shone like gold, [he advanced].
Yama brought the lords of the Daityas to the abode of Yama with his staff;
he, having pierced the mighty Hiraṇyākṣa with five arrows, [did so].
He laughed and roared at all the horses one by one;
then all those foremost of Daityas and Dānavas became distressed. ||8||
He discharged arrows shaped like venomous serpents that had mangled flesh for their prey;
with swift action, he severed each one of them into three pieces in the battle.
And again, as if laughing, he struck him with terrible arrows;
then [he struck] Andhaka’s charioteer and his chariot along with its horses.
The servant of great prowess led Yama to his own city;
then Andhaka, mace in hand, roared like a cloud at the end of an eon.
He rushed swiftly toward Yama and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
Then the Lord of the Gods [Indra] struck his gold-adorned mace with his thunderbolt.
O Vyāsa, he split [him] into a hundred pieces, and he fell down, remaining upon the earth;
having rendered him weaponless and armorless, those best of gods [acted].
In the battle, they struck him simultaneously with a rain of weapons;
Yama struck him on the head with his staff, and Śakra struck him with his thunderbolt.
And Varuṇa likewise with the noose that brings about the loss of wealth;
and other gods with their own various unerring and supreme weapons.
They rushed forward in great agitation, crying out, "You are slain!
Yet, at that moment, no pain whatsoever arose within that Daitya.
Then that Daitya, springing up, took his stand behind Puṇḍra.
With a blow of his fist, he felled Yama from his chariot to the ground.
Likewise, the swift one seized Indra’s elephant by the tail once more, whirled it around, and hurled it far away, saying, "You are destroyed! (18)
Then the Daitya, frantic with rage, seized the wish-fulfilling palanquin of Dhaneśa and shattered it in many pieces.
Then, in that battle, elephants struck down elephants, foot soldiers by foot soldiers,
chariots by chariots, and horses by horse-riders.
Furthermore, even while being struck in battle, he leapt up from the shoulder of Mahendra’s elephant and then cast Śakra down.
Beholding that deed of the lord of the Dānavas in battle, all the gods, seeking to save their lives, fled in every direction. ||22||
To the east was the Blessed Lord Indra, together with Āditya and the world-protectors;
likewise to the south were the Rudras, the Vasus, and the two Aśvins.
The Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas fled toward the west along with the Pannagas;
likewise, others fled toward the north like deer.
When they were broken, the lords of the Daityas, with their weapons raised behind them,
rushed forward roaring and displayed terror to them.
Then, after proceeding for a moment, they were held back by Hiraṇyākṣa.
Having turned back, they all stood still, overcome by indignation.
Then Hiraṇyākṣa, skilled in speech, spoke these words as if laughing to those enraged lords of the Daityas and Dānavas: ||27||
"O Daityas and Dānavas, what is the use today of these weaklings of yours—these wicked-souled ones who are bound, imprisoned, and as good as dead? (28)
Those for whom this kingdom is held are already slain; of this there is no doubt.
Their life does not exist today. Do not be hasty, O most foolish ones!
Even those who are weak, though enraged and still desiring life, [are as good as dead].
They are indeed invincible by force and difficult to conquer; of this there is no doubt.
"Regarding union, liberation, and their cause...
[he] spoke thus, O Uśanas. (3.1)
That which they call "kingdom" is indeed the vital breaths of great-souled men;
he who would seize their kingdom seizes their very life-breaths.
"O lords of the Dānavas, today we shall fill the stations of the gods with deities who are equal to them in heart.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, they entered Amarāvatī together with Hiraṇyākṣa;
they seized the jewels and proclaimed their victory. There, those gods stationed guards and employed spies to keep watch over them.
And they comforted the citizens as well as the subjects.
Thus,
with respectful offerings, excellent gifts, and benedictions, they bowed down to Hiraṇyākṣa, the best of the Asuras.
Having comforted them and seated them upon excellent thrones, the lord of the Daityas—
Having performed the duties for all, he went to the abode of Varuṇa.
With lion-roars, various musical instruments, leaps, slapping sounds, and roars,
all those great asuras surrounded the lion-like king of the Dānavas on every side.
Thus ends the ninety-third chapter of the Varuṇālayagamana in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Seeing him rushing forward with speed like Garuḍa in battle, those sons of Varuṇa fled together with their father.
And all those Daityas, having reached that abode of Varuṇa, stood with shoulders squared,
having dispatched a messenger named Vātāpin, who had been sent by the king and was full of vigor, toward that city.
Having gone to that beautiful city and entered it,
O Vyāsa, the great Asura, being highly honored by the citizens, spoke these words to them with great pride:
"I am the king of the entire world, the delighter of the Daityas and Dānavas."
The glorious and powerful Hiraṇyākṣa, the son of Kaśyapa,
having conquered all the gods in battle, constantly issues this command to you:
"All of you, listen to my command and carry it out!"
"Bring the jewels and abandon the deities!
Whoever among the faction of the gods dwells here in this city, I grant him safety; let him go to the gods as if he were fearless."
O Vyāsa, Nārada and the other sages, having approached that Daitya,
then spoke these conciliatory words to the asura:
"He is a king, a Bhoja, a Virāṭ, a Samrāṭ, a lord of the earth, a Kṣatriya, and a ruler."
What wise person would not worship him who is praised by these words? ||9||
Thus you are a king (*rājā*), a lord (*bhoja*), a sovereign (*virāṭ*), and likewise an emperor (*samrāṭ*);
you are a ruler of the earth (*bhūpati*), a warrior-noble (*kṣatriya*), a monarch (*nṛpa*), and likewise one who endures all (*sarvasaha*).
The gods, including Indra, who possess great heroism, have been conquered by you;
who else in the world is your equal, except for the one external Lord Rudra? ||11||
"You are the protector of all the worlds, as well as their destroyer and creator; O Great King, what evil-minded person could ever thwart your command? (12)
"O Lord of Daityas, O Dānava, we all desire a boon;
for you are the granter of boons to all beings, so be the granter of a boon to us. (13)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of theirs, he replied, "I am the giver of boons.
Then those masters of speech spoke to the king of the Daityas.
The sages said:
"O Daitya, that which has been spoken by you regarding hell, disease, and death would not be so; let this boon be granted to us. (15)
The Daitya said:
"O best of Brahmins, O you whose wealth is asceticism, my vow was made long ago:
'If I am to be the king of the world, I shall increase the happiness of the worlds. (16)
O best of sages, I shall not act in such a way that I would become one of false promise, untruthful, and evil-minded. (17)
"Therefore, sirs, ask me for another boon that is very dear to you;
I shall do all of that accordingly. I entreat you with my head bowed.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, having heard those words of his, all those sages spoke again to the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa.
The sages said:
"O bull among the Daityas, in the past all this was performed by Brahmā for the sake of setting the worldly order in motion, and dharma was also established."
Having considered this world, the Dharma has been set in motion;
O Daitya, let it not be that what has come to be does not exist—therefore, grant us this boon. (21)
That vow would prevail which effects the avoidance of suffering for the worlds;
therefore, that imperishable work of Brahmā shall not perish.
"O Daitya, since you are indeed the king and the lord of the world, by this act today, your debt to Brahmā shall be discharged. (23)
Having heard their words and determined them to be sages, the king of the Daityas [thought]:
"Those who are hostile and partisans of Śakra, and those who violate my command—" || 24 ||
"For them alone shall there be death and torments in the hells.
Then the king said this, and they too spoke to the lord of men.
Having said to them, "So be it," he ordained their release from torment; having liberated all those in hell, he entrusted the protection of that place [to them]. (26)
Then, having proclaimed his victory before the sinless and mighty Vipracitti, the king of the Pitṛs,
and having honored those twice-born ones,
the exceedingly powerful Hiraṇyākṣa departed for the abode of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
Then those mighty Dānavas, making the city of the Lord of Wealth resound— which was protected by Andhaka—
surrounded Hiraṇyākṣa and advanced like clouds toward a mountain.
Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Visit to the World of Yama," in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, within the section on Hiraṇyākṣa’s conquest of the quarters.
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus reached Laṅkā, the auspicious city of the Lord of Wealth (Kubera),...
Armed with armor and weapons, they stood nearby, brandishing their uplifted [arms]. ||1||
Having seen the Dānavas standing there, arrogant in their strength,
as well as all the inhabitants of Laṅkā and the guardians of the treasures, [they spoke].
The treasures, such as Śaṅkha, Padma, and others, and the sages whose wealth is penance,
having taken up the respectful offering and jewels, presented them to the Dānava.
And they said: "O Lord of Daityas, we are under your command, there is no doubt;
O Lord of Dānavas, please instruct us as is fitting. (4)
Hiraṇyākṣa said:
"O Yakṣas, let there be no fear for you; you are mine, of this there is no doubt.
For this king here is the best among you, the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu. (5)
Prahlāda was the oppressor of all the hosts of gods;
therefore, having established that bull among the Daityas, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), there.
Furthermore, having established the lords of the Dānavas as the residents in all those places, he filled the abodes of the other hosts of gods once again.
Andhaka, moreover, consecrated [Virocana] as Indra in Amarāvatī;
the Daitya himself ruled over the entire Bhūrloka.
Furthermore, taking up his bow along with an arrow, the lord of the Daityas, resplendent like the sun, said to the Earth: "Reveal yourself to me."
Terrified and trembling before that Daitya, she stood with palms joined in reverence,
saying "Victory!", like another Lakṣmī standing before Viṣṇu.
Like a tiger to a doe, like the king of birds to a female serpent, like a lion to a tigress, and like the king of the śarabhas to a lioness— (11)
Like a mean crow toward a female swan, or like a madgura fish toward a peahen,
so did that son of Diti seize her with a wrathful countenance;
and, agitated, he spoke to the goddess who was overwhelmed by fear.
"O auspicious Vasudhā, I have been appointed by Brahmā as your husband;
you should honor your husband, for I shall protect you.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having gone to Rasātala near his own city,
he bound her with serpent-nooses as if she were a wicked woman.
Then the very powerful and wicked lord of the Daityas, Cala, besieged the distressed [city] with his conch, just as a heroic one might besiege a cave.
Then he appointed fourteen thousand Daitya chiefs named Kiṅkaras as guards, who were constantly engaged in her protection.
Having done exactly that, the lord of the Daityas shone with satisfaction, like a farmer upon seeing his field well-ripened. || 17 ||
Having united his eldest son with wives, like a self-controlled and virtuous man, that king formed the thought, "I have accomplished my purpose.
O observer of noble vows, no one else was able to find any flaw in him.

"O Dānavas, all of you, perform sacrifices and honor the Brahmins; and bow down again and again to the trident-bearing God, even as my own companion, the Brahmin who lives with hypocrisy, does. || 19 || 20 ||
At that time, he commanded: "Devote yourselves solely to the Dharma.
Not one of his followers—whether a Daitya or a Dānava—was unrighteous.
While he ruled that kingdom, there was no wicked conduct;
O Vyāsa, he himself became like Vāyu, Candra, and Sūrya in the worlds,
endowed with the power of asceticism.
While that king was ruling, medicinal herbs sprang up spontaneously;
they grew without cultivation and were sufficient for all the world.
That very king of the Daityas, however, took them away and carried them off to the ocean.
He indeed crushed him and led him back home;
he alone became the staff-bearer, and he indeed was the staff itself. Through his yoga, he constantly protects everyone everywhere from thieves.
No one among them falls ill, nor does anyone die;
nor is there ever one who is attached to another's wife, nor a slanderer, nor a violent person, nor indeed anyone unrighteous. || 26–27 ||
Ponds, lakes, rivers,
and springs exist everywhere even without rain;
for him, there are no Rākṣasas nor any harmful Piśācas.
No calamities existed for him, nor any pairs of opposites.
While that king reigned, the Brahmins did not offer oblations into the fire, nor did they study or perform sacrifices; at that time, society became a single caste.

O Vyāsa, those who were the Bhṛgu sages became the learned priests (vipras) who brought joy to the Dānavas; they studied and performed sacrifices in every way. Everything became joyful and well-nourished, entirely free from the suffering of disease.

The world, having abandoned the system of castes and stages of life, became equal for all people. Constantly engaged in festivals of dance and song, it slept in happiness and was devoted to the pursuit of pleasure.
Thus did the world shine while Hiraṇyākṣa, the son of Diti and lord of the Daityas, reigned as king.
Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of King Hiraṇyākṣa’s Reign," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
While that auspicious lord of the Daityas, the sovereign of the three worlds, was thus ruling as king...
And when the tax has been paid and the subjects are living in happiness. ||1||
"Deprived of their positions, the mighty gods were left without a foothold; afflicted by suffering, what did they do? Tell me all of this in detail. (2)
Sanatkumāra said:
Listen to the state that befell the gods; hear how they all, afflicted by suffering, acted there in due order.
Agni became the carrier of oblations for the gods, increasing their shares;
having cast him out, the Daitya then made another fire.
O best of Brahmins, in that ritual, there were mantras following it which, when recited for the portions of the Daityas and Dānavas, brought about auspicious results. ||5||
Then the Sacrifice itself approached those high-souled Daityas;
and when the Sacrifice had departed, all the lords of the Daityas were as if dead.
They lost their sense of direction, their vigor and prowess were diminished;
they were bereft of splendor, devoid of effort, without anyone to cry out for help, and filled with anxiety.
Like serpents burnt by mantras, like mountains pulverized by thunderbolts,
they are rendered as poisonless as snakes bitten by Garuda.
O Vyāsa, like trees deprived of water or women bereft of their kinsmen, those gods— deprived of their kingdom and robbed of their splendor—
brood in their hearts, wither away, and lament.
Then the self-existent god, the Grandfather, perceiving those gods to be in such a state, spoke these words from his sun-colored celestial chariot:
"O gods, you have lost your senses; for what reason are you so deeply distressed?"
"Or today, O foremost of gods, I shall grant you the power of asceticism and yoga."
"You are the creators and the destroyers of the world in every respect;
it is not fitting for you to remain like eunuchs today.
O mighty ones, abandon both your own power and mine, and endure this suffering."
Do not engage in grief; let the gods themselves proceed.
Just as darkness is not joined with the sun, nor heat with the moon, nor frost with fire, nor nectar with a serpent;
just as goodness does not belong to the wicked, nor ugliness to one of noble birth. (14)
The evil-minded man does not perceive unrighteousness either in his restrictive observances or in the Vedas.
"O gods, it is not fitting for you, who are high-souled, that this should be so;
for those who abide in their own splendor never despond in times of adversity. || 16 ||
Having encountered this calamity, you ought not to grieve;
do not despair, for the kingdom shall be yours once more. (17)
Endowed with the power of great yoga, Hiraṇyākṣa, the son of Diti, cannot be slain today by those of limited splendor, O deities. ||18||
"O imperishable ones, wait for the exhaustion of this penance;
when the penance is exhausted, Viṣṇu will slay the lord of the Daityas in battle.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by Brahmā, those lords of the gods, who had attained yoga,
bowed down to the creator of all beings and spoke as follows:
"The great seats of yoga have been seized from us by the sons of Diti."
Tell us, where shall we stay? Point out to us an imperishable place.
Brahmā said:
"All your abodes have been taken away; this is known to me. Listen to where you must dwell by means of your yogic power (yogamāyā)."
"O most excellent ones, O gods, all of you enter into bodies through yoga; from that, you shall obtain sustenance from all quarters for the sake of living beings."
Through their various kinds of food and drink, as well as through their transformative activities,
the earth— though bound by the nagas— will nourish you all.
Sanatkumāra said: Having been thus addressed by the God, all those gods, including Vāsava,
did exactly as Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, had spoken.
Remaining there, those best of gods constantly revolved [the wheel], abiding by the doctrine of the world-system as they observed the four ages. ||26||
Then, through his yogic power, Hiraṇyākṣa, whose self was absorbed in yoga, perceived the gods established among the creatures; he became enraged toward them.
Whichever deity he saw stationed there,
that best of Dānavas would approach and slay him.
I am constantly and diligently protecting my subjects from fear;
yet those of wicked conduct increase my very enmity.
"Ungrateful, slayers of their masters, insatiable, and evil-minded—
these wicked enemies of mine always nourish themselves with food, drink, and other provisions. Therefore, these women of depraved conduct deserve punishment from me."
Wherever all the creatures went, he slew them everywhere. || 31 ||
Then, by means of his yoga, the Dānava dried up all the ponds, lakes, rivers, and springs.
O you of noble vows, he destroyed even those medicinal herbs that used to grow cultivated on his land;
he also crushed the trees and creepers.
With its trees, shrubs, creepers, and sprouts destroyed, its grasses, herbs, springs, and reservoirs of water vanished,

and its rivers, ponds, wells, and pools dried up, the world appeared like the back of a tortoise. Devoid of the restraint of the duties of the castes and stages of life, with its sounds, cowherd settlements,
birds, and humans perished, and silent of its herds of elephants, horses, and offspring, the world shone like the fierce fire at the end of an eon.
Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Speech of Brahmā," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having seen the world in such a state, those gods were afflicted with grief.
Having reached the world of Vairāja, he beheld his grandfather once again.
Having all approached him together and bowed down again and again,
they, being deeply distressed, related the entire deed of the Daitya.
Having made their report, they spoke once more to the God, the cause of the worlds.
"O Blessed One, O Lord, we have been deprived of our kingdom and are weak;
thus, O All-pervading One, we are incapable of standing against that Daitya in battle.
Nor do we see any place where we might remain free from anxiety."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of the terrified inhabitants of heaven,
the Blessed Brahmā spoke to all the gods.
O gods, that great-souled yogin should not be feared;
all the fruit of that Daitya’s asceticism has been exhausted.
O gods, the time has arrived for him that brings an end to his life.
Therefore, all of you go with me and entreat Viṣṇu.
"Sirs, you are indeed powerless today and incapable of resisting him; Viṣṇu alone is capable, and he shall deprive that Daitya of his life. (8)
For previously, when he was born, an incorporeal voice spoke:
"This one cannot be slain by a human nor by a god in any way whatsoever. (9)
Nor will this Great-Souled One be born among the animals, nor on earth, nor in fire; nor in space, nor in any of the worlds. (8.97.10)
This very one, the lord of the Daityas, a high-souled and righteous deity, shall then be incapable of being slain by any living beings; he shall be slayable only through sorrow.
Having assumed the form of a boar, it was neither divine nor human;
nor was it born among the animals, for it was indeed a man-boar (naravārāha). Having entered the netherworld (pātāla), it was neither earth nor sky.
It is neither fire nor this world; it is entirely liberated from all things.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then they were all delighted, and having bowed down to the Grandfather,
they said, "O Lord of Gods, we shall depart, for our time is passing away."
Then they all went to Śveta, the best of mountains,
[to see] Viṣṇu— the patient and victorious one who crushes hosts of Dānavas.
Having prostrated with great reverence, they praised him with desired words:
"Obeisance to the destroyer of all enemies and the end-maker of the Dānavas;
obeisance to the victorious God, Vaikuṇṭha, the Great Soul."
Homage to the one whose dust has been shaken off; and indeed, homage to Truth itself. ||17||
Salutations to the deity Sādhya; salutations to the Abode, the well-knowing one;
salutations again and again to the deity Yama and to Jaya;
salutations to the son of Aditi and to Nara-Nārāyaṇa.
Salutations indeed to Namassumati, and let there be salutations to Viṣṇu as well.
Salutations to the one in the form of Vāmana and to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana;
salutations to Rāma, to Rāma, and indeed salutations to Dattātreya.
Salutations to you, O Narasiṃha; salutations again and again to Dhātṛ.
Salutations to Sādhya, to the Veda, and indeed salutations again and again to the wielder of the discus.
Salutations to the slayer of Śakuni and salutations to Dāmodara;
to him who performs penance in the water and who is fond of his serpent-couch.
Salutations to the one in the form of Kapila and to the Great Puruṣa.
Homage to him who has the form of a cloud and who is dear to Mahādeva;
homage to him whose form is half that of Rudra and likewise to him who takes the form of Umā;
homage to the host of Maheśvara, who holds a discus and a mallet in his hands.
And let there always be salutation to Śipiviṣṭa, the bearer of the Śrīvatsa mark;
to Dhundhumāra, the heroic slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
and to the four-armed Kṛṣṇa, the wearer of the jewel Kaustubha.
To the one who traversed the three worlds with three strides, who stands in the sky, who wears yellow garments, and who is well-attired. || 26 ||
Homage to the slayer of Puruṣa, who wields the mace and the fierce sword;
to the yogi, the sacrificer, and the one who ravaged the wife of Bhṛgu.
To him who has the form of a bull, the eternal best among the Ādityas,
to Cekitāna, the self-controlled, to Śauri, the kinsman of the Vṛṣṇis.
Salutations to you, the Śārṅga bow, for the destruction of Mura and Aśvagrīva, likewise for the slaying of the Asuras, and for the destruction of Saubha and Śālva.
Salutations to you, O Padmanābha, who have entered the body of Brahmā;
salutations to Jayā, to Śarva, and to him who has been granted boons by Rudra.
Salutations to the Lord of all, the one who sets forth the lost dharma;
salutations to you, the most excellent Puruṣa, the hundred-armed one.
By your grace alone, O Supreme Person, we shall indeed cross over this great hardship.
O mighty-armed Vaikuṇṭha, you do not know that we have all been robbed of our kingdom by Hiraṇyākṣa; destroy him, O mighty-armed one!
Sanatkumāra said: That mortal who, endowed with supreme devotion, constantly recites this Vaiṣṇava hymn, is liberated from all sins.
And having died, he rejoices in all the worlds for fourteen crores of years, honored by all the gods; of this there is no doubt. ||34||
He who merely recites this for the sake of living beings is liberated;
without reaching the world of death, he wanders free from suffering.
Sanatkumāra said:
He spoke thus, always honoring those tigers among the gods:
"From here that evil-minded Daitya, accompanied by his allies, hates the gods. Assume for me the form of a boar in human guise; let me be established [therein]. (36-37)
"That great-souled lord of the Daityas is indeed powerful and righteous;
I cannot slay him alone—I tell you this truly.
[I shall assume] the form of the Boar, which consists of all the gods and increases prosperity."
Having assumed that form, I shall slay that exceedingly powerful lord of the Daityas.
O best of gods, in that very form,
Brahmā attained the status of Brahmā, and Yama likewise became the one who presides over departure [Death].
"O best of gods, Varuṇa shall be the Udgātṛ there, and from him the sacrificial animal;
I, the mighty one, shall be the Śamitṛ for his sake.
Today let all beings behold both me and him. (41)
As if two rutting elephants dwelling in the forest,
having heard those words and the roar of that great-souled one,
they all gazed at one another with eyes wide with joy.
They thought that the exceedingly powerful lord of the Daityas had indeed been slain.
Their faces, which possessed the luster of full-blown lotuses and were radiant with beautiful eyes,
reflected how that Daitya had previously been killed by the one in the form of Narasiṃha, just as his own mighty preceptor had been slain long ago.
Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Means for the Slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then those tigers among the gods assumed his form.
The lords fashioned his body out of the seven worlds. ||1||
All his bones are the mountains, and his channels are the rivers;
the seven oceans are his blood, and the qualities of phlegm, bile, and wind are his [elements]. (2)
His feces became the herbs, and his dharma was the semen;
his urine became the clouds, and the seven vital airs became those residing within the body-cavities. || 3 ||
The Sādhyas became his head, and Rudra took up residence in his crown;
Dharma was on his forehead, and the self-possessed Vāyu was his nose.
The sun and the moon became his eyes, and the quarters of space became his ears;
his vital breaths became his eyebrows, and day and night became his eyelashes.
Fire became his mouth, while the submarine fire (vaḍavāmukha) was situated within it;
the intermediate space became his lips, and serpents became his teeth.
Indeed, the four great weapons were made into his large fangs.
First the Pāśupata weapon, and secondly the discus itself.
The third was the Brahmadaṇḍa, and the fourth was the head of Brahmā;
Soma became his neck, and Rudra was situated upon his shoulder.
Likewise, his two cheeks were fashioned by the Ādityas, and his two hands by the Rudras;
his fingers are Kīrti, Lakṣmī, and Siddhi as well. ||9||
...and their movements, as well as their claws, serve as weapons in every way;
likewise, they possess the staff of Yama, the staff of Time, and the staff of Death. || 8.98.10 ||
O Lord, Rudra and Daṇḍa became his four arms; the Sādhyas were his chest, and Soma was his heart, O best of sages. The great elements became his belly.
O best of Brahmins, Nābhi became his mother, and Aditi was his father.
Prajāpati was his penis, and Mitra stood upon its sheath;
the Vasus were at his sides, and Dharma was at his back. (13)
Death, Time, and Yama are situated on the soles of his hands and feet;
the two Aśvins are his tail, and the ancestors reside in his joints. 14.
Necessity, the noose of time, and even the strife of the God of Death, as well as whatever diseases there may be—all these have taken refuge in his glance. (15)
The Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, and together with the Pannagas—all of them, having taken refuge in the skin, stood gathered together. (16)
Likewise, all the meters, the Vedas, and the sacrifices themselves—
all these remained individually within the pores of his skin.
So too did the acts of charity, the observances, the restraints, and all the Mothers.
The gods who pride themselves on their stations, as well as beasts and birds, are indeed [subject to this]. 18.
All the hairs on that high-souled boar became [the stars],
and likewise the Viśvedevas became the toes of his two feet.
At that time, the Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirases became his gods;
all the sages were established within the pores of his skin and in all his limbs.
Thus, O Vyāsa, he became the Boar Nandivardhana;
in that form, he shone, touching both heaven and earth. ||21||
In ancient times, the blessed Self-born Lord Madhusūdana, being about to uplift this earth, shone forth in that form,
radiant like Mount Himavat blazing at night.
Then all those sages, by means of their great ascetic power at that time, [performed the rite].
Each having attained his own splendor, they further inflamed that [splendor] of his.
With the splendor of those ṛṣis of supreme power,
Viṣṇu blazed forth at the end of time like another fire of the dissolution of the age.
And having let out a tremendous roar, he caused the surface of the earth to tremble.
He said to all those sages, "I shall slay the Daitya, the enemy of the gods;
having killed that king of the Daityas, like a lion-king killing a śarabha. (26)
"Having entered the subterranean realm (rasātala) today, I shall liberate the distressed earth;
and having established her in her own place and restored the kingdom to the gods, you, whose wealth is asceticism, must now recite prayers for victory and for auspiciousness. (27)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, said: "Exert your strength; this Daitya is possessed of very great power."
O Lord of the Gods, exerting great effort and remaining vigilant, slay that king of the Daityas; this is my considered opinion, for this is indeed a difficult situation. (29)
In former times, there was no Daitya equal to him; this lord of the Daityas, Hiraṇyakaśipu, possessed great strength and was endowed with the power of asceticism and yoga.
Then, O Vyāsa, the blessed Lord whose banner bears the bull was there with the gods,
including Brahmā, and with the sages whose wealth is their austerity.
Having bowed to the Lord of Gods, he said: "O Lord, O Master of All, augment Viṣṇu with your own splendor so that he may slay the enemy of the gods. (32)
The Blessed One said:
"At that time, all those who possess the splendor of the lords of the gods shall enter into Hari, who is composed of light;
thereafter, he will swiftly slay the Daitya."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Brahmā himself performed the protection of that high-souled one;
learn that correctly from me as I speak it today, O you of pure vows. (34)
Brahmā said:
"O best of sages, may the Ordainer and the Creator protect you;
and may Rudra, the creator of all, oversee the deeds of you as you fight."
May Kapālī, Tālaketu, Gandhādhipati, Rasādhipati, and Sūkṣmarūpa protect [me]. ||3.6||
He who is the subtle knower of touch, the possessor of sound, and the high-minded;
he who is the lord of the senses and indeed Nīlalohita. ||37||
May the Great Yogin protect you, as well as the Lord of the Seed-syllables, the Garland of the Empowerment of the Seed-syllables, and the Lord of Consciousness. ||38||
He is the Lord who knows the time of both worldly engagement and withdrawal;
he is the Lord who grants the fruits to doers according to the course of dharma and adharma;
he is the one who provides the function for the qualities (guṇas) and remains indifferent toward actions.
He who is the author of the cosmic law and the knower of all actions;
he who functions for the sake of the instruments even without instruments;
he who is omniscient, omnipresent, and the self-existent presiding controller. || 8.98.40-41 ||
There is nothing whatsoever that is not presided over by Him, nor does anything exist in any way apart from Him.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere, possessing ears everywhere, He exists pervading all, the immutable one. (42)
He whose sovereignty is inexhaustible and who likewise possesses a thousand forms;
he who is the creator of all beings and of the principles, and who is of great renown;
he who is the maker of this cycle of existence and likewise its bringer to an end.

That which the followers of Sāṃkhya do not recognize, even though they are practitioners who have mastered the scriptures; that which the contentments and the perfections constantly bewilder living beings through illusion—in this Great Self, all principles are woven like warp and woof. ||44–45||
He who pervades all things, beginning with the Puruṣa, and is himself not pervaded by anything;
knowing whom there is no liberation, and by whom this entire world is bound. (46)
By whom I was formerly made the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) of all the worlds;
by whom you, as well as Sacrifice and Viṣṇu, were created in the beginning, O Ancient One.
May that high-minded god bestow upon you great strength, vigor, and splendor,
as well as memory regarding weapons acquired without effort in all circumstances;
and may the omnipresent deity grant protection to you as you fight.
"Having properly performed your protection, go and destroy the Daitya.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Brahmins, those who were stationed within his pores praised him with hymns.
And the gods praised him with desired words out of great reverence.
And all the various beings cried out, "Victory!
Then, auspicious divine drums resounded spontaneously in the sky.
There, where the Boar had appeared, the divine beings cried out;
and showers of fragrant flowers fell everywhere upon the Boar, greatly increasing the joy of the gods. (52)
Then, saying "Success! and having offered salutations to Rudra, he went to the abode of Varuṇa while chanting the *Jayāvaha* Rudra hymn.
He was attended by sages rich in asceticism, as well as by many victorious birds.
And with many divine deer circumambulating him to his right, the god set out toward the great ocean for victory.
Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Departure of Varāha for the Abode of Varuṇa," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
That righteous-souled one set forth, roaring like a thundercloud.
The God who consists of all the worlds is the Boar, the Increaser of Joy. || 1 ||
Then, having reached the ocean, that one of exceeding strength beheld it roaring like a cloud, submerging itself like a lion-king,
dancing like a female dancer, and leaping like a warrior.
As he thus traversed the earth with many diverse circles,
like one skilled in wrestling and expert in mace-fighting,
Nandivardhana then beheld that manifold wonder.
He worshipped that Lord of Gods, the all-pervading one who embodies all the worlds,
with a worthy offering, as well as the gods and the sages who had assembled there.
Taking him for victory and honoring the great ocean,
he turned back all beings and entered the vast sea.
As the omnipresent Lord plunged into the ocean, playing about, he shone with splendor.
Having reached a vast lake, like a rutting great elephant,
he entered it and went very deep until he became invisible,
like the sun with its full orb covered by a streak of clouds.
Then, having entered the water and agitating the great ocean,
O Vyāsa, he was seen by the world-protectors like a moon reflected in the water;
he [swallowed] even the *timi*, *timiṅgila*, and *timiṅgilagila* fish.
In that very same way, he likewise swallowed other donkeys, as well as even elephants.
And likewise those with the forms of sea-monsters (*makara*) and conchs, as well as those with the faces of horses;
similarly, others resembling birds, and even others in human form;
and those shaped like chariot wheels, as well as those with the faces of lions and tigers.
as well as fish with the faces of śarabhas, bears, and cats, and many other kinds of fish.
Whirling [the mace], he of great splendor and immense strength proceeded;
some entered him out of curiosity, while others indeed merely sniffed him.
Hundreds and thousands of fish with flaming mouths bite him;
yet he circumambulates the auspicious, divine Hayashiras.
In an instant, having passed through the midst of Mount Maināka and also through Bhogavatī,
he went to the city of Varuṇa, the wise lord of the waters.
Having reached the world-elephant Parjanya and performed a circumambulation,
and having arrived at the city of Surabhī and beheld the cows of radiant luster—
O Vyāsa, those which always yield nectar and the very essence of immortality— || 16 ||
That divine lake is Kṣīroda, where those twice-born ones subsist on foam.
Having drunk from that lake water which was equal in luster to the nectar of fame,
he dwelt there for that night, duly honored by the foam-drinkers (the froth-eaters).
Having stayed there, he went to the imperishable city of Kaṅka;
and having reached the cities of Vāsuki and the wise Takṣaka,
the Lord of Gods attained immortality there in the abode of Śeṣa.
Delightful, charming, and divine, it was even more excellent than heaven itself.
Having heard him, King Ananta honored him with the arghya offering; bowing down with great respect, the imperishable king invited him.
As he was thus worshipping him, the slayer of Madhu, filled with supreme affection, said:
"You ought not to create an obstacle to the work of the world."
"O Lord, this great task must be performed for the sake of the inhabitants of heaven.
We shall do it again together with you, if you so desire;
let not this opportunity pass away for the sake of the Daitya. (23)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having dismissed that serpent, he went to the netherworld (rasātala).
There dwelt the Daitya Suprabha, the guardian of the ocean, who moved within the waters.
Then he saw him approaching toward the city of Hiraṇyākṣa,
and he beheld the subtle gods within the limbs of the Boar.
And because of that form of his, the Asura, being terrified, did not approach him;
moreover, that evil-minded one was paralyzed by his splendor.
For they were about to report this quickly to that Hiraṇyākṣa;
meanwhile, the Boar exerted his speed toward the city ahead of him.
Desiring to go to that king of the Daityas, who was Ananta in the form of a boar and the bringer of death,
he approached the Daitya to bring about the end of his life, like the wind bearing a blazing flame and a garland.
Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Entry of Varāha into the Ocean," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
When that fear had arisen, there appeared omens indicating the threat of destruction.
At that time, indeed, terrible portents occurred in the city of Hiraṇyākṣa.
The watchtowers crumbled and the deities seemed to cry out;
jackals howled in the houses and assembly halls of the Daityas.
Suddenly, a terrifying roar arose there from the citizens.
And trees, uprooted from the earth, fall even without wind;
the sun appears like a headless torso (kabandha), and a battle is also seen here.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having observed these and other great omens at that time, the king spoke thus to the Asuras among the Daityas: ||4||
O foremost of Asuras, great omens are being observed;
these are certainly not without cause, for a great danger is seen.
O lords of the gods, having been deprived of your kingdoms, you will not remain inactive;
surely, relying upon someone, you are preparing for battle.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of his, Prahlāda, the best of the asuras,
bowed properly to his father and spoke these words.
Prahlāda said:
"O Lord of Daityas, I am your son, and you are my father according to dharma.
O best of Daityas, your intellect should not be influenced by those such as me."
Nevertheless, out of affection and desiring an imperishable kingdom, we have spoken thus out of our childish nature; you ought not to hold that against us.
"Last night in a dream, I saw him in human form;
having assumed the form of a boar, he seized you. Act properly so that this does not come to pass. (8.100.10)
Hiraṇyākṣa said: "It is exactly so; there is no doubt regarding that which you have seen according to dharma at that time. It is precisely as it truly is; of this there is no uncertainty."
Today I went in a dream to the abode of Tryambaka;
then the Blessed One, whose banner is the bull, spoke this to me.
O Daitya, such is your kingdom and even your status as Indra:
that you, my son, give this beloved Suprabhā along with the yakṣas to him. (13)
"Quickly bestow upon him today this crown and the necklace, as well as the armlets, the bracelets, the sword, and the golden circlet. (14)
Then, taking both the royal insignia and the fine linen garment, as well as the upper robe, from me even though I was unwilling, he gave them to Śakra.
Thereupon the Blessed One said to me: "You must always remain in my presence."
"O Lord of Daityas, you must dwell [here] starting from tomorrow; what use have you for a kingdom?"
For that which has been seen by me shall not be false;
in every way, there is no possibility here for the Daityas to exist through me alone.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, all the Daityas then spoke:
"This is false; O King, these things occurring in dreams are proclaimed to be false. (18)
That Andhaka, who is invincible and powerful, and who is to be slain by all beings, shall fight together with us against the gods. (19)
Relying upon him, we shall all fight happily and free from anxiety; O crusher of the hosts of gods, do not you yourself fight against the gods.
All the vital breaths of the Daityas, together with the Dānavas, are established in you. While you live, we live; but if you do not exist, how can we remain?
Or rather, abandoning the city this very day, let us all enter the great ocean.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of theirs, the great asura Hiraṇyākṣa,
the best among speakers, laughed and spoke this to them properly.
He who is the creator of all beings, and likewise their bestower and their destroyer—he who ordained it in the beginning, who else could alter that again? (23)
O Dānavas, if death has been ordained for me inevitably by him,
he will come and slay me while I am sitting and not fighting.
"Behold that place of mine, O all you best of Asuras, where Death shall not come and lead me away while I remain. (25)
Or rather, O Dānavas, death has not been ordained for me by him;
he shall not lead me away while I am fighting as I did before.
How could one such as I do this, which is censured by the virtuous—first bringing death upon a child, and then casting my own gaze upon another? (27)
O lords of the Dānavas, even one such as I, having alone and repeatedly wrought the slaughter of enemies in battle, would turn my back upon them once more. (28)
Vipracitti said:
"All the gods have indeed been conquered by us many times and have perished in every way; we shall now strive so that they may never return again. (29)
Hiraṇyākṣa said:
"Knowing ourselves to be immortal gods, though it is very difficult to attain, we shall live for a very long time and obtain [our desires] once again. (8.100.3)
Understanding that it is merely a kingdom, they constantly flee;
O best of asuras, we do not possess immortality at all.
Therefore, even for us who are ruined, there is no hope for life;
since that [hope] is absent, we see that whatever we have obtained is indeed better for us. (32)
Do not set your mind on destruction; my resolve is fixed on battle.
Let our lives depart in fair combat in the field, and not like those of cowards.
Sanatkumāra said:
While those enemies of the gods were speaking thus in the assembly,
a Dānava appeared, agitated by forceful breaths and rage.
Then, like an elephant in a desolate place terrified by the king of beasts,
or like a serpent by the paw of a lion, or like a snake by a Garuḍa,
he clenched his fist and gazed in all directions.
Sighing with vehemence, he went to the gate and spoke to the doorkeeper.
The Dānava said:
"O keeper of the assembly hall, announce to the king that Anala himself has arrived;
he is the protector of the ocean, and he is said to be swift, acting quickly even when it is not the appointed time. (37)
Then, having laughed and addressed him, the doorkeeper and assembly master spoke to him:
"Do not fear; from what could you have fear, O great asura? (38)
"There is no lion here, nor any thief, nor any other beast of prey; there are no cattle or other animals either. Cast away your fear and take heart."
Thus addressed by him, that best of Asuras became calm;
yet, filled with rage, he then let out a great sound that made the quarters of the sky resound.
Having approached the king, the lord of the Dānavas, at that time, O Vyāsa, they said:
"Tell us, what has this god seen today?
Having properly consoled this Daitya, O King, that highly illustrious one—
"O son of Diti, ask for the benefit of the Dānavas.
O best of Brahmins, having heard those words from that Dānava, Vyāsa spoke this to the king of the Dānavas, who was possessed of great strength: |||43||
"O Daitya, out of fear you are unable to approach me;
take heart and tell me everything exactly as it was seen, just as it is."
Sanatkumāra said: Thereupon, O Vyāsa, that Dānava, freed from his fever, bowed down to the king with joined palms and spoke these words properly.
May the king, who brings happiness to the Dānavas, be ever victorious for us;
may all our enemies, who bring us misfortune, perish. ||46||
"O Great King, by your command I wander everywhere day after day, accompanied by my men as far as the edge of the ocean. ||47||
Today, O foremost of Daityas, I see there a boar resembling the peak of Mount Meru, blazing like a fire.
O Great King, all the gods and the sages whose wealth is austerity are seen stationed upon his limbs, assuming subtle forms. ||49||
O Indra among kings, you are possessed of great strength and are always a source of fear to the gods;
yet Bhīma is even greater than you—no one such as he exists here in this world.
"O bull among the Daityas, neither seen nor even heard before in person, I was struck by him with his glance and fell violently to the ground. (51)
With their necklaces and garments slipping off, terrified as if struck by a thunderbolt,
all those Dānavas of fearsome prowess who were my followers fell down, deprived of life, by his force. ||52||
O Indra among kings, he is approaching right toward your city. ||53||
Shaking the entire earth and agitating the oceans,
O Lord of Daityas, he deprived the aquatic creatures of their lives.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of his, Prahlāda, the best of the asuras,
spoke these meaningful words to the king of the Daityas.
Prahlāda said:
O King, such is the form of that Boar as I have heard it described;
consisting of all the gods, the Boar is considered to be beyond the reach of material nature (aprākṛta). ||56||
Therefore, you must act in such a way that he does not delude us;
having reached a firm decision, O Lord of Daityas, let it be carried out without delay. (57)
It is clearly intended by Brahmā that this form of the Boar, which bears the discus and the plough, is composed of all the gods. 58.
O Lord of the Dānavas, you are incapable of being slain by any of the gods;
this illusion was indeed created by them because they were powerless, and not otherwise.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa spoke these meaningful words to the Daityas and Dānavas: [8.100.60]
Hiraṇyākṣa said:
"If this evil-minded slayer of my brother comes here, today at long last that desire in my heart will be fulfilled. (61)
Today, having repeatedly cut that evil-souled slayer of my brother in battle, I shall offer him as a beautiful sacrifice to Paśupati.
Today, O Daityas, having severed from his body that head with its wondrous eyes and earrings, I shall offer it to Rudra, the Supreme Self.
That Keśava was not encountered by me previously in that battle;
today, having encountered him, I shall send him to the abode of Yama.
Now, when he is slain, all the gods will become hopeless and overwhelmed by fear; falling into a state of helplessness, they will surely fall into servitude. (65)
Sanatkumāra said: Then he spoke to the heroic Dānavas and the exceedingly powerful Daityas,
those Dānavas renowned by the name of Kiṅkaras.
"O you of great strength, go those ten thousand [soldiers] and find out who this is;
then I myself shall go. || 67 ||
Thus addressed, all those great Māyās emerged delighted;
the foot soldiers were armored, having bound on their leather finger-guards and gauntlets.
Those sons of the Dānavas and Daityas were possessed of great strength, adorned with golden variegated garments, necklaces, and threads.
Uttering many cries and greatly provoked, they went forth just like venomous serpents. ||69||
Thus ends the hundredth chapter, titled "The Command to the Kiṅkaras," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having emerged with speed, those Daityas and Dānavas were clad in armor.
They rushed toward the boar like terrified deer toward a lion. ||1||
O Vyāsa, those lords of the Asuras, being led away by that boar-eyed one, appeared like bound sacrificial animals consecrated for slaughter. ||2||
Having struck them down with the rod of Kṛtānta and bound them with the noose of Death,
he then led those Daityas away like a man leading cattle.
Having traveled eight yojanas, they all beheld the boar who had emerged from the waters of the ocean, like small animals seeing a lion.
Having gazed at him for a mere moment, those enraged Daityas and Dānavas rushed about on all sides, stretching their bows.
Then, observing those Daityas as they were rushing toward him from all sides, that most powerful lord of boars spoke these words: ||6||
Varāha said:
"O sons of Diti, why do you all attack me from every side?
I do not harm you in any way, nor am I your enemy."
Then, as he was speaking thus, all those sons of Diti, the Daityas, filled with great wonder, surrounded that Boar and asked:
"Who are you here in the form of a boar, having crossed the ocean by your own power?"
For what purpose have you come here, or where indeed are you to go? ||9||
Having heard those words of theirs, that noble-minded and great boar,
whose voice was like the rumbling of a cloud, then spoke to all the Dānavas.
"I am Varāha; behold my form such as it is!
I have come to this region for the purpose of wandering about, of this there is no doubt. (1)
O foremost of Daityas, having had my wife stolen by another, I am despondent;
as I wander about, I am reflecting upon the household of that wicked man.
The Dānavas said:
"This is not your way; this is the abode of the Daityas.
Disregarding the Daityas, how have you come to this place? (13)
"O lowest of the deer species, we shall all slay you today;
having killed you, we shall indeed carry you before the Lord of the Daityas. (14)
Then all those Dānavas struck him violently with their excellent weapons,
just as uplifted clouds strike a mountain with rain.
Though being struck by those Daityas, that powerful Lord in the form of a boar, possessed of immense strength, spoke these words to them. (16)
"O best of Asuras, I have not committed even the slightest offense against you here; nor shall I commit one, nor do I commit one now. (17)
"For what purpose do you all strike me with sharp weapons as if against an enemy?
Indeed, there is no enmity between you here, nor is there any business for me with you. (18)
"Now, O Dānavas, if you have need of my flesh, then kill me;
however, let my life not be taken by sharp weapons, for I have no fear of you. (19)
"O sons of Diti, I stand here with these two arms outstretched;
when you all come to a standstill, then I shall slay you all. (8.101.20)
"Today, O Daityas, you shall know the strength of the deer here;
for you are intoxicated from having conquered the gods, and I shall destroy that pride of yours. (21)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that venerable Vyāsa stood with his two arms extended like Indra’s banner, rising up like the Lord Śaṅkara himself.
Having heard those words of his, those Dānavas, overwhelmed with rage and exerting themselves intensely, struck him violently with various weapons and missiles in their hands. ||23||
As a great wind disperses the clouds, as Garuḍa [disperses] serpents, as a tiger [overcomes] deer, and as a lion [subdues] hares; ||24||
O venerable Vyāsa, like a fire kindled by oblations or an elephant [surrounded] by jackals, so was that Blessed One Varāha, the increaser of joy. ||25||
Being tormented by them, he stood firm like a mountain, counting [the blows];
when he was struck by those arrows, as well as by maces, clubs, and spears, ||26||
Being struck by slings, bhuśuṇḍī weapons, swords, iron-tipped arrows,
and many other such missiles, the lord of beasts shone forth invisible; then all of them were exceedingly delighted.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, as they were roaring, the Boar, the increaser of joy,
emerged from the heap of weapons and crushed their heads.
He tore them apart with his two hands, his two feet, and his fangs;
he cut down others with the weapons released by them and let out a roar.
All of them were likewise torn apart by his hands, feet, fangs, and the tips of his tusks, from which their weapons had been cast off.
"Like great accumulations of wealth being constantly consumed by many, they are utterly exhausted.
Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, "The Battle with the Kiṅkaras," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, seeing that they had all been slain by the boar,
one who had escaped with great difficulty entered the city of Aśmaka.
Having gone there, with disheveled hair, covered in dust, and drenched in blood, he spoke these words at the door of that assembly hall.
"O Daityas, announce this to the wise lord of the Dānavas!
Thus urged, the gatekeeper, with his weapon raised, announced it to the king. (3)
Those best of asuras who had gone to see that king of beasts—all those sons of Diti were indeed slain by him through his prowess. (4)
"Do not fall into negligence, O Lord of Daityas; do not despise the Lord of Beasts.
Do not wait for time, nor recognize him as a mere deer.
He is great; of this there is no doubt, and he cannot be conquered by the Dānavas. (5)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, the great asura Hiraṇyākṣa,
becoming violently enraged, then sprang up from his seat.
He rose up like the banner of Indra, roaring like a rain-cloud,
his face contorted with a frown, blazing like a fire enveloped in smoke.
Then, as he rose from there, the Daityas and the Dānava Vipracitti bowed and spoke these words to the Daitya in smooth syllables and phrases: ||| 8 ||
"You are the king of all the Daityas and the bringer of victory to all beings;
while we remain here, it is not fitting for you to exert yourself yourself. (9)
"O Great King, having slain him along with the gods and those who are his protectors, we shall cut off his flesh and bring it here. (8.102.10)
Of the Ādityas, along with the Rudras, the Vasus, and also the Aśvins;
together with the Pitṛs of the Bhṛgus, and likewise of the Aṅgirases. (11)
And whatever Viśvedevas there may be, as well as the Sādhyas;
and of the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas, together with the Uragas.
O Daitya, the Gandharvas, birds, and humans—
even those exerting themselves along with the world-protectors and Death himself—
are capable of warding off and slaying those evil-minded ones.
And when it is time for their suppression, do not depart from here yourself;
behold today, O son of Diti, how we shall strike them down with our efforts,
wherever our king, master, and lord of subjects commands us.
"We shall all carry that out with our heads bowed, there is no doubt;
O best of Asuras, whatever task we are unable to perform,
you yourself shall perform it— do not look upon us as if we were strangers."
"For the sake of the deer, the king himself, who is a Daitya of great strength, has gone out;
there are no other Daityas, yet they will speak of his power.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that king commanded all the Daityas,
just as Indra at the proper time commands the clouds that possess the luster of crushed collyrium;
and having received his command, those Daityas were filled with joy.
Those of great stature put on their armor and mounted their vehicles. || 19 ||
Prahlāda and Anuhlāda, Śini and Bāṣkala,
as well as Jambha, Kujambha, Vātāpi, Ilvala, and Virocana.
Bali, Bāṇa, Vāta, Śambhu, Kaśyapa, the massive-bodied Śambara, and Kālaśambara; ||21||
Pradīpta, Asiloman, and Śili; the Dānavas Śarabha and Śalabha, as well as the Dānava Dhundhu and Mūka;
and the famous Śatodara, as well as another, Hradodara. ||22||
Tāra, Tāraka, Maya, and the renowned Kāla. ||23||
Aja, Namuci, Vyaṃsa, Kārtasvana, Śubha, Ilvaka, Vilvaka, Vipāka, and Pāka. ||24||
Hastin and Duryodhana, as well as the Dānava Vipracitti;
Hayagrīva and Mura, Naraka and Kuṇḍa as well. ||25||
Śakuni, Vṛṣaparvan, Śataketu, Mahārava, Saraka, Rāhu, Svarbhānu, and Kāla; ||26||
Virādha, Kabandha, Dundubhi, Śatadundubhi, both Śālva and Druma, as well as Mayūragrīva—these were they. (27)
Kālanemi, Meghanāda, the very heroic Andhaka,
Mahiṣa, Ānanda, Śamaka, Vāṭi, and Baka—
then these tigers among the Dānavas, possessed of great illusion and great strength. ||28||
All were experts in every weapon and had attained their mark in combat;
O Vyāsa, with chariots, horses, and elephants, as well as others on foot, they went forth to slay that boar like gods against an asura.
And that powerful Lord Varāha, the increaser of joy and possessed of great splendor, being thus praised by the sages dwelling within himself,
slew all those servants and went to the city of Aśmaka.
Roaring like a cloud at the end of an eon, releasing a torrent of rain.

Having gone there at that time, O Vyāsa, the Lord, who consists of the world, turned to his right and approached the southern gate. There, he was fiercely assailed by many Dānavas stationed at the southern gate.
By him the cry of "Halāhala! was raised, by which the city was provoked to anger.
For he, the Imperishable One, having shattered the *śataghnīs*, the door-panels, the sledgehammers, the wheels of time, and the mechanical engines, reduced them all to powder. (34–35)
Then those great chariot-warriors of the Dānavas arrived, possessed by intense fury,
covering the Lord of Beasts with a fierce shower of weapons.
Then he was struck by them with javelins, discuses, and bhindipālas.
Having abandoned the gate and emerged, he took refuge on level ground.
O Vyāsa, even though they knew him to be broken, those asuras then pursued him from behind, striking him with excellent weapons. || 37-38 ||
Being carved by showers of arrows, *tomaras*, great maces, clubs, and iron-tipped spears,
he then emerged and fought the sons of Diti, presided over by the hosts of gods.
Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Instruction to the Asuras," in the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, having reached level ground, he spoke deeply to all those bulls among the Dānavas, like a lion to deer in a lonely place.
"O lords of the Dānavas, all you Dānavas and Daityas of great strength,
while I fight again most fiercely in battle as a deer,
there is no shame for you to come forward in the fray."
Or perhaps you have no strength at all, for it is through deceit that the gods have been conquered by you. ||3||
"I am a powerful forest-dwelling deer, and I do not think that you possess the wisdom for a righteous battle, O best of Dānavas. (4)
"I possess no bow whatsoever, nor any such weapon by which I might fight with you many armed lords of the asuras. Therefore,
if you so intend, cast away your weapons now."
And by me, one by one, you shall all fight, abiding in righteousness.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of his, Sunda, the lord of the Dānavas,
spoke to all the lords of the Daityas, roaring like a cloud at the end of a Yuga.
"It is exactly as this great chariot-warrior Mṛgasura has said:
'Let us cast aside our weapons today and fight one against one.'"
Prahlāda said:
O lords of the Daityas, this is a lack of wisdom, just as this lowest of beasts [has spoken].
Among equals, a battle with equals is what is praised. (9)
"Neither weapons nor the strength of arms belong to the deer;
yet they are always slain by weapons—this is the dharma recognized by the virtuous. How then can we, the lords of the Dānavas, abandon our own dharma?"
Adopting the nature of deer, let us fight like beasts.
"This lowest of deer, being of wicked conduct, is not to be slain by those such as us;
let there be no consideration whatsoever regarding this deer. (12)

"O lords of the asuras, has this wicked-souled one, some defiler of the gods, ever been heard of or seen resorting to illusion? This evil-minded being desires to deceive us. "And where, O lords of the asuras, has such a thing been heard or seen among deer?"
He engaged in hand-to-hand wrestling with men in battle, just like a human being.
This Viṣṇu is ill-behaved and evil-minded; a thorn to the Daityas, he remains here having resorted to illusion because he is incapable of his own prowess.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O Vyāsa, that powerful lord of the Asuras, filled with rage, overwhelmed him with many arrows from his bow and let out a roar.
Andhaka and Vipracitti— all those Daityas and Dānavas—
besieged him with sharp arrows by the hundreds and thousands.
Then Daiva, having been deeply pierced by those enraged Dānavas,
shone like the Himalayas struck by the rays of the sun.
Having exerted great speed and brandishing his sharp arrows,
the god proceeded with ease toward the Dānava Prahlāda.
Having suddenly reached him, he [attacked] his charioteer and the chariot itself.
And with his fangs and his hands, he indeed reduced him to nothing but a name.
Then, leaping down from his chariot even while being struck by the Dānavas,
the god struck that Daitya on the head with the chariot’s banner-staff.
Then Prahlāda, having leaped up, struck the enraged god on the chest with his club of terrifying form, just as an obstacle strikes one established in dharma.
Struck by him, the god then abandoned his chariot.
He returned to that very place where he had previously been stationed.
Then Andhaka, Vipracitti, Śambara, and Kālaśambara pierced Nandivardhana with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
O Vyāsa, pierced at that time by those straight-knotted arrows and being split in many ways, he moved in circular maneuvers.
At times he leaps and roars like a lion,
and at times he casts himself upon the ground in battle like a tiger.
Having spread his bow, that one of great heroism stood firm, enduring the arrows;
then, rising on his foot, he shook them off like a bull.
Like a bird, the lord of beasts then circled in circles through the sky and then stood motionless like a mountain, while the boar remained as he was.
Having thus traversed many kinds of paths, the mighty one,
roaring aloud, seized the two chariots with his hands with great speed;
the powerful one [seized] that of Vipracitti, and the radiant one [seized] that of Andhaka.
Having whirled them around for a moment, those two, together with their horses and their charioteers, [were struck down].
Having lifted them up, he threw them onto the ground and again struck them with his foot;
while they were still mounted on their chariot, he struck them once more upon the head.
Raising their clubs with great fury and moving with speed,
those two struck Varāha on the head simultaneously and roared.
Powerful and enraged, with blood-red eyes, he seized the two clubs with his hands,
just as the lord of beasts seizes them by force.
Then Janārdana,
who was highly skilled with the mace, performed many various and wonderful foot-strikes in a perfectly correct manner.
Then the drawn-in, the scattered, and the non-scattered circle;
likewise the raised, the scattered, the released, and the running. ||35||
The turned-back, the returned, and also the half-moon;
the supported, the raised, and likewise the swan’s whirl. ||36||
Skilled in the mace, having properly whirled it in various circles,
he hurled the mace above Andhaka, making it resound.
And the powerful Nandivardhana [fought] against Aparā and Vipracitti;
those two Dānavas were exceedingly swift and very difficult to approach with their maces.
Having deceived Varāha in battle, the two Dānavas rushed toward him once more,
like two portents of destruction springing with great speed toward their destined place.
As they were both rushing toward him, that immensely powerful Varāha struck Andhaka with his fist and slew Vipracitti with his foot.
Andhaka seized his fist and Vipracitti his foot;
both Daityas, enraged, cried out, "You are slain! (41)
Like two dark clouds thundering at the proper time,
those two then seized that high-souled one, the best of gods.
Kāśyapa leapt into the sky with speed like the king of birds;
standing in the air, that lord of beasts shone brightly as he carried the two Daityas.
Like Garuḍa, the lord of birds, roaring in the sky and shaking his arms, that powerful one [seized] the elephant and the tortoise for the sake of devouring them.
And he kicked his foot at those two Daityas, who were like two serpents;
seeing them thus struck, O Vyāsa, those two Dānavas, intoxicated with the pride of battle— (45)
The two of them rushed toward the earth like two terrible thunderbolts fallen from the sky;
and that powerful Lord of Gods, Varāha, the increaser of joy,
crushed all the chariots of the Daityas.
Seizing someone by the forehead-piece of his chariot, he hurled him into the great ocean;
striking another with his foot, he brought him to union with the dust.
Having struck down a chariot with a chariot, a foot-soldier with a foot-soldier,
and an elephant with an elephant, he sent them to the abode of Yama.
Sanatkumāra said: All those tigers among the Daityas and Dānavas were put to flight; overcome with supreme shame, they retreated according to their strength.
Seeing one another's faces, all those heroes who had conquered the lords of the asuras were filled with shame; they once again addressed the Lord Varāha... [as follows]. (8.103.50)
Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, "The Battle with Varāha," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, then those Dānavas, roaring fiercely, [pursued] that deer.
Then, filled with intense rage, they hacked him severely with their weapons.
Like deer attacking a tiger, or elephants a lion cub,
the enraged Dānavas struck him— the Boar— with showers of missiles.
And that tiger among deer, having approached the great ocean, drank it down as he sat there, like the submarine fire entering the mouth of the mare.
In the same way, thousands of weapons were hurled at him by those Daityas.
Opening his vast mouth wide, he swallowed and roared.
Having devoured all those weapons,
that one of great strength rushed toward the Dānavas with the force of another ocean.
As a lion toward elephants, as the king of the śarabhas toward lions,
as Garuḍa toward serpents, and as a tiger toward deer;
as the wind toward a mass of clouds, and as the king of birds toward pigeons.
In that same way, O Vyāsa, that Blessed One, the protector of the world, [acted] toward the Dānavas.
He exerted such force that his mind was swiftly directed toward the senses;
and having encountered those Daityas, he, whose roar was like that of a great cloud,
put them all to flight, just as Rudra scatters herds of animals.
Highly enraged, he struck some with his feet and others with his hands.
There, with his fangs, he dispatched others to the abode of Yama;
with his snout, he struck Śambara and Kālaśambara down to the earth.
He swiftly struck Naraka with a kick, Hayagrīva with his fist,
and both Namuci and Mahāmāya with his chest.
Striking again and again, the enraged guardian of the gods felled them;
and as he was thus putting them to flight and roaring like a lion,
Vipracitti struck that boar on the chest with his fist.
He struck the fierce Vipracitti in the side with his fist.
Struck by the boar, he, frantic with rage,
once again struck that boar in the chest with his sword, making it resound.
Unable to endure that blow, the exceedingly powerful boar struck the Daitya on the head with his fist, which was like a thunderbolt.
Then, whirled by that blow from the discus, the Daitya fell violently upon the earth like a tree struck down by the wind. Approaching Vipracitti as he lay fallen, the Lord of Creatures [spoke].
The Lord of Gods seized with his two feet the son of Diti as he was fleeing.
Then, having whirled him around and roared repeatedly, the powerful and high-souled Nandivardhana hurled him toward the city.
Thus hurled by him, the mighty lord of the Dānavas shone forth.
Like a cloud cut through by the blazing flashes of lightning. || 1.9 ||
With his pearl necklace and garments slipping off, and his garlands and ornaments falling away,
he fell with great force upon the palace of Hiraṇyākṣa—
a mansion situated like a celestial chariot, complete with towers and upper chambers.
O Vyāsa, it crushed that vehicle as a thunderbolt crushes the king of mountains.
Then, by that great sound, Hiraṇyākṣa himself,
the son of Diti and lord of the Dānavas, arrived with speed and beheld him.
That tiger among Dānavas was likewise being tormented by the boar.
And because of that very distress, he became senseless for a moment. ||23||
Then the king, the son of Diti, comforted him with cool water,
with many palm-leaf fans, and with jewels.
Once he had recovered and risen, he sat down upon an excellent seat.
The king, having come to a state of great astonishment, questioned that Daitya. ||25||
Hiraṇyākṣa said: "O Daitya, by whom has the Himalaya today, or the earth with its oceans,
been suddenly lifted up by one of great strength, as if by Viśvakarman?"
By whom has Mandara been cast down today? By whom has Death been defeated?
O Lord of the Dānavas, by whom have you been thrown; who is the powerful one on earth? (27)
