Just as the weighing of the earth or the shaking of Mount Mandara, so too is this great destruction of yours like the death of Death itself. 28.
Resembling Rudra, Indra, and Death, and terrifying to the world-protectors—by whom have you been equaled in battle, like a strong man by one who is weak? (29)
Whose is this inexhaustible strength? By whom has such great strength of arms been proclaimed throughout the three worlds? O Lord of the Dānavas, let it be told.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of his, that exceedingly powerful Dānava sighed deeply and, looking at him again and again, spoke to him.
Vipracitti said:
"O King, this is superhuman, and likewise it surpasses even the gods;
O Lord of Daityas, it also surpasses the Daityas themselves, for such a thing has never been seen or heard of anywhere. (32)
Such strength as belongs to Varāha is not found anywhere else;
indeed, O King, I do not perceive anyone equal to that great-souled one.
O Lord of Daityas, even while being hacked by many missiles and weapons in battle, he felt no pain nor any suffering, and his consciousness was not lost.
O King, for one who has been bitten even by a mosquito, there would be no relief;
yet for one who slays the Daityas and Dānavas, there is likewise no fear.
Just as a lion [devours] small deer, or as a serpent [swallows] frogs,
so did he seize all those lords of the Daityas and Dānavas.
I do not consider him to be a deer, nor a god, nor even an asura;
some misfortune has surely befallen the sons of Diti. (37)
Struck on the head by that fist, I fell to the ground;
having been seized, I was suddenly lifted up and dropped upon your house. (38)
O Dānava, I do not know the whereabouts of the Dānavas, the Daityas, and the others; I believe they have all been slain. (39)
"He is invincible, possessed of great splendor and strength, while we are weak.
Having heard this, do that which is for the benefit of the sons of Diti.
All the sages together with the deities are seen within her limbs;
it is my thought today that she has been created for your sake as a magical creation (kṛtyā). 41.
O Lord of Daityas, turn back your mind which is resolved upon battle;
act instead for the welfare of the Daityas.
"The Daityas are powerful and heroic, while we are mere mortals and he is immortal;
he is invincible, yet the Daityas have been conquered. Do not involve us in battle. (43)
"Having abandoned the city of Aśmaka, we have all taken refuge at Samudrastambha.
O King, let us remain here; do not engage in battle with him again.
Do not despise this Daitya in any way, thinking, 'He is but a deer; he is a deer.'"
In the past, Narasiṃha was also a deer, but he was destroyed by him.
O Daitya, as long as you remain, bringing happiness to the Dānavas, all the gods will continue to live; of this there is no doubt.
"Let not the sons of Diti and the very foolish sons of Danu be provoked to anger;
O Lord of Asuras, let us depart from this city in every direction.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa spoke to the lord of the Dānavas, who was terrified of that great-souled one. ||48||
Without doubt, O best of Dānavas, that deer is a great-souled being by whom you, who are like Mount Mandara and possessed of immense strength, were weighed in the balance. 49.
O bull among the asuras, four thousand great divine years have passed while I have enjoyed sovereignty;
now five hundred [years] have arrived, and during that time the gods have been destroyed.
Though once powerful through many terrible battles, I have become like one who is weak;
though I am thus endowed with strength and have enjoyed a kingdom free from thorns, how shall I remain, having entered the water in fear like a serpent? (51-52)

O Lord of the Dānavas, if that Viṣṇu should appear in the form of a deer or assume the form of a boar, that shall be my task; do not fear. My strength, too, is inexhaustible, and therefore I am powerful.

"O Daitya of great strength, what regard could he have for this mere deer, he who abandoned his own form out of fear of me and took the form of a beast? He who would slay an elephant in battle, as well as a lion or even a *śarabha*— " ||54-55||
Out of fear of me, that boar, presided over by all the gods, challenges me, O Lord of Daityas;
therefore, victory shall indeed be mine.
"O Daitya, you alone shall be my messenger;
therefore, O bull among the Dānavas, go with haste to the world of death, [to tell] that slayer of my brother, who brings terror to the Dānavas. (57)
"I shall not return without having slain him; I swear this by my truth, O Dānava! (58)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having then commanded the charioteer, he had the chariot readied;
to console his wives, he entered the house once again. (59)
Having been honored there with auspicious rites by them, and having gazed upon all those sons of Diti from every side,
that one of great strength took up everything splendid and fit for battle, capable of warding off enemies.
Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Felling of Vipracitti," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having equipped himself with a bow, armor, and having bound on his leather arm-guards and finger-protectors, he [set forth].
With quivers fastened to his back, carrying arrows and a sword, he was possessed of great strength. ||1||
He had a tawny beard, four fangs, spike-like ears, and large jaws; his arms reached down to his knees, his eyes were long, and his body was as well-proportioned as a banyan tree.
He holds a lotus and a conch in his two hands, and a wheel and a fish on his two feet;
he has webbed hands, webbed feet, and a small penis.
With eyes resembling the rising sun and a countenance like a mountain of collyrium,
O Vyāsa, he then went forth with his face adorned by a frown.
And at the gate, he saw by the charioteer a chariot prepared, measuring a thousand nalvas, and equipped with divine horses. || 5 ||
O Vyāsa, accompanied by ten thousand [attendants] and provided with all necessary implements,
and joined by his skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) and a banner possessing the brilliance of the sun,
he ascended while being told "Victory! by many Dānavas at that time.
Just as the divine Sun, the lord of lights, shines upon his chariot,
so did that son of Diti shine while mounted upon that chariot;
he was like a sapphire set within a golden vessel.
The crown upon his head shone with great brilliance,
like a forest fire situated on the peak of a mountain of collyrium.
And that Daitya urged his charioteer toward his destination.
Beside him stood Vyāsa, and Vipracitti was stationed like a counter-sign against a banner in the sky.
There were conchs, kettledrums, clay drums, tabors, and flutes. || 8.105.10–11 ||
As musical instruments were being played, King Hiraṇyākṣa departed from the city of Aśmaka;
O Vyāsa, all the gods went before him, behind him, and on both his sides, just as the planets surround the sun.
And as he was departing from the city, birds appeared, foreboding fear.
Vyāsa, the lord of the Daityas, saw them but did not take them to heart; meanwhile,
a serpent with a black body cut off his path,
and a vulture with a red mouth perched upon the top of his banner.
As his chariot moved along, a vulture circled above it;
the great banner of the chariot, possessing immense luster, snapped,
and the left side of his body throbbed again and again.
The horses did not neigh and the elephants became devoid of their rut;
these and many other such things occurred, O best of sages, regarding the Daitya.
He repeatedly observed omens that portended danger to himself;
then, having gone out from the city not very far, he beheld the lord of beasts.
The Dānava beheld him fighting fearlessly in the fray;
that illustrious and powerful chief of the Daityas, his eyes bloodshot with rage,
drew his great bow and rushed forward on his chariot.
The mighty-armed Varāha, having put the sons of Diti to flight,
rushed with impetuous speed toward Suvarṇākṣa in a rage.
As he was thus swiftly attacking, the exceedingly powerful Dānava [prepared for him].
He drove many sharp-pointed arrows into all of its joints. Though pierced by those shafts in every joint, O observer of noble vows, that king of beasts did not waver; supported, it stood firm.
O Vyāsa, seeing that mighty one thus paralyzed, the gods then rendered him free from the stake with mantras that remove the shaft.
Having been freed from the stake by the gods, that great lord of beasts was restored.
Again, exerting great speed, he went toward the son of Diti.
Though being struck by many arrows, that great and imperishable lord of beasts reached the chariot of the lord of the Daityas and desired [to board] the chariot. ||24-25||
Making a loud sound as he sought to seize it, Vyāsa, assuming his universal form,
acted as the charioteer and, having formed a circle, caused that chariot to whirl about.
The Daitya bound that exceedingly powerful deer with outstretched paws using a serpent-weapon; once bound, it fell to the ground.
And as he fell, the lords of the Daityas, with various weapons in hand,
exerting themselves intensely and overcome by manifold rage, struck him violently.
Garuda swiftly liberated Nandivardhana from the lords of serpents, even as he was bound, being struck, and fallen.
Once released, that highly illustrious one then leapt up and, fleeing from the sons of Diti, swiftly charged toward the chariot of Hiraṇyākṣa.
As he was running, the Daitya again [struck] him with a straight-knotted arrow.
O Vyāsa, roaring like a thundercloud, he pierced him in the heart;
and that lord of beasts, his heart pierced, fell to the ground overcome by delusion, like the banner of Indra at the conclusion of a festival. ||3.1-3.2||
Then a cry of "Alas! Alas! was raised by all the assembled leaders of the gods;
the sages offered hymns of praise to him, and the Sun became lusterless.
Then he was restored there by the sages, the foremost knowers of Brahman.
Having then regained consciousness, he spoke these words: ||34||
"O gods, strengthen me quickly; I am utterly bewildered.
This Daitya cannot be fought in battle by one of little prowess. (35)
Then all those deities and the sages whose wealth is austerity completely gratified that god with their own ascetic power. Indeed,
as he was being nourished by the sages and the deities, [he grew strong].
His form shone with a splendor equal to the fire at the end of an eon and to Death itself.
Blazing, that Great-Souled One appeared resplendent, praised by all the gods and the ṛṣis;
then the God of Gods, like seven suns combined, seemed as if he would consume the worlds.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Nourishment of Varāha," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, having been thus nourished, he became powerful and possessed the radiance of the sun.
Moving in circles, he performs various, numerous, and rapid maneuvers;
having performed leaps like a lion, he gazes about once;
then, turning both backward and forward, he acts again like an elephant.
Again, opening his mouth wide, he swallowed the weapons of his enemies;
again, with trees and rocks, he slaughtered the Dānavas;
and again, becoming a traveler through the sky, he glided about like the king of birds.
Then, filled with rage, he laughed again, a sound resembling the crash of a thunderbolt.
And again, making himself subtle, he stood before him;
thus did the Dānava leap about and roar.
With a face contorted by a frown, Hiraṇyākṣa spoke, making the earth resound:
"O wretched deer, O evil-minded one, you shall not obtain liberation!
Having slain you, I shall offer you as a sacrifice to Rudra with my own might."
"My eldest brother was slain by you, O evil-minded one, through deceit;
today you have reaped the fruit of that deed, you wicked soul.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of Hiraṇyākṣa in the battle,
the Blessed Viṣṇu, proceeding with wrath, spoke to the son of Diti:
"That powerful Daitya has been slain by me in the form of Narasiṃha."
Having displayed your prowess in battle, your own death is likewise certain;
even if you were to go to the sky, or to the netherworld, or beyond this,
or to a mountain or the ocean, even then you would not escape.
O Asura, whatever strength you possess, whatever ascetic power, and whatever illusion you have—
all that, along with your life itself, I shall expel from your body this very day.
Hiraṇyākṣa said:
"You were pinned down by me with arrows and released by the gods through mantras; furthermore, when you were bound again by a weapon, the king of birds liberated you. (1-2)
"O evil-minded one, you have died again and were brought back to life by the gods;
yet I shall kill you once more, like a lion kills a deer in the wilderness. (13)
What power do you have here today, other than the boon of Maheśvara, even to touch me with your hand, like a man [attempting to touch] a fire? 14.
Having resorted to this body composed of the elements and presided over by them all,
you have come against me in battle, having been nourished by them all.
I am endowed with my own ascetic power and strength;
nevertheless, you are not able to overcome me today, just as a deer cannot prevail over a lion.
Whether to fight or even to advance together with the gods, that evil-minded one is incapable; for this indeed is the very great difference between us two.
He who is of noble birth, or learned, or established on the path of the virtuous, should consider himself already victorious by this alone and abandon the battle. (18)
Who else but you could be so pitiless, shameless, a striker at vulnerable points, and evil-minded? This does not belong to a mere beast, nor is it characteristic of a Daitya. (19)

"You have not brought about my death; rather, I shall slay you in combat. Let these Siddhas and thousands of Cāraṇas behold the difference between us as we fight in many ways in this battle. (8.106.20)
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, the enraged Hiraṇyākṣa struck the Boar— who possessed a splendor like that of a thunderbolt— with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Then, although being tormented by him, the exceedingly powerful boar,
filled with rage, rushed forward with speed, letting out a roar as he seized the chariot.
Having grabbed it by the pole, he violently shook it and tossed it about with great force.
The god hurled him along with his horse and charioteer, and he let out a roar.
But by his thrusts and side-blows, those horses had their traces severed;
the excellent chariot reeled about, and its joints became dislocated.
Then the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa, abandoning his chariot and standing on foot with his bow, struck the lion-king with a bewildering weapon (mohana-astra). ||25||
Delusion indeed overcame that god Nandivardhana;
however, by the power of the mantras of the gods, he was once again freed from delusion.
Indeed, this lord of the Daityas, filled with rage, struck him with various kinds of weapons,
yet he did not inflict any pain upon him.
Then that boar of great splendor, as if laughing,
uprooted a tree with speed and struck the Daitya on the head.
By that blow, as the Daitya was struck,
his bow fell with force, along with his five-fingered hand-guard.
Then, crying out "Alas! Alas!", the Daityas and Dānavas, deeply distressed, furiously struck the Boar with many weapons. (8.106.30)
Being struck by those Daityas, that one of great strength opened his mouth wide;
he swallowed all their weapons and let out a roar.
Seeing him thus transformed, the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa,
filled with rage, took up his trident while uttering "Salutation to Rudra."

Then the enraged Daitya hurled at Varāha a great trident of immense brilliance and loud roar, resembling the fire at the end of an eon. As it came rushing toward him, roaring in many ways and vomiting forth flames and sparks—
Seeing this, all the gods and hosts of Siddhas, their minds bewildered by fear, cried out, "Alas! Alas! (34).
Thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Hurling of the Trident," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
The deer did not see the trident as it was rushing toward him with great speed.
Intent on the alliance with the Daityas, he [created] that which causes fear to all living beings.
O Vyāsa, struck in the heart by that spear which remained unnoticed, the son of Indrāṇī fell down as if dead.
Then, O best of sages, the invisible spirits raised a cry of "Alas!
Alas!", the oceans overflowed their shores, and the sun became lusterless. (3)
Meteors fell everywhere, the flowers of the gods withered, there was a battle among the planets, and celestial chariots crashed down. (4)
When Varāha had thus fallen, all the sages cried out;
then, having paid homage to Mahādeva, Brahmā called him to mind.
Then everything became free from darkness and auspicious as before;
having paid homage to Mahādeva, Varāha rose up.
The divine, Maheśvara’s splendor entered Madhusūdana;
his body invigorated by that, Mādhava drew forth the trident.
Suddenly that mighty one became like fire;
then, with that very spear, the delighter of the gods [struck] that Daitya.
Enraged, he struck the Krauñca in the heart with his spear, just as Guha did; yet,
though his heart was pierced by that boar,
O Vyāsa, the great Asura felt no pain, remaining like a wise man in the midst of hardship.
Having split it in the middle and drawn out that trident, he cast it aside;
then, drawing his sword with speed, he struck Varāha on the head. By that excellent blow, Varāha Nandivardhana—
O Vyāsa, he did not suffer any pain; drenched in blood, he became like the Himavat mountain, variegated with its various minerals.
The divine Boar, the crusher of all asuras, shone forth;
O observer of noble vows, with a blow of his open hand, he caused the sword to fall from the hand of that Daitya who desired to strike him again.
Then both of them, who were skilled in wrestling, engaged in combat.
Like two elephants in a rage, like two buffaloes in their pride,
like two lions roaring, like two bulls in fury,
like two śarabhas exerting themselves, and like two tigers devoid of mercy— so were they.
Desiring victory over one another, they fought each other with goads,
hand-ropes, lassos, and maneuvers for retreating; again with various circular movements, as well as with advances and withdrawals.
With palms, fists, arms, and even feet,
with nails and teeth, as well as other means, those two of great strength thus engaged in combat,
both the god and the demon.
Eighteen days, as well as another fourteen,
and another thousand years passed; that was the human time there, and from that the Daitya became powerful.
Perceiving that powerful lord of the Daityas to be declining, a disembodied voice of very beautiful sound spoke thus in the sky: ||21||
Listen to this, O divine Varāha, and having heard it, act accordingly.
Indeed, this exceedingly powerful Daitya cannot be slain by you in this manner. ||22||
"Surely this cruel one has been rendered weak by Maheśvara;
behold him indeed through his splendor, for his time has now come."
"Having released this king of the Daityas, destroy him with your discus;
O Vaikuṇṭha, he shall then meet his death by means of the Māheśvara [weapon].
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having agreed to that, the Blessed One Nandivardhana released the king of the Daityas, striking him on the chest with his foot.
Released by that god, the bull among the Daityas shone forth like the sun released from its eclipse by Rāhu, the son of Siṃhikā.
The Blessed One, beholding that Daitya blazing with splendor,
then remembered his discus and paid homage to the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Then, O Vyāsa, all the directions appeared like fire-pits,
and there arose a tremendous sound resembling the clouds at the end of an eon;
the Siddhas fell to the earth, and fear entered the gods.
"May there be well-being for all beings," the sages then said.
The oceans dried up, and the nāgas and birds perished;
all the daityas and dānavas likewise entered into a hole.
Terrified by fear, living beings dropped firebrands from the sky as the brilliantly shining discus approached like the fire at the end of an eon.
That great wheel has edges like razors; it destroys aquatic creatures that sink within it.
It is difficult to behold, all-destroying, impenetrable, and striking down its foes. ||32||
Then, an unimpeded divine spear, capable of bewildering all embodied beings and possessing a sound like a hundred thunderbolts, came into the hand of Varāha.
Beholding it falling from every direction, all living beings [were struck with fear].

They fell to the ground in great terror, seeing nothing at all. Then that god, assuming a vast and imperishable form that pervaded the three worlds, let out a roar and hurled [his weapon] toward the Dānava.
Resembling the fire at the end of an eon, with edges sharp as razors and rending the sky,
it swiftly struck the Dānava as if burning all the directions.
O son of Śakti, that tiger among Dānavas, remaining unperturbed, struck the approaching Mahāraṇa with various kinds of missiles.
And that [weapon], O Vyāsa, reduced those great discus-weapons to ashes like fire; and it departed, making a thunderous roar.
Then he brought forth an illusion consisting of fire and earth, as well as that of wind and water, and also one of darkness whose nature is the senses. (39)
In that very manner, he employed in the battle the illusion of causing flight, as well as that which causes delusion, paralyzes, turns back, and crushes; and he produced others too.
Then, with a terrifying roar, that discus destroyed them all.
Having gone there, he tore his head from his body like a mountain.
By him, that great head was severed—its mouth wide open, its fierce eyes like fire, possessing fangs and emitting most wonderful and terrifying roars; it fell like a lofty peak of Mount Meru.
With its body crushed by the wheel of the chariot, the face, devoid of luster and exceedingly dejected, no longer shone.
Like the orb of the moon at the end of the night, its rays withdrawn and its form lusterless;
like that, the severed head of the Daitya—its lower lip biting the row of teeth and repeatedly gnashing the teeth—fell down like a massive peak of a mountain. || 43–44 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
When that Daitya had been slain, all the gods offered praise.
And sages engaged in asceticism fell as showers of flowers. ||1||
Invisible celestial drums resounded with a great sound, all beings attained peace, and the world shone in its natural state. ||2||
Then the discus vanished from sight, and the gods became at ease;
likewise, the sages and the worlds beheld that Daitya slain.
All those asuras, having closed the gates of the city on every side with great effort and being fully armored, took their positions upon the ramparts.
Terrified, with disheveled hair, covered in dust, and afflicted by fear,
they stood upon the ramparts at that time, seeking to preserve their lives.
The Blessed One too, like a fire kindled by oblations with blazing flames,
searched the earth while terrifying all the asuras.
Having searched everywhere outside and uprooted the trees,
he sought her on all sides like a cowherd searching for a lost cow.
Then, uprooting mountains, he pulverized the gardens of the Daityas;
he destroyed groves and ponds, and let out a roar.
Then, having gone a short distance to the south, that best of gods reached Mount Śaṅkha and roared like a rain-cloud.
For even the Asuras, standing within their inner walls, gazed in fear at that lion as he rushed toward them from every direction.
Then that god, having uprooted the excellent mountain Śaṅkha,
beheld the earth bound and guarded by the Dānavas.
Having cast that best of mountains, Śaṅkha, into the waters of the ocean,
he slew all the Dānavas who were protecting the earth.
Then, having put the lords of the nāgas to flight and forcibly seized the earth,
he went forth, delighting the Daityas and taking all kinds of jewels from every side.
Carrying her, who was caught upon the tip of his fang,
that lord of beasts shone like a king of elephants carrying a hanging lotus stalk caught on his tusk.
Carrying her through the midst of the ocean, he shines like the Lord of Beasts;
he appears like Brahmā in the form of a boar lifting up the earth at the end of the aeon in ancient times.
Having crossed to the edge of the ocean, the Blessed One Nandivardhana indeed established that earth once again in its own place. ||16||
Then that Madhusūdana gave the three worlds to Śakra and said,
"O sinless one, you are now my king and I am your friend."
Furthermore, there will be certain others who become lords of the asuras;
I shall undoubtedly carry out their terrible slaughter as well.
Then all the sages and the deities, including Indra, [spoke].
They said, "Assuming your own form, become as you were before.
Varāha said,
"O gods, this form has been attained by me, who possess supreme splendor."
And yet, no pleasure at all comparable to this has been obtained by me anywhere on earth. || 8.108.20 ||
"Having spent some time here happily in this form, O Lord, I shall become a god once again; I tell you this truly.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, all the gods, together with Indra, circumambulated him and departed for their respective abodes in every direction. 22.
When the hosts of gods had departed, the Blessed One Nandivardhana dwelt there in happiness, having slain the preeminent Dānava.
There, assuming the forms of thousands of Ṛgvedic verses, the radiant celestial nymphs (apsarases) attended upon him; with them, he took his delight.
Wandering with them, that high-souled god Nandivardhana took his pleasure like a rutting great elephant with female elephants in the forest. ||25||
Like a lion among lionesses, or like a roaring tiger,
he took his pleasure on the shore of the ocean like another Airāvata.
As he was enjoying himself, the Siddhas and the sages whose wealth is asceticism,
stationed in the sky, caused beautiful showers of flowers to fall.
Others constantly praised him and performed circumambulations around him; all the celestial drums resounded incessantly,
and the Apsarases danced before that Boar at that time.
And the Gandharvas play instruments and sing for the Great-Souled One. ||29||
The gods, led by Indra, as well as the Yakṣas who generate merit and those who are the folk of the gods, delighted that excellent boar.
And whatever Yātudhānas there may be, and all the Brahmadhānas;
as well as humans, animals, and all the Ṛṣis. ||21||
All the royal kṣatriyas and all the various communities from every quarter arrived there, desiring to witness the auspicious festival of the Boar.
O Vyāsa, for that high-souled Varāha, there was thus a great, divine festival every day, filled with many wonders and always abounding in spectacles, which increased his joy. || 3.3 ||

That lake of his is frequented by throngs of seers, and is always resorted to by gods, perfected beings (siddhas), gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, rākṣasas, and vidyādharas together with the apsarases. || 34 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, "The Festival of Varāha," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: O son of Śakti, as he was sporting for a long time...
From his wife Citralekhā, a son named Vṛka was born.
That powerful Vṛka, constantly roaming this earth,
roared and slew hundreds of beings in the world, for he was a great one.
Then he approached Himavat, the lord of mountains and great mountain,
near Gaurīkūṭa, to the auspicious abode of Kārttikeya;
having arrived there, he then [assaulted] him with force and insolence while he was unaware.
He passed by beautiful trees adorned with jewels and gold,
which bore flowers and fruits in every season and granted all desires;
they were radiant, made of precious stones and crystals, as well as of refined gold.
Uprooting and repeatedly uprooting other stones made of yellow orpiment as well as slabs of red arsenic, he shattered them with force like one enraged;
roaring incessantly, he was like another elephant in rut.
He shattered that splendid grove of the wise Kārttikeya.
By the sound of his roaring and by the noise of the destruction of the forest,
the heroic leader of Skanda’s hosts emerged from his abode.
Known as Kokavaktra, the great-souled and powerful one, who was a firm favorite of Skanda, went and beheld Vṛka.
Having seen him—of massive body, youthful, and pleasing to behold;
roaring like a thundercloud, with his face slightly flushed with anger—[he was struck with wonder].
With a joyful heart, Kokavaktra spoke these words as if smiling:
"Whose auspicious divine abode have you, a child, arrived at here? (1.1)
Do you not know what this is? It is the residence of the great-souled Skanda, frequented by gods along with gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, and kinnaras.
Having accomplished the purpose of his beloved master and being highly honored by the Gaṇas, Kumāra departed for Mount Mandara along with all the lords of the Gaṇas. ||13||
"Having stationed me here for the sake of protection, I shall therefore ward off those [enemies] for you;
for I am pleased with your beauty, as well as with your strength and your form. (14)
Cease from this, for that reason I tell you, O one of great strength:
I shall indeed restore what has been broken exactly as it was before.
O Lord of Śūkara, for your sake I shall fully describe that God in such a way that He will not be angry with you, but will instead grant you His grace.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, that lord of beasts, Vṛka, with eyes bloodshot with rage, then spoke this to Kokavaktra. 17.
I do not fear you, O Prince, nor your evil-minded followers;
for this prince, together with his hosts and lords, is no match for my strength. (18)
Whatever strength and pride you possess, exercise it without hesitation;
I shall leave you with nothing but your names at the end, having turned this forest into a wasteland.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having uprooted a golden tree with leaves of lapis lazuli,
he hurled it at Kokavaktra and bellowed like a bull.
Then, laughing, Kokāsya seized that very tree and,
filled with rage, struck Vṛka on the head with it.
Having whirled in a circle due to that powerful blow,
the deer fell senseless upon the ground like the great banner of Śakra.
Then, seeing him fallen, Kokāsya laughed aloud and bound him with many nooses, leading him into the house.
Seeing him bound and fallen, all those deer who were his companions suddenly fled, afflicted by fear and desiring to save their lives.
Then, at that moment, he arrived surrounded by many leaders of the herd.
Kārttikeya, accompanied by his followers, was on a crying peacock;
Kokavaktra, the lord of the Gaṇas, informed him of this and showed him the mighty Vṛka bound with nooses.
Kokavaktra said:
"O Blessed One, it is said that the illustrious Vṛka was the son of the one who took the form of a boar;
he was the one by whom the Dānava Hiraṇyākṣa, a thorn to the gods, was slain. (27)
This evil-minded one, together with his companions, has destroyed your forest;
therefore, he has been bound by me with snares—now let whatever further action is required be done to him. ||28||
Skanda said:
"This lowest of the deer-tribe cannot be released by me here today;
if it were released, there would undoubtedly be censure in the world. (29)
"The god will certainly speak to me; it is Skanda who is afraid, there is no doubt—who released his son, that boar who had committed an offense. (8.109.3)
"I have been addressed and sent away today by Sthāṇu, the Supreme Self:
'Do not forgive the Boar; he might summon you. (3.1)
And this exceedingly radiant power has been granted to me by him today;
it is renowned as Saṃvartikā, the destroyer of the strength of all weapons.
"Let this evil-souled one of wicked conduct, who oppresses all the world,
be seized and swiftly executed by force!
Sanatkumāra said:
Then all the leaders of Skanda’s hosts bound him from the outside with various kinds of nooses and tormented him by the thousands.
Being dragged along, afflicted by suffering, he lamented like a man of evil conduct dwelling in hell, tightly bound by his own deeds.
Seeing him being carried away, Nārada, of great ascetic merit,
went and informed that Varāha of immeasurable soul.
"This son of yours, Vṛka, bound by numerous snares, is being led away like a sinner by the servants of Kārttikeya.
Indeed, this is not fitting for you, O God, who are striving for the sake of the world. (37)
Skanda offers obeisance out of childishness and anger;
or perhaps Skanda considers his own impurity to be more powerful than yours, and for that reason he has bound your son with your own nooses. ||38-39||
"Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, before he puts him to death,
you must go and release him without delay.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard the words of Nārada, Varāha, the increaser of joy, roared with a furious face like a cloud at the end of an eon. ||41||
Then, from his anger, a fiercely blazing fire issued forth from his two eyes,
as if destroying the entire world with its brilliance.
Rising suddenly from his seat, the god looked upward with an intense gaze.
The Lord of Beasts himself set out for the divine peak of Gaurī. ||43||
Making the entire earth tremble and being praised by the great-souled ones,
he proceeded unhindered, beholding portents that had arisen.
As that god was going, a serpent cut off his path.
The fang, having struck the tree, fell to the surface of the earth;
blood flowed from his mouth and his heart trembled. Fear arose within him there at the very moment he was struck by that blow.
The winds blew contrary to the natural order, and he fell to the earth upon his chest;
moreover, as he remembered his beloved, an intense longing arose within him.
These and many other such portents occurred, foreboding fear.
Disregarding him, that mighty lord of beasts departed indeed. ||48||
O observer of noble vows, seeing him set forth and observing the auspicious omens,
the gods in the celestial realm prepared their worship.
Followed by hosts of Siddhas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and great Nagas, he departed.
Accompanied by hosts of Rākṣasas, Cāraṇas, and Kinnaras, the high-souled one went to the peak of Gaurī.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Binding of Vṛka," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Kumāra, having emerged from his own delightful abode, at that time—
He sported together with the lords of his hosts through many auspicious games. Then the Lord brought that son of Varāha there;
releasing Vṛka from his bonds, the omnipresent one let him go while laughing.
He seized it again with speed as it was released and running away;
releasing it once more, he seized it again and again.
Thus he sported with that boar, and the boar approached him.
Seizing a massive rock, resembling the enraged Antaka,
he hurled it at Kārttikeya, roaring like a rain-cloud.
As it came hurtling through the sky, making many sounds, it bore a form equal to Death itself.
Kokāmukha seized with great force that weapon of extreme velocity, which was like a blazing meteor.
Then the Lord hurled a thousand-spoked discus, radiant as the fire at the end of an eon,
at the undistracted host of Vināyaka.
That discus, resembling the end of all things and the slayer of all enemies of the gods, quickly entered along with its attendants; then it turned back from there.
Having turned back, that discus did not perform its brilliant task once again.
At that time, Viṣṇu did not seize it and then disregarded it. Disregarded by Viṣṇu, the slayer of Dānavas, that discus then quickly departed toward its own abode.
When that wheel had then passed away, the Blessed One Nandivardhana uprooted a tree with great force and struck the prince.
Disregarding that blow, the Blessed One, the son of Agni,
in his wrath hurled the Saṃvartikā spear and let out a roar.
Scorching as it were all splendors and roaring in many ways at that time,
the spear sped forth like a divine arrow to slay the boar.
As she was thus fleeing, the Blessed One Nandivardhana,
roaring like a king of lions, struck her with various kinds of missiles with great force.
Having reduced them to ashes, that auspicious Saṃvartikā spear entered his heart like a firm and beloved woman entering her lover.
With his heart pierced by her through that supreme yoga,
he abandoned that body like a yogi and remained in another body.
Having assumed another body, that best of gods,
surrounded by all the deities, went to the abode of Bhava.
There he beheld Mahādeva, wearing a crown of matted locks.
[He was] one who had dispelled the mass of darkness by the flood of the network of rays from the crescent moon.
Seated upon an auspicious throne made of gold and adorned with jewels,
he shone exceedingly with splendor, with Pārvatī stationed at his side.
He was constantly surrounded on all sides by many hosts of various forms who could assume any shape at will and were ever fond of dance and song. (19)
Having beheld Śaṅkara, Viṣṇu, with a serene inner soul,
praised him with various hymns and spoke these words in a melodious voice.
O Blessed One, having assumed the form of a boar and exerting my prowess in battle, Hiraṇyākṣa was slain by me, who was strengthened by your splendor.
O Lord, you are the eternal cause of both creation and dissolution;
this entire world is pervaded by you, whose form is unmanifest.
"O Lord of Gods, by your grace, Brahmā, I, and Śakra, as well as the other inhabitants of heaven, are always honored in the world. || 23 ||
O Mahādeva, O Lord, when you are pleased, we are all pleased;
if you are angry, our destruction will surely follow—of this there is no doubt. (24)
To Viṣṇu, who was thus offering praise, the Blessed Lord Śaṅkara, whose crest is the crescent moon and who possesses the splendor of a thousand suns, spoke with delight.
"O Viṣṇu, I am pleased with your devotion and with your exertion for the sake of the gods' mission.
Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—whatever dwells in your mind. (26)
Viṣṇu said:
"O Lord, if you are pleased with us, and if a boon is to be granted to us, then you ought to prescribe that divine vow which removes all sins. (27)
Relying upon which, we all, together with Śakra, shall be freed from suffering and grief and conquer the Daityas in battle, fulfilling every desire. (28)
The God of gods said:
"Behold, I shall declare to you this eternal secret,
the divine Pāśupata vow, by which you shall attain all your desires."
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the gods, desiring the welfare of the deities,
took leave of the Goddess, the daughter of the mountain king, and ascended to heaven.
Then the Blessed One mounted his excellent bull, whose beautiful form was like that of the snowy mountain.
Accompanied by the hosts of gods, the Lord Śarva went to Mount Sumeru, intending to instruct him in his vow. ||31||

Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Departure of the God of Gods to the World of the Devas upon the Withdrawal of the Boar Form in the Slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said: When Mahādeva had gone to heaven to prescribe the supreme vow...
"What did the Great Goddess do immediately thereafter while she was alone?
Sanatkumāra said:
"When Mahādeva had gone to heaven, [the Goddess remained] the daughter of the best of mountains."
The highly fortunate goddesses, the mothers of the world, presented themselves;
likewise Mālinī, renowned as the daughter of Agni,
and the imperishable Śucāvatī, the daughter of the god Parjanya.
Sāvitrī, Veda-mātā, Gāyatrī, along with Durgā;
Śrī, Kīrti, Lakṣmī, as well as Dhṛti and Prajñā;
Khyāti, Diti, Danu, Aditi, Siṃhikā, and Khaśā.
Rākā, Kuhū, Sinīvālī, and likewise the auspicious Anumati;
Gaṅgā and Sarasvatī, as well as other auspicious rivers;
and those who are the wives of the Ṛṣis, of the gods, and of the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas.
And likewise for the serpents, the birds, and the gandharvas as well. || 6 ||
Having approached and paid homage to Pārvatī, all these women,
who were knowers of all dharma and devoted to the purpose of dharma, questioned her concerning dharma.
O Lord of Gods, O lady of auspicious countenance, by what dharma or by what austerity is that which is proclaimed as a very great merit, even something imperishable, attained? (8)
The Goddess said:
"O you of excellent vows, for the sake of your own welfare and that of the worlds,
I shall proclaim the Dharma exactly as it is, in its proper sequence."
Indeed, there is no gift whatsoever superior to the gift of food;
for all beings arise from food, and therefore it is remembered as the most excellent.
He who, having prepared food well, bestows it upon a twice-born man,
obtains all his desires and is honored in heaven.
The giver of food indeed goes to heaven in a celestial chariot that shines like the sun, yoked with peacocks and swans, and which fulfills all desires.
If that best of men should ever return to the human state, he will be born into a noble family, endowed with beauty, and possessed of abundant wealth and grain; moreover,
such a man would give according to his ability day after day.
By that deed, he attains the same world as Prajāpati. || 14 ||
If one should ever give consecrated food to a Brahmin,
that gift shall accrue to him a hundredfold and even a thousandfold;
it remains present in all worlds, and he shall be happy even in this world.
He was cast out, despised, and even treated with contempt.
O auspicious goddesses, whatever kind of food one may give,
even for him who is being dragged into a terrible hell by Rākṣasas,
satisfaction will attend him in many ways, by which his hunger shall be appeased.
If that man should ever again attain human birth,
he becomes a possessor of enjoyments among the Mlecchas and rejoices like an immortal;
for there is no food on earth more distinguished than this.
Food is declared to be Prajāpati, and he is considered to be the year;
the year is that sacrifice, and everything is established upon the sacrifice.
From it, all beings—both stationary and moving—come into existence.
Therefore, food is indeed superior to all things; such is the Vedic revelation.
Indeed, there is no gift whatsoever superior to the gift of food;
for all living beings arise from food, and therefore that gift is highly praised. ||22||
Listen to the fruit of the gift of one who bestows upon Brahmins water that is fragrant, cool, and endowed with divine flavors:
he obtains a celestial chariot (vimāna) resembling the sun and resounding with the voices of throngs of Apsaras. || 23 ||
Having ascended that [vehicle], he goes to heaven and attains co-residence with Varuṇa. ||24||
Having dwelt there for eighty thousand years, happy like a god, he is born into a great, unadulterated family, possessing wealth and grain. (25)

He who gives a vessel full to the brim to a Brāhmaṇa finds that the essences attend upon him, and having gone to heaven, he is honored. O fair-faced ones, he who gives vessels that are well-filled [enjoys these benefits].

He shall become a vessel for enjoyments and shall deliver his ancestors from fear. Furthermore, he who constructs a prosperous reservoir of water, where all living beings indeed drink water—[he attains great merit]. (27–28)
And having delivered his fathers,
as well as his grandfathers and great-grandfathers, that bird [resided] among the worlds of the Kāmicas.
The goddesses move about like gods for six hundred thousand years;
and again, in the world of humans, he is free from all diseases. (8.111.30)

O women of pure smiles, the man who constructs a well filled with water becomes an enjoyer of pleasures and is born as a king; he is a donor, a performer of sacrifices, powerful, radiant, and pleasant to behold. (31)
And having fed the Brahmins according to the rules, one should give that [gift] to them;
it should be adorned with eight variegated banners,
with the Vaijayantī flag, and beautifully decorated with flowers.
Having delivered his ancestors by means of a celestial chariot,
that best of men goes to the world of Varuṇa, accompanied by the songs of Apsarases.
Listen to the fruit of merit for him who would give gold, or wrought gold, or land, or sesame seeds, or even jewels to all beings: he,
accompanied by all the worlds, shall travel in a great celestial chariot.
Having attained the world of Indra, he rejoices like a god.
And having fallen from there, that righteous-souled one, possessing the fulfillment of all desires, is born into a great family in this world and becomes truly fortunate. || 37 ||
But that virtuous man who plants a tree that provides shade, flowers, and fruit by the roadside, truly delivers his ancestors. || 38 ||
In the same way, having given [the land] to Brahmins and having redeemed it once again,
listen, O you of great splendor, to the fruit that man obtains:
for as long as embodied beings make use of the flowers of that tree.
And indeed, the fruits of that which has borne fruit are eaten by living beings.
Having delivered even his ancestors for that many thousands of years,
he shall reach the world of Soma and obtain the fruit of immortality.
He who, with a concentrated mind, bestows fruits upon Brahmins shall indeed partake in many fruits and become truly fortunate. || 42 ||
O Goddesses, that best of men who provides firewood to Brahmins during the winter season attains the world of Agni;
likewise, he who provides a vessel made of gold and adorned with jewels [attains the same]. || 43 ||
He who gives a beautiful silver vessel to Brahmins rejoices in heaven in a celestial chariot crowded with hundreds of apsarases.
Having attained the station of the Gandharvas, he rejoices together with Urvaśī.
He who gives a copper vessel, especially to Brahmins,
shall become a Yakṣa endowed with great power under the king of the Yakṣas.
He who bestows a house, however, which is replete with all desired objects, [shall likewise attain great merit].

Having reached the world of Brahmā, he enjoys all his desires. Having dwelt there for four times ten million years by virtue of that deed, when he is born as a householder, he becomes a donor and one possessed of enjoyments. ||47-48||
He who bestows medicinal herbs and various kinds of grains enjoys the world of Soma, which is enriched with all objects of desire;
having remained there for seven thousand years, that man returns once more.
In this world, he who bestows a field that is already cultivated and productive is born endowed with all wealth and possessed of enjoyments;
having become a lord of fields, he attains the realm of Prajāpati.
He who bestows land upon a high-souled Brahmin shall dwell happily in all the worlds,
traveling in a resplendent celestial chariot for many thousands of years, assuming whatever form he desires.
For that man who, by the turning of time, comes again to human birth— ||53||
In that regard, for him who is of great renown and gives clothing to a Brahmin, the earth becomes a cow of plenty in every respect;
having attained the Vairāja world, he shall dwell in happiness for ten million years.
He who indeed provides a covered seat to a Brāhmaṇa attains a position in a kingdom and reaches heaven free from all distress. Furthermore,
that best of men who provides a well-spread bed—
He enjoys many beloved wives, goddesses devoted to him;
yet he who bestows a well-adorned maiden upon a Brāhmaṇa [attains even greater merit]. (57)
Having gone to the world of the ancestors, he shall indeed dwell there for a hundred thousand years;
and being born again here, he will be endowed with all his desires fulfilled.
He obtains devoted wives and is born with offspring;
he who bestows a horse adorned with gold and endowed with auspicious marks,
by that deed, O goddesses, attains the world of the Gandharvas.
A chariot, a horse, an elephant, a maidservant, a maiden, or even a house.
And he who bestows land is born as a king upon earth;
through the ritual joined with mantras, his fruit of merit is great.
That [land] stands before him, becoming a cow that milks all desires.
He who gives a water-cow (jaladhenu) obtains a great fruit from that gift;
having constructed an auspicious pond, a reservoir, or even a well that is very abundant,
he should fill jars to the brim and adorn them with perfumes and garlands.
And having honored the best of the twice-born with flowers of various forms, || 64 ||
Once they have been well-satisfied with various kinds of food and drink, one should cause them to be given vessels of sesame seeds;
one should give them abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and then cause them to touch those [vessels].
May the auspicious and gentle waters satisfy my ancestors;
may the ancestors always be granters of desires and move at will.
Having thus given that cow, and having then purchased it back,
one should cause that water-shed— which bestows the world of Brahmā— to be maintained, O Goddesses,
after giving vessels of sesame seeds and a pair of new garments.
One should provide the presence of gold and various kinds of fruits;
then, having bathed and become pure, one should give these to the Brahmins according to the prescribed rule.
"From clarified butter cows are born; clarified butter is established upon the earth."
"Clarified butter, fire, and the gods—may clarified butter be granted to me.
By giving [a cow] according to this injunction, one shall attain the world of Brahmā.
That man who bestows a cow along with her calf and a bronze milking vessel [attains the same].

Having gratified the Brahmins with perfumes and garlands, [he should give] a cow with golden horns and silver hooves, draped in fine linen and silk, provided with bedding and coverlets, and accompanied by many flowers and fruits. (72)
At the time of her gift, the gods took refuge in her limbs:
Brahmā stood upon her head, Śakra resorted to her footwear, the moon and sun were situated in her eyes, and Vāyu was established in her nose.
Fire rests in her mouth, and the Lord Soma himself is her tongue;
all the directions are in her ears, and the Rudras have taken refuge in her veins.
The guardians of the worlds are in her feet, and all the mountains are her bones.
The seven oceans are situated within his belly, and the suns are resting upon his neck.
The Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, is his dewlap, and the auspicious Vasus are on his two flanks.
Prajāpati is his generative organ, and all sacred fords are his urine.
His feces became Śrī, and the Nāgas became his weapons in every respect;
the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and the worlds remained stationed, taking refuge in his tail.
The mantras, sacrifices, gifts, and restraints along with the sages;
the lunar mansions, the planets, and those which are in the form of stars;
as well as the Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, Jagatī, and Paṅkti meters. || 79 ||
The Anuṣṭubh, the Ṛg, the Yajus, and likewise the Sāmans and the Atharvaṇa;
the mothers of the world, as well as the clouds and the rain;
Dharma, Nārāyaṇa, the elements, and the rivers.
Residing within her pores are established the gods,
as well as yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas together with birds;
likewise, the sacrifices, the sacrificial fees, and the auspicious apsarases.
O Vyāsa, the high-souled Gandharvas and others such as these all took refuge in her two horns—
the fruits of sacrifices and gifts, as well as the various types of destinies. || 83-84 ||
All [the deities] have taken refuge in the calf; it is entirely composed of the gods and is auspicious.
It is presided over by the gods and is honored by all the worlds. (85)
With a well-concentrated mind, he should place into the hands of the Brahmins, accompanied by the sacred mantras, kusha grass, gold, seeds, sesame, and white mustard seeds. (86)
Then, O observer of noble vows, one should give a cow with water while reciting this mantra:
"The milch-cow consists of all the gods and likewise consists of all the worlds;
[I give her] for the sake of all the worlds and for the welfare of all the worlds. (87)
"I bestow this Great Being for the sake of inexhaustible virtue. || 88 ||
Thus, having given that cow, wherever he is reborn,
there she goes and delivers that person from fear;
she is indeed the fulfiller of all desires and the bestower of all worlds.
It bestows all knowledge and likewise yields the fruit of all sacrifices. || 8.111.90 ||
Having gone to all the worlds by means of that [gift], he rejoices like an immortal;
and being born here, he attains that very cow which grants all desires.
Born as a human, he becomes a possessor of a thousand cows and possesses great strength.
One who gives a cow with her calf facing both ways (ubhayatomukhī) according to the prescribed rite shall be born handsome, wealthy, and possessed of many sons;
he shall also attain the power of recollecting his past lives. || 92-93 ||
He who bestows a cow upon Brahmins in accordance with the prescribed rule—
he too protects them from fear and even from hell.
And he who gives a black antelope skin to a vow-observing celibate student—
He obtains the fruit of the earth, and yoga proceeds for him.
That self-controlled man who provides a dwelling for yogis, celibate students, and Brahmins shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice. || 95-96 ||
He obtains the Āptoryāma sacrifice, the Pauṇḍarīka, and a thousand cows;
and having attained supreme memory, O observers of noble vows, he attains Yoga.
Furthermore, that best of men who gives a water-pot to a Brāhmaṇa [attains these same rewards].
By that deed, O Goddess, he attains constancy in Dharma.
But he who, O Brahmin-sage, rescues according to his ability one who is diseased, miserable, deluded, or senseless, shall be liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin. || 98-99 ||
O deities, he who bestows gold upon a poor twice-born man obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
O Goddesses, he who bestows all these gifts mentioned here in their entirety at once shall become the sole sovereign of the earth.
He who constantly hears this and gives according to his own capacity [shall likewise attain such sovereignty].
And those of great fortune who should recite it, they too shall go to the third heaven.
Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The Goddess said:
"Listen further, O gods, to how [beings] may become auspicious even without giving."
O Goddess, this very dharma is obtained through fasting.
O Goddess, he who passes the month of Mārgaśīrṣa eating only one meal a day shall,
by that deed, always possess cattle.
By performing [this vow] in the month of Pauṣa, one obtains many righteous sons;
and by doing so in the month of Māgha, one further attains beloved ones. || 3 ||
He who constantly observes the practice of eating only one meal during the month of Phālguna attains good fortune with women, and women become most dear to him.
That best of men who passes the month of Caitra eating only one meal [attains the same].
That man who passes the month of Vaiśākha eating but a single meal a day will be born handsome in a family abundant with wealth and grain;
he shall attain preeminence in the world, honored and possessed of riches.

He who observes the practice of eating only one meal a day during the month of Jyeṣṭha-mūla becomes the eldest among his brothers and attains abundant enjoyment. He who likewise observes the practice of eating only one meal a day during the month of Āṣāḍha—
Having attained the respect of the king, he obtains abundant sensual pleasures.
Furthermore, that man who acts in this same manner during the month of Śrāvaṇa attains the position of a general and is born powerful.
O goddesses, he who observes the practice of eating only one meal a day throughout the month of Bhādrapada is reborn wealthy as a result of that deed.
Furthermore, for one who subsists on a single meal during the month of Āśvayuja,
his trade bears fruit, as do his agriculture and his herds of cattle.
And he who likewise subsists on a single meal during the month of Kārttika—
Having obtained the fruit of a horse sacrifice, he is glorified in the world of Agni.
That best of men who passes his entire life eating but one meal a day goes to the world of Śakra by means of a sun-colored celestial chariot.
He who remains for a full year eating but one meal a day becomes equal to a king and protects the earth like Mahendra.
Furthermore, that best of men should observe a fast for one day and night.
He obtains the auspicious fruit of ten gold pieces. That best of men who observes this fast for one day and night every month becomes pure through that deed, wise, and righteous.
He who passes the fourteenth and the eighth days of both fortnights for an entire year, day and night, without exception— || 17 ||
Endowed with that merit and freed from all sins,
O goddesses, he does not go to hell, nor does he behold Yama.
And the wise man who performs a three-night fast month after month—
Having reached the world of Kubera, he shall obtain supreme happiness.
That man who, self-restrained and pure, eats on the fourth day,
reaches the realm of the Gandharvas and rejoices in heaven like Śakra.
He who eats on the fifth day, remaining diligent month after month,
reaches the world of Vāyu and goes to the heavenly world.
He who, constantly adhering to this discipline, eats only on every sixth day,
reaches the world of Varuṇa and shall attain the great state.
He who, having conquered the pairs of opposites and being firm in his vow, eats on the seventh day,
reaches the world of the Sun and shall attain the great state.
The man who, being pure, eats on the eighth day alone,
having reached the world of Viṣṇu, shall become possessed of supreme luster.
The man who, established in his observance, eats on the ninth day, [attains the same].
Having become beloved of the Vasus, he moves together with the Vasus.
Having eaten on the tenth day, he obtains the fruit of ten days;
becoming equal to the Aśvins, he always blazes like the sun.
Furthermore, having attained human birth, he shall obtain ten wives,
possess inexhaustible gold, and shall not die an untimely death.
But the pure man who eats on the eleventh day,
having obtained the fruit of Ekādaśī, shall attain the state of being a follower of Rudra.
Having remained there for eight hundred years, endowed with supreme happiness,
he attains the status of a Brahmin and is born here as a performer of sacrifices.
That man who always eats on the twelfth day,
having reached the state of Śakra for twelve days, shall attain the world of Śakra.

Having dwelt there happily, that best of men is born again here as either a king, a royal official, or one who becomes exceedingly wealthy. As for the man who constantly eats on the thirteenth day, || 31 ||

Having reached the abode of Bhārgava, he shall dwell there endowed with divine happiness. Furthermore, if that man is born again as a human after his inauspicious karma has been exhausted, he will be born auspiciously into a noble family, abundant in wealth and grain.
But the man who constantly passes fourteen days [in this manner] shall reach the world of Tuṣita and become an excellent lord of the Gaṇas.
Furthermore, he who passes half a month always without weariness shall likewise attain that state.
Having become equal to the king of the gods, he dwells in heaven;
moreover, he is born again here on this great earth as a king—
[that] steadfast man who passes a month [in fasting], having conquered anger and subdued his senses.
Surrounded by celestial nymphs in a divine chariot,
being honored like a god and praised from all sides,
he, blazing like the sun, eternally enjoys happiness.
He dwells in all the worlds for many tens of thousands of years;
then, having reached the abode of Brahmā and being highly honored by Brahmā,
that best of men resides in the world of Brahmā just like Brahmā himself.
If, however, he returns again as a Brahmin who is a lord,
he attains yoga there and enjoys the sovereignty of yoga. Then, having become a lord of yogis, he shall become a leader of the Gaṇas of Śambhu.
O goddesses, listen from me to the procedure for all fasts, which bestows supreme merit, as it truly is and in its proper sequence:
having bathed, being pure, having sipped water (ācamana), having offered oblations into the fire, and being well-composed; ||41-42||
Having thus initiated himself, the wise man should observe a fast;
he should bathe at the three periods of the day and likewise offer oblations into the fire.
Restrained in speech, free from anger, self-controlled, righteous, truthful, and compassionate,
he should constantly mutter the Gāyatrī and always recite purifying prayers.

Then, at night, sleeping on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), having spread kuśa grass according to the rules, he should worship either the Rudras or the Gaṇas, remaining strictly avoided by women and Śūdras. 45.
Then, free from grief and devoid of envy, one should eat together with the goddesses;
for as many days as one remains, for that long one should feed Brahmins.
Then, when the period is complete, one hundred excellent Brahmins [should be fed].
Or else, having worshipped a thousand [times], or according to one's capacity, in every respect. ||47||
Having given sacrificial food, cows, and garments in sequence, one should cause gold and a vessel of sesame seeds to be given to each individual;
thereby one obtains that fruit which is difficult to attain through other vows. 48.
O highly fortunate ones, that best of men who would release a bull with a dark-blue body, or even another [type of bull], shall deliver his ancestors. ||49||
As many hairs as there are on that great-souled bull,
for so many thousands of years does he rejoice in heaven.
He who, with a pure mind and well-composed, having reached the new moon day of the dark fortnight, should give sesame vessels to the Brahmins; ||51||
Having gratified the ancestors, that bull among men attains the imperishable world of the fathers and enjoys happiness for a long time. ||52||
O fair-faced ones, this rule for the fast has been told by me;
now listen once more with full concentration to the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (53)
But he who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa penance as prescribed, with a well-concentrated mind,
shall reach the world of Soma and attain equality with Soma.
He who performs the Prājāpatya penance, whether once or many times,
becomes equal to Prajāpati and is glorified in his world.
And that best of men who performs the Sāntapana Kṛcchra—
He who delivers himself from distress goes to the world of Agni;
and he of noble mind who performs the Mahāsāntapana penance attains omniscience and finds the world of Brahmā.
And that best of the twice-born who performs the tulāpuruṣaka rite, being liberated from all sins, shall go to heaven full of vigor. ||58||
With great hardship, however, a man may go to the abode of Śarva;
likewise, through the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* penance, he may attain the status of a leader of the Gaṇas.
That best of men who performs all the *kṛcchra* penances [attains even higher].
Whatever desire he may pray for, that very thing he attains.
Whoever among these [practices] should be a performer with a well-concentrated mind,
he becomes purified by that and even finds godhood.
A man who might dwell for a full year constantly subsisting on milk,
or consuming barley-gruel prepared with cow’s urine,
or eating oil-cake and fruit, or even abstaining from pungent food and salt; || 62 ||
Having obtained the fruit of the horse-sacrifice, he attains the world of Brahmā.
Completely freed from all sins and liberated from all bonds,
he moves about like Brahmā in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
O best of men, this applies to that excellent man who practices even one of all these [virtues] individually.
The Great-Souled One, his defilements destroyed, remains lying down as long as he breathes.
That Great Being, having attained either the worlds according to his wish, or even liberation,
or great sovereignty, remains resplendent.
All these very same acts of charity and austerities are constantly prescribed in every respect even for Śūdras, provided they are performed without mantras;
of this there is no doubt. Thus spoke Prajāpati.
All those Śūdras are remembered as being without mantras, yet they are free from defilement.
For women, however, the husband is their deity; nothing else is ordained.
He is their refuge, his abode is supreme, and he is remembered as their highest dharma.
Therefore, she who is authorized by him to practice this Dharma shall,
being well-composed, obtain the fruit of that Dharma.
But she who performs any religious duty without his permission does not obtain its fruit; however, being virtuous, she does obtain the fruit.
But that woman who, having been authorized by her husband and having performed dharma most excellently,
gives [the merit] to her husband, for her the fruit shall be infinite;
whatever she may pray for, whether in this world or in the next.
O goddesses, she obtains all that and becomes fortunate as well;
her husband shall be under her control, and she will then be dear to him.
She shall have offspring in the form of sons and shall never experience suffering.
"This Dharma has been declared by me for you, O mothers of the world.
Beyond this, what else do you wish to hear, O auspicious ones?
For this Dharma is exceedingly great, most radiant, and very difficult to perform for those who have not practiced. (75)
One who knows the Dharma should not speak of this to any other person who is deceitful or unrighteous.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then all those goddesses, the mothers of the world, gathered together...
Having worshipped the Great Goddess, they spoke with hearts full of joy:
"O you who are saluted by all the immortals, oh, the Dharma has been proclaimed by you!
By practicing it, a most great fruit is swiftly attained. (77–78)
"O Goddess, let us look from here at the auspicious forest of this mountain,
filled with various kinds of flowers and crowded with many flocks of birds.
Then that goddess, having risen together with the divine mothers (devamātṛs), [proceeded].
The great yoginī, casting her gaze upon that supreme forest which brings happiness, wandered about Mandara mountain to behold its divine splendor;
she gazed upon its peaks of realgar and its summits of gold.
The Daughter of the Mountain was delighted upon seeing the beautiful mountain cascades with their white waters,
the lakes filled with lotuses, and the most enchanting ponds,
as well as Nandin standing by her side.
Then a daughter of Meru named Śubhāvatī, who possessed a slender waist, spoke to the daughter of Himavat, pointing out the auspicious forest:
"O daughter of the mountain, behold this place, auspicious with its playful arts. (83)

This great forest, endowed with all seasons, produces well-spoken words according to its nature; and for the wise, in times of distress, it likewise produces well-spoken words as is appropriate. (84–85)
Thus the excellent mountain peak, consisting of gold, shines like a learned man endowed with auspicious marks, or like a singer of the Sāman hymns chanting aloud;
and this mountain summit, possessing jewels, is ever resplendent.
He shines like the rising sun at both ends of the great age (mahāyuga). || 87 ||
This peak of vaidūrya, with its surface-stones of indranīla, shines forth, O Śarvāṇī, as it bears the Lord of the Earth (Sthaleśvara) above Hara. 88.
"This elephant is intoxicated by me, as if surrounded by maddened female elephants;
having performed anointment for you, O lady of beautiful brows, he bows his head like a sprout.
Oh, look at this beautiful form, O auspicious one, endowed with the beauty of a forest grove! (89)
Behold him, who has been consecrated to the position of crown prince like Jayanta with chowries;
and see this tree, O Śarvāṇī, as he dances near his mother with his sprout-like hands, like a beloved biological son.
I believe this is the dwelling of the deity of the forest;
its splendor appears exceedingly beautiful, such as I have never seen before.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of Śubhāvatī, the daughter of the mountain,
the imperishable daughter of Himavat, gazed upon the young tree.
Thus, as that goddess of gods was wandering upon the great mountain, she saw a young *aśoka* tree in full bloom, shining like the rising sun. (94)
O Sage, seeing him standing there with his hands joined in reverence like hundreds of copper-colored young shoots, the goddess Girijā attained supreme delight.
And he thought in his mind: "This tree is my son;
this praiseworthy offspring of mine shall be a bringer of joy. (96)
For when the Blessed One has arrived, authorized by the Self-Existent One, I shall take my beloved son, who is like a young *aśoka* tree. ||97||
And for me, who am childless, O best of men, this excellent tree shall become a son, the foremost among those with sons, and the destroyer of the grief of losing a son. (98)
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus resolved, that beautiful Umā then approached another tree and, having moved to another place, she beheld it there.
Then, in that interval, terrifying portents occurred there;
there was a great force of wind that brought down mountains and trees. (8.112.100)
The peak of the lord of mountains fell without any calamity, and trees were uprooted even without the wind. ||101||
Meteors fell from the sky and an inauspicious wind blew;
moreover, O son of Kālī, the left eye of the goddess throbbed. (102)
Seeing them, the Goddess was struck with wonder and spoke thus to Śailādi and her companions,
all of whom were skilled in speech and capable at every time.
The Goddess said:
"This mountain, covered on all sides by those trees, appears as if intoxicated;
I consider this to be a great danger, for it is not thought to be accidental. (104)

"These ill-omened portents do not arise without cause; act in such a way that these inauspicious signs do not bring fear upon me. Then Nandi, having prostrated with palms joined in reverence, spoke to the Goddess of the gods.
"O Bhavānī, whence could there be fear for you, you who are the mother of the dwellers of heaven?
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, as he was speaking thus to the Goddess, the mother of the universe—
Then the Daitya Andhaka also went from Pātāla to Mount Mandara.
Surrounded by thousands of Daityas and Dānavas, headed by Prahlāda,
the illustrious great Daitya appeared like Śakra surrounded by the hosts of gods.
By the counsel of the most eminent Daityas, that great Asura came to Mandara to see it, just as Indra goes to the Nandana grove.
Prahlāda, Anuhrāda, Śini, Bāṣkali,
Tuṇḍa, Tuhuṇḍa, Vātāpi, Bali, Bāṇa, Virocana,
Ilvala, Namuci, Vyaṃsa, and the great asura Vipracitti.
Sunda, Nisunda, Naraka, Dhenuka, Ariṣṭa,
Mura, Kārtasvana, Hastin, Duryodhana, Maya,
Tāraka, Tārakākṣa, Vidyunmālin, and Prabhākara. || 111–112 ||
Hālāhala, Kumbha, Saṃvara, and Kālasaṃvara; Dhundhu, as well as Indradamana, Hayagrīva, and Śatodara;
Meghanāda, Siṃhanāda, Dundubhi, and Śatadundubhi. ||13||
Kālanemi, Baka, Daṇḍa, Vipāka, and Pāka;
Vṛṣaparvan, Śatāvarta, Puloman, and likewise Śarabha; Bala, Gaganamūrdhan, and the highly illustrious Sūcīroman.
Asiloman, Pralamba, Śambhu, Devāntaka,
Mahiṣa, Bhīmasena, Vāyu, and Vāditra—
these followers of Andhaka also arrived at Mount Mandara. || 1.16 ||

Armed with weapons, having conquered the hosts of gods, and possessed of great majesty, yet fallen from the path of dharma—all of them were indeed heroes who never retreated; together with Andhaka, they went to Mount Mandara.
Sanatkumāra said:
O son of Kālī, it was like a herd of intoxicated elephants,
like clouds raining down, like horned serpents, and like a fierce,
great breed of proud boars.
In that manner, he moved through the host of Dānavas on Mount Mandara.
While wandering there with her companions,
Śoṇḍaka then beheld the goddess of the gods, like a wolf spotting a lioness.
O Vyāsa, having seen the Blessed Goddess, that Daitya of deluded mind did not offer salutation; he merely gazed at her.
Seeing that Daitya staring unwinkingly at the Daughter of the Mountain, [she became enraged].
But the highly intelligent Prahlāda spoke these meaningful words:
"She is the mother of the world, the imperishable daughter of Himavat;
she is renowned in the universe as Umā, endowed with the power of austerity and yoga. (122-123)
He whose son was Brahmā, who bestowed the status of Prajāpati, and who, by a boon, attained the state of being Brahmā’s grandson through his son. || 124 ||
He who grants auspicious boons to us and to the gods—
he of great renown is to be propitiated by all the worlds and by the deities.
He who, abiding within, pervades the entire multitude of beings without exception,
by whose self this imperishable world is sustained.
She who, by her own will, can contract all this universe in half a moment—she is the wife of that wise Supreme Lord, the God;
for she is capable, O Lord of the Daityas, of dissolving the entire world in an instant. (127)
Whether to burn her, or to seize her, or to cast her into hell—O Daitya, deluded as you were, why did you not offer her a prostration? (128)
Sanatkumāra said: O sage, while the enemy of the gods was thus speaking words endowed with righteousness, the Goddess, together with her divine consorts, vanished in an instant.
Those women, the mothers of the world, became invisible.
Then, when those [trees] had perished, they reached on foot Mandara’s auspicious forest,
which was filled with many sights to behold.
With *balā* trees, clusters of *kalanīṣa*, *sātimuktā*, and *priyaṅgu*;
with *campaka*, *bakula*, *lodhra*, *aśoka*, and those called *nāga*. ||132||
It was beautified by *punnāga* trees, *tilaka* trees, forests of *devadāru*, *sarala* trees, coconut palms, and clusters of lotuses. (133)
Neither by its deep ravines, nor its ridges, nor its caves, nor even its waterfalls, is there anything found anywhere on earth more delightful than that place.
Then all those Daitya leaders roamed about on the great mountain,
which was filled with many waterfalls and crowded with various kinds of trees.
While wandering there, they beheld seven great sages, perfected ones (siddhas) engaged in yoga, situated by a certain waterfall.

Seeing them seated upon a stone slab, conversing with one another about stories that were consistent with dharma, varied in meaning, insightful, and bringing great joy, Sunda, filled with anger, questioned Prahlāda, the best of asuras.

"Who indeed are these sages here, and for what purpose have they gathered? To him, the wise Asura— the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu and thorn to the gods— having understood the situation, spoke while standing in their midst.
Prahlāda said:
O Indraka, these seven high-souled sages have assembled here:
Bhṛgu, Atri, Marīci, Viśvāmitra, and likewise Aṅgiras.
Bharadvāja and Vasiṣṭha, great-souled ones perfected in yoga and rich in asceticism, have come here, their sins consumed by penance. (141)
"O Lord, I do not believe this arrival of Mandara is without cause.
Having gathered here in this secluded place, all of us, the lords of the gods, shall find out what these practitioners are doing here. (142)
"These beings have indeed become silent; having remained quiet according to their strength, O lords of the Daityas, remain silent so that I may grasp the opinion of everyone. (143)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then those foremost of the Asuras, having made an agreement, remained [there],
saying, "Whoever among us should say anything [contrary], he shall be put to death by us."
While those evil-minded asuras remained there in such a state, those sages devoted to austerity spoke these words to one another:
"O twice-born ones, this region of the mountain is no longer pure; let us go elsewhere today."
Indeed, the arrival of these most wicked-minded Daityas is seen here;
you too have gone elsewhere, O Bhavānī, oppressed by fear of the Asuras—those evil-souled Asuras for whom this destruction is certain. || 146–147 ||
All those who destroyed the Dharma have gone to their destruction; had that Dharma not been destroyed by those cruel ones for the sake of the kingdom, [they would not have met this fate]. 148.

In this way, none of those enemies of the gods would have met their destruction, had they remained content with their own kingdoms. They too would have shone in all the worlds, worthy of worship like the gods. || 149 ||
Sanatkumāra said: Aṅgiras spoke this to them: "For those who are lustful here and engaged for the sake of sovereignty, unrighteousness has indeed arrived. (8.112.150)
Indeed, one who desires [worldly success] acquires a kingdom through dharma alone;
yet he should not practice that dharma if it results in neither stability nor any lasting sovereignty.
Atri said:
Those who desire sovereignty through unrighteousness always conquer in battle;
yet they are not beloved by the world, nor do they live for the welfare of others.
Those who are righteous, having slain their enemies without hesitation, are soon firmly established in their kingdoms; therefore, one should take refuge in dharma.
But those who, abandoning dharma, seek to seize a kingdom by force alone, delighting in evil—
Even though they desire it, they never obtain that kingdom. Furthermore, whatever kingdom they might obtain through cruel deeds does not endure for long for them, and they become objects of hatred.
Bhṛgu said:
"In ancient times, this dharma was obtained by Brahmā, who desired to create; it is indeed terrifying to the Asuras, yet they do not practice it. || 157 ||
And all of them are indeed cruel by their very nature and by birth;
moreover, they have resorted to that karma because of their cruel approach.
Sanatkumāra said:
While they were thus speaking to the Asuras,
those three— Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and Kṛtānta— arrived.
Having honored them according to the prescribed rites, those three sages and Manu sat down together upon the very rocks, devoted to one another;
and the ṛṣis bowed with great respect to those who were seated.
They said: "O sustainers of the world, where have you set out for today? (161)
Dhātṛ said:
"O twice-born ones, having returned from the world of Brahmā, we have arrived here today;
we were commanded by Brahmā to go to the presence of Kaśyapa."
Again the sages asked: "What was said to the twice-born Kaśyapa?
Then the Creator (Dhātṛ) told the sages what he had said to Kaśyapa.
"O Brahmin, since you have informed me that Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, has said:
'O Lord, even the Asuras are my sons, and the Devas are also dear to me.'"
O Creator of the World, O Best of Gods, act in such a way that there shall be no mutual enmity among them; through that, may I attain peace.
There, having been commanded by Brahmā, O great sage, I shall tell you all about the war between the gods and the asuras, their mutual friendship,
the production of the nectar of immortality, and the entire history of the kingdom and its dissolution.
"O best of sages, everything that was spoken by you has come to pass."

Lokeśa related the deeds of the gods and asuras; having reported all of that to him, he said, "We have been sent by Brahmā and have come here to see the Blessed One, the daughter of the Snowy Mountain."
Sanatkumāra said: O sage, all those sages, rich in asceticism and self-restrained, then questioned those very disputants once again.
"O auspicious ones, we wish to hear that which has been told regarding the past and future events of the gods and asuras, if your mind is inclined toward showing us favor. (8.112.170)
Furthermore, O best of gods, the goddess has been informed by you;
tell us all of that, if indeed we are worthy of your favor. (171)
Having heard those words of theirs, those three most excellent gods, possessed of great strength, spoke these words to Kṛtānta: "Speak! ||172||
