Then he related to them the future in its many wonderful details,
exactly as it had been ordained by the Creator of old as the cause of the world, including the gods and the asuras.
Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Ascent of Mandara," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
Tell me all that was previously told by that high-souled Kṛtānta to the sages on Mount Mandara.
Sanatkumāra said:
"There will be a son of the asura Hiraṇyakaśipu named Prahlāda, a bull among asuras, who will be a powerful and wise Indra."
Having prepared the nectar of immortality together with the gods, that lord of the hosts of deities,
the preeminent Daitya, having defeated the gods in battle, brought the nectar away.
He will be conquered in battle by Viṣṇu and shall consecrate his son upon the throne.
Vyāsa said:
O son of Brahmā, how was that nectar churned by the gods and the mighty asuras? This I wish to know.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, having approached Brahmā, Prahlāda, the preeminent among the Asuras, was then consecrated into the sovereignty of Śakra; he then protected the Asuras.
Then a battle between the gods and the asuras took place;
and the gods took counsel together with the blessed Grandfather.
The gods said:
"O Blessed One, the gods are being slain by the asuras in battle like mortals.
O you of noble vows, command such a way that the gods may not die."
Thus addressed, Brahmā said to those gods, including Vāsava:
"Go quickly and produce the nectar from the Ocean of Milk.
Whichever gods there may be in all the Manvantaras,"
Together with the asuras, they produced all the nectar from the Ocean of Milk. ||9||
Then the lords of the gods eat, and by that they attain satisfaction;
they rise up even from death, and having drunk it, they do not die.
The gods said:
"O gods, how do you, the lords of the world during the Manvantara, produce that nectar? Tell us the entire means for that."
Brahmā said: In the city of Soma, belonging to Varuṇa, lies that auspicious lake Kṣīroda,
where those seven auspicious oceans are always present.
Irā, Mālā, Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, Irāvatī, Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Surabhī, and Kadrū. ||13||
There Aditi and Diti, as well as Devikā, the source of the universe, reside; there are cows, patient toward all, auspicious, and yielding all desires.
The affectionate cows there yield milk of six flavors, which is indeed like nectar;
it is there that the sages, whose nature is asceticism, self-restraint, and tranquility, subsist on the froth.
O best of gods, whatever medicinal herbs there are in this world—whether cultivated or wild, divine or human—they exist there by the thousands. ||16||
Having thrown in trees, creepers, climbing plants, shrubs, and other such things, as well as medicinal herbs and King Soma himself. ||17||
Prosperity, fortune, as well as renown, fame, and contentment; glory, faith, and retention, as well as reasoning and analysis. || 18 ||
Strength, Dharma, as well as vigor, the goddess Tṛpti, Sarasvatī,
all the sacred fords (tīrthas), and various kinds of gifts;
the bull, the chariot, the banner, and likewise the elephant and the horse.
And here he cast down the eight auspicious objects as well as the Vedic meters;
the Vedas and whatever sciences there may be, those who are the mothers of the world,
the mantras, the sacrifices, gold, and the implements for the mantras.
Having cast into it whatever was beautiful, satisfying, and flavorful, they then churned the churning-stick—
Mount Mandara, the best of mountains— and the tortoise Akūpāra.
Having made Mount Mandara, the lord of mountains, the churning-stick upon its back,
and having likewise taken hold of Vāsuki as the rope— held by Viṣṇu—
the Daityas stood where the mouth was and the gods where the tail was.
Pulling that churning-stick, they shall churn for many years;
then, after a thousand years, the horse will emerge from it.
Cows together with their calves, an auspicious elephant in rut,
a bull with a terrifying roar, maidens, flutes and reed-pipes,
the eight auspicious symbols, and the physician Dhanvantari. ||26||
Śrī, Lakṣmī, and others such as these, as well as Vāruṇī, who is intoxicated with passion; ||27||

Likewise, the divine medicinal herbs—both those of the village and the forest, as well as those belonging to humans—and all things beginning with trees, as well as King Soma himself, [arose] from that. ||28||
Having gathered that nectar as well as that difficult-to-withstand poison,
and all those sacrifices and other things whatsoever had been collected there— ||29||
In this manner, throughout the Manvantaras here, the nectar is churned by the gods along with the Asuras and humans; and thus, O gods, it is produced.
Therefore, having gone from here together with the Dānavas, O deities, churn the nectar quickly; from that, you shall obtain that benefit.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, those lords of the gods returned to this world and acted accordingly in every respect.
While that [ocean] was being churned, a poison with a terrible tip arose;
it caused terror to both gods and asuras, and Śaṅkara then drank it.
Then, from that very ocean, once again many diverse jewels rose up, and the deities took them.
The Asuras seized them; I cursed those Asuras because they held the auspicious rites in contempt, and by that they met their destruction. ||35||
The jewels said:
"O cruel and evil-minded ones, since you do not rejoice in us, therefore that which you desire shall not come to pass. (36)
The Asuras did not drink the Vāruṇī wine which brings on the intoxication of pride;
for that reason, those Asuras were indeed evil-minded in every respect.
Then there was the horse named Uccaiḥśravas, most beautiful,
as well as a four-tusked elephant and the highly renowned physician.
The goddesses Ghṛtācī, Pūrvacitti, Rambhā, and Manoramā, as well as Amṛta and Soma, then took [their portions] and rose up, O gods. ||39||
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having cast aside those jewels, the asuras, being exceedingly arrogant,
seized the nectar by force from the hand of Soma.
The gods, having approached them together while they were bewildered by their own delusion, spoke with conciliatory words:
"It is not proper for you to act thus; we shall all enjoy [the fruit] together. (41)
"Let there indeed be a very firm friendship between us; O lords of the Dānavas, do not, out of pride in your strength, undergo this suffering here in vain.
To all of them who spoke thus, Prahlāda, the lord of the Dānavas, [replied].
Having placed the Dharma behind him, Mahāmāya spoke this. ||43||
Prahlāda said:
"O lords of the gods, when you were indeed taking up the jewels risen from the ocean, you were not addressed by us with anything at all."
"O deities, we shall all accept this jewel in this manner;
for indeed, we will not give it up today without a fight. (45)
"O gods, this nectar of ours is the source of all auspiciousness;
if you have need for war, take it if you are able.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by those cruel ones, the gods became as if terrified;
with pale faces and dejected, they said nothing at all to them then. || 47 ||
Ashamed by that, those great beings, the lords of the gods, turned back;
they became devoid of enthusiasm, thinking, "We have been struck."
While they were thus reflecting, the thousand-eyed Purandara said:
"What is the use of despair? Let us slay them in battle."
Viṣṇu said:
"O lords of the gods, this lack of wisdom regarding war belongs to Śakra;
for all the gods, being possessed of great strength, cannot be slain in battle."
"Therefore, while they are drinking that auspicious nectar, I shall seize it by resorting to illusion and through that deception. (51)
"Arm yourselves, all you gods; having formed a battle array, stand firm!
O dwellers of heaven, remain here until I return from this place having seized the nectar.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, employing a deluding illusion and assuming the form of the sacrificial splendor (Yajñaśrī), the Lord of the Gods went toward the sons of Diti.
Having gone there, that one of great strength spoke thus to the king of the asuras:
"He is endowed with the splendor and form of a sacrifice, holding a lotus in his hand and possessing stainless eyes. (54)
Viṣṇu said:
"Knowing the gods to be weak and the Dānavas— proud of their strength— to be powerful and difficult to overcome, I, the glory of sacrifice, have arrived."
"May all you Dānavas, enemies of the gods, accept me!
Those gods have met their destruction; you are the gods, there is no doubt.
Then the Asuras rose up, as did the Dānava Prahlāda.
Having circumambulated him, they placed the jar in his hand.
That god spoke to the Dānavas, whose minds were captivated by the female form:
"You ought not to hurl this at me today in any way whatsoever."
O wise ones, they never resorted to illusion;
for all of them were of evil conduct and relied upon deceit and guile. ||59||
Prahlāda said:
"I know that they are indeed masters of illusion, powerful, and deceitful;
yet we shall slay them, though they are well-prepared, by means of illusion alone."
"Those of evil intent who know deceit must be slain by deceit;
and those skilled in illusion must be overcome by illusions—thus has the Dharma been proclaimed. (61)
But you alone are our refuge here today, and likewise our ultimate resort;
O beautiful one, we shall subsist upon everything provided by you.
If you would restrain us, that indeed would be for your own supreme benefit;
and we, likewise, shall never hold you in contempt.
Then that wise one of auspicious appearance, smiling at him, said:
"I shall do for you that which you have sung as true.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, while they were looking on, the all-pervading Viṣṇu assumed his own form,
seized the nectar, flew up, and gave it to the gods.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Bringing of the Nectar," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
How did that terrible poison arise, possessing the brilliance of ten thousand suns?
How was it drunk by the Blessed One Śaṅkara, who possesses immeasurable splendor?
"And how did the blue color arise upon the neck of the God of Gods, which possesses the luster of the kunda flower and the moon? This I wish to know.
Sanatkumāra said:
In what highly meritorious land did this supreme narrative take place?
And at what time, O one of great splendor, was it told to the one preceded by Brahmā?
O one whose wealth is asceticism, tell us this correctly as it happened:
how did the god Śarva, the blue-throated lord of the three worlds, [behave]? ||4||
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, this was heard by me previously as it was being narrated by Vāyu, the life-breath of the universe, during a thousand-year sacrificial session.
By what cause is the throat of the trident-bearing God of gods blue?
I shall proclaim that; listen, you who have taken refuge in his vow. ||6||
To the north of the king of mountains are lakes, rivers, and pools,
scattered across regions and mountain peaks.
On lofty mountain peaks and in forest glens and caves, high-souled sages of celebrated vows subsisted on roots and fruits. ||8||
They praise Mahādeva here, worshipping him according to the prescribed rites with the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as through dance, song, worship, and other such offerings. (9)
When the wheel of the luminaries had begun its course and the sun had reached the meridian,
all the deities, self-restrained, remained during that hour;
for at that time, the observances of the dwellers of heaven were concluded.
The wind, which moves among them and is the source of life for living beings, the ever-moving one, said: "Salutations to you, O Blue-throated One. (12)
Having heard that, the sages of purified souls and firm vows, known as the Bālakhilyas, who travel along with the sun, [spoke]. (13)
Eighty-eight thousand sages of sublimated vital energy,
subsisting on air, leaves, and water, questioned Vāyu.
The Bālakhilyas said:
"O best of winds, O Prabhajana, we wish to hear by your grace that which was spoken by you regarding 'Nīlakaṇṭha'. (15)
By what means did the throat of the Lord of Ambikā become blue?
We desire to hear this correctly and in detail from your mouth. (16)
Whatever merit we have gained from this is indeed our supreme benefit;
for all the words that proceed forth are uttered by you alone. (17)
When the wind has reached its place within the vocal organs, the production of speech proceeds;
from you, O Wind, knowledge, discernment, and energy proceed. ... By means of yoga, all the phonemes have been set in motion.
From which words turn back, and which are difficult to attain even for those bound by a body. ||19||
Even there, O Wind, your existence is attested; you are all-pervading at all times.
O Samīraṇa, there is no other all-pervading deity apart from you.
And this very world of living beings is sustained by you, O Wind;
for this world of the living is manifest before you, O source of life. (21)
"Do you know the Lord Vācaspati, the master of speech and the leader of the mind? Tell me, by whom was this transformation of form brought about in this region? (22)
Having heard the words of those sages of purified souls,
Vāyu, of great splendor and honored by the worlds, replied.
Vāyu said:
O Brahmins, in former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was a righteous-souled mind-born progenitor named Vasiṣṭha, who was devoted to the determination of the Vedas. ||24||
He questioned Kārttikeya, who has the excellent peacock as his vehicle,
who brought about the end of the body of Krauñca, who delights the heart of the Goddess,
and who stole the collyrium from the eyes of the women of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
[He told] the story of the high-souled Mahāsena, whose voice resounded like the thundering of clouds,
who brought joy to Umā, and who appeared as a child in disguise—
a narrative filled with many auspicious signs and destructive of all sins.
At that time, Vasiṣṭha, the great ascetic, offered a prayer.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"I take refuge in Śuci, the giver of boons, devoted to Brahman, and possessed of immeasurable splendor."
To you who are eternally compassionate toward devotees, omniscient, and of pleasing appearance; [to you who are...
homage to you, O fountain of grace, whose womb is fire; homage be to you! || 28-29 ||
Salutations to you who were born in the reeds; salutations to you, the son of the Kṛttikās.
Salutations to the twelve-eyed one; let there be salutations to you, the six-faced one.
Salutations to you who hold a spear in your hand, O possessor of divine weapons...

Homage to Hiraṇyaretas; homage to you, the source of well-being for all beings! Homage to him who holds a cock in his hand, and likewise to him who is fond of goats! Homage to you, the one clad in red garments; homage to the one with the blue crest!
Salutations to the Youthful One (Kumāra), who is worshipped by all the gods;
salutations to the destroyer of Krauñca and the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura;
salutations to you, whose form is the ocean... || 33-34 ||
Salutations to you who possess the form of a child and who are playful like one intoxicated!
For what reason has this auspicious mark, resembling white collyrium,
appeared upon the neck of Śiva, which resembles the jasmine flower or the moon?
This [is for you], who are trustworthy, self-controlled, and devoted, as you ask me.
"Speak a discourse endowed with auspiciousness and resting upon merit.
Thus was he praised by the sage Vasiṣṭha, whose self was purified.
Having heard those words of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha,
the immensely radiant enemy of the Daityas, born from the fire, replied:
"O twice-born one, as for the question you have asked me, that which has been spoken by you— "
Listen, O best of speakers, to this which is being told by me—
just as it was formerly heard by me from the conversation between the high-souled Śaṃkara and Pārvatī, while he was seated upon Umā’s lap.
I shall proclaim that to you exactly as it is, O Great Sage,
on the delightful peak of Kailāsa, variegated with various minerals.
Resembling the rising sun and like molten gold,
with stairs of diamond and crystal and surfaces of variegated silk-stone,
it was divine, made of Jāmbūnada gold, and adorned with various jewels.
It was filled with various trees and creepers, and possessed various flowers, fruits, and waters. ||43||
It was filled with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, adorned by *cakravāka* birds, its lotuses resonating with the songs of bees, echoing with the falling of waterfalls,
and its caves resounding with the cries of intoxicated cranes and peacocks. ||44||
It was crowded with throngs of Apsarases and adorned by Kinnaras;
it resounded with the cries of Jīvañjīvaka birds and Dātyūhas,
was sweet with the warbling of cuckoos, and was frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
In that place rich with the lowing of cattle, echoing with the thunder of clouds,
where mountain caves resounded with the cries of elephants agitated by fear of the Vināyakas,
and filled with the sound of flutes enchanting to the sense of hearing; ||47||
In that place frequented by women and siddhas, with playful and graceful movements of the swing.
It was filled with the ringing of bells on suspended swings adorned with banners,
abounding in the sound of lutes, and crowded with the activity of dancing;
likewise, it resounded with the beating of drums and the clapping of hands.
In a cave resounding with the cries of playful activities and diversions.
While the Lord of the Gaṇas was sporting with faces that were terrifying with laughter and likewise distorted, and with various bodily forms—
some with the fierce faces of tigers and lions, and others with the faces of serpents and mice.
Others had the faces of deer and sheep, as well as the faces of elephants and horses; some had fierce feline faces, while others possessed the forms and shapes of jackals.
They were short, tall, emaciated, and stout, with protruding bellies and massive stomachs.
With short shanks, with protruding lips, and others with shanks like palm trees;
with ears like those of a cow, with a single ear, with large ears, and with no ears at all. ||54||
With one foot, with great feet, with many feet, and with no feet at all;
with a single head, most fierce, or with many heads, formidable.
And with the leaders of the hosts who were headless, as well as those with massive heads;
with those having a single eye, great eyes, or many eyes in every respect;
and with other leaders of the hosts who were headless and bodiless in form.
With one nose, with large noses, with many noses, and with no noses;
with one face, with large faces, with many faces, and with no faces;
with one tusk, with large tusks, with many tusks, and with no tusks. ||57–58||

Surrounded by such great yogis who were elemental beings— some with one hand, some with large hands, some with many hands, and some without hands; some with universal forms, some with deformed shapes, some with beautiful forms, and some devoid of form— the Lord of Beings was thus encompassed.
Seated comfortably upon a delightful golden stone surface, adorned with armlets made of pure jewels,
the daughter of the mountain king addressed these words to the destroyer of the god of love.
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, whose banner is marked by the bull!
O Mahādeva, that which shines upon your neck, O Great God, resembles a dark cloud."

"O Lord, destroyer of the body of Kāma, what is this auspicious, brilliant, and not overly intense [mark] on your neck that resembles a mass of blue collyrium? O Īśvara, what is the cause or what is the reason by which this [neck] has become blue?"
I wish to hear all of this in its true essence, according to the proper method.
Then, having heard the words of the goddess Pārvatī, Śaṅkara, the beloved of Pārvatī, recounted a narrative filled with auspiciousness.
Maheśvara said:
Formerly, while the Ocean of Milk was being churned by the gods and the dānavas,
a terrible poison arose first, possessing the brilliance of the fire of cosmic destruction.
It appeared like Death itself at the end of time, possessing the brilliance of the sun at the dissolution of the eon;
it shone forth on all sides with the splendor of the sun that destroys the three worlds.
O lady of beautiful countenance, having seen him, the hosts of gods and the Daityas all became dejected in face and went into the presence of Brahmā.
Seeing the hosts of gods terrified, the highly effulgent Brahmā spoke.
I have bestowed upon you the eightfold sovereignty.
You are all lords of the three worlds, free from all affliction;
you shall all travel in celestial chariots and move about according to your own will.
"Properly honored by the subjects and always highly esteemed by me, for what reason are these women of great wisdom so deeply distressed in mind? (69)
By whom has their sovereignty been revoked, that they have come before me?
There is no one else capable of turning them back from the creation of progeny, other than me who possesses such knowledge.
Regarding the internal, the elemental, and the celestial, as well as the ripening of the karma of living beings, you are eternally capable of acting. ||71||
"What is the task? What is the cause? Or from where has fear come, by which you are so agitated like deer tormented by a lion?
You ought to explain all this quickly and according to the facts."
Then, having heard those words of the high-souled Brahmā,
the lords of the gods, Daityas, and Dānavas, together with the sages, said:
"O Brahmā, while the great ocean was being churned by the hosts of gods and asuras..."
The terrible poison, resembling a serpent or a bee, appearing like a dark blue cloud and possessing a radiance equal to the fire of universal destruction, manifested itself. ||75||
It appeared like the Death at the end of time, possessing a brilliance equal to the fire at the destruction of the eon;
it shone forth on all sides with the splendor of the sun that destroys the three worlds,
standing there as a truly vast mass of radiance.
Seeing that great poison suddenly arisen, they were all dejected of countenance.
By that rising poison, which possessed a brilliance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction,
Janārdana— whose limbs were once red and fair— was scorched and turned black.

Having seen Janārdana, whose limbs were once reddish-fair but had been turned black, we were all terrified; O Brahmā, we have come to you alone for refuge. Having heard these fear-inducing words of both the gods and the asuras, [he acted].
The immensely radiant Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, replied.
"Listen, all you deities and sages whose wealth is asceticism!
When the great ocean was being churned,
there first emerged that poison known as Kālakūṭa, resembling the fire of universal destruction."
As soon as he has arisen, the deities do not shine;
neither Viṣṇu, nor I, nor all the preeminent gods together are able to withstand his impetus, except for Śaṅkara. ||82-83||

Having spoken thus, Brahmā— the lotus-born, who is not born from a womb, and who possesses the luster of the interior of a lotus and is the best among those who know the Vedas— began to praise me in this manner.
Brahmā said:
Salutations to you, O Virūpākṣa; salutations to you, the many-eyed one. Salutations to the one with the Pināka in hand, and indeed salutations to the one with the thunderbolt in hand. ||85||
Salutations to the one who holds a trident in his hand, whose hands bear a staff, a noose, and a sword;
salutations to the Lord of the three worlds, salutations to the Master of all beings;
salutations to the slayer of the enemies of the gods, whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire.
Salutations to Brahmā, to Rudra, and indeed to Viṣṇu. Salutations to Sāṃkhya and to Yoga, and salutations indeed to the multitude of beings.
Salutations to the destroyer of the body of Manmatha, and indeed to the Death of Time.
To Rudra, whose seed is wealth, the God of gods, the impetuous one;
to the turbaned one, the fair-faced one, the thousand-eyed, the bountiful giver;
to the one with matted hair, the formidable one, Śaṅkara, and Hara. ||89||
Salutations to the one who is deformed and the one who is beautiful, to Śiva, and to the giver of boons;
salutations to the destroyer of Tripura, to the destroyer of sacrifices, and to the Lord of the Mothers; and salutations to the awakened one, the pure one, the liberated one, and the absolute one.
And to the creator of the three worlds, to Śakra, the giver of boons, to the foremost, likewise to the fierce one, to the brahmin with infinite vision. ||92||
Salutations indeed to Rajas, to Sattva, and to Tamas, whose source is the Unmanifest; salutations to the eternal, to the non-eternal, and to that which is both eternal and non-eternal.

Salutations indeed to the manifest and to the unmanifest, and to that which is both manifest and unmanifest; salutations indeed to the conceivable and to the inconceivable, and to that which is both conceivable and inconceivable. ||94||

Salutations indeed to the subtle, to the non-subtle, and to the one who is both subtle and non-subtle; salutations to the destroyer of the afflictions of devotees and to the one who is dear to Nārāyaṇa. ||95||
To Śarva, the beloved of Umā, whose lap is marked by the face of Nandin;
to Him who is the fortnight, the month, the half-month, the season, and the year. ||96||

To the one of many forms, to the shaven-headed, to the bearer of the staff, to the protector, to the charioteer, to the archer, to the one with matted hair, and to the perpetual celibate student. ||97||
Salutations to you, O Blessed One, the Puruṣa and the Lord whose form consists of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas;
salutations to you, O three-eyed one; salutations to you, O Blessed Śiva. 98.
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; salutations to you, O Creator of all beings.
Thus praised with such deeds and words, to you, the one worthy of praise, let there be salutation! (99)
Having bowed my head, I prostrate before Rudra, the teacher of the world, the best of gods, the three-eyed one;
O storehouse of splendor, you are subtle and attainable through the excellence of yoga—I clearly approach that Rudra.
O God of gods, having recognized my devotion, be gracious, O you whose hair is drenched by the waters of the Gaṅgā!
With effort, I have gone for refuge to you, Śiva, whose vehicle is the variegated bull and clouds. 101.
Thus, at that time, I was praised by Brahmā, the creator of the world, with various hymns originating from the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. ||102||
Then, being pleased with that high-souled Brahmā,
I bowed to the Grandfather with the utmost devotion and spoke to him.
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, Sovereign of beings, O Great Ascetic!
What task for you must be performed by me, O Brahmā? Speak, O observer of noble vows.
Having heard these words, O lotus-eyed one, Brahmā then replied:
Brahmā said:
O Lord of the past, future, and present, O Sovereign of Causes, listen,
O God, while the great ocean was being churned by the hosts of gods and asuras.
A terrible poison appeared, resembling peacocks and bumblebees, like a dark blue cloud, and possessing a brilliance equal to the fire of universal destruction. 106.
It arose like Death itself at the end of an eon, possessing the splendor of the sun at the dissolution of the world;
it shone forth on all sides with the brilliance of the sun that destroys the three worlds,
rising up with poison and a radiance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction.
Janārdana, whose limbs were once red and fair, was burnt and turned black.
Having seen Janārdana, whose limbs were once reddish-fair, now made black,
we were all struck with fear and have come to you alone for refuge.
Drink that, O Mahādeva, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds;
for you are indeed the consumer of the first portion, you who are the Lord and the best of gods.
"Your Honor is capable of restraining his great impetus;
no other man whatsoever in this world of mobile and immobile beings is able to do so.
O Mahādeva, O you of great splendor, you alone are capable of protecting [the world]."
Of that very one of fierce power, whose splendor is equal to the fire of cosmic destruction.
"O Mahādeva, there is no one else capable of withstanding his force.
While the supreme Brahmā was speaking thus, O Goddess—
Saying "So be it," O fair-faced one, I accepted those words and began to drink that poison which was like the God of Death himself.

O you who are worshipped by the hosts of gods, O lotus-eyed one, as I was drinking the most terrible poison for the sake of the welfare of the three worlds in the presence of the lords of the gods and the daityas,
it quickly became black in my throat.
Seeing that great poison, which resembled the petals of a blue lotus, clinging to his neck like the serpent king Takṣaka with its tongue flickering— like a snake.
Then the immensely radiant Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, said:
"O Mahādeva of noble vows, you shine with this throat."
Having heard these words of his, O daughter of the mountain king, O lady of beautiful countenance, I [acted] while the hosts of gods and the Daityas were looking on.
The terrible poison was held in the throat by the yakṣas, gandharvas, siddhas, piśācas, uragas, and rakṣasas; therefore, I possess the state of Śrīkaṇṭha.
O daughter of the mountain king, seeing that deadly poison of fierce radiance held in his throat,
the entire host of gods and demons was delighted and attained the utmost wonder.
Then all the hosts of gods, along with the yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas, spoke with palms joined in reverence, O Goddess who moves like an elephant in rut: (121)
Oh, what strength, heroism, and prowess you possess! Oh, what a body and power of yoga you have!
Oh, what majesty you display, O God of gods, whose moon-crested head is bathed by the waters of the Gaṅgā! 122.
You alone are Viṣṇu and you are the four-faced Brahmā; you alone are the sun and you are the moon.
You alone are Time and you alone are Destiny; you alone are Death and you alone are the Giver of Wealth. 123.
You alone are the subtle, imperishable Puruṣa; you alone are subtler than the subtle.
You alone are the manifest, you alone are Prakṛti, and you alone are both Sattva and the source of existence. ||124||
You alone are the earth, you alone are the water; you alone are fire, and you alone are the wind.
You alone are space, the past, the future, and the present; you alone are all that has been, is being, and will be.
You alone are the sacrifice, you alone are the discipline; you alone perform every act of dharma.
You alone are the distinct distributor of all that is moving and unmoving, and you are the protector at the time of dissolution.
Having spoken these words, the lords of the gods and the hosts of Siddhas, being delighted, bowed to me;
their sorrows dispelled and the moon [of their minds] restored, they departed with joyful hearts and the fierce speed of the wind. (127)
This supreme secret, greater in merit than merit itself, is great;
this hymn that destroys all sins was spoken by the Self-Existent One himself. || 1.28 ||
But he who, devoted to Me and established in the observances, constantly retains this auspicious hymn sung by Brahmā, which indeed destroys all diseases. (129)
I shall declare the destiny of that embodied being both here and in the hereafter;
for him, O lady of excellent hips, poison—whether stationary or mobile—is as nothing.
O lady of beautiful hips, having reached one's body, it is quickly countered;
having attained tranquility, it removes both auspicious and terrible bad dreams. ||1.31||
He becomes beloved among women and in the assembly of the king;
he attains victory in debate and in battle—of this there is no doubt. (1.3.2)
And as he travels on the path, well-being and strength arise within him.
O fair-faced one, I shall describe his destination upon the dissolution of the body.
He has a tawny beard, a blue throat, and hair marked by the crescent moon; he is three-eyed, possesses an indestructible trident, has the bull as his emblem, and is endowed with great strength.
With a body equal to Nandin’s and prowess equal to Nandin’s,
that perfected one (siddha) wanders through all the seven worlds by my command;
his movement cannot be obstructed, like that of the wind in the sky.
Having become my attendant, he shall remain until the dissolution of all beings.
O lady of excellent hips, I shall also declare the fruit for those men who always listen to this, O you who possess a thousandfold fruit.
A Brāhmaṇa attains the Veda; a Kṣatriya gains the earth;
a Vaiśya obtains profit; and a Śūdra attains a happy state. ||138||
The diseased is freed from illness; the bound shall be released from bondage;
the pregnant woman shall give birth to a son; and the maiden finds a worthy husband. (139)
A mortal who hears this story obtains lost wealth both in this world and in the next; he attains that same fruit which is the reward for properly giving away a hundred thousand cows.
Whether it be a syllable, or a quarter-verse, or a verse, or even half a verse; ||141||
Alternatively, that man who daily recites this entire chapter in an assembly of gods and Brahmins, with his inner self absorbed in me; || 142 ||
One who is faithful and ever-exerting is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Recite this, O Goddess—may it be well with you—and teach it to your kinsmen. (143)
Therefore, there has never been, nor will there ever be, a hymn superior to this;
neither the yakṣas, nor the piśācas, nor the bhūtas, nor the vināyakas [possess such power]. 144.
They shall create obstacles in that house where this hymn remains.
Just as among all fields, the field of liberation is designated as the most excellent,
so too is this hymn composed by Brahmā the most preeminent among hymns.
And whoever should cause even a single foot of this to be heard by Brāhmaṇas at a śrāddha ceremony, [attains the highest reward]. || 146 ||
Indeed, inexhaustible food and drink attend upon his ancestors—whatever has been mentally conceived and whatever has been uttered by speech. || 147 ||
Everything is accomplished for one by reciting this hymn;
even those who are of sinful birth, having heard this supreme secret, [attain success]. (148)
Women and Śūdras also go to the world of Rudra here; and when, after the lapse of time, they occasionally attain human status once more. (149)
One who knows the truth of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas is born into a pure family; he becomes a devotee of the gods and then practices righteousness. ||8.114.150||
This meritorious history, which destroys all sins, has been spoken here by me, who am well-pleased, O lotus-eyed one. 151.
Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Hymn to Mahādeva Composed by Brahmā," within the Episode of Nīlakaṇṭha during the Churning for Nectar in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
When that nectar had been seized by Viṣṇu in a disguised form, [the gods were overcome with fear].
And what did the Daityas and the Dānavas do in the meantime? ||1||
Sanatkumāra said:
Deceived by Viṣṇu through his anger, all those lords of the Dānavas then armed themselves for battle and, reviling Viṣṇu, spoke as follows.
Fie on your strength! Fie on your heroism! Fie on your prowess, O wicked one!
You are a constant betrayer of trust, a performer of base deeds, and evil-minded. ||3||
In the past, Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain by you through deceit, as was Hiraṇyākṣa, the lord of the Daityas; and this nectar has been recovered by you.
You possess no strength in battle, for you are powerful only through deceit;
remain standing in battle, and you shall not attain liberation from us.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that king of the Daityas, enraged and vomiting flames of fire,
rushed toward Viṣṇu himself on a chariot whose roar was like the sound of clouds.
Then Vipracitti, the lord of the Daityas,
challenged the thousand-eyed Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, to battle with his elephant;
and Virocana, filled with rage, [challenged] the Lord of Wealth, the sovereign of the Rākṣasas.
On his elephant alone, he rushed forward like a rain-cloud toward the sun;
and Bali, the son of Virocana, on his chariot, rushed toward Yama, the lord of the ancestral hosts, as Vighna rushed toward another Vighna.
And Anuhrāda, the lord of the Daityas and son of Hiraṇyakaśipu,
rushed toward Varuṇa like the force of a river rushing toward the ocean.
But Maya, the best of the Dānavas, as well as Tāra and Tāraka,
were engaged with the Ādityas like great elephants with [other] elephants;
so too were Śarabha, Śataketu, Bala, and the Dānava Mūka.
The Rudras indeed overwhelmed them, like lions attacking other lions in the forest.
Śambhu, Kārtasvana, and the great illusionist Śambara were engaged with the Vasus,
as if vices were entangled with the virtuous.
Narakāsura, Hayagrīva,
and the asura Indradamana were engaged with the two Aśvins, like stars joined by two planets;
others, possessed of great illusion and great strength, were likewise engaged with other gods.
Calling out one after another, all the Dānavas fought with fury.
Vipracitti, the master of great illusions, afflicted the thousand-eyed Indra with three arrows,
making the ten directions resound with his roar.
As he was shooting, the powerful Indra, possessing a light hand, shattered his variegated bow into a hundred pieces with his hundred-edged thunderbolt. Then,
as he was grasping another formidable bow, his elephant [was struck].

The elephant trampled him so that he fell like a mountain. When the Dānava had leaped from the elephant, the powerful king of the gods struck him with his thunderbolt, just as Guha struck Krauñca with his spear in battle.
By that blow of the thunderbolt, the Dānava, his mind bewildered, fell swiftly to the earth like a tree shattered by the wind. ||8.115.20||
Then a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the host of the Dānavas, while the gods uttered shouts of "Well done! Well done! accompanied by lion-like roars.
Then, having regained his composure, he [the Asura] with that spear of fearsome form—
Mātaṅga led him away, intoxicated, to the abode of Yama.
Then that foremost of gods shattered his rear guards and his armor of great luster; abandoning the battle, he departed.
Bali, Yama, Puṇḍra, Kṛtānta, Kalaha, as well as Kāla, Niyati, the Kiṅkaras, and Pāśa; ||24||
As he watched each one, he pierced them with five sharp arrows each,
and he also struck Yama himself in the heart with sixty-four.
As he was crying out thus, Yama, becoming enraged, then laughed and,
striking his chariot with his staff, reduced it to ashes.
While the chariot, along with its driver, horses, and footmen, stood still, Bali, crying out "Stay! Stay!", rushed toward Yama. As he was thus attacking, Yama swiftly hurled his staff at him.
Then, from that blow to his head, he fell to the surface of the earth.
Then a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the host of the Dānavas; some cried out, "Seize him! Seize him!", while others exclaimed, "Woe! Woe! (29).
But the mighty Anuhrāda, having struck Varuṇa in the heart with a steel arrow, angrily felled him onto the seat of his chariot.
Rising up in an instant, that god drew his powerful bow.
Having fixed an arrow, the valiant one cut through his bow.
He struck the horses and struck off the head of the charioteer from his body;
as he was leaping down from that excellent chariot whose horses had been slain, [he was struck].
It quickly pierced his heart, and he fell down as if dead;
meanwhile, Maya, Tāra, and Tāraka severely oppressed the Ādityas.
They too, with three hundred arrows each, deprived all of them of their chariots—
Śarabha, Śataketu, Bala, and the Dānava Mūka—
while roaring in battle and afflicting the Rudras with various kinds of weapons.
Having warded off those weapons of theirs, the mighty ones [proceeded].
Like locusts, they destroyed the fields in an instant;
being driven away by those many Rudras, they were then deprived of their chariots.
Abandoning the battle, Mahāmāya fled in all directions; so too did Śambhu, Kārtasvana, and the great illusionist Śambara. ||37||
In the battle, they rushed at the Vasus like elephants charging at rival elephants;
then all the Vasus discharged the Svapana weapon against them. (38)
Stationed upon their chariots, they appeared like sleeping deer;
while they were thus asleep, the charioteers carried them away from that battlefield.
They struck down the heads of the charioteers as they were carrying away [the warriors]. When the charioteers had been slain,
the sons of Diti, while still asleep on the battlefield, were then whirled around by the bewildered horses.
Narakotha, Hayagrīva, and Indradamana as well; ||41||
The two Aśvins, those lords of the gods, fought with great resolve;
then, as they were charging forward, those two gods, the best of physicians, [encountered them].
With their staff-like weapons, they rendered them all chariotless;
then [they struck] all those who were rushing forward again, mace-bearing and frantic with rage.
With the Vāyavya weapon, they suddenly struck one another down in the battle;
and other gods then slaughtered the sons of Diti,
just as deer gathered in the forest are torn apart by lions.
And Prahlāda, the lord of the Daityas, was also united with Viṣṇu. ||45||
Having fought a great battle at that time, he became deprived of his chariot;
his horses were slain by the discus, and his charioteer and followers were killed.
Seizing his mace and leaping forward, he rushed toward Janārdana;
as he ran with his hand raised, O great sage— ||47||
Janārdana swiftly cut that mace with his very discus.
Then those heroic Dānavas, their prowess shattered by those gods,
were routed out of fear, like herds of deer in the forest by lions.
Seeing them broken and being broken, they abandoned the battle and departed. || 49 ||
Prahlāda also, abandoning the battle, followed after them;
when they were broken, Indra's cry of victory was greatly celebrated.
Then the gods, together with Nārāyaṇa and the world-protectors, made [the battle] equal;
they let out various lion-roars and sounded musical instruments.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the section on the Battle during the Churning for the Nectar of Immortality.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus, O Vyāsa, occurred that churning for the nectar,
as well as a most terrible battle with Prahlāda himself.
After a long time, having waged hundreds of battles,
that lord of the asuras bestowed the kingdom upon his son Virocana.
Furthermore, O Vyāsa, the mighty Virocana, for the sake of the kingdom—
Āṭībaka was slain in battle by the greatly powerful Lord of the Gods.
Vyāsa said:
How did that battle between Āṭi and Baka occur, so full of great terror?
O Blessed One, I wish to hear it, for my curiosity is indeed supreme. (4)
Sanatkumāra said:
Once again here on earth, there was friendship between the gods and the asuras;
and they, with faces full of wonder, beheld it from afar.
In that land of Āmilāvṛta, which was filled with terrors, they beheld a fierce Atharvanic *kṛtyā* of deformed appearance, striking fear into the asuras.
A dispute also arose among the Asuras regarding whether [the creature] was a *baka* (crane).
Then that terrible *kṛtyā* appeared before the gods;
for them she became known as *āṭi*, while for the Asuras she became a *baka*.
O great sage, they made a wager there concerning the kingdom:
"Whichever of us is defeated shall become the slave of the other, and the victor shall be the master.
Then she, in the form of Sītā, granted an audience to them all.
Then those defeated gods said, "We have not been conquered. (8.116.10)
"This is clearly Baka; you have been defeated, there is no doubt.
This is not a crane acting as a rogue, nor is this a rogue acting as a crane. (11)
Thus, as they disputed for the sake of the kingdom, a terrifying battle took place between those chief Dānavas and the gods;
it lasted for a thousand years until Virocana was slain.

When Virocana had been slain, Brahmā consecrated Bali, that great asura, in the position of Indra; and he indeed became king. Thereafter, O Vyāsa, that imperishable one overran the three worlds by his might.
He was born as the lord of the three worlds and indeed as the sovereign of the Asuras;
having conquered the Lord of the Gods in battle, that powerful one displaced him from his station.
That mighty being also assumed the office of Indra and the office of Yama.
He himself became Varuṇa, as well as the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) and Agni;
he became Āditya and Soma, and Parjanya who releases the rain.
He alone always performs everything that is to be done in the world.
While he was thus ruling the kingdom, the gods then experienced unhappiness;
deprived of their sovereignty, those great-souled ones wandered about like birds.
To those distressed high-souled ones, Brahmā granted an insight.
Having consoled them in many ways out of compassion, O Vyāsa, that best of gods,
Brahmā, said:
"O gods, this Bali cannot be harmed by you."
"He is a great-souled and righteous being, and undoubtedly immortal;
he is devoted to Brahman, exceedingly powerful, and has indeed obtained boons.
Let Viṣṇu go to him in the form of a brahmin and make this request. (8.116.20–21)
"Assuming the form of a dwarf, he will take three strides of the earth;
having seized that, let him stride over it in its entirety. (22)
He will undoubtedly make the entire ground level with his stride;
then, he himself will place his second stride in the intermediate space.
"And I myself shall grant you the third step;
thus, O gods, this attainment of your kingdom is seen to be possible, and not otherwise."
At the time when this Viṣṇu sets out for heaven,
at that very time, you must protect the Dānavas with every effort.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus, those lords of gods, being of great courage, deliberated in many ways on what was auspicious and said to Viṣṇu: "Let the word of Brahmā be carried out. (26)
O Lord, that best of Asuras has been initiated for a horse sacrifice today;
go to his concluding purificatory bath tomorrow morning and beg him [for the horse].
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been told by him, "So be it," the gods, clad in armor for battle,
all then stood ready, making Śakra their leader.
Then Nārada, having gone there and being honored by him with devotion, sat down comfortably and spoke these words, he who is the best among speakers. (29)
"I am pleased with your righteousness, as are the sages whose wealth is asceticism.
O best of Dānavas, this conduct of yours is free from anything demonic."
For all the Dānavas are cruel, slayers of Brahmins, and thorns to the worlds;
but you are devoted to Brahmins and likewise a benefactor to the worlds. (31)
Therefore, O bull among Asuras, you should always contemplate what is auspicious for yourself, so that you may indeed possess some measure of well-being at all times, O King. (32)
This Viṣṇu, dispatched by the gods, has assumed the form of a Brahmin;
intent on [restoring] your kingdom, he will demand three strides from you.
Therefore, you must not grant him that kingdom, lest it later be lost to you.
Beyond this, O King, Lord of Asuras, you are the authority.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, having heard those words of his, Bali, the son of Virocana and lord of the Dānavas, then spoke humbly to Nārada.
"O Great Sage, they are my firm enemies and I am theirs;
if they beg from me, then indeed I shall have achieved my purpose. (3.6)
If Madhusūdana, having completely abandoned his own duty,
should entreat me with a humble soul, my life would be fruitful.
O Brahmin, O great sage, this has indeed always been my vow.
"O Lord, I shall not say 'I will not give' when asked;
for, O best of Brahmins, the vital breaths of one who asks depart upwards, but when he says 'I will not give,' they depart toward hell. (38–39)
"Give! is the name for weeping; "there is nothing" is the response to weeping.
"O Nārada, let no other people see me weeping"—this is the thought of every man, O great sage. (8.116.40)
This donor who gives to me as I request—this is indeed the inexhaustible fruit. ||41||
Therefore, if I do not give this great thing requested by my enemies,
I shall undoubtedly fall into the hell named Raurava;
for that lowest of men who does not give to one who begs is indeed destined for it.
He destroys that suppliant who cuts off his hope; of this there is no doubt. || 43 ||
"O venerable one, my father is clearly [my lord], for I am bound by affection toward my son.
O best of Brahmins, I shall not give him up; may you find peace in this.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having taken leave of him and being duly honored by him in return,
he ascended to heaven unperturbed, reflecting on how [the world] might come to be.
When that day had passed, during the night, that one of great fame—
Viṣṇu, having become a brahmin in the form of Vāmana, made a request of him.
And that king, O best of brahmins, [offered] jewels and treasures, villages, female slaves, queens, cows, horses, chariots, and elephants. || 46-47 ||
Variegated vehicles, gold, couches,
beds, coverlets, garments, ornaments, and houses—
whatever the brahmin requests, in whatever measure and in whatever manner.
In whatever manner he was requested, that lord of the Daityas gave it without hesitation.
To him who was acting in such a way, the highly illustrious Vāmana said:
"Give to me whatever I tell you."
Having honored him with a respectful offering, water for his feet, a seat, and other such gifts, he said: "O best of the twice-born, tell me what you desire."
Vāmana said:
"O King, if you grant it to me as I ask out of my own desire, then I shall speak; otherwise, O Lord of Asuras, I will not speak."
Bali said:
"O Brahmin, having understood the matter, I would promise it if it were something to be given; and if it were indeed possible to give, then I would be eager to give it. (53)
Vāmana said: "O best of asuras, this has indeed been your constant vow:
'Whatever a brahmin asks for, that I shall give. (54)
"O Lord of Asuras, having been initiated for the horse sacrifice, you give whatever a brahmin requests; there is no doubt that you grant it all.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus, that king, who was skilled in speech, laughed and, having resolved within himself, spoke again to that one of great heroism: 56.
Bali said: "You are Viṣṇu in the form of a brahmin, yet you entreat me through deception;
having abandoned the duty of a kṣatriya, you speak with the timidity of a beggar. (57)
"Even to all those who are destitute, I shall give when requested;
for, with the exception of the kingdom, I shall grant you, O God, whatever you desire. (58)
Vāmana said:
"This is true; I am Viṣṇu, and our kingdom has been taken away by you.
We have no desire for sovereignty today, for we are indeed free from longing."
"We beg you for a dwelling where I may live in peace.
Bali said:
"O Lord of the Gods, what is the size of that house for which you beg?"
"O Vāmana, tell me in every detail: what kind of gift shall I give, and where?"
Vāmana said:
"O King, grant me, who am a petitioner for a house, a large dwelling endowed with all the qualities of the earth, measured by my three strides."
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O Vyāsa, Śukra, the great ascetic, spoke to Bali:
"O Great King, it must not be given; Viṣṇu alone is possessed of great power."
"This is that invincible slayer of all the Dānavas;
Viṣṇu has come here in this manner through a disguise—release him! ||63||
Disregarding his words, the son of Diti said:
"O Viṣṇu, I shall give you a house exactly as you request."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of his, Madhusūdana spoke to the sinless King Bali in the presence of everyone.
Vāmana said:
"O sinless one, I am the god Sādhya, the son of Dharma and grandson of Diti.
Therefore, O mighty one, there is no fault in my accepting this gift."
O King, Lord of Asuras, if you have no regret later regarding this middle-sized house being given, then pour the water into my hand. ||67||
Sanatkumāra said: Then,
having replied "So be it," that mighty one prepared to bestow a great house upon Vāmana with a golden pitcher.
Then those cruel Dānavas, eager for resistance and intensely intent upon Bali, arrived there, O great sage.
Prahlāda, along with his brothers— Maya, Jambha, Urdhvalocana, the valiant Vipracitti, and others of great strength—
went to him and, placing Prahlāda at their head, spoke to him then.
O Vyāsa, they were contemplating the defeat of Bali, the son of Virocana.
Prahlāda said:
"What is this great undertaking that you have resolved upon, O evil-minded son?"
"O one of great strength, this task of destroying the sons of Diti is not for you;
Viṣṇu alone, the master of great illusion and slayer of the Daityas, is the one.
For he will surely traverse even the three worlds—of this there is no doubt. (72)
O son, you are our refuge; you are our strength and you are our prowess.
Our very life depends upon you; do not destroy us so quickly.
O son, King Hiraṇyakaśipu and the Dānava Hiraṇyākṣa are not worth even a sixteenth part of you, the king.
"O mighty one, give this house to that wise man; I tell you this, for it is indeed for the welfare of all as well as for yourself.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of the high-souled Prahlāda, the righteous and highly illustrious Bali bowed down and spoke this: ||77||
Bali said: "I know indeed that this god is Viṣṇu, the destroyer of all asuras;
yet this is my very vow: whatever is asked of me must be given."
"I am a renowned lord of generosity, famous throughout the three worlds; O givers, while I still live, how could I act otherwise? (79)
"It is unrighteous, brings ill repute, leads away from heaven, and causes great fear;
how indeed could I utter a falsehood? Such is the vow I have undertaken. Having given my word, how could I, for the sake of dharma, again deceive you, O Asuras? (8.116.80)
Prahlāda said:
O son, among the Dānavas and Daityas, dharma was established by themselves; yet the sons of Diti and the Dānavas always prosper through unrighteousness. 81.
Deceit, falsehood, hypocrisy, the slaughter of all beings,
and the plundering of sacrifices— this indeed is our auspicious dharma.
Therefore, O Lord, do not grant [the horse] to that evil-minded one after having promised it.
"For in this way there would be prosperity for us; otherwise, there would be great danger here.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, the wise Bali reflected.
The tiger among asuras, skilled in speech, spoke these words:
Bali said:
"This dharma which has been urged upon you by dharma—"
For there is no infinite fruit for this cruel one, O best of asuras. (85)
King Hiraṇyakaśipu did not attain ultimate happiness, nor did Hiraṇyākṣa, nor even his son Andhaka; likewise,
our grandfather [Hiraṇyakaśipu] suffered through his cruel deeds.
Therefore, whatever wise people there may be do not praise this. || 87 ||
"Behold, O sages, how by means of truth and dharma the gods are established in heaven;
they are exceedingly victorious, and the planets indeed move through the celestial realm."
No one at all is seen in the sky; thus, by means of this cruel deed, I seek to propitiate you. O Lord of the Daityas, I speak to you as I ask for your forgiveness. (89)
Prahlāda said:
O Dānava, whether it be wicked or cruel, or even auspicious, one's own great ancestral tradition must not be abandoned. (8.116.9)
"O son, O great sage, this was practiced by our fathers and likewise by our grandfathers; it must not be abandoned by you. (91)
Bali said:
"O Grandfather, hear from me what was performed by my ancestors without hesitation, as well as that which is censured by the virtuous. (92)
There was a sage of undepressed soul known as Vāmadeva.
Having beheld Urvaśī, his seed fell due to infatuation.
That seed, indeed, was cast upon the ground and a mare consumed it.
A fetus formed within her, and immediately she became a female mule (*aśvatarī*).
Out of affection for his daughter, the sage nurtured her for many years.
Then, the powerful royal sage named Aṣṭaka arrived there.
O Indra among kings, he beheld her in the midst of the sage's hermitage; and filled with supreme joy, he thought thus within his heart: ||| 96 ||
"This woman is equal to my wife in the perfection of her auspicious marks;
if the Brahmin were to give her [to me], it would be most excellent for me. || 97 ||
"And this brahmin will not give her to me, for she is very difficult to obtain;
however, I shall employ a stratagem by which he will give that radiant woman.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the king, having gone to him, spoke to Vāmadeva with great reverence and humility, O son of Śakti.
The king said:
"O great sage, I have a certain task that must be performed by means of this mare;
requested as I am, please grant it to me for a full year."
"O best of the twice-born, when the task is again accomplished for you,
O lord of brahmins, I shall give her back to you— if she is to be given, let her be given.
Then that tiger among sages gave the blameless woman to him.
Having seized her, the king then departed, rejoicing at having obtained her.
Then, when a year had passed, that best of sages said to him; the brahmin then spoke to him: "Give me the auspicious she-mule."
For that evil-minded sage did not give it, and out of anger he killed him.
Thereupon, his son became the king, a bull among men.
Then the brahmin spoke to him as well, but he too did not give it at that time.
Then that evil-minded one died likewise from the wrath of the brahmin.
His son became king, the best of the Daityas;
then the brahmin said to him, "Give me the she-mule."
Then, having been entreated in that manner, that wicked-souled one replied:
"I will not give [it] to this evil-minded murderer of my father."
Then that brahmin, filled with rage, deprived him also of his life;
thereafter, his young son became a king of exceeding splendor.
Overwhelmed by anger, that brahmin spoke to him as well:
"I shall surely destroy the lineage of that evil-minded Aṣṭaka."
Having heard those words of his, the youth honored that twice-born man and said,
"I shall give the Vāḍava girl after consulting my ministers.
Then, O Lord of the Dānavas, he summoned his ministers and questioned them.
"Tell me, should this beautiful female mule be given away or not?
The ministers replied,
"In former times, this female mule was given to your grandfather by his father."
O Lord of Men, she was entreated here for one year and then brought back.
When the year was complete, O great sage, although the brahmin begged, it was not given; and out of anger, that brahmin died.
Then your grandfather became king, O lord of subjects;
likewise, he too died because of the anger of a Brahmin after having given her away.
But if you would follow the conduct of your ancestors, this evil-minded Death, appearing in the form of a Brahmin, must not be given [the gift]. || 11.5 ||
Having heard those words of his ministers, the one of great asceticism, filled with indignation, rebuked them— who were ignorant of dharma— and spoke as follows.
In the past, having resorted to folly, they committed an act that was exceedingly cruel, unrighteous, disgraceful, and censured by the virtuous. ||1.17||
I shall by no means follow the path they have taken; today, I will rescue those ancestors and grandfathers of unrefined wisdom who stand in the pit, as well as my very great lineage.
Having spoken thus at their passing, a son of great intelligence was born. ||119||
The king formed a firm resolve to give a female mule to the Brahmin;
then, having honored that ṛṣi with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings,
that lord of men gave him his own female mule.
Having indeed given wealth to him, he propitiated that seer.
Then that powerful tiger among sages, with a delighted inner self,
raised up that tiger among kings and spoke these words.
O mighty-armed one, by you, a virtuous son, your fathers and grandfathers dwelling in hell have been delivered, enveloped as they were by the property of a Brahmin.
"I have no need for the jewels, nor for the mares, O lord of men;
being pleased with you, I grant all of this to you, O lord of men. (1.24)
O mighty-armed one, if that evil-minded Aṣṭaka had indeed acted thus toward me, or his son, or even your own father, O you of wicked intellect! || 125 ||
If they have not met with destruction and if I am satisfied in every way, then I shall take my leave and depart; this wealth of yours is indeed mine.
Then that tiger among sages departed for the forest itself;
the king, having obtained the female donkey, enjoyed himself with her as he pleased.

"O King, all the twice-born ones and others who speak of dharma do not praise such an act that is devoid of righteousness, even if it was done by the ancients. Therefore, I shall give the kingdom to the high-souled Vāmana. (128)
Sanatkumāra said: Then that tiger among asuras duly poured the highly venerable water upon the hand of Vāmana.
As soon as that [discus] was cast into the water over the great-souled Viṣṇu, a shower of flowers fell upon the lord of the Daityas;
and there arose the sound of invisible beings crying, "Excellent! Excellent! (8.116.130).
And here the celestial drums resounded of their own accord without being struck;
auspicious winds blew, carrying fragrant scents, and a sound arose there saying, "All you Dānavas are slain! || 132 ||

Then, having observed that deed of his which was so exceedingly difficult to perform, all the sages whose wealth is asceticism praised the Lord of the sons of Diti and bowed from afar to Madhusūdana. Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter in the Vāmana section of the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the Blessed Viṣṇu spoke to that bull among the Asuras:
"Behold, O lord of Dānavas, O one of radiant luster; I shall stride with my steps."
"If [the earth] is filled [with the merit of giving], then what has been given is complete; otherwise, more must be given.
Therefore, O Dānava, take another portion of land and be true to your word.
Bali said:
"Stride, O best of Vāmanas, with three strides today in every direction;
if [the earth] is not filled, I shall be the giver—this I tell you in truth.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the imperishable Viṣṇu, intending to advance, prostrated himself with supreme devotion before Mahādeva, the Lord of Gods and the Consort of Umā.
Thereupon, the gods, well-prepared, armored, and eager for battle, [stood ready].
Through the sky, those great beings of immense power arrived there.
Then, on the continent of Puṣkara, Viṣṇu assumed a form of supreme radiance and strode across both the earth and the heavens.
Placing one foot on the mountain Udaya and the second on the lord of rivers,
he traversed this world from the north of Puṣkara;
then, having taken a stride, as he was lifting his single foot, [he reached the next world].
The lord of the Daityas named Aja seized that foot.
Madhusūdana, lifting him up along with the Asura, hurled him away;
O Vyāsa, even today that Asura has not returned.
Then, having resorted to the supreme second yoga of Rudra, he became a single stride alone in the intermediate space, the *bhuvarloka*. Thereafter,
from that intermediate space, he again resorted to the yoga of Brahmā.
O Vyāsa, he traversed the entire Svarloka in a single stride.
Having reached that world, the best of gods emerged from it;
having then reached Janaloka, he did not complete his stride there. || 11-12 ||
And as he was ascending, the Daityas there, with weapons and missiles in their hands, rushed forward with speed; the gods repelled them.
At that time, ten thousand sons of Bala,
his offspring fighting with various weapons in their hands, were slain by him.
Both Bāṇa and Vāta, these two sons of Bali, were possessed of great strength.
Therefore, O Sage Vyāsa, having fallen from that state, they both then departed from the battle.
Then Brahmā, the Grandfather of this world, having approached, established an agreement with the Lord of Gods:
"O Bali, you have restored the entire kingdom of the gods. || 16 ||
Abiding by truth and the sacred pledge, do not desire kingship again. ||17||
"O child, this auspicious period of yours shall last for the duration of this Manvantara; it must always be observed by you. Now go, as you please. || 18 ||
You will obtain this fruit of sacrifice perfectly, there is no doubt;
and by my grace, you shall indeed attain yoga once again.
Having been addressed thus, she took leave of him and entered Pātāla;
the gods, too, having regained their own kingdom, rejoiced greatly.
Vyāsa said: Of what nature was that Lord Viṣṇu, who, having abandoned his own exalted dharma,
recovered the three worlds, yet felt no sense of injustice regarding this?
Sanatkumāra said:
As that god Viṣṇu proceeded, his form shone with the brilliance of a blazing fire;
it was exceedingly fierce and difficult even for the gods to behold.
Then the gods, together with Indra, having accomplished their purpose, praised and extolled Viṣṇu, the supreme deity of great power.
Endowed with supreme joy, all of us bear divine weapons;
O Lord of the Gods, O best of deities, you have become our protector and the restorer of our kingdom as we were being oppressed by the Dānavas.
By you, we have all been made happy, just as those who perform meritorious deeds are by their own good actions. ||25||
"O Lord, by your power we shall enjoy the kingdom free from anxiety, just as the sons of the gods did in former times through the power of the Sun.
For you are our supreme light and likewise our ultimate refuge. (26)
And you alone are the supreme purifier, except for the god Umāpati.
Sanatkumāra said: As the wielder of the Śārṅga bow was thus being praised by the gods, he then experienced extreme satisfaction as well as great self-regard.
Then, O Sage, because of his pride, that supreme yoga of his fell away,
just as a fire is extinguished when drenched with water.
Then, O sage, having found that opportunity, that sinful and demonic woman,
being greatly delighted, entered into Janārdana with great joy.
O Vyāsa, possessed by that sinful woman, the imperishable Viṣṇu did not shine there,
even though he was radiant, just as virtuous men do not shine when they encounter a cruel person.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Traversing of the Three Worlds," in the Vāmana section of the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, at that time he was thus joined with that sinful, demoniacal nature.
That very form, the best of gods, assumed as the dwarf. ||1||
To him who was thus behaving, all the gods, including Indra, said: "O Lord, what is this strange transformation of yours?"
Having heard those words of theirs, the sages of celebrated vows—
Marīci, Bhṛgu, Atri, Aṅgiras, Kratu,
Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Ruci— [spoke].
Viśvāmitra, Vāmadeva, Bharadvāja, and likewise Auśija. ||4||
Gautama and Śaradvat, Kaśyapa and Uddala, Vatsāra and Naidhruva, and the self-possessed Cyavana as well. (5)
Dadhīca, Ṛcīka, and the renowned Jamadagni;
likewise Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, and Agasti of great asceticism. ||6||
Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Śakti along with Parāśara,
Kuṇi, Kuṇibāhu, and he who is Sārasvata—
these and other sages, as well as Nārada together with Parvata.
Then, O Vyāsa, being urged by Brahmā, the sages spoke to the gods: "O lords of the gods, we have arrived today from the world of Brahmā.
The sages said:
"O lords of the gods, we have arrived today from the world of Brahmā."
They were swiftly commanded by Brahmā for the sake of this very god.
Because that high-souled Vaikuṇṭha, the kinsman of the gods, abandoned his own duty and accepted the kingdom as a gift,
therefore the sin of the Asuras— which causes terror to all living beings— [departed].
Having completely abandoned the Asuras, she entered into Keśava.
Thus overcome, this god was unable to afflict his enemies;
yet behold, all of you, that his splendor is indeed as auspicious as it was before.
If you think that he, being well-composed, has bathed at sacred fords and is to sacrifice again with the horse-sacrifice along with the gods,
and that he will then see the wielder of the Pināka bow and be purified in every way by him— [then you are mistaken]. 13.
"Thus shall you be liberated from evil," so said the Grandfather.
Sanatkumāra said: Then all those gods, together with the hosts of sages,
undertook a pilgrimage to that place, taking with them the imperishable Viṣṇu.
They [reached] that delightful lotus pond, renowned as Suṣumṇā,
covered with groves of lotuses, resounded by the joyful cries of birds,
endowed with many trees and forests, and adorned with blossoming lotuses.

Abounding with many groves of trees, with fine golden sands, marked with diamonds, lapis lazuli, and sapphires, and possessing emerald creepers and palaces; rich with the songs of various birds, it was frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas. || 17–18 ||
It was sweet with the songs sung by kinnaras, frequented by apsarases,
rich with the songs of intoxicated bees, and served as the dwelling place of the abode of Śrī.
O observer of noble vows, having bathed in which, mortal men go to the abode of the immortals in their own bodies, traveling by means of a celestial chariot as radiant as the sun.
Having reached that Suṣumnā river, the gods, together with the sages,
then gathered lotuses, stalks, and fibers.
Then, having uprooted and taken a large, blooming, and most enchanting lotus there, covered with a thousand petals,
Agastya cast it upon her bank and then bathed at his pleasure.
And the omnipresent Lord of the Gods, unseen by anyone, seized it.
Then Agastya, having emerged, did not see that lotus;
addressing them all, the high-minded one said this: ||23-24||
Agastya said:
"O great gods, by whom has my large, well-blossomed lotus been taken?
Sanatkumāra said:
Then all those sages and the gods likewise, O sage of noble vows, each individually performed various acts of faith.
Indra said:
He who steals the lotus shall dwell eternally in heaven through many sacrifices performed with desired rites and abundant sacrificial fees.
Sanatkumāra said: Then they all thought, O Vyāsa, that the lotus had been seized by the high-souled Indra; and Indra spoke to him.
Indra said:
"How may we hear the principles of dharma from the sages?
Therefore, this means has been devised; take this water-born [lotus]. (28)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having worshipped there the fires, the gods, and the ancestors, and having gratified the brahmins, they likewise received the blessings of Viṣṇu. (29)
O Vyāsa, the sages and the gods, being well-composed, went to many other very meritorious and auspicious holy places.
Then they saw a single tree, a great tree that was withered.
And they saw a parrot within its hollow, withering away and its senses distraught.
Having seen him, those illustrious dwellers of heaven questioned him;
having perceived the parrot with their divine vision, they were filled with joy.
Indra said:
"O Lord of Birds, why do you remain upon this tree when it is dead—
devoid of flowers, fruits, and leaves, withered and no longer providing sustenance?"
Śuka said:
"This tree was indeed once very great, like the Kalpa-tree;
it was long lived upon by us with fruits that were like nectar."
Furthermore, when this lord of the forest has reached this state through the passage of time,
how could a wise and grateful person like me abandon him? O Lord, by forsaking one who has sustained me, I would become ungrateful.
O Lord of Śacī, may those worlds which belong to this tree be mine. ||36||
Indra said:
"O king of birds, you are wise, intelligent, high-souled, and a knower of the principles of policy; why do you treat yourself as if you were a fool? (37)
"O virtuous one, this tree is his constant duty;
O Lord of Birds, it was performed by him here spontaneously and without prior deliberation. (38)
This thought occurred to him:
"Let the birds dwell with me constantly; let them eat fruits as they please. (39)
Just as fire, water, and wind are in reality insentient, they nevertheless act for the benefit of living beings by their very nature and not otherwise. (8.118.40)
In the same way, O bird, having understood that this action of yours is born of your own nature, abandon it and go elsewhere to where there may be happiness. (41)
Śuka said:
"O Lord of the gods, I am not deluded; do not disregard my words.
Listen, O Lord of the gods, O Master, to what I say according to my own understanding. (42)
For just as fire, water, and wind are in reality insentient,
O tiger among gods, so too are trees, shrubs, creepers, and the like.
For this cycle of existence has been ordained for all who perform actions;
therefore, O Lord of the Gods, there is no lack of consciousness in trees.
Just as is the disposition of trees, so how shall we act in every way? Listen to me regarding this matter: "How may we be of benefit to living beings? (45)
Having created these principal beings, the highly illustrious Svayambhū spoke to them:
"Conduct yourselves in every way for the benefit of all creatures."
Therefore, O Lord of the World, they exist for the benefit of all beings, even down to their fruits, flowers, bark, and sprouts.
Wind, fire, and likewise water—what is unknown to you, O Lord?
For even the auspicious mountains proceed exactly as intended by intelligence. || 48 ||
Indra said: "How did you obtain this knowledge? What is your duty, and what is your toil?
We wish to know this; tell us, O Lord of Birds. (49)
Śuka said: "O Lord of Gods, from birth onwards, even when death itself had arrived, my mind never once inclined toward betraying a friend."
I am devoted to my parents and likewise intent upon my own wife; I do not despise living beings, and I approach my wife only during her season. ||51||
"O Lord of Devas, O Best of Gods, I do not eat the grain of others;
by that, stainless knowledge has arisen within me.
Indra said:
"I am pleased with this virtuous intellect of yours, O best of birds!
Choose a boon, and I shall grant whatever you consider auspicious.
Śuka said:
"O Lord of the Gods, by your grace, let this lord of the forest remain alive;
therefore, O God, I would choose no other supreme boon. ||54||
Indra said:
"The destinies of living beings are proclaimed to be determined by their own actions;
one falls by one's own action alone—what use is this [body] to you, O wise one? (5.5)
"Having ascended this celestial chariot given by me, O best of birds, go quickly to my world while being praised like a man [of merit].
Śuka said: "I do not desire the worlds, nor the celestial chariot, nor indeed happiness."
"Grant what has been requested; for this tree belongs indeed to those who are living. || 57 ||
Sanatkumāra said: Having understood his true nature and everything else, that best of gods restored the tree, endowed with all its qualities, just as it was before.

And Śuka, by virtue of that deed, as well as through his firm devotion and his assistance to the distressed, went indeed to the world of Brahmā. Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter in the Vāmana-tīrtha-yātrā of the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Then all those deities, having arrived at the city named Kṛmilā, beheld this very place there, O great sage.
There was a Brahmin woman named Gautamī, who was like another Rudrāṇī;
she was righteous, generous, and had burnt away her sins through asceticism.
While she remained devoted to her penance, her husband departed for the world of Brahmā.
My son was bitten by a great black cobra and died. A hunter named Arjunaka came to that place;
having arrived there, he saw him overwhelmed by poison.

Having gone there, he said to Gautamī, "O lady rich in asceticism, this son of yours has been bitten by a snake and has quickly died; do you not perceive this? Thus addressed, she approached and saw that her son's life had departed.
O Vyāsa, the woman of great vows, whose child had died, wept in many ways.
While she was thus lamenting, the hunter Arjunaka then dug a hole, extracted that serpent, and bound him.
Bound by that noose, that evil-minded black cobra, being extremely distressed, then spoke to that hunter who was known as Arjunaka. (8)
"What is the use of my being bound by you? Do you not see the unrighteousness?
We are certainly not to be eaten by mortals; why do you not release me? (9)
Arjuna said:
"Today, having cut you into pieces, I shall give you as food to the dog,
because this son of a seer was devoured by you and has indeed died."
The serpent said:
"Impelled by Time, I bit that son of the seer.
You ought not, O Arjunaka, to reproach me for this fault in accordance with the truth."
Arjuna said:
"O serpent, if you have been impelled by Time and have bitten me, you are indeed merely the instrument of my death; therefore, I shall kill you utterly. (12)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, that Gautamī met her end in the form of death;
afflicted by supreme sorrow, she passed away, and Time (Kāla) departed from there in fear.
Kāla said:
"I am indeed the Time of all living beings; there is no doubt about this.
Urged on by Death itself, I have slain the son of the ṛṣi."
Arjuna said:
"Whether urged by you or by Death himself, he bit me;
therefore, since he is the cause for my slaying, I shall kill him. (15)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Death, being of great mind and fearing the asceticism of Gautamī, approached that place and spoke these words in a melodious voice. (16)
I too am bound by destiny and act with full composure;
I kill [this being], yet you should not find fault in me, O lady of virtuous vows. (17)
Arjuna said:
Whether it be destiny, death, or even time that is the cause, the black serpent is nonetheless the instrument; therefore, he must be slain, without a doubt. (18)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Niyati arrived there, O Vyāsa, and being afraid, she spoke these words at that time to the sorrowful Gautamī. (19)
O virtuous lady of excellent complexion, subject to the power of Kṛtānta and ever unwearied, I bind living beings with nooses and bring them under the control of Death. (8.119.20)
Kṛtānta said:
"O virtuous lady, I am indeed a servant of the high-souled Yama;
impelled by him, I lead living beings to the abode of Yama. (21)
Arjuna said:
Whether it be Yama, or Kṛtānta, or even these [gods], they are merely the instruments for him;
such a man of evil conduct shall never be released in this manner.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, the high-minded Yama himself went there and spoke thus to that Gautamī.
Neither I nor these great beings are the cause of my son's death;
look at his passing and listen also to my words. ||24||
O auspicious lady, the union of living beings with a body is caused by merit and demerit;
likewise, their separation from the body occurs again through the exhaustion of those very two.
For embodied beings, dharma alone is said to be the sole cause of life;
when that is exhausted, death is proclaimed, and that is remembered as Time and Mortality.
In the Kṛta age, it is said that Time consists of four thousand years.
In the Tretā age, however, it was three thousand-fold; in the Dvāpara age, it was two thousand-fold. || 27 ||
In the Kali age, O observer of the great vow, they say the lifespan of a living being is but one hundred years;
however, there is that which is called untimely death beyond that—listen now to that as well.
In the case of this best of bipeds, those gods who dwell within his senses—
all those most excellent deities— take away one portion for themselves when he looks with an evil eye or speaks wickedly. (2.9)
Even for one who hears, reflects, understands, and beholds [the truth], [it remains difficult]. || 8.119.30 ||
Likewise, as one touches, smells, or even eats, and through grasping, moving about, and the discharge of pleasure,
