other beings indeed carry away another portion once again. ||3.1||
The diseases among them have become exceedingly malignant and have ceased [to be subdued].
Furthermore, the ancestors have taken one portion, and the gods another;
furthermore, the sages, the fire, the moon, the sun, and likewise the planets [have taken their portions]. || 32-33 ||
O virtuous lady, as long as that embodied being has food brought to him, for so long shall he live; and that shall be called untimely death.
And how a living being dies at an untimely hour when asceticism has been intensified—listen now to me as I speak of this here, O lady of excellent complexion. (35)
As long as the lifespan of that person has not been exhausted in the Great Vow (Mahāvrata), so long does he obtain life; at its conclusion, he dies again.
Whatever offense he has committed, by that the gods take away his lifespan.
Because of that, a great unrighteousness arose for him, which brought about the end of his life. || 37 ||
Then, O virtuous lady of great vows, a disease manifested that cut through his vital organs. With his vital organs severed and rendered helpless, he abandoned his body and,
having attained another body, proceeded to another state of existence.
That merit which does not cause disease for him through its grace,
even that he indeed destroys by other means— namely, by the falling of poisons and weapons, and by various kinds of living beings, for those gods who dwell within his body.
"And by many other terrible [means], there is no fault for one who perceives [the truth].
Sanatkumāra said:
"Then Gautamī, possessed of great vows, beheld [the truth] through her ascetic penance."
Free from sorrow, she spoke these words to that Arjunaka: ||41||
Gautamī said:
"Release him, Arjunaka! This serpent does not deserve death;
he was possessed by unrighteousness and bitten my son under the influence of the gods."
Those great-souled lords, having entered both sentient and insentient beings, employ them everywhere according to their true nature.
This one has died by his own dharma; there is no fault on the part of the ascetics.
"Go, all you deities, to your own homes; why do you remain here?"
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, all those goddesses, having been sent by the wife of Brahmā, spoke these words together to that Gautamī: ||45||
The gods said:
"We are pleased with you, O knower of dharma, whose sins have been consumed by penance.
Let this son of yours live, and let him abide in his own duty."
"O virtuous woman of great vows, behold this serpent; he is Adharma himself standing here in embodied form, while this hunter is Dharma. (47)
O you of great vows, this test has indeed been performed for you by these gods;
all the worlds shall be inexhaustible for you, without a doubt. (48)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then those gods, led by Indra, suddenly beheld everything there exactly as it had occurred, and I reported all of that to them.
Having bathed, all those highly fortunate ones, with concentrated minds, went again to other sacred fords, repeatedly visiting them one after another.
Wandering in due order, they arrived once again at the place where Kṛtyā had previously been slain by the highly powerful Indra, the lord of the gods.
Vyāsa said:
By whom was that Kṛtyā produced, for what purpose, or for whom, O Lord? And how was she slain again? This I wish to know.
Sanatkumāra said: There was a king of great strength known as Tṛṇabindu;
skilled in speech, he spoke these words to the seven sages.
"O Brahmins, please perform the sacrifice for me; I shall indeed give you much wealth.
They replied, "O virtuous lord of men, we do not perform sacrifices. (54)
When that high-minded man had been initiated for sacrifice, he was overtaken by another drought;
they, overcome by hunger, arrived at the sacrificial ground by chance.
Then the king said to them, "Tell me, what shall I give to you?
With faces flushed with anger, they replied, "O King, give us a son! (56)
Having bowed with great reverence, that king respectfully bestowed upon them both his son and his wealth; and thus,
as he remained prostrate, those whose wealth is penance relinquished their material possessions.
As he was returning carrying the food, that boy, on account of his extreme delicacy, [fainted]. || 58 ||
Afflicted there by hunger and thirst, and further exhausted by the journey, he died.
Having placed him in the forest fire, they stood watching.
While they were looking on there, O lord of men, Vyāsa arrived;
and wearing divine earrings, he spoke thus to those ṛṣis with a smile.
Tṛṇabindu said:
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, do not accept gifts from me;
nor, O sages nourished by penance, perform sacrifices for us. (61)
"O twice-born ones, you see no fault here in the death of this child;
yet your minds are fixed on dharma, though this is both unrighteous and disgraceful! Alas! (62)
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O Vyāsa, disregarding him and without saying anything at all,
they departed for another direction in the forest, tormented by hunger.
And at that time, O Vyāsa, Tṛṇabindu, through his ascetic power, instantly created many trees there out of a desire for their comfort and welfare;
and they, having reached that forest, [saw] many trees laden with fruit.
Then, O Vyāsa, they beheld it and attained supreme satisfaction.
Having taken [the vessels], they broke them open and saw therein gold, food, edibles, and likewise silver of brilliant luster.
Those sages, endowed with ascetic power, considered that to have been caused by Tṛṇabindu.
Thereupon, those seven ṛṣis of excellent vows abandoned that forest and departed for another direction; and Tṛṇabindu became enraged.
Having approached those sages, the lord of men, his soul overwhelmed with grief and deeply agitated, spoke to them with humility and joined palms. (68) Tṛṇabindu said:
O brahmins, I have not fallen [into hell], nor am I indeed a doer of evil deeds;
I have not been shunned by the brahmins, nor am I a non-sacrificer, nor a committer of sin.
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, I am born into the pure lineage of lords of men;
I protect my subjects properly—why do you not hold me in high esteem? (8.119.70)
Having heard those words of his, those sages of great vows said:
"O King, we do not accept them under any circumstances."
"You are excellent, endowed with virtues, a protector of subjects, and a lord of creatures.
We are satisfied; we do not accept any wealth from you, O King.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus to the king, O sage, they all departed. That king, filled with great wrath, then offered oblations into the blazing fire and from it produced a Kṛtyā of immense power.
Then he spoke these words to her, who was known as Yātudhānī:
"O you of great strength, go and devour the seven sages in this task,
having first learned the names of Vasiṣṭha and the other ascetics whose wealth is their penance."
Having gone to the auspicious and divine lotus pond named Śubhā,
she reached its bank and stood there waiting for them.
Those sages, too, were distressed, their senses agitated by hunger and thirst.
Searching for other regions, they then went to the auspicious pool.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, having seen the fault in their departure, Purandara [acted].
Dressed in the garb of a wandering mendicant and accompanied by a dog, he approached them.
Seeing him—the mighty-armed one laughing, with his hand occupied by a triple staff—all of them spoke to one another in gentle tones. (78–79)
The sages said: "Surely, because he has been eating here day and night, always untiring,
therefore he has become so stout."
"Or perhaps he has an outstretched hand and is a constant beggar;
he has become fat by selling his asceticism and Vedic study.
Having thus speculated in many ways about him, those sages whose wealth was their penance—
They questioned the one of immeasurable soul, saying, "Who are you?
Indra replied,
"O best of Brahmins, I am a wandering mendicant (parivrāj) coming from Daśeraka."
I shall go to the auspicious pond; my name, however, is Śunaḥsakha. (83)
"O best of the twice-born, dogs have always been dear to me, and I have always been dear to dogs; therefore, I am known by the name Śunaḥsakha (Friend of the Dog). ||84||
Sanatkumāra said:
Then they went together with him to that auspicious lotus pond;
they saw the Kṛtyā there and were repelled by her.
Or if it pleases you, O wise ones, to plunge into this [water], then tell me your names here and move about at ease, O imperishable ones. ||86||
Sanatkumāra said: Then they said to that maiden, "So be it. And then Śvasakha, the subduer of enemies, spoke thus to all those sages: ||87||
"O Brahmins, this is a sorceress; she is not an ordinary human being.
For she must have some purpose, judging by what she says to you. Therefore, if you consider it to be for your supreme welfare and highest benefit—"
Speak out their names in such a way that she may not recognize them. || 89 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Having replied, "So be it," O Vyāsa, those auspicious sages,
having caused her names to be heard, entered into their respective abodes as they pleased.
They spoke of etymological derivations and their own names, which were difficult to understand; she did not comprehend them, and therefore they entered the water. 91.
Sanatkumāra said: Without having ascertained their names, that Śikhodbhavā spoke to Śvasana: "Tell me [their names], and then you shall go or not."
Śvasakha said:
"I am a friend of dogs, and I associate with cruel dogs;
therefore, O night-roaming Yātudhānī, know me as Śvasakha."
The Yātudhānī said:
"O lowest of men, speak your name only once more;
then you shall go into the presence of the Brahmins, known by me. (94)
The Dog-Friend said:
"I am the friend of dogs, O Goddess; my friendship with dogs is ancient.
Because I am a dog-friend, I shall slay you, O sorceress; listen! (95)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus to that cruel woman, the Lord of the Gods struck her on the head with his triple staff; by that, she was instantly reduced to ashes.
And that son of Tṛṇabindu, having been struck down by a mere magical rite,
was quickly restored to life by Śakra and approached his father.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus, O son of Śakti, having slain her, Indra, the friend of the Wind-god,
once again carried off the lotus stalks, lotuses, and lilies belonging to the sages.
Then, having safely crossed over and not seeing them, they were filled with rage.
The Brahmins, devoted to one another, made oaths among themselves. || 99 ||
Then all those best of sages approached Śvasakha and said, "We have doubt regarding you; tell us how you may be liberated.
Śvasakha said:
"Whoever takes away your roots, flowers, and fruits—may he be happy, eating sweet food, together with his friends and his family. (1.01)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then all those sages, O Vyāsa, spoke to Purandara:
"The wealth that was taken by you from us—give that back to us again."
O Vyasa, the Blessed One, being pleased, took all their roots and fruits and spoke these words to those sages: || 103 ||
Indra said:
"O Brahmins, this sorcery (kṛtyā) which was previously prepared for your sake has been destroyed by me with my triple staff (tridaṇḍa) for your benefit, O you whose wealth is asceticism."
"This was done to you by King Tṛṇabindu out of anger.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the gods and the sages, whose wealth is their asceticism, having approached him...
They bathed Viṣṇu in that sacred ford (tīrtha) worshipped by hosts of sages.
Then, having arrived at the Himavat mountain filled with joy,
those of noble vows caused Viṣṇu to be consecrated with the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha).
While he was performing the sacrifice, Tryambaka, the Lord of Gods and Master of the Gaṇas,
arrived through the air, filled with joy for the sake of the sacrifice.
Vyāsa said:
"O son of Brahmā, alas! You have related to me this account of Yātudhānī, which is supremely secret and very difficult to understand."
For this is a supreme secret, full of great significance, ever glorious and most purifying;
it has been correctly proclaimed by you, O Great Yogi, like the nectar possessing the luster of the full moon. 10.9
Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Yātudhānī," within the "Pilgrimage to Vāmana-tīrtha" section of the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said: Hereafter, I shall describe how that Blessed Lord, the Supreme Controller, proceeded.
Having observed that sacrificer performing the sacrifice, tell us [about him].
Sanatkumāra said:
That Lord, the divine wielder of the trident whose banner bears the bull,
spoke these words on the eighth day of the dark fortnight to the Goddess, the daughter of Himavat.
"O auspicious goddess, today in this world is the auspicious eighth day of the dark fortnight;
tonight we shall go to behold the cremation grounds."
The Goddess said:
"O God, O Protector of the World, let it be as it pleases you;
whatever is desired by you, O Mahādeva, that shall indeed be twice as much for me."
Then, O great sage, on that day in Ujjayinī,
the young son of a Brahmin— pure and learned— died.
Having performed his funeral rites and having adorned him according to the prescribed rule, Vyāsa [proceeded].
Crying out and weeping, they led him right to the cremation ground.
Having brought that boy Raktapādaka to the cemetery, they,
overwhelmed by grief out of affection for him, wept intensely and profusely.
Seeing them thus weeping, the vulture, filled with hunger and provoked to anger,
addressed those twice-born ones like a wise man:
"O Brahmins, listen to my words, which I speak to you as humans."
"You are clearly devoid of intelligence; listen to my words!
This man has indeed died by the power of time; why do you grieve like fools?
He will not come back to life by weeping; perform your own duties, free from distress."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, they then departed, leaving their son behind while looking back at him again and again; then the jackal spoke to them: || 11 ||
"Alas! Shame on all you humans! Behold, how devoid of intelligence you are—devoid of affection and ungrateful—that you depart indeed, having abandoned him.
A son is obtained with great difficulty, and in such a manner is he even born."
Furthermore, the cruel one increases through suffering, being afflicted by disease. || 13 ||
Indeed, he has forgotten the many endearments you have shown; this boy has done these things today—oh, what a lack of affection on your part! 14.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O Vyāsa, having heard the words of the jackal,
they gathered together and stood weeping, surrounding him in that cremation ground.
Then, at night, the Lord of Gods, Kapardin, arrived with his beloved,
surrounded by all his attendants and accompanied by Nandīśvara.
Approaching them, that Lord, who brings happiness to all beings,
replied to those who were weeping there, "I am the giver of boons."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, with voices full of distress and eyes clouded with tears, they said:
"O Lord, by your command, let this Jīva be our son. (18)
Having restored their infant son to life there, the Blessed One granted him divine lordship over the Gaṇas and an imperishable dwelling in that very place.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having thus spent that night, he went according to the prescribed rite to the cremation grounds and proceeded to the auspicious Vaidūrya peak of the Himavat.

He, of blazing splendor, the omnipresent one of imperishable nature, the wielder of the Pināka bow who dwells upon mountain peaks, spoke to those initiated for the supreme sacrifice: "Choose a boon, you who have taken refuge solely in the triple heaven."
Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having beheld Mahādeva, the sole kinsman of the seven worlds...
With palms joined in reverence, they all spoke, bowing with their heads to their knees. ||1||
O Blessed One, O best of gods, Hari, desiring the welfare of the world, formerly accepted [the gift] from him by which sin has now come upon him. (2)
Therefore, O Lord of this world, O Lord of the gods, being entreated by us, grant welfare to this devotee who is prostrate before you. (3)
"Let this sacrifice be completed; let Hari be released from evil;
and let all the gods, together with Indra, regain their own vital energy."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of theirs, the Blessed One, with a joyful countenance,
completed the sacrifice and obstructed that mountain with his trident.
From that [opening], due to that very division, waters as white as nectar, conchs, and the moon issued forth;
there, they then bathed Viṣṇu.
Then, as soon as he had bathed, there emerged from his body a most terrible and deformed Asura woman of evil nature with a distorted face;
she rushed toward the gods to slay them, but was held back by the Kinsman of the Gods.
He said to her: "All the gods, including Indra, must not be slain.
Your station shall remain right here, highly honored;
it shall be more meritorious than all other sacred fords (tīrthas) and the destroyer of all sins."
"You shall constantly deliver seven ancestors and seven descendants;
you are renowned in the world as Sandhyā, the auspicious one, the best of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
You are a divine stream of water, auspicious, and the bestower of the fruits of all sacrifices."
"By worshipping you, men shall cause seven generations of their lineages to be saved.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, at that time, all those deities, by the word of Rudra...
Having worshipped the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, according to the prescribed rule.
Having constructed a temple for the god, they departed for the third heaven itself.
When the hosts of gods had gone, Hari then remained on Śivakūṭa,
having performed the horse sacrifice, and continued to worship the god.

Then, after six thousand years and six months, the Lord of Gods, whose banner bears the bull, was pleased; Soma, together with Nandin and his attendants, spoke this to him again: 14. "Soma, along with Nandin and his hosts, spoke this to him once more."
Rejoicing and with a deeply satisfied soul, he said: "Tell me, what shall I give to you?
Viṣṇu replied:
"O Blessed One, O Lord of the World, whether by means of sin or even by means of ascetic penance,"
O Dispeller of Time, tell me that by which there may indeed be no loss for me. || 1.6 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, smiling and being well-pleased, the Lord of Gods, the Prajāpati, addressed Viṣṇu and said: "Practice this secret, great vow."
Then, having performed the protective rite, he [taught] that auspicious yoga, the yantra, and the vow which bring about all dharmas and accomplish supreme sovereignty.
Having performed that divine Pāśupata rite which fulfills all desires for twelve years, he attained supreme sovereignty;
the trident-bearing God himself was pleased upon seeing him in such a state.
He gave him half of his body; thus it became Viṣṇu-Śaṅkara.
That mortal who should always hear this on every sacred festival day (parvan),
and who should worship Śiva and Viṣṇu, shall go to the supreme goal.
Thus, that Vāmana Viṣṇu, possessed of great strength, having conquered...
He offered the entire three worlds back to all the gods.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O bull among sages, when the three worlds had been reclaimed by the gods, [the gods spoke].
Those who remained among the asuras, having taken refuge with two dānavas, [fled]. || 23 ||
Tāraka and Maya waged war together with the immortals;
and both Maya and Tāraka were surrounded by their sons and grandsons,
as well as Vipracitti, the son of Danu, and those who are known as his offspring.
All the Nivātakavacas, the Paulomas, the sons of Kālakā,
the valiant Saiṃhikeyas, and likewise the Bāleya host—
these and many other Dānavas were arrogant in their strength. || 25 ||
Armed and filled with rage, they then challenged the gods. Seeing them thus challenging, the gods also, well-armored and eager for battle,
approached them and engaged in combat.
Between them there occurred that tumultuous battle, hair-raising,
for eight hundred and sixteen thousand divine years;
yet in that conflict, victory did not belong to either side.
Then, in that battle, the gods were confronted by the unassailable sons of Siṃhikā.
The great beings were defeated like herds of cattle by lions;
observing their power, the thousand-eyed Purandara went for refuge to Rudra, the imperishable Lord of the gods of gods.
Having gone there, he took up residence on the peak of Mount Svarṇacūḍa and beheld Mahādeva together with the Goddess, surrounded by his attendants;
he was blazing like fire, difficult to behold for those who have not disciplined their souls.
Having been previously described by Nandin as the best of gods, Tamas saw him, bowed his head in salutation, and spoke these words: ||| 3 || 3 ||
"O Lord, sixteen thousand and eight hundred divine years have passed since the battle of the gods began.
And the two Dānavas, Tāraka and Maya, are intoxicated with the pride of war."
Relying upon those two, all the asuras slay the gods as if they were cattle. ||35||
O best of gods, grant life to those gods who are being slain, or do whatever else is appropriate, O Lord. (36)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, the Blessed One whose banner bears the bull reflected upon them and then spoke there, "Rāma, Rāma."
The Blessed One said:
"O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one! You have performed most great austerities.
Go and, through fair combat, make all the gods free from their feverish anxiety. (38)
Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus, the powerful Rāma, son of Jamadagni,
bowed down with great reverence and spoke in a piteous voice.
Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, I am of little prowess and am greatly emaciated by asceticism;
furthermore, O Lord of Gods, I am unskilled in weapons and shall not be able to withstand battle, O All-pervading One."
Devāvaha said:
"Go, O Brahmin; you will be able to fight today, so do not grieve.
I shall nourish you; do not feel distressed, O Bhārgava. ||41||
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the Blessed Lord Hara spoke to Indra, the lord of the gods:
"He shall slay your enemies; give him a chariot."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Śakra, having bowed down and taken Rāma with him,
went to that very place where the battle had occurred.
Then, having equipped him with that preeminent chariot, Śakra Purandara himself said to Rāma: "Summon the sons of Siṃhikā."
With that preeminent chariot, Rāma—the best among strikers—was equipped with armor, fastened his quiver, and took up his arrows, sword, and bow;
he also donned his leathern finger-guards and raised his standard and banner. || 45 ||
He rushed with speed toward the unassailable sons of Siṃhika.
A most terrible and fearsome battle ensued between them and him, like that of tigers in the forest against a lion. ||46-47||
There, the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Cāraṇas beheld a marvel:
that even though he was but one person on the stage, he appeared as many forms at once—neither taking up his variegated arrows nor yet fixing them to the bow. ||48||
Then Bhārgava was seen drawing his bow;
his great bow appeared drawn into a complete circle,
and he became difficult for his enemies even to look upon.
Turning back, that mighty Bhārgava, filled with wrath,
O Vyāsa, discharged ten sharp arrows at each of their mouths one by one.
There they beheld the wonderful dexterity of that wise man.
"Excellent! Excellent!"—such was the great sound made by the beings there. || 52 ||
Sanatkumāra said: With their faces pierced by those arrows, the mighty sons of Siṃhika fell to the earth with their fragrance [still upon them], like palm trees struck down by the wind. ||5.3||
Then that host of ten thousand enemies of the gods was consumed by the descendant of Bhṛgu, just as the world is consumed by Time;
thereafter, the gods, along with the ṛṣis, Gandharvas, and Cāraṇas, [rejoiced].
Saying "Excellent! Excellent! to him, they praised him with joyful faces.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having observed that deed of his, the Blessed Lord Pākaśāsana [was moved].
Having honored Bhārgava with great reverence, together with the gods.
The one of great splendor, having embraced him again and again, said this:
"This deed belongs to you alone; its like is not found among others even in heaven.
If those sons of Siṃhikā have been slain by you so suddenly,"
"Truly, this great deed of yours was like that of Tryambaka against Tripura;
there is no one equal to you in the world—I speak this truth.
These [beings] are not the equals of the God, nor of any human being whatsoever."
"All beings are not to be slain, yet you alone have destroyed them.
Therefore, we are pleased with you and grant you immunity from death,
as well as inexhaustible strength in battle and supreme fame upon the earth."
And Tryambaka, with divine boons and protections, will stand by you;
and in battles, you shall conquer the host according to your desire.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by those gods who were pleased, that ascetic of great austerity,
with a joyful and contented mind, went to the god Tryambaka;
and the gods, too, remained well-prepared against Tāraka, who was intoxicated with the pride of battle.
Then, together with Maya, they swiftly showered [him].
Those mighty ones, whose own momentum was checked by the force of the Daityas— possessing a speed like that of the ocean—
rushed down and struck the hosts of Daityas violently, just as wild lions strike elephants in the forest.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Bestowal of Boons upon the Son of Jamadagni," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having witnessed the slaughter of Saihikeya and likewise the victory of the gods, [the Lord spoke].
Suddenly, the Daitya armies were shattered on all sides.
Tāraka was struck down by another, as were the heroes Maya and Virocana,
along with Vipracitti, Ṣaṇḍa, and the great Asura Prahlāda.
Then Kālanemi, enraged in the battle against Keśava,
mounted his great chariot— which was adorned with a hundred banners and possessed a lofty standard—
and the Dānava rushed with speed toward Keśava.
Then, O Vyāsa, as he was still falling, Keśava discharged a great, irresistible discus; he then brought it to a standstill.
Seeing it thus obstructed, all the gods were filled with wrath.
For they were utterly defeated and deprived of their weapons by Kālanemi.
Having put them to flight and turned them back, that lord of the Daityas,
the imperishable one, then assumed the office of the world-protector.
Then, pervading both the earth and the heavens, that one of great strength moved through the three worlds by means of his power over the world, like Svayambhū himself. Sanatkumāra said:
Seeing the Daitya stationed in that manner, the gods, together with Indra,
terrified by fear, then went for refuge to the imperishable Hari.
And that Lord of gods, Hari, the protector of the three worlds, is the one worthy of seeking refuge.
He granted them protection from fear, desiring the slaughter of the Dānava.
Then, having pervaded both heaven and earth in every way with his form,
he called to mind that lotus-wheel which had been fashioned by Rudra.
Then, O Vyāsa, he struck off the great head of the Dānava like a ripe fruit from the top of a palm tree blown down by a violent wind.
When that Daitya had been slain, both Tāraka and Maya—
Having turned back, the two great warriors rushed with speed toward Pātāla.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus, O Vyāsa, there occurred that fierce battle for the sake of Tāraka,
wherein Kālanemi was slain and Virocana became renowned.
The valiant Saiṃhikeyas, the great asura Tuhuṇḍa, Surocana, Śatāvarta, Hāla, and likewise Gārgyaśiras; || 15 ||
Vipāka, Saha, Pāka, Caṇḍa, Kārtasvana, and Kubha—
these and other lords of the Daityas were slain during the Tārakāmaya war; furthermore, the cruel Vipracitti was killed along with his younger brother when the banner [was raised].
Vyāsa said: How did that battle between the gods and the asuras take place? And how did he come to have the name "Dhvaja"? (17)

And having performed that deed so difficult for all beings to accomplish, Jāmadagnya, the upholder of the Bhṛgu lineage, came into the presence of Tryambaka. I wish to know what he was told by the God of gods. || 18 ||
Sanatkumāra said: Then the son of Jamadagni, himself sent by the immortals,
went to the secret city of the god, the abode of Puruṣcandra.
Vyāsa said:
"O you of firm vows, tell me how that divine city of Purīcandra came to be— that secret abode of Maheśa."
Sanatkumāra said:
O high-minded one, I shall relate to you here an ancient account, hearing which even a doer of evil deeds may attain the supreme goal. (21)
In former times, there were two high-souled sages, Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
it is said that for the sake of the gods' mission, they committed the slaying of a Brahmin.
Overwhelmed by that evil of immense power, those two gods lost their senses and became utterly degraded, having entered the state of animal births.
Then, when a divine year had passed, the self-controlled one—
Brahmā himself arrived there, accompanied by the gods and the sages.
Then Brahmā, the lord of the gods, sought to awaken him along with the man;
yet even so, those two did not wake, being completely shrouded by their karma.
Then Brahmā spoke to all those inhabitants of heaven.
For the sake of Nārāyaṇa, you must practice the supreme dharma.
"Then the god, together with Manu, shall be liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
To him who spoke thus, all the gods then bowed their heads in salutation and, with palms joined in reverence, said: "Instruct us as to what penance and what deed we must perform."
Brahmā said:
"All of you, being self-restrained, subsisting on air alone, and having conquered your senses, chant the Heart of Rudra correctly; thereby you shall attain yoga. || 28 ||
Sanatkumāra said:
Having said, "So be it," those lords of the gods, dwelling in the waters, performed silent recitation (japa) together with the sages for six hundred thousand years.
Then, after a long time, for those of disciplined soul,
a subtle yoga manifested, because of which a pure fire arose.
By that fire, Nara and Nārāyaṇa [consumed] the sin of killing a Brahmin at that time.
Having been consumed by fire, she abandoned her body and entered the water.
The waters, though entered by the *nāstya* [demons], did not become flavorful;
they were indeed without fragrance, devoid of color, and lacked luster.
The earth became weak in vigor, and fire lost its sharp intensity. (3.2)
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having seen it thus, they joined their minds once more and, with concentrated thoughts, they recited the *hṛdaya* of the Rudras.
Then the Blessed Lord, the god who bears the trident and has the bull as his banner, arrived.
He said to the gods, "I am pleased; tell me what you desire.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then those deities, having beheld Rudra perfectly, rejoiced;
and bowing down, they praised Yajña-jīmūtavāhana.
The gods said:
Salutations to the Supreme Deity, whose splendor is like the fire at the end of an eon;
to the one who is salt-like and who performs ascetic penance; to the heart of the Rudras;
to the one with the great axe in hand; and to the one whose abode is gold.
Salutation to the Lord of the Vasus and to the Lord of the Gods;
salutation to the Pure One, to the Licking One, to the Newly Born, and to Wrath;
salutation to the Lord of the Planets and to the Heart of the Planets. ||37-38||

Homage indeed to the King of Planets, who is followed by the great planets; homage to the fierce one who possesses self-restraint and tranquility, and to the wielder of the fierce rod. Homage to Yama, the Lord of Restraint, and to the wielder of Yama’s rod.
Salutation to the supreme deity, the highest of the high;
salutation to the Lord of the great ones and to the bearer of the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
Salutation to Vāmadeva, the eldest, and to the Lord of all creatures.

Salutation to the Lord of Pradhāna, to the one who sets Pradhāna in motion; salutation to the thousand-faced one, to the wielder of the mace, salutation to the wielder of the trident. Salutation to the one whose form is the wind, to the multiformed one, to the Creator.
Salutations to the destroyer of sacrifices and the extinguisher of the fire of desire.
Salutations to him whose form is the limbs of the Vedic meters, and to the one with deformed eyes.
Salutations to the destroyer of the collection of the senses and to him who has reached the end of the Vedas.
Salutations to you, the destroyer of the thunderbolt, and to the one who is beyond the mind through the mind;
salutations to you, who wear the garland of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, and who are adorned with a lotus garland.
Salutations to the burner of the mountains and to the one born from that which is born of the mountains.
To the one of great universal form, who is magnified by the great;
to the one with a hundred thousand eyes, and the one with an eye in his forehead;
to the leader of the great yoga, and likewise to Tatpuruṣa. ||46-47||
Homage to the secret essence of the Vedas, who is praised by the gods and the Vedas;
to the yogi who is meditated upon, who laughs with the falling thunderbolt. ||48||
Salutations to you who dwell in the heart; salutations to the omnipresent one;
to the supreme lord of Kumāras, and to the progenitor of Kumāras;
to the one who wanders with staff in hand, to the Ender, and to the unconquered.
To the auspicious one, whose form is auspicious, who sets all that is auspicious in motion; to Śiva, the Lord of Śiva, who is eternally the source of all auspiciousness;
to the secret of the science of archery, and to the one who originated the science of archery.
O destroyer of all sins, O dispeller of all evils,
O auspicious and gentle Lord of Gods, grant us that which is in our hearts.
Whatever has been wrongly spoken by us, O Blessed One, O All-pervading Lord—
Out of affection for your devotees, you ought to forgive all of that from us.
O Lord, this kinsman of the gods, whose soul is overwhelmed by sin, shall become as pure as the moon along with Nara, O Lord of Devas. (53–54)
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, the man who, being self-restrained and full of devotion, constantly recites this hymn to Tryambaka, is liberated from sin. ||55||
One shall be liberated from all sins and regain what was lost;
nor does one fall into an evil state of existence, even if one has indeed committed great evils.
Sanatkumāra said:
O son of Satyavatī, having been thus praised by the gods and being pleased, that Blessed One, the Lord of the World and Master of the Gods, spoke to all the deities.
The God of gods said:
"O gods, I am well-pleased; choose whatever boon you desire.
I shall grant it, O highly wise ones; do not remain silent, but speak everything."
The gods said: "O Mahādeva, this Hari has his mind struck by sin;
quickly dispel it for him, as the sun dispels the mist. (59)
O Lord of Gods, this one of great strength performs his work for the sake of the welfare of the world and the gods; therefore, destroy his evil.
"And may we, O Lord of all gods, always attain equality with you and membership in your assembly, standing in the midst of your retinue, if you so deem it fit, O All-pervading One.
Sanatkumāra said:
While those gods were speaking thus, O best of sages, the blessed Lord Śarva, with a joyful mind, spoke laughingly:
"O gods, this is Viṣṇu; he shall immediately be released from this sin."
And this highly fortunate Pāpmā shall arise from saline soil;
likewise the resin of trees, the foam of waters, the scent of great serpents, and the censure of women. (64)
The proclamation of the ill fortune of an initiated Brahmin, the censuring of Brahmins, and the speaking ill of cows; ||| 6.5 ||
The non-kindling of fire and the binding of rivers—
if a man, possessed by passion and delusion, should perform these acts, he would incur this [fate] in this world, even if he were the Self-Existent Lord of the World himself. ||66||
But when Viṣṇu becomes the son of Vasudeva,
then this man Nara shall enjoy her in embodied form.
Having enjoyed her there, he, the granter of boons, shall then take his sister who has been born from Hari.
Freed from evil, he shall once more wander through this world. || 68 ||
However, so that even this sister of his shall not cause him any hindrance,
let him practice severe asceticism that is exceedingly difficult to perform;
and you all, together with the seers, remain right here, perfectly composed.
Perform the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) with undistracted minds, by my command.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by the God, all those deities then spoke to Hari: "Perform severe austerity; through that, you will indeed attain the highest good."
Then, having ascended Candra, the king of mountains, he practiced very great austerity with a well-composed mind, which scorched the collection of his senses.
Even the high-souled gods, together with the sages of firm vows, [approached him].
On the lord of mountains, Hiraṇyavarṇa, they performed penance with concentrated minds. ||73||
Then, when their vow was completed, the wielder of the Pināka bow commanded them to undertake that great and radiant Pāśupata vow.
With a satisfied soul, he addressed the foremost of the gods with a voice as deep and resonant as the thundering of clouds and drums;
the God of Gods spoke:
"O guardians of the world, this very *puraścaraṇa* has indeed been well-performed by you yourselves.
Having practiced this *Pāśupata* rite, go forth in peace and free from fear. (76)
This is the supreme, purifying vow, superior even to Sāṃkhya and Yoga;
there exists nothing higher than this, nor anything subtler anywhere. (77)
With all his limbs smeared with ashes, naked, and truly pure, one who brings stability to the body is liberated from all sins by Rudra.
Ashes are superior to bathing with water; for when it is wet, the killing of living beings is certain.
One should know that the primary nature (prakṛti) is moist, and that this primary nature is also bondage.
For the sake of abandoning this primary nature, bathing with ashes is prescribed, as well as nakedness and purity, by means of which [bondage] shall never arise again. || 80 ||
There exists no other supreme yantra than this yantra,
which possesses six limbs, fulfills all desires, and is honored by all the worlds;
it is pure, the most sanctifying, auspicious, and the destroyer of all sins.
Let them, being composed in mind, practice that which increases austerity;
for the machine (yantra) is to be known as sinless, and it is remembered as primordial nature (prakṛti).
Bondage is said to be threefold, as is the fruit of renunciation (sannyāsa).
Therefore, for the sake of abandoning everything, one should practice this yantra.
By means of this, one is never disrespected in the world and never decays;
having attained the supreme yoga, which is the greatest among all yogas.
Because there is nothing higher than this six-limbed [yoga] which fulfills all desires, by means of which the yogi, once liberated, does not fall again into death and the like. (85)
Having fully attained that yoga, the perfected one through divine action—
the great yogi— is not smeared by actions performed or left undone.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus commanded by the God of gods, those celestial beings, having completed that formidable vow, became the attendants of Śaṅkara. ||87||
Having attained the status of his attendants (*gaṇa*), those who were intensely purified by asceticism took possession of that region of the trident-bearing god.
The gods said:
Because our preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) were perfectly performed here even unto the end, this is therefore remembered as the secret abode of Maheśvara. ||89||
The city known as Pūrīcandra, radiant throughout the three worlds,
was five yojanas in width and just as many in length, and it was beautiful.
Crowded with perfected beings and celestial musicians, resounded by throngs of Apsarases, filled with the cries of many birds and the noise of rivers and waterfalls,
that grove of ascetics rich in penance shall become a place of great merit. (91)
He who comes here, prepares the sacrificial oblation (caru), feeds a Brāhmaṇa, and worships the Lord of the Gods, rejoices in the world of Rudra. ||92||
And whoever, having made a vow in this regard, remains for even a moment as one who bathes in ashes and is restrained in his vows, shall attain the status of being among the Gaṇas—
indestructible, immortal, and free from old age and disease.
Having become a leader of Rudra’s hosts, he shall attain the sovereign power of yoga.
Even one of very sinful nature who acts according to his own will, if he should dwell here for a single day, attains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and is liberated from all sins. ||95||
Even one of evil conduct who, filled with desire, should here give up his life,
he too, having reached the assembly of the gods, shall move about together with the gods.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then all those deities, having attained that supreme ascetic power, performed worship and ritual bathing for the Lord, the Supreme Self. (97)
Then all those inhabitants of heaven, having accomplished their purpose and endowed with the power of great yoga, set their minds upon going toward Hari.
O Vyāsa, approaching that Hari on Mount Hariścandra— who was like the blazing sun— the mighty ones beheld the imperishable Lord.
After a long time, he too, having shaken off all evil and performed great austerities,
attained equality with the gods and became joyful in soul.
Then, O best of sages, rising swiftly from that peak,
he descended and quickly stood in their midst.
Then, filled with joy and properly united with Hari,
they joined that peak of the mountain together with the fruit.
Because this Hari shone here, stainless like the moon,
through his great asceticism, therefore he is known as Ucaleśvara.

"He shall undoubtedly become famous as Hariścandra; because this descent was made here by one who was not of his own accord, therefore let this Bhṛgu be meritorious in every way throughout the world. (104)
O Lord of Gods, whatever man approaches this place of Bhṛgu’s leap and accomplishes his purpose there, he shall go to the exceedingly radiant world of Hari;
even one joined with great sins or afflicted by disease [shall attain it].
Whoever accomplishes the vital breaths here shall also be liberated from great fear.
Or whatever a person constantly prays for here at this precipice, he shall obtain all that without delay; so indeed it is remembered.
Sanatkumāra said:
Whoever, knowing the dharma, recites or even hears this story of Hariścandra and Purīścandra, shall destroy his own sin.

But that man who, being pure and free from malice, always recites this in the assembly of the hosts of twice-born and the gods, he dwells in heaven like an excellent immortal, stainless and blazing with splendor like the sun. (109)
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Mount Hariścandra," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: O Śaktinandana, having reached that Hariścandra, Rāma...
With his mind afflicted by the asuras, he beheld the Supreme Lord. Having seen Mahādeva together with Ambā, the Gaṇas, and the Imperishable One,
he stood before him, bowing down with palms joined in reverence and deeply humbled.
Sanatkumāra said: Then that high-minded god, the source of all speech, being pleased, spoke these words of profound resonance to the son of Jamadagni.
Covered as if with *kiṃśuka* flowers and as if sprinkled with sandalwood paste,
he was likewise drenched on all sides with blood,
like another great mountain from which red mineral ore was flowing.
The God of gods said:
"O son of Jamadagni, a great deed has been performed by you today in battle for the sake of desiring the welfare of the gods, as you strike down the sons of Siṃhika."
"O mighty-armed one, I am well-pleased with this deed of yours;
I shall grant you seven boons—name them as you wish.
Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, if you are pleased with me, O Lord, grant to me yourself the origin of all knowledge as set forth in all the Vedas;
may I be invincible in battle, and bestow upon me the science of archery."
Grant me these boons, O Lord: an axe that slays all, a chariot free from attachment, a vast collection of weapons, and likewise imperishable immortality;
salutations to you.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, as he was speaking thus, the Lord Hara laughed and said,
"All this shall come to pass for you by my command."
"You shall observe the vow of the science of archery for one year;
therefore, O scion of Bhrigu’s lineage, you must dwell right here.
Then the Blessed Three-eyed Lord himself [spoke] to him.
He prescribed a formidable vow, and he, being self-restrained, performed it.
When the vow was completed, the god Yajñahā himself came there and bestowed upon him the science of archery (dhanurveda), together with its mantras and the methods of its practical application.
He likewise [received] the extensive collection of weapons, along with their cords, protective enclosures, projectiles, and slingshots, as well as the corresponding counter-weapons.
Ishana bestowed that upon him and spoke these words in a melodious voice:
"This Dhanurveda, together with its weapons, is exceedingly powerful; [it has been given] by you."

Remember my command that [this] must not be given to the Kṣatriyas. If, out of delusion, you should ever give it to the Kṣatriyas, you will suffer humiliation at their hands, and you shall have no victory in battle.

Sanatkumāra said: Then, having given him the axe as well as a chariot that moves at will, he bestowed upon him an inexhaustible vehicle that appeared before him whenever it was thought of in the mind.
The wielder of the Pināka bow suddenly vanished from the sight of Amara, the Yakṣa king who was the charioteer.
Having received those boons, O Vyāsa, he too went into the presence of his father;
however, he did not see him there, for he had been slain by the sons of Kārtavīrya.
Having failed to perform that service for him, the powerful Rāma also [departed].
He deprived the earth of its kṣatriyas seven times over, including the three [previous] occasions.
With their blood, O Vyāsa, he created seven lakes at Samantapañcaka; with them, he gratified his ancestors. Then, having rid the earth of the Kṣatriyas, that best of the Bhṛgus—
By the grace of Mahādeva, he shone as the lord of the three worlds.
Śrī, Tuṣṭi, Dhṛti, Siddhi, Kīrti, Yaśas, as well as Śraddhā, Medhā, Kṣānti, Anasūyā, and Prasamaya attended upon him. || 22–23 ||
For Reasoning, Refutation, Logic, Self-restraint, and Tranquility—all these personified Mothers approached Bhārgava. ||24||
Then he said to them all: "Enter me without hesitation;
but let this Lakṣmī, who is ill-behaved, remain far away. (25)
Sanatkumāra said: To him who spoke thus, the virtuous Śrī said to Mahābala:
"O mighty-armed one, why do you not welcome me, who am so difficult to obtain? (26)
Rāma said:
"O beautiful one, you are fickle, intoxicating, and unstable; therefore, I do not welcome you. Stay far away from me! (27)
If every man possessed by you were himself a lord, he would, deluded by the intoxication of power, engage only in improper acts. ||28||
Sanatkumāra said:
That illustrious and high-minded king of the Bhṛgu lineage performed sacrifices;
and formerly, O twice-born one, the earth sank down during his sacrifice.
Vyāsa said: For what reason did the Earth enter Pātāla during his sacrifice?
What do you consider to be the cause in that matter? I wish to know this.
Sanatkumāra said: Having gone to Kaśyapa, the best of sages, that protector of the earth said,
"O best among the courageous, please become my officiating priest (hotṛ)."
O Vyāsa, while he was speaking thus,
Kaśyapa, being enraged, spoke there to the lord of men while censuring the best of the Bhṛgus.
"You are fallen, of wicked conduct, broken in character, and a great evildoer;
how shall I perform a sacrifice for you, who are guilty of the murder of an embryo? || 3.3 ||
Sanatkumāra said: Then, with those words, he spoke to that best of sages:
"O best of munis, do not remain within my domain today."
"O Brahmin, I am the lord of the world; go where I am not.
Thereupon, having abandoned that region, he then departed;
yet he did not reach that place where this Lord might not exist.
Failing to find [a way out], he then took refuge in the forest;
having become invisible, he wandered there for many years.
Then he saw a pigeon perched upon a tree, sitting together with a female pigeon; bound by the god of love, it had fallen into a state of helplessness.
The pigeon said: "O fair-hipped one, O beautiful lady, from the moment I first beheld you, I have withered away; I find no pleasure, O beautiful one. (38)
The female dove said:
"Do not speak thus, O man of evil conduct; for it is never right to act unrighteously.
The male dove said:
"If you will not give this to me of your own accord, O slender-waisted one, I shall take it from you by force; grant it, for I bow at your feet."
The female dove said:
"O cruel one, do you feel no fear of the mighty son of Jamadagni,
by whom you would thus insult me here, a devoted wife deprived of her husband?"
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by her, O son of Śakti, that pigeon spoke: "O Rāma, who indeed is this person who is equal to me? There is no one like me. (41)
While he was speaking thus, an arrow marked with the name of Rāma then swiftly struck off his head; Kaśyapa witnessed that.
Seeing him acting in such a manner, that high-minded one became afraid of that mighty being and caused the king to perform a sacrifice for the son of Jamadagni.
Kaśyapa said: "O King, O best of the Bhṛgus, I shall perform the sacrifice this very day, provided that you grant me the auspicious sacrificial fee I desire. (44)
Rāma said:
"What you say is beyond doubt; I shall grant that great ascetic merit.
Make me perform the sacrifice according to the rules, for today I am at your disposal. (45)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, there took place for him a very great horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha) accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, at which the gods attained satisfaction. 46.
Then, at the time for the sacrificial fee, the powerful son of Jamadagni said to Kaśyapa: "Tell me, what gift shall I give you?"
He said, "Give me the entire earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves,
as well as whatever wealth you possess in your house.
Having done so for him with a pure inner soul, he [bestowed it].
Taking his bark garments, he said to Kaśyapa, "What shall I do?
Kaśyapa replied,
"O sir, abandon this region and go to another land."
"O descendant of Bhṛgu, you must not dwell in my country today.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having replied, "So be it," he performed a circumambulation [of the sage].
He went to the ocean, the source of rivers and the abode of Varuṇa. Having reached that formidable sea, the descendant of Bhṛgu said to him:
"O great ocean, grant me a place for my residence."
The Ocean said:
"Since you are now under my control, employ me according to what is right;
standing near the shore, draw your powerful bow."
"Release your arrow, O Rāma, desiring this most excellent region;
as soon as that arrow, impelled by your life-force, is discharged, at that very moment I shall deliver your dwelling. (53-54)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that tiger among the Bhṛgus, having shown due respect and being unwearied,
drew his powerful bow and fixed an arrow upon it, O Vyāsa.
Having then formed the resolve in his mind, "He shall indeed go a hundred yojanas," Śambhu then consecrated him with mantras;
at that time, he was praised by Sāgara for the sake of his pacification.
For the sake of the welfare of the gods and for the purpose of drying up the ocean, he [Rāma] warded off that incomparable arrow discharged by the son of Jamadagni;
thus obstructed, it traveled for twelve *yojanas* and then fell. ||57-58||
And at that moment, the ocean, as if laughing, withdrew its waters from that region;
and the son of Jamadagni, endowed with great splendor and resembling the lord of the gods, likewise took up residence there,
his heart filled with joy, in that place frequented by herds of deer and flocks of birds.
The goddess made it like a glorious city filled with the terrifying roars of lions, lordly elephants, sharabhas, and bears.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter in the Rāmamāhātmya of the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
In that manner, the earth was given by the son of Jamadagni to that high-souled one.
Then, like a mountain peak falling from above, she descended to the ground below.
Enraged, the sage said to her: "Stop, stop, O Vasundharā!
For what reason, O auspicious one, do you abandon me and go down below?"
The Earth said:
"O Sage, with my heart captivated by his virtues, I am unable to remain without my beloved husband Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, who possesses exceeding splendor. (3)
O bull among sages, if you do not grant me to Rāma today, O Lord, I shall go down [to the underworld]; I cannot remain otherwise than this.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of hers, Kaśyapa, the best of ascetics,
spoke to the Earth, as if burning her with his splendor in his anger.
Kaśyapa said:
"Go, O woman of wicked conduct, down once more to the lower state!
I shall become the earth; behold the power of my asceticism! (6)
Then the Blessed Vyāsa, having resorted to supreme yoga,
attained the state of the earth and sustained human beings.
When this earth had shone for many thousands of years,
she then became despondent and propitiated Kaśyapa.
The Earth said:
"O Blessed One, O All-pervading Lord, by virtue of your austerity, yoga, and power, there is no one at all equal to you, whether in heaven or on earth. (9)
I propitiate you with my head bowed; behold this supreme power of mine.
O great sage, forgive whatever slight offense I have committed against you.
"By your command, O best of Brahmins, may I alone indeed become the earth in the worlds; you ought to show favor to me, who am distressed."
Sanatkumāra said: Seeing her thus present before him, the Blessed One, the best of sages,
then spoke with a smile to the goddess Earth who was bowing down.
Indeed, it was through your own misconduct that I did this to you;
now, enjoy the sovereignty of the earth granted by me.
"O Vasundharā, having become my daughter and being born of the lineage of Kaśyapa, you shall be known in the world as Kāśyapī. (14)
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, having thus gone downwards, that earth remained once more;
having regained her state as the earth, she became free from distress.
This state of the earth belonging to the great sage Kaśyapa, as well as the arrival of the earth and its subsequent transformation—[all this has been told]. || 16 ||
Indeed, whoever, having become pure, should always listen to or recite this, shall obtain imperishable worlds as well as the fruit of the entire earth. ||17||

O Sage, that best of men who, having repeatedly bowed here to her who is the source of all worlds, shall constantly proclaim this earth which bestows wealth, attains the imperishable world of the Rishi. || 18 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Earthhood of Kaśyapa," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the powerful battle of the banners.
There was a glorious and immensely powerful son of Danu named Vipracitti, who brought about the destruction of the life-force and yoga of both the gods and the asuras;
it is heard that he, with a disciplined mind, performed austerities at Bhastrāpada. || 1-2 ||
Having propitiated the Lord of Gods, the three-eyed Blessed One, there, he chose the boon of immortality; and that Lord of Devas granted it to him.
The divine, all-pervading, auspicious golden banner, composed of illusion,
spoke to that lord of the Dānavas with a satisfied soul.
"O son of Danu, this Viśvarūpa is your supreme banner.
Relying upon him in battles, you shall be invincible;
moreover, O mighty-armed one, you shall be immortal, provided that you do not utter a sound."
Otherwise, however, victory in battle will be yours through your good fortune.
Thus addressed by the god Dhvaja in that great battle,
O best of Brahmins, he challenged all the gods along with the Danujas.
Then a terrible, tumultuous, and hair-raising battle took place.
For eighteen hundred years, it was indeed most terrible. || 8 ||
There they beheld a marvel performed by the wise son of Danu:
that with his banner of universal form, he alone slew many.
And as he fought in battle, relying on his banner through the power of illusion,
the gods did not strike him, for though they beheld him, they were rendered bewildered.
In that battle, the gods did not see the sons of Danu nor the Daityas;
all those deluded dwellers of heaven saw only the banner.
Whatever infallible weapons the gods discharged, [they were met by it].
For those [demons] were indeed covered by the shadow of the banner and the wind;
from the front, from behind, from the sides, and even from above,
they saw only the banner, and neither the Daityas nor the Dānavas.
There, O Vyāsa, those sharp arrows, blazing like the flames of fire,
issued forth from his banner and tore asunder the foremost of the gods.
Maces, iron clubs, slings, and javelins,
as well as other various weapons, were seen indeed emerging from the banner.
All those gods, having taken refuge in that banner on every side, [were protected] by that Daitya.
Broken in battle, deprived of their senses, and stripped of their prowess, they were shattered.
Seeing all those best of gods broken and being broken,
the Dānava roared while leaning upon his banner, like a rain-cloud.
Perceiving that opening, the Blessed Lord Pākaśāsana,
filled with supreme wrath, aimed at the banner and hurled his thunderbolt;
that thunderbolt blazed like the sun and emitted a terrifying sound.
He made Sadhvaja, the lord of the Dānavas, his target in battle;
having fixed his aim upon the banner, the high-souled Indra, the lord of the gods,
slew all fourteen thousand of those Nivātakavacas.
Perceiving that they had been struck by that sound, those beings of great majesty,
who were like the lords of the gods and bore emblems equal to Indra’s, all placed their own insignia upon the banner of the god-king’s army with the power of his thunderbolt.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Battle of the Banners," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
O imperishable son of Brahmā, you have mentioned the place called Bhastrāpada.
"How did that come to pass? I wish to know this matter.
Sanatkumāra said:
"There was a lord of subjects named Bāhu, born in the lineage of Ikṣvāku."
O best of brahmins, his kingdom was seized in its entirety by the Haihayas and Tālajaṅghas through their prowess; accompanied by his wife, he departed for the forest.
Having gone to the hermitage of Ṛcīka and being hospitably received by him,
he dwelt in the midst of the forest together with his pregnant wife.
O son of Śakti, at the time of that wife's delivery, however—
Out of passion and delusion, her co-wife caused a poison to be administered to her.
Having experienced that [poison], she became tormented and afflicted with pain;
crying out, "It is cold water!", she fell to the ground in a swoon. ||4-5||
Seeing her fallen in that manner, the king, consumed by grief,
took his water-pot and went to the river for water, even though he was old.
Having filled that jar and carrying it upon his shoulder, he, being distressed by old age and exhaustion, fell down and died. ||7||
When the sages had thus proclaimed, "He is dead!
He is dead!", that goddess, struck by grief for her husband, rose up from her swoon.
Stricken then by the heat of the poison and by the death of her husband,
O Vyāsa, she cried out like a female osprey.
All the sages, Vasiṣṭha and the others, arrived at Bāhu’s [hermitage].
Having properly performed the piling of the sacrificial altar and preparing it for the consecration,
Śaibyā— though defiled by her pregnancy— was about to enter that fire;
she was, however, forbidden by the sages and by the high-souled Aurva, O Vyāsa.
O Vyāsa, on that day at evening, from her womb there emerged, together with the poison, this child who was like fire in brilliance and the destroyer of wrath. Then the sage gave him the name Sagara.
And filled with compassion, he performed for him every single consecration rite.

He bestowed upon him the science of archery (dhanurveda), as well as the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches (sāṅga), a vast collection of celestial weapons, and an inexhaustible, unimpeded chariot.
With that preeminent chariot, he indeed struck down his enemies in battle;
and having aimed the Aurva weapon, he destroyed their dharma.
Having thus slain them, O Vyāsa, and having obtained the kingdom as well, he—
Having obtained Śaivyā, the slender-waisted sister of Vainateya,
that mighty-armed lord of men, though childless, being possessed of great splendor, propitiated Tryambaka, the best of gods, for the sake of obtaining a son.
To him, the Lord, the powerful master, granted sixty thousand sons of great soul who would continue his lineage.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having obtained that boon, the high-minded King Sagara spoke to his two wives— the sister of Vainateya and Śaivyā. (19) Sagara said:
And my lord has granted me a son, auspicious and a perpetuator of the lineage,
as well as sixty thousand sons of great soul.
In that regard, which of you two goddesses chooses the boon—be it auspicious or beneficial?
Speak, for I shall not make a division among you who have realized the Self. (21)
Vainateyasvasā said, "O lord of men, may I have sixty thousand sons.
Śaivyā replied, "May I have but one son who shall perpetuate my lineage. (22)
Sanatkumāra said: Then Śaivyā gave birth to the son of Asamañja; she gave birth to a large egg, which was the sister of Vainateya.
Then,
O Vyāsa, from that vessel, those ten thousand [beings] multiplied by six were born, possessing great strength.
Then Sagara abandoned his son Asamañja,
knowing him to be unrighteous and established in improper conduct.
His son was Aṃśumān, who, though still a child, was exceedingly righteous.
At that time, Sagara, the best of kings, felt great joy in him.
Having renounced Asamañja, he was consecrated for the horse sacrifice;
he appointed sixty thousand [guards] for the protection of the horse.
While those great-souled ones were thus exerting themselves to tend the horse,
Śakra, having become invisible, snatched away that best of steeds.
Having gone everywhere throughout the worlds and not seeing that best of horses, they approached their father who was consecrated for sacrifice and reported the matter concerning that horse.
Then the king, enraged and as if burning his sons with his gaze, spoke with eyes copper-red from fury: "Perish this very day!
O cruel ones, do not come back today unless you have found the horse!"
"What use have I for sons or for you? Go all of you to the abode of Yama!
Sanatkumāra said:
O best of Brahmins, having been addressed thus, they then [departed] throughout the entire three worlds.
Having searched, they caused this entire earth to be excavated. Then they saw the elephants of the quarters and the sages of restrained vows;
seeing them all supporting the earth, they bowed down to them.
They beheld the sage Kapila sleeping in the pool of water; and not far from him, they saw the horse, whereupon they became enraged. ||34||
Impelled by their destined fate, having reached maturity in time and being on the verge of death,
they then spoke to Kapila, the best of sages, because of their father’s curse.
"This evil-minded one has stolen our preeminent horse while we were asleep;
today we shall all lead him before our father.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then all those mighty ones, bound by the noose of Time and subject to the power of destiny, struck him with their feet.
Afflicted by them, he became enraged and then discharged ten thousand arrows.
He suddenly released the suppressed wind, just as a great serpent sheds its skin.
Emerging from his mouth, that wind, consisting of fire,
burned all the oceans that were excluded from the path of justice and dharma.
When all of them had been consumed by fire, the sages, Nārada and the others, related to Sagara exactly what had occurred— that most difficult of deeds.
Thereupon, the king, afflicted with grief, steadied himself by his own self.
The high-minded Sagara commanded his beloved grandson Aṃśumān: "Mount this chariot and go to that excellent horse.
Sagara said:
[41] "Mount this chariot and go to that supreme horse."
Bring them here, O mighty-armed one, so that our time does not pass us by. || 42 ||
"You should act according to those words so that this best of sages does not direct his anger toward us; then our progeny will certainly endure.
Sanatkumāra said:

Thus addressed, that high-souled king, honored by gods and *siddhas*, mounted his chariot and proceeded with speed— possessing the prowess of the lord of the gods— to where the *yogin* who had brought about the end of Sagara’s lineage was shining.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Origin of Sagara," in the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having gone to that region frequented by great elephants, he saw those [beings] turned to ashes and the sage, who possessed the brilliance of fire. 1.
Then, bowing down in his presence with words joined in praise,
he asked forgiveness for all the evil deeds he had previously committed.
Kapila said:
"O King, here in this secluded place I was standing, disciplined and free from fever.
Being suddenly assailed by them, I released wind from my mouth."
For a thousand years he was restrained by me within that wind;
once suddenly released, he consumed all those ancestors of yours.
"O King, they were not burned by me intentionally, nor even out of anger;
they were slain by the fruit of their own ripened time, just like birds [falling from a tree].
This horse standing by my side has been recognized by someone who knows the self."
Their hearts have been stolen away for their own destruction; do not be angry, let the horse be led back.
Sanatkumāra said: With his permission, O Vyāsa, that high-minded lord of men, Aṃśumān, proceeded to give them water.
Vainateya said this to him: "O mighty-armed one, water must not be given to my sister's sons; it will not reach them."
Aṃśumān said:
"O Kaśyapa, how indeed may those ancestors of mine attain the divine worlds? I desire this to be told by you. (9)
Vainateya said:
"In the world of the gods, there is a sacred river named Gaṅgā that removes all evil.
Your bones shall remain in its waters here on earth for the sake of your kinsmen in every way."
O King, when these [limbs] are touched, they shall attain liberation from evil, O tiger among kings; otherwise, what use is water to you? (11)
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O Vyāsa, having taken the horse back, that virtuous king returned and presented the horse to his grandfather.

Then that high-minded king, having performed the horse sacrifice and being tormented by the slaughter of his sons, set his mind upon the destruction of the ocean. Thereupon, the lord of rivers bowed down to him and propitiated him.
He became his son and then spoke these words to him.
"O King, O mighty-armed monarch, it is said that I must indeed be made radiant by one born of your lineage, so that I may be filled to the brim with the waters of the Gaṅgā. (15)
"Do not be angry; I am your son, O you of immeasurable splendor who creates glory!
I shall bestow jewels upon you; come to peace with me, my lord. (16)
Then, O King, the anger of that monarch toward the ocean was pacified;
and Viṣṇu, being pleased with him, granted him his desired boons.
He obtains more than a hundred horse-sacrifices, as well as eternal and imperishable residence in heaven;
his lineage becomes forever undecaying, and he gains foremost and everlasting fame. (18)
Having obtained these boons— friendship as well as supreme steadfastness in dharma— and having enjoyed his kingdom free from all obstacles, he [ruled].
Then he went to the forest, and after performing austerities, he ascended to heaven;
thereafter, King Aṃśumān shone forth, righteous and true to his promise.
Having consecrated his son in the kingdom with the intention of descending to the Gaṅgā,
he who possessed great strength and prowess ascended to heaven after performing austerities.
Then his son, the high-souled and mighty Dilīpa, having ruled the kingdom like the king of the gods, retired to the forest, O Vyāsa.
There, having exerted himself for the sake of Gaṅgā and performed austerities, he went to heaven;
yet, without even attaining that desire, he was born again as his son. (23)
There was a virtuous king named Bhagīratha, the auspicious lord of Jambūdvīpa; he was righteous, truthful in speech, and heroic, like Dharma personified. ||24||
O best of sages, O Lord, from the very moment of his birth, the desire for the descent of the Gaṅgā has resided in his heart: "How shall I bring it about? (25)
Then, after a long time, having performed all his duties,
the king practiced a very great austerity by which the Lord of the World was pleased.
Then Brahmā himself, approaching him who was firm in his vows, spoke to him.
"Speak, O lord of men; choose whatever boons I may grant you.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that king, seeing him, bowed down with a joyful countenance.
He spoke of the inexhaustible dharma as well as the imperishable residence in heaven.
And he granted him the imperishability of his lineage, as well as a hundred excellent sons—heroes who were righteous and never retreated in battles. (29)
Victory in battle at all times, as well as imperishable fame in the world,
and also the unsurpassed descent of the river Gaṅgā—
so that she may become most renowned in the world as Bhāgīrathī.
"I desire this, O Lord of Gods, if you, O All-pervading One, so deem it.
Sanatkumāra said:
"When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One [expounded] all of this in its entirety."
The Creator himself gave it to him and spoke these words to that king: ||| 3.2 ||
"O tiger among kings, you are Gaṅgā; you shall lead her from heaven to the earth.
No one is capable of supporting her as she falls from the sky, except for the God who is the Teacher of the World, the three-eyed wielder of the trident."
Therefore, with restrained vows, you should propitiate the Lord of the gods;
that omnipresent one will clearly grant you a boon.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed, that lord of kings, subsisting on air and blinking his eyes,
became breathless there upon the auspicious peak of the Himavat.
The Lord, the god Kapardin Nīlalohita, was pleased with him who had been intent upon that for a thousand years and sought his blessing. Having said, "I am the giver of boons," the Lord spoke again:
"I grant you divine vision; behold me, O best of kings!
Having seen that great archer, the three-eyed Lord and Master, he said to the goddess:
"O Goddess, sustain [this] river; I choose a boon."

"O Imperishable One, if you are pleased with me, let the divine Gaṅgā, which flows through the three paths, fulfill my desire, O Mahādeva: [to bring] my deceased ancestors and grandfathers [back to life]."
"Having delivered them from hell, I shall lead those virtuous ones to heaven;
for their sake, O Mahādeva, this effort has been undertaken by me. By your grace, they shall go to heaven, having bathed in the Gaṅgā. (8.127.40)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, the Blessed One whose banner bears the bull spoke to that tiger among kings with a deeply satisfied inner soul.
The God of Gods said: "O Bhagīratha, it shall be so for you; there is no doubt.
And by my grace, that Gaṅgā shall become your daughter."
"And for your sake, O best of kings, I shall sustain her as she falls from heaven, for the purpose of astonishing the worlds and for the benefit of all beings. Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of his, Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, said:
"O supreme among gods, who will sustain my force?
Today, having suddenly seized him, I shall flow forth most difficult to endure."
I shall go to the Pātāla, which is so difficult to reach; of this there is no doubt. ||45||
Whether he be the Self-Existent Brahmā, or Śakra the lord of the gods, or even Viṣṇu the son of Aditi—I shall certainly lead him away; of this there is no doubt.
Today let the worlds behold my great and unassailable impetuosity.
As she was falling to the earth, that river spoke thus to the invincible one.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of hers, which were full of arrogance, Śaṅkara—
He formed the resolve to restrain that best of rivers.
By his mere resolve, a fever indeed entered the gods;
their garlands withered, portents arose, the worlds were overturned, and their celestial chariots fell. (49)
And the Asuras, intoxicated by their strength and possessed of great power, were seen calling out to the sons of Diti, who were radiant like blazing suns. (8.127.50)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having observed that transformation, the gods spoke to Śatakratu:
"O Lord, this reversal has not occurred without cause; let it be investigated quickly."
And at that time, the delusion of that god together with the sages arose; Brahmā, having approached them, enlightened them.
Brahmā said:
"O all you dwellers of heaven, do not remain despondent.
Understand what I say; let this time not pass you by."
This god, the great archer with matted hair who rides upon the clouds,
possessed of terrible prowess, set his mind upon destroying the Gaṅgā.
When the gods were thus meditated upon by him in his mind for the destruction of the world, [they trembled].
Act without delay so that this reversal may not occur.
Having gone from here with me and joined with the sages, seek refuge in Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, by means of this state of calamity. 55–56.
Sanatkumāra said: Then those gods, together with Brahmā, the lotus-born,
went to a peak of the Himalayas adorned with all kinds of jewels.
By name it was called Hiraṇmaya, where the river Hairaṇvatī flows;
and there the gods beheld the Lord of the Gods through their asceticism and devotion.
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, perceiving him to be as if enraged, possessing the brilliance of the fire at the end of an eon,
and difficult to behold, they then sought refuge with the Goddess.
The gods said:
"O Vibhāvarī, you are the mother of the worlds together with the gods; you are the bellows, O Rudrāṇī. Grant us that state which bestows both [worlds]. (8.127.60)
We have come to you for refuge, O Mother; we are your sons, O Auspicious One.
Protect us, O Goddess of the lords of gods; this is what we desire. (61)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of the gods who were terrified and seeking refuge, the Goddess granted them fearlessness, an unsurpassed boon.
Then, having bowed her head to that Lord of the gods, the Blessed One who wields the Pināka bow, the Daughter of the Mountain spoke like one who was afraid.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the Lord raised up that frightened woman, who was prostrate with her head at his feet,
using his hand which possessed the luster of a lotus petal.
And then he said to the virtuous lady, "O daughter of Himavat, you are afraid;
for what reason? And what is your fear, O fair-browed one? Tell me, O lady of auspicious countenance. (65)
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, at that time the daughter of Himavat spoke to him like one frightened:
"O Lord, I am truly afraid upon seeing your exceedingly radiant form. (66)
Resembling the fire of universal destruction and difficult to behold even for the gods,
O Lord of Gods, the worlds, along with the deities and the sages, were despondent.
All these lords of the gods worship you, trembling with fear.
O Mahādeva, I am afraid of you; these gods are even more afraid than I.
They have come to me for refuge; grant them fearlessness.
You are the creator of all worlds, together with the gods and the ṛṣis.
Do not destroy them; bowing my head, I entreat you.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of hers and having seen the gods, the destroyer of the sacrifice said,
"O best of the thirty deities, there is no fear for you from me."
But this river, by her very nature as a woman, O daughter of Himavat, having set her mind on me with ill intent, will fall upon me. (71)
"I shall arrest that river as it falls from heaven;
you too, O sinless ones, may go to your respective abodes with confidence.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having heard those words, those best of the gods bowed down and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke with voices full of shame: (73)
The gods said:
"This best of rivers has been created by you for the sake of the welfare of the world;
yet rivers are fickle, and such is the nature of women. (74)
By that very nature of hers, and through her reliance upon us, she has become filled with great pride and, being fearless of anything, she indeed boasts. (75)
And hear from us, O Lord of Gods, the reason for this pride of hers by which that river boasts; do not be angry, O you of terrible prowess. (76)
"For everyone becomes arrogant when being requested for the sake of some task;
O Lord, this is so even in the case of a mere trifle in this world, how much more so for this best of rivers?
O Great God, this very river is desired by you to be sustained."
Then, the god, who is the most excellent of all, spoke with pride:
"Supported by you, the lord of the gods, this best of rivers shall become meritorious in this world, destroying all sins. (78-79)
"O Lord of the Devas, no god is capable of holding back this falling river; yet, there would be no greater benefit than that.
Therefore, O Kāla, you have been entreated by the gods and by this king."
"O best of gods, becoming auspicious, sustain this river.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus was the Blessed One addressed by the gods with words that were truthful and free from contradiction.
The god was addressed by the deities together with Brahmā, along with Nārāyaṇa and the world-protectors. ||8.2||
Having repeatedly considered that granting of the boon to the king, the Lord of Gods spoke these words in a deep voice to the gods: || 83 ||
O best of gods, it was for the sake of this king, whose senses were overwhelmed by hunger, and at the request of you venerable ones, that [this was done]. || 84 ||
O sinless ones, listen to this which I shall not destroy:
the destruction of this pride, O great beings, as I speak it. (85)
A great destruction of this pride of the lord of mountains shall come to pass;
furthermore, the righteous Jahnu will destroy his pride again.
And this great river, corrupted by my curse, shall become one of ill conduct.
Having approached a human husband, she will kill seven sons. ||87||
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus to the gods, Śarva, the best among the deities, then said, "Speak; what else do you desire? I shall grant it today according to your wish."
The gods said:
"O Blessed One, we desire a place for the god of great supernatural power—a sacred field (kṣetra) called Samantapañcaka that is never bereft of your presence. (89)
Because the imperishable daughter of the Himalayas was addressed by us as "Bhastre," and because they desire a state of fearlessness (*abhaya*), it is therefore remembered as Bhastrāpada.
Whoever comes here with self-restraint and worships the Bull-bannered Lord shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice and attain the world of Rudra. ||91||
O best of gods, he who offers a *caru* oblation after fasting for a day and night shall become equal to Nandīśvara.
O Lord of Gods, whatever man here should give up his life while observing the rules, or even without such rules, O God, through death by chance; ||93||
Having become equal to the Gaṇas, he too shall remain until the dissolution of all beings,
