endowed with a divine body and having entered into the service of following you.
"Salutation to Bhastreśvara! Whoever, having performed this, remains ever pure—whether rising or even sleeping—he rejoices in the world of Śakra. (95)

Whoever should constantly recite this great, divine [hymn] of infinite benefit in the assembly of the twice-born and the gods, he shall become a lord of the Gaṇas of great majesty and great speed; O God, this is through taking refuge in your divine praise. (96)
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Descent of the Gaṅgā," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
In that delightful abode of Sthāṇu, the gods, together with Brahmā, [assembled].
Having installed the *liṅga*, all the holy sites (*tīrthas*) performed their respective rites individually. ||1||
...and the famous Ādityatīrtha, as well as the Aśvamedhika [tīrtha]. ||2||
Rudratīrtha, Sthāṇutīrtha, and the Tīrtha of Brahmā;
Indratīrtha and that of the Vasus, and another known as that of the Aśvins. ||3||
There is another sacred ford (tīrtha) of Yama, and then another sacred ford of Vāyu;
there is also another sacred ford of Viṣṇu, renowned and worshipped by the gods.
O brahmin-sage, having bathed in these [waters], prepared a sacrificial oblation (caru), and offered it,
one indeed wanders through these divine places free from fear from any quarter.
Even today, O Brahman-sage, that sweet sound is heard there, mingled with the jingling of waist-bands and bracelets, and intensified by the resonance of flutes and lutes,
as the beautiful-limbed women sing and likewise dance. (6)
O Vyāsa, he is eternally praised by the Apsarases as they laud the Three-eyed One.
Sanatkumāra said: Then those gods, together with Brahmā, spoke to the best of gods:
"O Blessed One, may we behold the supreme retention (dhāraṇa) of this."
The God of gods said: "O lords of the wise, see me tomorrow at dawn as you desire,
holding the river that flows through the three paths, which is proud of its own qualities."
Having been addressed thus, they bowed to the Lord and then went to the vicinity of the Gaṅgā;
thereupon Brahmā spoke to that goddess who brings happiness to the world.
"Do not be proud, O Gaṅgā; do not meet with destruction. Abiding in rectitude, you shall descend, O best of rivers, praising the three-eyed Soma while endowed with supreme devotion. || 11 ||
Having understood your intention, that Lord Śambhu was intent on your destruction;
yet, desiring your welfare, he was propitiated with great difficulty.
Do not commit such an offense again, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
"O best of rivers, from your destruction the world would surely perish.
Having thus consoled her, the gods, including Brahmā,
the lords of the world, arrived on the second day, desiring to see her.
The great and divine peak of the Himavat, named Vajropala.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Ananta, as well as men and sages;
the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the hosts of Maruts.
The Sādhyas, gods, along with the Pitṛs, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas;
as well as Piśācas, Asuras, horned creatures, and those with speckled coats. || 18 ||
The seers Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Marīci, Pulaha,
Pulastya, Aṅgiras, Bhṛgu, Kaśyapa,
Auśija, Vāmadeva, and Gautama of great asceticism; || 1.9 ||
Cyavana and Bharadvāja, as well as Indrapramati;
Raibhya and Jamadagni, and the heroic Kuṇibāhu;
Atharvan, Śvetaketu, and the renowned Dattātreya. || 8.128.20–21 ||
Ruci, Dharma, Dakṣa, and those who are the Sāvarṇi Manus;
Agni, Vedabāhu, and he who is named Śaṅkhapāt. ||22||
Ambarīṣa is renowned, and Ketumān is another;
these and many other sages as well as deities [are there],
along with all the celestial chariots and the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases.
The Jambhakas, the Seasons,
and all the various classes [of beings] arrived there, filled with joy and possessing supreme splendor.
While those gods remained in the sky, they were watching at that time.
On that most excellent peak, which resembled Mount Meru and Mandara,
the Lord of Gods, accompanied by Umā, suddenly became visible,
shining with a mass of matted hair tawny like a flash of lightning.
Standing above, he spoke to Bhagīratha with a great voice.
The God of Gods said:
"O Bhagīratha, where is that Gaṅgā who delivers your ancestors? Summon her, O mighty-armed one; I shall sustain her, of this there is no doubt. (28)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that tiger among kings, O Vyāsa, having remembered those words of Brahmā, bowed his head with joined palms and called the river to mind.
Summoned by his mind, that river whose abode is the heavenly world arrived in an instant, the auspicious goddess coming from the celestial realm to the earthly world.
Reaching that region, the river moved with a speed equal to the wind of thought.
Possessing great speed, she who is the source of hundreds of auspicious things adorned everything.
Then, having come obliquely from the sky, that great river became known as the Ākāśagaṅgā by the name Oghavatī.
That great river, the celestial Gaṅgā, possessing great velocity, emerged from the path of the sinful [Asura] saying, "May there be auspiciousness for me";
therefore she was called Śivagaṅgā, for she is indeed most auspicious by name. (33)
Making a vast sound like the roar of a thunderbolt, the river was seen by the gods from that place; therefore, it is known as Devagaṅgā.
Seeing her, all the sages and all the inhabitants of the world of the gods suddenly recited peaceful mantras, their hair standing on end with joy.
O Vyāsa, while they were reciting prayers, that river, which brings happiness to the world,
split into three parts and fell to the earth as if trembling with fear while offering praise.
As she was falling with great speed, Mahādeva caught her with his mass of matted hair in three swift movements, right in the presence of the gods.
Having reached that mass of matted hair, the triple-streamed river, though normally surging,
was checked by his yogic power and could not reach its end;
for she, trembling with fear, then fell down while offering praise.
Therefore, she is called Bhītagaṅgā and Stotragaṅgā. ||3.9||
Since that best of rivers has fallen with three currents,
she is therefore called Trisrotas by those who discourse upon Brahman.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having fallen there, she was sustained by the God through his illusory power (māyā);
searching for the opening in his matted locks, she dwelt there for many years.
When a full thousand years had passed while she remained in her hut of matted hair,
all the gods beheld her as if she were situated within the hollow of a tree.
Then those gods, having suddenly prostrated before the bull-bannered Lord, [spoke].
Dejected, they said, "O Vyāsa, do not destroy the river! (43)
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of theirs and having seen the king, the God of gods, who is full of compassion, shook out his mass of matted hair.
As he shook his mass of matted hair, drops indeed fell there;
resembling pearls and as pure as the rays of the full moon,
they created the divine Bindusaras, possessing the splendor of the ocean's form.
Therefore, exactly seven great channels have issued forth. ||46||
The Nalinī, the Hlādinī, and the Plāvanī flow toward the east;
the Sītā, the Cakṣus, and the Sindhu—these three indeed flow toward the west.
The middle stream followed the path by which King Bhagīratha went;
therefore, that Gaṅgā is called "Bhāgīrathī" by those who discourse on Brahman.
Then that best of rivers, tearing her way through, went toward the Himalayas;
she was obstructed at the foot of the Himalayas by a mountain peak of jewels.
Then, O Vyāsa, beholding her thus obstructed, King Bhagīratha, with a dejected countenance, remembered Brahmā in his mind. (8.128.50)
Then the Blessed Brahmā said to the great elephant Supratīka:
"Tear this mountain peak apart with your two tusk-thunderbolts."
Where that king of mountains was split by the elephant Supratīka, that place is called Gaṅgādvāra, and it is remembered as being exceedingly meritorious. ||52||
As long as the highly illustrious elephant did not stand facing him,
it was carried away by the current for a distance of twelve yojanas, lost to its path.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, this most meritorious descent of the Gaṅgā which I have described is the sacred place known by the name Bhastrāpada.
That mortal who shall always hear this on every sacred festival day (parvan),
having attained the world of the gods, shall wander together with the deities.
This auspicious [work] is a great liberator from sin, providing the means for celestial chariots and the company of Apsarases.
He who constantly listens with an undaunted mind goes to the worlds known to the inhabitants of heaven. ||56||
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Descent of the Gaṅgā," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the Hālāhala [poison] in its entirety.
The battle between the sons of Diti and the gods, which brought terror to all.
O Vyāsa, that host known as Hālāhala, possessed of heroic prowess,
appeared formidable to the Asuras as a thorn in the side of the Brahmins.
When the sons of Danu had departed, that host was overcome with rage.
Summoning his strength, he challenged all the gods to battle.
A most terrible battle took place between them;
yet victory always belonged to the Asuras.
Consequently, all those gods became dispirited, their prowess destroyed.
Having been deprived of their kingdom, they approached Brahmā, the cause of the world.
Gathering together, they said to him: "O Lord, we have now been deprived of our kingdom;
how may we regain our kingdom through your power? (6)
Having heard those words of theirs, the god born from the waters said to the gods,
"Propitiate the Lord of Gods without delay."
"That three-eyed god, of great heroism and strength, shall be your giver [of victory],
by whom you shall conquer all those in battle through your prowess.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus, the gods propitiated Śaṅkara, the Lord of Devas, through their ascetic penance;
with palms joined in reverence, they said to him, "O Slayer of the Sacrifice, grant us strength.
While they were thus chanting, Hara was gratified by their austerity.
Then he bestowed that invincible mantra, the supreme among all mantras.
Having obtained him, O brahmin-sage, the gods, having performed their protection,
all moved among the asuras like those who were deluded, though they themselves were undeluded.
Then the asuras, seeing all the gods to be deluded, [acted accordingly].
Those of evil conduct thought, "These are fools," exactly as it was;
"All these gods have had their passion stolen away by a deluded mind; they wander about like madmen—behold them, O you who are not gods! (12–13)
Others reviled them, struck them harshly,
bound them at will, and likewise released them;
such was the conduct, O Vyāsa, of those who were then performing auspicious deeds.
The Dharma became exceedingly great and destroyed the Asuras.
Because of that transgression of those evil-minded Asuras,
the hosts of deities perceived that their strength had waned due to the destruction of Dharma.
Sanatkumāra said: Then all those wielders of divine weapons, having been addressed by Brahmā,
challenged all the tigers among the asuras and slaughtered them in battle.

Wherein Bala was slain in battle by Devendra with his hundred-jointed thunderbolt after he had displayed his prowess; for that reason, he is remembered as Balahā (the slayer of Bala). Sanatkumāra said:
And there was another battle, dark and most terrifying,
lasting ten thousand and one thousand years.
Furthermore, there was a glorious son of Danu known as Devatāntaka.
In former times, desiring to obtain Māyā, he propitiated Rudra. O Vyāsa, when a thousand years had passed and the time for the boon had arrived, Brahmā granted a boon to that wise son of Danu.
He chose the Tāmasī Māyā, which afflicts all beings,
which is impenetrable and irresistible, and which no one knows.
He gave that illusion to him and then spoke these words to him:
"O mighty one, this illusion shall indeed come to pass exactly as it was described to you; provided, O son of Danu, that you do not make a sound according to your will. (23)
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O Vyāsa, having obtained the boon, that Asura, desiring to deceive [the gods],
oppressed all the worlds together with many Dānavas.
Even the gods did not stand before him out of fear;
all the gods, agitated by terror, did not remain at all in his presence.
Abandoning their respective positions, they remained here and there. (25)
Summoned by the harsh cries of the Dānavas, who were arrogant in their strength,
the gods nevertheless did not stand before them.
Having approached them, all the sages, filled with indignation, spoke as follows.
"Provide protection for the worlds; do not remain despondent. And we, O gods, shall maintain ourselves through self-restraint and asceticism.
Let there be no fear for you; fight and make the world free from fever."
O Vyāsa, having been addressed thus by those sages for the sake of the world,
they did not stop before that bandit out of fear.
When the dwellers of heaven still did not stop despite being told this, [the sages spoke again].
Then those best of sages spoke of another expedient:
"O supreme gods, let all the Apsarases be summoned and dispatched to the presence of the Asuras,
whose minds are possessed by desire."
"Having attacked those whose hearts were attached to them and who were intoxicated by drinking maireya wine,
you gods shall then slay the more powerful enemies of the gods by force in battle.
Then, those [apsarases] were dispatched by the gods for the purpose of deceiving the enemies of the gods.
The cranes listened intently to the humming sounds and cries of their tinkling anklets;
their slender bodies were tossed by necklaces over the expanse of their full, high breasts; and their long eyes resembled those of startled young does. (33–34)
Others had pale cheeks rubbed by swinging earrings and wore fine garments with the luster of a peacock’s neck.
The rows of their lower lips were as copper-red as freshly cut coral; their sprout-like hands were clinging to the ends of their garments and to flower-crests.
Their arms were adorned with armlets studded with the radiance of various jewels, and their beautiful, curly hair resembled the plumage of a peacock. (37)
Adorned with garlands of flowers produced from the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma), their breasts were encased in bodices as green as the body of a parrot; they displayed the graceful,
playful, and elegant gait of an elephant in rut.
Uttering cries as melodious as those of intoxicated cuckoos and gallinules,
they revealed themselves as causes of obstacles even to the great austerities undertaken [by the sages], acting as instruments for the destruction of their enemies. (39–40)
Then, having seen those celestial nymphs, the sons of Diti, deluded by passion, struck one another for the sake of those beautiful-limbed women with maces,
iron clubs, discuses, swords, spears, hammers, and javelins.
"With bows, thunderbolts, sharp-pointed weapons, slings, and axes—this woman of beautiful limbs and slender waist belongs to me, not to you.
Or rather, let battle be the bride-price; release her and strike at me!"
Having spoken these various words, the Daityas, impelled by Time,
encountered one another’s slaughter and went to the abode of Yama.
Those Dānavas who remained there as survivors, their prowess extinguished, [remained behind].
Even they were all slain in battle by the gods of fierce splendor.
That man of pure intellect who recites this account of the destruction of the lords of the Dānavas in an assembly shall obtain,
even in this very world, young women equal in beauty to the Apsarases.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Battle with Andhaka," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
How was that Daitya Andhaka struck down by Hara?
He under whose power the entire three worlds remained out of fear—
Sanatkumāra said: In the beginning, there was a lord of Daityas named Andhaka, who was a thorn to the three worlds.
Having obtained boons from Brahmā, he became incapable of being slain by gods or humans.
When he was enraged in battle, neither Viṣṇu, nor Śakra, nor Yama was able to stand before him; how much less so the other inhabitants of heaven?
Once, while wandering this earth, intoxicated by his own power,
that lord of the Daityas beheld on a ridge of Mount Mandara the goddess, the daughter of Himavat. Upon seeing her, his consciousness was struck down by lust.
"I alone am the lord," he thought, conceiving malice toward the goddess.
Having reflected thus, he spoke to his Dānava followers:
"Bring this daughter of the mountain quickly into my presence."
Having heard those words of his, Prahlāda, the best among speakers, whose mind was possessed by the god of love, spoke these words: ||7||
O Lord of the Dānavas, since speech that is beneficial and pure for the future must necessarily be spoken by me, especially out of affection for my kinsman. (8)
She is the daughter of Himavat and the wife of the wise Śarva;
you must not entertain any ill-will toward her, lest she consume you with her splendor.
O tiger among Dānavas, you ought not to revile Umā here— the goddess who is the mother of the world, worthy of worship, and possessed of a brilliance difficult to behold.
Why, with a deluded mind, do you wish to cross the deep-swirling, fearsome river by binding a great stone around your neck? (11)
"O Lord of the Dānavas, why do you, out of delusion, desire to touch the blazing crest of the fire like a moth, only for your own destruction?
O Lord of the Dānavas, do not lead us all to ruin along with our very roots."
"Let the mind of the queen be turned back; this is not fitting for the wise."
You are wise, of noble birth, and born into the lineage of the noble;
you are a performer of sacrifices and ever-devoted to dharma—this [act] is not fitting for you, O Lord. (14)
"You have many wives, all of whom possess enduring youth and are naturally endowed with beautiful limbs; let the Queen's heart be turned away [from her]. (15)
"He who, being pleased by our asceticism, grants the boons we desire—
you wish to commit a sin against that God of gods and his Goddess."
You wish to take away half the body of that God of gods, by whom Dakṣa, Kratu, Kāla, and Kāma were brought to destruction.
How can you disregard that Goddess, the sustainer of the world, who is worshipped in the lingas by gods, asuras, and great serpents? 18.
And you must not conceive of that god, the wielder of the Pināka bow, as being alone;
for if he so desired, he could indeed create hundreds and thousands of forms.
Thousands of *pramatha* spirits, yogins of terrifying deeds,
march before him just as your *dānavas* do for you—
he who would take away the brilliance from the sun, the luster from the moon, and the forbearance from the earth.
He who would seize the fang of Vāsuki would seize Pārvatī from him;
his entire head would shatter into a hundred pieces—that fool who would insult that noble lady, the wife of Śarva. || 21–22 ||
O son of Diti, you ought to remember those words spoken by your grandfather, the lotus-born one, at the conclusion of the granting of the boon:
"This prosperity, so difficult to obtain, has been bestowed upon you by me."
"O Dānava, through your own misconduct, this [kingdom] shall go elsewhere.
Those men who, possessed of wicked conduct, do not listen to the words of their kinsmen—even if they are bitter but beneficial—go to their destruction. (24-25)
"O Lord, for the sake of your pleasure, we shall seek out Śaṅkara;
having met him, we shall all follow you to the abode of Vaivasvata.
Having been addressed with these auspicious words by that kinsman, he then [replied].
"Driven by Time, he laughed and said, 'It is not so.
Regarding that which is unavoidable—both what must be done and what must not be done—I consider even defeat in battle to be my victory. (27-28)
"For it is Time alone that ordains the auspicious and the inauspicious for all beings by means of the mind, whether in this way or otherwise.
Then, out of passion, the lord of the Dānavas rejected Prahlāda.
He set his mind on touching the queen, like a moth upon the flame of a fire.
Then the Blessed Lady, having perceived the evil intent of the wicked-souled one,
commanded her hosts of great power to go to battle.

Then, commanded by the Goddess, those [gods], with various weapons in hand and led by Somanandin, set out toward the Dānavas. Having engaged in a great battle with the followers of the Dānavas, they...
Scattered by the lord of the Dānavas like clouds by the wind,
in that interval the Goddess, seeing Andhaka risen up,
herself rushed toward him, grasping her bow with an arrow.
She struck Andhaka between the breasts with twenty-five sharp-pointed arrows; he fainted and fell. Having regained consciousness after a moment, that Dānava was filled with pride.
He rose up swiftly with great speed, his formidable bow raised high.
Then that great asura, rising up once more against the goddess,
released showers of arrows like a rain-cloud pouring down rain.
Thereupon, raising his trident, which possessed the brilliance of a blazing fire, [he struck] the goddess.
The God gradually restrained her as she had begun to slay Andhaka. || 38 ||
"This lord of the Dānavas is to be disciplined by me alone; do not trouble yourself.
I myself shall pierce his heart with my trident in battle."
Thus addressed by the God of gods, the goddess Pārvatī then desisted from the battle and became invisible.
Then the Lord himself spoke to Nandin, the leader of his attendants.
"Fight together with the Dānavas, having summoned the hosts from all sides. || 41 ||
Then, having summoned all those hosts by the command of Śarva, Nandin spoke again to the Lord of Gods: "Listen to which hosts have arrived."
By you, these eternal beings were created as distinguished objects of desire within your own creation;
their true nature, which manifests as diversity through the state of progeny, is exceedingly difficult to describe.
"Bearing bull-emblems, with bulls as their vehicles, and adorned with portions of the moon—
these Rudras, dear to you, O Rudra, have arrived.
There are one hundred times ten million times one hundred of these great-souled ones."
O Lord, there were as many thousands and hundreds,
as well as sixty thousand of those blue-throated deities of great soul, for whom no equal is found. || 45-46 ||
These heroes, fierce in their forces and possessing formidable, supreme prowess,
will bring joy to your heart as they fight.
They are indeed the counterparts of these Rudras in terms of their power.
These gatekeepers are indeed powerful, courageous, and of fierce wrath.
Thus, these lions among monkeys, possessing the strength of lions, will fight with the Dānavas in battle like elephants against elephants. ||48-49||
The Rudras, the sons of Rudra, and those who are the attendants of the Rudras—
O Lord of the Rudras, for them there is indeed nothing that cannot be accomplished.
O best among those who have sons, each one of these Rudras has sons.
Five by five, these great heroes, wearing the feathers of crows on their heads, have suddenly arisen from your arms;
born of your wrath, they stand here together with Vīrabhadra at their head. || 51-52 ||
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, sixty crores and sixteen thousand of these leaders of the Gaṇas, who are dear to you, have arrived here.
Thus, O God, for the sake of pleasing you, Dakṣa’s sacrifice has become prosperous."
O God, slayer of Pura, behold those by whom you were struck down, now returned once more! O sinless one, these who were meditated upon by you when they had fallen into a state of calamity—
these very ones, numbering hundreds of thousands of crores, have now arrived.
Like great fires fanned by the wind that consume trees, these [beings] shall utterly burn the Dānavas who take delight in what is displeasing to you;
they who sport even with Guhya while he dwells in his cave. || 57 ||

O Maheśvara, O sinless one, three hundred million leaders of the Gaṇas, with faces like those of various hundreds of animals, have arrived like blazing mountains to do what is pleasing to you; they were given for your sake. || 58-59 ||
These lords of the Gaṇas, wearing red garments and adorned with red garlands and unguents, are named the Raktas, for they were born from the blood of Oṣṭhaja. || 8.130.60 ||
These sixty thousand crores of Aṅgāraka’s followers, possessed of great strength and prowess, have now presented themselves before you;
O sinless one, you must not consider their strength to be merely this much.
For these, O Great Lord, bearing the eightfold sovereignty born of your grace,
will bring many worlds— including gods, asuras, and humans— under their control when they are fully exerted. || 62-63 ||

O Lord of the Gaṇas, these who resemble kunda flowers and are adorned with golden lotuses— all clad in armor and eager for battle— could consume the gods and Dānavas at the end of the age in combat. || 64 ||

"O Lord of Rudras, behold these heroes devoted to Brahman, adorned with the crescent moon as their ornament; they have arrived, eager for battle—possessing the luster of the rising sun, bearing weapons, and endowed with four arms. (65–66)
O Lord, these gatekeepers indeed have faces resembling those of the lords of monkeys;
they wear red garments, red garlands, and are anointed with red sandalwood.
They are devoted to Brahman, bestowers of boons, heroic, and lifelong celibates from their youth.
All of them are mounted upon peacock-feathered vehicles, holding spears in their hands.
These boys named Skandas have displayed great prowess;
they wear golden garlands and possess horses equal to Uccaiḥśravas.
O God, they shone as they stood there, dressed in yellow silken garments,
possessing a luster like that of the rising sun, with eyes like the petals of a young blue lotus.
O God, those whom you see here, dressed in white garments and with white faces, are your sons named Viśākhas, the Rudras who hold spears in their hands. ||71||
Shining with their bodies like many risen moons,
wearing side-locks of hair, shaven-headed, and perched upon copper-colored cocks—
these are those youths of renowned prowess known as the Śākhas.
These who stand here like goats and rams, with the luster of *kiṃśuka* and *aśoka* flowers—
brave, noble, and possessing the lotus-like faces of children—
are equal in their retinue to you, the son of Naigameṣa. (73–74)
O God, these youths known as the Naigameṣas—
who possess the luster of dark clouds and voices resembling the rumble of dark clouds—
these Pramathas born from your hair have now appeared before you.

And these many red-clad hosts, crushers of enemy forces, are equipped with chariot-fences and armor; they are chariot-warriors who fight with diverse skills, all bearing various weapons and all being experts in battle. ||76-77||
All were skilled in action, fierce in battle, and fully armored;
they possessed the brilliance of white and black clouds and of mountains,
and like surging oceans filled with crocodiles, fish, and sea-monsters, they were formidable.
With faces like lions, tigers, and boars, and with iron clubs and thunderbolts in their hands—
these Pramathas have arrived before you solely through your grace.
Indeed, these are the heroic attendants of Skanda, the Supreme Self.
"O Lord, the army of the Pramathas—given by the thirty gods for your sport, now standing before you in its entirety—is haughty, joyful, and vast;
it is my conviction that it is capable of shattering the host of the Dānavas. ||81||
Setting aside all other duties and maintaining the highest reverence,
he immediately began to destroy [the enemy] for the ruin of the gods' foes—
[those warriors] whose splendor, like that of young suns, was equal to the radiance of the Karigiri trees and gateways.
O Lord, these leaders of the Gaṇas are indeed intent on conquering the enemy force. O Lord of the moving and the unmoving, then Andhaka, standing in battle, attains equality with you.
Surrounded by hundreds of hosts of Gaṇas, O All-pervading One, dispatch the lords of the Gaṇas.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirtieth chapter, at the commencement of the battle with Andhaka, in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Then the Blessed One beheld the leaders of the Gaṇas who had arrived.
With their own troops, they were many times arrayed, eager for battle and fully armored.
And Diṇḍi and Bhārabhūti and Somaśarman,
Karika and Meghanāda and Udaremaṇi,
Āsatti and Dhūtapāpa and Candramauli. ||2||
Ādityamāla, Vikrānta, Sukeśa, and Mahābala. ||3||
Tālaketu, Jvara, and the powerful Daṇḍapāṇi—these and other renowned leaders of the Gaṇas, both secret and manifest. ||4||
Having worshipped Mahāgaṇapati as well as Khoṭhāmudgara, the Blessed One propitiated them all again and again. ||5||
With a voice like the roar of clouds and a sound like a hundred kettledrums, he said:
"O best of beings, you together with the Dānavas ought to fight for me;
you alone, as leaders of the hosts, are sufficient to repel them."
"Therefore, you great beings, together with your hosts and followers, go forth for the sake of his destruction; I have been honored by you, O ones of great power.
Having been addressed thus by the god, they bowed their heads to Hara.
The high-souled ones departed, and the god also took his leave.
Then there arose a sound like that of the ocean being split asunder,
produced by the army of the demon Andhaka as it approached Mount Mandara.
Hearing that roar of the Dānavas, which was exceedingly distressing to the ears, [he was struck with fear].
The Pramathas roared fiercely, like clouds at the end of an eon.
Those two armies, agitated by each other's strength,
became like two great oceans tossed up at the time of universal dissolution as they clashed.
The God of gods said:
"O Brahman, offer oblations for the destruction of our enemies and for our victory;
and you too, Nandin, protect [us], surrounded by all these attendants."
"May these [beings], who reside in the sky and roar like clouds pouring rain,
afflict these enemies, the Dānavas, as they move through the very heavens.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed, the two began to carry out the word of the Blessed One:
Bṛhaspati offered oblations into the fire, and Nandin protected him;
meanwhile, Mount Mandara was held up by the great Pramathas with great effort.
He appeared as if he were fleeing, with his elephant-like mane disheveled.
Then, seeing the army of Andhaka arrogant like a lion’s strength,
it quickly shook him as he ascended, as if he were a mountain.
Then a tumultuous roar arose from the Pramathas as they warded off the Daityas in battle with trees, stones, and arrows. ||17||
But the Dānavas, though being restrained by the Pramathas who appeared victorious, then swiftly broke through the army of the Pramathas and ascended [the mountain]. || 18 ||
For the Pramathas, resolved that they must fight without attachment, cut, pierced, and struck down the enemies of the gods.
"Seize him! Release him! Stay still! What will you do while standing there? they cried.
Thus did the cries arise from the armies of the Pramathas and the Asuras.
With excellent trees from root to tip, and with mountains together with their vegetation,
the pitiless Pramathas and Asuras crushed one another.
Then, by the sons of Dākṣāyaṇī, those destroyers of Dakṣa’s sacrifice were not able to be turned away, for they were never averse to devotion. Sanatkumāra said:
Perceiving that the enemies were defeated and powerless, and that they had ascended to the peak of the moving mountain,
the God took hold of the Pramathas and restrained them all without exception.
The God of gods said:
"O leaders of the Gaṇas, let the sons of Danu ascend Mount Mandara with its beautiful caves; for the sake of sport, fight with them!
They heard the terrifying roar released by the king of beasts dwelling within many lovely groves.
The region was strewn with the flowers of trees broken by the impact of herds of elephants in rut;
the darkness within its beautiful stone chambers was dispelled by the lamps of the crest-jewels of the lords of serpents;
and the openings were visible through the lattice-work of great stones shattered by the force of the cool, pure waters of the mountain torrents. ||26||
In some places, the mass of rays from the young sun was obstructed by the tips of fresh copper-colored sprouts;
in other places, there were clearly fashioned beautiful leaf-designs upon the moon-like faces of celestial nymphs;
and in yet other places, regions of the forest were made variegated by clusters of lovely blossoms shaken by the wind.
His own body was gazed upon by a troop of monkeys seated and standing upon a surface of crystal gem-stones. ||28||
[The mountain] where the caravans of Siddhas are awakened to the pleasure of hearing the cries of the peacocks in the dwellings of the young wives of the gods;
which is delightful with the sweet warbling of ruddy geese resting in waters fragrant with the pollen of lotus petals;
and where the mineral gold is melted by the fire trickling from sun-stones heated by the rays of the sun.
In some places, the water was scattered by mountain rivers flowing forth from moonstones that had been struck by falling rays of light.

In some places, its expansive banks were adorned with heaps of pearls scattered from the frontal globes of great elephants split open by the impact of the boar, lion, and vajra, appearing like a profusion of white flowers;
while its interior was filled with the great roar of the loud, joyful laughter of the Gaṇas and Bhairavas.
Delightful with the dancing of joyful siddha-wives hidden within bowers of creepers in the dense thickets;
with intoxicated elephants roaming through many mountain fastnesses; where the waters of waterfalls were drunk by many young fawns;
filled with many rugged slopes, precipices, and groves, and abounding in various shrubs, climbing vines, and spreading trees.
In that place, the tips of every tree were variegated by the radiance of emeralds, rubies, and peaks;
its beautiful forest interiors resounded with the abundant warbling of swarms of bees and the cries of cuckoos.
There, those who had conquered death and sorrow—accomplished masters of the elixirs of yellow orpiment, collyrium, and black stone—dwelt forever in joy.
The Siddhas, always joyful and accompanied by their consorts, dwell there with beautiful necklaces like the rays of the moon.
There, the Vidyādharas, bound by passion for their beloveds, paint various flower-ornaments upon their full, high-sloping breasts using heaps of minerals in green, red, and orange hues. (35–36)

In which place the Apsarases, their slender bodies always exhausted by amorous dalliance, with their lotus-like hands resting in the grasping hands of their beloveds, joyfully enjoy the breeze that has arrived, exceedingly cooled by its intimacy with the waters of mountain cascades. (37)
The swans were awakened by the sound of anklets; the lotuses were brushed by the down of her laughing body;
its pure waters were reddened by the pollen of the lotuses; and its golden peaks were adorned with water. || 38 ||
There, sandalwood trees sprouted from the mountain peaks, and flocks of cuckoos perched upon those trees;
the sound of lordly elephants trumpeting was released by the herds, while bears and hyenas were agitated by the fear of that roar. ||39||
Its groves were inhabited by bears and hyenas; from the openings of its bower-caves issued lions;
many frontal globes of elephants had been torn open by lions; pearls and gems emerged from those frontal globes;
its back was illuminated by the rays of those jewels; and upon its back rested the foot of Śaṅkara.
The forest groves were filled with trees rising from their roots, and the paths were strewn with heaps of flowers from the thickets and creepers. || 41 ||
The path was variegated with jeweled archways, and those jeweled archways were adorned with colorful silk banners;
upon those silk banners were placed flowers, and those flowers were kissed by bees.
Its slopes were made beautiful by various minerals and it was delightful with many houses formed of flowering creepers.
Resounding with the songs of various intoxicated birds, it was inhabited by siddhas perched upon various peaks. ||43||

Then all those Daityas, desiring victory for themselves and permitted entry by the Blessed One, ascended that delightful Mandara mountain, which was inhabited by various throngs of Cāraṇas and Siddhas and had been personally occupied as a dwelling by the Three-eyed Lord. ||44||
Then, released by the Pramathas, the sons of Diti climbed [Mount Mandara],
thinking quickly that the Pramathas, being terrified, had retreated.
Thereupon, on the ridge of Mount Mandara, which was crowded with various trees, [they arrived].
The Daityas, possessing a radiance like that of the sun, stood with their shoulders bound.

That Mount Mandara, with its terrifying rocks, boulders, and trees, and its many tigers, hyenas, and elephants, was violently scattered by the great asuras—who rode upon proud horses and elephants—just as a cloud is dispersed by the winds. ||47||
In some places, those who resemble white clouds hurl rocks and, having uprooted trees, roar like thunderclouds;
though being warded off, they strike down the Pramathas, just as lions in the forests attack the leaders of deer herds. 48.
Then, surrounded by gifts of elephants, chariots, and horses, that [mountain], possessing the splendor of the agitated great ocean and protected by the arms of the sons of Diti,
shone like a forest protected by the arms of the lord of beasts.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Mandara," in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, at the commencement of the battle with Andhaka.
Sanatkumāra said: Having reached the peak of Mount Mandara, Andhaka, the lord of the Dānavas,
with palms joined in reverence, spoke this to Śukra, whose splendor was like that of Indra and the sun.
Andhaka said:
"O Blessed One, we have reached Mount Mandara with its beautiful caves,
its rocky surface occupied by the Pramathas who are terrible in appearance."
The leaders of the Gaṇas—those who move through the air, those possessed of illusory powers, and the yogins of great strength—cannot be forcibly conquered by the Dānavas. ||3||
For generally, even those who are powerful act with skillful means at the outset in their undertakings; it is only later that they act otherwise.
Therefore, being especially composed, one should rely upon such means.
Let us utterly crush the Pramathas, or do as you please.
Desiring our victory and for the sake of conquering the Dānavas,
O Lord, form the mountain-array that shatters the enemy's formations.
And who are these beings who possess bodies with the color and brilliance of ten million suns?
Standing in the midst of the hosts of the Pramathas, they look upon me repeatedly.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having heard the words of Andhaka, the preceptor of the Daityas became enraged.
He spoke to the lord of the Daityas, as if pointing out the Lord of Cows (Śiva).
Śukra said:
"This one who has eyes tawny like honey, who is three-eyed and adorned with the moon—"
This god, the wielder of the Pināka bow, is clothed in a tiger skin.
"He who has the face of a lion among monkeys, wears blue garments, and possesses four arms;
he who shines like the rising sun—this is Nandin, the leader of the Gaṇas. He whose body is tall and resembles fire, blazing like a flame—"
This is indeed Bṛhaspati, the lord of the Brahmins, possessed of vast intelligence;
and this one standing not far from the bull-bannered god, bearing a trident,
is the great Gaṇapati Andhaka, of massive body and preeminent excellence.

Mounted upon a peacock that cries out and is adorned with variegated plumage, he shines like the rising sun; he is mighty, holds a spear in his hand, is devoted to Brahman, intent on Brahman, a celibate student, and firm in his vows. (13)
This Skanda is indeed the leader of the gods in battle against the Dānavas.
He who stands upon the Tāmracūḍa [mountain], possessing the luster of the Tāmracūḍa stone,
shines while brandishing his spear like a cloud flashing with lightning.
For he, who bears the side-locks of youth, whose face resembles the full moon, is named Viśākha;
he is a youth, observing the vow of lifelong celibacy from his childhood.
Young and possessed of youthful wisdom, like a tree endowed with branches,
this son of Svāhā is indeed named Śākha, of great splendor.
He who stands here, having taken his place at his left side—
Repeatedly pointing with his index finger both at me and at you,
that powerful one, though appearing as a mere child, stands mounted upon a ram;
he is known as Naigameṣa, the son of Andhaka and Hara.
Surrounded by these four sons,
this slayer of the Asuras appeared like the Grandfather (Brahmā) himself when accompanied by the four gods;
he was the divine Lord, the great archer, preceded by the son of Nandin.
O best of gods, protected by my mantra,
I shall raise up the Daityas who have been slain by the Pramathas by the hundreds and thousands, just as a cloud revives the crops. ||22||
Sanatkumāra said:
Having addressed that lord of the Dānavas as "O Bhārgava," he then proceeded to array his army against the Dānavas by means of a mountain formation.
Having rendered his chariot, along with its pole, shafts, horses, and driver, blind,
he struck down his feet with many thousands of foot soldiers.
Within those thousands of feet of the mountain formation,
Bhārgava caused the Dānavas to construct masses of trees, crags, and boulders.
With ten crores of those high-souled Dānavas,
the Lord of Planets (Rāhu) struck the hips of those copper-eyed beings.
On the slopes variegated by the outflow of minerals,
Bhārgava likewise placed the Dānavas like blades of grass and shrubs.
With another thirty crores, he who possessed a radiance equal to the sun fashioned the peaks of the mountain-array for the enemies of the lord of the thirty gods.
Then, upon those lofty peaks, the descendant of Bhrigu pointed out the armed Dānavas, saying, "These are the precipices. (29)
Standing on the precipice, those Daityas, possessing the luster of dark rain clouds,
stood there joyfully as if discharging showers of weapons like water.
Those Daityas, who were strong and endowed with speed— the thorns of the gods—
having whirled about like hawks, hid themselves within the mountain range.
The divine descendant of Bhṛgu rendered all the Nivātakavacas, who bore various weapons, like the peaks of a mountain array;
likewise, he [confronted] Prahrāda, Saṃhrāda, Anuhrāda, and Śini.
Jambha, Kujambha, Tāra, and Maya, as well as Namuci. ||33||
He meditates upon Virocana, Bali, Bāṇa, Vāta, Kārtasvana, Kuśa, Śambhu, Aṅga, Ilvaka, and likewise Vilvaka.
Vita, Vṛtta, Tuhuṇḍa, Huṇḍa, Daṇḍa the Dānava, Añjana, Ruṣaṇa, Rāhu, Svarbhānu, Ajaka, and Gaja. ||35||
Hastin and Duryodhana, as well as Pāka and the Dānava Dhundhu—these and other powerful Daityas who were thorns in the side of the gods. ||36||
"Guard the formation! Fight! cried the lord of the asuras, who was like Himavat, the king of mountains, or the Vindhya with its wondrous caves. (37)
That mountain formation, with its trees bristling like thorns from weapons,
shone like a massed darkness or a gathering of clouds.
Seeing that mountain formation again and again, the Pramathas were filled with wonder.
Beholding the mountain-array, those stationed within the mountain-array [advanced].
Those tigers among gods could not pierce him, just as clouds cannot at the end of an eon;
and they said, "Indeed, he cannot be pierced even by the gods led by Indra."
"What can the Pramathas do, possessing such meager strength and prowess?
Śukra will bring us back to life even from death, there is no doubt.
Fight, O best of Dānavas, with fearless hearts! ||41||
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having seen the mountain-array constructed by the best of the Bhṛgus, the god Kapardin spoke thus to Bṛhaspati of great intellect: 42.
O Vācaspati, behold this mountain-array fashioned by Śukra, possessing peaks and caves like the Himavat mountain;
it encompasses the worlds along with the watery nether regions (pātāla), together with Viṣṇu and Pitāmaha. ||43||
If this mountain array is ignored, it will devour us;
neither the gods, nor the gandharvas, nor the nāgas,
nor the trees would be able to break it even if they exerted themselves, were it not for these leaders of the hosts.

O best of Brahmins, O wise one, I see no other means of breaking this mountain-array than the great Vajra-array, which pierces all arrays. Therefore, you who are the foremost among the knowers of Brahman, [employ] that which shatters the mountain-array.
"Form today the Vajra array, surrounded by ten thousand Pramathas!
Thus addressed by Śambhu, Bṛhaspati, the lord of brahmins,
then formed that new array in response with the Vajra formation.
The wise one stationed many thousands of mighty-armed and devoted leaders of the hosts in the midst of the Vajra array,
along with Skanda’s heroic attendants, who were destroyers of both gods and demons.
He fashioned for that Vajravyūha an array of a thousand joints;
that twice-born one stationed ten million of the foremost Pramatha strikers at every point where the thunderbolt-edges fell.
The divine Aṅgirasa made Kumāra, Viśākha, Śākha, and likewise Chāgamukha the buds of the Vajravyūha formation. ||52||
At the tip of the bud stands Nandin, possessing four arms and the face of the lord of monkeys; he holds a raised thunderbolt in his hand, possesses the luster of the sun, and dwells here.
[One should also worship] Kuṇḍodara, Nandiṣeṇa, Ghaṇṭākarṇa, and Mahodara.
He placed the bud of that vajra upon its rear half.
But before it stood the lord of the gaṇas, Somanandin, who has the face of a tiger;
he resembles ten thousand suns and moons and stands armed with a paṭṭiśa weapon.
The gatekeepers of the Rudras, as well as the Rudras themselves and those who are the sons of Rudra,
have been stationed here and there to protect the adamantine array (vajravyūha).
In the center of that adamantine array, however, he was established upon an excellent chariot.
The Lord Bhava, Śarva, Kapardin, Nīlalohita, remained there. ||57||
His great white banner shines forth like Indra’s standard;
it is like Mount Mandara, its peak graced by the orb of the moon. ||58||
With a hundred streams and many joints, adorned with beautiful buds,
the array of thunderbolts became like one desiring to pierce the mountain array.
Having seen that manifested array, the gods, gandharvas, and guhyakas—
"Excellent! Excellent! they cried out, their eyes wide with wonder.
Then, amidst the divisions of the army, there arose lion-like roars mingled with the sounds of kettledrums, clay drums, and conch shells.
They set forth, striking fear into the sons of Diti, resembling the roar of the agitated waters of the ocean. ||61||
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Formation of the Array," in the *Andhakamathana* section of the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having seen those two armies of the Pramathas and the Asuras thus arrayed,
the gods quickly obstructed the sky on all sides with tens of millions of celestial chariots.
The entire expanse of the sky shone, filled with splendors,
like the beautiful forest on the peak of Mount Meru being consumed by fire.
Abounding with the sound of celestial drums and crowded with hundreds of divine women,
that divine assembly shone just like the orb of the sun.
Strewn with divine flowers, perfumed with celestial fragrances,
and filled with hundreds of spectators, the surface of the sky shone like heaven itself.
Musical instruments were struck, and the celestial singers sang;
Rambhā and other divine women with beautiful side-glances also danced.
Then the two arrays of diamond-mountains, each desiring victory over the other,
clashed together with great roars like two oceans tossed by the wind.
Though addressed with "Do not hasten" by the high-souled Śukra and restrained by him,
the warriors engaged in unrestrained combat.
Then conchs and kettledrums, cymbals and cow-horns,
āḍambaras and ḍiṇḍimas, as well as maṇḍūkas and paṇavas, [resounded].
Kettledrums, war-drums, clay drums, *kiṃkharas*,
and *ānakas* were sounded intensely by the thousands on both sides of the army.
Then, having heard the sound of musical instruments from the two armies of the Pramathas and the Asuras, the hosts of gods, along with the Gandharvas and Cāraṇas, raised shouts.
At Mount Mandara, lions, tigers, and elephants roared fiercely at the sound of Bala’s musical instruments and the lion-like roar of the gods.
Their prowess was drenched by that sound of the resonance of the musical instruments.
Without breaking their own formation, the Pramathas and Asuras fought.
But at their first encounter in battle, those self-controlled warriors let out a terrible roar, like the trumpeting of elephants.
The gods and asuras, by the thousands, with weapons held in their hands,
distinguished themselves in battle, each desiring to slay the other.
Due to the excessive joy caused by the firm blows of spears, vajras, stones, trees, and arrows,
the battle of the attendant asuras increases in intensity, becoming as exceedingly terrible as the age of Kali (Tiṣya-yuga).
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
While the tumultuous conflict between the armies of the Pramathas and the Asuras was underway...
The sounds of bowstrings and terrible lion-roars are being heard. ||1||
The gods, Cāraṇas, Uragas, and Guhyakas, with their fingers interlaced, [paid homage].
The ends of their garments fluttered upward as they roared with the excitement of battle. ||2||
At the sound of that heroic roar,
the proud Pramatha demons, their valor incited by it, performed deeds that were unbearable.
Mangled by drawn swords, their chests split open by *paṭṭiśa* spears, and their vital organs cut away by arrows, the Pramatha demons fall down. (4)
In that battle between the Pramathas and the Asuras, heaps of many severed heads were seen there along with thighs.
Hundreds of chariots were seen with their wheels shattered, their banners destroyed, their fenders torn away, and their poles broken; they were deprived of horses and their charioteers slain.
Adorned with banners, armlets, armor, weapons, and standards, the preeminent elephants fall, their tusks and trunks protruding. (7)
With their limbs shattered by the strike of arrows, horses resembling the steeds of the sun—resplendent with their crests of chowries—are brought down along with their riders. (8)
With its terrified horses galloping wildly and even its dānavas fleeing with their chariots,
that army shone like a frenzied ocean with its crocodiles wandering in confusion.
With garments, parasols, crowns, jeweled earrings, necklaces, half-necklaces, armlets, rings, and the finest garlands; || 8.134.10 ||
Covered with severed hands and fallen feet, the battlefield shines like the sky filled with rising stars. 11.
Clad in garments dripping with blood and adorned with various ornaments,
the earth shone like Death itself, its limbs covered in crimson robes.
Then there flowed a terrible river, carrying blood for its water, which bore away the throngs of horses and elephants and carried them toward the abode of Yama.
It was crowded with deer, elephants, donkeys, horses, camels, and great sea-monsters;
it had flesh, fat, and liver for its mud, and hundreds of bows and banners for its trees. (14)
It was strewn with hundreds of stones whose heads were severed, with hands, beasts, faces, and serpents;
it was covered with hair like moss, and its hundreds of bowstrings formed its threads.

Indeed, it was filled with the joy of white-robed [warriors], crowded with the multitude of crowns and turbans, brimming with kettledrums as its tortoises, and resounding with excellent ornaments as its frogs. 16.
It was teeming with arrows as its fish, difficult to approach due to swords as its crocodiles, with great chariot-wheels as its large crocodiles, and churned by maces as its aquatic monsters. 17.
With its sand scattered by the breaking of necklaces and its foam produced from phlegm,
it was like a garland of red lotuses or a discarded wreath of saffron.
Like the tongue of the king of serpents, like the wondrous command of Yama—
inspiring fear in timid warriors and increasing the joy of the brave—
a river carrying waters of blood has begun to flow, streaming toward the heavenly realm. (19)
With smoke increased by the enraged lords of the Daityas and its interior set ablaze by the fire of Nandīśvara,
that army shone with a roar like the ocean, like the world at the time of universal destruction.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
While that battle between the attendants and the Asuras was increasing in intensity...
Standing upon mountain ranges and precipices, those best of Dānavas were filled with rage.
In their fury, those tireless ones rained down a shower of spears, javelins, double-edged swords,
and maces upon the army of the Pramathas, like clouds pouring forth rain.
Though struck many times by the falling rain of weapons,
they disregarded it all and set their minds solely upon battle.
For just as clouds [destroy] crops, as elephants [uproot] trees, as tigers [slay] spotted deer, and as śarabhas [overcome] elephants; ||4||
Just as thunderbolts [shatter] mountains, as messengers of Death [overcome] men, as obstacles [hinder] those seeking peace, and as lack of discipline [overcomes] protectors; 5.
Just as entities appear as entities, and faults appear as faults or otherwise,
so too did he [strike] the Nivātakavacas with showers of spears, javelins, and double-edged swords.
The heroic Pramathas struck them down by the hundreds and by the thousands.
With their chests torn open by spears and their heads split by maces,
the Dānavas fell to the earth, their limbs withered by the blows of the thunderbolt.
The exceedingly dreadful roars of those shouting warriors were heard on all sides,
like the thundering of the clouds at the time of universal dissolution.
Pierced in many places by arrows, their hips and spines were broken.
For the Asuras move upon the ground like serpents with broken backs. ||9||
Then, beholding that extreme slaughter, hundreds of heroic great asuras there turned back, their eyes bloodshot with rage.
O Vyāsa, those Pramathas were also severely pierced by them and became filled with shame,
closing their eyes like bulls when rain falls upon them.
The Pramathas endured that rain sent forth by the Dānavas;
yet even they, having waged a tumultuous battle, were then afflicted at the end. 12.
Broken and turned away, their joints and limbs shattered,
the foremost of the Pramathas were then broken within that army as it was being crushed.
Ten [others], equal to a hundred great elephants, created a mighty force;
there was the powerful Śaṅkukarṇa and the heroic Ghaṇṭākarṇa. 14.
Mahākāla, who is dark-hued, and the renowned Nandiṣeṇa;
Piṅgala, Lohitākṣa, and the powerful Somanandin. ||15||
And Vināyaka, and Nandin... ||
Chāga, Kuṇḍodara, and Skanda, who is mounted upon a magnificent peacock. ||16||
These [heroes] emerged together like water-bearing clouds, and they entered the army of the Asuras as crocodiles enter the ocean. ||17||
The Daityas were slain by Śaṅkukarṇa, torn asunder by Ghaṇṭākarṇa, struck by the arrows of Nandiṣeṇa, and driven away by Mahākāla. ||18||
With their weapons and ornaments crushed by the force of Kuṇḍodara’s mace,
they perished— stirred up by Piṅgala and torn asunder by Skanda’s spear.
With their mouths split by blows from fists, their heads struck by palm-fronds,
and being cast here and there by the force of blows from open hands.
With their weapons, garments, and armor cast off, and their hair-braids loosened, the Danavas were utterly shattered; thus, the breach of the formation occurred swiftly.
Being split apart, the mountain array appeared terrible to behold, like the great Vindhya mountain in ancient times when struck by Indra’s thunderbolt. 22.
Then, the Pramathas, appearing victorious, scattered the Daityas whose battle arrays were broken;
they fled by the hundreds like birds from ripe trees.
Then once again there occurred a fierce battle between the heroic Pramathas and the Asuras, filled with a great tumult. 24.
Furthermore, when those [armies] met in a terrible clash like that of elephants, the gods, along with the gandharvas and siddhas, rejoiced and shouted in heaven. 25.
Then, various kinds of sounds from musical instruments arose from the retinues of the Dānavas.
Terrible sounds were heard, like the roaring of thunderclouds. ||26||
And with elephants resembling the Blue Mountain (Nīlācala), and with chariots equal to the celestial palaces of the Gandharvas;
Indeed, the Daityas, fearless in battle, move about on horses whose speed is equal to that of the wind. 27.

The lords of the Gaṇas and the foremost of the Dānavas set about destroying one another with spears, javelins, double-edged swords, *bhuśuṇḍi* missiles, and arrows; with rocks and stones, discuses, tridents, and thunderbolts. (28)
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Now, Virocana, the lord of the Daityas, who was as radiant as the sun, spoke thus.
He entered the army of the Pramathas like the sun entering a mass of clouds.
Mounted upon a four-tusked elephant adorned with ivory ornaments, which resembled the peak of Mount Mandara, possessed tusks as long as plowshafts, and was exuding rutting ichor, [he advanced]. (1–2)
There, that bull among gods shone while mounted upon the neck of the elephant,
like the thousand-rayed sun blazing as it stands upon the peak of the mountain of sunrise.
With his maces and arrows, which shone like the rays of the sun, he struck down the Pramathas by the hundreds and thousands. ||4||
Just as Vainateya [Vishnu] drives away the serpents, or as a lion drives away bulls,
so did the heroic Virocana put the Pramathas to flight.
Whether moving away, coming toward him, not yet reached, already reached, or situated at a distance—
the Asura seizes hold of whichever Pramatha he beholds.
Just as deer upon seeing a lion, and as serpents upon seeing Garuḍa,
so did the Pramathas flee in fear upon seeing Virocana.
Seeing the strength of Gaṇeśvara, Vināyaka, the excellent lord of the Gaṇas and leader of the Pramatha army, quickly turned back.
Stretching out his terrible trunk like Airāvata in the east,
Virocana rushed toward Soma like a tiger toward a deer.
Seeing that elephant-faced one with sharp tusks rushing toward him,
the Dānava pierced him between the temples with a lance.
Drawing that javelin from the tip of his trunk, Vināyaka tore Virocana apart with that very same weapon hurled from his hand.
Pierced by that lance and distressed by the blow of the hand,
Virocana staggered, overwhelmed, and bled profusely.
Beholding the lord of the Dānavas, Virocana, reeling at that moment,
Vināyaka pierced him with his two tusks, which were as white as the moon.
Beholding that deed of Vaināyaka, the gods, including Śakra, let out loud cries;
a garland of flowers fell upon his head, just as the triple-pathed river [Ganges] falls upon the Lord.
Adorned with that garland of various flowers, the god then shone resplendent in battle, possessing a beauty as charming as a row of star-clusters, standing like another lofty Mount Meru. (15)
Seeing Vināyaka rending open the radiant [demon] whose blood was gushing forth, Jambha, terrified by the cloud-like [elephant], cried out and fled, saying, "Do not fear! ||16||
As Jambha approached, roaring in many ways like an immeasurable cloud in the sky,
Nandin checked him and struck him with his mace, just as the wielder of the thunderbolt, when enraged, strikes a mountain with his vajra.

From that blow of the thunderbolt, he became slack in his actions like a son of the Dānavas fallen from heaven; he fell to the ground and rose again repeatedly, like a fire in an assembly hall when sprinkled with clarified butter. ||18||

When Jambha, Vasanī, and Nibala were overcome and [the Lord] was gracious, the six Dānavas—like enraged Mlecchas—mangled that elder brother of Ṣaṇmukha with axes, spears, swords, and battle-axes. (19)
Vināyaka, having been struck by them, tore out two tusks from his own body and released him,
who was drenched in blood, just as Rāhu releases the sun after half-eating it.
Deprived of his splendor by that [curse], Virocana, though naturally charming, did not shine intensely;
he was like the full-orbed moon in the sky during the season of new clouds, when it is shrouded by clouds. ||21||
But Vināyaka, resembling the six-faced one (Kārttikeya), being himself without a leader, rendered those six Dānavas— who were like leaders—
futilely fleeing with blows from his broad teeth that were like thunderbolts, just as a lion drives away lordly elephants.

With the face of a lordly elephant, raising his trunk like an elephant of the gods filled with pride, he drove away those foremost of Dānavas, just as a proud lion cub drives away elephants. Like bulls stared down by a lion, or like men stared down by Death; ||| 23 ||
When they were gazed upon by the Leader, fear then seized the watching armies as they were being struck down. 24.
Whichever way that god looks, he is like an elephant raising its own trunk.
Then and there the Daitya army was shattered, like a flowering forest by a fierce wind. 25.

Seeing that army overwhelmed by the powerful one, this son of Bali, the most excellent among the strong, set out in battle with the intent to slay Vināyaka, like a rutting lord of elephants against another in rut. 26.
As he rushed forward like the enraged Kāla at the end of an eon, blazing with the splendor of the sun, Kuṇḍodara advanced in battle to obstruct and fight him, like one lion against another lion. (27)
Like two lion cubs filled with pride, or like two elephant calves with their trunks extended,
Kuṇḍodara and the son of Bala met, intoxicated by the passion for battle.
Drawing five hundred bows that resounded like thunderbolts, he released excellent arrows at Kuṇḍodara, roaring like a rain-cloud discharging its shafts. 29.
Then Kuṇḍodara struck all those sharp-pointed arrows of Bāṇa, which were like enraged serpents, with a mountain-peak, just as an obstacle strikes down one's desires. 8.136.30.

Seeing those arrows, struck down by the enemy of the gods and rendered fruitless as they lay upon the ground, he (Skanda) struck Kuṇḍodara with a spear, just as Guha once struck the lord of mountains, Krauñca, with his spear. 31.
From the chest of Gaṇeśvara, that spear drank the blood of Bāṇa, just as the wife of the wielder of the thunderbolt drinks the beautiful, fragrant nectar brought by Śakra. 32.
But the Yakṣa Kuṇḍodara, resembling Mount Udaradara and Mandara, was struck by the blow of the spear.
He fell down, losing his vast consciousness, like a tall tree consumed by a forest fire. ||33||
Seeing Kuṇḍodara slain, that Vināyaka, his lotus garland fallen away,
rushed toward Bāṇa, desiring to kill him, like an elephant with its trunk raised high as if holding a water-pot.
Then Bāṇa pierced that leader, who was already stretched out by arrows resembling thunderbolts shot from his face,
and having pierced him, he roared like a cloud in the sky at the end of summer.

Disregarding the falling arrows as if they were the dropping of blades of grass, the elephant-faced god shattered Bāṇa’s chariot—along with its fender, wheels, horses, and driver—with a mere glance from his eye. 36.
As Vināyaka was crushing Bāṇa’s horses like an elephant fallen to the ground, Rāhu, like a lion pouncing upon a lioness’s cub, seized him with the noose of his arms and bound him. 37.
Bound by Rāhu at many points, that leader, wearing a garland of a thousand serpents, with the tips of his trunk quivering and whirling, was like an elephant crossing the celestial river. 38.
Seeing Vināyaka, whose movements were then restrained by Rāhu’s arms, the gods dwelling in heaven—including Śakra, along with the Yakṣas and Siddhas—cried out "Alas! Alas! again and again. (39)
Then Kuṇḍodara, the best of Yakṣas, having sighed like a grain of corn watered by rain,
took up an axe and struck Rāhu between the collarbones with a clenched fist.

Struck by the blow of an axe and firmly beaten with fists by the preeminent Yakṣa, Rāhu, though possessed of terrible strength, released Vināyaka just as a man of noble birth abandons an unwholesome deed. 41.
Turning back toward him like an intoxicated elephant dwelling in a forest thicket, Gajānana—whose hands were formidable—struck Rāhu with his feet, his tusks, and his trunk. 42.
Struck by the Guide, Rāhu—enemy of the gods—abandoned his pride, arrogance, and strength;
like a lordly elephant struck down by a lion, he stood there resembling a cloud devoid of water. 43.
While Rāhu was being tormented by Kuṇḍodara with blows from his fists and Vināyaka likewise, Kujambha, Saṃhrāda, Maya, along with Tāraka, Huṇḍa, and Tuhuṇḍa, then approached him. 44.
Maya struck Kuṇḍodara with a spear, and Tāra struck him in the belly with a club;

Balasura, moreover, struck him—who resembled a hanging cloud—with a fist like a thunderbolt. And the son of Hiraṇyanetra’s younger brother struck the one of terrible strength, Vināyaka, with his palm;
and his son also, the powerful Tuhuṇḍa, having gone there, struck him out of rage.
Then Vināyaka, moving with terrible speed, seized Tuṇḍa in battle with his trunk;
having dragged him and lifted him up, he hurled that one who resembled a messenger of Yama far away.
Then that god struck Prahlāda, and Maya, whose chest was like that of a rutting elephant, [did likewise].
Having uprooted that tree of terrible sound, he roared like a cloud filled with pure water in the sky. ||48||

And Kuṇḍodara, that best of Yakṣas, having struck down Bala along with Satāra and Kujambha, stood in battle with both elephant-herd leaders, their garlands shaken off and their anger greatly aroused. (49)
Those two released a fierce shower of arrows, like two roaring clouds releasing a torrent of rain;
then again, they discharged a multitude of weapons, like the flashes of lightning and the thundering of storm-clouds.
Those powers of the Asura attendants had reached a state of supreme attachment. 8.136.50.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thereafter, there occurred once again a great conflict between the armies of the attendants and the asuras.
He appeared as wondrous as the manifestation of sea-monsters from the agitation of the ocean. ||1||
Armed with spears, swords, and bows, the Dānavas and the Pramathas shone there like clouds charged with lightning, eager for battle. ||2||
"Endure! Strike! Perish! You are already destroyed!"—such were the words repeatedly heard from those who spoke thus. (3)
With spears, tridents, and discuses; with *huṇḍa* weapons, maces, and whirling clubs; with *bhindipāla* slings, hand-held missiles, and even scattered javelins.
With axes, sharp-edged spears, lances, nooses, battle-axes, and pattisas;
with blows from trees, stones, and boulders, and even with the peaks of mountains. ||5||
With these weapons, they indeed slaughter one another:
"I am Ghaṇṭākarṇa, O Asura; I am Jambha, O Lord of the Pramathas;
I am Somanandin, O enemy of Indra; I am Kujambha, O Lord of the Gaṇas."
O Yakṣa, I am Bilvaka, a Dānava named Piṅgala.
"I am Prahlāda, I am Nandin, Śaṅkukarṇa, and indeed Bala; who are you? I am Kuṇḍodara, and I am Vṛtra, O Kuṇḍakodara! (8)
I am Nandīṣeṇa, I am Śambhu, and indeed I consist of Mahākāla;
I am Viśākha, I am Bali, I am Bāṇa, and indeed I am Guha. 9.
"I am Prahrāda, I am Śākha, I am Naigameṣa, I am Andhaka"—thus spoke the terrible ones among the Dānavas and the Pramathas. (8.137.10)
In the heat of battle, the insults of those fighting were heard due to their excess of pride, like the trumpeting of rutting elephants, like the roar of clouds at the onset of the rainy season,
like the crashing of splitting mountains, and like the tumult of oceans during their cataclysmic ebbings.
Like the speed of great winds at the end of cosmic dissolution. ||12||
A great clamor arose from them as they struck one another.
Enraged with one another, they slaughtered each other violently with weapons that resembled the staff of Brahmā and were like the staff of Yama. 13.
Then, as the weapons were being hurled, there arose a crackling sound like that of thunderbolts striking mountains or of bamboos burning.
Struck with great force by the Śaktis released by Gaṇeśvara, they fell down screaming like clouds accompanied by meteors. ||15||
With their limbs shattered by blows from tree trunks and their joints crushed by maces, the Dānavas fall upon the earth like horses whose lives have departed. 16.
With their banners and flags severed, and their axles, yokes, and poles broken,
chariots resembling celestial palaces were seen there, utterly destroyed.
With elephants, horses, and shattered chariots,
that ground became impassable, as if the Vindhya mountains had descended upon it.
There, the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Kinnaras, made the sky exceedingly resonant with the sound of their loud cries of "Excellent! (utkruṣṭa-vara-śabda).
A rain of divine flowers, most wonderful and fragrant like nectar, fell upon those who were fighting in that battle.

Thus, roaring with the deep thundering of clouds, those sons of Diti and the proud hosts of Pramathas fought one another with great ferocity, discharging showers of arrows, swords, spears, double-edged blades, and maces. ||21||
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
While the Daityas were thus being oppressed, the leaders of the hosts of the Daitya commanders—
Those of great speed exerted their force like the oceans at the ends of the eons. ||1||
Prahlāda, Anuhrāda, Saṃhrāda, Śini, and Bāṣkala;
and those four sons of Prahlāda who were of terrible prowess. (2)
Bali, Bāṇa, Vāta, Śambhu, Kārtasvana, Kubha, Karabha, Namuci, Tāra, Tāraka, and Indratāpana. ||3||
Anjana, Rūṣaṇa, Vyaṃsa, Gaviṣṭha, and Pṛthivīñjaya.
Ilvaka, Pilvaka, Dhundhu, and the Dānava Mūka. ||4||
Khaṛa, Mura, Naraka, Keśin, and Dhenuka; as well as Lamba, Pralamba, Ajara, Bhāvaya, Vyoma, and Mārdava. (5)
Vṛṣaparvan, Śatāvata, Gavākṣa, Gomukha,
as well as Saran, Nisunda, and Sunda— all possessed of great strength and prowess.
Pāka, Vipāka, Santāpa, Hastin, Duryodhana, Mohana, Mathana, Sacakra, and Cakra as well. (7)
Kālakāvadana, Kāla, Kālanemi, and Kalidruma.
Hyashīrṣa, Indraśiras, Triśiras, and Śaṅku as well. ||8||
Likewise, Gaganamūrdhan, Aviroma, Mahāmanas, Asiloman, Tuhuṇḍa, Huṇḍa, and the Dānava Vṛtra. ||9||
Daśagrīva, Bāli, Meghanīla, Prabhākara,
and he who, arrogant in his strength, seized the wheel from the chariot of the Sun.
That Vipracitti returned with his army, clad in armor;
these and other sons of Diti were like elephants in rut.
They made an effort to emerge after crushing the Pramathas in battle,
like lions for the sake of meat or like elephants for the sake of a female.
In that same manner, the Dānavas entered, desiring to slay the Pramathas.
As those enemies of the gods rushed forward, their onset was terrible,
like the fearsome torrent of the lord of rivers filled with crocodiles and sharks.
With weapons, stones, rocks, trees, and thunderbolts in their hands, they were indeed checked by the fierce Pramathas, like the currents of rivers held back by the oceans. 14.
Nandin, the lord of the hosts of Gaṇas; Mahākāya, who is full of vigor; Ghaṇṭākarṇa; Śaṅkukarṇa; Kuṇḍodara; and Mahodara. 15.
Nandisena, Somanandin, Karika, the Lord of the Ganas, Vighna, Vinayaka, and he who is the Universal Vinayaka. || 16 ||
Piṅgala, Lohita, Mayūra, and Kukkuṭa as well.
Pañcākṣa, Vīrabhadra, Viṭpati, and Pāvakārdana; ||17||
The nourishment of the Ādityas, the nourishment of Soma, another which is the nourishment of the ocean, and likewise the nourishment of the purifier (fire). ||18||
Varabarhidhvaja, Viśākha, Śākha, and the powerful Naigameṣa—all possessed of the heroism and prowess of Rudra. (19)
And those Pramathas of terrifying form who were born of Bāhuleyā—
those Dānavas rushed at them in battle like bulls against bulls.
And between them all, a tumultuous battle broke out, as fierce as that of scent-elephants against śarabhas in a forest. (21)
Like elephants by great elephants, like mountains by mountains, like oceans by oceans, and like fires by fires. ||22||
Likewise, the gods, their pride aroused and enveloped by the fire of anger,
were restrained by heroic attendants, just as obstacles are held back by those devoted to dharma.
Mountain peaks, torn apart on all sides by pickaxes,
fall by the thousands upon the earth like circling vultures.
Discuses were cut by discuses, and spears were split apart by spears.
Arrows, pierced by other arrows, fall like serpents.
With faces resembling the moon and lotus, and arms like iron clubs, the earth, strewn with them, shines as if covered with garments of tiger skins. (26)
The terrible battlefield became like a cremation forest, stained with the mire of fat, marrow, and bones, and thickly strewn with the filth of hair.
Horses, elephants, and even chariots were seen crushed here and there upon the surface of the earth by the lords of the Dānava hosts. 28.
O enemy of the king of the gods, you must now be examined in the assembly of the non-gods.
Then, as Nandin was speaking thus, Kujambha— whose prowess was equal to that of Śakra, Candra, and Vāyu—
knitted his brows into a three-pronged frown upon his forehead and spoke to Nandin.
O monkey-faced one, why do you wish to terrify me with words?
I am the grandson of Hiraṇyakaśipu, not some ordinary demon. (31)

Standing on the battlefield, I feel no fear from Yama with his staff, nor from Varuṇa with his noose, nor from Indra with his thunderbolt, nor from Kubera with his mace; I have no fear of the Daityas, nor do I flee from them.
Today here, let your face—with its tawny, rolling eyes, once beautiful but now a vessel of deformity—fall to the earth, severed by my arrows like a perfectly ripe palm fruit from its stalk. (33)
Having spoken thus, the cloud that was the king of the Dānavas covered Nandīśvara with a rain of showers of arrows,
just as a lion, letting out a mighty roar, covers a great mountain with a cloud.
Just as birds enter a tree laden with ripe fruit, or fierce serpents enter a high anthill,
so did the arrows discharged by the king of the Dānavas— with their blazing tips— penetrate Nandīśvara.

But the wielder of the thunderbolt, having warded off those floods of arrows as a mountain wards off torrents from the clouds, hurled his own thunderbolt toward Kujambha and roared loudly like a cloud in the sky. (36)

That thunderbolt, possessing a terrifying form arising from its sparks and emitting a roar like the cry of a struck beast, rushes toward the asura to slay him, just as the thunderbolt of the king of the gods rushes toward a mountain. 37.

In that manner, Kujambha struck Vajra with many sharp-toothed, well-sharpened arrows and poisoned barbed shafts from close range, just as a cloud strikes the fire of universal destruction at the end of an eon.

Struck by the force of his arrow, its excessive speed checked, its unerring velocity neutralized by the mountain and other defenses, the thunderbolt returned like that which was given back after being delivered for the purpose of causing a state of madness. (39)
Beholding the excellent Vajra obstructed and hearing the roar released by Kujambha,
Nandi, filled with rage, rushed toward that enemy like Rahu through the sky toward the moon.

Seizing the chariot by force with his hand at the tip of the pole, the protector of the Pramathas pulled it back and hurled it along with its driver and horses; having thrown it, he roared again most terribly. 41.
With its horses reeling and their bridles unfastened, its charioteer, sword, head, and rim fallen away.
Kujambha’s mount fell from the sky like a mountain whose wings have been severed by a thunderbolt.

Therefore, having descended from the chariot driven by the elephant Nandi, Prahrādi—whose spirit was undaunted and who was no longer despondent—took up his spear and stood firm like a cloud accompanied by lightning and thunder. (43)
Licking it like the tongue of a serpent, like death itself hungry and desiring to devour, and blazing like the crest of a great fire, Jambha released that [missile] at Nandin. (44)
That spear, released from the arm of Indra’s enemy, fierce and blazing like a Kṛtyā of Aṅgiras, was struck down by the fire from Nandin’s mouth and consumed like a female moth in a flame. 45.

Having burnt that spear with the fire of his mouth, the lord of monkeys, who possessed the splendor of the sun, swiftly struck him with his own thunderbolt, just as the blessed Lord Indra struck Mount Meru with his vajra. 46.
With his bones crushed by the blow of the vajra, his teeth shattered, his eyes destroyed, and his knees broken, Kujambha fell hunched upon the earth like a mountain struck by Śakra’s thunderbolt. 47.
When he was slain, the hosts of gods shouted for joy, while the enemies of the gods sank down in dejection;
and the Lord of Beings honored the God who is the Lord of Creatures, whose emblem is the moon. 48.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Battle of the Gaṇas and the Slaying of Jambha," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Having seen Kujambha slain by Nandin, the delighter of the gods...
The gods, the cāraṇas, and the great serpents raised a loud cry. ||1||
At that sound of the gods and at the destruction of Kujambha,
Jambha, the tiger among the Dānavas, summoned a great rage.
From the limbs of him who was enraged, sparks of fire flew forth on all sides,
like those from Mount Meru when struck by a thunderbolt.
Jambha, who resembled a cloud flashing with lightning and was overwhelmed by rage,
rushed toward Nandin to kill him, like a lion-king toward an elephant.
Carrying a massive iron club weighing five hundred thousand bhāras,
the Daitya rushed toward Nandin, wielding his terrible mace.
"Stay now, you of evil conduct! Having been seen by me, where will you go?
This iron club, resembling a thunderbolt, shall crush you. (6)
Having spoken thus with a terrible voice to Nandin in his presence,
Jambha hurled his iron club at him like a second Yama with his staff.
Released from his hand, that iron club— resembling a serpent freed from its slough and like the fire of cosmic destruction— advanced toward Nandin to slay him.
Nandin struck that great [mace], which resembled the serpent Vāsuki and was like the staff of Brahmā,
with his thunderbolt as forcefully as the King of the Gods.
Regarding the blow of the thunderbolt as if it were a blade of grass,
he rushed toward Nandin with his iron club, appearing as difficult to behold as Indra or Agni.
A great roar was raised by thousands of Pramathas;
hearing the roar of the gods and seeing the approaching iron club, [they were struck with fear].
Śaṅkukarṇa, rushing forward with great speed, charged toward the iron club—
that weapon resembling the serpent Karkoṭaka, which was difficult to ward off.
