Seeing Śaṅkukarṇa grasping a club by his strength, [he spoke]. ||13||
The gods rejoiced and cried out, and Śaṅkukarṇa offered hymns of praise;
then the powerful Śaṅkukarṇa again seized his iron club.
He roared, aiming at Jambha, and he who delighted in battle rushed forward.
Then that tiger among the Dānavas, eager for battle, rushed forward.
Then, likewise, in the army of Gaṇeśvara and in the army of the Dānavas, [the battle raged].
The sound of musical instruments arose, mingled with the roars of lions. ||16||

Then, in the expanse of the sky, there arose a sound resembling the roar of the agitated ocean's waters, as the denizens of heaven heard that battle between the lord of the hosts of Danavas and the Lord [Śiva]. 17.

The foremost hosts of the Pramathas along with the Nāgas and Rudras, as well as the best of the Asuras together with Andhaka, having ceased their quarreling, stood there at that time, watching the battle between the Lord of the Gaṇas and the Dānava. 18.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the exceedingly powerful [Gaṇa] rushed toward Jambha as Śaṅkukarṇa was charging against him.
Vṛtra rushed toward him to slay him, like a lion toward an elephant. ||1||
Leaving Jambha aside, Śaṅkukarṇa, the preeminent among the Gaṇas,
rushed toward Vṛtra just as a restrainer pursues one who is undisciplined.
Then Śaṅkukarṇa, the lord of the Gaṇas, struck him with an iron club,
just as Śakra strikes a great mountain with his hundred-jointed thunderbolt.
Then Vṛtra, the lord of the Daityas, struck by that iron club,
whirled about excessively like a tree driven by the wind.
Streaked with flowing blood from that excellent blow,
he shone like the Blue Mountain (Nīlācala) disgorging liquid gold.
While Vṛtra, the lord of the Daityas, reeled after being struck violently by the iron club,
the gods and Gandharvas raised a roar, honoring the Lord of the Gaṇas.
Then, after recovering after a long time, Vṛtra, the preeminent among the Dānavas,
uprooted a mountain peak and rushed at Śaṅkukarṇa;
that [peak] was covered with trees and bears, and possessed minerals, stones, and serpents.
And he hurled the peak of Mount Acala at Gaṇeśvara and let out a roar.
Nandin shattered that great mountain peak, which had been released by the arm of Vṛtra,
with his thunderbolt, as a lion strikes down an elephant.
Then those two lords of the hosts of Daityas, both skilled in hand-to-hand combat, joined together with their arms like enraged serpents, making a terrible sound.
They were like two suns roaring and like two blazing fires.
Like two thundering clouds, like two massive elephants.
Like two intoxicated tigers, like two hissing serpents,
like two roaring lions, and like two leaping bulls.
Like two great mountains in motion, like two oceans surging,
like two clouds filling the sky, and like two rivaling sea-monsters.
Thus Śaṅkukarṇa and Vṛtra, the bull among the Asuras,
both skilled in combat, engaged in battle with the desire to slay one another.
With fists like thunderbolts, with palms resembling lightning, with terrible kicks of the feet, and likewise by tossing [them] upward. (15)
By means of reproaches, as well as distractions, draggings, and thrustings away;
by fierce demonstrations of manliness, and even by making his name heard. ||16||
With the piercing of their fingernails, with throat-seizing throttles,
with lion-roars accompanied by musical instruments, and with trees, mountains, rocks, and stones—
Śaṅkukarṇa, the leader of the Gaṇas, and Vṛtra, the son of Danu [assailed him].
Then those two, seeking each other's weak points, struck one another.
By Śaṅkukarṇa, Vṛtra— like a tree with deep roots—
was suddenly uprooted by the binding of his arms and cast down upon the earth.
Then, between the army of the Lord of the Gaṇas and the army of the Dānavas, [the battle raged].
When Vṛtra had been struck down, a loud cry of "Well done!
arose. Then, having struck Vṛtra with his fist and cast him to the ground, Śaṅkukarṇa departed from the body like the swift life-force.
But Vṛtra, though possessed of great heroism, became overwhelmed by the blow of the fist;
he rose up like Indra’s banner and rushed toward the Lord of the Gaṇas.
As he was charging, Śaṅkukarṇa, the Lord of the Gaṇas, [struck him] with a tree.
He struck him with a śāla tree and said, "Come here! ||2 3 ||
The powerful Vṛtra, having approached, forcibly seized Śaṅkukarṇa by the foot as he was angrily striking a śāla tree. Having seized Śaṅkukarṇa, Vṛtra was like a serpent seizing a bird.
He whirled the helpless world about like rising delusion;
as Śaṅkukarṇa was being whirled in every direction by Vṛtra, his ornaments fell from his body by the thousands. || 25-26 ||
Seeing him being thus whirled about by Vṛtra, all the gods and the lords of the Gaṇas then cried out "Alas!
Alas! and, grasping their weapons and arrows, they fled in order to liberate him.
Seeing all those lords of the hosts approaching with sharp weapons in their hands,
Vṛtra released that elephant Śaṅkukarṇa toward them, just as Garuḍa, the king of birds, would [attack] a snake.
But the mighty leader of the hosts, Śaṅkukarṇa, having been released from Vṛtra,
turned back toward Vṛtra again, desiring to fight like a lordly elephant.
Then once more, lion-like roars and the sounds of kettledrums arose on all sides within that army.
The heart-stealing cry of "O Śaṅkukarṇa! O Śaṅkukarṇa! arose as a cry of praise for him in the battle.
Thus ends the one hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having whirled Śaṅkukarṇa around and cast him to the ground, Vṛtra crushed the army of the Pramathas like an elephant in rut crushing a forest. ||1||
Having struck Nandin, Nandiṣeṇa, and Somanandin,
and having put them to flight, he roared like a rain-cloud.
Then, as he was roaring, Rudra, the best of the lords of the Viśvedevas,
released an arrow that was like the fire of a thunderbolt and brought about the destruction of his enemy.
Released from Viṣṇu’s hand, that arrow, radiant as the rays of the sun,
pierced Vṛtra after rending him asunder, like a cloud in the sky split by a thunderbolt.
Then that Dānava raised his trunk, like an elephant raising its trunk.
In the battle, he rushed toward the Lord of the Viśvedevas like the wind rushing toward a cloud.
Nandī, possessed of a massive body, struck that Dānava with a trident; Somanandī with a thunderbolt; and Nandiṣeṇa with an axe and a palm-strike.
In the battle, the Lord of the Viśvedevas, being exceedingly enraged, pierced Vṛtra with a thousand arrows,
and again with another twenty-one.
Struck by the leaders of the monkey hosts, the mountain-like Dānava roared loudly as he was being cast down, like a tree inhabited by deities.
Then Maya, Bala, Mūka, Tāraka, Jambha, Namuci, Gaṇa, Ilvala, Bāṇa, and Bāṇa’s son stood with various excellent arrows and weapons, seeking to ward off the most heroic leader of the Gaṇas. ||9||
Adorned with beautiful necklaces of radiant gold and shimmering waist-bands, resembling the great Indra himself,
these sons of Diti— possessing forms of extreme joy yet appearing as Death itself— roam among the hosts of the Pramathas.

With their mouths torn open by maces, clubs, and arrows, and their limbs crushed like mountain peaks by thunderbolts and lightning, the lords of the Gaṇas fell distressed to the earth like mountains struck by the thunderbolt. || 11 ||
Sprinkled with droplets and drops of blood from their wounds, their white necklaces, ornaments, and garlands fallen away,
those hosts of Pramathas, their faces trembling with fear and severely tormented by their enemies, fled in all directions.
Like white, stainless clouds raised high in the sky, pouring down fresh rain, they scattered.
The sons of Diti discharged a rain of arrows, fierce with great velocity and capable of crushing [the enemy].
Then, resembling elephants, mountains, and clouds, and possessing splendor equal to blazing fire and the sun,
the chief Daityas— discharging nets of stainless, sharp arrows— struck the hosts of Pramathas.
Then, having entered the fray, the hosts advanced, spreading terror among the enemies of the gods with hundreds of mechanical devices on their hands that resembled iron clubs, arrows, and swords;
there were excellent elephants resembling mountain peaks and many preeminent horses of swift gait. || 15 ||
And terrible chariots, resembling beautiful palaces, fall shattered and burnt at the front of the battle.

(16) The sons of Danu, hundreds of them, were struck down; their mouths were firmly pierced by arrows, and they wore fine garments sprinkled with blood from their wounds. With their eyes wide open, yet their vital spirits departed, they lay prostrate. (17)
With the fallen white elephant-pearls, earrings, crowns, tiaras, gems, garlands, and garments,
the earth at the front of the battle shines like Urvaśī adorned with exquisite and beautiful ornaments.
Like the great ocean agitated at the time of the deluge, or like the vast sky [filled with clouds],
so did the army of the hosts of Asuras become, with its swift elephants, horses, and Dānavas.

Yama, Varuṇa, the Lord of Wealth, and Vāsava; Bhaga, Vasu, Sūrya, Śaśāṅka, and Māruta—these hosts of gods, their lotus-like eyes and faces blooming with joy, though arrogant in crushing the enemy ranks, stood obstructing him.
He [the Buddha] moved through a place where lordly elephants wandered like clouds and where horses galloped like the wind.
The storm at the edge of the battlefield, turbid with hundreds of thunderbolts, arrows, and lightning flashes, did not cease.
The earth shone as if covered with lotuses by the faces of the sons of Danu, which resembled the petals of a lotus and were like the sun and moon, the day-maker and the night-maker.
[The earth] was sprinkled with the blood and fat of the lords of the Ganas and Danavas who had been crushed.
The battle was extremely fierce and terrible, watched by the hosts of Garuḍas and Piśācas.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
While that battle between the hosts of the Pramathas and the Asuras was raging,
the sound of bows was heard like the roar of clouds in the rainy season,
along with the trumpeting of great elephants and the neighing of horses.
The terrible cries of the yak-tail-wielding *cāmaras* and the *rākṣasas*, who were devoted to the music of war,
caused distress to the ears like the roar of thunderbolts;
for they were heard to increase just as the interests of those who act unrighteously do.
Then the Dānava named Kārtasvana, whose voice was like the roar of clouds,
struck down the Pramathas in battle like Death himself arrived among mortals.
He was a chariot-warrior, equipped with a bow, arrows, armor, and earrings.
Like fire consuming dry grass, he dried up the pride of the host of Pramathas.
Great golden arrows released from his golden bow pierced the Pramathas without obstruction,
tearing through the battlefield.
Like locusts [devouring] fields, like wolves [attacking] men,
like birds [seizing] ripe trees, or like Garuḍa [slaying] serpents—
so did those broad arrows, released from the Kārtasvara bow, [strike].
They threw the Pramathas into confusion, as birds agitate the trees of Indra;
showers of arrows fell upon the army of the Gaṇas like [torrents] upon a mountain.
The sound of musical instruments was silenced, and they were utterly terrified by the blows of the arrows.
The army of the lord of the hosts became like a forest of bandhujīva flowers;
as the wind [scatters] clouds, as Vainateya [devours] serpents,
as a tiger [overcomes] spotted deer, and as the sun [dispels] masses of darkness.
Likewise, the enraged Kārtasvana, with his most terrible thunderbolt-like arrows,
scorched the leaders of the Gaṇas just as the fire of universal destruction consumes the worlds.
Seeing the army of the Lord of the Gaṇas burnt, devoured, and afflicted by disease,
the divine Lord of the Earth became enraged and spoke to Kārtasvana.
Then Rudra, whose prowess is fierce, stood firm within the range of his arrow's flight.
Enraged, he drew an arrow from his quiver at the lord of the Dānavas.
Your wealth, strength, valor, and majesty are supreme, O son of Kārta-vīrya;
why do you slay these weak ones, the lords of the hosts of Dānavas?
Come, if you possess the power or if you have any strength!
"O giver of honor, create a crush with me; behold my strength!
O Daitya, today I shall strike down your head—adorned with earrings and decorated with sprout-like fangs—just as the wind blows a fruit from a palm tree. (16–17)
"Even though the Dānavas protect you in this pitch-dark battle today,
nevertheless, O disgrace of the Asuras, I shall take away your life!"—
thus spoke the roaring Dānava to the bellowing lord of the Vitah.
He discharged an arrow and roared like a rain-cloud;
that blazing arrow, like a fire sprinkled with clarified butter and resembling the sun in its heat, rushed toward the Lord of the Demons.
There, by the radiance of that bird, the sun became lusterless;
by the sound of its golden wings, birds fell to the earth. That arrow, joined with the radiance of the bird, was like the fire of universal destruction.
He was submerged in the bracelet of the village headman like a wrongdoer in hell. || 22 ||
Then, having extracted that very arrow sent by the Dānava,
the Lord of Trees (Viṭpati) hurled it at Kārtasvana and let out a roar.
That arrow, released by the Lord of Trees, brought about the destruction of the Dānava.
By means of ten arrows, he struck off the heads of the Dānava’s charioteer from his body.
When the charioteer was slain, his horses— fickle and dappled— became bewildered in the battle and, seizing the chariot, fled like hawks after meat.
"Go toward the chariot of gold! Why do you sit idle?
Seize it!"—such was the great roar of the lords of the Dānavas.
That supreme chariot shone as it circled upon the vast plateau of Mount Mandara.
Like the sun with its seven horses, that excellent chariot revolves around Mount Meru. ||27||

Then, leaping down from that excellent chariot drawn by swift horses, Kārtasvana, bow in hand, rushed toward the lord of the Viśas. Thereupon, a roar of "Excellent! Excellent! arose from the two armies.
When Kārtavīrya desired to fight again with the Lord of the Viśas (Viṣṇu). || 29 ||
Like a cloud drenching a mountain with torrents of rain, that Dānava covered the lord of the Viṭpas with many sharp arrows resembling thunderbolts;
he was overwhelmed by the floods of Kārta-svana’s shafts, just as the ocean is by masses of clouds.
Even while being filled [with arrows], Viṭpati did not experience any distress at all.
Then that powerful one, drawing his bow with force as far as his ear,
cut each of the Daitya lord’s arrows into two, and likewise some into three.
Having struck down those arrows with feathered shafts that consume life-breath,
he pierced Kārtavīrya with a thousand and let out a roar.
With those arrows whose tips were visible from behind,
the Dānava shone like a mountain with excellent serpents emerging from its crevices.
Then the enraged and powerful Rudra cut asunder his bow, sword, and five quivers, and he tormented him.

Then the Lord of the People discharged an arrow—equal to Indra’s thunderbolt, like an enraged lord of serpents hissing, and moving straight toward the destroyer of Nandana, who was exulting in his noble strength. (36)
That king of arrows, dispatched by the boon-granting Rudra, spreading clouds of smoke upon the field of battle,
forcibly struck off the head of the Asura in combat, just as a sage of noble intellect plucks a lotus.
Then a roar was raised by the gods, the best of sages, and the Pramathas with terrifying sounds;
for they beheld his enemy’s face in battle, which had been deprived of its power by that subduer of the submarine fire.

That lord of the Viṭpas, the commander of the Pramatha host, skilled in the arts of war and the subduer of the lion-like enemies of the gods, was approached by the Lord of Beings (Śiva) and honored by him for a long time. (39)
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Having slain the enemy Kārtasvana with a golden arrow, [the Lord...]
The Lord of the People (Viṣṇu) consumed the Daityas like fire consumes moths.
That god, with his drawn bow and beautiful golden earrings,
roared while discharging arrows at the Dānavas, as the sun radiates its rays.
Those arrows, with shafts made of gold and feathers of Garuda’s plumage,
fell upon the Danavas like calamities sent by fate.
With their faces severed, their hands severed, and their feet, bellies, and thighs mangled,
hundreds of Dānavas fell upon the earth like mountains.
Some were struck on their backs, some were torn on their sides,
others were pierced in their eyes, and still others wandered about like the blind.
Like a tiger among deer or Garuḍa among serpents, [he pursued them].
Just as one who is ungrateful [destroys] good deeds, or as the sun [dispels] the darkness,
so did the divine Viṭpati, the consumer of oblations, annihilate those Asuras with sharp-pointed arrows whose tips were like the fire of a thunderbolt.
Deprived of their chariots, with their elephants struck down and their horses afflicted by arrows,
the Dānavas fled in terror, driven by the arrows of the Lord of the People.
Then, seeing the army of the asuras— with its weapons cast aside and its splendor destroyed—
broken in battle by the Lord of the Demons like a forest by an elephant;
those various among the followers of the gods who were there, renowned and fierce in their strength, [were overcome].
They were pursued by the lord of the people, like other deer by a lion.
Prahlāda, Anuhrāda, Saṃhrāda, Śini, and Bāṣkala; Jambha, Virocana, Bāṇa, and that Dānava Bali;
Ajaka, Namuci, Vyaṃsa, Ilvaka, and likewise Vilvaka.
Vipracitti, Stuṇḍa, Huṇḍa, and the Dānava Vakra;
Maya, Tāra, Tārakākṣa, Vidyunmālī, and Prabhañjana; Ariṣṭa, Riṣṭa, Añjana, Rūśabha, and Kubha. || 12–13 ||
Kāla, Kālanemi, and likewise Kālakavadana;
Saṃpāti, Ilvala, Bala, and Naraka as well;
and the two sons of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, the Dānavas Dhundhu and Mūka.
Hastivipāka, Pāka, Vikarṇa, and Śambhu— these four,
enraged and roaring like lions, rushed toward Viṭpati with many uplifted weapons that blazed like falling meteors. || 15-16 ||
With spears, stones, and arrows that sounded like thunderbolts, they struck him with terrifying roars, like clouds striking a mountain;
just as clouds driven by the wind discharge a rain of water.
In that same manner, those Dānavas released a shower of arrows upon the god.
The Lord of the enemies, the crusher of enemy hosts, swiftly cut down that hostile shower of weapons, just as one might dispel a quarrel with affection.
Then those sons of Danu, stationed in the sky toward the lord of trees,
let loose a rain of words like clouds thundering;
while others, situated on the peak of Mount Mandara, remained there like garlands of mandāra flowers.
They released *sāla*, *sarala*, and *devadāru* trees upon the Lord of the People.
Severely oppressed by the Dānavas stationed in the sky and on the earth,
the Lord of the Viśvedevas turned away, like a fire doused with water.
Seeing the Lord of the Viśvedevas turned away and covered by the mountain-like Dānavas, [he spoke].
Those renowned lords of the Gaṇas who possess terrible strength cannot endure this:
Somanandin, Nandin, and the attendant Nandiṣeṇa;
the radiant Vīrabhadra and Sūryāpyāyana as well. ||24||
He has five eyes, is a guardian of wrath, possesses three eyes, and has tawny-colored gaze;
he is a Rākṣasa, is tawny-hued, and roars while dwelling in the cremation ground.
Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Śaṅkukarṇa, and the powerful Kuṇḍodara; Airāvatamukha, Annapāla, and Kapāladhṛk;
Pralamba, Pīvarakara, and Vināyaka himself. || 26 ||
These and other leaders of the hosts, numbering in the hundreds and proclaimed by their troops, entered to burn the Dānavas as fires enter dry trees. || 27 ||
All those lords of the Gaṇas, surrounding Viṭpati like young lordly elephants trumpeting, advanced with battle-minds, tridents, discuses, arrows, and *bhuśuṇḍi* weapons in their hands. ||28||
Then, between those various warriors who were exultant in battle, there ensued a close-quarters combat,
like that of great elephants intoxicated with rut and accustomed to living together in the forests.
Beholding that chief battle of the Dānavas along with their lords of the hosts, those dwellers of heaven moved through the sky in divine celestial chariots,
uttering lion-roars and striking the palms of their hands.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-third chapter, "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Those Pramathas and Asuras were filled with great fury and were arrogant.
They fought a close-quarter battle, each having committed offenses against the other. Kālanemi, who was like Death itself, engaged Viśākha in combat with Kumāra, whose hand brandished a spear.
And he who, arrogant in his strength, had seized the wheel from the chariot of the Sun—that Vipracitti, eager for battle, became entangled with Śākha. 3.
Naigameṣa fought Hayagrīva, and the son of Agni fought Sugrīva, the lord of the Dānavas, just as Madhunihā fought Madhu.
Jambha fought with Nandin, and Tuhuṇḍa with Somanandin.
The Dānava Huṇḍa fought against the heroic Vināyaka. ||5||
Mahākāya was with Kāla,
Namuci with Ghana, Ilvaka with the two Piṅgala Gaṇeśas, and Pilvaka with Śaṅkukarṇa; Hrāda was with Anuhrāda, and Viṭpati likewise.
Rudra, who nourishes the sun, was joined with Saṃhrāda;
and Kuṇḍodara, the lord of Yakṣas, along with his attendant Ghaṇṭākarṇa,
were engaged in combat with Bala and Ilvala, like two elephants against two lions.
The Dānava, the father of Bali, was joined by Pañcākṣa along with Bali, and by Rudra, who possesses the splendor of the sun,
as well as by Vīrabhadra.
Sumukha rushed against Tāra along with Maya, while Durmukha assailed Mayūra;
Vajraroman encountered Kukkuṭa, and Mura approached Śeṣa.
Indeed, all the remaining leaders of the hosts likewise engaged with their respective remaining Daityas.
Elephants locked together in combat were like lions in a fight;
there arose a "taṭataṭa" clattering sound from weapons being struck down, like that of bamboos burning in a secluded place by fire.
"Do not flee! Run! Stay! and "Look! Look!"—thus shouting, the hosts of Gaṇas and Dānavas, locked in combat, struck one another;
their limbs were smeared with fat and marrow, and their faces and hands were severed and mangled.
The Dānavas and Pramathas rushed forward, their weapons unceasing, with their faces, thighs, feet, hands, teeth, and even their eyes [mangled];
they were covered with scattered necklaces, armlets, garlands, garments, and ornaments. || 14–15 ||
With the blankets that were the housings of the lordly elephants and with their weapons,
that battlefield shone like the sky with stars and planets;
it was variegated with drops of blood produced from the tips of claws and teeth.
With her limbs smeared with red sandalwood paste, the ground shone like a woman;
having discharged that arrow, radiant as the sun, at Vināyaka, Tuhuṇḍa laughed aloud, further increasing his wrath. || 17-18 ||
As he was laughing, Vināyaka cut his face— adorned with large earrings— with a sharp-edged sword.
Seeing Tuhuṇḍa slain, Huṇḍa was distressed by the slaughter of his brother.
He hurled his spear at the mouth of the Naga, as Śakra hurls the thunderbolt at a mountain.
That spear of Vināyaka, studded with hundreds of gems, fell upon the jewel;
resembling a blazing crest of fire, it drank the blood from his chest.
Clinging to the lap of Vināyaka, that spear shone forth like a streak of gold upon a sapphire gem. || 22 ||
Drawing forth the Huṇḍa-shakti, which was like a ray of the sun, from his lotus-like hand,
the Lord suddenly struck Huṇḍa with it, just as the younger brother [Indra] struck Mount Krauñca.
Seeing that Tuhuṇḍa and Huṇḍa had been slain by Vināyaka, the subduer of enemies—
The entire force of the leaders of the Gaṇas became like the intoxicated Gaṅgā.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fourth chapter, "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
When Huṇḍa and Tuhuṇḍa had been slain by Vināyaka,
that battle between the lords of the Gaṇas and the Asuras appeared utterly chaotic.
Roaring like clouds swollen with water at the onset of the rainy season,
they rushed at one another with great haste while fighting;
their limbs were stained crimson by streams of blood, and their lips were bitten in fury.

They struck one another with spears, javelins, double-edged swords, and battle-axes. Amidst the whizzing of hurled javelins, the falling of swords, the shouting of names, and the twanging of bows, [the battle raged].
Hearing sounds that caused distress to his ears, Jambha, the best among the powerful and indignant at the slaughter of his brother, entered the army of the Pramathas.
Piercing the Lord of the Gaṇas, who was preceded by Vyāghra, with his trident, Jambha—
Having slain the buffalo, he roared like a forest-lord in the woods.
As he was roaring, the first of the demons,
Maga, struck him on the head with a spear and then fled, leaving the remaining Daityas behind.
Then those renowned leaders of the Gaṇas, famous for their prowess, glory, and learning,
advanced against the Asuras in battle like śarabhas against elephants. Thereupon, a great clash occurred between the lords of the Asura hosts.
Like a collision of thunderbolts against the golden mountains,
Virocana and Andhaka, both indomitable and highly enraged,
rained down showers of arrows like two clouds pouring down torrents of water.

Afflicted by the shower of excellent arrows, those two Daityas, who were discharging volleys of shafts, were turned away from the front of the battle by Svayaṃprabha. With numerous arrows released from his bow-mechanism, Svayaṃprabha [assailed] the ocean-like army of the Dānavas.
Like the sun with its blazing orb at the end of the world, he dried up the ocean.
Then Andhaka, the charioteer of the world of the Dānavas, with rolling eyes, spoke to his own charioteer:
"O charioteer, take me toward Śukra; he is our constant remover of suffering and our preceptor."

Saying "So be it," he brought that chariot— drawn by excellent horses and resounding like a rain cloud— to the place where Śukra, the best of planets and a twice-born one, was stationed with the hosts of Dānavas.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having withdrawn from the battle, Andhaka, the best of the Asuras, [departed].
Approaching Śukra with his face bowed, he said this:
"O Blessed One, relying upon you, we always consider the gods along with their followers to be equal to blades of grass; I speak the truth."
Like elephants before lions or serpents before Garuḍas,
the gods are always afraid of us through your grace. Protected by you, we shall withstand the formidable array of the hosts of gods.
The Daityas entered [the lake] fearlessly, like those tormented by the heat of summer entering a pool.
Having become your refuge and remaining as motionless as stones,
we shall slay the lord of the Brahmins and the lord of the Indras in battle without hesitation.
And because of our state of distress, we— along with our wives and sons— serve your feet, which grant us happiness, day and night.
Always protect us, who have come to you for refuge.
In times of danger, he constantly sought refuge with the gods like a second Nārāyaṇa.
Behold Huṇḍa and Tuhuṇḍa, Kujambha and Jambha,
as well as Pāka, Kārtasvana, and the great Asura Vipāka.
And him, the hero Indradamana, the slayer of heroic immortals,
who was assailed by the Pramathas of terrifying prowess— those who had overcome the pain of death and other such afflictions.
These men, slaughtered and fallen like sandalwood trees by lions—
having formerly drunk the smoke of grain-chaff for a thousand autumns and thereby obtained from Hara the boon of knowledge— the time for that [knowledge] has now arrived.
Now let all the Pramathas and all the worlds behold with wide-open eyes that fruit of your knowledge as you bring the Dānavas back to life. ||11||
Seeing the Dānavas restored to life by you in battle,
all the Dānavas, casting aside the fear of death, will fight with the Pramathas.
Indeed, that knowledge was [obtained] by you, who were seeking the welfare of the Dānavas.
"Having propitiated the God, she has attained that [power]; show it to me, salutations to you!
Hearing these words of Andhaka, the sage Bhārgava remained firm in his resolve. (14)
Then, with a slight smile, he said to the lord of the Dānavas:
"O lord of the Dānavas, that which has been uttered by you is indeed true."
Indeed, this acquisition of knowledge for the sake of the Dānavas was accomplished by me after drinking, for a thousand years, the most unbearable smoke of grain-particles. (16)
This lore, which brings happiness to my kinsmen, has been obtained by me;
by means of this lore, I shall [resurrect] these Daityas who have been slain by their enemies.

"I shall raise up the crops that have withered, just as a cloud revives them; I shall make you see the Dānavas free from wounds, free from disease, and restored to health, as if they had risen again after sleep.
O Lord of the Dānavas, you shall behold this in this very moment. (18)
Seeing the Dānavas who had risen up slain in battle by the lords of the Gaṇas.
"Out of both wonder and fear, the lords of the hosts will flee.
Having spoken thus to the lord of the Dānavas, that descendant of Bhṛgu [then departed].
The wise one caused the Vidyā to revolve, aiming it at each Daitya individually;
and by that Vidyā being thus revolved there by the Brāhmaṇa, indeed—
The Dānavas, who had been sleeping, rose up like those awakened from sleep upon their beds;
they arose like the meanings of the Vedas when mastered through study, or like clouds at the appointed time.
Just as comets meet their destruction at the appointed time,
so too were those Daityas utterly destroyed by Śukra along with the Pramathas.
When they were raised up, those ancient Dānavas shone as if they were restored to their former health; seeing them thus revived by Śukra, the lords of the Gaṇas [were amazed]. (24)
"This is a marvel, O lords of gods," they said to one another;
and seeing those great asuras, Tuhaṇḍa and the others, restored to life,
the former gods roared like clouds filled with water.
Seeing those thousands who had risen up, others with axes, thunderbolts,
lightning, and spears in their hands rushed toward the army of Śiva’s servants, which resembled a surging great ocean;
there, once again, occurred a meeting between the hosts of Gaṇas and the Asuras, accompanied by an exceedingly terrifying roar.
Like the surging of oceans driven by the winds at the end of an eon. ||27||
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Revival of the Daityas in the Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
When the Daityas had been raised up by Bhārgava of fierce deeds, [the battle resumed].
The gods, along with the gandharvas, and the dānavas together with the Andhakas, raised a roar.
Then, mingled with the sound of conchs, there arose the blaring of mādruka drums and kettledrums, as well as lion-like roars accompanied by the sounds of chariots and elephants.
Huṇḍa, Tuhuṇḍa, Jambha, Kujambha, and the great asura Śaila fought against the enemies of the gods with mountain peaks, spears, and blows from rocks.
So too did Pāka, Indradamana, Kārtasvana, and Bali.
Desiring to retaliate against their enmity, they crushed the army of the Pramathas.
Having warded off their assault, the proud Pramathas,
all bearing rocks and trees in their hands, rushed toward the Dānavas.
In that terrifying battle, the lords of the Gaṇas among the gods were heard making the sounds of their bows and the fearsome clatter of their chariots;
some were intent on conquering the Pramathas, while others were engaged against the Dānavas.
They raised a terrible clamor and likewise winged cries in the sky;
the sound of the shouting and rushing forces became like the roar of oceans at the time of universal dissolution.
Intoxicated by the extraordinary nature of the battle, the Siddhas, Gandharvas,
and Cāraṇas raised a great clamor and showered down heaps of various flowers;
those diverse blossoms, as they fell, shone with splendor.
The stars, released by the Siddhas and Cāraṇas at the end of their course,
shone forth; the musical instruments of the gods and Gandharvas resounded manifoldly, and the cries of those intent on battle ceased again and again.
But having remembered his defeat in battle by Vināyaka, Jambha,
filled with rage, rushed toward him like one elephant charging another.
Seeing the Dānava Jambha attacking him in the fray, [he stood firm].
Like an enraged lion against an elephant, that Vināyaka blocked his path.
Raising his trunk, which resembled the trunk of Airāvata, that Vināyaka, whose face was like that of an elephant,
struck the Dānava in battle.
Then Jambha, the elephant among Dānavas, [struck him] between the two frontal globes (kumbhas).
He pierced it with the tip of his excellent arrow, just as a Siddha pierces the solar orb.
That arrow indeed sank between his two frontal globes,
like a lightning-charged cloud between the two peaks of the lord of mountains.
His mind incensed by that arrow, he shook off [the foe] along with his head and hand.
Bending down the great Daitya with the tip of his hand and striking him, he roared.
But Jambha, quivering as he was struck by Vināyaka’s hand,
became enraged and assailed Vināyaka with fierce arrows,
like locusts upon a field or bees upon a tree. || 18 ||
Then those Jambheṣas entered the god Vināyaka.
With their faces torn open by tridents, those arrows, dripping with blood,
shone upon the leader like serpents coiled around Mount Meru.
His body deeply pierced by Jambha’s arrows, his eyes crimson with blood flowing from his temples,
the god shook the tips of his hands and his head and rushed toward Jambha like one parched for water.
Having struck him repeatedly and firmly with the tip of his own firm hand and having roared again and again, he—
Seizing the chariot, the powerful one hurled it in that battle along with its horses, banner, weapons, and wheels.
With its flags and banners shattered and blown away, its thousands of swords, spears, double-edged blades, and arrows fallen,
the chariot of the joy of the Asuras fell like the intense desire of a man destitute of wealth.
But Prahrādi, whose splendor was like that of Indra’s rain-cloud, abandoned the falling chariot.
Standing in the sky, the wielder of the spear shone just like the wielder of the spear standing in the sky.
The son of the Asura king, his power fully aroused, hurled at Vināyaka that spear, which was adorned with a bell, bright as gold, and blazing like a streak of fire.
Falling from the sky, that weapon-woman, like a female serpent with a flaming face, [descended].
Struck by the lord of the Viśvedevas with an arrow, the spear fell like a preeminent power when its personified essence has been destroyed.
While that sacrifice of battle was thus proceeding— a source of wonder to the Pramathas and Asuras—
the son of Śilāda, indignant at witnessing the deeds of Bhārgava, approached Maheśa.
Having cried out "Victory!", Nandin spoke to the fierce Jayayoni, who was as radiant as gold:

"O Lord, that feat of war which is difficult even for the lords of the Gaṇas, let alone for the gods including Indra, has today been rendered futile by Bhārgava; for he does not restore the lords of the Dānavas to life."
For these leaders of the Dānava hosts have today returned once more from the abode of Yama.
Charging about and putting the Pramathas to flight like elephants in battle, these proud Śarabhas roam;
for if this one always revives the foremost Daityas once they have been struck down,
O Maheśa, how indeed can there be victory for the lords of the Gaṇas, and whence can there be peace?
Moreover, he stands in a crooked position; O bull-vehicled Śukra, he is not to be slain as he does not fight. ||31||
By your grace, there shall be no destruction for you, and you bring favor even to him who has struck [us].
O Īśāna, let it be as you deem fit that he be slain, so that your victory in battle may be eternal.
Act accordingly, O Buddha of supreme intellect; O Maheśāna, there is none equal to you in wisdom.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by Nandīśvara, the lord of the Pramathas, the God of gods, the Lord,
then spoke with a smile to Nandin, the leader of all the lords of the Gaṇas.

"Nandin, proceed with extreme speed; having torn him from the midst of the sons of Diti—the kinsmen of the lords of the twice-born—bring him here, just as a wealthy man brings a sacrificial offering. (34)

Thus addressed by the bull-bannered Lord, he whose banner is the bull, that lion-like roar of virtue, swiftly plunged into the army and went to where the lamp of the Bhārgava lineage was located. (35)
While he was being guarded by those sons of Diti, who held nooses, swords, trees, stones, and spears in their hands,
the bull-king Nandin agitated the Daityas and carried off Śukra, just as a śarabha seizes an elephant.
With his garments slipping, his ornaments fallen, and his hair disheveled, he was seized by the enemy.

As if seeking to liberate [him], the enemies of the gods rushed forward, uttering lion-like roars. Like fierce clouds, those lords of the Dānavas rained down upon Nandīśvara a shower of thunderbolts, spears, arrows, axes, discuses, clubs, stones, and tremors. || 37-38 ||

Having reached Bhārgava, Nandīśvara—the foremost of the leaders of the Gaṇas—burned hundreds of weapons with the fire from his mouth; then, seizing Śukra by the hand, he approached the leader of the Dānava hosts.
Thereupon, a most terrifying downpour of released missiles and weapons occurred between them.
"Kill! and "Seize!"—such was the great battle of the disputants, which delighted the mind of the God.
In that interval, Nandīśvara, his eyes pale with rage, approached the side of Bhava and quickly reported to the Lord: "O Blessed One, this is that Śukra. || 8.147.40-41 ||
And that God of gods took the semen, just as an offering is accepted when presented by one who is pure;
the protector of beings swallowed the semen situated in his mouth without saying anything at all. (42)
Then, once again, the lords of the Gaṇas slaughtered that army of Dānavas and Daityas.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Battle of the Gaṇas" and "The Abduction of Bhārgava," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, like serpents that have swallowed the semen of their own progenitor,
all the Dānavas became inactive like the poor;
they were like souls without bodies, or like Garuḍas deprived of their wings.
Like elephants deprived of their trunks, like bulls without horns,
like great serpents rendered venomless, like Brahmins devoid of sacred knowledge,
like oceans that have run dry, and like winds that have lost their force. || 2-3 ||
Like clouds that are silent, like fire without flames, like days whose festivities have passed, and like trees devoid of flowers. ||4||
Like deer terrified by a lion, like wingless birds,
like planets whose luster has faded, or like crocodiles dragged from the water—
such was the state [of the gods] when Śukra was carried off by Nandin and swallowed by Kapardin.
The heroic Dānavas were born, possessing meager honor and prowess.
Having fallen into extreme despondency, that Dānava, the incendiary of battle for the Dānavas,
standing in the midst of the fray, spoke with a voice like the roar of clouds.
"By Nandin, the best among those who know the right course of action, having displayed his prowess while leading Śukra away,
the lives of all have undoubtedly been taken today.
Who, moreover, will restore to life the Daityas slain by the Pramathas?"
"Except for that descendant of Bhṛgu, Śukra, who else will sustain us? Since the divine Śukra has been carried away,
our fortitude, valor, splendor, essence, heroism, strength, and resolve—
all have been seized by our enemies."
"Even though the Lord has been carried off by the descendant of Bhṛgu, my mind is also distressed;
yet, even if assailed by the Pramathas, I shall not abandon the battle.
Steady yourselves, do not fear, and fight with the enemies!"
I shall destroy all the Pramathas along with Nandin;
today, having rendered them helpless and having slain even the gods,
I will liberate Bhārgava like Hari from his cage.
"And even if that yogi, by means of his yoga, were himself a lord capable of emerging from his bodies, he would still be protected by us remaining here.
Having heard these words of Andhaka, the Dānavas roared like clouds.
Having resolved that they must die, the Pramathas began to crush them.
There, with floods of spears, swords, and thunderbolts, and with axes, sharp-edged stones, and boulders,
they hacked one another and wrought a great slaughter.
A most terrible sound arose from the drawing of bows, the discharge of feathered arrows, and the falling of swords.
Their banners and flags were broken, their weapons exhausted;
they were variegated with streams of blood and blossomed with wounds;
they were parched with thirst and weary, their horses and elephants having been slain.
Their forces were like the ocean-girt earth, extending everywhere on all sides.
Then once more, by that lordly elephant— roaring, possessing four tusks,
resembling a mountain of collyrium, with the luster of a black antelope,
equipped with quivers and banners, and goaded by the hook— [the chariot was struck].
Jambha, the tiger among Dānavas, rushed toward Nandin.
Seated upon the shoulder of his elephant, the Daitya Jambha, bearing a lance,
shone like a cloud with a flight of cranes resting upon the peak of a black mountain.
With his trunk, eyes, and ears stiffened, and his great tusks extended,
the great elephant, urged on by the lord of the Dānavas,
rushed forward with a speed like that of the incomparable wind at the end of an eon.
The speed of that elephant as it ran was likewise incomparable;
the horses, the elephants, and the Pramatha demons fled from its path, just as men flee from Death. || 24-25 ||
That powerful Vināyaka, exerting his prowess, restrained that mad elephant as it rushed forward like a thundering cloud. ||26||
That best of gods, the tusked one, struck that mountain-like elephant with the tip of his trunk extended forward.
Thus was the leader of all elephants assailed by the Leader.
Driven by that terrible pain, he became insensible for a moment. ||28||
Then, having rested his horse and summoned his own strength, the elephant,
trumpeting loudly, struck Vināyaka on the chest with his trunk,
which was like a peak of the Vindhya mountains. Struck by that elephant, he—
The Great Being, the Guide, did not move even a single step from his place. || 8.148.3 ||
Seizing that elephant of the Dānavas by the trunk with his own trunk,
Vināyaka, who possesses the stature of a great mountain, hurled him down and cast him to the ground;
he was felled like a lion struck down by another lion in the midst of the forest.
The serpent, quivering, hissed like a cloud driven by the wind. ||3.2||

As that best of Dānavas was releasing his feet from the neck of the elephant, the elephant-riding [Arjuna] quickly struck the elephant, which was vomiting blood, with a lance— just as the sun pierces a cloud with its rays. ||33||
Then Vināyaka struck him with that very same lance.
Struck by that excellent blow from the elephant-faced one, the Dānava Jambha bled profusely,
like a mountain discharging waterfalls.
Furthermore, desiring to slay him, the valiant one seized his sword; as he raised the blade and roared, intent on cutting off Jambha’s neck, [the Lord acted].
Kujambha cut that sword as Garuḍa cuts a serpent;
then, with a well-drawn blood-drinking arrow,
Kujambha struck him on the arm, just as Indra strikes a mountain with his thunderbolt.
Struck forcefully by him, he reeled like a *sāla* tree.
The god, with his hand raised high, rushed toward that Dānava as a lion rushes toward an elephant with its mane bristling. (39)
Vināyaka, arrogant with power, appeared like Airāvata;
but as he rushed forward, desiring to slay Kujambha,
Vyaṃsa checked him with his shoulder and cast him down to the ground.
Having struck Vyaṃsa with his shoulder, the mighty Nāgavaktra reached the presence of Kujambha like a śarabha reaching a lion.
Kujambha, however, pierced his raised arm with an arrow. || 41-42 ||
He struck him on the head with a mace and on the chest with a club;
smeared with blood from those three blows, Vināyaka shone like an elephant with its temples split by three [goads], possessing the strength of ten thousand times ten thousand serpents. ||43||
Having seized Kujambha on the earth, the immensely powerful Vināyaka hurled him away, just as a man might throw a sacrificial offering of beings.
When Kujambha, who resembled Mount Mandara, was cast forth by the arms of Vināyaka, [he fell].
All the Dānavas became enraged and showed no mercy toward Vināyaka. ||45||
Though pierced by hundreds of weapons and struck by the arms of the Dānavas,
the god moved among the Daityas like a lion among deer;
he did so with his tusks, his feet, and his extended trunk.
Enraged, he crushed the Dānavas as an elephant crushes reeds.
Then the Gaṇeśas, seeing Vināyaka wounded by hundreds of weapons by the Dānavas, seized their own weapons;
possessing the prowess of elephants and lions, they let out loud roars and rushed forward by the hundreds.
Then once again there occurred a great battle, terrifying with thousands of weapons, unbearable due to the falling of arrows, swords, spears, and double-edged blades;
it was the destruction of the life-force of the hosts of Asuras, wherein horses and elephants were slain.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
Having been swallowed by that bearer of the lunar form,
what did the descendant of Bhṛgu do while remaining within the stomach of that God of gods?
And how was it that the twice-born one, the best of ascetics and a yogi of great penance,
did not depart from the body of the god by the power of yoga?
And at that time, Andhaka, the foremost of the Asuras, was without Bhārgava.
"How did he, while being pursued by the lords of the Gaṇas, manage to take his stand?
O best among those who know the Vedas in their entirety, tell me all of this in its full detail; for I am never satiated as I listen to the deeds of the Lord."
Sūta said: Then, as Vyāsa was thus questioning him, that best of sages related the deeds of Śukra performed by Sanatkumāra.
Sanatkumāra said:
When Bhārgava had been swallowed by that Bhūtamātṛ, the kinsman of the gods,
Andhaka became lusterless, like the sun obscured by a cloud.
Seeing his own army being repeatedly crushed by the Pramathas,
Andhaka himself mounted his chariot and rushed toward the Gaṇas;
with those thunderbolt-like strikes of arrows, they were like the earth struck by bolts of lightning.
The Pramathas fell elsewhere like waterless clouds;
pierced by arrows in their chests, thighs, cheeks, backs, arms,
and bellies, the Pramathas roared like elephants.
Whether moving away, coming toward him, not yet reached, already reached, or standing at a distance—
he pierced each one of them violently with arrows;
he pierced a hundred with one, and again a hundred with a hundred.
A thousand with a thousand, and likewise ten million with ten million;
banners, flags, parasols, victory standards, goads, rugs, chowries, crowns, earrings, and garments. || 11–12 ||
Whatever among the forces of the Pramathas trembled or even fled,
all that the Dānava Andhaka swiftly cut asunder with his arrows.
Just as fire emits sparks, as a cloud pours down torrents of rain, as the king of rivers sends forth its surges, and as the sun radiates its rays; ||14||
Like lions in the forest letting out roars, or like elephants spraying their spray,
he released sharp-pointed arrows that crushed the enemy host.
While Andhaka, the best of the Asuras, was fighting with resolve,
the other Asuras also fought with resolve following Andhaka.
Those Nivātakavacas were exceedingly similar to one another.
Those many [demons] fought a battle with many Rudras.
The sixty thousand Kāleyas, great Asuras who were like Death itself,
fought with sixty thousand Pramathas born from his arms.
Prahlāda, Anuhrāda, Saṃhrāda, Śini,
Bāṣkala, Virocana, Bali, Bāṇa, Kujambha, and Avinijaya.
Añjaka, Kālanemi, Namuci, and Vyaṃsa—
these eleven are renowned, possessing the splendor of eleven suns.
Eleven Pramathas, seeking a quarrel, tormented Vīrabhadra, who was composed of light, as well as Piṅgala, the lord of the Viṭs. || 21 ||
Vegapa, Pavanāda, and those who nourish the Moon and Sun;
Saṃvarttakānala and those who nourish the Fire;
the powerful Yakṣonnada and the Rākṣasa Vidyutkeśa.
O foremost of gods, by these Dānavas headed by Prahlāda,
the gatekeepers of the Rudras and those who were the sons of the Rudras were rendered helpless, stripped of their weapons and armor, and covered by hundreds of missiles. ||23-24||
The attendants of Skanda and those who were lords of the hosts of Śaktis,
together with the sons of Danu and those belonging to the lineage of Danu’s sons—
those who delighted in strife and resembled the God of Death— engaged in a quarrel. (25)
While that battle was thus being waged, with the ornaments, garlands, and weapons of the gods shattered,
and their garments disarrayed, the gods and hosts of Siddhas stationed in the sky cried out, their beautiful eyes wide with wonder.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Battle of the Gaṇas," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
[I shall describe] the illusory power and the heroic prowess of Andhaka, the enemy of the gods.
It was perfectly created by the Blessed One, arising from the signs of the divine form.
Since the sage Bhārgava was swallowed by the God into his body,
what did he do while remaining within the body of the God of gods? And how did that twice-born one [act] through the power of his asceticism and the power of his yoga?
Like the moon emerged from white clouds, so did the descendant of Bhṛgu emerge.
O best of sages, this curiosity has arisen within me today;
please relate the life-story of the wise Bhārgava.
Sūta said:
Having been thus addressed by Vyāsa, the lord who was the son of Padmagarbha related the departure of Śukra from Śiva as told by Sanatkumāra.
Then, within the body of that Śambhu, his semen, its luster destroyed,
wandered about seeking an exit, like the homeless wind.
He beheld worlds with the radiance of fire, surrounded by hundreds of millions of Rudras,
frequented by the daughters of Rudra,
and [filled] with beings possessing fangs and claws whose color was like that of jasmine, the moon, and a conch shell. || 7 ||
Of those endowed with long tails, full of pride, yet possessed of patience. || 8 ||
Of lions with hair blazing like fire, bearing the *nandyāvarta* mark,
with tongues the color of *kiṃśuka* flowers, possessing the stature of Mount Kailāsa,
bound by fiery fetters, and of terrifying form.
The descendant of Bhṛgu beheld within the body of the God of gods a thousandfold vision:
he saw the gods together with Indra, along with the Ādityas, the hosts of Apsarases, and human beings;
and remaining within the body of Hara, he also witnessed the battle between Gaṇeśa and the Asuras.
Wandering within Bhava’s belly for a hundred years,
he did not find a single opening, just as Kali finds none in a pure person.
Even his yoga, endowed with sovereign powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the other qualities, [could not prevail].
Mahādeva struck down those whose minds were restrained in thought and speech.
Then a great clamor arose between the armies of the Pramathas and the Asuras;
hearing that sound, Bhārgava was alarmed and awakened.
Within that [forest], a Brahmin whose asceticism had increased praised with various hymns the god Soma, who is adorned by the moon, the husband of Umā. To him,
who had fallen into a state of distress, the trident-bearing god [granted his wish].
"Go forth by means of this sign"—thus was the rise of his grace accomplished. || 1.6 ||
Then, having become subtle in form, that Śukra, the best of sages, emerged like semen from the linga of the wise God of gods. || 17 ||
Because the delighter of the Bhṛgus emerged from his penis like semen (*śukra*),
that best among those who possess movement attained the renown of "Śukra.
And as he was offering salutations, he was addressed by him, the cloud-bannered one (Kārttikeya):

"O descendant of Bhṛgu, since you have emerged from me like semen, by that deed you are Śukra; you are my son as well, so depart. Thus addressed by the god, Śukra, whose splendor was like that of the sun, [departed].

He entered the army of the Dānavas like the moon entering a mass of clouds. Upon seeing him, who resembled the moon and whose appearance was like the rising of the moon, the enemies of the gods felt as much joy as men do at the rising of the moon. || 21 ||
Having seen Śukra, who possessed a radiance equal to the moon, those sons of Danu were filled with wonder.
All those who were eager for battle, filled with great joy, let out lion-like roars.
As for the Dānavas who had been slain by the Pramathas, who appeared radiant in victory,
they regarded them as having already entered the jaws of death because of the arrival of Bhārgava.
The great asuras paid homage to him, rejoiced, and were filled with serene joy.
That great ocean of Dānavas attained joy at the rising of Śukra, just as the ocean, joined by the Rākṣasas, always does at the rising of the moon. || 25 ||
Then Śākha and Viśākha, Chāgavaktra and Caturmukha, Nandin and Somanandin, and the heroic Nandiṣeṇa;
Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Śaṅkukarṇa, Kuṇḍodara, and Mahodara.
Viṭpati, Vīrabhadra, and that god who consists of light; Saṃvartaka, Anala, Urva, and Vibhākara, who is radiant with fame;
Vegapa, Śikhaṇḍin, Tāmracūḍa, and Kukkuṭa. || 27–28 ||
The Yakṣa Piṅgala, the food-giver; the clever boy Piṅgala;
Vidyutkeśa and Sukeśa, two invincible Rākṣasas;
these and other leaders of the Gaṇas, whose splendor is equal to that of the world-protectors.
They entered the army of the Dānavas, which was uplifted by the rising of Śukra. Then the sounds of musical instruments, together with the roars like the cries of lions,
became fierce in both armies, causing all living beings to tremble.
Then, having encountered one another with terrible blows from their tusks and palms that extinguished [the enemy's] force, they struck each other down;
placing Nandīśvara and the six-faced Kārttikeya at their head.
The Pramathas crush the Daityas in battle, just as Tārkṣya crushes serpents.
With their heads severed by falling swords and their skulls crushed by maces, the Dānavas lie upon the ground like mountains split apart by thunderbolts. (34)
Shattered and broken by arrows, their thighs and arms crushed,
the Daityas writhed in battle like serpents tormented by Tārkṣya;
their triple-jointed thighs and hips shattered, they were oppressed by thick showers of shafts.
The Daityas, afflicted with pain, wailed like clouds filled with water.
During that exceedingly fierce crushing of the Daityas by Gaṇapa,
the earth became filled with Daityas, just as the sky is filled with clouds.
With crowns, diadems, necklaces, bracelets, ornaments, armlets, bangles, upper-arm rings, waist-bands, and earrings; || 38 ||
With brilliant crest-jewels,
radiant necklaces, garlands of beautiful flowers, and eyes with arms foremost in gems.
With missiles, weapons, garments, and umbrellas possessing a luster like that of the moon,
her limbs were variegated with red saffron, and she was adorned with various ornaments.
In various places, the battlefield shines like women adorned with abundant wealth;
it resembles the appearance of proud lions or likewise of elephants. ||41||
The Gaṇeśas became emboldened as they struck down the Dānavas.
Being slaughtered, defenseless, and afflicted by fear, those Dānavas sought refuge;
pursued by the Pramathas, they took shelter in the ocean.
Having seen that army abandoned by the Dānavas, who were tormented by the Pramathas; ||| 43 ||
When the Daityas had entered the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters,
the descendant of Bhṛgu, possessed of great splendor like a blazing fire,
became enraged and severely cursed those Daityas who dwelt within the sea.
"Since you, O weak women, have abandoned your companions and even me— who am as beneficial to you as a father—
and have entered the ocean for the sake of saving your lives,
therefore, remain right there, devoid of shame and scarred by my curse."
Having attained the state of fish, you shall remain born or unborn as long as the worlds exist, along with the mountains and the oceans; for that long,
you shall be aquatic fish dwelling in the water.

"O sinful ones, you shall become eaters of human flesh and devourers of men. You shall endure my curse for hundreds of millions of years. Having thus reduced the remaining inhabitants of the ocean waters to being struck by his curse, [he departed].
The one of great splendor, Śukra, whose radiance was like that of the moon, ceased speaking.
Sanatkumāra said: Then those Asuras, struck by the preceptor’s curse, [fell] into the waters of the ocean.
They were seen equipped with weapons, wearing armor, and clad in mail.
Then Śukra, touching Andhaka with his hand as if to restore him to life, spoke to him who was overwhelmed by the fear of the enemy of Śukra:
"Do not fear, O best of Dānavas; fight against your enemies! (51)
"I shall sustain you as food sustains life.
Having been addressed thus by Śukra, Andhaka, the lord of the Dānavas,
replied, "So be it," and besieged the Pramathas in battle.
Then, as the Asuras had entered the ocean and were being struck down by the followers of Śaṅkara,
Andhaka held back all the Pramathas, just as the sea of vast waters holds back the rivers and streams.
Then that Andhaka pierced Nandin with twelve arrows and the son of Agni with five.
With one hundred and ten arrows, that Dānava struck Viśākha and Śākha,
as well as Naigameṣa. He pierced Vīrabhadra, Viṭpati, and the radiant Piṅgala, the foremost of Yakṣas,
with arrows adorned with golden ornaments, just as an elephant-driver strikes an elephant with the tips of goads.

There was no horse, nor elephant, nor even any other creature, before him or behind him, who could withstand the arrows discharged by Indrajit—arrows resembling the blazing fire of cosmic destruction and the sun. ||57||

Torn apart like sandalwood trees by the lords of the hosts, the sons of the enemy stood repeatedly on their arms, bellies, chests, and heads, rendered motionless like elephants confined within the bonds of a cage. ||58||
Then the asuras let out lion-like roars, intensified by hundreds of conchs, kettledrums, and drums;
once again, a terrifying battle broke out between the lords of the Gaṇas and the lords of the Dānavas.
Thus ends the one hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Battle of the Gaṇas and the Curse of the Gods," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
While the battle with Andhaka was underway and the Gaṇas were fleeing,
the Grandfather spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the thirty gods.
"Behold them, O Lord of the Immortals—may it be well with you—as they turn their faces away and are being crushed in battle by the terrible Dānavas and by Andhaka. (2)
Śukra remains reviving those dānavas slain again and again by the foremost warriors in battle,
just as a rain-cloud revives crops.
And here he is, with his bow drawn, resembling a cloud accompanied by Indra’s bow (the rainbow).
Andhaka was raining down a shower of arrows, destroying his enemies.
Why did you remain patient with this defeat—this which afflicts the Pramathas, brings harm, and is disgraceful? (4-5)
"Indeed, having conquered all of us, this Andhaka, the lord of the Dānavas, will utterly uproot even our very foundations. Therefore,
before he brings our Pramathas to destruction with his arrows,"
At that very moment, we shall seize the rear of the one clad in animal skins.
"In this way, O Lord of Devas, your purpose will be accomplished,
and a great favor will indeed be done for Rudra as well.
Having heard these words of Svayambhū, the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra—
Having said, "This is right," the Lord of the Gods spoke to the deities:
"Armed with armor, weapons, and missiles, and possessing swift prowess,
let us provide assistance today to the hosts as they fight in battle."
Then Nārāyaṇa, Ananta, the two lords of men (Nara and Nārāyaṇa), and Candra;
Svayambhū, Anala, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Dhanada;
Pūṣan, Aryaman, Bhaga, Mitra, and Yama, the son of the Sun.
Aṃśa, Tvaṣṭṛ, Jaya, and Jayanta, the son of Śakra;
the Maruts, Vasus, Sādhyas, as well as the Aśvins, Garuḍas, and Uragas;
the Tuṣitas, Lekhas, Viśvedevas, and Guhyakas.
The Gandharvas, the Yakṣas, and whoever else were on the side of the gods— all of them rushed into the battle, desiring to slay Andhaka.
Then, the sounds of kettledrums and terrifying lion-roars arose among the divine armies, bringing joy to the Pramathas.
As the gods descended, they churned that army of the Dānavas like a lake with abundant fish and dwindling water being stirred by royal swans.
Then, a tumultuous roar, most terrifying, arose.
While the army of the Dānavas was crowded and presided over by the gods,
it was like the sky filled with thick clouds and sea-monsters,
like a body overwhelmed by phlegm and bile, or like serpents beset by Garuḍas.
Thus, in a mere moment, that army of the Andhakas was entirely rendered helpless, its armor and banners destroyed by the might of the inhabitants of heaven;
on one side were the gods led by Indra, and on the other were the lords of the Gaṇas.
The host of Dānavas was being slaughtered like a flock of goats by hundreds of wolves.
The god who holds a raised thunderbolt in his hand, the preeminent among the gods,
was their leader like the syllable *oṃ* is for the Vedas;
with the fire of the thunderbolt-weapon, Indra consumed his enemies in battle.
But all misdeeds [are consumed] by the fire of expiation, just as [fuel is consumed]. || 22 ||
While he was being struck by the gods and the Pramathas, Bali,
the lord of the Dānavas, blinded by anger and passion, spoke to the Dānavas.
Having provoked enmity with Rudra, the protector of all the worlds,
it is not possible for you to defeat the Pramathas along with the immortals, even if you remain undaunted.
"You must not fear death; fight, O Daityas and Dānavas!
For here stands Bhārgava, who will restore us to life. (25)
Therefore, O lords of the hosts of gods, being fearless, ward off these [demons] according to your strength and according to your energy, while consuming them with your vital breaths;
do so by means of many secret illusions against those who are themselves hidden in form.
"Repel all the assembled gods with battle!
Thus addressed, they unleashed terrible [missiles], like clouds at the end of a kalpa. ||27-28||
Making sounds with their bows and likewise uttering lion-like roars,
the Dānavas, urged on by Andhaka, rushed toward the gods.
Having drawn his great bow, the Dānava Andhaka, who roared like the ocean and the clouds, rushed with speed toward Rudra.
As that lord of the Dānavas, difficult to restrain, was charging forward,
Śailādi warded him off as one wards off unwholesome thoughts from a mind fixed on Dharma;
he struck Nandin with three arrows resembling blazing suns.
Andhaka, out of rage, squeezed [him] between his arms, crushing him. ||32||
Severely torn by that Dānava, the Lord of the Gaṇas,
Nandin, then reeled like a tree shaken by the wind.
Reeling, Nandin shone with his polished earrings as ornaments, like an ashoka tree rich with swaying sprouts and flowers. (34)
Then, having recovered after a long time, Suyaśas, the lord of Suyaśas,
raised his powerful thunderbolt and hurled it at Andhaka.
Andhaka checked that powerful thunderbolt, which resembled the fire and the sun, with a flood of arrows, and he laughed aloud. || 36 ||
As he laughed, drops of tears flowed from his eyes and beautiful eyebrows,
just as rays stream forth from the radiant orb of the sun.
The King of the Bhūtas uprooted that tree with its agitated foliage, and crying out, "O Indraka, you are slain!", he hurled it and roared. (38)
As he ran through the sky, bees fanned him with the wind from the trees, following him just as friends follow a companion who has fallen into misfortune. (39)
Andheka also cut that [arrow] of his with shafts adorned with beautiful gold,
just as the slayer of serpents (Viṣṇu) once cut the embryo of Diti while it was still within the world-supporter (Indra).
Then Nandin, having fashioned a tree from the peak of Mount Mandara— which was filled with deer, wild beasts, and serpents—
uprooted it and rushed toward Andhaka in battle.
Nandin, whose abode was among the mountain peaks and forests, hurled that mountain crag at him.
He brought down his chariot upon the Vindhya mountain, as the slayer of serpents hurls the thunderbolt.
Struck violently by that bull Nandin with its horn, the chariot— along with its wheels,
pole, and horses— was reduced to a state of union with the dust.
Then, seeing Andhaka’s chariot— complete with wheels and axles— pulverized,
the gods along with the Gandharvas, Pramathas, and Guhyakas raised a roar.
Thereafter, Andhaka, thundering like a dark cloud, [advanced] with his trident.
He struck Nandin as a lordly elephant strikes down a tree.
(45) Struck by that trident by the one whose beloved weapon is the trident, Nandin, with all his limbs overwhelmed, trembled like a mountain peak in a great flood of water. (46)
While Nandīśvara was reeling, severely afflicted by the blow,
a lion’s roar arose repeatedly from the army of the asuras.
By that lion’s roar of the enemies, Nandin was awakened.
The kinsman of all beings struck Andhaka with his battle-axe. Struck by the battle-axe, the Dānava Andhaka bled like sandalwood exuding its resin when struck by an elephant’s tusk.
Seeing Andhaka deprived of his chariot, the enemies of the gods protected him;
the deities remained stationed in their respective quarters, just as they protect this world.
Then there was Bāṇa, the son of Bali, whose radiance was equal to the bāṇa flower.
"O Dānavas, prepare Andhaka with a chariot!
Then Andhaka, the lord of the Dānavas, ascended that chariot,
just as the blessed Sun rises with its full orb.
Then again, the gods and dānavas, desiring to engage in a most dreadful conflict, joined battle;
with tridents, thunderbolts, lightning, and arrows, the fire kindled in the fray blazed forth even more intensely. (53)
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Battle between Andhaka and Nandin," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Viṣṇu, the destroyer of the Dānavas, was being oppressed by the Dānavas.
Making a roar like a thundercloud, the Dānava Jambha rushed forward.
But seeing Jambha approaching with a sound like a cloud,
the god was not at all alarmed, just as a lion is not frightened upon seeing an elephant.
Kujambha and Jambha, the younger Dānava mountain,
obstructed the infinite and finite enemies and roared;
Vṛtra, resembling a mountain of collyrium and appearing like the fire at the end of an aeon, [did the same].
Desiring to seize him, he approached Indra, roaring like a cloud.
As that Dānava was running and roaring, Purandara, who possesses a hundred eyes,
struck him— who resembled a mountain— in a cave.
Fighting with a mace, he [struck] Śatāyu, who was like Vāyu, in the battle.
Desirous of fighting, he rushed forward quickly, roaring and laughing.
The two great asuras Tuhuṇḍa and Huṇḍa fought with the Aśvins; Bhaga fought with Prahlāda, and Virocana with Anśa.
Aryaman and Yama fought against Vilva and Kelvala;
and those great asuras led by Vipracitti, foremost among the powerful,
fought by the thousands against the lords of the hosts and the gods.
The bull among Dānavas, Andhaka, having approached Nandin,
mangled him with calf-toothed arrows discharged from his bow; he,
in turn, was deeply pierced by Andhaka with arrows that tear through the vital organs.
Nandin grew enraged, and in that great battle against Andhaka,
he rushed forward; raising his hand which held a thunderbolt and shone like the rays of the sun,
the agitated Nandin roared like a cloud at the time of universal destruction.
With the hundred-edged thunderbolt, the Lord of the Gaṇas [struck] Sondhaka. || 12 ||
He crushed the horses, the charioteer, and likewise the chariot;
then [he struck] Andhaka at the root of the ear, which was adorned with earrings and locks of hair.
The boon-granter, who possessed beautiful earrings and a voice as deep as a thundercloud, struck him;
then, he too, whose hand resembled the trunk of an elephant, raised his hand.
He was thrown onto the lap of Nandin like an elephant in battle;
struck by that Dānava with a backhanded blow,
the Lord of the Gaṇas retreated eight steps, only to fall back again upon those very same spots.
Then the Daityas said to Andhaka, "Excellent! Excellent! (1.6).
Incensed by that excellent blow directed at the Dānava,
he summoned a fierce rage and indeed rushed forward.
Having seized his variegated bow and his armor of great luster, [he advanced].
He indeed cut it into pieces with a hundred-edged thunderbolt.
Having bound him with the noose of his arms, the Lord of Beings himself desired to crush him upon the ground; but Andhaka released him.
Having freed himself, he resorted to a deluding illusion.
He rushed toward Śailādi, crying out, "Stay! Stay! (8.152.2).
As he was rushing forward with great speed, all the most eminent lords of the Gaṇas,
their minds filled with rage and various weapons in hand—
Nandiṣeṇa, Somanandī, Śaṅkukarṇa, and Mahodara— [rushed against him].
Ghaṇṭākarṇa and Vīrabhadra—that god who consists of light—were the foremost among their attendants; protecting their lord, they fought Andhaka just as lions attack the elephant of Śakra. ||22-23||
Nandiṣeṇa struck him with a spear, Somanandin with a fist,
Vīrabhadra with an arrow, Ghaṇṭākarṇa with a sword,
Śaṅkukarṇa with the tip of his trunk, and Prabhāmaya with a tree.
The gods cut Andhaka to pieces, just as the Draviḍas cut sandalwood;
but Nandīśvara, the leader of the Gaṇas, struck the lord of the Dānavas, Andhaka, on the head, after he had been turned away by the other Gaṇas.

Seeing the lord of the asuras pursued by the gods and the leaders of the gaṇas, a cry arose within the army of the asuras: "Run! Seize him! Then the asuras, led by Prahlāda, quickly assembled together.
Having risen up and come forth, Viṣṇu alone held back all those rivers.
But seeing him thus valiant at the head of the battle with the discus in hand,
Andhaka, overwhelmed by rage, launched a truly massive assault.
Whether he was striving, motionless, rushing forward, or roaring—
whomever and wherever he saw him, he pierced him with arrows.
Broad, yellow, and sharpened, bearing the feathers of Garuḍa’s body,
Andhaka’s terrible arrows, inexhaustible from his bow,
fell upon [his enemies'] faces, gums, bellies, and hands. ||31||
When pierced by Andhaka, even elephants abandon their excessive rut;
some [of his followers] take refuge in the Lord of Gods, others in Indra, the sovereign of the deities;
still other hosts resort to the god Nārāyaṇa, and others to Nandin.
Other gods stood leaning upon Śākha and Viśākha, and others upon Kumāra as well, like birds perched upon trees;
just as mortals do out of fear of a thunderbolt, or as deer do out of fear of a lion.
Just as serpents are always terrified of Garuḍa, the devourer of snakes,
so too did the gods— the enemies of the deities— stand trembling in battle before Andhaka; afflicted by his mass of arrows, they wandered about like those who are bewildered.
Just as a forest of bandhujīva trees shines when bent down by their blossoms,
so did that host of attendants appear, their limbs drenched with blood from their wounds.
Just as trees in the forests tremble when stirred by the wind, [so did they shake].
Likewise, at the front of the battle, the gods were terrified by the fear of Andhaka.
Then Nārāyaṇa, Ananta, the powerful Śakra, the two Aśvins, the eight Vasus, and the twelve Ādityas [all fled]. || 38-39 ||
Nandī, Viśākha, Śākha, Vīrabhadra, Prabhāmaya, Viṭpati, Śaṅkukarṇa, Somanandī, and Vināyaka—
these were present while Bala was being struck down by Andhaka’s surging forces.

The gods, armed with various weapons, rushed toward that lord of the hosts of Dānavas. Surrounding his excellent chariot, which resembled the palace of a Gandharva, they shattered it and roared like clouds.
As the great chariot-warrior Andhaka was being shattered by the gods,
he was like a desire set upon unrighteousness thwarted by obstacles;
that Dānava struck the wielder of the discus with his own discus and Śakra with his thunderbolt.
With a single infinite arrow and a trident, [he struck] Vināyaka. ||44||
Having swiftly struck Nandin with his fist, Prabhāmaya with his spear (paṭṭiśa),
Pūṣan with a crescent-headed arrow (bhalla), and Yama with his mace,
that fire of battle quickly assailed all his enemies.
Leaping up into the sky, he roared like a water-saturated cloud;
that deceptive warrior, resembling a mountain,
hurled mountain peaks along with trees, shrubs, and serpents, and let out a great roar.
That terrible rain from the mountain peaks—accompanied by trees, bears, and great serpents—fell upon the divine armies like a shower on lotuses;
it was incessant, without pause, breathless, and filled with terror. (48)
With their noses, eyes, teeth, and lips severed, and their feet, hips, and hands broken,
the Pramatha gods are seen terrified, bewildered, and trembling.
Standing upon the clouds, he shines as he repeatedly hurls a rain of stones and weapons from the peaks of the palace towers.
To me... ||51|| ...the sound;
a great lotus shrouded in smoke, and a powder of great fire resembling fireflies. ||52||
That enemy of the hosts of gods, having ascended into the sky, let out a roar like that of the surging ocean;
he repeatedly discharged a great rain of water, just like the fierce downpour from the cloud at the time of universal dissolution.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-second chapter in the *Andhakayuddha* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said: Then Andhaka, standing in the sky like a mass of great clouds, rained down a shower of stones, just as a cloud rains down water.
Again, seizing his bow which resembled the bow of great Indra,
he released a tempest of arrows, and it became an exceedingly dark storm.
Then [he loosed] those arrows with feathers like those of the *suparṇa* bird, possessing wings like the *suparṇa*.
Of those who fly like Garuḍas and possess beaks as lofty as Garuḍa’s.
The lord of the Dānavas created a hundred [demons] who pierce bodies and consume the essence of the body; and, filled with pride, he roared as well.
Drawn and discharged from the fully drawn bow, moving through the field of battle, following their own paths as guides for the arrow's flight, and equal to thought or wind in speed—
those great arrows of Andhaka fall upon the gods.
Just as the rays sent forth by the sun [are repelled] upon great mountains;
likewise, elephants struck by arrows, horses struck by arrows,
and the hosts of lords of the gods were struck by arrows on every side.
With their entrails and blood protruding, their necklaces and ornaments scattered, and the binding of their hair loosened, they fall down in intense agony. ||8||
Whether standing, moving, rising, running, or leaping—
just as he perceived the horse, the elephant, or the god from whichever direction,
Andhaka then struck that enemy with arrows whose forms were like darkness.
Having forcibly cast him down, he roars like a cloud at the arrival of the rainy season.
With the cries of those afflicted by wounds and the horses wandering in confusion,
the army shone like a river in flood, its sound of trumpets having been silenced.
Torn asunder, cut, split, burnt, devoured, and shaken down—
like a forest whose trees have been destroyed by an elephant blinded by rut;
some were struck upon their faces, while others were struck upon their eyes.
Others likewise were struck on the chests, and others on the backs.
Just as the *śataghnīs* were covered with arrows, so too the hosts of Maruts and the groups of beings of terrible prowess, being struck down, reached neither the sky nor the earth.
Then the river of blood began to flow, set in motion by the gods and the asuras;
it was teeming with great elephants as its crocodiles, with chariots as its beautiful tortoises,
with severed arms as its serpents, and with bows and excellent banners as its trees.
With the peak of his crown as its frog and the bowstring as its cord, [the earth trembled]. 16.
With scattered pearl necklaces for its pebbles and white garments for its abundant foam,
this river— set in motion by the gods and demons— is as difficult for gods and demons alike to cross.
Then the Piśācas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas, whose brilliance was like that of collyrium and who laughed with flashes of lightning, being greatly tormented by thirst,
drank the blood just as the gods drink the excellent nectar.
Then once again, a wonderful and tumultuous battle took place when Andhaka had been struck by Nandin with that great arrow.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Battlefield," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
While that army was being slaughtered by the gods together with the lords of the Pramathas, [the battle continued].
The twenty-four formidable Dānavas, filled with pride, became enraged:
Prahlāda, Anuhrāda, Saṃhrāda, Śini,
Bāṣkala, Jambha, Virocana, Vṛtra, Bali, Bāṇa, and Avinijaya.
Likewise, Tuhuṇḍa, Huṇḍa, Śambhu, Kārtasvana, Kubha,
Śambara, Vipracitti, Ilvaka, and Pilvaka; as well as Maya, Tāra, Tārakākṣa, Vidyunmālī, and Pramohana.
Thus, these twenty-four Dānavas fell under the power of Mṛtyu. ||4||
They rushed toward the god Nandin, who stood there armed;
those beings, resembling dark mountains, assailed Nandin— who was like a mountain of gold—
with spears, javelins, double-edged swords, and sharp-edged axes.
Thus struck and obstructed by those enemies with their weapons,
Nandin was neither agitated nor did he fall into distress or pain;
then the Blessed One drew back his great, fully drawn bow.
With three arrows at a time, he swiftly pierced all those foremost of Dānavas;
by the streams flowing from the paths of his arrows, those Dānavas began to bleed.
Like the lords of mountains exuding liquid gold, they shone;
then Nandin, emboldened by rage, was revived once more by Śukra.
With terrible arrows, he sent Kārttavīrya to the abode of Yama.
Having encountered that which causes the loss of life, that great mountain-like Dānava fell instantly like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt, its rocks shattered.
When he had fallen to the ground, slain by the arrow of Nandin,
Bali uprooted a mountain peak and hurled it toward Nandin.
That mountain slope, containing minerals, wild beasts, and serpents, along with bears and trees— [fell upon him].
The serpents and other creatures rushed with speed toward the Lord of the Gaṇas, who was like a tree shaken by a windless storm, as he was released from the power of Śṛṅgin.
