Like kinsmen abandoning a man who has fallen into distress,
the heroic Nandin then pierced that falling mountain peak with an arrow,
splitting it like a great wind dispersing the clouds, and let out a roar.
Having split that mountain peak, he whose abode is upon a mountain peak pierced Bali with an arrow, as if Bali were a risen obstacle. ||15||
Struck by Gaṇeśa and rendered helpless like the son of Prahlāda,
he suddenly fell to the ground like a tree felled by the wind.
Then, when Bala had fallen, struck by the excellent Nandī, [the battle continued].
Afflicted by arrows, the Dānavas fled from the battlefield in terror. || 17 ||

Then Andhaka, who resembled a cloud and possessed a form like a cloud, having reached the earth from the sky amidst clouds that looked like spreading masses of water, spoke these words to the Dānavas: || 18 ||
O sons of Dakṣa’s daughter, listen today to my words;
if you so deem it right, carry out the beneficial instructions spoken by me.
"Born in noble families, heroes who have mastered all weapons— why do you flee, driven by sharp iron arrows? Where are those words of yours, spoken and proclaimed in the assembly?"
Where now is that abundance of hostility toward the gods?
Having been defeated by a single Nandin hundreds and thousands of times,
how is it that you feel no shame as you chatter here in the courtyard of our home?
"Turn back, O you who know not dharma! Fight! What is the use of fleeing?
There is no place where death does not exist for us; there is no such opportunity.
Let the judges stand by our side, free from enmity and devoid of malice."
"Behold now this duel with Nandin!
Having heard these words of Andhaka, all those Dānavas in the battle turned back once more for combat, grasping their excellent weapons.
Then, mounting another chariot adorned with banners and measuring a *nalva* in size,
Andhaka advanced toward Nandin along with the foremost of the Dānavas.
Their broad and pleasingly shaped [weapons] had sharp points and were fashioned from gold.
The great arrows discharged from Andhaka’s bow fly forth like locusts over a field,
like bees toward a tree,
like clouds toward the lords of serpents, and like sea-monsters toward the oceans.
By means of great arrows released [by Andhaka], possessing a luster equal to that of serpents and the sun,
the gods were rendered like the finest *śataghnīs* by Andhaka;
they became as irresistible as the wind, just like death or old age.
And just as the blessings of Brahmins are said to be unimpeded and certain. ||8.154.30||
Thus, those sharp and fierce great arrows of Andhaka were like uplifted Brahma-staves; for they were irresistible and unfailing in battle,
wherever all the Asuras and their enemy Andhaka went.
Then, from that point on, the Pramathas along with the gods were being torn asunder.
He too, with his bow perpetually drawn like the sun surrounded by its halo,
discharged volleys of arrows just as the sun radiates its rays.
Encountering his arrow-wounds, all the leaders of the Gaṇas and the gods together with Vāsava faltered, like trees on a riverbank.
Having pierced Viṣṇu with one arrow, Ananta with two, and Śakra with three, he—
Having rent asunder Yama, Soma, the Lord of Waters, and the Vasus, he let out a terrible roar.
Having pierced the two Aśvins with two arrows, as well as Bhaga, Aryaman, Candra, and Pūṣan,
the one of fierce deeds then mangled Nandīśvara and the lords of the Gaṇas with his shafts. Thus did the assailant Andhaka burn them, just as the blessed Fire burns moths.
Then those leaders of the celestial warriors were repelled and shattered by Andhaka;
they were unable to stir or even look upon Andhaka in battle, just as men cannot gaze upon the sun in the sky.
Thereupon, abandoning their blazing glories, the gods, together with Nārāyaṇa and Devapāla, departed.
Afflicted by the arrows of that Andhaka-demon and distressed by the piercing of the Dānavas, they fled in all directions. || 38 ||
Viṣṇu, Pitāmaha, Ananta,
and Śatakratu were all defeated in battle by Andhaka with arrows resembling tongues of fire.
The Ādityas, the Vasus, the Sādhyas, and the two Aśvins, the best of gods,
were broken in battle by Andhaka with blows from his thunderbolt, like winged mountains.
So too were the Tuṣitas, the Viśvedevas, and the gods who partake of the Svadhā offerings.
They were shattered by Andhaka’s arrows, like trees broken by the wind. ||41||
The Lord Moon, Vahni, and the Rākṣasa Vittapāla were broken in battle by Andhaka with arrows resembling venomous serpents;
so too were the Gandharvas, Guhyakas, Sarpas, Garuḍas, and Mahoragas.
Broken in battle by Andhaka and pierced by arrows resembling fire, [the following were struck]:
Viṭpati, Śaṅkukarṇa, Somanandin, Prabhāmaya, Piṅgala, Nandiṣeṇa, Ghaṇṭākarṇa, and Mahodara. || 43-44 ||
Vidyutkeśa, Sukeśa, and that god Vināyaka, as well as other heroic Pramathas led by Vīrabhadra. ||45||
Broken by Andhaka in battle by the hundreds and thousands, the entire triple world, including all things mobile and immobile, was forcibly overwhelmed. 46.
In that battle, Andhaka shattered the divine host along with Nārāyaṇa and the gods,
leaving only the Lord of the Gaṇas as the sole survivor among the celestial forces.

No one remained standing before him who wore the great jewel upon his crest; then, within the host of the asuras, there arose a terrible and great roar of lion-like shouts from all living beings, mingled with the wonderful sounds of musical instruments. ||48||
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter in the *Indhaka-vijaya* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said:
In the meantime, all the gods, led by Śakra, [arrived].
Accompanied by Brahmā, they went to the wielder of the trident, the one worthy of seeking refuge.
Having prostrated before Mahādeva, they, afflicted by fear, said this:
"We have all been utterly defeated; why do you neglect Andhaka?"
Then the God of gods spoke to the deities, headed by Brahmā:
"Because I have granted him a boon, you have been defeated;
furthermore, he was overlooked by me in battle solely for the sake of sport."
Now, for your sake, I shall subdue Andhaka.
Then the God, having smiled, looked at the trident standing by his side;
knowing the true intent of the God, the trident blazed up instantly.
Having rushed swiftly toward Andhaka, who appeared victorious,
he suddenly displayed his prowess in battle and pierced him between the breasts.
Then, having pierced through Andhaka, that trident brought the mighty and massive-bodied lord of the Dānavas into the presence of Śaṅkara.
From that [body] pierced by the trident, drops of blood flowed forth;
having fallen, they became men who fought with unbearable ferocity. ||8||
Possessing forms equal to his own and equal prowess to his,
they too, equipped with various weapons and missiles, fought against the lords of the Gaṇas.
...with dice in their hands; some of those exceedingly powerful ones struck even the Gaṇas as they were fleeing. ||8.155.10||
Among those fighting, not a single lord of the Gaṇas remained;
out of fear of the lords of the Dānavas, they all fled from the battle.
Seeing all those Gaṇas fleeing along with the lords of the gods, [he...]
Mahādeva emitted... ||1 2||
...doing so, they then made this request: "You ought to grant us your command. Then the God of gods spoke to all of them as they stood with weapons raised:
"Devour these great Asuras who have arisen from drops of blood! || 14 ||
Thus addressed, all those powerful mistresses of yoga slaughtered the asuras in battle again and again and devoured them.
Then the god, the destroyer of Andhaka, spoke to his blazing trident.

"Cook Andhaka in the fire of the sun for a hundred thousand years! || 16 || For even Andhaka, while being cooked on the point of a trident by the brilliance of the sun, attained a state of sattva when the full thousand years had passed. || 17 ||
Having attained a state of sattva and shaken off rajas and tamas,
he recognized the bull-bannered God as the cause of the worlds.
Having realized that, he then, with devotion and a stainless inner self,
though remaining with only sinews and bones left, praised the God who bears the crescent moon upon his crest.
Andhaka said:

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, who is the creator of this entire world with its moving and non-moving beings, as well as the author of what is created and the bestower of pleasure and pain; he who is also the cause of dissolution at the time of the end.
To him, the yogis—whose delusion, darkness, and passion have departed, whose minds are one-pointed through devotion, and whose desires have ceased—[go for refuge].
Those of firm intellect meditate upon that Śaṅkara, who possesses such divine nature; I go for refuge to him, the giver of protection. ||21||

I seek refuge in that Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, who out of affection bears upon his head the stainless crescent moon with its spreading rays, and who offered half of his own body to the daughter of the King of Mountains. 2.2.

I go for refuge to Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, who bore upon his head the Gaṅgā—whose beautiful waters are frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas, and which falls from the sky with the impetuosity of great waves—as if she were a garland of flowers that never droops. || 23 ||

I go for refuge to Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, who, when the peak of Mount Kailāsa was being shaken by the ten-faced Rāvaṇa— who himself resembled a peak of Kailāsa— bore it up by pressing down with his lotus-feet.
By him the sons of Diti, the sons of Danu, and the hosts of Vidyādharas and Uragas were repeatedly granted all their boons.
The best of sages, subsisting on fruits and roots, have been joined together; I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of protection. ||25||
He destroyed Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the eyes of Bhaga, and likewise the row of teeth of Pūṣan;
he paralyzed the arm of Mahendra equipped with the thunderbolt—to that Śaṅkara, the giver of refuge, I go for shelter. ||26||

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the bestower of protection, who has attained liberation from the threefold bonds and who, though not even endowed with the qualities of knowledge, spiritual lineage, or sacred learning, becomes an enjoyer of happiness for those men who have taken refuge in him. ||27||

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, who, at the time of the world's dissolution, possessed a splendor equal to ten million suns and struck terror into the foremost of gods and demons, and who drank the violently surging Kālakūṭa poison. ||28||
From battle, the Lord Maheśa granted many boons to Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, the Maruts, and Ṣaṇmukha;
the Lord also rescued Nandin from the jaws of Death—I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of refuge. (29)
And Kāma, the wielder of the bow who possesses five arrows on earth, was then rendered bodiless by the Blessed One out of sport;
yet in ancient times he destroyed Tripura with but a single arrow—I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of refuge. (8.155.3)

Salutations ever to Śiva, the bringer of auspiciousness, who is attainable through the supreme reality; he who was propitiated with great austerity in a Himalayan bower by means of the smoke-vow (*dhūmavrata*) in a place inaccessible even to the minds of others, and who bestowed the *sañjīvanī* [life-restoring] power.

[Salutations] to him who is surrounded by the lords of the hosts (*gaṇendra*), the powerful ones who crushed Dakṣa’s sacrifice, possessing various faces resembling those of elephants, cats, and other creatures.
I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the bestower of protection, who is worshipped by the hosts of gods together with the world-protectors. ||32||

For the sake of sport alone, the Blessed One created the seven worlds—adorned with various rivers, birds, and trees, together with Brahmā and dedicated to the welfare of the righteous; I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of shelter.
He under whose control this entire world eternally remains, and who enjoys the worlds through his eight very forms.

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, who is the cause even of the greatest causes. Having cast me down, O you followed by the daughter of the Lord of Mountains, I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, whose limbs are adorned with ornaments.
I seek refuge in Śaṅkara, the bestower of protection, who is binding that white-clad sage as he is being led away by those terrifying and most fierce men devoted to the enforcement of restraints. 36.
Reflecting thus upon that Śaṅkara, the giver of refuge, I go to him for shelter.

(38) Those who are deluded by the nature of worldly bondage do not understand this world; bound within the sphere of the defects of power, they experience the same suffering as I do when they emerge from it. (39)
...Indeed, through that grace... at that time, Śubhakarmā reached the world of Śiva.
Sanatkumāra said:
While he was thus praising him, the god Śaṅkara, the trident-bearer whose banner is the bull, being pleased at the completion of a thousand years, said:
"O son, I am satisfied; may it be well with you; you have now become stainless."
"I grant you divine vision; behold me, O Lord of the Dānavas!
Whatever supreme fruit you desire, I shall grant it all to you; speak, O best of the Dānavas! (42–43)
"Whether it be the station of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or Indra— difficult even for the gods to attain—
or else become the king of all the worlds as you were before.
Andhaka said:
The station of Brahmā, that of Viṣṇu, and that of Indra— all characterized by return—
I have known all of that even with my mind.
O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, grant me the status of a leader of the Gaṇas.
It is undifferentiated, pure, and eternally imperishable.
46. The God of gods, who is honored by all the worlds, said: 47.
The great yogi, capable of assuming any form at will, possessing great strength along with living beings,

The Lord, the God himself, having raised her up, sat down upon a seat shimmering with the rays of jewels, accompanied by her.

"This Andhaka, your son, was born from my very eyes;

When the Lord of Gods, Śaṅkara, had spoken thus, the Dānava Andhaka—
Bowing down with palms joined in reverence, he addressed Pārvatī:

"Know me, O Mother, as one who is patient, self-controlled, devoted, and solely intent upon taking refuge in Him; I am established here with a pure disposition.

With palms joined in reverence, he bowed down and praised him with words worthy of the Āhavanīya fire. || 14 ||
Vibhāvarī, Vāricarī, Śarvarī, Śarvavallabhā;

Puṣṭi, iṣṭi, tuṣṭi, gṛṣṭi, dṛṣṭi, truṭi, taḍit;

She is initiation (*dīkṣā*), the most excellent of the skillful (*dakṣāvarā*), protection (*rakṣā*), and instruction (*śikṣā*); she whose abode is the armpit (*kakṣaniketanā*).
She is fragrant (*sugandhā*), fortunate (*subhagā*), auspicious (*bhavyā*), and the maker of what has been, what is to be, and what is becoming (*bhūtabhavyabhavatkarī*).
She is the earth (*dharaṇī*), the supporter (*dhāraṇī*), the blessed one (*dhanyā*), the source of heroes (*vīraṇī*), and indeed the cave-dweller (*guhāraṇī*).
Lā, Golā, and likewise Maṅgalāvidhā. ||8.157.20||
She who is surrounded by the virtuous, who delights the kṣatriyas, who is as variegated as the starry sky, who is the earth, who is action, and who is memory free from greed. 2.1.
She is purity, purification, the wise one, and fame; she is the beloved of the wearer of the elephant-hide garment.
She is the bowstring, the victorious one, the worshipful, the object of sacrifice, the path of the righteous, and the bestower of victory. ||22||
She is the most excellent among the best, the giver of boons, the noblest woman, and the field for speech;
she is prosperity, the mother of all beings, the embodiment of merit, the well-disposed, and delight.
Bhāratī, endowed with splendor, who bears well-joined and impassioned speech; Ājñā, Prajñā, and Saṃjñā; Ulkā, born from the nose;

She is the upholder of dharma, the mother of dharma, the sharpening one, the most excellent among those possessing splendor; she is the night, the delighter, the steadfast, the source, and the forest-eyed one. ||25||
Seeking wealth, she was like a river of Danu; possessing the meaning of sacred learning, she was more learned than the most learned.
Wearing bracelets like whirling firebrands, she was a girdle herself, yet wore a girdle.
"May the Mother of the World, Śyāmā, who is clad in dark garments—Umā herself—be pleased with me.
Thus was Īśā praised by Andhaka with hundreds of hymns.

Sanatkumāra said: Having beheld Bhavānī, the bestower of boons, Andhaka, the foremost of the Gaṇas,
bowed down with palms joined in reverence and spoke to Umā, the daughter of Himavat.
And whatever boon you grant me, O Goddess, beloved of Īśāna, by all of that may my devotion to you remain steadfast. (8.157.30)
Having heard those words of his, the Blessed Aparājitā approached Andhaka and, being well-pleased, spoke to him once again.
"I am indeed pleased, my son, with this auspicious knowledge of yours, since you have today sought devotion from me, O most excellent lord. (32)
"O sinless one, this leadership of the Gaṇas has been granted to you by the God of gods himself solely because of your own desire; therefore, I am well-pleased with you.
Furthermore, O son, it is because of your solar oblations and your excellent combat."
There was a great expenditure of wealth; for that reason, you were made preeminent. ||34||
Immortal, abandoned by old age, powerful even among the powerful, an ascetic, imperishable, and a conqueror—you shall become like Nandin. (35)
"You shall be dear to my Lord and also to me as his servant;

Thus addressed by Pārvatī, honored and esteemed by Andhaka,
and permitted by Pārvatī, he rejoiced as he remained at the side of Hara.
Having thus favored Andhaka, the god, whose ornaments were made of darkness,
sported at his pleasure upon that mountain.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Bestowing of Boons upon Andhaka," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said: Having made Andhaka a leader of the Gaṇas, Maheśvara, together with the Goddess, [departed].
Tell me what occurred after that; dispel my curiosity. ||1||
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, having then conquered Andhaka and made him the leader of his attendants,
the destroyer of the gods' afflictions sported together with the daughter of the Lord of Mountains.
Then the Mother of the Lord of Beings, who had assumed the form of the Six-faced One and was the best among those skilled in questioning, asked a question concerning her son.
For what purpose, O Lord, is this supreme verse sung by the virtuous:
"Five trees are better than ten granaries"? (4)
After piercing through the sixteen limbs of the embryo, the son is born;
therefore, how could a son born from the womb be superior to one born from a vessel? (5)
To Umā, who was thus inquiring about conduct, initiation, consecration, ritual action, and the intellect—
the peerless goddess— the God spoke these words:
"O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, O fair-faced one, this matter you ask about is subtle in its meaning."
I shall declare that to you, O daughter of the Lord of Mountains,
for a son born from the womb is superior to a son born from the earth;
[and I shall tell you of the sufferings] in the Śālmalī, the Vaitaraṇī, and the forests of sword-leaves.
In Kumbhīpāka, Raurava, and Mahāraurava,
as well as in other such hells,
those who are enveloped by their evil deeds are punished at the command of Death by Rākṣasas of cruel actions.
O Goddess, a virtuous son protects his ancestors when they are surrounded by terrible, inauspicious beings and afflicted by Rākṣasas; no one else who is resolved upon evil can do so.
Furthermore, it is not the case that all men possess virtuous sons.
In this world, there is truly only one [son] who protects his ancestors from fear;
those sons of wicked conduct do not attain the status of a son,
O King, just as a rogue bull or even a eunuch does not.
In this regard, it is further objected: "The wise know that suffering is hell;
because he protects his ancestors from that [suffering], he is therefore remembered as a *putra* (son). (13)
O Goddess, there is no other connector between both the father and the son;
therefore, the father protects the son, and the son protects him from fear.
But because of the power of the senses, O Pārvatī, they commit even sinful acts toward their sons; yet they become true sons indeed.
For these trees, O Goddess, have had their senses destroyed by the curse of Dakṣa.
They do not commit evil deeds, for they possess restrained senses.
For this reason, O Goddess, even from among a hundred sons born of the womb,
a single son born of the soil is praised, but not one born of the womb.
O sons, the night-stalkers are causing the trees—the fathers—to be cut down, split apart, terrified, and torn asunder. 18.
Uma said:
How do the trees ward off cutting, splitting, and terrifying by means of the hell-bound Rākṣasas for the ancestors in the abode of Yama? 1.9.
The God of Gods said:
"Listen, O daughter of the Naga, to how these trees endure the cutting and splitting in the abode of Yama, O delighter of the Nagas."
"O Goddess, these trees are devoid of effort and indeed destitute of sense organs;
they are sought after by the gods for sacrifices.
O Blessed One, by the curse of Dakṣa, our senses have indeed been impaired. (21–22)
Having reached a state of excessive darkness, inactive and unable to move about,
unhappy, deprived of our senses, and shrouded by a great gloom—
make us, who have fallen into this condition, endowed with righteousness.
Having heard these words of theirs, the god born from the waters, the Lord of Trees, spoke these words to the trees for the sake of the sacrificial tree:
"O immovable ones, welcome to you! I am pleased with those who seek refuge."
"O children, I shall destroy this darkness caused by Dakṣa’s curse."
Śāl trees, Bilvas, Palāśas, Varuṇas, and Kiṃśukas, as well as Rohītakas and whatever other trees originate from the components of sacrifice; ||| 26 ||
Having been well-employed in sacrifices as bark, leaves, fruits, and branches,
you shall attain radiant forms and dwell in my world.
"You too shall be followers of these sacrificial trees;
employed in sacrifice, go to the very same world as them.
And those [trees] used as *sthāṇu-liṅgas* by people preceded by devotion," || 28 ||
With bodies purified by dharma, you shall attain your desired goal;
and as you serve the objects of sacrifice in the sacrificial grounds,
freed from the darkness of Dakṣa’s curse, you shall wander in my world.
"Whatever man is bereft of a son, you shall provide him with sons; and you shall protect him from fear. Your dharma shall be great. (3.1)
The trees said:
"How can we be the sons of those fathers who have gone to hell—
those who sell Soma and those who are murderers of the trusting?"
Those who are intent on the slaughter of living beings, those who eat the flesh from the back [of animals],
those who revile kings, and those who steal the funeral offerings (piṇḍa)—
these are enveloped by their own terrible deeds that cause the hair to stand on end.
They are cooked in the terrible hell, crying out with terrifying sounds:
"Alas! We are violently assailed by inauspicious torments! (3.5)
They will be threatened with death by Rākṣasas of terrifying prowess;
how shall we rescue those very ancestors who are being tormented and beaten by the Rākṣasas, and who are submerged in hell?
Brahmā said:
"You shall deliver those ancestors who are being thus tormented and beaten by the Rākṣasas, and who are submerged in hell."
"O trees, listen with attentive minds to what I say: how you shall deliver these ancestors who dwell in hell.
You are of the nature of sons; to whomever you shall belong," [38] ||| "you will become his very sons."
O sinless ones, as soon as you remember him, you shall go to that place.

"...Understand this: how you shall sustain your ancestors who have fallen into hell and are tormented by sufferings, for their happiness, even as immobile beings, through the performance of the final consecration for you according to the rules and with mantras. (8.158.40)

Having performed the rites beginning with the conception ceremony (*garbhādhāna*), a man may designate [others] as his sons. Furthermore, those who have been previously born and are without possessions— whom you shall make into sons according to the prescribed rule— you will cause them to cross over [to liberation].
"You shall grant all desires and likewise supreme happiness;
you shall effect the exhaustion of karma for all and likewise grant imperishable worlds.

Then, when the sun had set behind the western peak with its hundred thousand rays,

Where learned Brahmins who know the mantras do not consume the supreme oblation,

For him, nothing is spilled, nothing is disturbed, and darkness does not overcome him.
This is the most excellent of all gifts: that which is offered into the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa. || 51 ||
In the state of being a *brahman*, O Great Being, the element of food (*anna-dhātu*) is for consumption.
Because he consumes the *brahman*, he is therefore remembered as a *brāhmaṇa*. Furthermore, those who are born again—having been consecrated by high-souled men—are [true *brāhmaṇas*].
Therefore, O Goddess, the name "dvija" is eternally applied to them.
The word *viyat* refers to the sky (*vyoman*), and the verbal root *div* is traditionally remembered in the sense of "attaining.
Since these Brahmins cause others to attain heaven (*divam*), they are therefore known as *vipras*, O Goddess. ||53-54||
For these Brahmins were created by the Self-born One as being composed of the essence of truth;
success cannot be attained when they are displeased, even by the gods themselves. ||55||
"I am Nārāyaṇa, Ananta, Brahmā, Śakra, Anila, and Agni;
we do not rejoice in that gift, O Brahmins, in which you are not honored.
Through your grace, long life, dharma, strength, and happiness are easily obtained."
A wise man should honor those Brahmins for the sake of prosperity, fame, and residence in heaven.
Then, having invited the Brahmins, she—clad in pure garments and possessing a pure smile—should lie down upon the ground strewn with Darbha grass, having offered her salutations. 57–58.
Having passed that night, when the sun has risen,
he should take food— both solid and soft— and go to where the tree may be.
Then, having adorned it with banners, a parasol, and ornaments, [he should proceed].
Having made a bower of creepers, the young woman followed the shade of the tree.
Having fed the best of the twice-born with whatever food was available,
and having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made— either by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) or by himself—
he should [disclose] his own true intention to the satisfied Brahmins.
Having made this announcement with supreme sincerity for the sake of the highest goal, she said:
"O Blessed Ones, I am childless; I shall take this tree which has the nature of a son. O sinless ones, you ought to grant me permission to do so."
Then, O beloved, having been authorized by them, one should take that young tree as a son in the presence of the gods of the earth.
O Goddess, by this rite, the tree-like son who has been accepted rains down honey and Soma for the ancestors dwelling in hell.
"O fair-browed one, this son of the Earth has been taken according to this rite;
when auspicious, he brings happiness, but by the contrary method, he bestows suffering. (66)
O Goddess, O moon-faced one, even compared to a hundred virtuous sons, a single tree planted as a son is considered superior in the status of a son. (67)
Thus has this excellent instruction been taught by me to you in clear words;
just as the son born from the earth is superior to the son born from the womb.
Then the goddess of gods, having again prostrated before Maheśvara, spoke these words out of affection and curiosity: ||69||
"O Lord of Gods, while I was wandering on Mount Mandara during your absence, I beheld an Ashoka tree, tender and most beautiful. (8.158.70)
And at that time, this thought occurred to me: "When Rudra has returned without obstacle, this young tree shall become my son. (71)
And from these two breasts of mine, O Mahādeva, purifier of the twice-born, milk has flowed—a stream of nectar that bestows happiness through maternal affection for my son. (72)
O Lord, I would take that tree which is like a son to me, if you would grant me your permission; I am under your command. (73)
When the gods cast it as the fruit of a son, that young tree-shoot was indeed granted to me; for, O sinless one, it shall become a son who grants joy to me, who am childless.

While Bhavānī was speaking thus, the blessed Lord Bhava, the scorcher of enemies, spoke these words that issued from his true nature: ity evaṃ bhāṣamāṇāṃ tu bhavānīṃ bhagavān bhavaḥ | sadbhāvān niḥsṛtaṃ vākyam avadat paratāpanaḥ ||75||
O Goddess, with eyes like full-blown lotuses, how indeed could my son not become the supreme sovereign of this ascetic woman? (76)
"O blameless lady, you are capable of procreating sons through your ascetic power;
and I, too, shall grant you most excellent sons. (77)
Or rather, O beloved, this Ashoka tree is to be favored by you;
O Queen, permitted by me, make the Ashoka tree your son. (78)
Recognizing her husband to be well-disposed toward her, that lotus-eyed woman, satisfied and bowing down to the imperishable Maheśvara, spoke this: 79.
"O King, I know the dharma that for women there exists no deity to be worshipped other than the husband who must be honored. (8.158.80)
"For whatever a woman gives or worships without first addressing her husband, she does not obtain the fruit thereof; such indeed have we heard. (81)
But that woman who, honoring her husband, practices her duty— O Lord, the gods are pleased with her, and her merit is exceedingly great.
However, that woman who disregards her husband, who is her deity and her guru...
She who performs meritorious acts according to her own intellect falls into hell;
yet that beautiful woman who, even regarding a husband who has passed away, consults him as if he were still living, honoring him in the proper manner. || 83–84 ||
For she, O Lord of the Gods, being authorized by him with a joyful heart, obtains abundant fruit in the performance of religious duties:
austerity, fasting, charity, uprightness, and truthfulness itself. || 8.5 ||
These do not equal even a sixteenth part of the service rendered to a husband.
For she who, though fickle toward other men, performs service for her husband with true devotion while on his bed or seat, she alone is truly recognized as virtuous.

Having thus spoken to the Lord of the Mountains on the mountain peak, which was variegated with heaps of flowers from the mountain trees, the beautiful Bhavānī wandered with him, like the radiance of the sun together with the sun itself. (88)
Thus, those two, honored by the gods and honoring one another,
wandered together, revered by the foremost lords.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sons of Bhūmija," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having understood Pārvatī’s resolve, the Lord Tryambaka,
the best among those skilled in speech, then addressed the yakṣa Sumāli Piṅgala.
There, the Lord Śaṅkara himself will take as his son Nandin, who stands by his side— a devotee, a great yogi, a Gaṇa who previously received boons,
and who shall remove the sorrow of the daughter of the Mountain King.
And all that is dependent upon you; therefore, act according to my command.
O Hero, O Lord of the Gaṇas, act in such a way that where the Aśoka tree stands, abundant food may be found there,
and that the region of that mountain shall become delightful. (4)
O Lord of Yakṣas, act in such a way that [the tree] where the Aśoka tree stands [is protected]. ||5||
Thus addressed by the Supreme Lord, Piṅgala, who had tawny eyes,
spoke together with Somā to the Lord of the gods.
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, O Destroyer of Sacrifices, I shall do exactly as you have commanded, so that Soma and Nandin will both be gracious toward me. (7)
Having spoken thus and being permitted by him, that Yakṣa, who dwells in another world,
then fashioned an excellent seat at the side of that Aśoka tree.
When Sumālā had departed, the three-eyed Siṃhakrodha,
a mass of splendor, spoke to Nandin and Diṇḍi, O Caṇḍeśvara.
"O highly intelligent one, tomorrow at dawn, the goddess Nandin will worship the Brahmins who are devoted to the Veda with a sacrifice; for that, there is need for the Brahmins. (8.159.10)
Therefore, O Lord, sent by me, go wherever I tell you and,
having arrived there, invite the brahmins to three places.
In the watery realm, O Virūpākṣa, there are Brahmins born of Brahmā who,
dwelling in the depths of the netherworld, worship Varuṇa.
Invite without delay those known as the *phenapa* (foam-drinkers), including the gods, *asuras*, and others, who drink the supreme essence of the rasa.
Likewise, O Lord of Beings, invite those Brāhmaṇas who dwell in Saṃyamanī and wait upon Yama; they are equal to Brahmā himself.
Likewise, on the peak of the mountain of sunrise, there is a great lake named Satya, frequented by royal swans and covered with lovely lotuses. (15)
There dwell those virtuous ones, whose wealth is their austerity, who are truly named "Truthful," and by whose truth the sun perpetually conducts its course through the day.
Having bathed in that lake, the stainless Lord Divākara, the performer of auspicious deeds, makes his daily departure from it. (17)
Having bowed to them with your head and having offered yourself to them,
O Nandīśvara, invite them while displaying your true devotion before them.
And those Atharvāṅgirases who constantly travel surrounding the chariot of the Sun— invite that host of twice-born ones as well.
And those perfected ones who wander with wheels, those who subsist by gleaning like pigeons,
and those who worship Śakra— invite all those twice-born men.
Then, having gone to the assembly hall of Brahmā, invite those who are devoted to Brahman and dear to Brahmā,
as well as Brahmā himself with his consort and the Brāhmaṇas.
"Invite the Bālakhilyas, who dwell on the shores of the Ocean of Milk and reside in the forest of asceticism, after they have come from the abode of Brahmā. (22)
Those who, together with their wives, sons, and the implements for the *agnihotra* sacrifice, are my devotees—to them I am eternally well-disposed in my grace, being their foremost leader. (23)
O Lord of Speech, O husband of Suyaśas, having become illustrious yourself, address those Bālakhilyas who are as difficult to approach as venomous serpents.
Moving through the three worlds like the unimpeded wind,
invite all those brahmins whomsoever you see from there.
And whatever Pramathas there are within your range, O slayers of the enemies of the gods, may they all come as servers of food for the Brahmins. (26)
Thus addressed by Kapardin, Nandin, who possessed a radiance equal to the sun,
raised his flaming trident and set out for the abode of Varuṇa—
the ocean, which has the sky as its garment and whose range of vision extends to the heavens.
He approached him as he was leaping about like an elephant in an arena;
that leader of the Pramathas entered the ocean crowded with hundreds of whales, just as the blazing sun enters a mass of clouds. || 28-29 ||
On the surface of the earth and in Pātāla, he of the prowess of the lord of elephant-kings beheld the Earth flowing with divine milk, that very source of nectar.
Having saluted Surabhi, Nandin, a follower of Śaṅkara, entered here where Varuṇa dwells, honored along with his attendants. || 3.1 ||
He saw Varuṇa, the guardian of the waters, accompanied by his hosts of sons and grandsons, adorned with celestial garments and ornaments, and resplendent like ten thousand suns;
he was announced beforehand by the gatekeeper.
Then Nandin entered the abode of Varuṇa.

And King Varuṇa himself, seeing Nandin from afar, rose up as if greatly delighted, honoring him who subdues the god of love. Having personally offered him the guest-water, a cow, and water for his feet—
To him as he sat, the protector of the waters, the best among speakers, asked:
"O Blessed One, why have you waited for us for so long today?
We consider the sight of you to be the very sight of the God of gods."
O sinless one, your face appears like that of one desiring to speak, as if filled with indragopa insects;
tell me all your intentions, for I shall accomplish them—of this there is no doubt.
Thus addressed by Varuṇa, who was intent upon that task, the son of Śilāda then spoke to Varuṇa,
who had been unconquered by the Dānavas:
"The daughter of the mountain will take as her husband your son, Aśokataruka."
Hara invites you along with Umā for the sake of sport.
Therefore, O God, surrounded by your sons, accompanied by your wife, and together with the Phena-pas,
go tomorrow to Mount Mandara and increase the joy of the wielder of the trident.
Having spoken thus and being permitted by Varuṇa, that lord of the Gaṇas emerged from Varuṇa’s abode like the sun from a white cloud. ||41||
Being honored by the Siddhas, the Cāraṇas, and even the gods,
Nandin reached the Mountain of Sunrise, just as the arrow of Hara reached Tripura.
Then, upon that mountain peak reddened by the scorching rays [of the sun],
the bird Garuḍa alighted like a gust of wind in the path of the atmosphere.
There he saw a lake resembling the ocean, adorned with golden lotuses.

He saw that lake, rich with waves of withered lotuses and surrounded by celestial nymphs. On the shores of that lake, among thousands of *aśoka* trees, he beheld truthful sages who resembled ten thousand suns. || 44-45 ||
Seeing those ascetics, who were as radiant as the sun,
Nandin approached them with palms joined in reverence and saluted the twice-born ones. Those ascetics, though established in their vows, set aside their formal observances to greet him.
They gathered around Nandin, as birds flock to a tree that provides shelter;
surrounded by them— who were tanned by the sun’s rays and clad in yellow garments— Nandin shone like Jambudvīpa encircled by mountains.
Being thus honored by the truthful ones whose wealth is asceticism, that leader of the hosts, Satya,
shone exceedingly, O Vyāsa, like Maheśvara at sacred fords.
Those truthful ones, whose wealth was asceticism, [approached] Satya as he sat comfortably upon Nandin.
With faces and eyes wide with wonder, they spoke words agitated by joy.
O Nandīśvara, after a long time, today indeed there is a rising, a rising radiance;
for by you, dear one, [this place] has been overcome through righteousness, just as hell is by dharma.
"O sinless one, has the Lord of Gods—the three-eyed destroyer of Tripura—come here for recreation?
Was that deity seen by us, and then were you seen?
O Lord of the Gaṇas, our penance has been well-performed, pure, and true."
"Accompanied by you, we shall behold Śaṅkara here. ||53||
Thus the son of Śilāda, whose speech was truth, spoke these words to the ascetics who were bowing like the lord of monkeys:
"The Unborn One would never, under any circumstances, abandon Mount Mandara."
I have come to this hermitage of yours on account of some business.
The Daughter of the Mountain will take the Aśoka tree as her son;
there Śarva invites all of you, O best of the twice-born. Honoring Bhava along with Ambā, all of you go quickly to the Lord of Ambā.
"O you who are constant in austerity, go tomorrow to Mandara, the upholder of the earth."
"There you shall behold Śarva, the lord of the immortals, the sovereign, the auspicious one adorned by the moon,
the Lord who crushes the asuras, the remover of all the afflictions of the gods, the destroyer.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Summoning of the Brahmins during the Seizing of the Tree-Sons," in the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having taken leave of all those ṛṣis, who were endowed with truth, heroism, fame, and sacred learning,
Nandin was dismissed by them and departed toward the chariot of the Sun.
At the command of Hara, that lord of beings approached the divine Sun with those seven excellent horses and that best of birds as his charioteer.
He saw those ascetics, who subsisted on rays of light, seated comfortably amidst thousands of sunbeams like birds in the shade. (3)
Then, having quickly approached the chariot of the Sun, which has Aruṇa as its charioteer,
he [beheld] the garlanded one (the Sun), Atri, and also Atharvan and Aṅgiras.
Then the auspicious Nandin invited the gods, sages, serpents, and horses, along with the Ādityas, Aśvins, and others, desiring to please Rudra. 5.
Having said "So be it," the Lord of Beings then quickly departed from Sūryavāha,
after taking leave of the gods, the ṛṣis, and the serpents.
Swift as the wind or like Garuḍa, the bird of prey,
Nandin reached Kailāsa, the abode of the Lord of Wealth.
Beholding that mountain, the abode of the Giver of Wealth, which shone like white clouds and possessed the luster of kunda flowers, the moon, and silver, he rejoiced.
That Lord of Beings, who carries out the words of the Lord of Mountains, [remained there].
He reached a beautiful golden palace on the summit of the mountain;
it was situated upon the peak of Kailāsa and possessed a splendor equal to the peak of Kailāsa itself, endowed with mansions and palaces, shining as if it were perfectly complete. || 8.160.10 ||
It resounded day and night with banners and flags adorned with rows of tinkling bells, with the laughter of the city-dwellers,
and with the blaring of hundreds of most terrible drums and musical instruments.
The members of the assembly here are perfected in sacrifice and Vedic study. || 12 ||
Then he reached that assembly hall of Rudra, graced with splendors,
where the son of the sage Viśravas was seated;
he saw him endowed with supreme prosperity and likewise attended by divine fortune.
Nandin beheld the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), attended by throngs of celestial women.
O lady with eyes as long as a single tawny bee, you were surrounded by the lords of the yakṣas whose ears were like mother-of-pearl, while being sung to by the gandharvas. ||15||
Intoxicated by his friendship with Maheśvara and by the pride of granting boons, he was adorned with a pure and shimmering necklace of gold.
And Dhanada, seeing that excellent follower of Śaṅkara, quickly rose from his seat while worshipping Śaṅkara and Soma. (18)
Rising from his golden throne,
Dhanada shone like the sun emerging from a lofty mountain rich in flowers and adorned with Aśoka trees.
As he sprang up, the Yakṣas quickly leapt after the lord of the Yakṣas,
just as blazing planets follow the lord of the planets at the waning of the day.
Then, having offered that guest-water and water for the feet to Nandin, the bestower of wealth,
together with his sons, wife, and ministers, bowed mentally to Hara.
Then, after engaging in various kinds of conversation concerning Maheśvara, Dhanada asked Nandin why he had taken so long to arrive. Nandin said:
"The daughter of the mountain will take the son of the Aśoka tree."
There, the Great Lord, the Master of Wealth, invites you.
"Tomorrow, O Lord of Wealth, go to Mandara together with your sons, your wife, your followers, and the hosts of Apsaras; the Lord of Gods is pleased with you."
Having thus addressed the Giver of Wealth, and being dismissed by the Giver of Wealth, Nandin, who resembled Yama himself, went to Saṃyamanī, the city of Yama. ||24||
That leader of the hosts saw Yama, the proclaimer of dharma, the lord who takes away living beings, together with Agni, Dharma, and Vyādhi. ||25||
Seeing Nandin approaching, Yama, surrounded by hundreds of spirits, fell at Nandin’s feet and was filled with joy;
indeed, having performed unsurpassed worship for him as if for Rudra himself, Yama [honored him]. ||26||
He inquired of Nandin with great effort why he had taken so long to arrive.
Nandin said:
"The daughter of the mountain will take the Aśoka tree as her son;
there, the divine Śaṅkara invites you along with your followers."
And the god, having honored them with great respect, addressed those twice-born ones who dwell within this realm.
"Since the Blessed One is healthy and the time is auspicious, you ought to go to Mount Mandara, honoring the Lord Īśāna who is fond of the mountain.
Having been addressed thus by Yama and by those twice-born ones who were like fire, [Yudhiṣṭhira agreed].
From the abode of the son of the Sun, Nandin then went to the world of Śakra;
he quickly entered that wonderful world of Vāsava, the dwelling place of the virtuous, just as the slayer of serpents (Garuḍa) enters the womb of Diti.
In the Sudharmā assembly hall,
Nandin beheld Śakra, who was surrounded by the immortals and listening to celestial music;
and Śakra, in turn, saw the god Nandin, the servant of the God of gods.
Out of joy, he brought [the vision] before his thousand eyes and beheld it perfectly.

Having received worship from the Lord of the Gods that was equal to that given to Rudra, he of immeasurable soul sat upon an excellent seat near Śakra. As he sat there, the subduer of enemies, the performer of a hundred sacrifices, approached him.
Drinking with his thousand eyes, he did not reach satiety.
Then Vṛtrabalarī, with joy, questioned Nandin, who possessed the splendor of the sun: "Why have you come after such a long time?"
Thus addressed by the god who dwells in heaven,
the wielder of the thunderbolt, his mind perfumed by the Mandāra flowers, spoke without agitation:
"The daughter of the mountain will take as her son the offspring of the Aśoka tree."
There, the Lord, the protector of beings, invites you along with the gods.
Śaṅkara also invites those twice-born ones who were previously there, as well as those who now dwell in your abode, together with their sons and wives.
"O Lord of Gods, accompanied by your wife and son, go to Mount Mandara at the command of the God of gods and greet the Lord of Mountains.
O best of deities, when you have gone there for the festival of the Ashoka tree,"

The Lord of the Gods, the remover of the suffering of gods and men, will attain supreme joy. Having prostrated before the powerful Maheśa— the wielder of the sharp trident and the Pināka bow, the husband of the daughter of the king of mountains— you shall once again return to the assembly of heaven.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "The Addressing of the Brahmins," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been granted permission by Śakra, Nandin, the leader of the Pramathas, [proceeded].
The one of great splendor set his mind upon going to the abode of Brahmā. || 1 ||
In a mere moment, that attendant of the Four-faced One, possessing great speed like the wind of great velocity, reached the Vairāja abode. ||2||
The radiant Nandin entered that assembly hall, which was free from fatigue like Mount Meru, just as a ray of the sun enters it.
Nandi beheld that assembly hall, which was like a story full of wonderful meanings, endowed with many diverse subjects, and filled with great marvels;
therein he saw him seated with the ascetics in a wondrous manner.
Nandin beheld the lotus-born Brahmā, surrounded by five deities, expounding the meaning of the Vedas to ascetics who were questioning him;
and he heard all those masters of the Bhāṣya exclaiming, "Excellent! as they spoke.
Nandin quickly and properly worshipped the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Then the Grandfather spoke to Nandin, the leader of the Gaṇas:
"Why have you come so late? And he replied to him.
The daughter of the mountain will take Aśokataruka as her son.
There, O Blessed One, the god Śaṅkara invites you, as well as these [sages] who shine like fire through their asceticism, who possess the Vedas, and who proclaim the Vedic teachings. || 8-9 ||
The Lord of Gods, having invited ten million sacrifices, invites you along with all the ascetics to Mandara, to its variegated caves.
O giver of honor, go; thus does the Unborn One command the gods.
Having heard these words of Nandin,
the Grandfather (Brahmā), whose nature was joyful, spoke thus to him who is fond of recitation:
"O Nandīśvara, go forth safely and without obstacle."
I too shall come to Śiva's presence along with these;
and this Aśoka shall be released from the darkness caused by Dakṣa’s curse.
"The goddess who is the daughter of Himavat will take this boy as her son.
Having been addressed thus, the leader of the gods, honoring the Lord, [departed] from the beloved of the Lord.
He quickly went from the abode of Brahmā to the Ocean of Milk;
he reached the shore of the ocean, which was like a garland for the sea yet devoid of its usual blossoms,
that formidable boundary presided over by the foremost assembly of the lords of the Gaṇas.
The leader of the hosts saw the Brahmins dwelling on the shore, the Vālakhilyas rich in asceticism,
who were engaged in various observances;
and seeing him, Gaṇeśa, the lord of great fame, bowing down, [he greeted him].
Those whose wealth is asceticism rejoiced with favorable blessings;
standing in their midst, Nandi shone amidst the delighted ascetics.
Just as the moon situated in the midst of the planets of gentle form [is honored], so too,
having worshipped the god Nandin with the offering of water for the feet, the arghya, and the bestowing of fruits, the Bālakhilyas spoke to him.
O Lord of the Pramathas, why have you come here after such a long time?
O Lord of the Gods, shall we behold Bhava, the husband of Ambā, together with Ambā?
Then Nandin, the most excellent lord of the Pramathas, addressed these words, adorned with formal courtesy, to the best of the twice-born in that assembly of brahmins.
"O ascetics rich in penance, Lord Śaṅkara, accompanied by Ambikā, does not come here to Mandara; hear from me the reason for his not coming here. (22)
The Daughter of the Mountain will take Aśokataruka as her son;
there, the divine Śaṅkara, the Lord of Cattle, invites you.
"Tomorrow, O foremost of Brahmins, all of you, together with your wives, disciples, sons, and sacred fires, go to Mandara and show favor to me and my mother."
Thus addressed by Nandin, the great sages, the Bālakhilyas,
spoke these words to Gaṇeśa with intense devotion toward the Lord.
"O Nandin, we shall come tomorrow at dawn, O Lord;
go without hindrance to Mount Mandara with its beautiful caves.
Thus addressed and honored by the Bālakhilyas, he [departed].
Having invited all those best of the twice-born to his three-footed throne,
he returned once more to Mount Mandara,
where he remained together with the Goddess.
Then, having approached the Lord of Beings, the master of the worlds and of the gods, the boon-granter of Kubera, who was like a bee at the lotus-face of the Daughter of the Mountain—
Then Gaṇapatīnātha spoke this:
"Those brahmins who move about in heaven and on earth,
endowed with tranquility, self-control, restraint, purity, and courage— "
O subduer of Tripura, O destroyer of Kāla, all of them have been invited by me at your word. (29)
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Invitation of the Brahmins for the Seizing of the Tree-Son," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: When the Brahmins had been invited to the three steps of Nārāyaṇa...
Then, when Nandin, the leader of the hosts of the Gaṇas, had departed, the Blessed One— the destroyer of the sacrifice and the desires of Kama, the shatterer of Pūṣan’s teeth,
the garlanded one, the crowned one, the powerful one, Time itself— spoke these words at the proper time.
"O Ambikā, all Brāhmaṇas in the world are equal to a Brāhmaṇa.
Being invited, O lady of beautiful hips, do that which is in your heart.
Wherever that Aśoka tree stands, there your son shall be."
There, O beloved, Piṅgala, the giver of food, prepared the meal.
O Goddess, O Daughter of the Mountain King, act in such a way that tomorrow at dawn we may go to the side of the Ashoka tree together with Nandin, O Joyful One.

O Mother of the World, O Daughter of the Mountain, for the sake of your own welfare, this entire universe— including the sky, the waters, and the netherworld— shall indeed be condensed into that [liṅga].
And while Nandin was thus addressing the best of the twice-born,
he stepped upon the three strides of Nārāyaṇa that had been traversed by Trivikrama.
"Therefore, O lady of excellent hips, O most excellent one, O giver of boons,
O granter of boons, I shall grant you a boon, O beloved, if it is pleasing to you.
Then the Goddess [spoke to] Hara, the lord of heaven, the master of Dindimunda.
She spoke to her beloved, the granter of boons, who was adorned with the crescent moon.
This god Nandīśvara is our supreme benefactor;
he deserves thousands of millions of boons from you, without a doubt.
"For you are the granter of boons to the worlds, and indeed the Lord of the worlds. If you are pleased, O Lord of the Mountain, grant a supreme boon.
Then the god Kṛttivāsas, having smelled the head of Nandin, [bestowed it].
He said to the Lord of the Pramathas, "Let the desired boon be chosen."
Then Nandin, the beloved of Śaṅkara, whose face was like that of the lord of monkeys and whose splendor resembled that of the lord of the gods, bowed his head and said:
"O Lord of Gods, by your power I am a granter of boons, free from old age and death."

I am wealthy and honored by the gods, dānavas, and kinnaras who are themselves worthy of worship. O Śarva, what need have I for a boon, since I behold your feet—which are worshipped by millions of boons and adored by the Pramathas—along with those of Ambā? || 14–15 ||
"O Lord of the Cows, if you are pleased with this boon of mine,
O Maheśvara, let my devotion toward you and Sāmba be eternal.
And let me be the lord of the hosts of those disciplined ones who are superior to me, O Lord of the Gaṇas."
"O best of gods, what more than this will you do for me?"—thus spoke Nandin as he bowed;
then the three-eyed god, who has the moon as his crest-jewel, looked upon him with affection. (17–18)
Then, having wiped [his face] with a hand as blue as a lotus, the Blessed Lord Hara spoke with joy, greatly gladdening Nandin:
"O Nandin, you are devoted to me, together with your wife and the refuge of your attendants."
And placing that devotion foremost, I have kept you by my side.

O Lord of the Gaṇas, compared to truth, dharma, austerity, charity, cows, and the Vedas— compared to all these, you are dearer to me. O Lord of the World, whoever shall proclaim your name at dawn, [for him you will grant his desires].
He shall obtain the full fruit of a horse-sacrifice properly performed.
And whoever hates you, though he be devoted to dharma, is hateful to me;
whereas he who is dear to you shall always be dear to me.
"For that man who, having uttered 'Salutation to Nandīśvara,' shall go to sleep,
there shall indeed be no fear from the kings of the Kuṣmāṇḍas.
As he was speaking thus, [he offered] this hymn of praise to the virtues of Nandīśvara.
The extremely fierce twilight, the body of Brahmā, drew near.
The Lord, the knower of time, who is Time itself and the destroyer of Time, observed that the hour for dancing had arrived and considered it the proper moment. Then,
having performed his ablutions with water, the Creator and Protector of the three worlds [prepared to depart].
The Blessed One sat through the twilight, protecting the established order of the world.
With his hands outstretched and his knees placed upon the ground,
the Lord appeared like the sun in the sky with its rays spread abroad.
Having recited that supreme mantra, which is born from the essence of the three Vedas,
Bhava, dancing skillfully and gracefully with four faces,
saw his lord dancing with hands like tender sprouts extended.
The queen, his partner in dharma, danced with her husband.
Seeing the couple dancing, Nandin, the leader of the Gaṇas,
then began to dance with loud laughter, bringing joy to the two deities.
Having beheld the God, Ambā, and Nandin dancing,
the Pramathas, who resemble dark clouds, began to dance to the sounds of musical instruments.
Then there were kettledrums, jharjharas, kikhis, ānakas, and maṇḍukas.
Kettledrums, ḍiṇḍimas, and conch shells resounded loudly.
Again and again Ambikā performed a graceful dance;
Nandin let out a laugh, and the Pramathas roared loudly.
That place was rich with the sounds of excellent musical instruments and filled with the tumultuous roar of Śiva’s thunderbolt.
The fierce face of twilight shone like the mouth of the submarine fire.
Some danced and laughed, while others muttered prayers;
and still others sang most sweetly like Gandharvas, the attendants of the Lord.
Then, upon the surface of the sky, there appeared the exceedingly pure, full orb of the moon.
For when the moon, the lord of deer, has risen, he whose ornament is a digit of the moon [appears]. ||37||
Having completed the observance, the Lord, accompanied by Ambā and the attendants of Nandīśa,
ceased from that festival and spoke thus to Pārvatī:
Having stayed this night, O you of immeasurable prowess,
tomorrow you shall take up your son, the Ashoka tree,
from the earth where Darbha grass grows— she who supports the world, the Earth herself.
At the word of the god, she who was firm in her vow slept for one night.
Then, when the sun, the thousand-rayed one, had risen,
he said to Umā, "Let us go to where that son of yours, Aśoka, is."
Then the blessed Dhanyā, the giver of wealth, honored by the Giver of Wealth,
said to Bhava, "Let us go," while her ornaments tinkled;
and the Blessed One, the protector of trees, [proceeded] on foot toward the tree.
Accompanied by Nandin and Ambikā, Hara reached the Aśoka tree.
There he saw the tawny Yakṣa, who resembled a blazing fire, together with his Pramatha attendants, as he was preparing food and distributing it. 43–44.
Then, the lord, the best among those who know the stars, beheld there heaps resembling mountains of food to be chewed, swallowed, sucked, and licked. ||45||
Then, seeing the food prepared by the Yakṣa, the wielder of the Pināka bow,
together with Ambikā and Nandin, experienced incomparable joy.
Thereafter, the divine Grandfather, along with the gods, Apsarases, and serpents, [arrived].
Having become joyful, he went there, where the husband of Ambā and Ambikā resided.
Having prostrated before Mahādeva, those gods, honored by him,
then surrounded that Aśoka tree and spoke these words in the presence of Hara:
"From this day forward, may this tree be endowed with every form of happiness."
O denizens of heaven, he shall be liberated from the darkness of Dakṣa’s curse;
he shall become immortal, freed from old age, and devoid of all suffering;
he shall be enriched with every ornament and flower, and endowed with every fragrance and flavor.
He shall indeed be the granter of all desires, with flowers and fruits appearing at will; of this there is no doubt, and he will be very dearly beloved by the Goddess. 51.

Sanatkumāra said: Then the Lord of the Mountains, the destroyer of the distress of those who bow before him and the granter of desires, spoke to the daughter of the Mountain King: "Behold these mountains of food."
Beholding those towering mounds of food and drink, resembling mountains,
Piṅgala, the son of Guhā, the lord of the gods, was deeply gratified;
so too was Parvata’s daughter toward Sumālin, the foremost of Yakṣas, and Piṅgala.
Maheśvara joined her with the granting of a boon and said to her:
"O Goddess, all this excellent food—both that which is chewed and that which is eaten—is ready for you.
Perform whatever task you desire; why do you remain sitting?"
Then she, exceedingly joyful and dwelling in celestial raiment,
having obtained permission from Śaṅkara, the Lord of the World, who possesses the speed of thought—
that goddess who bestows sorrow upon the Daityas became the night Aśokā (the "Sorrowless" one). ||56||

With affection, she adorned him with various kinds of ornaments. And before him, the Daughter of the Mountain raised a parasol illuminated by strings of pearls, together with peacock feathers. || 57–58 ||
And with fragrant sandalwood paste of various colors, the queen marked her body from head to foot with excellent streaks. (59)
And with bands made of Jāmbūnada gold, adorned with jewels,
she decorated her beloved Aśoka tree on all sides. Upon its branches and twigs, Pārvatī [hung] strings of pearls.
He shone with them bound upon him, like the moon with the stars. ||61||
Then Guhāraṇi, the mother of the worlds who yearned for her son, clothed that Aśoka tree with pairs of white garments. || 62 ||
Then, she who grants boons to the gods offered incense consisting of *śrīveṣṭaka*, *nameru*, *guggulu*, and clarified butter all combined together.
Then, with the sounding of conchs and the noise of divine musical instruments, [she worshipped].
Bali’s wife performed austerities.
As she was thus worshipping that tree, which shone with the luster of nectar from the moon and was adorned with pearl necklaces,
milk flowed from her breasts due to the intensity of her maternal affection for her son.
That Aśoka tree, the illuminator of the forest, was worshipped by Umā.
He shone exceedingly there, like a handsome man in the springtime.
He caused the Brahmins, who were equal to Brahmā himself and had been brought by Nandinātha,
to recite the *puṇyāha* (auspicious day) benediction, having given them whatever they desired.
Then, at the conclusion of both the proclamation of the *puṇyāha* and the bestowing of blessings—
Having obtained her husband’s permission, the queen spoke to those seers:
"O venerable ones, I am childless; today I shall take this son from the Ashoka tree. You ought to grant me your consent."
To the goddess Pārvatī, who was speaking thus and longing for a son, all the twice-born spoke together: "Take [a boon] according to your desire."
Then the divine sound of the conch shell, accompanied by the sounds of all musical instruments, resounded,
filling the entire threefold domain of Nārāyaṇa.
While the Brahmins were chanting the Vedas, throngs of Apsarases danced;
and all the Pramathas, along with the Gandharvas and great serpents, raised a roar.
And the six seasons, exulting with their respective collections of flowers, adorned both the Aśoka tree and that circle of deities. || 73 ||
The gods, filled with joy, behold that festival at the Aśoka tree, where celestial music is played and throngs of Apsarases dance. (74)
Playing his kacchapī lute, Nārada—the best among lute-players—dances with joy like a fire fanned by the wind. (75)
Adored by those whose wealth is asceticism and by the gods who honor the Giver of Wealth (Kubera),
she shone there like the radiance of the sun. Then,
having completed her religious observances and taking the aśoka sapling, she departed.
The daughter of the Lord of Mountains shines like the earth sprinkled with water. ||77||
Then, commanded by Nandīśvara, those thousands of Pramathas,
who are devoted to Brahmins, quickly offered their own seats to the Brahmins.
There arose the sound of seats made of gold, silver, and radiant crystal, being strewn about by the Pramathas. ||79||
The roar of the Pramathas, who bore seats made of great *kuśa* grass as if they were the peaks of Mount Meru,
resounded like the thundering of clouds that have shed their rain and are free from desire.
With their weapons resting on their shoulders, held in their hands, or even placed upon their heads,
the Pramathas shone like mountains with the sun and fire;
some brought them quickly, while others bore them.
Those Pramathas, joyful in appearance and possessing great seats, were seated;
each was a hundred yojanas in extent, with an interval of one yojana between them.
A row of unattached seats was thus constructed by Viśvakarman.
On the auspicious back of Mount Mandara, they emerged from the rows of Brahmins. ||84||
When all those [streams] had emerged from the heat, they drenched them like clouds at the time of the rains;
having bathed, their seats and ornaments shone like a path seen after rain.
Those thousand rows [of seats] were spread out upon Mount Mandara.
Having summoned the twice-born, who were anointed with yakṣa-unguents mixed with mud, adorned with crests and garlands of flowers, and standing ready with uplifted [offerings],
[he honored them] with mandāra, santāna, and likewise pāribhadra trees.
And the twice-born ones, accompanied by their wives, shone like gods amidst the breezes. ||88||
Then the gods scattered very fine, fragrant, and golden-hued scented powders all around those gods of the earth (the Brahmins).
Marked with divine sandalwood paste, they were sprinkled with divine powders.
The Brahmins shone, gathered together in one place like fires in a single spot.
Having caused divine incense to be wafted everywhere, and having issued a command to me in every respect,
the servants of Śaṅkara then provided hand-washing for a moment, which was as clear as crystal and as fragrant as the pollen of lotuses. ||91||
Then those heroes, girding their loins like elephants with girths fastened,
began to surround the bull-like Brahmins.
There were vessels made of gold, silver, and crystal.
In a moment, the gods humbly gave [the gifts] to the twice-born. || 93 ||
Having repeatedly seized the sky, the staff, and the circle of waters,
they properly provided foods to be chewed, eaten, and drunk, as well as drinks, on all sides;
likewise, they took possession of meaningful cities, forts, and royal capitals.

The lords of the Pramathas gave water that increases virtue—situated in their eyes, situated in their hearts, situated in their mouths, and indicated by their hands—to the Brahmins and the wise; some offered this water from golden ewers. || 95-96 ||

Even while pointing out the way, these Pramathas, joyful and fanning the Brahmins with fragrant whisks as white as moonbeams, said, "Water! Water! [97] They were like the wind itself to those engaged in austerity.
Divine celestial women dwelling in the three worlds serve each one of those Brahmins there, just as they serve Vāsava;
and hosts of Apsarases, adorned with every ornament, [attend them]. || 98-99 ||
Viśvāvasu, Nārada, Tumburu, and Parvata likewise danced, stealing away the minds of the gods in every direction. (8.162.1) 100.
Kustumburu, Śāliśiras, Parjanya, Gaṇḍamaṇḍaka,
Citrāṅgada, Citrasena, Citra, and Citraratha—
these are the Gandharvas of the gods who delight in musical instruments and are dear to Hara.
Upon divine instruments, they sing songs that kindle the god of love.
There, an excellent incense, a blend of *nameru* and *guggulu* sprinkled with streams of clarified butter, is wafted about by female door-keepers.
For this purpose he wanders through the three worlds of Nārāyaṇa, being honored by the gods including Indra; he is the verse marked with the three types of incense:
of guggulu, of nameru, and indeed of clarified butter incense.
The gods do not reach satiety, just as one does not from the sight of beloved ones. || 1.05 ||
The winds did not obstruct the course of these three types of incense:
that of guggulu, of nameru, and indeed of clarified butter incense.
Seeing that festival of the trees, the Lord Śiva, who bears the moon upon his crest and bestows joy upon Pārvatī, repeatedly experienced unsurpassed delight.
While Paśupati, the lord of vows, was repeatedly rejoicing, O Hari, the entire three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, were filled with joy.
The assembly of dancing Apsarases was perfumed with divine incense. || 108 ||
That assembly hall, strewn with seasonal flowers, became like the sky.
Then, [he served] rice cooked with milk quickly...
by that food, which was like nectar, all those best of the twice-born were [satisfied].
Honored by the world, they were satiated with various kinds of food, both solid and soft, as well as drinks.
Then there arose a sacred sound of "Auspicious Day," pleasing to the ear, terrifying to the Rākṣasas and Asuras, and filling the three worlds, produced by the Brahmins. || 111 ||
Then, having greeted that Aśoka together with Sāmba, Hara, and Nandin— with flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and blessings—
all those great ones, possessing beautiful voices, wearing sacred threads and matted hair, [proceeded].
Bowing down to Virūpākṣa, the brahmins departed as they had come. And all the gods, having been honored by the wielder of the trident with gifts and words of praise,
returned as they had come, surrounding Śatakratu.
And all the Gaṇas, together with their leaders, having been honored by the Guardian of the Gaṇas, departed for their respective abodes, their garments fluttering with joy.
"Oh, how great is the good fortune of the Goddess! Oh, how beloved is Hara to her! they exclaimed.
"Ah! We have indeed observed such great agitation on the part of the Lord for the sake of the Goddess."
How can she who is not so beloved by her husband as the Daughter of the Mountain is by the Lord be called fortunate, and why does she even bear the nature of womanhood? || 117 ||
I believe that the daughter of the mountain performed a most radiant penance,
for by that penance she conquered the bull-bannered Lord, who granted her a boon.
Oh, how subtle is the power of women, which is exceedingly difficult even for the gods to overcome!
By which lords equal to Rudra have been brought under the control of women. || 119 ||
There, other high-souled leaders of the hosts said to them:
"This is indeed a god who remains here having become her wife in this form.
Do not despise that goddess; why do you not perceive this through your yogic power?"
Conversing thus with one another, those leaders of the hosts departed for their own abodes, shining like blazing fires;
and the god [Śiva] also went together with Nandin and the beautiful Soma.
Seated beneath an Ashoka tree and worshipped by the Apsarases,
Soma— the source of all speech— then bowed to his lord, the granter of boons who is adorned with the moon, and addressed the Lord of the hosts of beings with these words: || 122-123 ||
I have become fully liberated, O destroyer of Tripura and Andhaka,
since I have made the Ashoka tree my natural-born son.
O Creator of the World, the entire triple world, both in its totality and its individual parts, is yours.
"Through your power, you have come to this festival for my son, who is like a tree.
Surely, O Lord, my merit and my asceticism must be supremely radiant, since I have obtained you, O God, the Lord and Master of all beings. (1.25–1.26)
"O Lord, whatever fruit of a beloved son was formerly stolen from me by the gods,
all of that has now vanished upon obtaining my son, the Ashoka tree.
O Lord, there is no other woman in the triple heaven more blessed than I."
"O Hero, O Maheśvara, you are the husband and the lord of vows for me," having spoken thus out of love to Bhava,
Bhavānī—
wearing a string of pearls and her eyes filled with tears— fell at the feet of the God.
Having raised her up and embraced her as she was distressed, Giriśa, seating her upon his own thighs, spoke these words with affection: ||| 8.162.130 ||
"O Goddess, you are virtuous, chaste, and my partner in dharma;
you are devoted to Brahman, a refuge for others, and always dear to me, O beloved.
Therefore, O Goddess, even though it is an improper act, it must indeed be done by me for your sake."
How much more so,
O Goddess, since you have gratified the Brahmins and the gods along with their hosts with such merit mingled with fame;
and this beloved Aśoka tree has been taken by you as a son, my dear.
"Come, O Queen, let us go home; your heart's desire is fulfilled.
We shall see that son of yours once more, adorned with clusters of blossoms.
Thus addressed by her husband, the virtuous woman, her face and eyes filled with joy, [replied].
There, the deer-eyed woman spoke these words to Hari:
"O Hari, protect this fawn-eyed one who stands here, my dear son; guard him with effort from elephants, horses, and the falling of bird-eggs."
"Or if this little Aśoka tree of mine should be adorned with clusters of blossoms, then you ought to come and see me.
Having thus instructed the gardener, she whose eyes were like those of a startled doe—
Having cast a sidelong glance with her eyes, the goddess Umā entered her abode together with her husband, like the splendor entering the orb of the sun.
Thus, the goddess, having taken her son, embraced the young Ashoka tree even as she was with the Lord of Creatures.
Surrounded by a joyful retinue, she then entered her own palace with a heart full of delight.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Seizing of the Son by the Aśoka Tree," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
Having taken up the splendor of Śarva, what did Vahni do then?
How did Skanda arise, and in what place was he of great splendor?
How was he consecrated as commander-in-chief by the supreme gods?
For what purpose was he consecrated, and in which land, O Lord? (2)
And how was Tāraka slain by him at the forefront of the battle?
O great sage, I desire to know this through your grace. (3)
Thus addressed by Vyāsa of unwearied deeds,
the wise son of the Grandfather, the best among speakers, then spoke.
Sanatkumāra said: Then even the radiant Pāvaka was unable to sustain that three-eyed splendor, which had arisen from the son’s resolve.
Although he was of a burning nature and was himself being consumed by that brilliance,
he entreated Gaṅgā to bear that radiance.
Requested thus by him, the goddess Hutāśanā, who traverses the three worlds, spoke with a sweet voice and with apprehension: "So be it. (7)
Then that radiant bearer of oblations, the fire of the God of gods,
transferred that heat into the Gaṅgā by means of his yogic power.
Although she knew it was difficult to fulfill, that fair-faced woman consented,
fearing the reproach of failing to satisfy the petitioner, like the best of rivers.
Then, by the power of his splendor, she quickly became slow-moving, her face and breasts turning dark.
With her slender line of body hair, which had the luster of crushed collyrium,
she shone like a streak of the cool-rayed moon across a mass of clouds at the end of the rainy season.
Then the queen, her eyes somewhat clouded, fell into a state of languor;
she found no pleasure at that time in beds or seats.
Though touched by the cool, nectar-dripping rays of the moon,
that sinless woman withered then, being consumed by his splendor.
[She dwelt] in a place resplendent with a thicket of reeds.

Then, on an auspicious day, he discharged that fierce energy of Hara. From the midst of the arrow there emerged a boy of youthful prowess, with six faces and twelve arms, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns. || 14-15 ||
Then Viśvāmitra, whose splendor was like that of fire, kindled the sacrificial fire there according to the prescribed rites and performed the birth-ceremony for the noble-born child.
Then the Kṛttikās, their breasts overflowing with milk upon seeing him,
came into his presence.
And the Vedas, along with the Upavedas and the Saṃgrahas, waited upon him.
All the arts and sciences, Lakṣmī, Medhā, and Sarasvatī. || 1.8 ||
Beauty, righteousness, compassion, forbearance, fortitude, courage, valor, yoga, splendor, strength, wisdom, stability, profundity, and noble conduct. (19)
Then, taking up his divine bow, he of wondrous prowess effortlessly fixed an arrow and released it at the mountain;
by that [arrow], the excellent peak of the mountain was suddenly split asunder.
It fell swiftly, causing the birds to fly about in terror and fear.
Seeing that great marvel, wonder and fear arose simultaneously among the beings dwelling there. (21–22)
Then, perceiving that danger from him, the destroyer of Bala dispatched his mothers to bring about the destruction of the one of immeasurable luster.
Having arrived there and beheld that treasure-house of splendors, the mothers,
their minds captivated by his brilliance, sought refuge in him alone.
Then, mounted upon the shoulders of the elephant Airāvata, Pākaśāsana arrived, enraged and accompanied by hosts of gods.
Seeing the gods approaching, the one of great splendor let out a loud roar and,
filled with rage, rushed toward them like a lion toward intoxicated elephants.
By that roar, the inhabitants of heaven were repeatedly rendered bewildered.
Even the rut-fluid on the temples of Airāvaṇa was destroyed;
and he, the son of the Three-eyed One, the destroyer of the pride of the gods, emitted thousands of blazing rays. || 27-28 ||
The faces of the enemies of the asuras, their luster destroyed by the flames,
became like lotuses in lakes scorched by frost.
Then, taking up his thunderbolt, which blazed with the brilliance of fire,
Śatakratu, the corners of his eyes copper-red with rage, hurled it.
By that stroke of the thunderbolt, he then became two-bodied.

He rushed toward Purandara with both his forms. Then, quickly casting aside his pride, the subduer of Pāka bowed down before that treasury of splendors and, being utterly defeated, spoke thus to him: ||| 3.1–3.2 ||
"Accept even this kingdom, which is to be desired by the wise;
you alone, O son of Agni, are fit for the protection of the worlds, even though there exist other splendors that destroy darkness. (33)
"Only in the fire is the meritorious oblation offered...
(34) Having laughed, the best among the powerful spoke to the lord of the gods:
"O Śakra, you yourself rule this kingdom that you have long desired. (35)
"O Purandara, because of these many faults, I have no desire for it.
Having heard those words of Skanda, whose mind was untainted,
the glorious Lord of Śacī spoke again in speech that was meaningful and gentle.
Show us the various kinds of manifold effects—
those that are united and those that are divided— and the eternal acquisition of sovereignty over the three worlds that follows from them. (39)
When he had spoken thus, the one possessing the brilliance of fire replied with these words,
preceded by a smile, in a voice that was both affectionate and deep:
"O Śakra, my mind cannot be forcibly shaken."
The water of the lord of rivers is not heated by firebrands;
O lotus-eyed one, I would never, even in my mind, desire sovereignty, which is the eternal abode of faults, O Subduer of Pāka. || 41-42 ||
Having heard those words of his, he desired to speak again, as if bathing Skanda with eyes dripping with nectar:
"O Lord, this is not surprising in you, a praiseworthy mine of splendors. || 43 ||
The capable ones do not thus become attached even to very great enjoyments.
"Be consecrated as the commander-in-chief for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods;
I honor your person here, O Lord, but I do not issue this command. || 44-45 ||
Then, having heard those words, the mighty-armed and immensely valorous one with twelve eyes spoke thus to the thousand-eyed Puruhūta:
"The illustrious, imperishable Lord of the worlds has power over me."
O Purandara, he who is the peerless, immeasurable self, whose banner bears the bull—
having propitiated that Lord with devotion, O Śatakratu, accept his command;
I shall carry out whatever that Lord shall grant me.
Having understood his intention, the God of gods, whose banner is the bull,
arrived then with his consort, desiring to see his son.
Vahni accompanied by Svāhā, Gaṅgā the best of rivers,
and the Kṛttikās, all greatly delighted, [went to] Śveta, the best of mountains.
Then, simultaneously, on that highest peak of Śveta, they reflected as they approached: "Who among us shall go to Skanda? (51)
Then, having understood their intention, Skanda, the best among the wise and lord of yogis, manifested in six forms, becoming exceedingly powerful at that time.
