Skanda went to Mahādeva, Viśākha to the daughter of Himavat,
Naigameṣa to Gaṅgā, and the highly effulgent Śākha to Agni.
Accompanied by Svāhā, Guha, wearing side-locks of hair like crows' wings, departed full of joy;
and the glorious six-faced one rushed forward with speed toward the Kṛttikās.

The Lord, the son of the God of gods, the Master of yogins, simultaneously fulfilled the desires of them all with his various forms. Then Śambhu bestowed upon him the fourfold collection of divine weapons.
And Pārvatī’s crest-jewel was dripping with drops of nectar. ||56||
With eyes blossoming with joy in the cave, Gaṅgā gave him a single-string necklace that was as pure as her own mind, stainless, and born of nectar; likewise,
Havyavāhana gave him a heavy, unfailing weapon that takes the lives of enemies.
And he gave to his capable son the spear named Arciṣmatī.
Svāhā gave to the Great-Souled One a great, divine, red banner, radiant like a blazing fire and resounding with the tinkling of small bells.
And the Kṛttikās gave him a garland of full-blown, most holy-scented lotuses, tinged with their own pollen and adorned with filaments.
Then all the gods arrived, led by the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Desirous of beholding the Bull-bannered Lord, they ascended the beautiful peak of the White Mountain.
Then, seeing all those inhabitants of heaven arrived there together, Mahādeva honored them with a gracious countenance.
Having bowed to the Lord of the gods of gods and received his permission, the inhabitants of heaven [proceeded].
Those of immeasurable luster sat upon the moon-white rocks.
Even the lofty-peaked, white,
and radiant mountain became even more resplendent by the convergence of their splendors.
Then, urged by all the gods, the lord of the gods—
the best among speakers— bowed to Mahādeva and addressed him:
"O Lord, our prosperity has been forcibly seized by the one named Tāraka."
The vajra struck his chest and became blunted against its hardness.
The thousand-spoked discus of Hari, blazing with radiant power,
having reached the throat of that enemy of the gods, attained softness;
even the staff of Vaivasvata, shining with the brilliance of a kindled fire, [was softened].
Like a firebrand extinguished in a torrent of water, he was quenched upon the chest of Dānava. 68.
In battle, that great noose of Varuṇa, which was difficult for enemies to withstand,
fell around his neck as if brought under control by a mantra.
Having violently uprooted the wish-fulfilling trees in the Nandana grove, he—
They were settled according to their desire in the grounds of their own houses and gardens. ||8.163.70||
In his presence, the wind, though as vast as a palm-leaf fan, waits upon him apprehensively;
the Seasons, fearing him, attend to him with heaps of their own flowers.
He forcibly seizes the oblation offered into the sacrificial fire.
While all the gods looked on, O God of Gods, the son of Diti consecrated the highly resplendent Skanda as the commander-in-chief;
and now, O Śaṅkara, by your grace, the gods desire to conquer the lord of the Daityas. || 72–73 ||
Thus addressed there by the wielder of the thunderbolt, the bull-bannered god granted permission to Skanda for his consecration as commander-in-chief.
Then he, who is worshipped by the hosts of gods, the one worthy of adoration,
the destroyer of Madana’s body, whose crest is adorned with the crescent of the young moon—
having gazed upon his son, his eyes blossomed with affection.
He quickly disappeared within the mountain white as the rays of the moon. ||75||
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "The Permission for Skanda’s Consecration," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Then those gods, led by Brahmā, took Skanda with them.
Those of immeasurable splendor arrived at the meritorious Samantapañcaka.
On that bank of the Sarasvatī, which was level, sloping toward the northeast, extensive, and free from pits, stones, thorns, and saline soil; || 2 ||
Then all those best of gods, their hearts filled with joy and possessing the splendor of blazing fire, sat down on every side around Skanda.
That sacred place, already frequented by the immortals, became even more holy.
The waters of the Yamunā became as if united with the waters of the Gaṅgā. ||4||
Then,

when the consecration of Skanda had taken place, the Earth herself, her eyes blossoming with joy, arrived at that region in embodied form. Immediately thereafter, that land became filled with golden sands.
Variegated on all sides with various shimmering rays from gems,
that region was inhabited by high-souled men free from envy;
there, through their splendors, all evil was cast out.
Then Himālaya, together with the mountains, arrived taking with him a divine, well-crafted golden throne. ||8||
Taking golden jars filled with jewels, medicinal herbs, perfumes, and meritorious waters, and adorned with garlands of blooming lotuses.
Greatly agitated, with their jeweled earrings swaying and their chests radiant with necklaces, they arrived there in haste.
The Gaṅgā [brought] beautiful jars made of jewels, radiant with flashing luster,
adorned with golden lotuses as crest-ornaments, and filled with the most excellent water.
Taking all the rivers with her, she whose garment is the river,
then arrived out of joy, stumbling even on level ground.
Having caused well-prepared consecration jars to be brought forth, which were colored by the radiance of various jewels so as to rival the rays of the sun; 13.
Pārvatī arrived together with many goddesses of the gods,
as if overwhelming their splendors with her own radiance.
Having caused [the priests] to take up well-consecrated, bright crystal jars, filled with supremely meritorious waters and adorned with garlands of jewel-like rays. (15)
And he wore a great crown, worthy of praise, radiant and beautiful in form,
its interior shimmering with the mass of variegated rays from various jewels.
And a necklace, stainless and pure, with the brilliance of moonbeams;
lovely, a canopy of pearls, captivating the heart and perfectly immaculate. (17)
Then the lord of aquatic creatures arrived there in great joy,
his armlets scarred by the tusks of the elephants belonging to the lords of the Dānavas.
The Lord of Wealth, taking beautiful and radiant jeweled armlets—
the very essence of all riches— approached.
Taking up fly-whisks with jeweled handles— long, radiant, and as white as the rays of the moon— the one of great splendor [approached].
Vaivasvata also approached his presence, wearing upon his chest a necklace as pure as the rays of the full autumn moon.
Under the pretext of a royal parasol, he bestowed upon that great-souled one the entirety of the fruit of sovereignty over the gods, as if Vāsava himself had given it; meanwhile,
the trees there adorned themselves with the appearance of sky-flowers blooming in profusion.
Then the Seasons, with contented hearts, arrived at that place:
Arundhatī, Śacī, Svāhā, Sinīvālī, the daughter of the Mountain King (Pārvatī), Aditi the mother of the gods, Niśā, Anumati, and Kuhū. ||23-24||
Hrī, Śrī, Puṣṭi, Diś, and Dyau were all daughters of Prajāpati;
Rākā, Dhiṣaṇā, and Surabhi were the celestial women;
the medicinal herbs were personified, as was Kauśikī, the deity of the forest.
The day, the kāṣṭhās, the muhūrtas, the months, the years, and the kalās. || 26 ||
Airāvaṇa, Supratīka, Vāmana, Kumuda, Añjana, Puṣpadanta, Mahāpadma, and Sārvabhauma— the elephants of the quarters—
brought everything required for the consecration of the high-souled one.
Having bound their matted locks, which possessed a radiance equal to blazing fire, the excellent sages dwelling on the Himālaya mountains—
delighted and empowered by the strength of their intense austerities— approached the son of Fire.
Devoted to the abode of the gods, blazing with splendor, and having lotus-feet worshipped by the deities,
the hosts of sages— whose powerful and constant rites of austerity were restrained [by his presence]— hurriedly approached Guha.
With minds joyful and eager, the sons of the Lotus-born Brahmā,
endowed with great majesty and bearing noble fame, approached him who possessed the preeminent power of the Three-eyed God’s son.
The lords of the serpents also hastened toward him, their hoods overspread with the radiance of their own jewel-crests.

Even those who bear poison assumed exceedingly gentle forms, while the Garuḍas, free from envy and possessing the rising strength of being mounted upon the king of serpents, approached the son of Fire whose prowess was insurmountable;
they moved with great speed, possessing a luster like the rising sun, and caused the trees to tremble by their wind-like velocity. || 31-32 ||

The celestial nymphs (apsarases), endowed with long and tremulous eyes, filled with the essence of various emotional expressions and graceful charms, possessed of the highest youth, beauty, and virtues, danced about, exceedingly joyful and full of delight.
At that time, the winds blew, their forms reddened by the pollen of various flowers and carrying fragrant scents;
free from dust, exceedingly gentle in their movement, and bringing delight to the hearts of the gods.
Having properly kindled the fire, Bṛhaspati performed the entire ritual for his consecration according to the rules prescribed for one born under the Śara constellation.
Then the sages, having embraced the son of Śiva—the abode of blessings—with their own blessings, praised him who is worthy of praise with the most excellent hymns. (36)
Then the Gandharvas and Nārada, having tuned their lutes to a high, sweet, and steady pitch, sang auspicious songs for him.
Then, having taken him by the right hand and performed the auspicious rites,
the Guru seated him upon that lion-throne facing the east.
At that moment, the drums of the gods resounded loudly in the unstruck sky.
The various drums resounded intensely, perfectly captivating the mind.
Showers of flowers fell—variegated, possessing holy fragrance, and glowing with the reddish luster of their own filaments, accompanied by the songs of intoxicated bees. (8.164.40)
Praising Skanda with words from his four mouths, Prajāpati first took up the pitcher, which was filled with meritorious water. ||41||
Then Viṣṇu, having donned his yellow garment, took up the pitcher of the Kaustubha gem, which was touched by its rays. ||42||
Then Indra, having quickly adjusted his upper garment which was inlaid with the luster of gems from his armlets, took up the water-pot.
Having bound their matted locks— which were marked with crescent moons and tawny as fire—
the Rudras, adorned with bracelets made of serpents, took up their water-jars;
though they possessed supreme radiance, their forms were pleasant to the touch.
The Ādityas took up full jars with holy waters. ||45||
Vasu, whose chest was wounded by the tusks of the elephant that was the enemy of the lord of the gods,
took up jars there filled with meritorious water. The two Aśvins also, well-prepared, took up jars filled with pure waters.
Then they took up two golden jars, garlanded with the rays of jewels.
There, blazing beings of radiant splendor took up jars covered with golden lotuses, variegated by the beams of gems.
The kings of the Nāgas and Gandharvas, the world-protectors, the hosts of Maruts,
the Ṛṣis, the Bālakhilyas, the ancestors, the lords of birds,
Dharma, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Kāla, Mṛtyu, and Vasundharā. ||49||
Twilight, beauty, fortitude, intelligence, fame, fortune, and eloquence.
The oceans, rivers, Vedas, sacred fords, mountains,
and planets there took up jars filled with the supreme water.
Then, with joyful minds, they [honored] the son of Agni, who was himself exceedingly delighted.
Then they all consecrated the one of great splendor in the command of the army.
Thereupon, all the inhabitants of heaven and the assembled sages raised a shout of victory for the victorious son of Śarva.
Maghavā seized his white sunshade,
which was like a halo surrounding a canopy formed by the mass of radiance from all kinds of jewels;
and they fanned him with long yak-tail whisks, as pure as the rays of the autumnal moon.
And the world-protectors [honored] the one of great splendor on all sides with jewel-staffs. ||55||
The daughter of Himavat placed upon her son’s head a divine crown that had arisen from the nectar of immortality and was brought forth by Pracetas;
it was as bright as gold, expansive, and possessed the luster of the moon’s rays.

The best of rivers fastened a necklace upon his chest. At that time, a doubt arose in the assembly of the gods as to whether it was his chest adorned by the necklace, or the necklace resting upon his broad chest. ||57-58||
Arundhatī fastened well-adorned armlets upon the arms of the mighty-armed one, which were as thick as the pillars used for tying elephants.
Then the son of Pāvaka became even more radiant,
like a fire blazing at a sacrifice when it is offered oblations of clarified butter.
The four-faced Lord, being pleased, gave to that high-souled one great attendants who were heroic, powerful, and able to assume any form at will:
Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Suraktākṣa, and the invincible Nandiṣeṇa.
To him [Kumāra], Sthāṇu gave the fourth great attendant, Kratu, who was renowned as Kumudamālin, the best among the powerful and possessed of great heroism;
this occurred when the terrible Tārakāmaya war had then commenced.
Enraged, he slew fourteen yojanas of Daityas;
and the gods gave him an army teeming with Nairṛtas.
The son of Vivasvat gave to him two great attendants, who were invincible, possessed of universal forms, and the destroyers of Daityas and Yakṣas.

Greatly rejoicing, he gave to Kārttikeya two followers of the Sun— Unmātha and Pramātha, who possessed great heroism and prowess, were brilliantly radiant, and were exceedingly difficult to conquer in battle.
[The two Aśvins gave him] two [horses] shaped like the peaks of Kailāsa, adorned with white garlands and unguents.
Candramas also gave to him the Maṇi and the Sumaṇi; likewise, Vibhāvasu gave to his son the Jvālājihva and the Jyotis. ||67-68||
Being exceedingly pleased, he gave [to Skanda] two weapons for the destruction of enemy armies:
the formidable iron club (parigha) and the terrifying drum (paṭaha), as well as the two burning missiles, Dahana and Atidahana.
Aṃśu also gave five attendants to the wise Skanda.
Utkrośa and Satvara, both of whom bear the vajra-staff.
The joyful Śatakratu gave to the son of the God of gods the discus,
the Vikramaka, and the exceedingly invincible Saṃkrama.
The highly illustrious Viṣṇu, being pleased, gave these to the son of Agni.
The two Aśvins, of great strength and well-pleased, gave to Skanda both Vardhana and Nandana, who had reached the end of all branches of knowledge;
as well as Kundara, Ugra, and the mighty Kumuda. || 72–73 ||
The Creator gave both Ḍambara and Aḍambara to the son of Agni; and Tvaṣṭṛ gave two great illusory attendants,
Vakrānuvaktra, who were powerful, ram-faced, and invincible in battle,
to Skanda.
Mitra gave [her] to the high-souled one, who was of excellent vows and true to his promise.
The Creator bestowed upon Skanda Suprabha, Mahāmāya, and Śubhakarmā—those two who were destroyers of the enemy host. (76)
Pūṣan gave two attendants to Skanda of immeasurable splendor: Pālin, who possesses great heroism, and Kālaka, who possesses great strength. ||77||
And Vāyu, being pleased, gave to the high-souled Kārttikeya two beings of great body and great strength, namely Bala and Atibala. (78)
Varuṇa gave to the son of Agni two noose-bearing [demons], Ghasa and Praghasa, who had mouths like whales and massive bellies;
as well as Suvarcas, of great heroism, and likewise Ativarcas.
Himavat gave to Skanda both Atibala and Mahāmāya; likewise, Meru gave two attendants, Kāñcana and Jīmūtamālin, to the son of Agni.
Furthermore, Mahāmeru gave to Skanda of immeasurable splendor both Sthira and Atisthira as his two attendants. || 82 ||
Vindhya gave to Skanda, who blazes with splendor, two beings of great courage, Ucchṛṅga and Viśṛṅga, who fought with rocks and stones.
Then he gave to Kārttikeya two great attendants, Saṃgraha and Vigraha, as well as Samudra and Gadādhara;
[and] Unmāda, Puṣpadanta, Śaṅkukarṇa, and Durjaya.
Pārvatī gave those of great heroism and great being to her son. 85.
The Nāgas gave victory and great victory to the Great-Souled One;
and the Bull-vehicled Lord, being exceedingly pleased,
granted to Skanda many heroic attendants who are invincible by enemies in battle.
Gajakarṇa, Nikumbha, Padma, and Kumuda; Sananda with twelve arms, as well as Kṛṣṇa and Upakṛṣṇaka;
Kṛtagrīva, Kapiskandha, Kāñcanākṣa, and Jalandhama. ||87-88||
With eyes that pierce through, a blunted nose, a neck curved to the side, and a large belly;
having one eye, twelve arms, and a single foot, with massive matted hair. ||89||
He has a thousand arms, disheveled hair, a tiger’s face, and makes the earth tremble;
he has a face on his back, a beautiful name, and faces on his sides and a great face [on his chest];
he is flowing with wine, as red as a lotus, and fond of garlands and ointments.
Ajodara, Gajaskandha, Skandhakṣa, Śatalocana;
Jvālājihva, Karāla, Śitakeśa, Tatodara;
Aṣṭajihva, Caturdaṃṣṭra, Meghanāda, and Pṛthūdara. || 91–92 ||
Vidyudakṣa, Dhanurvaktra, Jaraṭha, Mārutāśana,
Udarākṣa, Jhaṣākṣa, Vajranābha, and Suprabha.
Samudravega, Gokarṇa, Śailakampana,
Patrameṣa, Prabāhu, as well as Nanda and Upanandaka;
Dhūmra, Śveta, Kaliṅga, Siddhārtha, and Varada.
Priyaka, Gardabhāsya, Gonarda, and Bhūtatāpana. ||95||
Ānanda, Pramoda, Svastika, Dhruvaka, as well as Kṣepavāpa, Sujāta, Siddhayātra, Mahāvara,
Govraja, Kanakāpīḍa, Mahāpārśva, and Mahodara.
Gāyana, Hasana, the Lord Bāṇakhaḍgadharin,
Vaitālin, Atitālin, as well as Śaṭhika and Vātika, Māṃsaja, Paṅkadigdha, Samudronmātha, and Avyaya. || 97–98 ||
Raṇotkaṭa, Prabhāsa, Śvetamūrdhan, Acyuta, Kālakaṇṭhaśarīra, Kuṣmāṇḍa, and Śatrutāpana. || 99 ||
Gomāyuvaktra, Śyenāsya, Bhūtalonmāthana,
Yajñavāha, Pravāha, Kākāsya, Kākalocana,
Mañjula, Vakranāsa, Mahānāsa, and Gajodara.
Tuhana and Tuhāna, Citradeva, Aja, and Khara;
Madhura and Suprasāda; Kirīṭa, Bhakuṭotkaṭa, Vasana, Madhuvarṇa, Kalaśa, and Kalaśodara. || 101-102 ||
Revanta, Manmathakara, Sūcīvaktra, Gajānana, Śvetavaktra, Suvaktra, Cāruvaktra, and Pāṇḍara. || 103 ||
Kaṇṭhabāhu, Subāhu, Baka, and likewise Kokilaka; Acala, Kanakākṣa, and Balānāmagranāyaka;
Sañcāra, Kokamukha, Gṛdhrāsya, and likewise Jambuka.
Lomaśa, Jarāsyaka, Uṣṭragrīva, and Kamaṇḍalu. || 105 ||
Daṇḍaka, Dīrghavaktra, the mighty Haṃsavaktra, Ṭuṇḍuka, Śatapāda, Śatākṣa, and Cāpapṛṣṭhakrama. || 10.6 ||
Śikṣaka, Apavaktra, Śākhavaktra, and Kuṇḍaka—
these great beings of great yoga are constant practitioners of celibacy.
Invincible, possessed of great heroism, slayers of enemies in battle, armed with various weapons and missiles, of diverse forms and immense power;
surrounded by hosts with various faces, these were the leaders of the Gaṇas. || 108 ||
Clad in the skins of lordly elephants, they wore garments of tiger-skins and black antelope hides.
Some had red hair and tawny beards, while others were shaven-headed or naked;
some wore matted locks and had tawny eyes, with girdles made of serpents.
These heroes wore armlets of snakes and were coiled by the hissing lords of serpents.
Their limbs were smeared with purifying ashes as white as the moon.
[He saw] the leaders of the Gaṇas, surrounded by many other Gaṇas, dancing and leaping with eyes wide open in laughter;
some having the faces of tortoises and cocks, others the faces of rabbits, iguanas, and wolves.
With terrifying faces of donkeys, camels, and horses; with the faces of boars and buffaloes; with human faces and faces of rams; with faces of dogs, jackals, and deer;
and with terrifying faces of crocodiles, porpoises, and bears.
With faces like those of cats and wolves, with long faces, and even without faces; |||1.14||
With faces resembling those of mongooses, owls, kites, and lotuses;
with mouths like mice, tawny cats, and other creatures; with faces like goats and rams, and others with faces like parrots and kāraṇḍava ducks—[they were] difficult for enemies to conquer. (11.5)
And with faces like those of bears and tigers, as well as those of elephants and lions.
With terrifying faces of elephants, as well as faces of hyenas;
with faces of Garuḍas and jackals, and faces of crows and cuckoos;
with faces of cows and monkeys, and others with faces of hawks and vultures.
With great bellies, feet, and limbs, with eyes like stars, and possessed of great strength.
Others had faces like pigeons, as well as faces like cocks;
some had mouths like quails and partridges, and others even had faces like lizards.
Some wore garments of yellow silk, while others wore rags and bark;
some had their bodies entwined by lordly serpents, and others wore bracelets made of variegated snakes.
Some had large bellies and thin limbs, while others had thick limbs and slender waists.
With short necks and large ears, adorned with various serpents,
wearing the skins of lordly elephants, they were heroes invincible in battle;
some had faces on their shoulders, some were faceless, some had mouths on their backs, and others had faces on all sides.
By heroes of various forms and many arms, terrifying with diverse serpents;
by those of various guises, great yogins dwelling in various places;
and by others wearing various garments, various garlands, and various unguents. || 123 ||
Others were clad in various skins and garments, wearing diverse ornaments.

With those who have protuberances on their heads, those wearing crowns, those with necks like conch-shells, those well-proportioned, those wearing diadems, those with five topknots, and those bearing matted locks and crowns. ||1.25||
Some had three tufts of hair, some two, and others seven;
some wore crests, some had long matted locks, some were shaven-headed, and others had tawny hair.
By those with variegated eyes, variegated faces, and adorned with diverse garlands and ointments;
by heroes wearing variegated garments who were always fond of combat;
and by those with dark, fleshless faces, long backs, and slender bellies.
With thick backs, large necks, and pendulous bellies and great stomachs.
With great arms, great mouths, short necks, and emaciated faces;
with hunchbacks, long shanks, ears like those of elephants, and necks like those of elephants;
with long lips, long tongues, long eyes, and long noses.
With great fangs, excellent fangs, and variegated fangs, they were possessed of great strength;
their bodies were well-proportioned, radiant, and well-adorned;
some had tawny eyes and large ears, others had ears like spikes, and some were entirely earless.
With long fangs, broad chests, thick lips, and tawny hair;
with various feet, lips, and fangs, and various hands and necks. (13.2)
Covered with various skins and draped in diverse garments,
they were joyful, leaping about, dancing, and making a great clamor.
Some had long ears, broad chests, blue throats, and three eyes;
some resembled the belly of a parrot, while others were like collyrium in hue.
With white bodies, red necks, tawny eyes, and fearsome appearances;
with hands and feet variegated like the colors of vermilion and cinnabar;
resembling golden crests, they were white with streaks of red.
Some were the color of lapis lazuli with splendor like that of peacocks;
some had nooses raised in their hands, with gaping mouths and loud roars;
others had tawny eyes and blue throats, with arms like great iron clubs.
With *śataghnīs* and spears in their hands, with maces and clubs in their grasp,
and some with tridents and swords in their hands— great-bodied and possessed of great strength;
with *bhuśuṇḍīs* and javelins in their hands, and heroes with axes in their grasp.
With nooses and mallets in their hands, discs and javelins in their grasp,
those heroes bearing various weapons filled every direction;
their limbs were bound with networks of bells, and they wore clusters of tiny tinkling bells.
Surrounded by hosts, the leaders of the hosts—beings of great courage and great strength—waited upon the high-souled and illustrious Kārttikeya. || 141 ||
And he gave him as mothers those born from the body of Kauśikī—
women of great strength and great courage, unconquered in battles.
Prabhāvatī, Viśālākṣī, Palitā, Vṛṣanāsikā,
Śrīmatī, Bahulā, Siṃhī, Vijayā, Bahuputrikā,
Gopālī, Suprabhā, Ṣaṣṭhī, Bṛhadambālikā, and Kṛśā.
Jayāvatī, Mālatikā, Dhruvaratnā, and Prabhākarī. || 144 ||
Suprabhā, Vasudā, Viśokā, and likewise Nandinī;
Vajracūḍā, Mahācūḍā, Vajranemi, and Mahāprabhā; Añjanī, Bharatsenā, Kamalākṣī, and Śaśiprabhā.
Śatruñjayā, Mahānāsā, Krodhanā, Śalabhī, and Khaṣī. || 146 ||
Mādhavī, Śukavaktrā, Kīrtinemi, Aninditā,
Gītapriyā, Mahāmāyā, Vāyasī, Amṛtā, Satī,
Sarasvatī, Bhogavatī, Subhrū, and Kanakāvatī. || 147 ||
Suta, Lakṣmī, Vīryavatī, Vidyunjihvā, and Mahābalā; || 148 ||
Padmāvatī, Sunakṣatrā, Kandarā, Bahuyojanā,
Santānikā, Śivā, Kamalā, Maladā,
Sudāmā, Bahudāmā, Suprabhā, and Yaśasvinī. || 149 ||
She who loves dancing, possessed of beautiful hips, and wearing a white mortar as her girdle.
Śataghaṇṭā, Śatānandā, Śatanetrā, Yaśasvinī,
Vapuṣmatī, Śīlā, Bhadrakālī, and Bhairavā.
To Saṃhārikā, Niṣkuṭikā, Bhūtā, and Catvaravāsinī;
to Sumaṅgalā, Svastimatī, Vṛddhikāmā, and Janapriyā;
and to Dhanadā, Supradā, Bhavadā, and Sukhadā as well. || 152 ||
Ailī, Bhelī, Samelī, Vetālī, Jananī, and Niśā. ||153||
Kaṇḍū, Piṅgalikā, the illustrious Devamitrā,
Lambuṣī, Sanakā, Citrasenā, and then Acalā;
Kukūnikā, Śaṅkhinikā, and likewise Jharjharikā.
Kuṇḍālikā, Kolavilā, Kaṇḍarā, and Śatodarī;
Utkvāthanī, Jurelā, Mahāvelā, and Kaṅkaṇā; Manojavā, Kaṇṭakinī, Vighasā, and likewise Pūtanā. || 1.55–1.56 ||
Vaiśayā, Carcikā, Vāmā, Krodhanā, Mukhamaṇḍikā, Maṇḍodarī, Tuṇḍā, Koṭarā, and Meghavāsinī. || 1.57 ||
Subhagā, Lambinī, Lambā, Vāmadhūlī, Vikatthanā, as well as Ūrdhvaveṇīdharā and Lalāṭanayanā;
Pṛthubharhā, Mahākāyā, Madhukumbhā, and Taḍitprabhā. || 1.58 ||
Manthānikā, Unmanikā, Jarāyū, and Jarjarānanā. || 1.59 ||
Khyātā, Dahadahā, and likewise Dhamadhamā; Khaṭaṅkhaṭā, Mahāvīryā, Vṛṣaṇā, and Maṇituṇḍikā.
Baddhaveṇī, Dharādhārā, Piṅgākṣī, Lambakarṇikā, Āmodā, Pramodā, and likewise Lambapayodharā. || 161 ||
One with the face of a hare and an owl, black, with legs like those of a donkey and a great roar;
one with the face of a porpoise, white, with red eyes and terrifying. ||162||
Jaṭālikā, Kāmacarī, Dīrghajihvā, Lolupā, Kanelikā, Vāsanikā, Mukuṭā, and Mahābalā. || 163 ||
Lohitākṣī, Mahākāyā, Haripiṇḍī, and the invincible Durjayā;
Paśudā, Vittadā, Vīrā, and the mighty Aṅgadā; Payodā, Gopradā, Śaṅkhā, Suniṣaṇṇā, and Tarasvinī. || 164 ||
Pratiṣṭhā, Supratiṣṭhā, Rocamānā, and Surocanā. || 1.65 ||
Gokarṇī, Aśvakarṇī, Śirā, Kharikā,
Kacakracā, Megharavā, Meghamālā, and Virocanā—
these and many other Mothers were the givers of wind to Māruta.
Ekākṣarā, Sugandhā, Kṛṣṇakarṇī, and Dāruṇā. ||1 67||
Kṣurakarṇī, Catuṣkarṇī, Karṇaprāvaraṇā, as well as Catuṣpathaniketā, Gokarṇī, Mahiṣānanā,
Kharakarṇī, Mahākarṇī, Bherīsvanā, and Mahāsvanā.
And Śaṅkhakuṃbhaśravas, who was indeed unconquered in battles.
Gaṇā and Sugaṇā, as well as Vātī who goes at will, Catuṣpatharavā, Bhūtinī, and Vanyagocarā—
these followers of Kārttikeya are of various forms, numbering in the thousands.
With long teeth and extremely long nails, they had elongated faces and were exceedingly terrifying. ||171||
They were clever and sweet-spoken, in the prime of youth, and well-adorned;
endowed with majesty, they could assume any form at will and possessed great strength. Their limbs were fleshless and white, yet they shone with a luster equal to that of Jāmbūnada gold.
They were black, with the color of clouds, and possessed smoke-colored hair; they were most terrifying.
The Asuras had large fangs and long fangs, wore white garments,
had ears and lips turned upward, possessed tawny eyes, and wore hanging girdles.
They had protruding bellies, drooping lips, and long ears, breasts, and eyes;
they had copper-colored eyes and copper-colored faces, with tawny eyes and golden hair.
They dwelt in trees and open squares, making their homes at crossroads.
Dwelling in caves and cremation grounds, they have their abodes in mountains and springs. ||176||
Wearing various ornaments, adorned with diverse garlands and unguents,
clad in various garments, and likewise bearing various weapons—
these and others Kauśikī joyfully gave to Skanda.
Viṣṇu gave him the Vaijayantī garland, with its lovely filaments, rich in various fragrances, in full bloom, and beautiful to behold;
he also gave him two stainless garments, radiant like the rising sun. (178–179)
Being well-pleased, Pārvatī gave to Skanda, whose mind was joyful,
a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) filled with the nectar-like waters arising from immortality.
Being pleased, Gaṅgā gave [it] to Kumāra, who possessed a profound heart.
Garuda, being well-pleased, gave his beloved son, the powerful and shape-shifting Citrabarha Śikhaṇḍin, to Skanda;
and Aruṇa gave the heroic Tāmracūḍa, whose weapon is his feet, to Cāraṇa. || 181–182 ||

Varuṇa gave to Skanda a most powerful goat, endowed with the speed of the vigor of existence, pleasing to behold for Skanda, capable of bearing a great burden, able to go anywhere at will, and able to assume any form at will. 18.3.
Brahmā gave to the one devoted to Brahman a sacred black antelope skin for a garment;
Bṛhaspati gave to that treasury of splendors a staff, which was as dark as the interior of an eye and shimmering with the movement of playful women.
Being exceedingly pleased with Skanda, he [gave] a garland of beautiful gold.
Having duly consecrated that son of Agni as their general,
the assembled gods, possessed of great power, were filled with joy for the sake of destroying the lord of the Daityas.
Together they undertook an expedition for victory over the enemies of the gods.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Consecration of the General," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Placing Skanda at their head, all the gods quickly prepared their army;
they struck hundreds of kettledrums with massive sticks, firmly adorned with gold and various jewels.
[They readied] the elephants of the quarters, which resembled the peaks of mountains, their bodies drenched by the waters of the Mandākinī.
Having summoned them, the leaders of the army honored them with various perfumes and garlands;
then, having fastened colorful armor around their flanks with the utmost care,
they secured golden trappings for those chief elephants and horses, as well as the harnesses for their weapons.
Variegated banners and flags with beautiful golden poles were raised up;
they fastened various garlands of razor-edged arrows to the sides and hung bells upon them.
And there was a battle-chariot with beautiful wheels of refined gold, variegated with the rays of jewels.
They yoked two horses that moved through the air, possessed of noble forms and joyful hearts.
Śakra fastened upon his chest a costly, polished breastplate, as fair as the interior of a lotus,
anointed with yellow sandalwood, and radiant with a brilliance blazing like a thunderbolt.
Restraining their tawny matted locks with hissing serpents, they bound them high;
the delighted Rudras placed variegated armor upon their chests, which were scarred by the tusks of the Daitya-elephant.
Wearing that wonderful armor, the one of great splendor was equipped with a girded sword, a shield, and finger-guards.
Though bearing a strung bow and possessing intense prowess, the Moon did not abandon his innate gentleness.

The suns, with great effort, fastened their armor—which was made of impenetrable iron, yet beautiful and adorned with gold—though it was somewhat dimmed by their own radiance at that time, as they were repelled by the arrows. || 8-9 ||
With his radiant armor fastened, his excellent bow ready, and a broad sword girt at his side;
holding his staff and with his crown securely bound, even Yama himself became exceedingly terrifying.
Enveloped in an exceeding radiance and repeatedly flashing with his forebody held high,
the noose seems to proclaim the defeat of the enemies in the assembly of Varuṇa.
The Lord of Wealth (Kubera) too, with his massive arms wielding a mace, cast a fire-tawny glance at the mace and,
by his own power, brought about the destruction of the enemies of the gods during their slaughter.
Then, large meteors with flickering sparks of fire fell upon the army of the enemies of the gods.
Without clouds, the sky resounded dreadfully, and the earth with its trees and mountains trembled.
Dust, grey as the back of a donkey, driven by the wind, fell everywhere from the heavens.
Banners with sturdy golden staffs fell down, and the clouds released a rain of blood-red water.
Again and again, their hearts overcome by dejection, the horses shed warm tears;
the ichor of the elephants, dark as the neck of a pigeon, ceased from the surfaces of their temples.
In blazing places, flocks of birds, beasts, and horses shrieked loudly with piercing cries.
A harsh wind, having increased in strength, blew about, crushing the rows of banners on all sides.
The great and joyful army of the gods advanced, roaring, toward the lord of the Daityas;
and the Daitya, having learned of the arrival of the gods, then caused his own army to arm itself.
Those armies of the thirty gods and the asuras, with weapons raised, encountered one another.
Like the waters of the great ocean in the dissolution of the world, agitated to an extreme degree from east to west,
the Daityas— mighty, filled with pride, and eager for victory— hearing the sound of the battle trumpets,
set out for the fray with weapons grasped, their auspicious rites unfinished due to excessive joy. (18–19)
The dust raised on the field of battle by the chariots, horses, and infantry— dusky with the throats of monkeys—
and their exceedingly fierce and great roar, then pervaded the sky and all directions.
Likewise, the weapons of the Dānavas and gods were uplifted, along with banners, flags, sunshades, and parasols.
Then the sky shone like a lake filled with rows of swans, accompanied by lightning, the moon, and the bow of Indra. || 21 ||
Weapons falling upon their armored limbs against one another produced,
during the clash between the Daityas and the immortals, a sound mingled with the sparks of flashing fire.
Seeing the Asuras endowed with courage and strength, some gods, disregarding their allies, [advanced].
The female elephants, their temples darkened by flowing rut-fluid, halted like intoxicated male elephants. ||23||
Having rushed forward with great speed from afar, the leaders of the gods and asuras—
having cast aside all hope for their own lives and having displayed their prowess— struck one another there,
their minds possessed by an intent of extreme enmity as they sought to kill each other. (24)
Then that tumultuous battle between the gods and the asuras became immense in that great conflict.
Mangled by lances and spears, the elephants fell; the horses, struck by arrows, collapsed;
and the warriors, having received heavy blows, fainted while vomiting blood from their mouths with foam.
In that great battle, the lotus-faces of the chief Dānavas and gods, adorned with earrings, fell severed by sharp razor-headed arrows as they displayed mutual pride and wrath.
Those Mothers and those hosts roamed about, crushing the multitudes of enemies in the fray.
With blows from fists, strikes from palms and heels, and by dragging, twisting, and crushing,
the hosts of the Dānavas slaughtered the leaders of the Mātaṅgas with rutting elephants, the best of horses with steeds,
chariots with chariots, and throngs of infantry with foot soldiers in the battle.
Leaping up with speed, the leaders of the Gaṇas struck the warriors of the lord of the Daityas— who were mounted upon elephants—
with sharp arrows, fist-blows, and fierce blows like thunderbolts, until their brains were shattered and their eyes protruded.
Filled with intense rage, they cut them down with battle-axes, hacked and pierced them with swords and spears;
and with their arms, as thick as the trunks of great elephants, they crushed the enemies.
The goddesses also struck those hosts of Daityas who had taken up their weapons in that great assembly—
those mounted upon excellent horses, those stationed in chariots, and those standing at the necks of elephants— leaping up to attack them.
Then that demonic army, its foremost leaders crushed by the lord of the hosts,
was violently agitated like the unfathomable great lake of the ocean when struck by the wind from Garuḍa’s wings.
Then, beholding his forces being violently slaughtered by the leaders of the hosts, Tāraka—
his long eyes copper-red with rage— advanced, protected by the Mauli-bala.
Having drawn his bow, which resounded like Indra’s thunderbolt and blazed with the luster of jewels,
he covered the expanse of the sky with a shower of arrows— feathered with the plumes of herons and peacocks— that pierced the vital organs.
Having learned of that lord of the Daityas' arrival from his mouth,
the son of Analas then beheld the spear held in his own hand, beautiful with its bells of variegated gold;
and then that roar of Kārttikeya, having pierced the sky and the intermediate and cardinal directions, [resounded].
He forcibly bewildered the minds of the enemies of the gods in that great assembly. ||37||
Then, beholding Tāraka approaching in that great battle, protected by a vast force,
Guha released a spear blazing with the brilliance of fire for the destruction of the enemies of the gods.
Released by him, the son of Agni, it enveloped the sky and the quarters with its flames.
In many ways it became most terrible in the sky, like an illusion (māyā) utterly deluding the Daityas.
It fell upon the chests of those enemies of the gods who wore variegated armor;
with irresistible speed, it simultaneously tore through all their bodies and quickly entered within.
Struck by them, all those enemies of the gods— with eyes wide and bloodshot,
their tongues and lips bitten and their limbs convulsing— gave up their lives, vomiting blood,
just as the sun pierces through dense darkness with its rays.
In that same manner, the son of Agni shattered the forces of his enemies on the field of battle with his spears.

Having slain all the enemies of the gods on the battlefield—those possessed of towering pride and valor—the spear, like the radiance of the sun after it has scorched the worlds, then returned to Skanda. ||42–43||
Having slain the Daitya king Tāraka at the head of the battle together with the hosts of the sons of Diti, who were free from distress,
he was praised by the joyful leaders of the assembly of the gods.
Possessing immeasurable splendor, he returned to the presence of the wielder of the trident.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, "The Slaying of Tāraka," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, endowed with the power of great yoga!
I have heard this entire great life-story of Skanda from you,
O supreme lord of yoga, as well as the supreme secret of the Blessed One.
Beyond that, the Lord of Gods, the enemy of Tripura, whose banner bears the bull— || 1-2 ||
Having dispatched Guha as the commander-in-chief of the great army together with the gods,
and having entrusted the deities to Skanda, what else did the Lord do?
Where did the Lord of Gods go, and what did the Daughter of the Mountain say?
"And what did Umā say to him? Recite this for me as I ask.
Sūta said:
Thus questioned by Vyāsa, he then began to relate it.
Sanatkumāra, the son of Brahmā, who possesses great ascetic power and knows the supreme meaning of all scriptures,
said:
"Then Bhava, the god of gods, having renounced [his sovereignty] to the six-faced one, [departed]."
Accompanied by the goddess, he went to Mandara, which possesses golden caves.
He stood there upon that great, radiant golden throne,
strewn with various jewels and as lofty as a golden peak.
Standing by his side, the goddess, daughter of Himavat, shone like Rohiṇī beside the full moon in a cloudless sky. ||8||
Then Girijā, having bowed to the Supreme Lord, spoke:
"Since I am your partner in dharma and exceedingly dear to you, and since I was won through our former affection, I ask this without hesitation. (9)

"O Giver of Desires, O Lord, I wish to hear from you as they are told those meaningful names of yours which are purifying and sacred. Thus questioned by Gaurī, the Lord of the Gods then spoke everything.
O Goddess, the awakening to the meaning of my names is equal to the fruits of all sacrifices;
it is my supreme secret, which even Brahmā and the other gods know.
O Goddess, I shall declare that to you by means of which divinity is attained.
Because I cause all pervasive suffering to melt away within this world, I am called Dravara.
O beloved, because I destroy weeping, I am called Rudra;
and because I withdraw the entire universe at the time of the end, I am so named.
Because he removes death, he is celebrated as Hara;
"pura" is declared here to be the body of all living beings.
Since that city, which is my bed, is situated within all living beings,
therefore my name is "Puruṣa," possessed of great supernatural power (maharddhimat). I have never been born at any time, nor is there any birth of mine anywhere.
Therefore, O Īśānī, I am always proclaimed as the Unborn (Aja).
Having entered into non-existence within me, the world of moving and unmoving beings arises again from me; for that reason, I am designated as Bhava.
Even among the great gods, I alone am the greatest;
for there is no other greater than I, and thus I am Mahādeva. 19.
Because I protect the animals and create them according to my will,
and because I am their very lord, I am known as Paśupati. I alone am the Lord of others, and no one else has power over me.
I lead my devotees to lordship; therefore, I am celebrated as Īśāna.
The directions are indeed my garments, for I dwell in all directions;
since I am the clothing of the directions, I am remembered as Digvāsas (Clad in Space).
Because I am the bringer of welfare (*śaṅkara*) to all beings, I am remembered as Śaṅkara;
because I am the creator of bliss (*śiva*) for the worlds, I am therefore remembered as Śiva.
Since my body is dark blue, yet blood-red and glowing with a crimson luster...
"Therefore, I have been proclaimed by him as 'Nīlalohita' (the Blue-and-Red One). ||24||

When addressed as "Śūlin," he is praised with the word "Śūla"; when addressed as "Lakulin," he is called "Lākulin. O Goddess, when he is celebrated as "Rudra," the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is said to be attained.
Furthermore, when he is addressed as "Hara," one obtains the fruit of the Gosava sacrifice.
By reciting "Bhava," one is immediately liberated from all sins. ||26||
By saying "Puruṣa," one attains supreme happiness; by saying "Aja," one attains residence in the same world [as the deity];
by saying "Īśāna," one attains great sovereignty; and by saying "Mahādeva," one attains the imperishable.
By "Digvāsas" one attains supreme liberation; by "Śaṅkara," great happiness;
by "Śiva," extreme auspiciousness; and by "Śūlī," supreme strength. ||28||
By proclaiming the name "Lākulī," a man gains renown in the higher worlds;
by praising Nīlalohita here, he obtains the fruits of all sacrifices. O Goddess, my devotee attains eternal residence within me.
Thus, O Vyāsa, has that which awakens one to the meaning of names been told. 8.166.30.
"By the wielder of the trident, the God of gods, out of a desire for the welfare and pleasure of the Goddess—what else do you ask, O Brahmin? Speak, and I shall tell it to you.
Vyāsa said:
O Sage, knower of the supreme dharma, you previously stated that Rudra is the bestower of white life; tell me that in brief.
O Lord, how did Īśāna give that life back to the sage?
For what purpose and where, O Master of Yoga? And who is this one called Śveta? (3.3)
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, my child, to how a second birth was granted by the wielder of the Pināka bow to Śveta,
whose life had expired and who was being carried away by Yama.
There was a sage named Darbhadhvaja, equal to Bṛhaspati,
whose self was disciplined by all branches of knowledge; his son was Kuśadhvaja,
who possessed great splendor and was like another Viśvāmitra.

He had a beloved son named Śveta, who was possessed of great luster. From the very moment of his birth, devotion toward the one whose banner is the bull (Śiva) remained constant with that son of Kuśadhvaja, like a shadow that never departs.
Whether standing or walking, sleeping or performing austerities, the great sage remained absorbed in meditation upon the Lord of Gods with his whole being. (38)
Then, O best of Brahmins, after some time, the powerful Dānava named Vipṛthu went to Śveta’s father and chose his daughter.
And he did not give his daughter to that enemy of the gods;
by him, even Darbhadhvaja was slain at night by force.
O observer of noble vows, Viṣṇu, the supreme righteous soul who bears the discus and mace, was desired as a son-in-law by him; and his daughter [likewise] desired him.
When his daughter learned that her own father had been killed, [she acted accordingly].
The virtuous woman of great vows departed for the sake of another to practice asceticism. 82.
Śveta, too, having understood that from it, established himself in supreme detachment;
reaching the banks of the Narmadā, single-minded and with senses conquered,
he offered his entire being to Rudra alone, remaining fixed in him and devoted solely to him.
Performing severe austerities, that one whose wealth is penance remained steadfast and disciplined.
Then, as that wise man was performing his penances, a very long time passed;
the lifespan ordained for him by the Creator reached its end.
Then, perceiving that Śveta’s lifespan was exhausted and that death was manifesting its activity,
the son of Vivasvat joyfully [confronted] Kāla, Mṛtyu, and their attendants.
He dispatched his servants to bring that best of the twice-born.
Then those messengers approached him and stood there with the intent to kill Śveta.
Seeing those messengers of Yama standing there, Śveta then—
Crying out "Alas! Alas!", terrified of death and overwhelmed by distress, he reflected with composure upon Śaṅkara for protection.
Then, the moment he was thought of, [the Lord] standing upon the peak of the king of mountains appeared.
The Lord Śaṅkara, the master of the gods and bestower of grace upon his devotees, perceived Śveta who was afflicted;
knowing that devotee to be thus distressed and fallen under the power of death,
he spoke these words to the Goddess while smiling.
O Goddess, there is a sage named Śveta who is devoted to me and has flourished through his ascetic penance.
His life was exhausted; he became deluded, bewildered by the noose of death.
This rule was established of old by Brahmā, the creator of the worlds:
that there is a loss of lifespan for living beings when the duration of time comes to its end. (52)
For even Brahmā, O Daughter of the Mountain, becomes deluded while creating the worlds, since he creates them filled with death and suffering;
yet that Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, is also exceedingly devoted to me. || 53–54 ||
And because of her exceptional devotion and reverence toward the Daughter of the Mountain King,
O Goddess, this creation, accompanied by death, was authorized by me as well;
for that sage, O Goddess, had dedicated all his actions to me.
"O Pārvatī, because of his single-minded devotion, I am firmly pleased with him.
I shall become his protector and I will restore that sage to life.
Then, having heard her husband's words, Girijā spoke these words: ||56-57||
"O Great God, act thus to grant the desired favor to your devotee;
for what other refuge could there be for this devoted sage? (58)
Thus addressed by Pārvatī, the God of gods, whose banner bears the bull,
the Lord of the Gaṇas, spoke to those lords of the Gaṇas headed by Nandīśvara.
The wielder of the trident sent Śaṅkukarṇa, the leader of the Gaṇas, as well as thousands of others,
for the protection of the sage Śveta.
Having received the command from the mouth of the Supreme Lord, those lords of the hosts, possessed of great power,
quickly went to the presence of the sage Śveta, like the messengers of Antaka (the God of Death) desiring to incinerate [their enemies].
Having gone there, they beheld Śveta being tormented by the messengers of Yama.
Like a single deer in the forest surrounded by many hunters,
his neck bound by the noose of Time and his hands and feet constrained by shackles,
he was being dragged away by Death himself, whose eyes were streaming with blood.

He was being hurled from all sides by the most terrible messengers of Yama, who had deformed faces, large fangs, and blood-red beards and hair; whose eyes resembled lightning, and who held fierce iron clubs in their hands.
Seeing the sage thus distressed and crying out repeatedly, "O Lord!", the lord of the Gaṇas quickly released the sage from those bonds, just as the Lord releases the fetters of bound souls (paśus).
"Go away, servants of Yama! Leave the sage here with his firm bodies; for he is a devotee of Śambhu, the unborn, the cause of the universe, and the lord of gods and demons."
He who is the creator of the wind, fire, Indra, and the Maruts, praised by Brahmā and the other gods, the protector, he whose banner is the bull, the unconquered one—Yama shall not even behold him.
Seeing those leaders of the hosts, the messengers, preceded by Kāla and Mṛtyu,
stood at a distance and spoke to the sage Śveta, releasing him from fear.
"O lords of the Gaṇas, the time for this sage is full; his lifespan is exhausted.
What is the use of him? Release him! Let us lead him into the presence of Yama.
Then Nandīśvara, as if burning them with his wrath, spoke to them.
Go quickly, unharmed, while these wretched servants of Yama have not yet become enraged;
lest those most wrathful lords of the Pramathas seize you,
like lions in the forest seizing elephants maddened by rut.
"Having struck them down all at once, they shall bring an end to those whose lives have run their course.

Then, having been addressed thus by Nandīśvara, the leader of the hosts and possessor of immeasurable prowess, the messengers of the King of the Ancestors departed in fear; and having gone, they reported the matter to Yama.
Having then heard those harsh words spoken by Nandīśvara,
the son of the Sun (Yama) became enraged out of delusion and resolved to go there himself.
Then he advanced, his eyes reddened with anger, surrounded by all those [attendants] led by Mṛtyu.
Sighing like a fierce serpent, he alone seemed as if he wished to incinerate the entire world. ||72||

Having seen the white sage, free from delusion and surrounded by the lords of the Gaṇas whose forms were like Śiva’s, the son of the king of planets said to Nandīśvara and the others, "Release him with speed! ||74||
"Who are you, O Yama, that seeks to lead away the white sage Śveta, who is blessed by Bhava and devoted to the Lord of the Pramathas?
Go away, O fool of unrefined soul, for he is being protected by the Lord himself! Thus spoke Nandin. (75)
Then, having heard those harsh and severe words of Nandin, Yama, filled with rage, spoke this to the lord of all the attendants: 76.
"O leaders of the Gaṇas, this Brahmin’s life has departed; he remains here like one who is unconscious.
Why do you hold him? Release him, lest you undergo vain exhaustion.
For even if he were protected for a long time, he would surely come back to me."

When the full span of time has elapsed, someone here whose life is exhausted does not live on, even if he is wise and endowed with austerity and dharma; for whatever karma he has performed, whether righteous or indeed censurable, [that determines his end]. (78–79)

Having cast off this body, let him attain the state of a leader of the Gaṇas. This entire examination of the multitude of living beings, as well as the investigation of the merits and demerits of their actions, is dependent upon me.
"Therefore, quickly hand over this white one whose life has reached its end.
Or else, all you lords of the hosts, take him and go here to the presence of the Wielder of the Trident; he will certainly release him."
Having heard the words of the King of the Ancestors, Nandīśvara and the others said to Yama, who was overcome by anger, "So be it.
Then all of them together, as well as Śveta, the best of sages—
They came to the Vindhya mountain to behold Hara, the Lord of the World. ||84||
Nandi, the leader of all the attendants, having bowed with supreme devotion to Bhava of immeasurable splendor, reported everything exactly as it had occurred.
Then the Blessed One heard the words spoken by Nandi.
He spoke directly to Vaivasvata with an affectionate and deep voice:
"O Lord of the hosts of the departed, Śveta possesses supreme devotion toward me;
therefore, even though his lifespan is exhausted, death shall have no power over him. || 86-87 ||
"O Tāpana, by means of great austerity and devotion, Śveta has purified his mind in me; through my grace, he has conquered death.
By my command, you must never cause him any harm."

Do you not know, O son of Ravi, that those foremost of men who are devoted to me do not behold your abode even when the dissolution of the body has arrived? Being thoroughly gratified by this exceptional degree of devotion, [I have granted them this]. || 8.166.90 ||
"I shall grant you immortality with this very body.
Thinking thus, free from doubt, go quickly to your own abode.
Having heard these words of the god and having prostrated, the son of the Sun [departed].
Without understanding the ultimate truth, he spoke thus to the wielder of the Pināka bow.
"O Blessed One, this ancient state was created by you alone.
I am appointed to this task of investigating birth and death;
for even Śakra’s authority ceases upon the completion of his office, O Bull-bannered Lord. (93)
"O Lord of the Gods, both the wind and I were indeed created by you alone.
O Mahādeva, this path—which consists of time, death, and destruction—has never been transgressed by anyone through the maintenance of the suspension of time. || 94-95 ||
"O Lord of the wise, having thus reflected upon this supreme creation, you ought to release the foremost of brahmins when his time is full and his life has come to an end;
in this way, the established order shall remain unbroken and I too shall not be held in contempt. (96)
"Death, dwelling within the body, shall obtain that white [elixir] as his boon.
Having heard these words spoken by the King of the Dead, the bull-bannered god [Śiva], like a glowing ember or like the fire of universal destruction, [blazed forth]. || 97-98 ||
Then,
O Vyāsa, perceiving that Nandīśa had mounted Yama’s shoulder, the wielder of the Pināka bow spoke these words, appearing like a sudden upheaval of the world. || 99 ||
"Oh, behold the harshness of the reply uttered by this son of the Sun, who speaks with such deceit! 'Śveta has been rescued by me; go to Yama,' he said. (8.166.100–101)
"Release Śveta!"—thus he spoke to me, his consciousness departed.
But is this man merely a fool, or is he arrogant in his prowess? "Go!"—when commanded by me, who is capable of remaining here?
Standing before me, he spoke this reply once more.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, the cause of the origin of the world, cast a sidelong glance and looked at Yama with wrath. (103–104)
Burned by that eye, he fell to the surface of the earth like a great tree in the forest felled by a mighty wind;
he was quickly reduced to ashes, and then Bhava laughed aloud. || 105 ||
Then the enemy of the Tripura Asuras touched the white sage—who was prostrate, speaking with a choked voice, and despondent from the fear of death—on the head, saying, "Do not be afraid.
And the wielder of the trident granted him this boon: "O Brahmin, death shall not be yours."
And the Lord, being thoroughly pleased, granted him the status of a Gaṇapati and spoke thus to him. || 1.07 ||
"Since I am angry with the son of the Sun on this most sacred mountain, I shall dwell here upon the summit of the king of mountains;
therefore, I shall become Krodheśvara here.
In the Vindhya region, frequented by gods and Siddhas, men who [visit] the holy mountain Krodheśvara..."
Those who, free from delusion, shall cast off the body, their destination is remembered by me as equal to that of Śveta.
And those who behold Śveteśvara here shall also become my own divine Gaṇapas;
moreover, this most meritorious river shall be known by your very name as the Śvetagaṅgā.
"In that [place], there is an exceedingly vast abode for the ancestors, bestowing the heavenly realm, where various kinds of nourishing foods are provided.
As soon as the Lord of the Universe had spoken these words, the sage Śveta assumed a divine body.
Possessing qualities equal to those of Nandīśa and Caṇḍeśa, he bowed to the Lord and stood before him;
then, seeing his son lifeless, the Sun, tormented by grief, quickly rushed forward with speed.
Together with Brahmā and the others, headed by Śakra, they came to the Cause of the World.
Then those immortals made this petition to the Son of the Sun for the sake of restoring life:
"O Lord of the Lords of the World, because this man is deluded, he has therefore fallen into this intense suffering. (113)
"Be gracious, O Lord of Gods; grant us favor so that this king of the hosts of spirits may live.
May he now become as he was before; indeed, O Lord of gods and asuras, sever our affliction!
Such was the petition of the inhabitants of the three heavens, headed by Brahmā, Śakra, and Arka."
Hearing that Yama, the Lord, feeling compassion, said, "Arise, my son!
Then the son of the King of Planets assumed a divine body, resembling a mountain as before.
Rising up quickly, he immediately bowed to the Blessed One, suddenly grasping him by the feet;
then Brahmā and the hosts of the lords of gods, seeing them thus prostrate, spoke to them.

The Lord of Brahmā, the Sun, Viṣṇu, and Agni, the sole creator of the gods and the sovereign of the deities, whose crown is adorned with the moon and half of Śiva’s matted locks—O gods, depart for your own abodes! (118)
"This declaration has been made by you with its fruit; do not, however, fall again into self-delusion.
Having spoken these words to the Lord of the Pretas, the hosts of gods then departed after bowing down. (119)
Having quickly seized Sauri, the King of the Ancestors, Śveta also stood there, freed from death;
just as Nandin was free from the state of suffering, so too was that Brahmin devoted to the Supreme Lord.
Thus has this been told to you— the destroyer of untimely death— concerning Śambhu, the Lord Īśa, husband of the daughter of the Snowy Mountain;
it is the fruit of unerring devotion and the excellence of the attainment of all prosperity.
"I bow to that one refuge in the world, the worthy object of refuge.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, "The Granting of the White Boon," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
This supreme secret majesty which has been declared by you could not belong to anyone else, except for Hara, the remover of the world's suffering.
O great sage, here are the meritorious shrines of the trident-bearing God; having seen them, people do not grieve over birth and death.
"Tell those to me, O knower of dharma, if I am worthy of your favor;
by this means, O best of sages, I shall release myself once my purpose is fulfilled.
Having heard these words of Vyāsa, the son of Brahmā spoke as follows:

Excellent, O Vyāsa of great intellect! You are devoted to Śaṅkara. Since you desire to hear of the meritorious abodes of the Wielder of the Trident, you have achieved your purpose, O master of great yoga, being liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra. ||4-5||
Listen, my child, I shall tell you this supreme secret of mine:
a description of the abode of Śambhu that removes the fear of birth and death.
There is a beautiful peak on the Vindhya mountain named Ādityabandhana.
A highly resplendent liṅga was installed there by Tapanas.
Having seen that auspicious peak of the Snowy Mountain named Hemasomodbhava, O Vyāsa, a person does not grieve over birth. There is a holy sanctuary there,
established by Cyavana.

Those men who then go to that abode of Śambhu do not fall from heaven even when the dissolution of the world has arrived. [On the other hand,] on the sacred mountain Udaya, which is frequented by hosts of Siddhas— || 8.167.10 ||
There is a sacred lake named Satya, covered with golden lotuses,
where those truthful sages— possessing the radiance of truth, fire, and the sun—
those high-souled ones, sustain the Sun-god along with his chariot through their blessings.
O Vyāsa, a holy shrine of the wielder of the Pināka bow was established there by them;
it is worshipped by the immortals and surrounded by Siddhas and Vidyādharas.
Those devotees of Bhava who travel through the sky beheld that shrine at that time.
Having become dear to Bhava, they become lords of the Pramathas.
There, on Mount Uśīrabīja, the king of mountains,
is the great hermitage of Agastya Tṛṇāṅga, which is worshipped by gods and dānavas.
O Vyāsa, in that place there was a linga made of sapphire, of great height.
In that abode, that great Ṛṣi Tṛṇāṅga, assuming the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, constantly praises the matted-haired Rudra;
by worshipping him, the inhabitants of heaven become lords of the Gaṇas.
To the north, in a region devoid of light and bereft of sun and moon,
stands a great, lofty, golden peak of Mount Meru;
there, O venerable Vyāsa, resides the Lord who wields the trident himself, established as a great Liṅga.
O great sage, that *liṅga* was eternally worshipped by Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda, whose soul was devoted to Bhava;
it remains there, inaccessible even to the gods, except for the supreme and excellent Dhruva. || 18-19 ||
On the king of mountains, the great Liṅga of the trident-bearing God of gods was installed by the sage Jaigīṣavya.
Having seen that, O Vyāsa, a human being shall attain the world of Rudra;
they shall become masters of the sciences of liberation and experts in Sāṃkhya and Yoga. ||21||
Upon seeing that most wonderful linga, men become joyful;
it is the supreme linga installed by the King of the Gods in the Nandana garden. ||22||
Having seen that divine linga made of radiant gold, which the deities worship, they attain the supreme state.
In the Ocean of Milk, there is a divine [linga] fashioned by the Bālakhilyas themselves.
There is a great sacred site, meritorious and frequented by perfected *kinnaras*.
In that place is the *liṅga* named Candraprabha, made of crystal and adorned with jewels.
Having worshipped it, the Bālakhilyas went to the same world as the Lord. || 24–25 ||
On Mount Gandhamādana, the king of the Yakṣas established a divine golden linga of the Blessed One known by the name Kubereśa. ||26||
Having worshipped that Great Lord with devotion using divine mandāra flowers and golden lotuses, Kubera became filled with bliss.
By those gods and asuras who beheld that abode of Kubera at that time, [the same joy was attained].
The bull-bannered Lord bestows upon them the fruit of all sacrifices.
O one of great intelligence, hear now of those most meritorious places belonging to the moon-crested Lord that are accessible to human beings in this world. || 28–29 ||
On the auspicious peak of Himavat, the king of all mountains,
is the primordial abode of the Self-Existent One, renowned as Mahālaya.
O Vyāsa, it is there that all the immortals led by the four-faced Brahmā,
as well as the perfected sages and those who are masters of yoga on earth,
having worshipped Hara with devotion, have attained that supreme state.
Wherein Mahādeva himself has directly set down his own foot.
Having approached that Lord who dwells in Mahālaya, all men who bow down to him are liberated from all sins.
Having attained the dissolution of the body—wherever and in whatever manner—a mortal who has reached this unsurpassed perfection is not born again. ||34||
Neither those ignorant of dharma nor even men who have committed evil deeds can see him;
there stands the mighty Mahāgaṇapati, stationed at the gateway.
He destroys the progress of those men who are doers of evil;
where the yogins, gods, siddhas, and supreme rishis dwell—
having bowed to him, they went to the meritorious abode of Paśupati, which is perfection itself.

Merely by the thought, "I shall behold Mahālaya," a living being is liberated from those deeds known as the great sins (mahāpātaka). Mahālaya is a great and auspicious sacred field that bestows the attainment of liberation.
A person who has seen it protects seven lineages on both sides;
beyond that, O Vyāsa, is the most meritorious place known by the name Kedāra. It is the supreme abode of the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva), auspicious and situated to its very north.
It is said that on that most excellent mountain, the god Hara himself released holy water from his mass of matted locks; thus,
the water flowing forth from the crest of Hara’s head came to be there.
O Vyāsa, those men who drink that auspicious water which resembles nectar become Gaṇas known as Kuṣmāṇḍas, who are dear to Rudra.
Possessing great forms and great souls, with a splendor even exceeding that of Nandin,
Brahmā, Śakra, Viṣṇu, Soma, and the lord of the hosts of Yakṣas beheld the God of gods, the Lord of the universe, residing at Kedāra. ||43-44||
Those high-souled men who have drunk the water of Kedāra worship the Supreme Lord stationed there with devotion;
O Vyāsa, how could they grieve? For what happiness has not been attained by them?
May that water which flows from the head of the all-pervading Lord Śiva— the wielder of the trident and the Creator— on the peak of Mount Himavat at Kedāra,
protect you; for those who delight in unrighteousness do not obtain it to drink, except through the grace of Śiva.
Having drunk that, may all beings be liberated from the terrors of the bonds of existence. ||46||
Right here is the primordial station of Umāpati, Madhyameśvara;
having gone there to that Lord of Gods as well, one shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati. ||47||
Even there, O Sage, the Lord is always personally present;
having approached that Īśāna, one should not grieve regarding death.
[This occurs] in a region of the Himavat mountain, belonging even to the three worlds.
O Vyāsa, this is the most excellent, auspicious [mantra], which bestows all spiritual accomplishments. ||49||
Merely by approaching this [liṅga], the fruit of all sacrifices is said to be attained;
even for one who has met with disaster or through negligence, the supreme goal is the state of being a Gaṇapati.
There exists nothing more meritorious than this in all the worlds:
either the sovereignty of a universal monarch over the three realms, or death upon this mountain. (51)
Death here is superior to the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin);
for one who dies here goes to union with Śambhu, endowed with supreme sovereignty.
What higher state than this could there be for a living being who dies here by my word?
But there is another peak of Mahāhimavat, frequented by the Siddhas. ||53||
Where the Goddess performed penance with the desire to obtain a fair complexion,
that place became renowned throughout the three worlds as Gaurīśikhara. It is at the holy site known as Kucakuṇḍa, which was created by Umā.
Those men who go to that holy Gaurīśikhara, ||45||
Having obtained the fruit of the horse-sacrifice, they go to the supreme goal.
[There is] another peak, Ṛṣabha, resembling a diamond or crystal. ||46||
There, Nandi performed penance and obtained a boon from Śaṅkara;
having reached that peak, the sacred abode of Umāpati known as Ṛṣabha, one who beholds it becomes liberated from sin and attains the world of Rudra. ||57||
There is another peak of Himagiri, possessing a splendor equal to Hemakūṭa;
there is the auspicious sanctuary of Rudra named Bhastreśvara.
On that mountain, the god Rudra is known as Bhastreśvara.
The Kinnaras, Uragas, and Cāraṇas pay homage to that Mahādeva;
so too do men who are terrified of death and likewise afflicted by the sufferings of birth. (8.167.60)
Having reached that sacred site and fulfilled his desires as he wished,
a man who beholds it shall obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
[This is] at Gaṅgādvāra, the auspicious gateway, a place of great merit for the high-souled.
The Liṅga established by Dakṣa out of devotion for the one with matted hair (Kapardin) stood where there were trees named Kanakhala that were golden in nature;
however, due to the lack of virtue among men, those wooden trees appeared as if they had been cut down. ||62-63||
Therein dwells Śambhu, the Soul of the Universe and Lord of All, together with Ambikā;
he is known by the name Bahurūpeśvara and bestows many boons upon living beings.
Those seekers of liberation who do not behold him there undergo rebirth once more.
A man who beholds him obtains the merit of ten horse-sacrifices.

Having seen the Lord whose throat is like a dark blue cloud, the hosts of gods, vidyādharas, and siddhas, as well as gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, and dānavas, do not fall again into the mire of saṃsāra.
There is another shrine of the Lord known as Japyeśvara,
where in former times a twice-born man, having performed his recitation (*japa*), established a *liṅga*.
Those men who, having reached Japyeśvara, shall give up their lives there—
Released from birth and death, they shall dwell in the abode of Śiva.
O Vyāsa, there is another sanctuary of the one whose crest is the half-moon of the moon, which is renowned in the world as Mahābhairava, O Sage. (68–69)
There, the god who bears the trident, the bull-bannered one himself,
assumed a terrifying form that was fearsome even to the hosts of Nandi and Umā;
seeing which, the daughter of Himavat became overwhelmed with fear.
Where, for the sake of sport, Bhava caused the daughter of the Mountain King to tremble, he again assumed a gentle form and comforted her;
that sanctuary is therefore called Mahābhairava. || 71–72 ||
O Vyāsa, he who, having approached Bhairaveśvara, beholds the wielder of the Pināka bow,
shall not undergo birth and death again.
Whatever merit belongs to those in the stages of life (āśrama) as well as to those who observe the vows of the Lord, [he obtains that all].
Having beheld that Bhairava, the best of men attains its fruit. ||74||
And likewise Kumbhakāreśvara, as well as Utkuṭukeśvara, Chagalaṇḍeśvara, and the site born of Mahābhairava. ||75||
By beholding these three places, one becomes the lord of the three worlds.
Furthermore, another sacred abode of Śiva is called Rudrakoṭi. (76)
O Vyāsa, having recited three crores of Rudra-mantras there, Nandin attained the supreme status of a Gaṇeśa from Śaṅkara; likewise,
those who behold that sanctuary attain the highest goal.
And in the Devadāru forest is the excellent abode of Bhava;
it is covered with Devadāru trees and fragrant Sarala trees, and is constantly frequented by Gandharvas, Uragas, and Kinnaras. ||78-79||
There dwell the Vaikhānasa brahmins, devoted solely to the worship of Śiva,
rich in ascetic merit, and resplendent like the sun or fire.
It is said that the wielder of the trident entered that forest for the sake of alms;
there, the Lord of Gods was seen by the sages with his organ held erect.
Out of envy, O Vyāsa, that great liṅga of the god was cast down by deluded sages in the hermitage of the Devadāru forest.
When that liṅga had fallen, the world became devoid of a liṅga.
Everything, both the stationary and the moving, shone forth as neuter.
Then the gods, beginning with Brahmā, as well as the Siddhas who were seekers of liberation,
realized that everything was born of Śaṅkara and that its destruction would be most terrible;
having praised Śaṅkara with various hymns, they fully gratified him.
Then that linga of the wielder of the Pinaka bow became as it was before.
And from that [seed], the world immediately attained masculinity;
there, a linga of the Supreme Lord was installed by them with devotion. ||86||
Having seen that, one obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices;
such, O great sage, is the meritorious Dāruvana forest belonging to the Lord.
Having approached it, men are quickly liberated from all sins;
for by Dadhīca, this great, divine, and meritorious sanctuary was established. ||88||
Known as Sthāneśvara and renowned throughout the three worlds, a man who reaches Sthāneśvara and casts off his body there [attains liberation]. (89)
Having attained mastery through yoga, he rejoices in the heavenly world,
by virtue of his firm devotion to Śaṅkara as embodied by the serpent Takṣaka.
Thus, Takṣakeśvara was established on the bank of the Jāhnavī,
where the supreme presence of Rudra, the God of gods, resides.
By beholding that deity, a person obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
And another great, meritorious sanctuary was established by Agastya. || 92 ||
O observer of noble vows, it is renowned in the world as Āmrāteśvara;
having beheld it with supreme devotion, a man of pure conduct [attains his goal]. ||93||
Upon the dissolution of the body, he shall attain the world of Śarva;
having seen the Liṅga of Umāpati on Mount Kālañjara,
he shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and reach the world of Rudra.
It was known as Puṣpabhadraka, situated on a plateau of the Vindhya mountains and covered with trees. ||95||
The abode of Bhava is meritorious and frequented by gods and gandharvas;
it was established there by the rākṣasa Meghanāda, the son of Rāvaṇa, who propitiated Bhava, the lord of all beings. ||96||
There, Mandodarī’s son had his heart's desire fulfilled by Śiva, the moon-crested one, through the granting of a chariot of illusion. || 97 ||
Then, having seen [him], having gone there, and having bowed to the Lord of the World,
men go to heaven, endowed with divine yoga.
In Andhra, there is another sanctuary of Śarva, the Supreme Self.
By name it was Citraratha, the bestower of the boons of yoga-perfection.
It was there, O Vyāsa, that during the slaying of Tripura, the chariot of the wise god was adorned by the immortals— by Soma, Āditya, Yama, and the others.

Whatever fruit is declared by the wise for the correctly performed Aśvamedha sacrifice, a human being attains that same fruit upon reaching Citraratha. There is another auspicious abode of Bhava named Uktaratha.
It is auspicious and always frequented by *suras*, *kinnaras*, and *gandharvas*.

There, the mountain named Śrīparvata stands as an abode of glory; crowded with hundreds of *siddhas* and immortals, it is that most excellent field of spiritual attainment (*siddhikṣetra*). || 102–103 ||
O Vyāsa, it was there that one thousand meritorious, boon-granting Liṅgas of Śūlin were installed by the high-souled Śilāda.
Those men who behold that Lord residing on Śrīparvata shall never again experience the fear of birth and death; indeed,
with this very body, they shall attain liberation in that sacred field which is of the nature of Bhava.
Brahmins devoted to the practice of yoga attain their desired perfection. O Sage, those men who even mentally visit Śrīgirī do not go to the abode of Yama, even when death has arrived.
Then [he went] to Uttaragokarṇa, the hermitage marked by the liṅgas of Hara,
where fierce austerities were performed by flesh-eating rākṣasas,
such as the illustrious Rāvaṇa and others, and where their desired boons were obtained.
In ancient times, having performed austerities there and propitiated the wielder of the Pināka bow,
Rāvaṇa attained the status of a universal emperor over the three worlds;
a man who beholds that place obtains the merit of ten horse-sacrifices.
And upon death, one attains union with Rudra; of this there is no doubt.
Beyond that is the meritorious site of Dakṣiṇagokarṇa, belonging to the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Where, upon the peaks of the Malaya mountain in Laṅkā,
the Blessed Lord, the sovereign of all the foremost immortals, is worshipped with *spṛkkā* flowers;
and where even today Vibhīṣaṇa alone remains as a tiger among Rākṣasas.
Having fully worshipped the Lord of the Immortals, he enjoys his kingdom without fear.
Those men who go to the hermitage of the Gokarṇa shrine obtain the auspicious fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
There is a mountain renowned as Hariścandra, which possesses many waterfalls.
In which [place] a sanctuary was established by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni.
Where the gods, Siddhas, Yakṣas, Guhyakas, and Kinnaras, as well as those observing vows and practitioners of yoga, bow down to the Bull-bannered Lord;
by whomsoever the peak of Mount Hariścandra, Ākūṭa, has been beheld.
O sage, having become gods, they do not dwell among mortals again.
On the northern bank of the Narmadā, at a distance of one *yojana* along the path, is the great site known as Kārohaṇa, a magnificent sanctuary of the Three-eyed Lord.
It was there that Prajāpati ascended upon Kākī while she was performing austerities.
Because the Lord of Creatures ascended there where the crows were,
that region is celebrated by the name Kārohaṇa;
and it was in that very place that the Blessed One whose banner is the bull descended.
O Vyāsa, learn from me of that land which is more meritorious than all lands:
when the Kṛta Yuga had waned and the dawn of the Tretā Yuga had arisen.
Oppressed by unrighteousness, Dharma placed one foot upon that [era];
when the Dvāpara age arrived, he placed a second; and in the Kali age, he placed a third. (1.22)
And because that Lord, the Master, established himself there on the fourth day,
this region is thus remembered as most meritorious due to its association with Dharma.
Having become Bhārabhūti in that region, the wielder of the Pināka bow bound the burdens of the twice-born and cast them into the Narmadā.
Out of compassion and with the desire to liberate mortals from birth, Mahādeva,
as Diṇḍi and Muṇḍa during the Tretā age, cut off his own heads.
In the Dvāpara age, having become a blue jay, he favored them with his dance.
Thus, O Vyāsa, in every yuga, Śiva himself has descended in that region,
bestowing grace upon the Brahmins of pure mind.
O observer of excellent vows, these were the abodes of all of them.
By whom [these] have been seen, one shall attain the world of the Lord Īśāna;
even now, in the Kali age, having recognized that the world is afflicted by suffering.
Having created four persons from his own four faces, the Supreme Lord, desiring to bestow grace upon the worlds, spoke:
"All of you go to the earth, becoming ascetic twice-born ones."
O masters of yoga, having led these Brahmins to the supreme state, you shall come to me alone.
O Vyāsa, having spoken thus, they then became born separately among human beings as brahmins devoted to the dharma of liberation.
In Ujjayinī was the eldest elder, known by the name Kauśika;
the second was Gārgya, who practiced austerities at Jambūmārga;
and the third was the high-minded Mitra, who resided in Mathurā.
But let the fourth be a celibate student (brahmacārī), born of a noble lineage, O Kuru.
The Blessed One, the Lord of Gods, accompanied by Amareśvara,
[bestowed it] upon one born of the lineage of Atri named Somaśarman.
Having assumed a white-bodied form, Śaṅkara went to the auspicious home of the sage Atri;
there, the Lord favored that Brahmin knower of Brahman, Atri, along with his family,
by bestowing upon them the perfection of yoga.
Then, O Vyāsa, having shown favor to that best of the twice-born along with his family, [he departed].
The Lord went to Ujjayinī and entered the cremation ground.
There, the bull-bannered god, having smeared himself with ashes,
