sat down while holding a firebrand in his left hand.
There, the Lord first took Kauśika as his disciple;
then, on the Jambūmārga road, he took a second; thereafter, in Mathurā, and then another in Kānyakubja—thus the Master of the World showed his grace.
The Lākula [prophet] bestowed his own doctrine and spoke this Yoga:
"This supreme secret, known as the Pañcārtha, has been given to you in order to liberate the Brahmins from the bondage of mortality. (8.167.140)
By means of this initiation, cause the Brahmins to attain the supreme state. || 141 ||
"Your dwelling shall be on the pure banks of rivers, in sacred shrines,
in empty houses, or in forests, free from all attachments.
Having heard these words of the Blessed Lord Paśupati himself, the disciples [acted accordingly].
All those who possessed the splendor of Bhava failed to do as they were commanded. || 143 ||
Since existence has descended into that land marked by the footprints of the Dharma, that land is supreme; therefore, it is remembered as the most meritorious of all. (144)
O Vyāsa, where the hermitage of yogins, which destroys all sins, is situated— that place of the Great-Souled One known as Aṣṭāyatana—
is such that by seeing it, men attain the supreme state.
O best of sages, those men who go to Kārohaṇa, the abode of Śiva,
shall have no fear of lying in a womb.
[That land lies] between the Mahī and Narmadā rivers, and within the range of the Sahya mountains.
This is the ancient field of Paśupati, praised by the sages;
having come here, O Vyāsa, even if a man has been a perpetrator of great sins,
he shall be liberated from all evils and attain his desired goal.
The place Kārohaṇa is exceedingly meritorious, O wise one, for there are Śiva temples therein;
having gone to those which yield great fruit, men do not enter the house of saṃsāra again. (149)
And there is another sacred site, O best of sages, honored by the seven worlds, located in Vārāṇasī where Hara is ever present. (8.167.150)
There, the holy Bhāgīrathī flows toward the northern direction;
it is the field of perfection (Siddhikṣetra), the great field (Bṛhatkṣetra), renowned throughout the three worlds. It is known by the name Avimukta, for it has never been abandoned by Hara.
Having beheld there the Lord Avimukteśvara, the husband of Umā.
O great sage, the destination at the time of death is said to be that of the Gaṇas, where the mighty Gaṇapa Vidyutkeśa stands at the gateway. (153)
By the command of the Self-born, the great-splendored Daṇḍapāṇi did not see him; they do not behold Hara, the Lord of the God of Gods.
Even the high-souled yogis find the sight of him to be meritorious.
Having seen the pure Gaṇa Daṇḍapāṇi, who had been granted a boon by Hara, [he spoke].
Having attained happiness in this world, they go to the same world as Him,
where the great-souled Siddhas dwell, endowed with the power of yogic sovereignty.
Having circumambulated him, they bowed down to the Self-Existent One:
Śakra, Pitāmaha, Viṣṇu, Dhaneśa, Varuṇa, and Yama. || 1.57 ||
The consumer of oblations (Agni), the wind (Vāyu), Soma, and the Sun himself,
as well as the seven seers (Saptarṣis), the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Pannagas,
all of them firm in their vows, worship the Lord Avimukteśvara.
Therefore, there is no sacred field of spiritual attainment more meritorious than this; such is the traditional teaching.
There, for a living being who has met their end, liberation from the bonds of saṃsāra arises through the grace of Śambhu. This is remembered as the supreme secret.
The Gaṅgā is to the south of it, and Varāṇasī is to the north;
between those two lies the sacred field of the wielder of the Pināka bow, Avimukta.
Whatever fruit is obtained elsewhere by the installation of a Liṅga of Śambhu, [it is attained here without effort].

That [merit] is said to be a thousandfold when [the image] is installed at Avimukta. Whether a woman or a man installs it according to the prescribed rite, by him a thousand lingas of the Lord have been installed. || 162-163 ||
Having become a leader of the Gaṇas with three eyes, he shall attain union with Rudra.
Therefore, O best of sages, after this, all the supreme gods, led by Brahmā and Āditya, established Liṅgas there.
In that field of the Blessed One, in the city of Kāśī,
many liṅgas installed by great-souled ones are seen even today;
by the mere remembrance of Avimukta, one becomes established at the very end of the earth.
A living being is liberated from impurities and, upon death, attains happiness.
There, Brahmins who know the true meaning of the Vedas,
as well as Siddhas and Pāśupatas seeking liberation from the bonds of worldly existence,
release [their bodies] upon reaching the meritorious Vārāṇasī, the unsurpassed field of perfection.
Furthermore, what living being would have the intention to go out elsewhere? 168.

O Vyāsa, that sacred field of the moon-crested Lord is celebrated in the Vedas as bestowing liberation, perfection, and the supreme goal upon embodied beings who cast off their vital breaths there. Indeed, those men devoted to Rudra who dwell in Vimukti [are likewise blessed].
O Vyāsa, they dwell in the abode of Rudra; of this there is no doubt.
Whether standing, walking, sleeping, eating, performing action, or even laughing, if an embodied being remembers Vimukta, whence can there be fear of rebirth for him?
There is no field superior to Avimukta; there is no state superior to Avimukta; there is no merit superior to Avimukta; there is no goal superior to Avimukta. 172.
The same goal that belongs to one who constantly meditates and merges into the supreme Brahman is declared to be the goal for one who gives up their life-breaths in Avimukta.
This is the merit of the Lord of Umā, frequented by the best of gods, which always leads to spiritual perfection.
This place, which has been frequented by Brahmā and others for the sake of peace as "Avimukta" (the Unreleased),
those mortals who— supreme in their devotion to the Lord— serve it for the attainment of tranquility,
become liberated from the terror of worldly existence and go to the supreme liberation.
And at Prayāga, the field of austerity, there is a great sanctuary of the God;
having beheld it properly, a person shall attain the desired goal. ||175||
Having beheld the great sanctuary of Rudra, the God of gods, at Naimiṣa, one is liberated from sin and shall attain the heavenly world. || 176 ||
O best of Brahmins, by beholding that great abode of the Lord of Yoga at Kurukṣetra, the field of Dharma, one attains the status of a leader of the Gaṇas.
Upon death, he shall attain the world of Rudra, which fulfills all desires;
and at Gayā, there is another auspicious station of the Lord, the Blessed One.
By the name Gṛdhrakūṭeśvara, he is the liberator from all sins;
having seen him, the best of men are not deluded at the time of death. || 179 ||
There, by applying sacred ash, one is liberated from all sins;
a twice-born man shall obtain the fruit even of a twelve-year vow.
There is another meritorious shrine of the wielder of the Pināka bow in Magadha,
known by the name Prahasiteśvara in the city of Pāṭalīputra;
by approaching that Lord, one obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice.
In Magadha, eight places of the moon-crested Lord are renowned, which Nakulīśvara wandered about while surrounded by his disciples;
by beholding these, a person would immediately become free from sin. || 182–183 ||
Among the Yavanas, another sacred place of the Lord of Umā is remembered;
by beholding that Lord, a human being attains Tripiṣṭapa.
In the land of Aṅga, the supreme and holy site of the wielder of the Pināka bow is proclaimed.
Upon seeing him by the name Hemacūḍeśvara, one is not deluded. || 185 ||
Then, O Vyāsa, at the confluence of the Bhāgīrathī and the ocean,
there is a meritorious Liṅga of the wielder of the Pināka bow (Śiva) established by Brahmā.
Merely by approaching it, one is liberated from all sins;
by beholding it, one obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
Having beheld the Wielder of the Trident at Prabhāsa, one becomes a Gaṇa upon the dissolution of the body;
having beheld Śaṅkara at Puṣkara, one shall not grieve over birth and death.
Having approached the auspicious abode of Rudra at Mahendra, the best of mountains,
a wise man shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
[189] At Ujjayini, the one of great vows [should visit] the god Mahakaleshvara.
Having approached him, the wise man shall attain the status of a Gaṇa among the enemies of Tripura.
Having beheld the god Drimi-caṇḍeśvara, a person is saved;
he rescues seven generations on both sides of his family and attains the fruits of all sacrifices. ||191||
Having beheld Śaṅkukarṇeśvara on the peak of the Himālaya mountain, which is frequented by Siddhas and Kinnaras, a man shall no longer grieve over death.
Having approached and beheld that great abode of Rudra known as Ḍiṅgeśvara, he saw the Lord, the Master of the World.
O Vyāsa, one devoted to the worship of Śiva shall attain all desires;
and for the deceased high-souled person, the destination is declared to be the state of a Gaṇapati.
The supreme abode of the God of gods is remembered as Suvarṇākṣa.
O Vyāsa, having seen that, a person shall obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice. || 195 ||
Having beheld the meritorious site of Kapardin at Saptagodāvara,
a man shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice and dwell in the heavenly world.
There is yet another most holy site, renowned as the best in the world.
Known by the name Bhadreśvara, it is frequented by gods and gandharvas.
O Vyāsa, upon beholding it, a human being obtains the fruit of all sacrifices;
whatever great inauspicious karma has been committed since birth [is destroyed]. (197–198)
Upon seeing Hara Bhadreśvara, everything perishes in that very instant;
even if a man dies anywhere else, he shall attain the status of a leader of the Gaṇas. || 199 ||
Blessed are those men, O Vyāsa, who are devotees of Rudra and possess great luster,
who behold Bhadreśa, the remover of the fear of birth and death.
By seeing the abode of the Lord at Ekāmra, one shall attain heaven.
Having seen Hara at Virajā, one obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
And having seen the Lord Paśupati, the God of gods, in Nepāla,
one attains the merit of ten horse sacrifices and goes to the world of Rudra.
And upon the dissolution of the body, one is liberated from the state of being a bound soul (paśu). There is another place on the Himalayan mountain, the Lord of the uniquely lofty peaks. || 203 ||
O best of sages, having seen that, a mortal is not born again;
it is remembered as the granter of all desires to those who are devoted and prostrate before it. ||204||
Thus, O Vyāsa, these meritorious abodes of Rudra have been described by me to you, through which an auspicious state is attained. || 20.5 ||
The bull-bannered God grants union with Himself to that Brahmin who, with a restrained mind, recites these [verses] day after day. || 206 ||
A pure person should constantly perform the recitation of the names of Śambhu’s abodes, which is supremely auspicious, meritorious, purifying, and the remover of all fears. ||207||
Thus, this residence in the world of Viṣṇu— the wearer of the Gaṅgā and son of the king of mountains— bestows all desires upon you;
it is sanctified by the sons and disciples of the best of sages, and it effects the complete purification of sins.
Speak, O Vyāsa; what else may I say to you? || 2.08 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Abodes of Śiva," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sūta said:
Having heard this narrative connected with the sacred abodes of Him whose crest is adorned by the crescent moon’s orb, [the sages spoke].
The sage Vyāsa spoke these words to that lord of sages, the son of Brahmā and knower of Brahman:
"O Blessed One, this righteous and most meritorious secret narrative has been duly imparted to me by you.
Who else among the ṛṣis is capable of fully knowing the places so dear to Śambhu?"
I desire to know how Tripura was consumed by a single arrow by the wielder of the divine Pināka, who formerly granted boons to his devotees; O Sage, tell me that according to how it occurred.
Thus questioned by the sage, the Lord of Sages answered the inquiry exactly as it was asked, speaking these words:
"O son, listen to how that Tripura was burnt. ||4||
When that lion among the bull-like lords of the Daityas, the heroic son of Hiraṇyākṣa, had been slain,
and when the Daityas along with the Dānavas were broken, Maya became consumed by the pain of his lack of fortitude.
Deprived of the royal fortune of the foremost of Dānavas as if by Rati herself, he became like a fish-bannered god (Kāma) without his beloved.
Having taken the Daitya Tārakākṣa and Vidyutprabha, who possessed power equal to that of Indra, he—
whose deeds were never lacking— performed severe austerities along with those two Daityas, whose valor was like that of Andhaka.
During the cold season they stayed on the snowy mountains, and in the summer they were scorched by five fires.
In the rainy season, they performed their austerities with diligent effort upon ground drenched in water under a cloudless sky;
thus, as they remained engaged in such intensely fierce asceticism, a full thousand divine years passed for them.
Through the excellence of their penance, those lions among the sons of Diti became like fire in their radiance, with nothing remaining of them but skin and bone.
The heroes became equal in splendor to the sun and possessed a radiance like the body of the sun. ||9||

The Grandfather approached them all and, having spoken many kind words, addressed them: "Your asceticism has been perfected and your delusion has vanished; now, being joyful, choose a boon. (8.168.10)
With palms joined in reverence and his knees touching the ground, Maya bowed down to the Lord of the Gods and addressed him:
"Grant me invincibility, incomparable strength, divine knowledge, and supreme bliss. (1.1)
O God, grant us this desired boon so that death may not come to us;
O Lord of the Gods, I shall construct a fortress with three cities resembling divine celestial chariots.
"May that [abode] of mine be inaccessible to all the gods, with its own independent structure, location, and movement.
When he had spoken thus, Brahmā addressed these words to Maya, the lord of the Danujas.
"This boon cannot be granted to you; therefore, choose another that is different and yet superior.
O son, ask for it, and I shall grant it; let there be no further anxiety on your part regarding the Danujas.
Then Maya, being utterly bewildered, spoke these words: "Let the boon be exactly as it was requested by us."
O Lord of the Gods, I shall tell you something else; may you grant it to me this very day.
When a full thousand years have passed, the three cities shall come together for a mere half-nimēṣa.
O hero among the gods, at that moment when those three divine cities have converged— || 15–16 ||

"May he burn those three cities with a single arrow; may he be the destroyer of Tripura. Having heard those words of Maya, Brahmā, his inner soul thrilled with joy, granted that desired boon to the lord of the Danujas, and having bestowed it, he quickly departed for his own city.
Then Maya constructed that Tripura, just as the Creator fashioned the worlds at the beginning of the kalpa;
he first made it of iron, and after that, another of silver, resembling a mountain.
He quickly created another third city, golden and as lofty as a peak of Mount Meru;
once created by Maya, that triple-city eclipsed the divine form of heaven itself. (19)
It was well-furnished with charming doors, *vaḍabhī* balconies, and windows, as well as courtyards and walkways made of gold;
with palatial mansions whose floors were touched by moonbeams, providing a pleasant entry through the refreshment of cool breezes;
and adorned with pearls, corals, and fragments of gems, which, when suspended, shone like variegated lightning.
It shone intensely with various banners shaken by the wind and fluttering flags;

adorned with fragments of jewels set in rows upon the palaces, resembling the luster of great moon-like gems, and graced by gateways and lofty rooftops, that Tripura gleamed with splendor. || 21-22 ||
It was surrounded on all sides by very tall trees that bore blossoms and fruit of every season and were pleasing to the mind;
likewise, it was endowed with hundreds of delightful gardens where bees, peacocks, and swans wandered about.
It was filled with ponds frequented by water-birds and covered with blooming blue lotuses.
That abode of the Daityas shone likewise with lakes where cranes were dancing;
it gleamed exceedingly, crowded with women whose breasts were pressed by their nails, whose eyes had red corners reaching to their ears, and who cast slightly tremulous glances with modesty.
Having constructed that city of iron which he placed below, Maya gave it to Tārakākṣa;
he gave the second city, made of silver, to Vidyutprabha, the lord of the Asura kings;
and for his own sake, the king Maya himself took possession of the third divine city, made of gold.
Then that Tripura was presided over by those three lions among the Danava kings, who were equal [in power]. ||27||
Having conquered all their own domains on every side, accompanied by their beloveds, friends, and servants,
they enjoyed various pleasures there, unconcerned with the affairs of the three worlds.
Bound by pride and delusion, their passion was such that they considered the gods inferior in strength.
And perceiving this, they fell upon them with violence and inflicted various kinds of extreme torments.
They stripped the groves, headed by Vaibhrāja, of their creepers and flowers;
they rendered the ponds devoid of lotuses, and they ravaged the plantations, beginning with those of Rambhā.
The celestial women, their limbs trembling with fear, suffered great torment at their hands;
and as they continued thus to bring about the destruction of the gods, a very long period of time passed away.
Then, having become enraged, all the lords of the inhabitants of the three heavens assembled together and immediately reported everything that had occurred,
in its entirety, to the Grandfather.
Seated upon his lotus throne, the Lord addressed all those lords of the gods, consoling them.
"Those lords of the Asuras of Tripura are possessed of great strength; indeed, they cannot be slain by you through force alone.
Therefore, taking Viṣṇu and myself with you, let us go for refuge to Śambhu.
O lords of the gods, the moon-bearer is our eternal resort; he, the wielder of the trident, will slay them by his power."

"So be it," they replied; and those gods—Brahmā, Arka, Śakra, Anila, Pāvaka, and the others—having prostrated themselves and arrived at Kailāsa, beheld Hara, the Lord of the lords of the gods, and praised him with their purposes fulfilled.
"Salutations to the one worshipped by the lords of the three worlds, whose beloved is the Earth, and who possesses immeasurable valor!"
Homage to him whose crest is illuminated by the splendor of the mass of matted hair adorned with the crescent moon!

Homage always to the god of the three worlds; likewise, homage to the wielder of the Pināka bow! Homage to him who bears the blazing sword and battle-axe; homage always to the one who holds the trident in his hand! 36–37.
Homage, homage to the bestower of boons upon Nandi, the refuge of the world, the Lord of the gods;
homage to the eternal bestower of boons upon his devotees; salutations to the bestower of boons upon the Lord of Yakṣas. ||38||
Salutations ever to you who dwell eternally on Himavat, the king of mountains, and who reside on Kailāsa;

salutations to you who are liberated, whose abode is Śani, and who are present everywhere—homage be to you! Salutations ever to you whose limbs are smeared with ashes, who wear matted hair, and who are seated upon the bull.
Salutations to the sky-clad one, the bestower of white boons, who is endowed with all prosperity and is the ordainer of the world;
salutations to the god, the creator of Viṣṇu, the Sun, Indra, Agni, and Brahmā;
eternal salutations to the subtle, supreme Lord, the omnipresent Creator. 8.168.40–41.
Salutation to the Supreme, who is beyond the highest, the Primordial Person known as the Twenty-sixth;
salutation be to Śarva, the wielder of the bow, to Sarva, the eternal source of all.
Salutation be to the First Creator, whose nature consists of the Moon, Wind, Sun, Fire, Water, Earth, and Space.
Homage to Pūṣan, the destroyer of teeth; let there be constant homage to the destroyer of the limbs of desire.
Homage to the Primal Matter (Pradhāna), to the Supreme Spirit (Puruṣa), and always homage to him who is attained through yoga.
Homage again and again to the fierce one, to the gentle one, to the embodied one, and to the creator of the entire world.
Homage to the creator of knowledge, homage to the creator of dharma; homage to the creator of the sacrifice of gods and demons.
Homage to the bearer of the third eye, and repeated homage to the one with the blue crest-lock.
Homage ever be to the Supreme Person, and always homage to the dweller in the cremation ground.
Homage be to the destroyer of the Daitya Andhaka; homage always to the destroyer of delusion. || 46 ||
Salutations always to the destroyer of darkness; salutations always to the destroyer of ignorance.
Salutations always to the bestower of the boon of liberation; salutations always to Him who abides in the nectar of immortality.
(47) Salutations to the husband of the daughter of the mountain-king; salutations always to the father of Kumāra.
Homage to the one who grants boons to the Lord of Wealth; homage always to the one who grants boons to Śukra.
Homage to the one whose self is Brahman, who creates Brahman; homage, homage to the creator who brings forth the gods.
Homage to the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice and of the immortals; homage to Caṇḍeśa, the granter of boons. 48–49.
Salutations to Rudra, the supreme abode, the Lord of Yoga praised by the immortals;
salutations to Hara, Śarva, Śiva, the Protector, to Bhīma and to Śambhu.

Salutations forever to the one who is devoid of qualities, yet overflowing with qualities, who transcends qualities, yet abides in qualities; to the Puruṣa praised in the Sāṃkhya, established in the Yoga-Upaniṣads;
salutations always to the Great Purāṇa, higher than the highest, both gross and subtle.
"Being propitiated, O Supreme Lord, grant us your favor; being pleased, bestow a boon.
Thus did Śambhu respond to the gods, led by Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and the Sun, as they offered their praise.
Pleased by her exceptional devotion in this hymn of praise, he spoke these words of most wonderful meaning:
"I am satisfied, O gods; listen quickly today if there is anything you desire.
I shall grant it all today without exception; there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be given to you."
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Granting of Boons to the Deities," at the commencement of the destruction of Tripura in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The gods said:
"O Lord, by the three Dānavas—Maya and the others—who have been granted boons by Brahmā..."
"Having made that Tripura a fortress, we shall oppress [the gods] who are arrogant in their strength.
All the *apsarases* have been seized and the forests destroyed;
today we shall slay all the gods, and tomorrow we shall slay them," they said.
"Even Brahmā, the Grandfather, or Viṣṇu, or even Mahādeva, is not capable of subduing them; therefore, we have very great fear. ||3||
O best of gods, act in such a way that Tripura may be destroyed and they may be slain; grant us this boon. (4)
Thus addressed by all those foremost of gods, the immensely radiant Śambhu spoke these words as if consoling the deities:
"O lords of the gods, take indeed a hundredth part of my splendor."
Having become composed of the splendor of Rudra, they shall slay the Dānavas.
Then those gods spoke these words once more to the Lord:
"O Lord of the Gods, we are not capable of bearing even a thousandth part of you;
what power do we have against the supreme, great majesty of Maheśvara?"
O Lord, grant us your grace so that we may either see or hold [the weapon].
O Blessed One, O Śaṅkara, we are in no way able to slay those Dānavas by force; you yourself must destroy Tripura.
It is said that a boon was granted to them by Brahmā, the wielder of the trident:
"After a thousand divine years have passed, the powerful one shall come to the three cities;
in that moment, lasting half a blink of an eye, he shall destroy this triple city."
"He who, having discharged a single arrow once, shall utterly consume the Dānavas—he shall be your death;
for there is no other way for your death.
We are not able to do that; therefore, grant us your favor. (11–12)
Then that Blessed Lord, whose banner bears the bull, spoke again to reassure the dejected inhabitants of heaven who were bowing before him:
"O tigers among the gods, if it is thus that the great Tripura is so difficult to overcome,"
Having discharged a single arrow but once, I shall consume [them] in the twinkling of an eye.
Indeed, for the sake of pleasing Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and for the favor of Śakra,
I myself shall mount the chariot Tripura and destroy it.
"Let that chariot be made ready, ascending which, O dwellers of heaven,
I shall consume the triple city, though it is difficult to assail and occupied by the three classes of Dānavas.
O foremost of gods, let it be such as would indeed be capable of carrying me."
A chariot of such strength, comparable to the Himalayas, must be constructed.
Then the gods, having bowed to the Lord, became joyful in mind;
together they all fashioned an excellent chariot.
Then the blessed Brahmā, as well as Viṣṇu and Hutāśana (Agni), [prepared it].
They fashioned that supreme, divine chariot, which was composed of all the gods.
To Dhātṛ, Bhāskara, Śakra, Pavana, Dhanada, and Yama;
to the Vasus, the Rudras, as well as the Ādityas, the Gandharvas, and the two Aśvins.
[He saw] Garuḍas, mountains, nāgas, guhyakas, and the great oceans;
likewise ṛṣis, siddhas, yakṣas, and grahas... ||21||
...the white [half-month] and likewise the black, as well as the lords of the forest;
the days, the muhūrtas, the kṣaṇas, and likewise the kāṣṭhās and lavas;
the two solstices, the seasons, the months, the fortnights, and likewise the years.
Whatever is stationary and whatever is moving, as well as the constellations; ||23||
They arrayed those eight classes of gods upon that chariot;
some they placed upon the two wheels,
while others they assigned to the pole and the shafts of the chariot, O preeminent among the gods.
Having done so, they yoked the four Vedas as horses to that chariot.
They made the year into the wheel and likewise the mountain into the bow;
they made the goddess who sustains the world the bowstring of that bow.
Thus did the gods construct that foremost chariot of such a kind.
Having fashioned that supreme chariot, which was like a mountain and composed of all the gods,
Viṣṇu, Pitāmaha, and Agni bowed to the Supreme Lord and declared,
"The chariot is ready for the destruction of the enemies of the gods. || 27-28 ||
Then the Blessed Lord Śambhu, being praised by the three classes of gods, gazed upon the divine chariot fashioned from all the deities;
saying "Well done! Excellent!", he took up that great bow.
Then he took up that supreme, blazing bow, which was composed of all-pervading splendor.
Having gazed both downward and upward, the Lord of the World was gratified;
then, looking at the Grandfather, the Lord of Speech spoke:
"O Brahmin, this chariot and this bow have been well-prepared by you."
"Bring quickly that arrow by which Tripura is to be consumed.
Then Brahmā, having bowed to the bull-bannered god, said to him:
"O Lord, this chariot has been prepared for you, and this bow as well, by me."
"The Blessed One alone is capable of making that arrow suitable for its purpose.
Then, seeing Śambhu and Viṣṇu standing at his side,
the subduer of enemies summoned those two gods with a glance of his eye.
Having joined their palms in reverence, the two of them stood before the Lord of the Gods.
Then Śambhu himself fashioned Viṣṇu into the excellent arrow;
he fixed Soma, the lord of medicinal herbs, upon its nock.
Brahmā then appointed Śalya as the fire and spoke to him:
"O Brahmā, who has been appointed by you here as the charioteer on this chariot?
Thereupon, Brahmā, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to the Lord of the World.
If you give me the command, I myself shall indeed be the charioteer. || 38 ||
"O Lord, what else shall I obtain that is superior to being your charioteer?
Having said, "Everything shall be auspicious," the god who wields the Pināka bow then departed.
Taking the Lord of Gods by the hand, he ascended the excellent chariot;
and those who were the attendants of Rudra, led by Nandīśvara, [did likewise].
Led by Śaṅkukarṇa and including Caṇḍeśvara and others,
these lords of the Gaṇas were great yogis, three-eyed, with *paṭṭiśa* spears in their hands;
they wielded various weapons and missiles and were experts in diverse modes of combat.
Adorned with various ornaments and garments, and proficient in various branches of knowledge,
those fourteen thousand leaders of the Gaṇas arrived together, sounding many musical instruments along with the sounds of kettledrums and conchs. || 42-43 ||
Showers of thousands of various kinds of flowers fell upon the head of the wielder of the Pināka bow as he stood in his chariot;
and musical instruments themselves resounded in every direction.
And they were all yoked to the chariot of the trident-bearing God of gods. ||45||
Unable to bear the burden, the gods were utterly bewildered;
then the Lord of the Gods, perceiving those inhabitants of heaven to be deluded, [acted]. ||46||
The gods made his body capable of being endured, and consequently they were bewildered;
then, O Vyāsa, in this interval, the venerable sage Nārada appeared.
He went quickly to Tripura with the desire to see Viśvakarman.
Then, seeing that the sage had arrived, Viśvakarman Maya [acted] at that time.
Having worshipped him with supreme devotion, he bowed down to that best of sages;
and the latter, having bestowed blessings upon him, sat down upon a cane seat.
Having seated himself on that seat, the great sage spoke to Maya.
Having propitiated this bull-bannered god by all the deities, [he attained his goal]. (8.169.5)
"He has been brought here to destroy Tripura; therefore, do what is right.
Having mounted his divine, god-made chariot, the Lord of the World [is ready]. (51)
Having made Brahmā his charioteer, Śaṅkara himself came;
having heard the words of Nārada, that lord of the Dānavas then [prepared].
Having summoned Tārakākṣa and Vidyunmālin,
as well as his other asura brothers led by Bāṇa and Nemi,
he then made them hear everything that had been related by Nārada.
Having heard that, Tārakākṣa, the king of the Daityas, spoke this: ||54||
"O bull among gods, there is no one equal to you in the three worlds who could fight you without fear; do not harbor such anxiety on my account.
O King, what is there to worry about here, since we are all destined to be slain?"
O Dānava, who would possess the power to destroy those three cities?
"O Lord of Daityas, even if all the gods were to assemble here to fight,
behold them today slain by me alone!
A weak man employs division, bribery, or even conciliation."
"Let them always pay homage to a stronger enemy who is superior in power.
"Punishment must be inflicted upon a weak enemy by one who is strong and desires victory through valorous deeds"— thus did the preceptor Śukra speak at that time.
Therefore, we Daityas are powerful while the inhabitants of heaven are weak;
having slain them all with our staff, we shall remain at ease and in happiness.
Having heard the words of Tārākṣa, Vidyunmālī spoke these words:
"This auspicious speech of the king is also exceedingly pleasing to me.
Deprived of strength, the gods are not capable of fighting with us."
If those deluded ones should fight, they will then go to their destruction.
Therefore, we shall employ a stratagem against them rather than fighting one another;
for in battle, the Daityas do not always achieve supreme victory.
"Having slain all the gods today, rule the kingdom in the third heaven;
enjoy the three worlds in peace, become Indra, the creator of all!
Today we behold you as Purandara, the lord of the seven worlds. (64)
"O Lord of Daityas, remembering Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa,
who were the enjoyers of the kingdom of the world, you too should go to their destination.
Having heard these words spoken by Vidyunmālin, O Vyāsa, Maya [replied].
"O best of Daityas, he who is an enemy equal or inferior in strength to himself said, 'It is not so,' shaking his head repeatedly. (67)
Whether it be a child or one who is older, or those who possess bodies born of various lineages—
the wise apply toward them these four means.
"O leaders of the asuras, we gods are equal to you in strength; therefore, it is appropriate for us to employ conciliation and other such means toward those gods. (69)
This Blessed Lord Īśa, the Lord of the lords of all beings, is the sovereign who is both the creator and the destroyer of us and of the gods.
He comes himself to slay him; what kind of means can there be against him?
"Prostration and seeking refuge—these two are the means for attaining the qualities of the one with matted hair (Kapardin).
It is my conviction that these two methods alone should be employed against him.
If we were to fight the wielder of the Pināka bow by resorting to harshness... (71–72)
By his mere sidelong glance, the Asuras were struck down;
then Brahmā and the other gods, being tormented, went to Śambhu for refuge for the sake of peace.
But who could be a refuge for him by whom even he himself was overcome? (73)
O Daityas, he by whose mere thought this entire world, renowned from Brahmā downwards,
might perish in an instant,
or even come into being— he who is the cause of liberation and the cause of the world.
"What kind of battle did we have with that Śambhu, the God of gods? Do you not know the difference between the intelligence of a child and a mountain of earth?
Having become like clods of earth yourselves, you face the Lord of Umā, who is like a mountain. (76)
"You desire [this] in battle, deluded and bound by the noose of Time.
I am a devotee of Mahādeva; I know the extent of his power.
I shall approach him with prostration; I will not fight with Śambhu. || 77-78 ||
If you too are wise and wish to listen to me, do not engage in battle with Śambhu; go instead for refuge to Śiva.

Having heard those words spoken by the powerful Viśvakarman, the venerable Nārada addressed these words to the destroyer of the Dānavas: 80. "O you who are the creator of all, having heard him speak thus, the blessed Nārada spoke these words to the one who brings an end to the Dānavas."
"O Viśvakarman, that which has been spoken by you here at length and with purpose—all this is indeed appropriate; however, the time for it has not yet arrived.
Your ascetic merit has been exhausted, and your sovereignty has already been enjoyed."
Even by acting with cowardice, you Dānavas shall perish.
Śambhu, surrounded here by all the immortals for the sake of slaying you,
will destroy even you who are prostrate before him for the sake of his own pleasure.
"How is it that you Dānavas, though born as sons of Danu and being kings arrogant in their strength,
are afraid and wish to conquer death like wretched men?
You shall attain even greater sovereignty if you should give up your lives in battle."
If you perish without fighting, your destiny will be inauspicious.
Moreover, even if you are slain by the trident-bearing God of gods, O lords of the Pramathas, you will then become [his attendants]; of this there is no doubt. || 85-86 ||
There is no merit in your alliance with the gods;
your inclination toward war is appropriate, and that is evident, as are we to you.
Śiva, whose emblem is the bull, has at times been pleased by your valor.
O Daityas, he shall be the granter of boons; therefore, valor will be for your welfare. ||88||
"And I shall provide you protection that thwarts the strikes of weapons.
Arise, O sons of Danu, with the desire to fight for the sake of victory!
Having heard the words of Nārada, the exceedingly powerful Tārakākṣa [arose].
And Vidyunmālī, the lord of the Daityas, as well as Bāṇa and other great Asuras.
"Afflicted by the noose of Time, deluded, their merit exhausted and their lives spent, they said to him:
'This which has been spoken by Nārada is excellent and beautiful.
I too, having understood those words and realizing that destruction was at hand,"
He spoke these words: "What was said by Nārada is excellent. || 92 ||

Nārada also, delighted, having bound a protection through his illusory power (*māyā*) and having rendered the Asuras eager for battle, proceeded toward the chariot of Śarva. Then all those Dānavas became resolved upon combat.
Equipped with various weapons and desiring battle,
Tarakākṣa, Bala, Bāṇa, and the Dānava Vidyunmālī—
all having donned their armor— stood together at the front of the kings. || 94-95 ||
Then, thousands of conchs and musical instruments were sounded amidst the terrible army of the Dānavas, which struck fear into the hearts of the cowardly.
"Here comes the charioteer; that other one is seen there.
"How has he arrived?"—thus did the hosts of Daityas from Tripura speak to one another, free from fear and despondency.
With faces contorted in rage, they became ready for battle;
with excellent weapons in their hands, they followed close behind that chariot like animals following the sacrificial fire, gazing intently at it. ||98||
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Asuras in the Destruction of Tripura," in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that chariot arrived at the summit of the western ocean, where Tripura was situated.
With his crown resplendent and variegated with various banners, he was like Meru, the king of mountains, composed of golden stone. ||1||

Having beheld the impregnable Tripura, the leaders of the Gaṇas, headed by Nandīśa and Caṇḍīśa, stood well-prepared; those great heroes, desiring to fight with the lions among the Dānava kings, raised a roar together.
And Caṇḍeśvara, the high-souled one of fierce form, with a blazing, flaming, and terrible axe in his hand,
stood before Lord Śambhu with his mouth wide open, that hero among the lords of the Pramathas.
Grasping a radiant trident, the three-eyed Nandin, whose body was equal to that of Hara, set forth.
And that lordly elephant Śaṅkukarṇa stood at his side, grasping a blazing mace. ||4||
Bhṛṅgin, who is the very self of Hara, as well as Vīrabhadra and hundreds of heroic leaders of the Gaṇas,
stood there filled with joy, eager for battle, with thunderbolts, tridents, swords, and *bhuśuṇḍi* weapons in their hands.
Seeing that chariot arrived, the Daityas, overcome by delusion, sallied forth for combat.
Those heroic sons of Danu, headed by Tārakākṣa, having donned their armor with various weapons blazing in their hands,
engaged in battle together with the lords of the Gaṇas, overcome by the power of wrath.
Even the God whose crest is the abode of the half-moon did not discharge an arrow to consume the city.
He stood there just as before, repeatedly observing that battle between himself and the hosts of Daityas;
then Nandin engaged in combat with the foremost heroes of the Gaṇas, who were undaunted in spirit.
Vidyutprabha, his eyes bloodshot with rage, pierced Bhṛṅgin with ten arrows.
Having approached Bhṛṅgin, those arrows were unable to inflict any injury upon him.
Then Bhṛṅgiriṭi struck Vidyutprabha on the back with his flaming trident;
struck by that trident, he reeled and, abandoning Bhṛṅgin, fled, afflicted by fear.
Thus shattered, that lord of the sons of Diti abandoned Bhr̥ṅgin, the chief of the Gaṇas,
and pierced Vināyaka in the region of his shoulder with seven sharp, whetted arrows.
Again, with sixty-three and then ten more, Vidyutprabha struck him whose face is like the king of elephants.
Having struck him in his vital spots with unerring aim, the Lord of Vināyakas then grew enraged.
Then that lion among lordly elephants, having encircled the neck of the lord of the Daityas with the tip of his trunk,
tore the head from the body, just as a wild elephant plucks a lotus from a lake.
The severed head of the Daitya shone forth from that body, which resembled the lord of the Vindhya mountains,
like a lotus quickly uprooted from a lake resounding with the songs of swans and ruddy geese.
Then two other lords of the Daityas, Nemi and Bala— who were as formidable as Andhaka and well-armed—
approached Śaṅkukarṇa in a rage and pierced that lord of the Gaṇas with feathered arrows.
Śaṅkukarṇa, springing forward with force, rendered them both chariotless, their banners and horses destroyed.
Mounting two other chariots, those two once again approached the hero of the hosts.

Then, having gazed at those two kings of the Daityas for a long time, the enraged Lord of the Gaṇas violently struck them with many kinds of exceedingly sharp arrows resembling the impact of a thunderbolt. (17)
Having struck those two heroes with his blazing mace, he dispatched them to the city of Yama;
and other Daityas dwelling in Tripura, enraged, rushed forth to be met by the lions among the leaders of the Gaṇas.
With iron arrows, discs, swords, and axes in their hands, those lords of the Daityas waged a most terrible and great battle against the lords of the Gaṇas,
who were equal to Hari and had obtained the grace of Śiva.
Struck down, they indeed became breathless, like deer at the edge of a forest by lions.
With their various weapons, garments, and necklaces fallen away, and carrying blood from their severed arms,
they fell into the ocean like mountain peaks struck by thunderbolts.
Then, hearing that those two Daityas named Bala and Nemi had been forcibly slain by Śakukarṇa, [the others fled].
Having emerged from the city, Tārakākṣa, filled with rage, personally rushed toward the lord of the Gaṇas.
As that lord of the Daityas, who resembled a mountain, was swiftly discharging a fierce shower of arrows, Śaṅkukarṇa,
the leader of the Gaṇas, violently struck the Daitya on the head with a broad-headed shaft.
Having fallen and being struck somewhat by that broad-headed arrow (bhalla), the lord of the Daityas fainted.
Rising quickly, Tārakākṣa indeed hurled a discus at that leader of the Gaṇas.
Thereupon, that lord of the Gaṇas, Śaṅkukarṇa, became enraged at Tārakākṣa. || 23-24 ||
Having struck him down, he beat him on the head with his fist; thus struck, he fell into distress.
He reeled, wandered, fainted, stood still, and fell, casting aside his excellent weapon.
He vented his rage, shrieked intensely, and finally died, released from his life-breaths.
Having seen the lord of the Daityas fallen, the Daityas took him up and went to the abode of Maya;
having reported this to the king of the Asuras, their master, they raised a great outcry with various lamentations.
Then Maya, the lord of the Asuras, spoke these words to those weeping lords of the gods, consoling them.

"O Daityas, this nectar created by me remains here; therefore, raise him up quickly! Then, taking that supreme nectar, the joyful leaders of the Daityas restored Maya to life as he was before and repeatedly bowed their heads to him.
Then Tārakākṣa, desiring once more to fight, quickly went forth onto the path of battle.
Seeing him approaching— him who had previously died and now returned to life—
the Grandfather (Brahmā) spoke these words to the lord of the gods and asuras, pointing out the Daitya with his left hand.
O Śaṅkara, although this Tārakākṣa was slain, he was quickly restored to life by Maya;
for he possesses the supreme nectar of the gods, with which that lord of the asuras brings the demons back to life.

"This is a great fault, O Lord of the Gods, that he revives those who have died in battle because of my thought. Then Śambhu quickly withdrew that nectar situated within him merely by means of his meditation.
The Grandfather (Brahmā), being delighted, bowed again to the wielder of the Pināka bow and spoke these words to him.
I have witnessed this battle of the Gaṇas with the lords of the Daityas, who are undiminished in their vital strength.
A thousand divine years have passed, yet this Tripura has not gone to its destruction.
O Lord of the Gods, discharge that flaming arrow; let those enemies of the gods meet their end!
When the thousand years were complete, O Lord of the Gods, Tripura came together and once again became disarrayed.
"O God of gods, this arrow has been discharged by you; or rather, O Lord of the gods, what need is there for your effort?
By mere thought alone, O Lord, this Tripura—the abode of the Daityas—goes to its destruction.
If I am to be honored by you, O Lord, then quickly release that arrow at Tripura."
Thus addressed by the four-faced one, the slayer of Ananga,
having drawn his bow with great force, fixed that flaming arrow upon the Pināka; then,
by mere thought, the god [reduced] those three cities together to ashes.

The creator and destroyer of the world set it in motion, and the universe immediately became motionless. The god discharged that fierce arrow, which was of the nature of Viṣṇu, with fire and moon as its feathers, blazing like the dissolution of the three worlds; and having shot it, he cried out, "Alas! Shame! || 38-39 ||
Then Nandin, having approached Maheśa, bowed down and spoke these words: "What is it?
The Blessed One said to that Nandīśvara: "Desiring to perform a favor for my devotee Maya, O Lord of Nandins, Viśvakarman is my devotee; he shall so construct his city that fire shall not burn it."
"Likewise, by my command, go and restrain the two gods Anala and Somahari.
Then Nandin, having received the command of the Lord of the Gods, quickly went to that city of the Creator;
possessing a speed equal to his, he arrived even earlier than Jyotiṣmat.
Seeing there that lord of the Dānavas, his body bowed with his head before the bull-bannered god,
afflicted by the fear of death and seeking refuge, Nandin comforted him as a devotee of the Lord.
"Do not fear; you are protected by me; you shall become a devotee of Bhava," he spoke these words.
Having seen Nandīśvara and having heard that pleasant favor from Śiva, the king of the Dānavas [replied]. ||44||
Just as he had bowed his head to Rudra, he likewise offered salutation to him.
Then Agni arrived, desiring to consume Tripura, having set it ablaze on all sides;
resembling the fire of universal destruction at the end of an eon, he blazed as if to annihilate the world.

When he had arrived—the abode of the Creator of All, Viṣṇu joined with the Moon, and the blazing Fire—Nandin, by the command of the Lord, quickly spoke these words: "This must not be consumed by you, O Consumer of Oblations.
Then that Fire said to the God: "Why should this not be consumed by me?"
Then Nandi spoke to Hutāśa: "I remain here, a devotee of the Lord of the Immortals."
Then Vahni spoke these words to the Asura king Māya: "Depart quickly from here!
Taking the golden Liṅga of Maheśa, the Asura lord Māya emerged from the city and, rejoicing and offering salutations to the Beloved of Umā, swiftly entered Pātāla.
Nandīśvara also, having approached the presence of the Lord of the Gods and reported this, remained there.

Then Tripura became ablaze; its machines and bolts were shattered, its houses destroyed, and it was filled with the great, fierce cries uttered by many asuras, while the wives of the lordly daityas were overwhelmed with terror.

In the windows of their palatial mansions, women with moon-like faces and full breasts lay sleeping upon couches, their eyes clouded by intoxication; they gazed repeatedly down the path toward their beloveds, their limbs anointed with copper-hued unguents and their fair complexions contrasted by broad hips.
Their eyes were reddened by the color of their cosmetic ointments.
The wives of the Daityas saw themselves ablaze, embraced by the fire of the arrows;
staying upon their palaces, they fled, afflicted by fear like Kinnarīs dwelling on mountains out of terror.
Then, beholding their beloveds returned, they fell into a swoon and were utterly overwhelmed.
Then those sons of Diti, having seized their beloved ones, departed with speed, their desires fulfilled;
but as soon as they had emerged, being deprived of their strength and bewildered by the power of Śiva, they fell into the ocean.
Then, as those Daityas fell into the ocean, great fish resembling mountains,
along with fierce crocodiles and terrible makaras, devoured them— now deprived of strength and bewildered.
Other great lords of aquatic creatures seized those women who had fallen there, their necklaces shattered.
Deprived of their loved ones, those with terrifying fangs and gaping mouths set about devouring them. || 5-6 ||
Being devoured, those young women fell down; having gazed many times with great anger at their beloveds, the youthful maidens, tormented by intense pain, wailed most piteously.
Then, that furious gaze of those Daitya-wives shone forth intensely.
At the end of their dalliance, they were as weary as if their lovers desired to approach other women.

Then all those bull-like Daityas, together with their wives, being scorched by the fire of Tripura, sank into the ocean; pierced by sea-monsters, they lost their lives and fell under the power of death.

And that arrow, whose essence was Agni, Indra, and Janārdana, having utterly consumed that city of Tripura and cast it into the ocean, attained tranquility; it subsided and returned to the hand of Śambhu. When those Daityas had been slain and Tripura burnt, the Lord [re-established] the gods once again upon their chariots.

Just as previously he, the cause of creation, dissolution, and so forth, had made them endowed with divine bodies, so now Brahmā and the other lords of the denizens of heaven bowed to the Lord and spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, this deed you have performed is impossible; it is a great and auspicious act, yet one even more terrible than the fierce."
The Daityas have been slain, that Tripura has been consumed by fire, and peace has been established for us, O Lord of gods and asuras!

Homage to you, the creator of the gods, the Supreme Lord who is eternally present everywhere! Homage, repeated homage to you, the all-pervading one, whose movements and actions are forever unknown! ||63||
Then the Lord Brahmā said to those lords of the gods, headed by Brahmā, Arka, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Dhaneśvara:
"O gods, you must always protect and guard me just as you would your own sons."
With their desires fulfilled and their enemies destroyed, the gods departed for their own abodes, rejoicing;
then, having bowed to the best of gods, they went to their respective dwellings.
The god [Śiva] also, being saluted by the Siddhas and accompanied by the lords of the Gaṇas, proceeded to the peak of Kailāsa.
Accompanied by Caṇḍeśa, Nandīśvara, and Vīrabhadra, the three-eyed Creator of the universe departed.
Thus, O Vyāsa, this unbearable deed of the God of gods, known as the burning of Tripura, has been narrated by me to you.
The man who, being pure and a devotee of Śarva, studies this, becomes free from sin, a partaker of heaven, and one born among the gods.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventieth chapter in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the section on the Destruction of Tripura.
Vyāsa said:
"O Blessed One, I have heard this account of the burning of Tripura;
it is of wonderful meaning and exactly as it occurred—who else could have related it thus?"
Why did Guha, in his anger, tear asunder that king of mountains, Krauñca? And why did Vāsava sever the wings of all the lords of mountains?
Sanatkumāra said:
Listen, O Vyāsa of great intelligence, to that which you ask me:
how the Krauñca mountain, the son of Maināka, was split by Kumāra. (3)
Then, having approached Meru, the king of mountains and abode of all the gods,
Vāsava beheld Skanda like a mass of splendors;
he saw the youth, radiant as fire, in a grove of reed-thickets.
Śakra, overcome with the intoxication of sovereignty over the gods, questioned the six-faced one.
"Who are you, O child of divine form, who have taken refuge on Mount Meru?
Having seen me, the king of the gods, arrived here, why do you not honor me?
To Śakra, who was speaking thus, the son of the Trident-bearer replied:
Brahmā and the others, as well as the perfected ones and those who know the Vedas, recognize me.
"O Śakra, what purpose is served by you, who know this, or by one who has been honored, when you have already lost your kingdom through asceticism and will soon meet your end?
Then Śakra spoke again to that god, the son of Fire:
"There is none higher than me, except for Śarva and Pitāmaha.
O sinless one, why have you spoken thus to the lord of the gods who has arrived here, if you consider yourself greater than me? (8.171.10)

For this is the son of Maināka, the great mountain frequented by perfected beings (siddhas) and cranes, vast in extent and possessing many flowing waterfalls. Come, come with me; quickly perform a circumambulation.
"Whichever one of us two shall first advance against him,
he shall become our great leader by virtue of his power and splendor.
Having said, "So be it," the six-faced Kumāra then [departed].
Having joined with Śakra and mounted his excellent peacock,
he proceeded before Mahendra and circumambulated Mount Krauñca.
Then Mahendra, perceiving himself to be inferior to Anala, [was filled with shame].
Desiring to circumambulate the prince even with his mind,
he stood there, deeply satisfied, seated upon the surface of the rock. Then the prince, having swiftly performed a circumambulation of that curlew, [proceeded].
Seeing Indra, Guha then spoke in haste, "I shall be the victor.
Śakra said to Guha, "I alone am the victor.
As Śakra and Kumāra were thus speaking repeatedly to one another, || 17 ||
Approaching, the land-dwelling Krauñca spoke these words: "What is this?
Then Śakra addressed these words to the Kumāra:
"This very Krauñca, possessed of great strength, is the witness to our victory."
"For this excellent grandson of the Himavat mountain will not speak a falsehood.
O Śakra, let him be questioned; what harm is there? so said the son of Agni.
To him, Śakra spoke with respect: "By whom were you [seen] upon the mountain peak?"
"Having performed the circumambulation, speak, for you are indeed the authority for both of us.
Then the mountain Krauñca, his mind bewildered, reflected for a very long time:
"This husband of Śacī has performed the circumambulation here with me in front of him."
Laughing, the Lord of Mountains spoke thus to the gods;
then, as the mountain was speaking those words devoid of truth,
his peak suddenly fell down as if struck by a thunderbolt.
Thereupon, whatever beings were present there upon the Lord of Mountains, beginning with the gods, quickly abandoned him and fled in every direction.
Vāsava also rejoiced in his mind, honoring the mountain;
then the six-faced son of Rudra became enraged at Mount Krauñca.
At that time, Vāsava, seeing Guha so furious, [approached him].
When the two splendors are united and complete, like those of fire and the sun.
Then, raising his spear which possessed a radiance equal to the fire of Yama,
the Lord Skanda, filled with rage, hurled it with the intent to slay Krauñca.
That spear fell swiftly upon the summit of Mount Krauñca, like the noose of Death upon a man whose life has been exhausted. ||28||
But that best of mountains, Krauñca, his vital organs pierced by that spear,
with all his limbs shattered on every side and streams of blood flowing forth,
fell to the earth in embodied form, deprived of consciousness and life. (29)
Seeing their husband slain, his wives were deeply afflicted with grief.
Lamenting piteously, they then fell upon Mount Krauñca;
likewise Meru, Himācala, Vindhya, Kailāsa, Gandhamādana,
Pāriyātra, Sahya, Niṣadha, Udaya, and Vāmana.
And Maināka, the best of mountains, was also the progenitor of Krauñca.
All the kings of mountains, afflicted by grief, arrived;
surrounding Mount Krauñca, they wept, deeply distressed. || 33 ||
Knowing her brother’s son had been slain, the goddess of the gods, the daughter of the mountain king,
who observes great vows, came to Mount Krauñca accompanied by Śarva.
Seeing that her own kinsman, Krauñca, had been killed by Kumāra, she arrived there.
Then the queen was distressed upon seeing her father tormented. ||35||
Seeing the great mountain Himavat distressed by the death of his grandson,
Girijā grieved, looking again and again at the Lord of the Gods.
Then, seeing the Lord who had arrived with the Goddess, the wielder of the Pināka bow,
those of great strength, though deeply tormented by grief, paid their respects.
Then Himavat, the best of mountains, having bowed down to the Lord of Gods—
With a dejected soul, overwhelmed by pain and grief, he made this request. || 38 ||
"O Blessed One, by this Śakra, who considers himself so highly,
my grandson Krauñca-parvata has been brought to his destruction.
What rivalry could he possibly have with your son, O Lord?"
Out of pride, he did not perceive any difference between the prince and himself.
"Now that my grandson has been slain by Kumāra after a contest,
let this Vāsava remain at ease, his pride gone and his mind at peace. O Mahādeva, with his grandson killed, he is submerged in an ocean of grief."
I am unable to live; I shall go the way of my grandson. || 42 ||
As he was lamenting thus, his kinsmen, led by Meru and Vindhya, wailed, tormented by grief and pained by the loss of their relative. 43.
Seeing her father distressed, as well as her other kinsmen and the mountains,
Girijā, the sustainer of the world, was also consumed by grief.
Then, seeing them all in distress, he whose vehicle is the bull said,
"Do not grieve," and spoke to his six-faced son:
"O son, great men such as you, even when a kinsman has committed an offense— "
Why do you not commit an evil deed? Why have you slain the curlew? (46)
"O Six-faced One, this great mountain Krauñca is the son of your mother’s brother;
how have you slain this, your own brother? (47)
"This action is not worthy of you, my son born of me.
Tell me now, what deed do you consider most significant here?
To the god speaking thus, the six-faced one then [addressed] his father.
He spoke these most wonderful words with great modesty. ||49||
"O Lord, because of Śakra's interference, this Krauñca was slain by me;
since he acted with improper counsel, hear my further petition:
by your grace, I shall restore this best of mountains, the Krauñca, to life."
"Nothing at all is difficult for me, O God, since you are my son.
Then the six-faced one said to his brother Krauñca, "Arise!
Thereupon, in an instant, the lord of mountains, Krauñca, assumed his body as it was before. ||51-52||
Vyāsa rose up free from disease; that was a marvel at that time.
Thus, with his life restored and remaining unshaken, Ṣaṇmukha shone with the brilliance of fire. || 53 ||
Remembering the insult from Rudra, his eyes bloodshot with anger,
the mighty one [spoke] in the presence of all the gods, of Śakra,
of Vāyu, Viṣṇu, and Yama, and of the high-souled Brahmā.
Having prostrated before the Lord of gods, the Sovereign, together with Umā, who is indeed his own father; || 55 ||
The god, assuming the excellent form of Kumāra, spoke these words:
"O Lord of the Gods, this Śakra has spoken in my very presence, saying, 'I am greater than you.
At that, indignation took possession of me."
This great power, consisting of that [essence], has been buried in the surface of the earth.
Whoever, excluding the god who wields the Pināka bow, is capable of lifting it up—let him uproot this, for he alone is greater than I. ||57-58||
Having spoken thus, the god, whose splendor was like that of the rising sun,
became silent with a joyful heart and stood by his father's side. Then Indra, intoxicated by the pride of sovereignty, [stood] in the midst of the deities.
I strove to uproot that power which had entered the earth.
And even with great effort, the lord of the gods was unable to move him;
then, filled with extreme shame, he departed from that place.
Then other foremost deities, headed by Yama and Anila,
resolved to rescue him and exerted themselves with all their power, girding on their armor.
And the best of the immortals were unable to shake that power;
then Viṣṇu, of immeasurable soul, seeing the gods deprived of their vigor, [acted].
I strove to lift up the Śakti in the very presence of the gods;
yet, although it was being moved by me, that Śakti—possessing great heroism and endowed with the splendor and strength of Skanda—did not budge from the surface of the earth. || 64 ||
Then Viṣṇu, whose nature is immeasurable, having understood the true meaning of reality, became attentive.
Worshipping the Kumāra with devotion, he desisted from his exertion of power.
Then, O Vyāsa, all the immortals and Viṣṇu, the best of gods, having praised the six-faced deity, spoke these words to him of great luster: || 66 ||

...the Lord, the son of Mahādeva, the protector, the guardian, the creator, the destroyer of afflictions, the most excellent and great one. O Lord of Gods, with you as our protector, we are all perfectly at ease. || 67–68 ||
"We all stand here together; protect us from every side.
You ought always to forgive this transgression against Śakra, committed out of folly and delusion, for we have entreated you out of affection."
Thus was that Blessed One praised by all the gods and the princes.
He abandoned his anger toward Śakra and was gratified with the inhabitants of heaven.
Then all those mountains, the goddess who is the daughter of Himavat,
and Śakra, the king of the gods, being delighted, honored Guha.
The Blessed One, also being well-pleased, granted boons to his son;
and the leader of the hosts of Mothers went to the divine and auspicious peak of the Himalayas, together with Guha and the Goddess.
Accompanied by Krauñca, the mountains Meru, Vindhya, and others,
as well as Śakra, the god and king of the Suras, each returned to their own abodes.
Thus it was, just as with Krauñca and those dwelling among the cranes and saras birds.
It was torn by Guha with his spear, and subsequently an iron bolt (kṛtāmara) was hurled;
that wound caused by the spear is still visible on Krauñca, the best of mountains, which is vast and great, the abode of many deities. ||76||
Thus has all this wonderful account of the rending of Krauñca been told to you.
That mortal who hears this is liberated from all sins.
Vyāsa said:
O Blessed One, Supreme Lord, how is it that you are the leader of the Mothers? Who indeed are these Mothers? Please explain this to me as I ask.
How were the groups of Mothers born, and for what cause?
What is their vigor and what is their power, O Lord, by which those hosts came into being? (79)
"And what is their support by which these auspicious groups exist? By whom were they polished, or were they so of themselves? This I wish to know.
Sanatkumāra said:
In this regard, O descendant of Kali, I shall describe to you the auspicious origin of the Mothers.
For in ancient times, the Lord Brahmā, the sovereign of the gods, having created these various progenies,
wandered about observing them.
Once, when the time of twilight had arrived, that overseer of the people [was there].
Having reached a beautiful region on the shore of the great eastern ocean,
he performed his twilight devotions with unwearied diligence for ten million years in that lovely place.
Then the Lord, having performed his twilight rites while seated upon his lotus throne, reflected: "This region is delightful and captivating to the sight;
I shall establish here a beautiful city endowed with all desirable things."
Having reflected thus, O Vyāsa, that blessed Lord, the creator of all, [acted].
In that delightful region, he built an unsurpassed city,
possessing immeasurable splendor with pavements of red, black, and golden stones.
It was filled with loud, boisterous laughter and cries of "khātakas," and it stood like a four-legged structure with its crossroads and squares. ||87||
With houses joined by moats and ditches and filled with great wealth,
in its center was the Mandākinī— a divine, enchanting pond and river,
covered by lotus groves and resounded by the songs of joyful birds. ||88||
Having created that city, which was golden and adorned with jewels, Brahmā spoke these words, O Vyāsa, which were most wonderful and full of meaning:
"In this beautiful and excellent city shall dwell those who enjoy the fruits of their meritorious deeds."
Free from old age and endowed with splendor and strength, those highly fortunate ones shall become invulnerable by my grace; of this there is no doubt. (91)
Then that Blessed Lord, the best of gods, spoke once again:
"O most excellent of gods, the deity always rains down ten million desired objects here; therefore, the people in this place are happy."

Having spoken thus, O Vyāsa, that Blessed One, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the World, departed for his own divine assembly hall, which is frequented by many perfected beings (siddhas). After he had gone, [the gods were addressed] with the words of the Asuras and Daityas.
That city was indeed occupied by all those thorns to the Brāhmaṇas,
whose lord was Durmarṣaṇa, the best among all wielders of weapons—
a slayer of Brāhmaṇas, a destroyer of sacrifices, O Sage, and a killer of gods and demons. ||94-95||
Siṃhanāda, Bhīmanāda, Mada, and others—
then the Daityas, led by Haimakuṇḍa, having assembled and stationed themselves in that excellent city, caused manifold affliction. ||96||
For those haters of the world have slain thousands of Brahmins;
by those lowest of Asuras, sacrificial rites such as the *homa* and others have been destroyed. (97)
Having learned that they had acted in this manner, all the inhabitants of heaven approached the world of Brahmā and reported everything to the Lord.
Having heard the words of the gods and understood the conduct of the Daityas, [the Lord spoke].
Having said, "This cannot be done by me," Brahmā, together with the foremost of the gods,
went to see Bhava in the beautiful forest of the Himavat mountain,
where Gaurī was performing austerities to become the one who shares half his body. (8.171.100)
Having entered there, all those gods, beginning with Brahmā,
indeed instantly became women through the power of Pārvatī’s ascetic penance.
Then the wielder of the trident, the Lord of the gods of gods, questioned those best of deities who had indeed become women, asking, "For what purpose have you come?
Thereupon, they all together recounted their previous subduing of the Daityas.
Afterwards, having reported her own female state to Śambhu, she performed a penance (kṛcchra).
When those men said, "May we become exactly as we were before," the Lord of the Gods then spoke to those deities who had attained the state of women.
"Go, all you gods, having become women, to the presence of the Asuras;
for those Dānavas, arrogant in their strength, are to be slain by women alone."
Having assumed embodied forms, O auspicious Mothers,
you shall thereafter become exactly as you were before, O best of gods.
Then, bowing once more to the Lord, the deities spoke these words:
"O God, O Supreme Lord, assume for yourself a female form with a physical body,
so that together with her we may slay the Daityas by force."
Then the God created the goddess Rudrāṇī, the auspicious Mother;
and assuming a deformed form, he created a second Mother as well,
known by the name Bahumāṃsā, whose nature is the destruction of the world.
Then, by the command of the God of gods, the Lord Viṣṇu also brought forth two Mothers: Vārāhī, who belongs to Viṣṇu, and Brāhmī from Pitāmaha, as well as Śarvāṇī from Śaṅkara. (8.171.110)
Kaumārī also emerged from the six-faced one (Kārttikeya), Vaiṣṇavī from Viṣṇu,
Vārāhī from Mādhava, and the goddess Māhendrī from Purandara.
The auspicious goddess, composed of all splendor, is the most excellent among the Mothers.
From the bull-bannered Lord (Śiva), Bahumāṃsā became Mahāvidyā.
And from the bodies of all the gods, the auspicious Mothers emerged, assuming their own forms and powers, as destroyers of the Daityas. || 112 || 1 || 3 ||
The mighty Vāyavyā, Vāruṇī, Yāmyā, and Kauberī,
as well as Mahākālī, Āgneyī, and thousands of others,
went to that beautiful city [and encountered] the Daityas of fearsome prowess. || 114 ||
The goddesses struck [the Daityas] in many ways with terrifying, horrific roars;
they rendered that foremost city, adorned with gold, devoid of Daityas.
Then, all the Daityas having been slain, the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, [rejoiced].
He came to that region with the desire to grant boons to the Mothers.
Seeing all those Daityas, the enemies of the gods, slain,
the bull-bannered Lord was then highly pleased and granted them their boons.
"You shall become mothers of the world, acting as true mothers.
Those bulls among men, or even highly fortunate women, who become your devotees—assailants shall indeed not harm them. || 118-119 ||
Even my deceased attendants shall become free from old age and death.
This place of yours shall be known as Koṭīvarṣa;
it will become world-renowned and a liberator from all sins.
"I am indeed your cause, for you were created by me alone.
I shall remain here under the name Hetukeśvara as the bestower of boons;
I will dwell together with you, established in the role of leader."
But he who shall worship you along with me according to the prescribed rite, his soul liberated from all sins, shall attain the supreme goal.
Since the Dānavas were slain by you with this spear of many-fleshed power, [it is known as the Mahāmāṃsā]. || 123 ||
This sacred site (tīrtha) shall become renowned by the name Śūlakuṇḍa.
Having drunk the water from the trident here and having bowed down to Bahumāṃsa,
that best of men shall become invincible to all predatory creatures.
The delightful river Mandākinī, renowned for its pleasant waters,
shall here become for you a torrent of blood.
I, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the sages whose wealth is austerity [have revealed] the divine Mātṛtantras and the supreme procedure for the Mātṛ-sacrifice.
We shall perform meritorious sacrifices by which you will attain the Brāhma, the Svāyambhuva, the Kaumāra, and likewise the Yāmala [Tantras]. (128)
The *Sārasvata*, the *Gāndhāra*, the *Aiśāna*, and the *Nandiyāmala*—
these tantras shall belong to you, as shall thousands of others.
By means of these, men will worship you with devotion.
"You shall grant boons to men who perform sacrifices. || 8.171.1 || 30 ||

"You shall become goddesses who bestow divine perfections and possess divine yogas. And those women who shall always worship you with the secret rites, they too shall become mistresses of yoga (yogeśvarīs), beautiful women of divine prowess. (131)
Chagala and Kumbhakarṇa, my two leaders of the Gaṇas,
shall remain as your doorkeepers by my command.
This place Koṭīvarṣa is the most excellent and beloved abode of the Mothers.
"The cremation ground shall become a supreme, divine place that bestows happiness. Having thus obtained those boons, the Mothers, who are the mothers of the world,
bowed with devotion to the Lord of Gods and rejoiced greatly, their afflictions now dispelled.

From that time forward, all of them together with the moon-crested Lord dwelt in Koṭivarṣa, bestowing fearlessness upon all the worlds. Thus did the Blessed Lord, the leader of the hosts of Mothers, [conduct himself].
O Vyāsa, that which you have asked me has become clear:
Śaṅkara [has explained] this origin of the sovereigns of the world, who are honored by Brahmā, Indra, Śakra, and Anila.
That man who should constantly read or hear this account shall, upon death, attain the heavenly realm.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-first chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
"Formerly, how the mountains were made wingless by Śakra..."

I shall declare that to you, O Vyāsa; listen to it all in its entirety. Long ago, when the lord of the Daityas and Dānavas, Hiraṇyakaśipu, had been slain by Viṣṇu of supreme luster, who assumed the form of a lion. || 1–2 ||
His son, the Daitya Prahlāda, became enraged toward Viṣṇu;
for when his father was slain, that illustrious lord of the great Daityas [was left alone].
For many thousands of years he performed fierce and great penance.
Then the four-faced God, being pleased, approached that lord of the asuras himself and respectfully said, "I am the giver of boons."
Having bowed down, Prahlāda— his limbs burning with grief as he recollected the slaughter of his father— spoke this to the boon-granting Brahmā who had arrived:
"O Blessed One, if you are pleased and have come here as a bestower of boons," || 5-6 ||
"Viṣṇu killed my father, the king, through his illusory power (māyā) in battle; act in such a way that I may likewise slay that Viṣṇu. ||7||
Then Brahmā spoke to Prahlāda, the best of asuras:
"Viṣṇu is unconquerable in battle and cannot be slain by gods or asuras. (8)
"O great Asura, by the grace of the God of gods, the Creator of the world, the Lord of Umā, this boon cannot be granted to you by me."
"Choose another boon as you desire, for I shall grant it to you.
Then, having reflected further, that great-souled and highly intelligent asura spoke these words to the god seated upon his lotus throne:
"If Viṣṇu, the best of gods, is indeed unconquerable and unslayable,
then by your command, O Lord, may I become unslayable and unconquerable by that Viṣṇu, or by Śakra, or by any other enemy. (11–12)
"Let it be so," Brahmā said to him, O best of Dānavas; and having spoken, the divine Lord, seated upon his celestial lotus-throne, vanished right there.
Prahlāda, too, having obtained that most wonderful boon from Brahmā, [departed].
He stood on the shore of the western ocean, his senses agitated by anxiety.
"How may I slay Viṣṇu and Śakra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices?"— while Prahlāda, the enemy of the gods, was reflecting thus, [the following occurred].
The illustrious Himavat mountain, the lord of all mountains,
rose up with his two wings and came through the air as a sky-farer.
For in ancient times, O Vyāsa, the mountains were possessed of wings.
All those who move through the divine realm of the sky, as well as those who wander throughout all the worlds. || 17 ||
Then, seeing that Himavat mountain had arrived, Prahrāda,
having first offered a welcome, spoke these words with joy.
"O Lord of the foremost of mountains, we Daityas are the grandsons of Kaśyapa;
you too, O great mountain, are his sons, as are the gods. Thus, O Mountain, our origin and yours are from one and the same source."
The deities became our brothers, for they were indeed our gods. || 8.172.20 ||

"O Great Mountain, disregarding us asuras, those arrogant ones rule the kingdom. Let us join together and, having utterly defeated the gods, seize the entire three worlds and exercise sovereignty. (21)
O Lord of Acala, those regions where the sacrifice of the gods is performed, where the sacred fires are offered, and where the deities are gratified—[those are the places]. || 2.2 ||
"Accompanied by all the mountains, you must advance quickly and slay them! Then, once the gods have been deprived of their sacrifices, we shall kill them at our ease and be set at peace.
Thus addressed by the king of the Daityas, Himavat, the best of mountains, [replied].
"This is not proper," he said with apprehension to the lord of the Dānavas.
Then the great Asura spoke again to Himavat:
"O Lord of Mountains, if you consider it right, [then do so] from me."
"I shall lead you, together with this mountain, to death at the same time;
therefore, O Mountain, remain vigilant until I slay you.
Then, seeing the king of the Daityas enraged, that best of mountains—
"I shall do so," he said; thereupon, the Daitya was pleased.
Then, having heard the words of Prahlāda, Himavat, the best of mountains, together with those other mountains, brought about the destruction of the country;
He traversed those regions in which mountains are situated. || 29 ||
Then, when the regions had become desolate, Nārada, the best of sages,
reported the entire transgression of the mountains to Śakra.
Having heard that, Śatakratu, the king of the gods, was consumed with anger.
Having approached the immovable mountains, he spoke with indignation, "What is this? Then, O Vyāsa, the mountains said to the enraged lord of the hosts of gods:
"O Lord, out of fear of Prahlāda, the great lord of the Daityas, we [have fled]."
"We have incurred this transgression, yet there is no fault in us whatsoever.
But if you consider it a fault on our part, O Lord of the Immortals," [3.3]
"Come to the presence of Prahlāda; let us go there together quickly.
By that king of the Daityas, Bali, desiring to do you harm, all this destruction of the sacrificial ground has been caused."
"O Lord of the Gods, know that this is not our fault," they said.
At their words, Śakra became even more enraged;
hurling his thunderbolt again and again, he then rendered those mountains wingless.
Then all those lords of the mountains, their wings having been lost, fell to the surface of the earth like birds with clipped wings, O Vyāsa.
Thereupon, the lord of the Daityas, Prahlāda, the foremost among the Asuras, heard this. || 36–37 ||
Afflicted by the severing of the wings of the lords of mountains, the lord of the hosts of Daityas was deeply incensed. Reflecting for a long time on what he should do,
he arrived at the hermitage of Badarī and beheld Viṣṇu seated there.
He had a truly great and wonderful battle with Viṣṇu.
And Viṣṇu was not able to conquer that Prahlāda by his might;
a terrible battle took place between them for a hundred divine years in ancient times.
Viṣṇu knew himself to be inferior to the Dānava Prahlāda;
then Viṣṇu, the knower of the supreme dharma, exerted himself in battle.
Unable to conquer the Dānava, the Lord became filled with wrath;
then, having meditated upon Mahādeva and bowed down to him again and again, he called to mind Para... [Śiva].
[Recalling] that favor of the wielder of the Pināka bow—
namely, his invincibility and the state of being unconquerable by all the inhabitants of the worlds—
the supreme god Viṣṇu [acted]. ||43-44||
Having become possessed of the strength of a great being, the powerful one rushed toward the Daitya.
Then, realizing himself to be being overcome and perceiving Viṣṇu to be the stronger, the son of Hiṇyakaśipu retreated from the field of battle.
Deluded by the splendor of Śiva, Prahlāda, the lord of the Dānavas, perceived his own self as unconquered by Viṣṇu;
yet, having obtained a boon even from Brahmā regarding his own invincibility, he realized that his self was indeed conquered. || 46–47 ||
The great asura then considered himself already conquered.
That terrible battle between the asura Prahlāda and Viṣṇu, which struck fear into the gods,
lasted for a hundred divine years and was truly marvelous.
Neither by learning, nor by vigor, nor by heroism, nor by splendor [is he surpassed]. || 49 ||
Neither in wisdom nor in righteousness was there an asura equal to Prahlāda;
nor was there a great king like Hiraṇyakaśipu;
nor were Andhaka or Hiraṇyākṣa equal to Prahlāda in strength.
