It is said that he was Viṣṇu himself who had come into the state of a Daitya due to the curse of Bhṛgu. Even the perfected denizens of heaven envied the great-souled Prahlāda for his heroism, his learning, and his humility.
In his kingdom, the subjects were no longer beset by suffering and grief;
thus did that best of Dānavas wage war against Viṣṇu.
With his body tormented by remorse, he became free from longing for sense-objects;
having realized that the granting of boons and the fruit of asceticism are impermanent,
he became indifferent toward all undertakings and devoid of desire for sense-objects.
But having renounced all actions, he should be devoted to the practice of meditation. || 56 ||
The great Daitya Prahlāda, a knower of the supreme truth, went forth into the homeless life seeking peace for the sake of attaining liberation;
for he understood that birth leads to rebirth and perceived the ultimate impermanence of all things,
realizing that sovereignty is but a source of suffering.
Having consecrated his son Virocana upon the throne of the sons of Diti.
Having made that lord of the asuras the king of the Daityas and Dānavas,
and desiring the supreme attainment of liberation,
he became resolved upon renunciation in order to seek the excellent reality— the unborn, auspicious Śiva who transcends all qualities.
[He approached] the sage Āsuri, the direct disciple of the Blessed One Kapila.
Having approached him as a disciple, he attained the knowledge of liberation—
the supreme reality of the primal natures (prakṛtis) and likewise the supreme reality of the transformations (vikāras).
Having known the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the Person (puruṣa), the enjoyer who is himself devoid of enjoyment,
he became one who knew the supreme goal of the science of liberation and had reached the further shore of the Sāṃkhya system.
That best of sages became known by the name Pañcaśikha;
having attained supreme Yoga, that great sage and teacher of Sāṃkhya was liberated from the threefold suffering and reached the imperishable state. (63)
Thus the illustrious and high-souled Daitya king, the enemy of the three worlds, having maintained enmity for a long time with Viṣṇu, the preceptor of the gods,
eventually became perfected; thereafter, having attained yoga, he became the bestower of fearlessness upon the world.
Liberated thereafter, he indeed attained the immortal state, the primordial Brahman.
The knower of the field, awakened, liberated from the qualities (guṇas), freed from sufferings and the bonds of the snare of existence,
and released from the obstruction of darkness and delusion— this lord of yoga became the sovereign of the Daityas.
Thus, Purandara [beheld] all those mountains with their wings clipped.
The best of sages performed that which I was previously asked by you.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Severing of Parvata’s Wings," in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, within the narrative of Prahrāda.
Vyāsa said:
When the lord of mountains had been restored to life and Guha had been gratified by the gods, [the mountain] Krauñca...
Hara, accompanied by Pārvatī, went to the peak of the Himavat mountain. || 1 ||
O best of Brahmins, tell me what else the Lord did and what Pārvatī said to him;
for there is no satiety for me as I listen. || 2 ||
Sūta said: Thus addressed by the lord of sages, the imperishable son of Brahmā, the seer and supreme master of yoga, related the matter as it truly is:
"When the God of gods had departed for the peak of the Himalayas together with Umā..."
Having bowed to the Supreme Lord, the Goddess Girijā spoke to the God:
"Of Hiraṇya, who subsists by gleaning grains, who dwells in the Naimiṣa forest,
and who is indeed endowed with purity, austerity, devotion, and tranquility— " || 4-5 ||
Having witnessed that greatness of the ascetic brahmin, I myself went to receive worship from the twice-born.
"O Lord, I have reached a state of wonder that the twice-born are the most excellent;
it is my conviction that they are even weightier than the gods by virtue of Brahmā.
Therefore, I wish to hear from you the supreme majesty of the twice-born. (7)
The God of gods said:
"It is even so, O Mother of the World, you who are saluted by gods and asuras!
These excellent ascetics, the Brahmins, are even weightier than the gods. (8)
Those progeny of mine who were created first are indeed my source;
the Rudras and the twice-born of great power were previously created by me.
Having observed my creation, even Brahmā, desiring to create, [looked upon it].
The Brāhmaṇas, possessed of great splendor, were created first from my head.
Indeed, I was their foremost one, and at that time I became the best among the twice-born. Consequently, all those most excellent of Brahmins became my friends.
This is the supreme and highest creation of the Brahmins, the Parameṣṭhins;
the fourfold varṇas, beginning with Dharma, are all established upon them.
By the oblation that the Brahmins offer into the fire, the deities are satisfied.
Indeed, the entire world is established through the spiritual power (*tejas*) of the Brāhmaṇas.
That Pāśupata vow of mine, which removes both death and birth, cannot be accomplished by others of any other caste, except for the most excellent Brāhmaṇas. || 13-14 ||
I shall fully declare the characteristics of the twice-born; listen to this:
the rules for purity and uprightness, as well as their power and their duties.
One is a Brāhmaṇa by birth, but is called "twice-born" (dvija) through the sacramental rites.
Through knowledge one attains the state of a Vipra; Brāhmaṇya is thus remembered as being threefold. || 16 ||
Whether one be a Brahmin by birth or one who has mastered the Vedas,
it is recorded that the merit and demerit of protecting or killing these two are equal.
And as for one who is a Brahmin by birth and learned in all the Agamas...
One who is endowed with austerity and purity is called "pure in three ways.
If one feeds such a person at a śrāddha or even in a rite for the gods,
that offering becomes inexhaustible through the gratification of that pure one.
A Brahmin who is learned in the Vedas and constantly devoted to the fire-oblation, O Goddess, is considered the most excellent; when honored, he delivers his entire lineage.
O Goddess, even if someone were a Brāhmaṇa by birth alone in any circumstance,
he too would be honored as a teacher of the world and a bestower of heaven.
[The duties are] the Agnihotra fire-sacrifice, austerity, sacrifice, purity, and straightforwardness.
Truthfulness, devotion to the Vedas, and the performance of the duties of the twice-born are remembered as the highest [dharma]. ||22||
A Brāhmaṇa does not speak untruth; the twice-born does not kill a living being.
A Vipra does not perform service for others, nor does the twice-born become a doer of evil. (23)
A Brahmin who is also an ascetic does not undergo rebirth.
Having attained the state of a learned Brahmin, what indeed has not been gained by that embodied being?
Those eight forms of mine which are remembered as the Sun, the Moon, and the rest—
All of them lived with that Brahmin who was enriched by his ascetic penance. ||25||
For, O Goddess, by sustaining themselves upon the splendor of the twice-born as well as nectar and cows, the Brahmins always prevail; therefore, they are the most excellent. (26)
For those twice-born ones of supreme splendor, nothing is impossible;
when enraged or when pleased, they bestow both good and evil.

Those twice-born ones who are ascetics and proficient in the knowledge of the Vedas shall be bestowers of liberation; they are the deities even of the gods. Both I and the Grandfather (Brahmā) are remembered as their two origins.
O Goddess, they were born from me first, and thereafter from the Grandfather.
We two are the causes for the twice-born because of our nature, and you alone are that very nature;
you are declared to be Prakṛti, while I am indeed the Supreme Puruṣa.
Those who are remembered as Brahmā and Viṣṇu consist of the qualities of Rajas and Sattva.
From us two, those two Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis) are produced at the time of creation. || 31 ||
For I am Agni, you are Viṣṇu as Tamas; know that Sattva is established in Brahman, while Rajas is pervasive among the actions of the constituent qualities.
Both of these—tamas and rajas—are of the nature of delusion;
they destroy sattva, and that [sattva] arises from fire.
For these high-souled twice-born ones are known to possess the brilliance of fire;
they prevail everywhere, and there is no means to restrain them.
Know that straightforwardness and equanimity constitute the fiery power within the twice-born.
Honesty excels even those endowed with austerity and knowledge.
Freedom from deceit destroys sins, and equanimity destroys the bonds of delusion;
yet it is honesty practiced by the twice-born that destroys both of these.

Formerly, on the banks of the Bhāgīrathī, there was a twice-born man named Dānaruci, who was a knower of the supreme dharma and lived by the practice of gleaning. His soul was disciplined by all branches of knowledge, and he granted fearlessness to all living beings.
Together with his wife, my devotee was devoted to the fire-oblation. ||38||
O Goddess, having first fed the guest according to his arrival, he then eats at the sixth meal-time; this is his supreme vow. As he lived in this manner, a great deal of time passed.
When a guest has arrived, no hesitation arises in him. || 8.173.40 ||
Endowed with austerity and purity, and solely devoted to uprightness, that twice-born man became exceedingly radiant with splendor, like the sun and fire.
The Fire-god, pleased by his asceticism, attained supreme satisfaction;
desiring to bestow auspiciousness upon him, he became ready to grant the fruit of his desire.
Then, after some time, when the sixth mealtime had arrived—
The twice-born man was wandering about on a cold, cloudy day, thick with snow and mist. || 43 ||
Exhausted by hunger and fatigue, he did not see any guest;
even at the end of the day, no guest appeared anywhere for him. ||44||
Then, without having eaten anything at all, that foremost of brahmins became devoted to fasting; he did not even consider his own exhaustion.
His highly fortunate wife also, devoted to the vow of fidelity to her husband,
then acted exactly as her husband had done.
Her limbs were tormented by cold and hunger, and she was beset by many pairs of opposites.
O Queen, that twice-born man became exceedingly distressed by his great affliction. ||47||
When the second day arrived and it was the sixth mealtime, that twice-born man,
due to the affliction caused by the cold and the stormy weather, did not look toward a guest at all.
Then Agni, knowing his firm and supreme resolve, [acted].
For his form was indeed deformed, loathsome, and like that of a dog-cooker (outcaste). ||49||
Having done so, he stood at the foot of the tree and granted him his vision.
Then that best of brahmins, afflicted by hunger and wandering in search of a guest,
saw standing at the base of the tree one who was terrible and of deformed appearance.
A dog-cooker, drenched with cold and marked by hundreds of various wounds. ||51||
That best of the twice-born beheld one who was difficult to look upon, aged and afflicted, with worms and blood flowing from him, crying out, "O father!
Then, seeing that miserable dog-cooker, the best of the twice-born—
"Take heart, blessed one," he said, speaking these sweet words.
And for the purpose of removing the cold, the twice-born brought fire for her.
Then, once she had recovered from the contact with the fire, he spoke to her.
"Come, eat; may you be my guest, O blessed one," he said respectfully to that wretched man.
Then the outcaste spoke to that treasure-house of asceticism:
"O best of the twice-born, I am an outcaste; my food is indeed right here."

"Give it to one who is contemptible, just as you do for beasts and birds," he said. "I am not worthy to receive refined food. Knowing through meditation that Agni was present before him as he spoke thus, [the sage remained silent]. || 56-57 ||
O tiger among the twice-born, he who was skilled in speech spoke these words:
"O sinless one, I do not despise birth, nor do I honor it;
for this Self is all-pervading and resides within all living beings. (58)
I worship that very Self as the supreme Śiva with devotion;
perceiving the Supreme Lord, the Puruṣa, as present everywhere, I feel no contempt for animals, and especially not for those such as you. || 59-60 ||
"Everything is indeed that very same [Brahman]; devoted to austerity and purity, I worship it with an undistracted mind. Be free from doubt in this matter.
[This applies] toward worms, insects, mice, and snakes, as well as toward outcasts, gods, and the twice-born."
Since the self is indeed omnipresent, how then can there be any contempt for us? 62.
"O noble one, I am not contemptible; come to me as one who is not contemptible. Eat this prepared food and bestow your favor upon us.
Thus addressed by the lord of the twice-born, the outcaste (śvapāka) was then filled with joy.
He went to the house of that Brahmin, desiring to bestow his grace upon him.
Then, with a mind pure in its disposition, he who delighted in giving performed for him a hospitable reception according to the rules, as if for a guest worthy of honor. (65)
The fire-god (Havyavāhana), being pleased, appeared in personified form after having been fed;
he then bestowed upon him the unsurpassed power of yoga that he desired.
Having attained supreme yoga, that best of the twice-born, subsisting on gleaned grains,
was liberated along with his wife and reached the immortal state.
Just as the perfected sage Kapila, the supreme knower of reality,

so too a Brahmin endowed with uprightness and possessing the defining characteristics shall obtain nothing that he does not deserve; O Goddess, he shall attain from the auspicious an even more auspicious state.
O daughter of the Lord of Mountains, this supreme and most excellent majesty of the Brahmins, who possess the luster of immortals, has been told to you many times; it bestows merit and long life.
A wise and pure man who constantly hears this or recites it according to the rules shall obtain merit, happiness, longevity, desired fruits, splendor, and strength. (69)
O daughter of the great king of mountains, this majesty of the twice-born has been recounted to you exactly as it is;
from the beginning of creation, O best of the twice-born, they have been mine.
"Thus they indeed attained supreme majesty.
Sanatkumāra said:
"Having thus described the majesty of the twice-born to Pārvatī and Parameśvara,"
Thus occurred this auspicious and meritorious discourse, which destroys all evil.
[O] Pārāśarya, whose wealth is asceticism,
if you deem it worthy of being heard from me, then ask with a concentrated mind.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Twice-born," in the Skanda Purāṇa.

Vyāsa said: O Blessed One, regarding that which was spoken by you at the time of the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice—that Brahmā and the other denizens of heaven attained the Pāśupata Yoga—[I wish to hear more].
"O great sage, they indeed attained the supreme reality through knowledge;
tell that to me, your devotee and disciple who asks. || 2 ||
"What is that supreme yoga, the auspicious Pāśupata knowledge,
by knowing which perfected Brahmins attain the highest liberation?
Thus questioned by his disciple, the best of sages replied:
Sanatkumāra said:
Well done, O Vyāsa of great intellect! You are a seeker of liberation, my son, since you ask me about that supreme knowledge and yoga pertaining to Maheśvara.
That which is proclaimed as the reality of all yogic sciences— even those endowed with Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and the Āgamas, and being experts in all spiritual matters—
was not perceived even after they had attained the sovereignty of yoga.
O illustrious one, that knowledge spoken by Śaṅkara which they did not understand—
just as it was told to those gods by the Three-eyed Lord,
I shall now declare to you here in brief, the definitive certainty of reality.
It is not possible to describe that in detail even in hundreds of years; I shall, however, explain its established side, which is the arising and destruction of saṃsāra. ||8||
Having paid homage to Maheśāna, the Supreme Person who brings all beings into existence, I shall briefly declare this most excellent doctrine which bestows both liberation and spiritual perfection.
The supreme secret of primordial nature (prakṛti) is the Person (pudgala), the highest lord,

whom the Sāṃkhyas call the twenty-fifth— the unborn, all-pervading Puruṣa; and the Yogins likewise [call him] the twenty-sixth, the pervasive one, whose essence consists of the three qualities (triguṇa).
Having meditated upon Viṣṇu and Pitāmaha, the two high-souled lords of creatures who create the entire world,
he then bowed down to that Mahādeva, the three-eyed Lord and bestower of boons. ||1–2||
I shall proclaim his doctrine, the definitive conclusion of the system of Yoga;
know this definition of Yoga as it is being declared by me.
O great sage, through its practice, the bonds of the bound soul (paśu) are severed.

When the mind is established in the Self, there is the external removal of objective conditions; this very intention regarding both the Supreme Lord and the individual Self was proclaimed by Śambhu in the past as "Yoga," O Vyāsa. (1.4–1.5)
Subtle and the remover of existence and rebirth for the gods who have sought refuge,
[this state arises] when the mind of a person dwelling in the body is established within the Self—
free from discursive thought, turned away from the external, subtle, and joined with constant practice. || 16 ||

For one who exerts effort, there is the complete cessation of those subtle conditions produced by causal factors which are designated as pleasure, pain, and so forth. However, for the practitioner who applies himself to yoga, the supreme Lord Maheśvara is the one who joins him [to his goal] through His intention.
At that time, there is indeed an underlying intention regarding both the Lord and the self;

for by means of a single [practice], through the application of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there is the taking up of happiness for one who remains established in the state of *pra...* [the supreme goal]. 19.
For the practitioner, this mountain shall always be the fruit of accomplishment; thus it is established.
Now, the locus therein is proclaimed in due order:
first, one should know withdrawal (pratyāhāra), and likewise breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Meditation and concentration are indeed declared to be the practice of yoga.
Having transcended death through these three, the fourfold activities proceed;
O Sage, death has no power over them. ||21-22||
For the elements become subject to him; of this there is no doubt.
Consequently, he becomes a practitioner who has conquered death.
O Vyāsa, these are the ritual actions for the head and the heart.
Indeed, all those [deities] in the intermediate space have been proclaimed; of this there is no doubt.
Bound to the three stations and established in four characteristics, these rites cannot be accomplished anywhere by one who is negligent. || 24-25 ||
These three, characterized by delusion, are constantly engaged with death;
there is no separation from them in each of these activities.
Even ignorance trembles within those [states] that move both externally and internally.
The practitioner is thus engaged in the activities pertaining to the intermediate state.
Through his power, there occurs the cessation of the elements, the senses, the mind, time, and the directions.
The ten directions, the three times, the elements, and the expansion of the senses [are withdrawn]. (27–28)
"Accompanied by the cessation of mental activity and characterized by the absence of sense objects,
this was declared of old by the Blessed One himself as 'pratyāhāra' (withdrawal). When the mind remains unwavering due to the absence of movement toward other directions," || 29 ||

The arising of withdrawal occurs all at once upon the emergence of yoga. Knowledge regarding the three periods of time and the loftiness of sovereign power do not exist when the mind is restless; they come into being only when it is equally established in composure. (8.174.30–31)

Since the mind is the sole instrument for all yogic practice, one should therefore exert effort toward the stabilization of the mind. Meditation upon the restraint of the vital breath is known as *prāṇāyāma*.

For the *prāṇa* alone always acts as the charioteer of the vital airs (*vāyu*). A yogin should constantly practice the restraint of the *prāṇa* for the sake of progressively attaining mastery over the domain of the vital airs. (33–34)
One should know that the setting in motion of the light is a practice joined with constant repetition:
twice in the apāna, once in the prāṇa, and likewise in the samāna.
This is the third stage, the kumbhaka, which illuminates the fire of yoga. (35–37)
By these, the subtle course of meditation, which effects the restraint of the vital breaths, proceeds; by means of this, the yogin attains the supreme Person. || 3.8 ||
From the simultaneous withdrawal [of the senses] and the repeated liberation [from them], this is designated as *kumbhaka*, following the practice of *prāṇāyāma* and other techniques.
This vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the wind; it is the self (*ātman*), the living soul (*jīva*) within the body.
One should know that it has two forms everywhere: the gross and the subtle. ||8.174.40||
The unmanifest is of subtle form, whereas that which possesses characteristics of shape is gross.
Beginning from the gross, one should discern the subtle through the practice of meditation.
O Sage, from the cultivation of the subtle, the light of illumination arises.
When the mind, while meditating on a gross object, has wandered in all directions and a state of radiance arises, one should immediately stabilize it once again upon a mountain,
a tree, the back of a wind-swept place, a chasm, or rows of palaces. ||42||
One should practice the union of the mind whether at sea or upon the earth.
Having established the mind there, one should again undergo withdrawal;
through delusion, one might direct it toward insentience, but for this reason, the wind is seen otherwise.
Having withdrawn it from there, one should once more practice the course of meditation upon the pervasive.
For one who meditates constantly through practice, the mind and breath [become stilled].
For one engaged in the yoga of knowledge, when attachment to sense objects has been destroyed,
obstacles indeed arise— those born of the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest— which manifest as intuitive flashes (*prātibha*).
For indeed, obstacles to yoga arise for one who is practicing it. ||46||
Knowing these, one who is free from desire for sense objects and has conquered [the senses] through diligent effort should stand upon the path to Nirvana, freed from the three qualities (guṇas).
[One may attain] divine travel through the sky, born from union with hosts of Apsarases.

One may experience consecration by the gods, the undertaking of various poetic works, attachment to the pleasures of sovereignty, and the acquisition of much gold and jewels; one should recognize these as obstacles arising from the power of *sattva*, yet they are characterized by intuitive inspiration (*prātibha*). ||48-49||

One should recognize that those [visions] which involve the arising of pride, which follow a sequence of diverse behaviors, and which are obstructed by passion, are intuitive (prātibha) cognitions; of this there is no doubt.
One should designate as *tāmasa* those [visions] preceded by the emergence of torture, such as consumption, colic, fever, insanity, leprosy, snakes, and planetary seizures (51).
A sage should always recognize that intuitive visions (*prātibha*) arise from the three qualities (*guṇa*).
One who applies himself should observe quickly and indeed treat [the patient] with speed.

Having withdrawn the mind and having focused it upon the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth, one should destroy all obstacles on every side by means of the "pot-like" (kumbhaka) breath control (prāṇāyāma). ||53||
Rajas, sattva, and tamas are the three qualities (guṇas) of Pradhāna;
indeed, they are the causes for the Great Lord's association with created beings.
These [obstacles] arise for one who practices yoga with pride and delusion.
But when the conscious yogi, free from desire and at peace, applies himself,
then the intuitive insights proceed while the obstacles go to their destruction simultaneously.
Consequently, the manifestation of those qualities is the cause of delusion. ||56||
One should know that *tamas* belongs to Rudra, *sattva* is established in Brahmā, and one should know that *rajas* belongs to Viṣṇu; Maheśvara is the destroyer of these.
Having known Mahādeva as supreme, the twice-born man should be devoted to the practice of yoga.
Freed from the three qualities (guṇas), he shall attain absorption into Śaṅkara. ||58||
First, one should purify one's own body through restraints (yama) and observances (niyama);
thereafter, being free from both dharma and adharma, [one should proceed] according to that which is prescribed in the scriptures. (59)
One should practice the cultivation of meditation gradually according to the instruction,
having conquered the objects of the senses such as sound which fall within the range of the ears and other faculties;
remaining equanimous toward gods and animals, and free from the sense of "mine" regarding all things.
Freed from all undertakings and devoid of merit and demerit,
free from the pairs of opposites, one should practice yoga in a secluded place under the Lord,
having abandoned pride along with restrictive observances, and relying on the certainty of Sāṃkhya.
One should constantly practice the yoga of Maheśvara in another [state].
There are eight eternal primary natures (prakṛtis) and sixteen transformations (vikāras). || 63 ||
The twenty-fifth principle, which is the object of the Sāṃkhya school's tenets, is this very supreme secret among the Sāṃkhyas in their determination of reality:
having known the distinction between primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa), one is liberated. ||64||
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Pāśupata Yoga," in the section on the Rules of Meditation within the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
"Yoga and Sāṃkhya—these two everywhere are declared to be the two-fold knowledge."
Among them, some were devoted to Sāṃkhya, while others relied upon the path of Yoga. || 1 ||
The unmanifest (avyakta), primordial nature (prakṛti), and likewise the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra)—
these are indeed the eight primary natures (prakṛtis), together with the five subtle elements (tanmātras).
They say there are five organs of perception (buddhīndriyas) and five organs of action (karmendriyas).
The mind and the five elements are known as the sixteen transformations. ||3||
The twenty-fifth principle, the Puruṣa, is devoid of all undertakings;
it is eternal, omnipresent, subtle, conscious, and free from the three guṇas.
It is perfectly pure, stainless, the enjoyer, the non-agent, and stands like a witness.
Having understood this, they do not enter the cage of saṃsāra again. || 5 ||
These twenty-five principles have been proclaimed by the Sāṃkhya yogis,
for by knowing them one is indeed liberated from birth:
the subtle, unmanifest Prakṛti, which is the object of enjoyment, all-pervading, and mobile.
She should be known as eternal, insentient, and the fulfiller of all desires. ||7||
Tamas, sattva, and rajas—these three qualities reside within objects;
for it is through their invariable presence that all this is established.
Sattva produces illumination; rajas incites attachment;
and tamas causes delusion—thus is the expansion of the qualities described.
Of these, which are designated as "qualities," the operations and functions are distinct.
Livelihood is said to be superior when it is accomplished through human effort as its cause.
Divine [existence] is remembered as having eight divisions; animal existence is recorded as being sevenfold;
and human existence is undifferentiated—all of these consist of the qualities (guṇas).
Whether it be deluded or unconscious, gross or subtle,
formless or even possessing form— everything is said to consist of the three qualities (guṇas).
Indeed, these qualities of the yogin are proclaimed to be obstacles to liberation.
For bondage belongs only to one who is attached; one who is unattached is said to be liberated.
Due to [their] separation, the three qualities (guṇas) remain eternally present in that which abides in primordial nature (prakṛti).
Through separation, those situated in transformation resort to their respective dharmas.
The creation of beings is declared by the knowers of Sāṃkhya to be threefold:
it is called the perfected (saṃsiddha), the natural (prākṛta), and likewise the modified (vaikṛta).
Among these, those who are perfected through dharma abide in the yoga of Maheśvara.
O Vyāsa, those who are experts in the Sāṃkhya analogies do not accept origination; they maintain that dharma consists of fivefold nature through its connection with substance. 1.6
Those who rely on causes do not indeed maintain that an effect exists prior to its cause;

for from Pradhāna, through the transformation of the constituent qualities (guṇas) which are like water and other elements, the intellect (buddhi) arose repeatedly with a predominance of sattva, derived from Puruṣa. (17)
It is described as exertion, as well as form and determination.

For the intellect (buddhi) itself is the ego (ahaṅkāra), because other cognitions arise from it. Some, however, desire that [ego] to be the mind (manas), which is produced by action and is a collection of qualities. || 18–19 ||

"I alone am the doer"—this is declared to be *ahaṅkāra* (egoism). It is also considered to be the mental construction regarding the sphere of the senses. From the luminous *ahaṅkāra*, which has become the intellect (*buddhi*) and arisen from *sattva*, [the following proceeds]. || 8.175.20 ||
The five sense organs arise from the emergence of *sattva*;
because the seeker of liberation is awakened or perceives by means of them,
they are therefore proclaimed as the "organs of cognition" (*buddhīndriya*) by those who contemplate reality.
Therefore, they say that the organs of action are born from the *rajas* quality;
furthermore, from the *tamas*-dominated ego (*ahaṃkāra*), the subtle elements (*tanmātrāṇi*) came into being.
Some say that [the organs] are all-pervading.
...and that [body], arising from merit and demerit (dharma-adharma), goes everywhere for the sake of accomplishing its purpose;
it pervades all beings, is delusive, powerful, the substratum of all, subtle, and its path through the directions is unobstructed. || 24-25 ||
That which is called the *liṅga*, which is the cause for embodied beings, and that creation which was declared to be threefold, is further said to be ninefold. || 26 ||

The thousands of different types of bodies resulting from the modification of primordial nature (prakṛti) are known as the first creation, the creation of the principles (tattvasarga); after that follows the second, the creation of the physical body (piṇḍasarga);
and thereafter the third is declared to be the creation of the cognitive faculties (pratyayasarga).
Non-attachment, dissolution, contentment, and perfection—these are the four stages. ||28||
In the creation of cognition, however, other divisions are recorded due to their diversity;
there are fifty divisions in total, and for each of these, there are ten qualities. (29)
These sixty categories are indeed proclaimed by Kapila and others;
contentment is divided into nine kinds, and accomplishment (siddhi) is likewise eightfold.
Furthermore, the opposite of these very [categories] is recorded as being fivefold.
It shall consist of eight divisions, divided into three, and [further] categorized by ten bonds of action. ||3.1||
The sacred tradition states that these sixty categories constitute the knowledge of number; some recognize them as fewer by one, while others know them to be more by one. (32)
Indeed, O child, in the past, within my own five-footed footprint, I sought the essential reality that lies between primordial nature (prakṛti) and the spirit (puruṣa). || 3.3 ||
Having thoroughly understood and realized the Sāṃkhya system— that which is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti)—
one knows the twenty-fifth principle, the unborn, the enjoyer, and the one possessed of self-conceit.
Doubt did not depart until I had understood the Supreme Lord;
for when I was taught my own yoga by Śambhu himself, the God of gods and creator of the world,
O child, I became free from all doubt.
Then, having known the twenty-sixth principle, the all-pervading Lord, || 3.6 ||
I am liberated through the perfection of yoga and have become free from delusion.
O twice-born one, if the Puruṣa is indeed the enjoyer of Prakṛti, then he enjoys it himself. 37.
He who is beyond these two, the eternal, the twenty-sixth, the Lord, the all-pervading—by knowing Him as the supreme reality, one is liberated from the bondage of birth. (38)
Even having mastered the Sāṃkhya system entirely through an investigation into the distinctions between the guṇas,
liberation does not arise from the mere awakening to the twenty-five principles.
Bound by the guṇas born of Prakṛti, he remains fettered by the snares of the enjoyer.
The enjoyer consists of ego-inflation; because he is a person (puruṣa), he is not a liberator. Even by knowing him, there can be no liberation devoid of [further] cognition. || 8.175.40 ||
Thus has the detailed exposition of the Sāṃkhya doctrine been stated in brief.
I shall now proclaim the reality of Yoga, which brings about the destruction of suffering and rebirth. (41)
The origin of embodied beings and that by which dispassion arises;
the abandonment of both merit and demerit, free from truth and falsehood;
the practice of yoga, detachment from others, and faultless subtle knowledge.
It is liberated from all attachments, the cause for attaining the Lord;

it is the union with perfection free from dualities, the destruction of the arising of inauspiciousness, the consciousness that perceives the supreme, and the certainty regarding the state of ultimate reality. ||43-44||
"The Yoga that removes existence and rebirth, which is devoid of sense objects and the senses,
is the complete teaching of Paśupati, which attains the abode of immortality.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Pāśupata Yoga," within the section on the Rules of Meditation in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, I shall tell you how a living being is born, how it attains detachment, and how it indeed awakens.
Space, wind, fire, earth, and likewise water—
from the aggregation of these together, that which is called the body is born.
All fluids are of the nature of Soma, as is the fourfold food.
For embodied beings, the production of *rasa* (nutritive essence) results from the consumption of food.
From *rasa*, blood is produced; from blood, flesh is said to arise;
from flesh, fat is produced; and from that, bones come into being.
The marrow is known to arise from the bones, and from that, semen is produced.
Through the union of blood and semen, the embryo is formed in the woman, due to the conjunction of the fertile period and the influence of destiny and past actions. ||5||
At the end of their sexual union, both the woman and the man attain oneness.
Then, having attained oneness and impelled by the vital wind (*pavana*),
they become the *kalala* in one night, the *arbuda* in five nights,
the *piśita* in seven nights, and from the [end of the] month, the emergence of the limbs (*aṅkura*).
From that time onwards, O twice-born one, the differentiation of the embryo occurs.
Endowed with a head, hands, face, shoulders, neck, back, and so forth, the emergence of the eyes, ears, and other [features] occurs after five months. ||9||
With all its limbs fully developed and endowed with the nine apertures,
that embryo becomes manifest after exactly eight months;
when the ninth month arrives, it is complete with all its constituent elements.
That [body], consisting of the five elements, remains like the mind. || 11 ||
With limbs drenched by the moisture of the womb and beset by every suffering, the living being dwelling there remembers its birth from all origins:
"I have died and been born again; having been born, I have died once more. (12)
But now, as soon as I am born, I shall practice yoga alone. || 13 ||
"But I shall not enter again into that saṃsāra which arises from impurity.
While he was reflecting thus, the ninth month arrived. (14)
For the embodied being who is bound by his own karma, as soon as he is born,
the tamasic wind enters him and seizes away his memory.
By which the deluded one becomes joyless and finds no delight within;
[know that] the entire fourfold collection of beings consists of the nature of Agni and Soma.
O you of excellent vows, it has arisen from such a union and will continue to arise.
In that regard, those who— through association with the virtuous and through the arising of auspicious karma—
are intent on seeking the scriptures and avoid sinful conduct,
having realized that the affliction born of saṃsāra is tormented by the fear of birth and death; ||17–18||
Having cultivated detachment from birth by completely abandoning all undertakings, and being freed from the veils of desire, anger, passion, longing, greed, and delusion,
they indeed seek the auspicious goal— the secret vision of the inner self.
Having attained supreme yoga, they find that highest Brahman.
I shall fully explain to you that which is the cause of awakening to Brahman,
the secret of all yogins, and the manifestation of all yoga. Thereafter, I will describe to you that supreme Yoga of Maheśvara.

The fire of brilliance, the fire born of desire, the fire of anger, the fire of the gaze, and the digestive fire which is the self of beings—these five are the fires of the body. Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna. ||22-23||
These five winds are eternal, arising within the bodies of embodied beings;
for they originate from space, and the body abides within them—
[the body] which is filled with flesh and blood, and is a collection of sinews, fat, and bones.
It is enveloped in skin, foul-smelling, and filled with excrement and urine. ||25||
It is as impermanent as the flash of lightning or a cloud, resembling a clay vessel about to fall;
it is joined with all manner of misfortunes and is subject to destruction before long.
It is uniform in form, possessing nine gates, three pillars, and five deities.
It is muddled by the objects of the senses and afflicted by many diseases. || 27 ||
The body, held together like a machine by the vital breaths (prāṇa) and other winds,
repeatedly disintegrates when released from those winds joined with the individual soul;
through the passage of time, it perishes like a vessel of raw clay due to its lack of support.
The five elements, having departed from the body in every way, enter the self;
and the self likewise quickly enters them.
Among the elements, the wind is preeminent, and the living soul is bound to it.
The life-force of living beings is not separate from the wind and fire joined together;
there is no other form of the life-force that is seen apart from the embodied one at death. (31)
The God who is beyond the five forms is considered subtler than the subtlest;
he does not see, he does not smell, he does not hear, and he does not speak.
The individual soul (jīva), enveloped by the vital breath (prāṇa), neither knows nor experiences touch;
O twice-born one, that which is called prāṇa is the great wind that sustains the jīva.
Indeed, in all embodied beings, it both speaks and breathes;
that vital breath sustains the internal fire, and it is known as the individual soul (jīva). ||34||
For fire, when sustained by the vital air, circulates through the bodily functions;
that which possesses this fire within the body is designated as the "living soul" (jīva). //3.5//
For it is indeed contained within all beings as the bond for the commencement of action;
thus is this body composed of the qualities of the five elements. ||36||
When that transformation has perished, one is said to be "dead.
The elements, the senses, the mind, the individual soul, and the objects [of perception] are bound by the fetters of passion.
Yet, within the heart, in the pericarp, resides the treasure of splendors situated in the center.
The self is eternally omnipresent and devoid of sense objects and the like. || 38 ||
The all-pervading Lord abides there, by knowing whom one is liberated;
He is reached through the perfection of yoga by one who knows the practice of meditation and ritual action. (39)
Through the mastery of the practice of the channels and by means of constant application of yoga,
he was seen illuminated by rays of light and liberated from all transformations.
O best of Brahmins, liberation is indeed said to be seen [attained] from that,
for by fully knowing the twenty-sixth principle and dissolving oneself therein.
Subtle, pervading all living beings, and residing within one's own body—that which the perfected yogins, freed from bonds, clearly perceive. ||42||
"But as for that supreme means belonging to the Lord through the knowledge of Him,
O best of the twice-born, I shall explain to you that supreme practice of yoga.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Meditation," within the description of Pāśupata Yoga in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: The inner self (antarātman) is endowed with consciousness; the mind is known to be born of volition (saṃkalpa).
Due to the activity of the great elements (mahābhūta), the fire of agitation is called the individual soul (jīva). || 1 ||
There is no mind without the body; if that [body] does not exist, from where could it [the mind] arise?
Nor is there mind without the living soul (jīva), and that [soul] also does not exist without the mind.
Life-force (prāṇa) is said to be the living soul; it proceeds as something distinct from touch.
"The mind binds everything to the undertaking of action," so says the Śruti.
For all these, coming together, support the embodied being;
he among them whose mind is predominant is proclaimed as "the possessor of the mind.
By means of the mind, one discerns the basis of the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Having fixed that mind upon the consciousness, one should become constantly devoted to the inner self.
Having restrained the senses and transcended objects such as sound,
the embodied soul intent on the commencement of meditation shall be liberated from karma.
The senses do not bind the mind when it is situated within the body;
rather, the individual soul (jīva) should be known as that which is subject to bondage because of its attachment to the auspicious and the inauspicious.
[This occurs] through the two qualities of *rajas* and *tamas*, which are of an inauspicious nature.
From the predominance [of rajas] suffering is born; from sattva, happiness arises. || 8 ||
For embodied beings, suffering arises from the transformation of pleasure;
and pleasure, O Brahmin, arises again from the reversal of suffering. (9)
Thus, mutually connected and born from the transformation of the three qualities, consisting of pleasure and pain, and characterized by delusion, it remains pervading all beings. (8.177.10)
The destruction of that [mind] is declared to result from the concentration of the mind, from aversion toward sense objects, and from the complete avoidance of attachment;
likewise for those intent on restraining desire and who have abandoned anger and the like.
Free from the sense of "mine" and free from egoism, they are not bound by actions at all.
For this Self is omnipresent, subtle, and devoid of sensory enjoyment;
yogis perceive it through meditation by means of the cessation of the vital breaths.
A living being wanders through the cycle of existence among the creatures of the four wombs for as long as it does not seek the Self, nor is it weary of birth. (14)
Although one may perish without realizing Brahman due to attachment to meditative absorption (*dhyāna*),
nevertheless, through union with Brahman (*brahmasāyujya*), one shall not undergo birth again.
Furthermore, the sage attains supreme sovereignty born of yoga through meditation.
Having realized the Supreme Self, one does not return from there again. || 16 ||
Even those actions that are unpleasant, even those committed through great sins—
a living being intent on meditation brings them swiftly to exhaustion.
Having attained the total destruction of all karma through the method of meditation, O Great Sage, [he attains liberation].
The yogi, endowed with supreme sovereignty, remains fearless.
Desire, anger, attachment, hatred, passion, and dogmatic certainty—these are the most base states; being liberated from them, he is truly free.
Pride, hypocrisy, egoism, sophistry, arrogance, envy,
harshness, and cruelty— these are the dispositions bound to the kṣatriya.
He in whom these delusive states do not exist perceives the Self as the Lord.
Transcending the states of delusion, always equal in pain and pleasure,
and endowed with selflessness and other such qualities, he is recited as a "Yogin.
Having completely cast aside the sacrificial rites that are bonds of delusion pertaining to Viṣṇu, || 21-22 ||
A Brahmin who desires liberation should always be devoted to the inner self;
having completely renounced the three aims of life, he should find delight in the fourth aim.
He is worthy of worship by the gods and is called a *vipra*.
Through meditation, karma—whether evil or auspicious—is exhausted.
Once his karma is exhausted, the yogi then attains that supreme Brahman.
Whatever a sage who has attained yoga and is absorbed in meditation desires to do, [that he accomplishes]. || 25 ||
Whatever is conceived by the mind of that person, it immediately comes to pass.
Upon seeing the yogin, people are liberated from their sins at that very moment;
even he who merely converses with him attains a virtuous state.
O Brahmin, having understood yoga alone to be the supreme means of liberation from all that is inauspicious, the wise twice-born became seekers of emancipation. ||27||
Those who know meditation, the object of meditation, the supreme state, and the Sustainer,
are liberated from the bondage of suffering through burning away, scorching, and being purified.
This occurs by abandoning all undertakings and relinquishing notions of "mine-ness" and the like.
Sāṃkhya and Yoga are two distinct traditions regarding liberation from the principles;

however, for the foremost followers of Sāṃkhya, the Puruṣa is taught to be devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). Their departure at the dissolution of the body is recorded as being like the extinguishing of a lamp. || 8.177.30 ||
The Lord, liberated from everything, is known as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) by the yogins;
indeed, the yogins, endowed with supreme sovereignty, enter into Him through those very dhāraṇās along with the breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas). ||3.1||
He who unites the self attains the supreme sacrifice.
The yogi who is endowed with non-violence and other virtues, free from envy,
and who practices meditation, shall conquer both death and birth.

Free from qualities, free from ego, having conquered the pairs of opposites, and unimpeded by worldly constraints, one who subsists on food obtained through alms is called a seeker of liberation (mumukṣu). ||34||
One who remains equanimous amidst all undertakings, who is free from all dependence,
and who has transcended the path of action, is proclaimed a meditator (dhyānī).
O Great Sage, he whose mind does not tremble when encountering suffering—
He who does not rejoice even in pleasure is designated as a meditator (dhyānin).
The path that bestows the attainment of liberation is proclaimed to be threefold:
the first is said to be based on convention (saṃketana), and the latter is remembered as being based on discourse (saṃkathana). || 36–37 ||
The third is the "attached" (saṃsakta); hear now this distinction among them:
having fashioned an image of the Lord and being endowed with the ten restraints, ||38||
The sage who worships while meditating is called a *saṃketana*;
he is unattached to the pleasures sanctioned by the Vedas, performs actions with a pure mind, and has no kinsmen. (39)
Having abandoned [all else], one should meditate upon the Lord; this is called *saṃkathana*.
Through the renunciation of all undertakings, the path practiced by Kapila and others is known as *saṃkathana*, which illuminates the fire of yoga.
But one who is free from conceptual construction sees that everything is indeed Brahman alone. || 41 ||
One whose conduct and ritual actions have been shattered, yet who meditates, is said to be "attached.
This applies to the threefold path, including both its rules and its lack of rules. (42)
These very distinctions of conduct are proclaimed in many ways;
O Sage, these three causes for liberation are the paths of meditation. (43)
Having correctly understood these, the sage, free from the sense of "mine," resorts to one or another of them;
then he attains supreme meditation, by which he finds that which is beyond. All these rules for meditation being thus described by me—
Listen, O Vyāsa of great intellect, to [the teachings] that bestow the fruit of the sovereignty of yoga. 45.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Pāśupata Yoga," within the section on the Rules of Meditation in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Brahman is declared to be twofold: indeed, the perishable (kṣara) and the imperishable (akṣara).
For by knowing both of these, one is indeed released from all bonds.
The twenty-fifth principle is perishable, yet it is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti);
the imperishable and supreme Brahman is traditionally known as the twenty-sixth.
Having made the mind one-pointed through repeated applications of *dhāraṇā*,
one should perform the restraint of the vital breath (*vāyu*), preceded by *pratyāhāra*.
One should practice *pratyāhāra* for half a *muhūrta* or even for a single moment.
From that, three hundred [breaths] above constitute the basis for breath control (prāṇāyāma). ||4||
Having assumed a posture that has been mastered—such as the *svastika* and others celebrated in tradition—one should practice meditation in a secluded place. (5)
Whether afflicted by hunger, overfed, or even possessed by the pain of illness,
a wise man who desires meditation for himself should not meditate [under such conditions].
Then, having placed the right hand upon the left, he should assume the yogic posture.
One should be slightly downward-facing, looking at the tip of one's own nose. ||7||

Without touching his teeth with his lips, while recollecting the Brahman as the syllable Om, the wise man, free from the sense of "mine," should meditate, preceded by the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma). ||8||
Having joined the self with the Self, one should withdraw all the limbs;
motionless and with eyes closed, having fixed the concentration (dhāraṇā) in the heart,
the sage should practice meditation (dhyāna), as steady as a stone.
The fixing of the mind upon a single point, maintaining it without vibration, is known as *dhāraṇā*.
Thus, as that sage-yogi meditates day after day,
all transformations born of the *guṇas* that cause obstacles perish;
he then seeks the Supreme Brahman, which resides within his own body.
Having achieved unification through the restraint of the vital breath, the mind, and the senses. || 12 ||
By renouncing all things, one attains liberation without doubt,
having brought all the spheres of the senses under the control of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*).
Then, free from the pairs of opposites, one applies oneself to yoga, practicing the concentration of the mind.
Having established everything in the mind, one should discern the supreme reality.
(14) When, meditating upon the eightfold perfection pertaining to sovereignty, one perceives it through the complete attainment of yoga, then that person is proclaimed a yogi. (15)
When one who is disciplined perceives the gods beginning with Brahmā and Soma,
this is indeed called by the yogis the accomplishment born from the transformation of yoga.
The perfection of yogins is attained through the mind, and that of the Sāṅkhyas from the ascertainment of the principles;
there is no distinction among yogas except for the method of Maheśvara. || 17 ||
The yogi attains perfection in meditation, while the Sāṃkhya achieves the ascertainment of the principles;
yet these two—the meditation and the ascertainment of the meaning of the principles—are non-different.
One who has fallen away from all bonds and is freed from the defect of attachment [attains liberation].

One who has completely abandoned passion, delusion, and the like is called "liberated. When the disciplined one, through the perfection of yoga, no longer perceives objects such as sound by dwelling upon them, then he beholds that Supreme Reality. (8.178.20)
Agitated by the fear of birth and death and free from the defects of attachment,
one should enter the forest, observe silence, and meditate upon the imperishable syllable Om—
that sound which is proclaimed at the beginning of the Vedas and established at their conclusion.
That which is beyond him who is dissolved in primordial nature (prakṛti) is known as the Great One (mahat). ||2.2||
He who knows the threefold form, the three measures, the three Brahmas, and likewise the three syllables— both that which is devoid of measure and that which possesses measure— is liberated.
Therein is neither fire, nor wind, nor moon, nor sun.
They prevail within Maheśānī, the Sovereign who is free from the threefold conceptualization. ||24||
The syllable Oṃ is proclaimed as the supreme reality, the Self, and Brahman;
it is realized by the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas) through self-awakening and by yogis through subtle vision. ||25||
In this very way, always meditating, one should yoke the mind to the Self;
the yogi attains the Lord, having reached whom he is liberated.
Furthermore, [he should restrain] all the senses by withdrawing them from sound, form, and other objects.
Having understood that [the afflictions] are born of karma, the yogi destroys the defects without remainder.
Then, purified by the power of meditation, he attains liberation from all the Victors.
O Vyāsa, by practicing yoga every day, one attains perfection within six months.

And by means of that [knowledge], the great sage perceives the Supreme Brahman through which he may be liberated from bondage; having known that Self as supreme through the power of yoga, he shall attain the immortal state endowed with supreme sovereignty. ||29||
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Pāśupata Yoga," within the section on the Rules of Meditation in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
"That which has been described by me as the 'Great' (Mahat), perfected through the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)..."
In this [body], there are five organs of action and five organs of cognition. || 1 ||
The five elements and the mind are here known as the sixteen transformations. Indeed, the Great One (mahat), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), and the five subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi)—
these eight primary natures (prakṛtis), O Vyāsa, reside within the body.
These twenty-four principles have been declared by the yogis;
the body, pervading the three worlds, stands supported by these.
In the center of the navel, however, one hundred channels are established.
As for those other channels throughout all the limbs that carry water, food, and rasa,
thirty thousand of them are situated within the flow of the vyāna.
Other channels of the udāna are established at the crown of the head, the seat of Brahmā.
Resting upon the hub of the wheel, he is supported by the aggregate of the elements;
in his midst stands the one whose nature is action, touched by the qualities (guṇas) and the deluder of beings.
Resembling the radiance of the stars, his splendor is like a mass of moonlight.
Standing like ten thousand suns, he causes distress to others;
appearing like a portentous fire or like mountain mist, the twenty-fifth principle is the Puruṣa, the source of beings who abides in the qualities (guṇas). ||7-8||
Beyond that as well, there arises the pure one, like a great fire that has blazed up;
radiant, blazing on all sides, free from conceptual construction, and stainless. (9)
Resembling smokeless embers, his movement and arrival are imperceptible;
he is the twenty-sixth principle, the subtle Puruṣa, the Supreme Lord, the all-pervading.
O Vyāsa, this one who stands beyond the others has been described;
by knowing this Mahādeva, the sage is liberated at that very moment.
That which abides in the transformations of the three qualities is called the twenty-fifth.
Therefore, deluded by ignorance alone, he transmigrates further;
infatuated by passion, he wanders among gods, humans, and animals.
Through the absorption in the Twenty-sixth [Principle], his perfection arises from the transformation of those modifications. || 12-13 ||
Free from action and its effects, the omniscient, the creator of all, the Lord, fully endowed with supreme sovereignty, the Great Lord who has accomplished all that was to be done. ||14||
The Unborn, the Self-existent, the Twenty-sixth, is indeed the immutable, immovable, and eternal.
From Him the principles (tattvas) are born, as is the Puruṣa together with the qualities (guṇas).
And in that very Great Lord, the Twenty-sixth, they all dissolve.
Having known this Maheśāna, the perfection of liberation is attained.
Knowing this, one would not be smeared by actions that are bonds of delusion;
just as fire at the end [of time] would burn away the entire multitude of beings without exception,
so too one who knows the reality of the twenty-six categories would burn away all actions.

Just as space, which is all-pervading and subtle, is not defiled at all, so too the yogi through the twenty-sixth principle is not defiled by sins. There is nothing beyond the twenty-sixth; therefore, one should become devoted to that supreme reality.
Having abandoned oneness with that very [ego], he attains the body;
[he perceives] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and all others, the entire multitude of beings without exception. (8.179.20)
O Vyāsa, [the world] is born from Īśvara and dissolves into that very same one;
there is indeed nothing else superior to him, for one should know him as abiding everywhere. 21.
The perfected ones who know the inner self worship him as the Supreme Self;
he is this all-pervading god, the twenty-sixth, the Supreme Lord. ||22||
One should strive for the restraint of those five winds in the body: prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.
Having carefully made both apāna and samāna move as one, [one should proceed].
One should establish the prāṇa, together with the vyāna, within the udāna.
Then, by the power of yoga, one should cause the breath to reach the tip of the nose once;
having established a steady gaze, one should thereafter contemplate the Twenty-sixth [Principle].
Fifteen measures (mātrās) are prescribed for the first binding of the joints.
The fifth [chapter], concerning peace and war, should be understood as consisting of twenty measures (mātrās).
In a soundless and solitary place, free from desire and with senses conquered, one should assume either the Svastika, Padmaka, Bhadra, or Siṃhakacchapa postures. || 26–27 ||
Occupying a single seat and recollecting the Twenty-sixth [Tattva], having withdrawn all limbs [of the senses], one should practice meditation, free from movement. ||28||

One should gradually cause the breath, which resides in the channels and the flow [of the body], to circulate through the channels; one should remain thus with a disciplined mind, free from longing, through the yoga of breath-control. ||29||
As long as one perceives that which resembles a lunar disc situated in the heart,
and having seen it resting within the body of light, mastery over yoga proceeds.
Thus, from such constant practice and the resulting progression toward the perfection of yoga,
direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding objects of the three times arises for the yogin.
Diseases do not enter him, nor does he become possessed by suffering.
And a sweet fragrance arises from one's own body, and a divine form is produced. || 3.2 ||
His word shall be unfailing, effecting both curses and favors;
furthermore, there shall be no adverse consequence for him arising from his actions.
O Vyāsa, among all those who possess knowledge, among ascetics, those who observe vows,
and among Brahmins who practice austerities, the yogi is declared to be the most excellent.
Otherwise, a living being is not liberated from this worldly existence, which is beyond even darkness.
Apart from the thorough knowledge of the twenty-six principles, there is no bond to yoga.
Having conquered the eightfold binding of postures by means of the sixfold yoga as well as the fivefold [yoga], ||3.6||
Having mastered the fourfold prāṇāyāma by means of the excellence of the *mātrās*, and having conquered the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) with the senses, and the senses with their objects; ||37||
Free from egoism, fear, fatigue, anger, and greed, devoid of envy, attachment, affection, and desire;
having established himself in the state of yoga previously described, which is devoid of qualities (guṇas). || 38 ||
One should meditate upon that God, the All-pervading Lord of the Universe,
who is without beginning or end, tranquil, and entirely free from the three qualities (guṇas).
Placing the tongue against the palate and not allowing the teeth to touch one another— ||8.179.40||
One should join the senses and the mind within the Supreme Self;
having gathered all that [into] the mind and restrained both prāṇa and apāna,
one should repeatedly meditate upon the syllable Oṃ while withdrawing the limbs like a tortoise.
Having filled the entire body, one should project everything into the Self. ||42||
Having withdrawn that [mind], the sage should again repeatedly undertake it in such a way through the movement of the channels and the vital breaths, so as to enter the pervasive, expanded element.
That time during the first and last watches of the night is said to be sattvic for the mind.
At midday and in the afternoon, one should meditate upon the dark, tamasic form.
One should constantly practice the *rājasa* meditation during both twilights, and the *taijasa* meditation at all times; indeed, through meditation alone, one shall conquer the *guṇas*.

O Vyāsa, for one who always meditates in this way, that sovereignty proceeds by which, having realized the twenty-sixth principle, the Great Lord (Maheśvara) residing within the heart, [one attains liberation]. 46.
Having voluntarily abandoned its own body, it merges back into that very [source].
The Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, the Cause, the Great Puruṣa,
is declared to be the Lord, devoid of qualities, and the Experiencer— the Twenty-sixth.
And that which is both non-existent and existent, the pervasive and supreme one who has become the manifestation of all beings. ||48||
He is awake while [others] sleep; he eats, remains still, and gives.
He is the creator and the destroyer, the Great Lord who transcends the qualities (guṇas). ||49||
Thus has all this been told, the exposition of every yoga—the primordial Pāśupata yoga that bestows the state of liberation. 8.179.50
O sinless one, I shall proclaim to you that subtle and supreme knowledge, which is free from all conceptual attachments and has issued forth from the mouth of Hara;
through the thorough understanding of which, there remains nothing further to be known. ||51||
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Pāśupata Yoga," within the section on the Rules of Meditation in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, in ancient times, at the time of the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the deities beginning with Brahmā—
Afflicted by the fear of Vīrabhadra, they sought refuge with Śaṅkara.
When they were pursued by the lord of the Gaṇas, they took to heaps of ashes;
once they had entered the ashes, they attained the supreme splendor of Śaṅkara.
At that time, those fierce beings became like consecrated sacrificial animals, their limbs smeared with ashes as they observed the vow of Śaṅkara. ||3||
Then the Lord, the husband of Umā, bestowed his own yoga upon them—that which is the most preeminent reality among all the sciences of liberation. ||4||
O Vyāsa, that yoga which was initiated by the foremost of yogis, headed by Hiraṇyagarbha, is complete, yet it is accomplished through arduous means.
O great sage, by practicing this for thousands of other births,
they attain either the supreme light or the sovereignty of yoga—
this very supreme Yoga of Maheśvara which has been directly revealed by the Blessed One.
This has been told to you in truth for those celestial beings who have sought refuge;
by the complete understanding of this very [teaching], one attains knowledge within six months after undertaking the Pāśupata vow in this very life. ||7||
O Vyāsa, having attained the great sovereignty of yoga by which one is liberated,
and having cast aside all other dharmas through the power of the Partless One,
they enter that Maheśvara after receiving the Pāśupata initiation.
Endowed with all-encompassing knowledge yet excluded from the dharma of asceticism,
this vow was taught by Śiva as consisting merely of the practice of sacred ash.
Understand that great vow: whether they are most wicked or righteous, those who are devoted solely to the Lord are liberated by serving Him.
There is no righteousness without unrighteousness, nor is there any evil without righteousness.

These two are bound to one another; therefore, having abandoned both of them, one should practice the Pāśupata vow, free from both merit and demerit. Then, having attained this yoga, one obtains great sovereign power.
Merely by taking up the ashes, one is liberated from all bonds;
indeed, one is released as soon as one is touched by the ashes purified by Brahman.
Fire burns that which is produced by Soma; the wise know the Lord to be that fire.
Fire, when joined with Soma, consumes both the done and the undone.
All those possessed of ego, beginning with Brahmā, were liberated by the ashes.
Ashes are the vigor of his splendor; ashes are the purifying Lord.
O Vyāsa, he who performs the ritual bath with ashes uplifts himself;
through the yoga of Śiva and by means of ashes, he is liberated from the bondage of the fetters. 17.
The gods originate from Soma, and the ancestors originate from Agni;
therefore, the entire world is established as consisting of the nature of Agni and Soma.
Īśvara, Agni, and Soma—that is said to be the fiery ash.
Touched by his splendor, O twice-born one, one is liberated from birth.
Having abandoned Sāṃkhya, knowledge, austerity, and even Vedic duties, one who is purified solely by bathing in ashes goes to that supreme state. (8.180.20)
Even one who has indulged in sense objects and remained devoted to great unrighteousness is indeed purified by the ashes of Śambhu, provided he subsequently becomes intent on devotion.
He who, having consecrated himself with the sacred ashes of Brahman, makes himself the sacrificial animal and offers it into the fire of Mahādeva, becomes a sage performing the sacrifice of Śiva.
Having attained the supreme yoga very quickly, he shall be liberated from bondage;
thus, having undertaken this vow, the sage becomes a Pāśupata. || 23 ||
One should practice this supreme secret knowledge of Maheśvara;
the object of knowledge, the knowledge itself, and the knower—how these three abide within the body.
Who the self is, and how it is established in the three locations, and how indeed the self abides within the channels and within the self itself. ||25||
O Vyāsa, it remains hidden everywhere within all beings, just as butter is contained within milk; by knowing this, one is liberated. ||26||
That Self cannot be known in any way without knowledge;
who can know that Maheśvara, who transcends form, sound, and taste?
For thus it is, O illustrious one, by the grace of Tryambaka.
O sinless one, I shall tell you the means for attaining self-knowledge. 28.
Indeed, this entire world was formerly nothing but darkness;
there were no gods, no wind, no sky, no sun, and no moon. 29.
Nothing whatsoever exists as real in any way within the world;
rather, it is the pure, stainless, imperishable, and supreme Lord who shines forth. (8.180.3)

Listen now to how that imperishable Brahman is described: it transcends all states and qualities, is free from conceptual construction, and is stainless; it moves both externally and internally, is radiant, indestructible, supreme, and eternal. (31)
The single syllable "Om" existed first; from it emerged the perishable.
The three-syllabled and three-measured Oṃkāra is called Brahman. || 3.2 ||
In the syllable *a* is Viṣṇu, in the syllable *u* is Pitāmaha (Brahmā),
in the syllable *ma* is the Lord Īśa, and in the *mātrā* (the nasal bindu) Prakṛti is remembered. Those two gods, Brahmā and Viṣṇu, are known as having emerged from Īśvara.
Assuming their innate female nature, they two remain eternally by the side of Īśa.
In the form of his consort, that Prakṛti always worships Śambhu;
Prakṛti is known as the perishable, while the imperishable is the Lord himself.
For that Prakṛti, bound by the qualities (guṇas), emerged from Īśvara;
Mahādeva is her creator, from whom Viṣṇu and Pitāmaha [Brahmā] arose.
The two Prajāpatis were born bound by the three qualities; Maheśa, having taken hold of them while they remained in primordial nature (prakṛti) and consisted of those qualities, [acted]. ||37||
Abiding in the letter *ma*, the All-pervading Lord indeed enjoys and wanders about.
Having understood this supreme secret, I have declared this imperishable reality (*tattva*).
O Vyāsa, by that very meditator, this Lord is conceptualized.
Having entered that, the sage becomes one whose self is liberated and who has accomplished his purpose.
Those who stand on the wrong path, devoted to logic and reasoning, do not know him—
the enjoyer, the Lord of nature, the Supreme known as the Twenty-sixth.
The syllable Oṃ is eternal Prakṛti, and within it the Lord resides, just as clarified butter exists within milk, O Vyāsa. (41)
O Sage, he by whom the syllable Oṃ is meditated upon transcends primordial nature;
that great Lord is known, and he is liberated from the bonds of the bound souls (paśus). ||42||
Nature (prakṛti) is known as the sovereign (īśvarī), who deludes through the bonds of the qualities (guṇas);
for she is the nourisher (bṛṃhaṇī) by virtue of being Brahman, and she rests in manifestation (vibhava) by virtue of being Viṣṇu. ||43||
By the grace of the Lord, this primordial nature (prakṛti), consisting of the three qualities, possesses self-consciousness and is the creator of worldly existence; Maheśvara is its enjoyer.
She has eight arms, three feet, and likewise five bodies and faces.

She has two eyes, is established in the five actions, and is mounted upon a chariot drawn by seven horses. Indeed, she is remembered as the Mother of the World, born from the transformations of the three qualities (guṇas).
Both the auspicious and the inauspicious, as well as both knowledge (vidyā) and ignorance (avidyā), belong to her. ||45-46||
Manifestation, as well as destruction, the performance of action, and the causal source—these, in brief, are the states of existence. 47.
The syllable Oṃ was born from the Lord, and it is established in Him;
from the syllable Oṃ, the entire world, up to the abode of Brahmā, has arisen. (48)
Therefore, O highly fortunate one, the yogis such as Kapila and others, having understood this, worship the syllable Om as the supreme Brahman, free from conceptual construction.
For that alone is the all-pervading Self, and that alone is indeed the cause.

Thus, having known those two— the Lord and the object of enjoyment— who are of the nature of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), who originate from the syllable *oṃ*, who consist of the qualities (*guṇa*), and who are Viṣṇu and Pitāmaha (Brahmā),
and having abandoned the two [beings] created by them called the Vedas and sacrifices, which are the bonds of dharma; ||5 1 ||
The two great delusions are rooted in darkness (tamas) and joined with attachment to sense objects;
preceded by goodness (sattva) and having passion (rajas) in their midst, they are always accompanied by pleasure and pain.
They cause wandering in saṃsāra, are characterized by folly, and are joined with all that is impermanent.
The wise man, desiring the Lord, should become devoted to meditation and yoga.
Therefore, primordial nature (prakṛti), having arisen from Him alone, dissolves back into Him;
by means of that yoga, He is known as the Lord established within the self.
"Nature (prakṛti) does not bind him, and he is liberated from the ocean of existence.
Thus ends the one hundred and eightieth chapter, the seventh in the section on the rules for meditation within the description of Pāśupata Yoga in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
The self is subtle, as are the mind, the intellect, the ego, and the qualities; likewise the elements, the aggregate of the senses, the subtle essences, and the ten vital airs. (1)
O observer of noble vows, they are divided sequentially within the body according to their respective locations in the three states of dreaming, waking, and deep sleep.
Within the heart, there is a lotus facing in all directions, situated at the pericarp.
Above that, for all embodied beings, it is enveloped by subtle threads.
Therein the Self, together with the vital breath and the mind, is established;
the perfected Śiva-yogins call that state "deep sleep" (suṣupta).
[The five powers are] Jvālinī, Stimitā, Dhūmrā, Vidyunmeghā, and Viśālinī.
Mālinī, Śaṅkarī, Sumaitrī, and likewise Bodhanī. ||5||

These ten great channels are established in that living being; whether he is lying down or awake, they sustain the embodied soul. As for the Self, which is omnipresent, [it is distinct] from the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest.
Furthermore, that which is joined with fire and wind is called the individual soul (jīva). ||7||
Ego (ahaṅkāra), intellect (buddhi), the dispositions (bhāvas), and the mind (cetas) are considered to be born of the body;
they abide together with the individual soul (jīva), supporting the embodied being.
All these together, with the soul as the fifth, [constitute the subtle body].
The pericarp, established in space by means of threads, faces in all directions. ||9||
Subtle and situated within the mind is the thread named Śītāṃśu;

that alone is declared to be the consciousness (cetas), and that alone is remembered as the person (puruṣa). Furthermore, the ego (ahaṃkāra) and the individual soul (jīva) are the thread born of Bhāskara.
The mind is Soma, bliss is Brahmā, knowledge is Dharma, and likewise delight. || 1.1 ||
Taste, the self, great medicinal herbs, the expansion of dispositions born of *sattva*, ego-consciousness, fire, death, suffering, disease,
desire, anger, old age, thirst, and unrighteousness— these are the qualities of *tamas*.
Viṣṇu, intellect, as well as the effect, the cause, and the earth;
knowledge, detachment, and space—this is the extensive expansion of the rājasa state. Subtle and smokeless, it is the flame of fire situated within the living soul.
It is indeed the nectar of all beings and their supreme goal;
situated in its center is the gentle lunar orb, which is nectar itself.
In its center, the Lord Jīva is seen, resembling fire;
he is full of essence, red, foremost, joyful, and likewise possessed of flavor.
Vidhūmā, Amṛtā, Nikuṇṭhā, and Bahuvistarā—
these extremely subtle channels, having pierced through the ten fires,
constantly satisfy Soma, the support of all beings, with the nectar of milk. || 17 ||
Satisfied by those [waters] with all essences, juices, and potencies, that soma, having increased,
envelops that flame situated in the midst of the living being.
That indeed is declared to be the nectar, the supreme abode of the Lord;
for when the essence of the soma is drawn up excessively by the flame (śikhā), [then it is attained]. 1.9
At that time, this living being born from all wombs remains awake;
the other channel, called Amṛtā, is established in sleep.
When he has drunk the Soma and is said to be "asleep," then the sage,
having conquered both these states based on sleep and wakefulness,
should contemplate through the yoga of meditation, neither waking nor sleeping. || 21 ||
Those states such as the sense of "mine-ness," as well as those feelings of aversion belonging to the mind,
and that detachment which belongs to the intellect— by means of these, yogins perceive.
Whatever the mind conceives and whatever the intellect discriminates, [they perceive it all].
Or rather, whatever the ego may do, one should abandon it all through knowledge of that [Self].
For one who is actionless, whence can there be action? Without that, whence can there be bondage? Indeed, being devoid of the bondage of action and perfectly pure, how could he be bound? (24)
Those who do not know that these sense-objects originate from Soma—for them, Vahni is said to be the enjoyer; by what, then, can the knower of that be bound?
Having understood this, one should abandon anxiety and always remain devoted to Yoga.
The heat of fire is declared to be that sin, which is the property of fire;
that which is its nature is the individual soul (jīva), and that which is the flame is Maheśvara. ||27||
He who can burn the fire with his own brilliance is not himself consumed by it;
by him the primordial nature (prakṛti) has been transcended, and by him Maheśvara has been attained. ||28||
For this world is bound by the bonds of karma; how could one who is free from action be bound?
Those who know yoga, devoid of the sense of "mine," abide in the vow of Śaṅkara. ||29||
They depart, having abandoned their own bodies and cast off illusion, reaching the supreme state.
This is another supreme knowledge, which is moreover even more subtle than this. (8.181.3)
I shall proclaim it to you, O Vyāsa, for you are a devotee of Śaṅkara;
that which is a most wonderful secret, which other yogins do not know, exists in no beings other than the Siddhas who have attained the Pāśupata state. || 31 ||
The mind, the intellect, the ego, the senses, and the three qualities do not touch that Self; these modifications are external to it. It is seen everywhere, yet it is not perceived by all.

He is seen thus through meditation; by no other means whatsoever can he be seen. Those yogins who perceive the Supreme Lord—who transcends all states of being and qualities, and who is well to be contemplated—through wisdom, are remembered as the supreme ones.
This shadow which is seen resting within the range of the eye is declared,
O Vyāsa, to be the *jīva*, the cause of stability for embodied beings.
Within that [shadow] dwells the supreme Self, subtle, situated in the midst, and imperishable.
