The great nāga known by the name Vāyu has his domain in the sky. ||3.6||

Established in the ether, in the pericarp, in the channel, and in the individual soul (jīva) are Gāndhārī, Vijayā, and Sañjñā, who resides at the base. Within these channels, the serpent-like wind circulates.
Those two, Jayā and Vijayā, are known as the carriers of the prāṇa.
Apāna is associated with the two channels Gandhārī and Hastijihvā, which are joined with Nāga;
through yoga, these are impelled by the apāna and the mind by means of Nāga.
That vital breath, satisfying the fire that carries the oblation both externally and internally, sustains the aged body with both life-span and strength. (8.181.40)
Another channel, however, is called Suṣumṇā; it is situated within the moon, fire, and mind.
It resides in this body composed of the constituent elements (dhātus), as well as in the tortoise-shaped wind (kūrmāra-vāyu).
Fixed at the ankle and the palm of the hand, it is both contracted and extended.
Joined with the *samāna* and *vyāna*, they indeed nourish the blood and flesh.
As for the other wind, *udāna*, it is called the "tortoise" (*kūrma*);
these two are established in the channel connected to the navel, which is like a scale.
Now, one wind moves through the nāḍī, while the other moves upward;
the one situated below is connected to the feet, and the one moving upward is stationed in the head. ||44||
The wind known as Devadatta, which is conditioned, and the other wind, Nila—these two, bound by fire and moon, are the causes of the vital breath and possess great power. (45)
One increases the fire, while another satisfies the moon;
[these are] Devadatta, Mahānāga, Kṛtakūrma, and Dhanañjaya. ||46||
Those five vital breaths are renowned as the sacrificial fires for the sacrificer;
whatever is offered or sacrificed into them reaches the Soma.
Sacrificers enter the Soma; for them, there is no characteristic of liberation.
That which is known as the radiance of fire and the essence derived from plants—[these are their lot]. (48)
That which is the libation of Soma is situated within the pericarp;
it is this light seen in the eyes that illuminates the shadow. (49)
That *jīva* is the self of all beings, established therein; subtle and contained within the light, it is remembered as that supreme nature. || 8.181.50 ||
That is declared to be the nectar; it is said to be attainable through knowledge.
There is no goal higher than that, which is the culmination of theoretical knowledge (*jñāna*) and realized wisdom (*vijñāna*).
Having understood this, one should abandon delusion born from the transformations of the three qualities (*guṇa*).
Who else, even if skilled in yoga, could create a distinction for that indivisible Self, the twenty-sixth principle, the Lord?
One should not conceptualize that stainless, non-conceptual Sovereign. ||52-53||
Free from delusion, having abandoned worldly associations, and devoid of ritual actions and duties,
those who observe the vow of the Lord enter that Great Lord.
Thus, O Vyāsa, this yoga of Maheśvara has been declared to you;
it is the perfect union with the Lord, which is not found elsewhere. ||55||
O Brahmin, whatever doubt you have and whatever you deem worthy of inquiry, ask that of me immediately, O Brahmin; there is nothing that I should not tell you.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Pāśupata Yoga," within the section on the Rules of Yoga in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of all Yogins, honored by all the immortals!"
Oh, what knowledge you have proclaimed, which brings about the cessation of ignorance! || 1 ||
Today my doubt regarding the supreme Mahādeva has vanished:
that Prakṛti was born from Śaṅkara, and that Brahmā and Viṣṇu are of his very essence;
having known the Lord as the twenty-sixth principle, one is liberated from bondage. ||2||
Having previously explained the entire compendium from the path of all yoga, ||3||
"Who else could speak thus of knowledge that is both partless and with parts?
O best of Brahmins, by hearing this, I have realized that my body is liberated.
Through your grace, dear father, I have attained knowledge and am freed from all evil."
O venerable one, you are free from doubt and peaceful; I have something to ask you. ||5||
I inform you of this truth; you ought to explain the final state.
O Sage, thus endowed with such knowledge and having attained yoga, the sage—possessing the power of yoga—casts off the body without affliction.
How does one attain that Brahman, the partless Supreme Lord?
O best of sages, tell me the means for attaining the Lord—which is the attainment of liberation—for there is nothing else remaining for me to ask. (7–8)
Thus addressed by his disciple Vyāsa, the great-souled one,
that best of Brahmins recounted the definitive conclusion of the Śiva-siddhānta.
Sanatkumāra said:
Listen, Vyāsa, to this supreme knowledge which has the Lord as its foundation;
by means of it, yogins devoted to wisdom are liberated according to their own will. Having understood this threefold departure and having practiced it repeatedly— || 8.182.10 ||
Having abandoned one's own body like an enemy, one attains dissolution in the Twenty-sixth.
Those channels, held by the vital wind, sustain the embodied being;
of those hundreds of channels, a hundred are centered within the pericarp.

Depending upon that [central channel], the channels are situated at the navel; they extend downward into the feet, are known to be fixed at the head, and those same ones are further established in the hands. (13)
O Sage, depending upon those [channels], seventy-two thousand other channels called *nāḍīs* further depend upon the *karṇikā*.
The subdivisions of each of these are said to be increasingly subtle;
within them moves the vital breath (prāṇa), which arises from the space of the pericarp (karṇikā).
Therein, O twice-born one, the Self (ātman) abides as previously described, perceivable in its subtlety.
The sage who knows yoga should resort to that radiance of his which is difficult to perceive.
That energy is distributed throughout all the channels of all embodied beings;
by means of it, the channels make the mind, which has expanded outward, perceive external sensations.
Having withdrawn that fire by means of the eye, which is situated within all the channels, one should make the mind one-pointed and fix it upon the Self. || 18 ||
The wind named Dhanañjaya is that which always throbs within the heart;
they say it has three openings: the head, the navel, and the heart. These others are the nine vital breaths (prāṇas) which have been described by me as winds.
They were all under the control of Dhanañjaya and dependent upon him.
By their power these [channels] ascend; established therein, they remain fixed.
Having reached the binding of the navel, they occupy the openings of the channels.
The second is located in the pericarp, while the third is situated at the palate.
The razor, the axe, and the trident—these are said to be the threefold upward transition (utkrānti). ||22||
A spear is situated in the heart, a razor at the navel, and an axe resides in the palate;
or else, three [weapons] are bound to the palate and the heart, while they are established at the navel.
When the two palates are separated, everything releases the vital breath alone;
when the triad is drawn up, it is released into the pericarp at the navel.
Having joined [the self] within the Self, one should cast the mind upward;
through this practice, O best of Brahmins, the sage is liberated at that very moment.
This voluntary abandonment of the body has thus been described to you.
But by means of the actions previously performed, which are bound by merit and demerit. ||26||
Listen now to this by which the life-force (jīva) of the yogi is not bound:
death is said to be of two kinds, namely external and that born of the body. || 27 ||
Death by means of poison, weapons, fire, serpents, fanged beasts, wind, and water is known as external; now learn from me that which is bodily.
Death may be either internal, arising from disease or arising from time;
that which arises from time is said to be due to old age, while that which arises from disease results from the exhaustion of the bodily constituents (*vyadhi-saṃkṣaya*).
O Sage, this other kind of death, born from the application of yoga, is difficult to attain.
Listen briefly, O Vyāsa, to the distinction between these two: that which is brought about by the means of yoga and that which occurs through the exhaustion of time.
One arises from the exhaustion of time; the second is desired by the mind. || 8.182.3–4 ||
This sound produced by resonance which is heard through the connection of the ears first dissolves into the tortoise; by that [dissolution], fire abandons its radiance.
Then that fire becomes lusterless and is deprived of its connection with sound;
transcending the qualities of sound and touch, it relinquishes its connection with form.
When the fire has thus been extinguished, all the vital airs (anila) then,
desiring union as one, cut through the vital points (marmāṇi).
The tortoise, Devadatta, Kṛkara, and the serpent itself—having quickly joined with Udāna, they indeed enter the pericarp.
Thereafter, the breath becomes upward-moving; this is the departure of the mind and the life-force.
Then the light that is in the eyes quickly enters the moon.
The senses go toward the mind, and the mind [goes toward] the departure of the vital breath;
when all of these have dissolved, the wind [of the breath] should suppress the vital breaths. ||37||
Then, being oppressed, they all become unified in their vital breaths, having each abandoned their respective abodes and whatever actions were inherent to them. (38)
All the winds, gathered in one place, fill Dhananjaya;
for there remains only the tortoise-like vital breath (kūrmāra), which stays having abandoned the individual soul (jīva).
The mind, the intellect, the ego, the consciousness, and likewise the individual soul,
impelled by the vital wind, quickly depart from the body;
thereafter, another subtle body is produced for it, which was previously acquired.
There, that soul remains joined [to the body] once more, yet remains deluded. || 41 ||
Thus, indeed, this condition of all classes of beings is determined by time;
without yoga, the subtle state of Maheśvara cannot be attained.
Whether sitting or asleep, one who has practiced restraint regarding the departure of the soul [from the body] [achieves it]. ||52||
O Vyāsa, having known Maheśvara as the Thread (Tantu), one is liberated by one's own will.
Then the sage may wield a razor, an axe, or even a trident;
thereafter, all modifications dissolve along with the instruments of perception.
And he beholds the Lord, Brahman, the twenty-sixth principle, abiding within his own body;
yet the mind of the living being, though intense, remains inert as he falls into calamity. ||45||
Overcome by pain, he did not perceive the object of his knowledge;
yet, O Brahmin, by this very act, he was entirely freed from all suffering. (46)

Having understood the five categories of reality, he attains the bliss of the summit of the palace of Brahman as if from its very foundation; established in the final cessation of suffering, the twice-born man, purified by the five Brahmans and consecrated with ashes, [attains liberation]. 47.
The yogi whose mind is single-pointedly fixed on Śaṅkara attains this knowledge.
Even with great effort, they do not find this partless Māheśvara yoga— the cause of liberation— without having undertaken the vow of Śaṅkara.
Therefore, O Vyāsa of great intelligence, by practicing the Pāśupata vow and becoming devoted to Mahādeva, may you attain this knowledge.
Other yogins do not find this supreme Brahman in such a manner.
Except for those who have taken refuge in Mahādeva, there are no Śiva-yogins.
This entire method of liberation, O Vyāsa, has been described as being free from all objective perceptions, partless (niṣkala), and supreme, since nothing higher than it exists. ||51-52||
In this way, the Pāśupata brahmins, having entered that Maheśvara who is partless through yoga, are liberated and freed from rebirth. ||53||
I shall describe that divine abode of Mahādeva, which stands beyond the world of Brahmā and is the resting place for all; there those who are his devotees go. ||54||
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-second chapter, the ninth in the section on the rules of yoga within the description of the Pāśupata yoga in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
[Regarding] truth, greatness, people, and likewise austerity...
And it stands above the seven [realms] consisting of the past, present, and future. || 1 ||
The entire world, where Śambhu resides, is entirely auspicious (śiva);
it cannot be defined by logic, for all worlds are established within it.
Above, across, and below, all worlds have that as their support.
The entire universe is established within that world of Śiva.
It does not perish at the time of dissolution; it is eternal, immovable, and the abode of the gods, where I, Sanaka and the others, and Brahmā, the Grandfather, reside.
Led by the Bālakhilyas, the Siddhas such as Kapila and others,
having attained the yoga of Śiva and being freed from the qualities of sattva and the rest,
remain in bliss, O Vyāsa, serving that Lord.
This atom is the Lord, perceivable by the wise through their discernment.
There resides Vigraheśvara, endowed with supreme sovereignty;
likewise, forbearance, truth, fortitude, austerity, and detachment. ||7||
The state of being the creator, knowledge, dispassion, self-awakening, and supreme lordship—
these abide eternally in that Great Lord, the Divine.
This Self is the fire of yoga, the creator of Brahman, and the Supreme Lord.
Assuming a form through its totality, it maintains the stability of the world.
The eighth is the eternal, the syllable to be studied, the cause of liberation;
it is the abode of Māyā for that Lord, the cause of the dissolution of the world.
Above the world of Brahmā, at a distance of twenty million yojanas from that great-souled one, the city of Sthāṇu is situated.
This much is known as the upward movement and the end of the course;
in that city dwell those who are innumerable, eternal, subtle, and likewise imperishable. (12)
The primordial natures (prakṛtis) of Śiva, whose essential quality is the authority of knowledge, remain established;
from them were born the two Great Lords, Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the progenitors. To those two, who have become the primordial natures, He granted supreme creative power.
He is imperishable, stainless, subtle, partless, and yet also possessed of all parts.
Established in the stable, formal, supreme, and divine state at the level of the ultimate atom,
there first occurs the manifestation of that light from the primordial darkness of the mind.
When that golden egg was mundane, it then became the Great Principle (Mahat), which is eternal, all-pervading, and derived from the Lord, pertaining to both worldly existence and liberation. ||16||
Therefore, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is remembered as the omnipresent one who is without differentiation from the seed;
Prakṛti is declared to be Vaiṣṇavī, and she has emerged from him. 17.
For the sake of creating the gods, asuras, and others, she again assumed the state of Brahmā;
from the breaking of the cosmic egg, there arose the lotus-born Brahmā, whose nature is Śaṅkara, and before the city of Brahmaloka, there appeared a great city composed of light. (18)
O Vyāsa, that abode of the Lord of Form, the Supreme Self, the Sovereign, known by the name Śivapura, is the destination of the yogis who have attained mastery.
A hundred times one hundred thousand yojanas is said to be the extent of the terrestrial sphere; it is recorded as being spread out in the center of that [world].
It was beautifully encircled by a great wall made of gold, possessing a brilliance exceeding that of fire and shimmering with the form of the sun;
it featured four golden gates adorned with jewels and pearls.

That beautiful city, adorned and frequented by the Siddhas, shone brilliantly. O Sage, in that city of Śiva, inauspicious states such as old age, death, fatigue, disease, anger, delusion, and pride do not prevail.
That city of the bull-bannered god extends for a hundred times a hundred thousand yojanas in every direction; it is all-pervading and magnificent.
The divine emerald ground brought pleasure by its mere touch;
it was fashioned like lapis lazuli gems and resembled the rising sun.
In some places red lotuses shone, and in others white ones.
They were as large as great lakes, with stalks resembling vaidūrya gems. || 26 ||
Fragrant and highly precious, they were laid upon the surface of the earth, resembling sapphire and possessing the luster of great jewels. ||27||
In some places there were blue and half-red lotuses, bearing divine fragrances, and there were lotuses everywhere on all sides. ||28||
O son of Parāśara, learn now of those great rivers that flow with nectar-like water within that city of the Lord Śambhu:
Varadā, Vareṇyā, Vareśā, and Varavarṇinī.
Vārāhī, Vāribhadrā, and Varā are indeed great rivers. || 8.183.30 ||
They carry that nectar-like water mixed with various flowers;
neither gods, nor lords of sages, nor asuras, nor ancestors [can do so]. 3.1.
And no others would be capable of knowing that wondrous city,
except for those who have awakened within their inner minds, who are permeated by devotion on all sides,
and whose minds are fixed solely on Śiva; O Vyāsa, those men rejoice therein.
In the center of that city of the Lord of Gods, who possesses the brilliance of the blazing sun, stands a palace made of gold,
shaped like the peak of Mount Meru, auspicious in all directions, radiant as the sun,
a hundred thousand paces in extent, and capable of moving at will.
It was adorned on all sides with great jewels that were beyond the reach of sight.
With lapis lazuli that resembles the sky, with crystal possessing the luster of the moon, with coral resembling the sun, and with others made of sapphire; || 35 ||
Adorned with banners that in some places were as radiant as moonbeams and in others took the form of sunbeams, that place shone with pleasant breezes;
it was further beautified by variegated flowers of all seasons and by wish-fulfilling jewel-fruits.
That city, strewn with trees resembling mountains, shone brilliantly.
Just as Mount Meru is the great and preeminent among all mountains, so too did that city gleam, situated above all the worlds. (37–38)
There, Viśveśvara himself, Hara, the Lord of the great elements, the twenty-sixth Supreme Lord, dwells eternally together with his consort. (39)
Lakṣmī, Medhā, Dhṛti, Hrī, Śrī, Kīrti, and Sarasvatī, together with Umā—these mothers of the world rejoice there. || 8.183.40 ||

O child, those men who have dedicated their souls to the state of Śiva and are devoted to Rudra— wherever they may die, that very place is declared to be their abode. And those Māheśvaras, O Vyāsa, who dwell in the temple of Śaṅkara, [attain the same].
The sages are devotees of Śaṅkara; listen to them with a concentrated mind. ||42||
I myself, as well as Sanandana, Sanaka, and Sanātana;
Ṛbhu, Brahmā, the eldest of the gods, and also Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
[and] the perfected disciple Pañcaśikha likewise. ||43||
And the sage Hayashiras, as well as Yajnavalkya and the others. ||44||
Three-eyed, possessing the body of Śaṅkara, and endowed with supreme sovereignty,
they remain at the base of the Lord, beyond the qualities (guṇātīta), seeking liberation.
When the destruction of the world has occurred, known as the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), [they remain].
Having entered into the Lord, they attain that which leads to liberation. ||46||
And those by whom the Śiva-liṅgas were seen, O best of Brahmins,
namely Kedāra, Madhyama, and Girīśa at Mahālaya;
the Lord Catuḥśṛṅgeśvara, and Maheśvara on Śrīgiri.
Kārohaṇa is Deveśa, and Śaṅkara is at Gaṅgādvāra;
likewise, Mahādeva is Bhadreśa, and Śaṅkukarṇeśvara is also there. ||48||
Both Mahākāleśvara and Gokarṇa, as well as Avimukteśvara and whatever other [shrines] exist upon the earth. 49.
They too, O Vyāsa, go upon death to that city of the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain;
and this is the Pāśupata Yoga which has been fully described by me to you.
Having received the Pāśupata vow, he too practices it there.
Those excellent men who possess constant devotion to Bhava have achieved their life's purpose;
O Vyāsa, upon death they become three-eyed beings with tridents in hand in the city of Śiva.
Resembling Nandīśa and Skanda, they were endowed with the power of yogic sovereignty.
O Vyāsa, they always become Rudras standing by the side of Śaṅkara.
Thus has this entire supreme Māheśvara Yoga been told to you,
having thus known the Supreme Lord both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala).
Completely liberated from all bonds, you shall attain supreme liberation. ||54||
And by the power of this knowledge, you shall become a yogi whose very self is yoga,
a sustainer of the world, and a promoter of the Smārta dharma;
through the power of knowledge, you will be the cause of the manifestation of the universe of memory.
You shall compose the Purāṇas for the purpose of understanding the nature of the persistence of phenomena.
For the sake of propagating the dharma of sacrifice, you shall, having recollected through higher knowledge the Veda remembered by Svāyambhuva, divide it into four parts.
Throughout this entire, irreproachable Vaivasvata Manvantara,
the duties that establish the world— preceded by the Vedas and the Smṛtis—
shall be promulgated by you. You shall become a maker of sacred fords (tīrthakṛt).
And having undertaken the ash-observance, which brings about liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu). || 59 ||
"Endowed with the knowledge of Śaṅkara, you shall attain dissolution into the Lord.
Having been addressed thus, that best of Brahmins, his hair standing on end with joy,
approached the lord of sages and received the consecration of ashes.
At that very moment, O great sage, this yoga manifested for him.
Having saluted his preceptor, the son of Brahmā, Vyāsa of great splendor,
wandered over the earth in order to behold the abodes of Śarva.
Thus questioned by the wise Vyāsa, Sanatkumāra,
the lord of sages, recounted the Purāṇa concerning the birth of Skanda,
which is endowed with all the Āgamas and contains the description of the Manvantaras and the stability of the world.
This great meditation, born of Śiva-yoga, is a vast ocean of all knowledge.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, having understood this, practice the Pāśupata vow and the yoga of Śaṅkara, and attain absorption into the Lord.
Having investigated this scripture, that great sage Vyāsa,
the bull among munis, composed the various branches of knowledge connected with the meaning of the Vedas and the Smṛtis.
From this [source] emerged the Dharmas as well as the Yogavidyās;
O twice-born ones, Nandīśvara declared that the Purāṇa is the first and the primordial [text].
He who knows this in its true essence is renowned... 67.
By this, the three aims of life are attained; by this, liberation is born.
By this, one's lifespan is increased; by this, everything is obtained—just as Hara is the primordial creator of the entire world, O Brahmins. || 68-69 ||
Likewise, this Purāṇa is remembered as the supreme among all Purāṇas;
those Brahmins by whom this has been studied have attained union with the Lord. He who hears it attains the state of union with the All-pervading One.
By its practice, one attains perfection in yoga and the supreme liberation.

O best of the twice-born, this is the primordial merit of the Lord of Umā; it is a supreme recitation of hymns concerning the Goddess as well, containing a discourse on her great power and endowed with all the Āgamas.
Through the power of Skanda’s manifestation,
may they attain [liberation] by means of the lords of the nāgas, the lords of the asuras, the yakṣas, the gods, the siddhas, and even the best of the twice-born. ||72||
Those by whom he was served with hearts in which all states of being were offered to Śambhu—
all those became the best of the Gaṇas, attendants of the God’s face, three-eyed and possessing the brilliance of the moon, with bodies like the blazing sun and fire. (73)
